papers.title: Large Language Models for Agent-Based Modelling: Current and possible uses across the modelling cycle
papers.abstract: The emergence of Large Language Models (LLMs) with increasingly sophisticated natural language understanding and generative capabilities has sparked interest in the Agent-based Modelling (ABM) community. With their ability to summarize, generate, analyze, categorize, transcribe and translate text, answer questions, propose explanations, sustain dialogue, extract information from unstructured text, and perform logical reasoning and problem-solving tasks, LLMs have a good potential to contribute to the modelling process. After reviewing the current use of LLMs in ABM, this study reflects on the opportunities and challenges of the potential use of LLMs in ABM. It does so by following the modelling cycle, from problem formulation to documentation and communication of model results, and holding a critical stance.
papers.summary: Agent-based modelling (ABM) simulates systems as interacting individual agents, and the authors look at where Large Language Models (LLMs) could help modellers build such simulations. They first review how LLMs are currently used in ABM. They then go through the whole modelling cycle, from problem formulation through to documenting and communicating results, and assess the opportunities and challenges at each stage. The review takes a deliberately **critical stance** rather than an optimistic one, drawing on LLM abilities such as summarization, information extraction, dialogue and reasoning.

papers.title: Multi-LLM Systems Exhibit Robust Semantic Collapse
papers.abstract: Whether machines can originate novel content has been debated for nearly two centuries, from Lovelace's assertion that no engine can "originate anything" to Turing's question of whether a machine can amplify ideas brought in from outside. Interacting multi-LLM systems, increasingly deployed for autonomous generation, reopen this question empirically. Here we show that such systems exhibit semantic collapse, systematic convergence in semantic representations despite apparent lexical variation, with no retraining or weight updates. The pattern holds across model families and over 200 to 1,000 rounds. Thirteen intervention implementations tested, spanning decoding parameters, prompt design, agent composition, activation engineering, and reinforcement learning, did not reliably restore semantic diversity. Mechanistic analyses suggest that semantic collapse is not solely attributable to the alignment or conformity biases examined here, but is consistent with intrinsic properties of autoregressive generation. Our results point to persistent constraints on the ability of multi-LLM systems to sustain open-ended exploration in closed-loop settings.
papers.summary: When several LLMs interact in a closed loop over 200 to 1,000 rounds, their outputs show what the authors call semantic collapse. The underlying meanings converge even though the wording keeps varying, and this happens without any retraining or weight updates. The pattern holds across model families, and **none of 13 tested interventions reliably restored semantic diversity**. The interventions covered decoding parameters, prompt design, agent composition, activation engineering and reinforcement learning. Mechanistic analyses suggest the effect is not fully explained by alignment or conformity biases and is consistent with intrinsic properties of autoregressive generation, which limits how well multi-LLM systems can sustain open-ended exploration.

papers.title: INCARBench: A Benchmark for Scientific Configuration in VASP INCAR by Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being integrated into first-principles computational workflows, yet their ability to configure scientific calculations remains poorly understood. Here, we introduce INCARBench, a benchmark for evaluating LLMs on input configuration for the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP) through both configuration generation and repair tasks. Evaluating 19 model configurations reveals substantial capability differences among current frontier models. While several models achieve high semantic and policy accuracy, task-critical correctness remains substantially lower, demonstrating that parameter-level correctness does not necessarily imply scientifically valid configurations. Failure analysis shows that errors concentrate in physically coupled settings involving DFT+$U$, magnetism, and correlated materials, where multiple constraints must be satisfied simultaneously. Repair evaluation further reveals that correcting incorrect settings and preserving already-valid configurations are distinct capabilities, with configuration preservation remaining a major challenge. These findings establish scientific configuration as a measurable capability of large language models and provide a foundation for developing more reliable AI systems for computational materials science.
papers.summary: `INCARBench` tests how well LLMs can write and repair input configurations for the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (`VASP`), a widely used tool for first-principles materials simulations. Across 19 model configurations, several frontier models score highly on semantic and policy accuracy, but **task-critical correctness is substantially lower**. In other words, getting individual parameters right does not guarantee a scientifically valid configuration. Errors cluster in physically coupled settings such as `DFT+U`, magnetism and correlated materials. The repair tasks also show that fixing wrong settings and leaving already-correct ones alone are separate skills, and the second remains a major weakness.

papers.title: Fine-Tuning Small Language Models for Reliable VASP INCAR Generation
papers.abstract: Language models can prepare VASP INCAR files from natural-language requests, but so far only large proprietary cloud models come close to handling the tightly coupled, physics-sensitive settings reliably, a dependence that fits poorly with local, high-throughput materials workflows where privacy, cost, and offline deployment matter. We show that a small language model (SLM) can close this gap. The SLM is fine-tuned on reference VASP calculations and paired with VASPGuard, a deterministic post-processor that checks syntax, workflow, and material-dependent constraints; we call the combined model INCAR-SLM. On INCARBench, a benchmark for VASP INCAR generation, INCAR-SLM built on Qwen3-4B outperforms every general-purpose LLM evaluated, exceeding GPT-5.4 by 15.55 points on the 100-point INCAR Score. Most of this gain comes from fine-tuning, with VASPGuard correcting the errors that remain. We further find that model size matters less than expected: once fine-tuning and post-processing are applied, performance saturates at a few billion parameters, and Qwen3-4B outperforms larger models in the same family.
papers.summary: Generating `VASP` INCAR configuration files reliably has so far required large proprietary cloud models, which suits privacy-sensitive, offline, high-throughput materials workflows poorly. The authors fine-tune a small language model (SLM) on reference VASP calculations and pair it with `VASPGuard`, a deterministic post-processor that checks syntax, workflow and material-dependent constraints; the combination is called `INCAR-SLM`. Built on `Qwen3-4B`, it beats every general-purpose LLM evaluated on `INCARBench` and **exceeds `GPT-5.4` by 15.55 points on the 100-point INCAR Score**, with most of the gain coming from fine-tuning. Performance saturates at a few billion parameters, and the 4B model outperforms larger models from the same family.

papers.title: Web Agent Agentic Reinforcement Learning Decision Model Under Multi-Cost and Failure Risk
papers.abstract:
Intelligent agent interactions in real-world web environments are commonly constrained by request budgets, time delays, anti-crawling restrictions, and operational failure risks. Strategies solely optimizing task success rates often exhibit unusable phenomena such as "high success but high cost" or "low risk but conservative failure." This paper proposes a constrained agentic reinforcement learning model for web agents, unifying page access, search requests, and external API calls into a unified long-term decision-making framework with associated costs. It simultaneously incorporates cost budget constraints and tail risk control into the optimization objective: constructing a multidimensional cost vector comprising cumulative request count, total latency, and failure penalties to achieve budget compliance via Lagrange dual updates, while employing a CVaR risk term to suppress excessive exploration of high-failure-probability paths, thereby achieving an adaptive balance among "completion rate, cost, and risk."
  Experiments were conducted across 30-70 site/page templates and 800-1,500 end-to-end web tasks, including information extraction, price comparison, form submission, and cross-page navigation. Interaction sequences spanned 20-120 steps with tool scales of 30-200. Performance was benchmarked against unconstrained RL, budget-constrained RL, and rule-based/scripted web agents, quantifying task completion rates, cost-per-success, failure rates, and policy stability.
  Results demonstrate that at equivalent completion rates, our method reduces C-PS by 22%-31% and lowers failure rates by 18%-26% under high failure penalties. Under fixed budgets, task completion rates increase by 10%-16%, highlighting the necessity and effectiveness of constraint modeling for practical web agent deployment.
papers.summary: Web agents running in real environments face request budgets, latency, anti-crawling limits and failure risk, so policies trained only to maximize task success can turn out too expensive or too cautious to use. The proposed constrained reinforcement learning model treats page visits, searches and API calls as costed actions within one long-horizon decision problem. It enforces a cost budget covering request count, latency and failure penalties through Lagrange dual updates. A conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) term discourages exploring paths that are likely to fail. On 800 to 1,500 end-to-end tasks spanning 20 to 120 steps, the method **cuts cost per success by 22–31% at equal completion rates** and raises completion rates by 10–16% under fixed budgets, compared with unconstrained, budget-constrained and scripted agents.

papers.title: I$^2$-Med: Interpretable Medical Inference through Visual-Guided Dynamic Logits Calibration
papers.abstract: Medical vision language models have demonstrated strong potential for medical image understanding and reasoning. However, their interpretability and reliability remain limited because medical vision language tasks require precise visual grounding and clinically coherent explanations. This is particularly challenging due to complex imaging patterns and scarce expert annotations. These challenges reduce the effectiveness of conventional reasoning methods and lead to visual hallucination, defined as the generation of text that is not grounded in the given visual input, which further limits their applicability in clinical practice. To mitigate these challenges, we propose an interpretable medical inference (I$^2$-Med) framework that enhances visual faithfulness during inference without additional training to improve reasoning and explanation faithfulness in medical vision language models. During text generation, I$^2$-Med uses a visual guidance module to check whether each candidate word is supported by the medical image and consistent with the current reasoning. Based on this guidance, the model's output scores are adjusted to favor visually grounded words, without changing the model parameters. Extensive experiments on the OmniMedVQA benchmark, covering eight medical imaging modalities and five clinical question types, demonstrate that our proposed I$^2$-Med framework generates more clinically meaningful and visually faithful reasoning chains and reduces visual hallucination under standard medical VQA evaluation metrics. The source code is publicly available at \url{https://github.com/mtanveer1/l2-med}.
papers.summary: Medical vision language models often hallucinate, generating text that is not grounded in the input image, which undermines their reasoning and explanations in clinical settings. `I²-Med` (interpretable medical inference) is a training-free decoding method that tackles this. During generation, a visual guidance module checks whether each candidate word is supported by the image and consistent with the current reasoning, and adjusts the output logits to favour grounded words. On `OmniMedVQA`, which covers eight imaging modalities and five clinical question types, it **produces more visually faithful reasoning chains and reduces hallucination** without changing the model's parameters.

papers.title: Modeling Human Behavior in the Prisoner's Dilemma with Large Language Models
papers.abstract: The Prisoner's Dilemma has long served as a foundational framework for studying human decision-making and cooperative outcomes across social scenarios, yet human behavior consistently deviates from predictions of fully rational economic theory. Previous works have studied human and LLM outcomes in the Prisoner's Dilemma; however, these studies have lacked at least one key feature: a memory component for LLM agents, accessible open-source models, or comparison against empirical human data. This project investigates whether open-source LLMs, TII Falcon 7B Instruct, Google Gemma 7B, Meta Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, Microsoft Phi Mini MoE Instruct, and Qwen 2.5 7B Instruct, can model human cooperation patterns in repeated Prisoner's Dilemma games, while examining how an LLM's knowledge that its opponent will be shuffled affects its decisions. Using a standardized prompting framework, we simulated interactions in two trial types: a fixed-partner setting where both agents retain memory, and a shuffled-partner setting where a memory-enabled agent, informed that its opponent changes across rounds, interacts with a memoryless agent. For each trial, we measured cooperation rates over 100 rounds and 10-round increments and compared them to human data from Montero-Porras et al. (2022). Under both frameworks, all LLMs differed from the human cooperation rate. Open-source LLMs generally over-cooperated relative to humans, particularly in the shuffled framework, where human cooperation averaged 28.5% while several models exceeded 80%. Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct showed deterministic tendencies, while Phi-mini-MoE-Instruct displayed greater variability and briefly approximated human rates. These findings suggest that LLMs have potential as behavioral simulation agents and provide a benchmark across two interaction environments, although open-source models are not yet reliable substitutes for human participants.
papers.summary: The study asks whether small open-source LLMs can stand in for human players in the repeated Prisoner's Dilemma, comparing them directly with empirical human data. Five roughly 7B-parameter models, including `Llama 3.1 8B Instruct`, `Qwen 2.5 7B Instruct` and `Phi Mini MoE Instruct`, played 100 rounds in two settings. In one, both agents keep a fixed partner and retain memory; in the other, a memory-enabled agent is told that its opponent changes every round. Every model deviated from human behaviour and generally over-cooperated, most sharply in the shuffled setting, where **humans cooperated 28.5% of the time while several models exceeded 80%**. `Qwen` played almost deterministically, and `Phi` varied more and briefly came close to human rates.

papers.title: PolyGraph: Plan-Buffered CUDA Graphs for Adaptive Speculative Decoding
papers.abstract: Adaptive speculative decoding changes the active batch size B and draft length d from one decode step to the next, whereas a CUDA Graph replays a fixed launch configuration. The resulting verification width M = B d forces serving systems to pre-capture many shapes, capture new ones on the serving path, or pad every step to the largest draft. We present PolyGraph, a plan-buffer mechanism for custom Triton kernels that avoids this choice. PolyGraph captures one maximum-grid graph and writes the active shape to GPU memory before each replay. Kernels skip tiles beyond that shape, while graph topology, allocations, layouts, pointers, and launch grids remain fixed; the update transfers only 28 bytes. On one NVIDIA H800, a trace-driven prototype with Qwen2.5-3B dimensions replaces 64 shape-specific graphs with one, matches the warmed baseline in observed step latency (17.7 vs. 17.8 ms P50), and reduces measured pre-serving graph-build time from 3,915 to 93 ms. Fixed-draft controls show that the benefit comes from avoiding padded payload: the P99 difference from MaxPad is negligible at zero padding waste but reaches an 18.7% reduction at 100% waste. Our evidence establishes a bounded work-shape mechanism for custom kernels, not a production serving system, and is limited to synthetic traces on one GPU.
papers.summary: Adaptive speculative decoding changes both batch size and draft length at every decode step. CUDA Graphs, however, replay a fixed launch configuration, so serving systems must pre-capture many graph shapes, capture new ones while serving, or pad every step to the largest draft. `PolyGraph` instead captures a single maximum-size graph for custom `Triton` kernels and writes the active shape (just 28 bytes) to GPU memory before each replay, so kernels skip the unused tiles. In a trace-driven prototype on one H800 GPU using `Qwen2.5-3B` dimensions, it replaces 64 shape-specific graphs with one and matches the warmed baseline's latency. It also **cuts pre-serving graph-build time from 3,915 to 93 ms**. The authors frame it as a kernel mechanism tested on synthetic traces, not a production serving system.

papers.title: Forecasting Patient Trajectories from the Electronic Health Records with Action-Conditioned World Models
papers.abstract: We introduce a predictive world model for electronic health records (EHR) that represents patient histories as action conditioned latent trajectories. Rather than modeling clinical events solely through autoregressive token prediction, our framework explicitly separates patient states from observed clinical actions and learns their evolution through a state and action conditioned transition operator. At its core is a state dependent linearization predictor that propagates local changes in latent patient state, enabling time resolved prediction, multi step rollout, and action conditioned simulation. Empirically, we show that generated latent trajectories preserve downstream predictive signal, temporal structure, and subgroup level statistical relationships present in encoder derived representations. We further decode free running rollouts into the original clinical feature space and evaluate future clinical measurements against observed values using task matched forecasting baselines, demonstrating that the learned dynamics retain predictive information beyond latent space agreement. Across binary classification and time to event tasks, EHR WM achieves competitive, though task dependent, performance relative to substantially larger EHR foundation models while using a 30x smaller parameter footprint. Finally, perturbing observed action sequences produces corresponding changes in generated trajectories, demonstrating the action sensitivity of the learned dynamics. Together, these results support world modeling as a complementary framework for learning explicit, time indexed representations of patient evolution from longitudinal EHR.
papers.summary: Rather than predicting clinical events token by token, this world model for electronic health records (EHR) represents each patient's history as a latent trajectory in which patient states are kept separate from the clinical actions taken. A state-dependent linearization predictor learns how actions move the latent state, which supports multi-step rollouts and simulating alternative action sequences. Generated trajectories preserve downstream predictive signal and subgroup statistics, and when decoded back into clinical measurements they retain forecasting value. On classification and time-to-event tasks it is **competitive with much larger EHR foundation models at a 30x smaller parameter footprint**, though results vary by task.

papers.title: Measuring the Influence of Modality-Specific Node Representations on Graphs
papers.abstract: Multimodal attributed graphs combine graph structure with node text and image representations in recommendation and multimedia analysis. Graph predictors propagate these representations across connected nodes, so one input can change predictions at its own and nearby nodes. Measuring this distributed response reveals which modality-specific inputs a trained model relies on and how predictor design changes that reliance. We study influence measurement for modality-specific node representations. Given an encoded graph, a trained predictor, a training split, and fixed candidate representations, the task outputs one influence score per candidate and separate text and image rankings. We score a candidate by replacing it with its modality's training-node mean and comparing the original and changed predictions. Existing feature attribution and data valuation generally target one output, training examples, whole nodes, or graph elements rather than prediction changes across graph nodes. Our empirical study shows that nearby-node responses contain information missed by source-only scores and simple proxies, while response magnitude alone does not identify which class changes support the task. Guided by these observations, we propose MoGI (Modality-specific Graph Influence). It propagates training labels to define task direction, reads the same replacement response for the favored class and full class distribution, and averages the resulting ranks. MoGI requires no predictor retraining or learned scoring parameters. Under a shared five-dataset, eight-predictor benchmark, it achieves the largest aggregate held-out loss increase against all five external methods at every tested ranking cutoff.
papers.summary: In multimodal attributed graphs, each node carries text and image representations, and a graph predictor spreads them to neighbouring nodes, so changing one input can shift predictions across the graph. The authors define a task that assigns an influence score to each modality-specific node representation. They score a representation by replacing it with its modality's training mean and measuring how predictions change at both the source node and nearby nodes. Building on this, `MoGI` (Modality-specific Graph Influence) uses propagated training labels to judge whether those changes matter for the task, and it needs no retraining or learned parameters. Across a benchmark of five datasets and eight predictors, **removing the inputs `MoGI` ranks highest raises held-out loss more than with any of five baselines, at every ranking cutoff**.

papers.title: SAGE-CP: When Marginal Coverage Hides Route-Conditional Failures in Adaptive VLM Ensembles
papers.abstract: Adaptive VLM ensembles save computation by stopping early on easy images and escalating harder ones. Although a single conformal threshold can make the final predictor marginally valid, it can still fail severely along individual computational routes. We characterize this failure precisely: if a route has prevalence pi, marginal 1-alpha coverage allows its conditional coverage to fall to max{0, 1-alpha/pi}. To address this mismatch, we learn the router on development data, freeze all routing choices, and calibrate the returned score separately for early exits and escalated inputs. We call this pipeline SAGE-CP. Its calibration step applies Mondrian split conformal prediction to the operational groups created by the router. Under exchangeability, the resulting prediction sets achieve finite-sample coverage within each route. Across 10 benchmarks, 4 frozen VLMs, and 5 aligned splits, both global calibration and SAGE-CP achieve 0.900 marginal coverage at a 0.90 target, but their route behavior differs substantially. SAGE-CP raises mean worst-route coverage from 0.623 to 0.887 and reduces the mean route-coverage gap from 0.324 to 0.025, using the same routed scores and 1.177 source calls per image. The stronger guarantee increases the mean prediction-set size from 1.893 to 2.212; nevertheless, the sets remain smaller than those of the full ensemble (2.486) while requiring 70.6 percent fewer source calls. The route-level reliability persists across 6 fixed query fractions, while finer exit-depth groups demonstrate the need for additional calibration data on rare routes. Across 5 datasets, SAGE-CP also reduces measured batch-one latency by 58.8 to 63.4 percent and gross GPU energy by 55.7 to 57.5 percent relative to full inference. Thus, routing provides computational savings, while route-stratified calibration attaches coverage guarantees to the operational paths created by the router.
papers.summary: Adaptive ensembles of vision-language models (VLMs) save compute by exiting early on easy images and escalating hard ones. The authors show that a single conformal calibration threshold can be valid on average while failing badly on individual routes, and they derive the bound: a route with prevalence π can drop to coverage of max{0, 1−α/π}. `SAGE-CP` freezes the learned router and applies Mondrian split conformal prediction separately to early-exit and escalated inputs, which guarantees coverage within each route. Across 10 benchmarks and 4 VLMs, it **raises mean worst-route coverage from 0.623 to 0.887** at the same marginal coverage. The price is slightly larger prediction sets, and it still uses 70.6% fewer model calls than the full ensemble.

papers.title: GardenBench: A lightweight, daily evaluation of LLM capabilities
papers.abstract: We introduce GardenBench, a benchmark with 11 test suites that evaluate the capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) across a range of tasks. By systematically prompting LLMs with various lightweight queries, we document day-to-day changes in model performance, including run costs and times, that other benchmarks miss. This allows us to compare the accuracy and features of responses across model providers and versions. We account for daily variations in model accuracy, capturing both model progress and degradation, for instance, when a model is changed post-deployment or when a new model is released. We base our evaluation on general-use tasks and make our results publicly accessible via a live dashboard, diversifying existing approaches to LLM testing. Our main contribution is an innovative, lightweight, and inexpensive benchmark, designed to be consumer-facing and for everyday tasks.
papers.summary: `GardenBench` is a lightweight, inexpensive benchmark of 11 test suites that queries LLMs on everyday, general-use tasks every day. It records accuracy, cost and run time for each response. Because it runs daily, it can **catch day-to-day changes in model performance**, such as degradation after a model is silently changed post-deployment or shifts when a new version is released, which one-off benchmarks miss. Results are published on a live, consumer-facing dashboard so users can compare models across providers and versions.

papers.title: Composable Parametric Demographic Injection for Values Survey Simulation
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as simulated respondents in computational social science, yet accurately reproducing population-specific heterogeneous response distributions remains challenging. Existing methods such as demographic prompting are sensitive to prompt design and increase inference overhead, while parameter-based methods struggle to reuse demographic information efficiently, limiting generalization to unseen combinations. In this regard, we propose PARADE, a composable PARAmetric DEmographic injection framework that represents each demographic attribute value with a reusable and composable LoRA module. Specifically, PARADE separates task-common survey capability from demographic-specific value shifts via a shared Task LoRA and attribute-level Demographic LoRAs, with composition calibration to reduce parameter interference. At inference time, target population models can be constructed on demand by recombining the relevant modules, including demographic combinations not observed during training. Extensive experiments on the World Values Survey and SocioBench across three backbone models show that PARADE achieves strong population-level distribution alignment while maintaining competitive predictive performance, reducing KL divergence by up to 52.8% relative to the strongest baseline.
papers.summary: When LLMs act as simulated survey respondents, they struggle to reproduce how answers are distributed within specific demographic groups. Demographic prompting is fragile and adds inference overhead, while existing parameter-based methods generalize poorly to unseen combinations of attributes. `PARADE` addresses this with a shared Task LoRA for general survey ability plus one reusable Demographic LoRA per attribute value, combined with a calibration step that reduces interference between modules. Composing these modules on demand builds a model for any target population, including demographic combinations never seen in training. On the `World Values Survey` and `SocioBench` across three backbone models, it **reduces KL divergence by up to 52.8%** relative to the strongest baseline.

papers.title: Translating in style: An open-weight alternative to GPT-4 for culturally aligned machine translation
papers.abstract: Machine translation systems often preserve meaning but systematically flatten linguistic style, a failure that is most acute when translating into non-Western languages. The RASTA framework of Havaldar et al. (2025a) addresses this through retrieval-augmented stylistic alignment, but relies on GPT-4, a closed, proprietary model. We investigate whether an open-weight translation specialist, Hunyuan-MT-7B, can serve as an open-weight alternative. We evaluate three variants of the model, the base model, a LoRA supervised fine-tune, and a GRPO-steered policy. We do this across three style dimensions (formality, politeness, and intimacy) and twelve directed language pairs, measuring style alignment with the correlation-based metric $\mathcal{A}$. We find that fine-tuning does not reliably improve alignment: the three variants are statistically indistinguishable in aggregate. The open backbone does not match RASTA-GPT-4 overall, but the shortfall is concentrated in formality and largely closes for intimacy and Chinese directions, where the open model matches or surpasses GPT-4 on individual pairs. An accessible RASTA pipeline built on an open model is thus already viable for parts of the problem.
papers.summary: Machine translation tends to preserve meaning while flattening style, especially when translating into non-Western languages, and the existing `RASTA` retrieval-augmented fix relies on the proprietary `GPT-4`. The authors test whether the open-weight translation model `Hunyuan-MT-7B` can replace it, comparing the base model, a LoRA fine-tune and a `GRPO`-steered policy across formality, politeness and intimacy in twelve language pairs. **Fine-tuning gave no reliable improvement**, and the three variants are statistically indistinguishable overall. The open model falls short of `GPT-4` mainly on formality, but it matches or beats it on several intimacy and Chinese-language pairs.

papers.title: DUET: Decoupled Upper- and Lower-Body Execution for Task-Agnostic Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
papers.abstract: Changing a humanoid robot's manipulation policy should not require retraining the controller that maintains the robot's balance. This study introduces DUET, a decoupled execution framework that enables locomotion and manipulation controllers to operate simultaneously by combining their commands only at the robot interface. A reinforcement-learning locomotion policy controls the 12 leg joints and a waist yaw joint, tracking planar velocity, turning rate, and pelvis height from deep crouching to upright standing on a 23-degree-of-freedom Unitree G1. The 10 arm joints are excluded from the action space, while their positions and velocities are included only as observations, so that any compatible manipulation policy that generates arm-joint targets can control the upper body, and the locomotion policy keeps the lower body stable without requiring shared training or direct coordination. This study demonstrates the modular approach on hardware by pairing the same locomotion checkpoint with two different vision-language-action models, GR00T N1.7 and pi0.5. In simulation evaluation, the locomotion controller kept the robot's lower body stable with no falls while tracking the commanded planar velocity, yaw rate, and pelvis height with errors of 0.186 m/s, 0.142 rad/s, and 0.016 m, respectively. Ablation studies identify the upper-body pose curriculum as the dominant component, and removing this training step reduces episode survival from 20.0 to 7.4 seconds and increases the fall rate to 6.06 per environment minute. Robustness tests show no falls under pushes of up to 1.0 m/s within the trained payload range, and no falls at twice the payload limit for pushes below 0.7 m/s. These results show that a manipulation policy can be exchanged without retraining, restarting, or otherwise touching the layer that keeps the robot upright.
papers.summary: `DUET` separates humanoid locomotion from manipulation so that the manipulation policy can be swapped without retraining the controller that keeps the robot balanced. A reinforcement-learning locomotion policy controls the legs and waist of a 23-degree-of-freedom `Unitree G1`. It can only observe the arm joints, not control them, so any compatible manipulation policy can drive the arms and the two command streams are merged only at the robot interface. On hardware, **the same locomotion checkpoint worked with two different vision-language-action models, `GR00T N1.7` and `pi0.5`**. In simulation it had no falls while tracking commanded velocity and height accurately. Ablations show that the upper-body pose curriculum is the most important training component.

papers.title: Latent Multimodal Memory Reasoning
papers.abstract: Long-term personalized agents are required to reason over distributed history across modalities and evolving dialogue states. While existing flat cross-modal methods compress visual evidence prematurely and struggle with temporally stale observations, they neglect the necessity to unify multimodal and cross-session evidence. Crucially, raw multimodal memories are inherently entangled and heterogeneous, making fine-grained visual grounding and cross-modal reasoning computationally prohibitive. To this end, we present latent multimodal memory reasoning, i.e., LMMR, a novel neuro-symbolic framework that shifts long-term multimodal memory organization into a continuous latent space. Specifically, (i) instead of converting images to text and relying on static retrieval, LMMR maps both textual hidden states and visual patch features into a shared Sparse Autoencoder concept space, establishing sparse activations as common semantic addresses to dynamically construct a turn-level multimodal memory graph. (ii) A graph encoder then aggregates cross-modal and temporal dependencies across the task-specific latent subgraph, injecting the graph readout as a continuous residual rollout into the generation backbone while retaining native visual tokens to preserve fine-grained details. Extensive experiments on nine Mem-Gallery tasks and twelve MemEye settings demonstrate that LMMR significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in capturing complex multimodal dependencies while enabling faithful and grounded responses.
papers.summary: Long-term personalized agents need to reason over memories spread across images, text and many dialogue sessions. Converting images to text and retrieving them statically loses visual detail and handles outdated observations poorly. `LMMR` (latent multimodal memory reasoning) maps both text hidden states and visual patch features into a shared Sparse Autoencoder concept space, then uses the sparse activations as common addresses to build a multimodal memory graph turn by turn. A graph encoder summarizes the relevant subgraph and injects it into the generation model, while the original visual tokens are kept to preserve fine detail. Across nine `Mem-Gallery` tasks and twelve `MemEye` settings, it **significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines**.

papers.title: Language-Forcing: Advancing Humanoid Loco-Manipulation via Semantic Alignment of Whole-Body World Action Models
papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) jointly predict robot actions and future observations. However, their visual prediction objectives do not explicitly distinguish task-relevant transitions from incidental scene changes. For whole-body policies, this distinction matters because task progress depends on coordinated changes in body pose, contact, and object state. We introduce LANGUAGE-FORCING, a training strategy that uses language to emphasize task-relevant changes in the future visual representations of a whole-body WAM. Given paired current and ground- truth short-horizon future frames, a frozen vision-language model assesses task progress and predicts plausible subsequent state changes. We encode these descriptions with a frozen text encoder and align their embeddings with intermediate, action-conditioned future-visual features, complementing the original visual and action prediction objectives. All auxiliary components are used only during training, introducing no additional inference overhead. On HumanoidArena, LANGUAGE-FORCING achieves an average success rate of 79.17%, exceeding the strongest competing policy by 9.46 percentage points and the same WAM without language alignment by 10.77 percentage points. Across five real-world tasks, language alignment raises average success from 53.33% to 71.33% over the same WAM baseline.
papers.summary: World Action Models (WAMs) predict both robot actions and future observations, but their visual objectives do not separate task-relevant changes from incidental ones in the scene. `Language-Forcing` addresses this during training only. A frozen vision-language model describes task progress and the likely next state changes from current and future frames, and those text embeddings are aligned with the WAM's action-conditioned future-visual features. Because this happens only in training, it adds no inference cost. On `HumanoidArena`, it **reaches 79.17% average success, 9.46 points above the strongest competing policy**, and on five real-world tasks it raises success from 53.33% to 71.33% over the same WAM trained without language alignment.

papers.title: InJePA: Intention-First Latent Planning with Coupled JEPA World Models for Visual Navigation
papers.abstract: Visual navigation requires goal directed planning informed by predictions of environment dynamics. Representative navigation world model methods propose complete action candidates before predicting consequences for selection or search updates. For each candidate, predictions primarily evaluate proposed actions rather than guide its stepwise construction. To this end, we propose InJepa, an intention first planning paradigm centered on latent states. A goal conditioned JEPA proposes latent intentions, and an action conditioned JEPA continually predicts future latent states. Both operate in a shared latent space to align their predictive representations. Within each candidate, predicted consequences feed into the next intention proposal and action inference, forming a closed loop of intention, action, and consequence. This extends the world model's role beyond evaluation to leading candidate construction through latent intentions. We evaluate InJepa through closed loop image goal navigation in Habitat MP3D. The results show effective multistep navigation through intention guided action generation and consequence feedback. Experiments across encoders further support applicability across visual representations. These findings support latent intentions as the central planning object and show that world models can directly guide plan construction through coordinated reasoning about intentions and consequences. Code is available at https://github.com/zhuxun132/InJepa.
papers.summary: Navigation world models usually propose complete action sequences first and only then predict their consequences to pick among them. `InJepa` instead builds each plan step by step around latent intentions. A goal-conditioned JEPA (a joint-embedding predictive model) proposes intentions, while an action-conditioned JEPA predicts the resulting future states in the same latent space. Each predicted consequence feeds back into the next intention and action, so **the world model guides how plans are built rather than only scoring finished candidates**. In closed-loop image-goal navigation in `Habitat MP3D`, it achieves effective multi-step navigation across several visual encoders.

papers.title: EAGLE: Entropy-Aware Geometric Learning Enhancer for Partially Polygon-Supervised Object Localization
papers.abstract: Object detection is a critical application of computer vision, yet models trained uniformly on bounding boxes lack the geometric precision to be fully effective in inference settings, especially at high IoU thresholds. One common approach is the introduction of polygon-supervised localization, where a model is trained explicitly for localization but with access to polygon masks during training. Among such methods, partial polygon supervision is viable due to the higher annotation costs of developing fully supervised training datasets. However, this introduces a further challenge: in object classes of relatively low shape complexity, the addition of training masks and subsequent segmentation loss may obscure box localization, often worsening model performance despite access to deeper geometric information. To address the practical limitations of both full and partial polygon supervision, we introduce a mathematical framework for quantifying per-class geometric complexity by combining information theory and statistical shape analysis. With this framework, we develop Entropy-Aware Geometric Learning Enhancer (EAGLE), a lightweight, post-training model head that learns geometric information for the localization model, improving accuracy via edge refinement and localization rescoring using entropy-informed updates. Empirical analysis across MS COCO and Pascal SBD demonstrates the entropy framework meaningfully predicts shape reconstruction error and accuracy differences among mask-derived and standard box predictions, while the implemented EAGLE framework achieves consistent improvement on already SOTA detection frameworks (+0.9 mAP50-95 points on MS COCO) at minimal observed inference overhead.
papers.summary: Adding polygon mask supervision can improve object localization, but for classes with simple shapes the extra segmentation loss can actually hurt box accuracy. The authors define a per-class geometric complexity measure that combines information theory with statistical shape analysis, and they show it predicts when mask-derived boxes beat standard ones. Building on this, `EAGLE` (Entropy-Aware Geometric Learning Enhancer) is a lightweight head added after training that refines box edges and rescores detections using entropy-informed updates. On `MS COCO` and `Pascal SBD` it consistently improves already state-of-the-art detectors, adding **+0.9 mAP50-95 on `MS COCO`** with minimal inference overhead.

papers.title: Rethinking weakly supervised localization on chest radiographs: position nulls, protocol dependence, and PACE
papers.abstract: Weakly supervised localization on chest radiographs is reported as a single overlap accuracy, and those numbers are not comparable across papers. We measure what one contains. Against position-null controls that keep a readout's own box and move only its position, class activation mapping and its gradient-weighted variant beat the null on two to four of seven annotated findings on ChestX-ray14 and two of eight on CheXlocalize. The null is beatable: three board-certified radiologists clear it on four to seven. Three rarely stated choices each move a result by more than most reported method effects: the results regime, the extraction threshold, and the mask-to-box rule, whose cost is predicted by how fragmented the thresholded mask is. Predicted box area alone reverses a paired comparison. These measurements produced PACE, for \emph{population anomaly and class evidence}, which multiplies the finding identity from the label-trained head by the spatial evidence from a frozen radiograph backbone that never sees a pathology label. It is the case study that made the protocol dependence visible, and we report its costs beside its gain: in an exploratory matched-area analysis it improves strict-overlap accuracy on both corpora and beats a label-derived second map, but it is the least faithful of the three readouts to the classifier's causal map, its advantage depends on the box rule, and, this benchmark releasing no localization validation set, every design choice behind it was made on the boxes it is scored on. Its one clean transfer beats one baseline and loses to the other.
papers.summary: Weakly supervised localization results on chest X-rays are usually reported as a single overlap accuracy, and the authors show that these numbers are not comparable across papers. Against position-null controls that keep a method's predicted box but move it to a different position, class activation mapping and its gradient-weighted variant **beat the null on only two to four of seven findings on `ChestX-ray14`** and two of eight on `CheXlocalize`, while board-certified radiologists beat it on four to seven. Three rarely reported protocol choices (the results regime, the extraction threshold and the mask-to-box rule) each shift results by more than most reported method improvements. The authors also present their own method, `PACE`, and are candid about its limits, including that every design choice was tuned on the same boxes it is scored on.

papers.title: Your Self-Supervised Projection Head Captures Object Co-Occurrence Statistics
papers.abstract: Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) has achieved impressive success in learning semantic visual representations, yet the underlying principles driving this success remain underexplored. In this work, we hypothesize that common SSL pretext tasks implicitly model object co-occurrence statistics, a fundamental cue for visual learning. To test this, we curate three datasets of segmented objects from existing vision benchmarks using a state-of-the-art segmentation model. Through experiments across many SSL models, we reveal a hierarchical encoding of semantic information: while the visual backbone captures object categories, the projection head specializes in encoding co-occurrences between object categories. As a result, the projection head outperforms the backbone in aligning with human judgments of inter-category similarity. Furthermore, by controlling co-occurrence patterns during pre-training, we demonstrate that encoding object co-occurrences can significantly accelerate the emergence of category-level representations. Our findings uncover a previously hidden learning principle in SSL and suggest a path toward designing more effective pretext tasks by explicitly leveraging object co-occurrence structure.
papers.summary: Why self-supervised learning (SSL) produces semantic visual representations is still poorly understood, and the authors propose that common SSL pretext tasks implicitly model how often object categories appear together. They build three datasets of segmented objects from existing vision benchmarks and probe many SSL models. They find a hierarchy: the backbone encodes object categories, while **the projection head specializes in encoding co-occurrences between categories** and matches human judgments of inter-category similarity better than the backbone does. Controlling co-occurrence patterns during pre-training also significantly speeds up the emergence of category-level representations, which points toward pretext tasks that use co-occurrence structure explicitly.

papers.title: Announced Breaks Separate Conformal Reliability from Frequency Calibration
papers.abstract: An announced boundary reveals the partition before the first affected outcome, and a reset there serves one of two audits. The per-time audit reads conformal reliability, the expected distance of the threshold's coverage from nominal at miscoverage 0.1. The frequency audit reads frequency calibration, whether a closed window's error rate matched it. The reset rule, the post-boundary empirical quantile, attains the minimax per-time rate for independent scores. On bounded scores a recursion reset at the boundary attains a frequency gap of order one over the count when its floor adds a bounded total. At the 50th forecast after a large synthetic break, the reset rule's per-time gap stands below that of five adaptive methods, four from their authors' code, with every paired band below zero. After an electricity market reform, on 68 unseen scores, the band stands below zero against two, includes zero against two, adaptive conformal inference among them, and is a point at zero against one. After monetary policy decisions its pointwise band stands above zero against all five on 10 of the first 34 days. Of 9 announced boundaries one clears the smallest coverage difference its window detects, where every method's per-time gap at the 50th forecast exceeds the nominal miscoverage. Over the first 50 forecasts the reset recursion leads the frequency audit after every synthetic break.
papers.summary: The setting is conformal prediction when a structural break is announced before the first outcome it affects, and the authors argue that resetting at that boundary serves two different audits: per-time conformal reliability (how far coverage is from nominal) and frequency calibration (whether a window's error rate matched nominal). They show that a reset to the post-boundary empirical quantile **attains the minimax per-time rate for independent scores**, and that a reset recursion achieves a frequency gap of order one over the count on bounded scores. On synthetic breaks, the reset rule beats five adaptive methods, including `adaptive conformal inference`, on per-time gap at the 50th forecast. Results on an electricity market reform and on monetary policy decisions are mixed, and only one of nine real announced boundaries clears the smallest coverage difference its window can detect.

papers.title: Vocabulary-Incomplete Unsupervised Vision-Language Model Adaptation
papers.abstract: In certain real-world scenarios, obtaining labeled data is excessively expensive, motivating increasing interest in adapting models without annotations. Vision-language models (VLMs) provide pseudo-labels for unlabeled images through image-text similarity, enabling adaptation without manual labeling. The previous unsupervised vision-language model adaption methods assume access to an adaptation vocabulary containing all class names. However, a complete vocabulary is difficult to construct in real-world scenarios, as unlabeled data may contain classes that are overlooked or fall outside the current task scope. Thus, we propose Vocabulary-Incomplete Unsupervised Vision-language model Adaptation (VI-UVA), where only a subset of class names are available during adaptation. The vocabulary incompleteness induces an adaptation bias toward provided classes, which degrades omitted-class recognition. To address this issue, we propose Label Space Reconstruction (LSR), which reconstructs a latent label space from the unlabeled data and incorporates it into prompt tuning, thereby extending adaptation beyond the incomplete vocabulary and mitigating the adaptation bias. Furthermore, we derive an omitted-class semantic discrepancy bound for LSR and identify the key factors affecting the bound. Extensive experiments across eight benchmarks demonstrate that LSR outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods.
papers.summary: Unsupervised adaptation of vision-language models (VLMs) uses image-text similarity to pseudo-label unlabeled images, but existing methods assume the adaptation vocabulary contains every class name. The authors define Vocabulary-Incomplete Unsupervised Vision-language model Adaptation (`VI-UVA`), where only some class names are known, and show that this setup biases adaptation toward the provided classes and hurts recognition of the omitted ones. Their method, Label Space Reconstruction (`LSR`), reconstructs a latent label space from the unlabeled data and feeds it into prompt tuning so adaptation extends beyond the given vocabulary. They derive a bound on omitted-class semantic discrepancy and report that **`LSR` outperforms state-of-the-art methods across eight benchmarks**.

papers.title: Zero-Shot Tabular Learning via Hypergraph Reasoning with LLMs
papers.abstract: Tabular data are prevalent across diverse domains such as healthcare and finance. Zero-shot tabular learning aims to make predictions without labeled data. However, existing LLM-based approaches rely on row-wise prompting, resulting in high inference cost and limited use of inter-row dependencies. In this work, we propose TABHGR+, an efficient relation-aware zero-shot framework for tabular data that leverages LLM-generated rules to label and group rows. Specifically, based on column and task descriptions, we use LLMs to generate rules that assign weak labels to all rows. To refine these noisy weak labels, we construct a hypergraph by grouping semantically related rows using LLM-generated rules and perform hypergraph-based label propagation. Lastly, we further enhance the LLM-generated hypergraph for propagation, which is potentially sub-optimal, by assigning label-adaptive weights to hyperedges. By requiring only a constant number of LLM calls independent of dataset size, TABHGR+ substantially reduces inference cost while achieving higher classification accuracy than zero-shot and strong few-shot baselines.
papers.summary: Existing LLM-based zero-shot methods for tabular data prompt the model one row at a time, which is expensive and ignores dependencies between rows. `TABHGR+` instead has an LLM write rules from column and task descriptions; these rules assign weak labels to every row and group related rows into a hypergraph. Label propagation over that hypergraph, with label-adaptive weights on the hyperedges, then refines the noisy labels. The framework **needs only a constant number of LLM calls regardless of dataset size**, and the authors report higher classification accuracy than zero-shot and strong few-shot baselines.

papers.title: Improving Fake Profile Detection Through Multimodal Learning and Research-Guided Feature Integration
papers.abstract: Fake accounts continue to undermine online platforms, yet it remains unclear whether multimodal learning offers meaningful improvements over strong metadata baselines or graph-based approaches. In this work, we study bot detection by integrating textual, visual, and account metadata signals on the TwiBot-22 benchmark using a subsample of 30,000 users. We propose a multimodal framework combining pretrained textual (XLM-RoBERTa) and visual (CLIP) embeddings with structured account-level features such as follower counts, posting frequency, and account age, and evaluate multiple modality combinations using CatBoost alongside a Relational Graph Convolutional Network (R-GCN). Results show that metadata alone is highly predictive, while multimodal fusion yields only marginal and largely statistically insignificant gains. The graph-based model underperforms classical variants under the subsampled graph conditions of this study. Overall, our findings suggest that under practical constraints, feature quality and metadata richness matter more than fusion complexity.
papers.summary: The question is whether multimodal learning actually improves fake-account (bot) detection over strong metadata or graph-based baselines, studied on a 30,000-user subsample of the `TwiBot-22` benchmark. The authors combine `XLM-RoBERTa` text embeddings and `CLIP` image embeddings with account features such as follower counts, posting frequency, and account age, then evaluate modality combinations with `CatBoost` and a Relational Graph Convolutional Network (`R-GCN`). **Metadata alone is highly predictive, and multimodal fusion adds only marginal, largely statistically insignificant gains.** The graph model underperforms on the subsampled graph, and the authors conclude that feature quality matters more than fusion complexity.

papers.title: miniTE: Diagnosing and Bridging the Execution Gap in Native NVFP4 Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Native NVFP4 promises to accelerate reinforcement learning (RL) for large language models (LLMs), but achieving stable learning across separate training and sampling engines remains challenging. We show that matching model weights and numerical formats is insufficient to ensure consistent policy evaluation, highlighting the importance of cross-engine numerical execution. We introduce miniTE, a lightweight framework that combines execution diagnostics, cross-engine numerical alignment, and efficient native W4A4 (4-bit weights and activations) GEMM computation for LLM RL. It improves numerical execution consistency without modifying the RL objective, while reducing implementation overhead to realize the benefits of native low-bit computation. Long-horizon RL experiments on Qwen3-30B-A3B demonstrate stable training and benchmark performance close to BF16, outperforming naive Transformer Engine (TE) NVFP4 in evaluation quality. On single NVIDIA B300 GPU node, the optimized learner reaches 33,540 tokens/s, yielding 1.39x and 1.47x the throughput of BF16 and TE NVFP4, respectively, for complete learner updates. We released the framework, kernels, diagnostics, and training configurations to make native low-bit RL easier.
papers.summary: Native 4-bit `NVFP4` arithmetic could speed up reinforcement learning (RL) for large language models, but training stays unstable when the training and sampling engines evaluate the policy differently. The authors show that matching weights and numerical formats is not enough, and they introduce `miniTE`, a lightweight framework that combines execution diagnostics, cross-engine numerical alignment, and efficient native W4A4 (4-bit weights and activations) matrix-multiplication kernels without changing the RL objective. In long-horizon RL on `Qwen3-30B-A3B`, it trains stably with benchmark scores close to `BF16` and beats naive Transformer Engine (`TE`) `NVFP4` on evaluation quality. On a single `B300` GPU node, the learner reaches **33,540 tokens/s, 1.39x the throughput of `BF16` and 1.47x that of `TE` `NVFP4`**; the framework, kernels, and configurations are released.

papers.title: VERDICT: Visual Extraction-Result Decoder with Integrated Confidence and Traceable Evidence
papers.abstract: Enterprises run schema-guided structured field extraction on documents with frontier multimodal models, and accuracy keeps improving as new models and systems arrive. Two things have not kept pace: the evidence for each extracted value, meaning the location of the document it was read from, and how far to trust the value and that evidence. Neither is a component of most extraction systems today, so we build them as a framework that attaches to an existing extractor and leaves it untouched. We present VERDICT, a plug-in framework that uses a small Vision--Language Model (VLM) to ground/localize the evidence once per document over a fixed external extractor's output, then calibrates value and evidence confidence. Fine-tuning the VLM for evidence localization substantially improves visual evidence quality and, more importantly, expands VERDICT's selective-prediction operating range. At a strict confidence threshold $0.80$, VERDICT with the fine-tuned VLM gives usable precision--coverage trade-offs for both value and evidence confidence across the in-distribution and out of distribution datasets, whereas the frozen setting often collapses to little or no coverage. Running an open-weight VLM for localization rather than a closed API makes its internal states available to the calibrator, and they are worth more than output log-probabilities: in-distribution AUROC rises from $0.730$ to $0.914$ for value confidence and from $0.681$ to $0.906$ for evidence confidence. This advantage does not survive a distribution shift. We show that the signal is displaced rather than destroyed, and that labeling roughly $120$ fields from the target dataset takes evidence confidence from $0.641$ to $0.905$ on one dataset and from $0.675$ to $0.829$ on the other.
papers.summary: Enterprise document-extraction systems built on frontier multimodal models rarely say where each extracted value came from or how far it should be trusted. `VERDICT` is a plug-in that leaves an existing extractor untouched: it uses a small Vision-Language Model (VLM) to locate the evidence for each value once per document, then calibrates confidence for both the value and its evidence. Fine-tuning the VLM improves evidence quality and keeps usable precision-coverage trade-offs at a strict 0.80 confidence threshold, where the frozen model often collapses to near-zero coverage. An open-weight VLM exposes internal states that are far more informative than output log-probabilities, raising **in-distribution AUROC from 0.730 to 0.914 for value confidence**; this advantage is lost under distribution shift, but labeling about 120 target fields recovers most of it.

papers.title: Organizing LLM Inference for Aggregate Predictions from Behavioral Data
papers.abstract: When using a large language model (LLM) to simulate a user population, how should we combine individual behavioral histories to predict the fraction of users who take a particular action? We study this question in e-commerce, predicting observed product-level conversion rates from browsing sessions without task-specific model training. We vary two design choices, each involving a bias-variance tradeoff. Summarizing a product's sessions before inference reduces cost but can discard predictive detail, adding bias, whereas predicting outcomes for individual sessions and averaging afterward preserves that detail but requires many calls to reduce variance. Evaluating products together in one prompt can help the model infer what is typical in the setting, reducing bias, but also makes each prediction depend on which other products appear alongside it, adding noise. We evaluate both choices across five LLMs and two datasets. Our main finding is that predictions from individual sessions outperform predictions from summaries when products are evaluated separately, but summaries lead when products are evaluated together. Comparative summaries achieve the highest Spearman correlation with observed rates in 12 of 15 settings, with no alternative significantly better. Comparison thus helps summaries far more than session predictions, overcoming the advantage of behavioral detail. We interpret this difference through a Bayesian model of the second tradeoff, which suggests that comparison helps more when the inputs in a prompt reveal more about differences across products, consistent with our results for four types of comparative context. Comparative summaries also incur a small fraction of the inference cost of the session methods. With the best model for each outcome, they attain 66-89% of the correlation of the best supervised benchmark trained on thousands of labeled products.
papers.summary: When an LLM simulates a user population, the authors ask how to combine individual behavioral histories to predict aggregate rates, using product-level conversion rates from e-commerce browsing sessions without any task-specific training. They vary two choices: summarizing sessions versus predicting each session and averaging, and evaluating products separately versus together in one prompt. Across five LLMs and two datasets, session-level predictions win when products are evaluated separately, but **comparative summaries achieve the highest Spearman correlation in 12 of 15 settings** at a small fraction of the inference cost. A Bayesian model explains why comparison helps summaries more, and with the best model per outcome, comparative summaries reach 66-89% of the correlation of a supervised benchmark trained on thousands of labeled products.

papers.title: Factorization-Guided Training and Inference for Diffusion-Drafted Speculative Decoding
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference through parallel verification of tokens proposed by a drafter. Diffusion drafters further parallelize proposal generation, but greater proposal capacity or higher mean accepted tokens (MAT) need not yield higher throughput. Because verification accepts only a consecutive prefix, early rejections can render later correct predictions ineffective, limiting MAT gains, while even higher MAT may not improve throughput if per-round latency increases. We introduce DScout, which uses two complementary factorizations to guide diffusion drafter training and inference for higher throughput. For training, DScout factorizes position-wise loss into inclusion, weighting, and prediction loss. This guides the design and combination of mixed-horizon training, intra-block unmasking, and acceptance-weighted loss to align supervision with prefix acceptance and improve MAT. For inference, DScout factorizes throughput as the ratio of MAT to per-round latency, guiding target-conditioning depth, drafter depth, and inference block size selection to identify a high-throughput configuration for each workload. Across six benchmarks, DScout achieves $3.84\times$ and $4.14\times$ mean speedups over autoregressive decoding on Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B, respectively, improving mean speedup over the state-of-the-art baseline by 9.1% and 7.1%. Across models and concurrency settings, our inference configuration policy provides up to 9.75% additional mean speedup over DScout's fixed configuration.
papers.summary: Speculative decoding with diffusion drafters can propose many tokens in parallel, but a higher mean accepted tokens (MAT) does not guarantee higher throughput: verification accepts only a consecutive prefix, and per-round latency can rise. `DScout` uses two factorizations to address this. In training, it splits position-wise loss into inclusion, weighting, and prediction terms, which motivates mixed-horizon training, intra-block unmasking, and acceptance-weighted loss. In inference, it treats throughput as MAT divided by per-round latency to choose conditioning depth, drafter depth, and block size per workload. Across six benchmarks, it reaches **3.84x and 4.14x mean speedups over autoregressive decoding on `Qwen3-4B` and `Qwen3-8B`**, 9.1% and 7.1% better than the previous best method, and its configuration policy adds up to 9.75% more speedup.

papers.title: Beyond Prediction: A Component-Level Study of Concept Recovery in In-Context Learning
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) enables language models to make accurate predictions from demonstrations, but prediction success alone does not reveal the extent to which the underlying concept has been recovered. Existing evaluations typically assess recovery at the level of the whole concept, making it difficult to identify which components are recovered and to separate model limitations from ambiguity in the demonstrations. We introduce a component-level framework for concept recovery that decomposes concepts into their defining components and uses controlled structural interventions to evaluate both component-level and whole-concept recovery under identifiable demonstrations. Across four instruction-tuned LLMs and three composition forms, we find that models often achieve high prediction accuracy despite poor whole-concept recovery, with systematic over-specification of relevant attributes and level constraints. Individual structural components are generally insufficient for whole-concept recovery, whereas jointly specifying complementary components, particularly relevant attributes and their level constraints, substantially improves recovery. However, this improvement is fragile: a single plausible but unnecessary level constraint can substantially disrupt recovery. Finally, joint supervision of recovery and implicit prediction substantially improves recovery while preserving prediction performance, with the learned capability transferring across composition forms. Overall, our component-level analysis provides a more diagnostic view of what models recover from demonstrations than the existing holistic view.
papers.summary: Accurate predictions from in-context learning (ICL) do not show whether a model has actually recovered the concept behind the demonstrations. The authors break concepts into their defining components and use controlled structural interventions, with demonstrations designed so the concept is identifiable, to measure recovery of each component and of the whole concept. Across four instruction-tuned LLMs, **models often predict accurately while recovering the whole concept poorly**, and they systematically over-specify relevant attributes and level constraints. Specifying complementary components together helps substantially, but a single plausible yet unnecessary constraint can derail recovery. Joint supervision of recovery and prediction improves recovery without hurting prediction, and the gain transfers across composition forms.

papers.title: SECURE-AI: Multi-Signal Uncertainty Quantification for Trustworthy Acoustic Cough Detection
papers.abstract: Acoustic models for cough detection achieve high accuracy on curated benchmarks but fail silently in deployment, where speech, environmental noise, and audio unlike the training data induce confident misclassifications. In health monitoring, a confidently wrong prediction is worse than no answer at all. We present SECURE-AI (Self-aware Estimation of Cough Uncertainty for Reliable Evaluation of AI), a multi-signal uncertainty quantification framework that wraps a frozen MobileNetV3 cough classifier and estimates when its predictions should not be trusted, combining Monte Carlo Dropout, Temperature Scaling, and Mahalanobis distance in the embedding space. On a held-out split of 12,161 Coswara recordings, the probability-space methods are individually insufficient: Monte Carlo Dropout assigns lower uncertainty to incorrect than to correct predictions, and temperature scaling improves calibration but not discrimination. The strongest signal is embedding-space distance: Mahalanobis distance separates true positives from false positives (means 44.7 versus 63.4; Cohen's $d = 0.94$; AUROC 0.86) and, among predicted non-coughs, false negatives from true negatives (AUROC 0.82), so the same signal can flag both false alarms and missed coughs. At a descriptive operating point selected from labeled test data, retaining 90 percent of true-positive detections removes about two-thirds of false positives and raises precision from 59.9 to roughly 80 percent. A rejection threshold tuned on one split does not transfer to another (validation F1 of 82 percent falls to 34 percent on test), so we report threshold-independent AUROC as the main measure. An error taxonomy shows that failures are systematic, with most false positives related to speech. The pipeline runs on Raspberry Pi hardware costing 30 to 90 US dollars. Probabilistic calibration alone is thus inadequate for reliable cough detection.
papers.summary: Acoustic cough detectors score well on curated benchmarks but make confident mistakes in deployment, where speech, noise, and unfamiliar audio are common. `SECURE-AI` (Self-aware Estimation of Cough Uncertainty for Reliable Evaluation of AI) wraps a frozen `MobileNetV3` classifier and combines `Monte Carlo Dropout`, `Temperature Scaling`, and `Mahalanobis distance` in embedding space to flag predictions that should not be trusted. On 12,161 `Coswara` recordings, the probability-based methods fall short, while **embedding-space Mahalanobis distance separates true from false positives with AUROC 0.86** and also flags missed coughs. Rejection thresholds did not transfer between data splits, most false positives involve speech, and the pipeline runs on Raspberry Pi hardware costing 30 to 90 US dollars.

papers.title: Pack and Extract: An Effective Graph-Based Approach for Feature Selection
papers.abstract: Many molecular biology data sets contain thousands of features, such as genes in single-cell experiments or other omics data. Standard predictive models often perform poorly in such settings, as they tend to retain a large number of features and fail to adequately handle correlations among them. Combinatorial approaches, such as feature selection based on the Independent Dominating Set (IDS) model, have shown promising results, but appear to have been largely overlooked, possibly due to their high computational complexity. In this paper, we propose an improvement to IDS-based feature selection that (i) favors features exhibiting greater diversity and (ii) generalizes the notion of independent dominating set to a node packing model. The resulting formulation is used as an intermediate step within the feature selection process. We evaluate our approach on five genetic data sets and compare the results with those obtained using existing methods. Our experimental results demonstrate notable improvements in predictive accuracy over traditional models, as well as increased stability of the selected feature sets.
papers.summary: Molecular biology datasets such as single-cell and other omics data contain thousands of correlated features, and standard predictive models handle this poorly. The authors extend feature selection based on the Independent Dominating Set (`IDS`) graph model in two ways: they favor more diverse features, and they generalize the independent dominating set to a node packing formulation used as an intermediate selection step. On five genetic datasets, the approach shows **notable improvements in predictive accuracy over traditional models** and more stable selected feature sets.

papers.title: PeekKV: The First Content Token Already Knows Which Heads Matter
papers.abstract: The size of the KV cache grows linearly with context length, making it a major memory bottleneck in LLM serving. Motivated by recent progress in identifying the functional roles of attention heads, a growing body of work compresses the KV cache non-uniformly across heads. Existing methods either fix the important heads via offline profiling or select them using attention signals from the prefill stage. In both cases, however, accuracy fluctuates substantially across workloads. While investigating the cause of this instability, we find that the active heads shift between the prefill and decode stages even within a single input. Along the decode path, by contrast, the activehead composition remains stable across content tokens once format tokens are filtered out. Based on this observation, we propose PeekKV. PeekKV observes a single content token immediately after prefill - a one-token peek - to jointly obtain head-group scores and token-importance scores. Guided by these scores, PeekKV allocates KV cache budgets to head groups in proportion to their group scores and retains only the top-scoring tokens within each budget. PeekKV requires no offline profiling or training and thus applies directly to unseen workloads and new models. Across four public benchmarks, PeekKV achieves the highest accuracy in more than half of the per-model comparisons against state-of-the-art methods, and stays closest to the full-cache accuracy on RULER and LongBench. On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, PeekKV retains 95.7% of the full-cache accuracy at a 10% memory budget on RULER with 16K contexts and 95.9% at a 1.5% budget on LongBench.
papers.summary: The key-value (KV) cache grows linearly with context length, and methods that compress it unevenly across attention heads give unstable accuracy because the active heads shift between the prefill and decode stages. The authors observe that along the decode path, once format tokens are filtered out, the set of active heads stays stable across content tokens. `PeekKV` uses this by observing a single content token right after prefill to score head groups and token importance, then splitting the cache budget across head groups and keeping the top-scoring tokens, with no offline profiling or training. On `Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct`, it **retains 95.7% of full-cache accuracy at a 10% memory budget on `RULER` with 16K contexts** and 95.9% at a 1.5% budget on `LongBench`.

papers.title: Fast Construction of Inner Sphere Trees Using Machine Learning
papers.abstract: Collision detection for complex non-convex objects is a bottleneck in physics simulation, virtual reality, and robotics. Inner sphere trees (ISTs) answer proximity and penetration queries efficiently, but their greedy leaf-sphere construction is sequential and computationally expensive, which limits both large-scale preprocessing and runtime use. In this work, we present ML-IST, a machine-learning-based method that reformulates leaf-sphere generation as a single-shot set-prediction problem: a network predicts a fixed set of inscribed sphere candidates from multichannel voxel geometry, differentiable coverage feedback corrects the coarse prediction and fills residual gaps at finer scales, and a lightweight geometric projection enforces validity. Averaged over the test set, a single-GPU implementation of ML-IST reduces mean leaf-generation time by a factor of $2.0$--$2.6$ over single-core CPU construction across target capacities of 64--512 spheres, and qualitative results on complex models show multiscale sphere distributions that follow principal volumes and slender features. We further integrate ML-IST into the Jolt Physics and Bullet engines; in an alpha-puzzle benchmark it reaches 55.89~FPS, the highest among the compared representations (conventional IST, GImpact, and convex decomposition). These results support learned leaf generation as a practical component for fast, runtime construction of detailed collision representations.
papers.summary: Inner sphere trees (ISTs) answer collision and penetration queries for complex non-convex objects efficiently, but building them requires a slow, sequential greedy placement of leaf spheres. `ML-IST` reframes this step as single-shot set prediction: a network predicts inscribed sphere candidates from voxelized geometry, differentiable coverage feedback fills gaps at finer scales, and a geometric projection enforces validity. A single-GPU implementation cuts leaf-generation time by 2.0-2.6x compared with single-core CPU construction.
