Integrated into the `Jolt Physics` and `Bullet` engines, it **reaches 55.89 FPS on an alpha-puzzle benchmark**, the best among the compared collision representations.

papers.title: A Group-Aware Comparative Study of Classical Machine Learning and Deep Learning Methods for Sensor-Based Human Activity Recognition
papers.abstract: Human Activity Recognition (HAR) using wearable or smartphone inertial sensors is commonly evaluated with both classical machine learning and deep learning methods. However, reported performance can be strongly affected by sensor modality, dataset characteristics, and data-splitting strategy. This study presents a controlled comparative evaluation of four classical machine learning models and four deep learning models on two public HAR datasets, UCI-HAR and KU-HAR. Three sensor modalities were considered: accelerometer (ACC), gyroscope (GYRO), and their combination (ACC+GYRO). Classical machine learning models used handcrafted statistical features, while deep learning models operated directly on raw sensor sequences. The primary evaluation employed five-fold StratifiedGroupKFold cross-validation, with subject- or participant-level grouping to prevent group overlap between training and test folds. Macro-F1 was used as the primary performance metric. The results show that deep learning did not consistently outperform classical machine learning. On UCI-HAR, the evaluated deep learning models achieved slightly higher macro-F1 values, whereas on KU-HAR, LightGBM achieved 0.857 compared with 0.828 for the highest-performing evaluated deep learning model. Regarding sensor modality, the combined ACC+GYRO configuration generally outperformed ACC or GYRO alone on both datasets. The evaluation protocol also had a substantial effect: for CNNBiLSTMAttn with ACC+GYRO, random splitting increased macro-F1 by 0.033 on UCI-HAR and 0.093 on KU-HAR compared with grouped evaluation. These findings highlight the importance of model family, sensor modality, dataset characteristics, and group-aware evaluation when assessing sensor-based HAR systems.
papers.summary: Reported results for sensor-based Human Activity Recognition (HAR) depend heavily on sensor modality, dataset, and how the data is split. This controlled study compares four classical machine learning models using handcrafted features with four deep learning models using raw sequences on `UCI-HAR` and `KU-HAR`, with accelerometer, gyroscope, and combined inputs, under subject-grouped `StratifiedGroupKFold` cross-validation. Deep learning did not consistently win: it was slightly ahead on `UCI-HAR`, while `LightGBM` scored 0.857 macro-F1 against 0.828 on `KU-HAR`. Combining both sensors generally helped, and **random splitting inflated macro-F1 by up to 0.093** compared with grouped evaluation.

papers.title: ReTTT: Reflection-Driven Test-Time Training via Experience-Based Parametric Memory
papers.abstract: LLM agents accumulate valuable task-specific information through their actions, observations, and environmental feedback during multi-turn task execution. When effectively used, this information can help agents refine subsequent decisions and improve task performance. However, the learning value of an interaction depends on its context and subsequent feedback, making it challenging to extract reliable, actionable lessons and revise them as the task unfolds. In this paper, we introduce ReTTT, which enables experience-driven self-adaptation through test-time training on lessons constructed and continually revised within an episode. ReTTT lets the agent reflect on interaction feedback, maintain the resulting lessons in an explicit memory, and learn from them by updating an episode-local LoRA adapter while keeping the backbone frozen. The adapted model then performs both subsequent actions and reflection, coupling policy adaptation with the construction of future learning experience. We evaluate ReTTT on ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and SWE-bench Lite using two model families. ReTTT outperforms trajectory-based test-time training across all six model--benchmark settings, improving task success by up to 12.14 percentage points. A frozen-reflection comparison further shows a 7.14-point benefit from adapting the reflection policy, while trajectory analysis illustrates how adapted reflection derives more task-specific guidance from failed attempts. These findings suggest that learning to reflect on its own behavior can boost agents' performance on long-horizon tasks.
papers.summary: LLM agents gather useful feedback during multi-turn tasks, but turning that feedback into reliable lessons and revising them as the task goes on is hard. `ReTTT` has the agent reflect on feedback, keep the resulting lessons in an explicit memory, and train an episode-local `LoRA` adapter on them while the backbone stays frozen; the adapted model then handles both subsequent actions and further reflection. On `ALFWorld`, `ScienceWorld`, and `SWE-bench Lite` with two model families, it beats trajectory-based test-time training in all six settings, **improving task success by up to 12.14 percentage points**. Adapting the reflection policy itself adds 7.14 points over keeping reflection frozen.

papers.title: TeleTwin: A Calibrated Digital Twin of Telegram Crisis Discourse as a Ground-Truth Testbed for Detecting LLM-Powered Information Operations
papers.abstract: Large language models make it cheap to run influence operations whose messages never repeat, yet real platforms offer almost no ground truth for testing whether coordination detectors can find them. The problem is sharpest on Telegram, which moderates little and spreads content through broadcast channels and forwarding rather than a follow graph. We introduce TeleTwin, an LLM-powered digital twin of a Telegram crisis-discourse ecosystem in which channels are agents, each instantiated from the history of a real channel, calibrated on 1.07 million messages from 195 public channels on the Israel-Gaza and Iran-Israel conflict (March-August 2025). On a held-out period containing the June 2025 Iran-Israel war, the twin tracks daily dynamics better than statistical baselines (correlation 0.86 against 0.64) and reacts to the war unprompted, but it over-focuses on the conflict, over-amplifies forwarding cascades, underestimates the shock and writes recognisably LLM-like text. We then inject LLM-written campaigns with known membership into the real data and into the twin. In real data, identical-text, co-URL and synchrony detectors fail once a campaign rewords, staggers or drops links; multilingual semantic similarity recovers loud campaigns, including cross-lingual ones, but not quiet ones, and its false positives fall unevenly across political perspectives. Inside the twin all detectors fail, because the simulated background is about 40 times more semantically homogeneous than the real one. Digital twins can supply ground truth for campaigns, but not, without calibrating their diversity, a realistic background for evaluating semantic detectors.
papers.summary: LLMs make it cheap to run influence campaigns whose messages never repeat, and real platforms provide almost no ground truth for testing detectors, especially Telegram with its broadcast channels and forwarding. `TeleTwin` is an LLM-powered digital twin in which each agent is modeled on a real channel's history, calibrated on 1.07 million messages from 195 channels covering the Israel-Gaza and Iran-Israel conflicts. It tracks daily dynamics better than statistical baselines (correlation 0.86 versus 0.64), but it over-focuses on the conflict and produces recognizably LLM-like text. When LLM-written campaigns are injected, identical-text, co-URL, and synchrony detectors fail on real data once campaigns reword or stagger, and semantic similarity catches only loud campaigns. Inside the twin every detector fails, because **the simulated background is about 40 times more semantically homogeneous than the real one**.

papers.title: How Data Scales in Agentic Reinforcement Learning: Laws and Synthesis Strategies
papers.abstract: Pretraining scaling laws treat training data as a one-dimensional quantity: a token count. Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) inherits this scalar abstraction, but modern synthesis pipelines now generate \textit{tasks}, \textit{environments}, and \textit{trajectories} independently and at very different costs, turning data into a structured design space. This raises a question pretraining never had to answer: given a synthesis budget, \textit{which axis} should be scaled? We address this question end-to-end with three tightly coupled contributions. First, we decompose agentic data into three cardinality axes (task, environment, trajectory), plus a reward-density control variable, and fit per-axis scaling relations on different large language models (LLMs) across math+code, SWE, web, and UI/tool application domains. Across all model sizes, model families, domains, and RL algorithms (PPO and GRPO) we measured, the scaling exponents order as environment $>$ task $>$ trajectory. When environment diversity is decomposed into world and environment-structure diversity, its advantage is mainly driven by the former, while the latter is just comparable to the task diversity. Second, we use the fitted laws as a common ruler to price synthesis methods, capturing each method's efficiency as a per-axis discount factor and identifying critical synthetic-to-real ratios at which collapse begins; these ratios differ by an order of magnitude across axes. Third, we cast budget allocation as a constrained optimization under our laws and discounts, deriving a Chinchilla-style compute-optimal recipe and validating it at held-out scale. The empirical results demonstrate that following the recipe yields up to $1.7\times$ compute efficiency over the dominant ``scale-the-trajectories'' practice.
papers.summary: Pretraining scaling laws treat data as a single token count, but agentic reinforcement learning (RL) pipelines synthesize tasks, environments, and trajectories separately and at very different costs. The authors fit per-axis scaling laws across model sizes and families, math, code, software engineering, web, and UI/tool domains, and both `PPO` and `GRPO`, and find that **scaling exponents consistently order environment > task > trajectory**, with environment gains coming mainly from world diversity. They use the fitted laws to price synthesis methods and identify synthetic-to-real ratios at which training collapses. A Chinchilla-style budget-allocation recipe derived from these laws yields up to 1.7x compute efficiency over the common practice of scaling trajectories.

papers.title: Parameter misspecification in physics-informed neural networks: A closed-form audit and its limits
papers.abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) are trained to minimize the residual of a prescribed equation, so a low training loss does not indicate whether a coefficient in that equation was specified incorrectly. This study evaluates what can be inferred about the encoded parameter from the trained network alone. When the residual is linear in the parameter, written as $A - \nu B$, the least-squares estimate $\hat{\nu} = A^{\top}B/B^{\top}B$ is obtained from a single evaluation of the frozen network, without retraining or reference data. Its accuracy depends on how closely the network satisfies its own equation, quantified by a normalized residual $\rho$. Recovery error is associated with $\rho$ (log-log correlation 0.72 across 36 convection-diffusion networks), and empirical exponents of 0.63 to 1.20 across three equations decompose into one half plus a measurable angular term. For Burgers' equation, a single-model test based on a block-bootstrap standard error flagged 3 of 300 correctly specified networks (observed false-alarm rate 1%), all 2% misspecifications at a practical budget, and two thirds of 1% misspecifications after convergence. For the self-similar blowup rate of the C\'ordoba-C\'ordoba-Fontelos equation, where the rate also enters the architecture, the estimator recovers about half of the misspecification, whereas $\rho$ increases approximately quadratically and distinguishes a 0.2% error. When the incorrect rate enters both the equation and the architecture, errors of up to 2% were not detected at the precision reached. At practical budgets, the raw loss can be lower for the misspecified model, a scaling effect that $\rho$ does not share.
papers.summary: A physics-informed neural network (PINN) can reach low training loss even when a coefficient in its equation is wrong. When the residual is linear in the parameter, the authors recover a closed-form least-squares estimate from a single evaluation of the frozen network, with no retraining or reference data, and show that its accuracy tracks a normalized residual. For `Burgers' equation`, a bootstrap-based test **flagged all 2% misspecifications at a 1% false-alarm rate**. The method weakens when the parameter also enters the architecture: for the blowup rate of the `Córdoba-Córdoba-Fontelos equation`, errors up to 2% went undetected when the wrong rate appeared in both the equation and the architecture.

papers.title: DS-Net: A Dynamic Split Network for Edge-Cloud Collaborative Inference
papers.abstract: Collaborative inference serves as a critical methodology in edge intelligence. Existing collaborative inference methods operate by splitting the deep neural network (DNN) model between edge devices and cloud servers. However, these methods need to load different models for multiple split points when the communication or device changes, thus resulting in long switching times and substantial storage overhead on the edge side. To address this issue, we propose a Dynamic Split Network (DS-Net), which not only enables efficient split point switching but also enhances the collaborative speed and accuracy across various scenarios. Specifically, we design a dynamic switching framework that enables flexible selection among multiple split points within a single model, thereby reducing storage, memory, and switching overhead. To mitigate the feature distribution shifts and task-relevant information loss caused by dynamic splitting and high-ratio compression, we further propose a hierarchical compensation mechanism. Local alignment calibrates the decoded feature distribution at each split point, while task-specific global compensation restores task-relevant information at the global level. In addition, we incorporate sample-adaptive global compensation selection into split-point selection based on sample complexity and runtime resource conditions. Experimental results demonstrate that DS-Net reduces memory overhead by 74.6% and achieves millisecond-level switching latency. Moreover, under a 10 Mbps bandwidth constraint on the Nano platform, DS-Net outperforms state-of-the-art collaborative methods by achieving 1.2% higher accuracy on the COCO dataset, reducing latency by 42.5%, and improving throughput by a factor of 1.8$\times$.
papers.summary: Edge-cloud collaborative inference splits a deep neural network (DNN) between an edge device and a server, but existing methods load a separate model for each split point, which makes switching slow and costs storage. `DS-Net` supports multiple split points within one model and adds a hierarchical compensation mechanism: local alignment corrects feature distributions at each split, and task-specific global compensation restores information lost to heavy compression. The split point and compensation are chosen per sample based on its complexity and on available resources. It **reduces memory overhead by 74.6%** with millisecond-level switching, and at 10 Mbps on a `Jetson Nano` it beats prior methods on `COCO` with 1.2% higher accuracy, 42.5% lower latency, and 1.8x throughput.

papers.title: Compaction-Aware Reinforcement Learning For Ascend Triton Kernel Generation
papers.abstract: Automatically generating high-performance kernels with LLM-based agents promises substantial gains in development efficiency, but two obstacles remain. First, while increasing multi-turn interaction with execution environments is crucial for refining generation quality, continuous context accumulation rapidly exceeds the model's effective context window. Second, training long-horizon tasks via GRPO inherently incurs sparse rewards due to its reliance on terminal outcome evaluation, severely hindering step-level credit assignment; To address these obstacles, we propose ATRL (Ascend Triton Reinforcement Learning), a post-training method that refines GRPO into a compaction-aware, segment-level objective for long-horizon kernel generation. We also design a lightweight agent harness providing cascaded compilation, correctness, and profiling feedback, alongside an Ascend-specific knowledge base injected during agentic RL training and evaluation to compensate for the base model's missing platform expertise. Evaluations on NPUKernelBench and KernelBench, both executed on Ascend hardware, show that ATRL consistently surpasses all baselines, including GRPO, in both correctness and speedup.
papers.summary: LLM agents that write high-performance kernels face two problems: long multi-turn interaction with the execution environment overflows the context window, and Group Relative Policy Optimization (`GRPO`) gives only a sparse reward at the end of a long episode, which makes it hard to tell which steps helped. `ATRL` (Ascend Triton Reinforcement Learning) turns `GRPO` into a compaction-aware objective that assigns credit per segment, so context can be compacted during long episodes. It pairs this with a lightweight agent harness that returns compilation, correctness, and profiling feedback in sequence, plus an Ascend-specific knowledge base that supplies hardware expertise the base model lacks. On `NPUKernelBench` and `KernelBench`, both run on Ascend hardware, **`ATRL` beats all baselines, including `GRPO`, on both correctness and speedup**.

papers.title: LatLM: Line-Parallel Language Models with Deferred Commitment
papers.abstract: Line-parallel language models advance multiple lines concurrently for substantial speedups. However, frameworks like the Line-Coupled Language Model (LCLM) enforce a fixed commitment schedule across lines. Because dependencies vary within text, a fixed schedule cannot hold back a line whose prerequisites remain uncomputed, forcing premature commitments and cascading reasoning errors. To address this limitation, we introduce the Lattice Language Model (LatLM), making commitment schedules an adaptive decoding-time choice. Text occupies a 2D lattice where eligible frontier tokens are scored each round; a policy commits confident candidates while deferring unready ones for extended context. One forward pass supervises entire sampled trajectories via 2D causal masking, while an append-only cache retains exact states. At 482M parameters, we establish two findings. (1) LatLM matches a data- and capacity-matched autoregressive model on held-out text when decoded sequentially, while its adaptive parallel decoder achieves near-autoregressive accuracy on independent-line tasks using 25--41% as many decoding rounds. (2) When cross-line dependencies cause LCLM's fixed schedule to fail, deferred commitment substantially improves accuracy while retaining parallelism where dependencies permit. On mixed dependency chains, LatLM achieves 96.5% accuracy versus LCLM's 78.5%, using fewer than half the decoding rounds of the autoregressive baseline.
papers.summary: Line-parallel language models generate several lines of text at once for speed, but frameworks like the Line-Coupled Language Model (`LCLM`) commit tokens on a fixed schedule, which forces premature commitments when one line depends on another that isn't finished yet. The Lattice Language Model (`LatLM`) places text on a 2D lattice and scores the eligible frontier tokens each round. A policy commits confident tokens and defers unready ones, training uses 2D causal masking over whole sampled trajectories, and an append-only cache keeps exact states. At 482M parameters, `LatLM` matches a comparable autoregressive model when decoded sequentially and approaches autoregressive accuracy on tasks with independent lines using 25–41% as many decoding rounds. On mixed dependency chains it reaches **96.5% accuracy versus 78.5% for `LCLM`**, with fewer than half the autoregressive baseline's rounds.

papers.title: DISCERN: Identifiable Disease Evidence for Generalizable Medical Multimodal Learning
papers.abstract: Clinical multimodal models can learn enrollment shortcuts shared across modalities and fail on new cohorts. We model these data through a latent structural causal model: disease state and background factors generate physiology through shared mechanisms, while cohorts differ in selection and measurement. Holding acquisition fixed, we identify conditional disease evidence without observing disease-state labels or recovering the full causal model. In common Gaussian coordinates, cross-cohort state alignment and natural-parameter changes identify a minimal selection statistic; conditioning on it removes enrollment-dependent evidence and yields an identifiable reference posterior within the specified shift family. State-dependent interactions can carry evidence invisible to individual-modality posteriors, motivating joint, information-preserving representations. DISCERN combines an information-lattice encoder, a latent-state model, and an outcome head through joint training. Under reversed synthetic enrollment on known latent coordinates, conditioning raises state AUROC from 0.043 to 0.883 and from 0.265 to 0.825, while random conditioning does not. Exploratory cross-database mortality experiments between eICU and MIMIC-IV improve AUROC over matched empirical risk minimization by 0.036 and 0.035. Learned-coordinate diagnostics distinguish preservation of state information from identification of the coordinates required by the estimator.
papers.summary: Clinical multimodal models can pick up enrollment shortcuts, patterns tied to how patients were selected into a cohort, and then fail on new cohorts. The authors model the data with a latent structural causal model and show that disease evidence can be identified, without disease labels, by conditioning on a minimal selection statistic estimated from how latent states shift between cohorts. `DISCERN` jointly trains an information-preserving encoder, a latent-state model, and an outcome head. Under reversed synthetic enrollment, conditioning **raises state AUROC from 0.043 to 0.883**, and in exploratory cross-database mortality prediction between `eICU` and `MIMIC-IV` it improves AUROC by about 0.035 over matched empirical risk minimization.

papers.title: Physics-Aware Self-Supervised Pretraining on Multi-Domain Raman Spectra
papers.abstract: Raman spectroscopy generates large volumes of unlabeled data that are difficult to exploit with conventional supervised learning. This work introduces a multi-domain self-supervised learning framework based on a masked autoencoder (MAE) for learning transferable Raman spectral representations from heterogeneous biological, chemical, forensic, and materials datasets. The proposed pretraining strategy incorporates physics-aware objectives by combining masked intensity reconstruction with a sparse Voigt-profile decoder that models spectral peak structure through differentiable peak centers, widths, and amplitudes. A denoising objective is further included to improve robustness to spectral corruption. The learned encoder is evaluated on substance classification, component identification, concentration estimation, and spectral denoising under linear probing, attention-based probing, end-to-end fine-tuning, and training from scratch. Experimental results show that self-supervised pretraining is most beneficial for challenging tasks with limited labeled data. Attention-based probing also reveals substantially more useful information in the frozen representation than linear probing, indicating that conventional linear evaluation may underestimate representation quality. In addition, the benefits of pretraining become more pronounced with increasing encoder capacity. Overall, the proposed framework demonstrates that physics-aware, multi-domain self-supervised pretraining can improve label efficiency, robustness, and transferability across diverse Raman spectroscopy tasks.
papers.summary: Raman spectroscopy produces large amounts of unlabeled data, which conventional supervised learning cannot use. The authors pretrain a masked autoencoder (`MAE`) on biological, chemical, forensic, and materials spectra, using physics-aware objectives: masked intensity reconstruction, a sparse Voigt-profile decoder that models peak centers, widths, and amplitudes, and a denoising task. Pretraining helps most on hard tasks with little labeled data, and the gains grow with encoder size. **Attention-based probing extracts far more from the frozen representation than linear probing**, which suggests that standard linear evaluation can underestimate representation quality.

papers.title: Same Space or Not: Benchmarking Spatial Intelligence Through Cross-View Contradictions
papers.abstract: Spatial intelligence, the capacity to represent and reason about physical space, underlies embodied perception and real-world visual understanding. Existing benchmarks probe it through spatial relations, perspective-taking, and mental modeling. What remains underexamined is whether a model can maintain a coherent scene representation across views, since pairwise comparison alone cannot reveal which view departs from the truth. We thus introduce Same Space or Not (SSoN), a benchmark of cross-view contradiction resolution comprising 1,000 questions from seven indoor scene sources and six categories of controlled 3D edits. Each question presents three views of an unchanged scene and one view of an edited variant. Models must identify the inconsistent view and explain the contradiction without a designated trusted reference or a marked target. Our pipeline iteratively translates human review into generation constraints. Automated checks and exhaustive human validation screen out both trivial visual shortcuts and questions lacking sufficient evidence for a unique answer. Humans achieve 83.3% accuracy, compared with 39.7% for the strongest vision-language models (VLMs), falling to 34.9% when a valid visual explanation is also required. We investigate prompting, camera information, and 3D reconstruction as interventions. On a 100-question intervention set with a 24% baseline, prompting and 3D reconstruction remain below 50% answer accuracy, except when ground-truth camera information is supplied, which reaches 61% answer accuracy but only 48% True solve accuracy. On a held-out 201-question test set, Qwen2.5-VL-7B achieves 21.89% accuracy, 33.33% after answer-only fine-tuning, and 41.79% after fine-tuning on both rationales and answers. These results identify cross-view contradiction resolution as a substantial weakness of current VLMs that can be partly addressed by targeted supervision.
papers.summary: Same Space or Not (`SSoN`) is a 1,000-question benchmark that tests whether vision-language models (VLMs) keep a consistent representation of a scene across viewpoints. Each question shows three views of an unchanged indoor scene and one view of a 3D-edited variant, and the model must find the inconsistent view and explain the contradiction without being told which view to trust. Humans reach 83.3% accuracy while **the strongest VLM reaches 39.7%**, dropping to 34.9% when a valid explanation is also required. Prompting and 3D reconstruction stay below 50% unless ground-truth camera information is supplied, and fine-tuning `Qwen2.5-VL-7B` on rationales and answers raises its held-out accuracy from 21.89% to 41.79%.

papers.title: UltraData-Code: From Raw Repositories to Algorithmically Dense and Task-Oriented Code Data
papers.abstract: Code generation has become a core capability of large language models (LLMs), and code data is central to the pre-training process that develops it. As obtaining public code of sufficient quality becomes more difficult, further progress cannot rely on corpus expansion alone. Tiered data management instead applies increasingly targeted processing to smaller data pools, producing data states suited to different training objectives. Following this perspective, we present UltraData-Code as four connected data states spanning repository archival at L0, standardized natural code at L1, algorithmic selection at L2, and task-oriented synthesis at L3. L0 preserves repository data and provenance for reprocessing, while L1 applies scalable filtering, normalization, and near-deduplication for broad pre-training. L2 selects high-quality algorithmically relevant files using language-adaptive relevance signals and quality constraints, yielding approximately 400B tokens of UltraData-Code-L2 across 11 programming languages for focused continual pre-training. L3 converts selected implementations into structured programming exercises, yielding approximately 150B tokens of UltraData-Code-L3 across the same 11 languages for task-oriented mid-training or supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Under controlled 10B-token continual pre-training of a 1B model, L2 improves pass@1 over L1 by 7.80 percentage points (pp) on EvalPlus and 5.13pp on MultiPL-E. Replacing half of the L2 training tokens with L3 yields a further gain of 8.42pp and 8.07pp on the two benchmarks, respectively. Both gains increase when the training budget scales to 100B tokens. We have released our datasets and classifiers to support further research on LLMs.
papers.summary: As high-quality public code becomes scarcer, `UltraData-Code` organizes code pretraining data into four tiers of increasingly targeted processing. The tiers are raw repository archives (L0), filtered and deduplicated natural code (L1), about 400B tokens of algorithmically relevant files across 11 languages (L2), and about 150B tokens of synthesized programming exercises (L3). In controlled 10B-token continual pretraining of a 1B model, L2 improves pass@1 over L1 by 7.80 points on `EvalPlus` and 5.13 on `MultiPL-E`, and **replacing half the L2 tokens with L3 adds a further 8.42 and 8.07 points**. Both gains grow at a 100B-token budget, and the datasets and classifiers are released.

papers.title: A Controlled LLM Workflow for Evidence-Grounded Diagnosis of Risk Score Differences
papers.abstract: We propose a controlled Large Language Model (LLM) workflow for explaining risk score differences using similar historical transactions. The workflow combines reference retrieval and contrastive SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) evidence with reference-based LLM reasoning and deterministic validation. Experiments on a test dataset show that the workflow produces more consistent, evidence-grounded and traceable diagnoses than the same LLM without structured workflow guidance.
papers.summary: The authors build a controlled large language model (LLM) workflow that explains why two transactions received different risk scores by comparing them with similar historical transactions. The workflow combines reference retrieval, contrastive SHapley Additive exPlanations (`SHAP`) evidence, reference-based LLM reasoning, and deterministic validation of the output. On a test dataset, **the workflow produces more consistent, evidence-grounded, and traceable diagnoses** than the same LLM used without structured guidance.

papers.title: Geo-vision: Native-Resolution Geometry and Sampled Topology for Vehicle-Part Damage Classification
papers.abstract: Geo-vision classifies vehicle-part damage using a fixed representation combining appearance, multiscale geometry, orientation, and sampled digital topology. Connected components, holes, Euler characteristics, and spatial arrangement complement amplitude-sensitive pooling and a supervised tree classifier. We establish amplitude preservation, axial sign invariance, and conditional operator stability. Retrospective checkpoint evaluation on 55,303 crops from 4,916 source groups yields average precision 0.7577, exceeding 0.7458 for an ImageNet-pretrained frozen YOLO11n comparator on identical crops. The complete added structural block, comprising topology, occupancy, and component location, improves average precision by 0.00493 beyond appearance and geometry. Geo-vision uses no external encoder pretraining and has higher AP point estimates at every matched label budget. With approximately 25% fewer task labels, its AP point estimate exceeds full-data YOLO, although the adjusted interval includes zero. Complete serial CPU inference requires 26.98 ms per crop versus YOLO's 11.20 ms, with peak memory 185 versus 437 MiB. Independent external validation remains necessary.
papers.summary: `Geo-vision` classifies damage on vehicle parts from a fixed, hand-designed representation: appearance, multiscale geometry, orientation, and sampled digital topology features such as connected components, holes, and Euler characteristics, fed to a supervised tree classifier. On 55,303 crops, it reaches **average precision of 0.7577 versus 0.7458 for a frozen ImageNet-pretrained `YOLO11n`**, without any encoder pretraining. The topology and structure features add only about 0.005 average precision. It runs slower on CPU (26.98 ms versus 11.20 ms per crop) but uses less than half the peak memory, and the authors note that independent external validation is still needed.

papers.title: IMPULSE: Push First, Then Predict in V-JEPA 2 Feature Space
papers.abstract: Latent world models such as V-JEPA 2 forecast in the feature space of a video encoder, but one look at an object does not reveal how hard it is to rotate, how much it bounces or how much it slides. People find out by trying: a few pokes reveal how an object responds. IMPULSE, named after the impulse response it infers, gives a predictor in frozen V-JEPA 2 feature space the same ability. A Bayesian contact memory summarizes three short calibration pushes, a predicted object pose carries it into the predictor, and a lightweight random-Fourier pose head lets the predictor use the pose. On 512 fresh objects, in a pre-specified held-out confirmation with models sealed before the data existed, the memory lowers the 1-second feature-forecast error by 11.6-12.8% relative to the same predictor without experience, for all 8 training seeds, with a 95% seed-and-object interval excluding zero. The gain also holds for 128 objects with out-of-range physics (11.7-14.0%), and the full extension beats a plain predictor by 15.5-16.6%. An information-ladder argument, exact for ideal predictors, shows that physics reaches the features only through motion, so we measure how much the pathway lets pose help. On fresh objects, the Fourier head roughly triples the gain of a perfect memory over plain pose tokens (2.8-3.2x). Raw push measurements fed through the same pathway give a similar gain, so the Bayesian summary is not required; it condenses the trials into eight interpretable numbers. The gain is absent at contact onset and grows afterwards.
papers.summary: Latent world models such as `V-JEPA 2` forecast video in feature space but cannot tell from a single look how heavy, bouncy, or slippery an object is. `IMPULSE` lets a predictor in frozen `V-JEPA 2` feature space learn this from three short calibration pushes. A Bayesian contact memory summarizes the pushes, a predicted object pose carries that summary into the predictor, and a random-Fourier pose head lets the predictor use the pose. In a pre-registered held-out test on 512 new objects, **the memory cuts 1-second feature-forecast error by 11.6–12.8%** across all training seeds, and the gain holds for objects with physics outside the training range. Feeding raw push measurements through the same pathway gives a similar gain, so the Bayesian summary is not required; its main value is condensing the pushes into eight interpretable numbers.

papers.title: Spatio-Temporal Detection of Photovoltaic Systems on Industrial Building Rooftops Using Satellite Imagery and Machine Learning
papers.abstract: The global transition toward carbon-neutral energy systems is heavily dependent on the rapid deployment of solar photovoltaic (PV) infrastructure, yet the speed of this expansion has outpaced the ability of administrative registries to maintain accurate records. While high-resolution commercial imagery is often used for monitoring, its high cost and infrequent updates can create an information gap for grid operators, energy infrastructure developers and policymakers. This study addresses the lack of scalable monitoring for industrial-scale rooftop PV systems by developing a machine learning framework that utilizes open-access, multispectral Sentinel-2 satellite imagery. By integrating building geometries from OpenStreetMap with Sentinel-2 reflectance data, a Random Forest model was trained to identify the specific spectral signatures of PV modules. Moving beyond theoretical modeling, this work emphasizes practical implementation through the development of an interactive web-based prototype for on-demand site monitoring. The application enables users to retrieve up-to-date satellite observations and assess the presence of PV systems on industrial building rooftops. The tool incorporates quality metrics that inform users whether a prediction is supported by sufficient training data density or requires manual verification. This end-to-end framework demonstrates that open-source medium-resolution data can effectively bridge this monitoring gap.
papers.summary: Rooftop solar has spread faster than official registries can track it, and high-resolution commercial imagery is expensive and updated infrequently. The authors combine building outlines from `OpenStreetMap` with open multispectral `Sentinel-2` imagery and train a `Random Forest` model to recognize the spectral signature of photovoltaic panels on industrial rooftops. They package the model as an interactive web prototype that fetches recent satellite observations on demand and **flags whether each prediction has enough nearby training data to trust or needs manual checking**.

papers.title: Super-resolution as Spatial Downscaling: Coherence, Structure and Task Utility in Earth Observation
papers.abstract: Learned satellite super-resolution is commonly assessed by pixel fidelity and potential downlink savings, but these criteria do not establish whether the reconstructed field preserves spatial structure or supports reliable downstream analysis. We treat single-image super-resolution as a spatial downscaling problem and evaluate four lightweight networks, including our compact 0.36 million-parameter model, against interpolation using pixel metrics, directional variograms, spectral band correlation, codispersion and observation coherence. On 735 satellite tiles from 190 scenes, the networks differ by at most 0.03dB and outperform bicubic interpolation by $1.39-1.42$dB at $\times 2$. They recover about 30% of the spectral power above the observation's Nyquist frequency and, at $\times 4$, produce more isotropic fields than the reference (range anisotropy 0.59 against 0.49). Energy-based metrics can favour invented detail. Enforcing coherence reaches the quantisation limit, yet at least 99.7% of the remaining error lies in the observation operator's null space, which coherence cannot constrain. Under spatially blocked, paired evaluation with two backbones and a sharpening control, learned reconstruction changes land-use accuracy by $-1.0$ to $+3.1$ percentage points (significant in 7 of 24 comparisons) and building-change F1 by $-0.015$ to $+0.024$ (none significant) relative to bicubic interpolation, and amplifies spurious change between two observations of an unchanged scene by $1.3-1.5$ times where interpolation attenuates it. Full-resolution JPEG\,2000 matches or exceeds reduced-resolution transmission with reconstruction at every matched bitrate. Learned reconstruction is most useful when only low-resolution imagery is available, and its evaluation should combine pixel metrics with spatial structure, observation coherence and task-level tests under spatial validation.
papers.summary: Satellite super-resolution is usually judged by pixel fidelity, which does not show whether the reconstructed images preserve spatial structure or support downstream analysis. Treating super-resolution as spatial downscaling, the authors compare four lightweight networks, including a 0.36M-parameter model of their own, against bicubic interpolation using pixel, variogram, spectral, and coherence metrics on 735 tiles. The networks beat bicubic by about 1.4 dB, but their effect on land-use accuracy and building-change detection is mostly not statistically significant. They also **amplify spurious change between two images of an unchanged scene by 1.3–1.5×**, and transmitting full-resolution `JPEG 2000` matches or beats sending reduced-resolution images and reconstructing them at every matched bitrate.

papers.title: FrameScout: Scouting Query-Relevant Frames for Long Video Understanding
papers.abstract: Long video understanding requires VideoLLMs to answer queries about videos spanning tens of minutes to hours, but such long videos produce far more visual tokens than current VideoLLMs can process. To address this issue, keyframe selectors are proposed to select the most query-relevant frames by computing the similarity between frame and query embeddings. Existing selectors either encode frames independently without temporal context or process chunks in isolation with ranking objectives that are difficult to optimize. To alleviate those limitations, we propose FrameScout with two core designs: (i) a streaming selector architecture that leverages a sliding-window KV cache and successor aggregation to produce temporally-contextualized frame embeddings; (ii) a frame-query contrastive objective that aligns frame and query embeddings in a shared space, directly training the selector to distinguish relevant frames from irrelevant ones. Extensive experiments on three long-video benchmarks and six base VideoLLMs demonstrate that FrameScout consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance. Code is available at https://github.com/Hubert-1102/FrameScout.
papers.summary: Long videos produce far more visual tokens than video large language models (VideoLLMs) can process, so keyframe selectors pick the frames most relevant to the query. Existing selectors either encode frames without temporal context or are trained with ranking objectives that are hard to optimize. `FrameScout` uses a streaming selector with a sliding-window KV cache and successor aggregation to produce frame embeddings that account for neighboring frames, and trains it with a contrastive objective that aligns frames and queries in a shared space. Across three long-video benchmarks and six base VideoLLMs, **`FrameScout` reports state-of-the-art results consistently**.

papers.title: LLM Evolutionary Search Strategies Should be Compared by Tokens
papers.abstract: LLM evolutionary search is currently evaluated by counting proposals (candidate programs). We demonstrate this metric hides the true cost of search, and redo the comparison using tokens. By replaying 600 logged runs across 5 tasks and 3 methods, we show that proposal costs vary wildly from 16k to 39k tokens. In equal-proposal comparisons, this silently grants some methods up to 1.9x the compute of others, and gives evolution roughly 6x the budget of independent sampling. When we match token budgets, giving sampling six times more attempts, and remove scorer exploits, the evolutionary advantage largely vanishes. Evolution beats independent sampling by 5% or less on 12 of 15 task-method pairs, retaining a 23 to 28% margin on only 3, all on one task. A replication with Claude Haiku 4.5 reproduces this split, though a third backbone shows its size depends on the model too. The performance margin justifying these systems is often an accounting artifact. Reporting tokens, not proposals and not model calls, fixes this and costs nothing, as the logs already hold them.
papers.summary: LLM-driven evolutionary search methods are usually compared by the number of candidate programs they propose, but proposals vary in cost from 16k to 39k tokens. Replaying 600 logged runs across 5 tasks and 3 methods, the authors show that equal-proposal comparisons give some methods up to 1.9× more compute than others and give evolution about 6× the budget of independent sampling. **Once token budgets are matched and scorer exploits are removed, evolution beats independent sampling by 5% or less on 12 of 15 task-method pairs**, keeping a large margin only on one task. A replication with `Claude Haiku 4.5` shows the same split, and the authors recommend reporting token counts, which the logs already contain.

papers.title: SPELUNKA: A Framework for Finding Unanticipated Associations in Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are the backbone of many state-of-the-art multimodal systems, but often encode spurious and harmful associations from their training data. While prior work focuses on removing known biases from VLMs, methods for discovering unanticipated associations for retrieval tasks remain underexplored. We introduce SPELUNKA, an automated, inference-time framework for finding unanticipated distributional biases for retrieval tasks in VLMs without pre-specified labeled subgroups, inference-time human supervision, or model fine-tuning. Given a concept of interest, SPELUNKA generates captions for related images, extracts relevant entities from captions, and selects semantically meaningful associations. A frequency-based detection rule then identifies spurious associations by measuring over- or under-representation of these attributes in a VLM's top-ranked outputs relative to their full dataset distribution. We evaluate SPELUNKA across four datasets, and find that it 1) successfully recovers both synthetic and naturally occurring spurious correlations, 2) achieves an average AUROC of 0.93 across four datasets in identifying images strongly associated with a query, and 3) outperforms baselines in finding features that are strongly associated with a given query.
papers.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) absorb spurious and harmful associations from their training data, and existing methods mostly remove biases that are already known. `SPELUNKA` discovers unanticipated biases in retrieval at inference time, without labeled subgroups, human supervision, or fine-tuning. For a given concept, it captions related images, extracts entities from the captions, and flags attributes that are over- or under-represented in the model's top-ranked results relative to the whole dataset. Across four datasets it recovers both planted and naturally occurring spurious correlations and **reaches an average AUROC of 0.93** at identifying images strongly associated with a query.

papers.title: Weakly Supervised Discovery of Motion Styles for Compositional Robot Control
papers.abstract:
When a robot possesses more degrees of freedom than a task requires, multiple trajectories can achieve the same objective using distinct motion styles. Compositional robot control aims to preserve a selected style while simultaneously executing an independent task command, effectively balancing these potentially competing objectives. In this paper, we present CODES, a framework for compositional robot control that discovers a coherent style repertoire from diverse recordings and composes it with independent commands. First, motion retargeting maps the recordings to motions executable by the target robot; next, weakly supervised consensus encoding and density-based clustering identify styles within and across recordings without a prescribed count; finally, reinforcement learning trains a policy to compose the discovered styles with independent commands. We evaluate CODES on a Unitree Go2 quadruped across two simulators and physical hardware. Compared to baselines, CODES significantly improves kinematic coherence. Furthermore, our controller successfully tracks velocity commands that generalize beyond the support of the recorded data, exhibiting robust and distinguishable style characteristics during both cross-simulator and real-world hardware deployments.
  Project website: https://www.proroklab.org/compositional-motion-styles/
papers.summary: A robot with more degrees of freedom than a task needs can complete it in several distinct motion styles, and compositional control aims to keep a chosen style while following an independent command. `CODES` retargets diverse motion recordings to the target robot, finds a repertoire of styles with weakly supervised consensus encoding and density-based clustering (without fixing the number of styles in advance), and then uses reinforcement learning to train a policy that combines those styles with commands. On a `Unitree Go2` quadruped in two simulators and on real hardware, it **substantially improves kinematic coherence over baselines** and tracks velocity commands beyond the range of the recorded data while keeping styles distinguishable.

papers.title: SPADE-KD: Peer-to-Peer Collaborative Learning under Heterogeneous Settings
papers.abstract: Peer-to-peer collaborative learning is an emerging distributed deep learning paradigm that eliminates the need for a central aggregator and disseminator, avoiding the single-point-of-failure and bottleneck issues they can bring. Many such approaches use parameter averaging, requiring clients to have homogeneous model architectures, whereas others use knowledge distillation as an alternative while leaning on shared public data or centralized control infrastructure. Many of these approaches also make a one-size-fits-all assumption, i.e., jointly training a single, globally optimal solution for all clients, when in reality, clients' underlying data distributions might differ such that a globally optimal solution may not be locally optimal for all clients. To enable collaborative learning in environments with both model architecture and data distribution heterogeneity, we present SPADE-KD -- a fully decentralized model distillation framework that optimizes collaboration towards personalized rather than global performance. SPADE-KD leverages two mechanisms -- adaptive distillation and utility-driven peer selection. Adaptive distillation modulates the strength of each incoming model transfer by the performance advantage of the incoming model compared to the native model measured by their task losses, such that a client will distill more aggressively from incoming models that outperform it on its own local data. Utility-driven peer selection uses the loss-informed utility derived from adaptive distillation to rank prospective partners, focusing on exchanges that measurably improve the local model while suppressing low-utility transfers. Using federated classification tasks, we demonstrate that SPADE-KD consistent outperforms naive decentralized distillation with lower loss and faster convergence and that its individual components are more effective together than independently.
papers.summary: Peer-to-peer collaborative learning removes the central server of federated learning, but existing methods either require every client to use the same model architecture or depend on shared public data or central coordination, and most train one global model even when clients' data differ. `SPADE-KD` is a fully decentralized knowledge-distillation framework that optimizes each client's own performance. Each client distills more strongly from peer models that achieve lower loss on its local data, and uses that same loss-based utility to choose which peers to exchange with. On federated classification tasks it **achieves lower loss and faster convergence than naive decentralized distillation**, and its two mechanisms work better together than separately.

papers.title: TWIN-MoE: Two-stage Intra-Expert Imputation Network for Incomplete Multimodal Learning
papers.abstract: Recent Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) approaches address missing modalities either by routing each missingness pattern to a dedicated expert, which scales poorly as the number of modalities grows, or by imputing the missing modality from representations contributed by multiple experts, which requires a costly retrieval mechanism. We show that routing induces expert-conditioned representation neighborhoods and derive an imputation-error bound controlled by their local feature dispersion. When these expert-conditioned neighborhoods are more compact than the global representation space, intra-expert aggregation admits a tighter worst-case reconstruction bound than unconstrained global aggregation. Guided by this analysis, we propose TWIN, a two-stage intra-expert imputation framework. Pre-imputation generates a context-conditioned estimate in the encoder embedding space and radially soft-clips it using modality-specific statistics maintained in an observed FIFO queue, this ensures that the pre-imputed modality stays in empirically calibrated region of the target modality space. Post-imputation refines the missing representation after MoE by aggregating expert-conditioned observed representations within the same sample. Across four missing-modality benchmarks under natural, random, and asymmetric dropout protocols, TWIN achieves state-of-the-art performance while using substantially fewer parameters than competing MoE-based imputation methods.
papers.summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) methods for handling missing modalities either dedicate an expert to each missingness pattern, which scales poorly, or impute missing data from many experts via costly retrieval. The authors show that routing creates compact neighborhoods of representations for each expert, which gives a tighter worst-case error bound for imputing within one expert than across the whole representation space. `TWIN` first produces a context-conditioned estimate of the missing modality, clipped to a calibrated range using statistics from a queue of observed examples, and then refines it after the MoE layer using observed representations from the same sample. Across four benchmarks and several dropout protocols, it **achieves state-of-the-art results with substantially fewer parameters** than competing MoE imputation methods.

papers.title: Unified Multiparadigm Fusion Intelligence for Rare Disease Diagnosis
papers.abstract: Rare diseases (RDs) affect an estimated 300 million people globally, leaving patients to navigate a protracted diagnostic odyssey constrained by clinical scarcity and fragmented medical knowledge. Artificial intelligence (AI) has progressively advanced RD diagnostics, from symbolic methods and deep learning to large language model (LLM)-based systems. However, each paradigm carries structural limitations: symbolic methods are bounded by knowledge completeness, neural models sacrifice interpretability, and LLM-based systems are vulnerable to evaluation biases like data leakage. In this study, we introduce FusionRare, a unified multiparadigm fusion framework integrating knowledge-driven symbolic reasoning, deep-learning pattern recognition, case-based patient retrieval, and LLM-based heuristic inference via statistical meta-aggregation and knowledge-enhanced agentic reflection. Evaluated on 2,528 strictly isolated clinical cases, FusionRare achieves state-of-the-art RD prioritization, attaining a macro-averaged Recall @1 of 51% for phenotype-only diagnosis and 79% for phenotype-genotype joint analysis. These results represent decisive advantages over the advanced agentic system DeepRare, frontier LLMs including GPT 5.5, and specialized tools like PhenoBrain and LIRICAL under stringent anti-leakage protocols. A randomized, crossover clinician-AI validation demonstrated that FusionRare elevates the true diagnostic rank in 45% of decisions, improves physician confidence in 62%, and reduces time to diagnosis by 21%. These findings indicate that reconciling these orthogonal AI paradigms significantly enhances diagnostic capabilities, bridging the gap between computational benchmarks and actionable clinical reliability. More broadly, this work provides a replicable framework for deploying trustworthy diagnostic AI across complex, high-stakes, and underserved medical domains.
papers.summary: Rare-disease diagnosis has been attempted with symbolic methods, deep learning, and large language model (LLM) systems, each with structural weaknesses. `FusionRare` combines symbolic knowledge reasoning, deep-learning pattern recognition, retrieval of similar patient cases, and LLM-based inference through statistical meta-aggregation and an agentic reflection step that draws on medical knowledge. On 2,528 clinical cases screened to prevent data leakage, it reaches **macro-averaged Recall@1 of 51% from phenotypes alone and 79% with phenotype plus genotype**, outperforming `DeepRare`, `GPT 5.5`, `PhenoBrain`, and `LIRICAL`. In a randomized crossover study with clinicians, it moved the true diagnosis higher in their ranking in 45% of decisions and cut time to diagnosis by 21%.

papers.title: Dynamical Kernel Attention: Estimating the Present from a Record of the Past
papers.abstract: Standard self-attention compares tokens by similarity but does not account for how much of a past state survives to the present. We introduce Dynamical Kernel Attention (DKA), which derives attention from robust estimation of a latent state evolving under stochastic dynamics. As a past state decays toward equilibrium under the dynamics, the information it carries about the present vanishes, bounding the total evidence a head can draw. Unlike recency biases, DKA can abstain when relevant evidence is weak and guarantees a bounded error when old tokens are discarded. DKA preserves the parallel structure and computational cost of standard attention. We present the model and its theory; empirical evaluation is deferred to a subsequent version.
papers.summary: Standard self-attention compares tokens by similarity but does not model how much information from a past state still applies to the present. Dynamical Kernel Attention (`DKA`) derives attention weights from robust estimation of a latent state evolving under stochastic dynamics: as a past state decays toward equilibrium, the evidence it provides shrinks, which caps the total evidence a head can draw. Unlike a simple recency bias, `DKA` can abstain when evidence is weak and **guarantees bounded error when old tokens are discarded**, while keeping the parallel structure and cost of standard attention. The paper presents only the model and its theory, and empirical evaluation is left for a later version.

papers.title: Do Knowledge and Reasoning Oriented Benchmarks Induce Stable Representation Signatures in LLMs?
papers.abstract: Internal signatures could support monitoring, adaptive computation, and mechanistic analysis, but benchmark prompts can be separable without any shared computational distinction. We test whether a prespecified knowledge/reasoning label defines a reusable internal signature in five contemporary 7B to 31B models. We treat the \textbf{task} as the unit of inference probes hold out complete tasks, labels are permuted across tasks, and the best layer and stream are reselected for every permutation. Raw probes recover an eight-versus-eight-subject MMLU partition in all five models (macro-F1 $0.78$--$0.81$), but prompt text predicts it nearly as well: under an identical probe configuration, the activation advantage is only $0.017$--$0.070$ macro-F1 and is not significant. At the prespecified $0.01$ level, lexical adjustment removes significance while the adjusted states still identify individual subjects, and the selected site changes across task panels and selection rules. Additionally, two released base-training trajectories show no common direction. These pooled layerwise measures recover the task label but identify no transferable knowledge/reasoning signature at the tested sensitivity, which cannot exclude moderate effects. The resulting protocol gives future internal monitors and intervention studies a sequence of tests to pass. Project page: \url{https://parsa-ra.github.io/lmbehave/}.
papers.summary: The authors test whether a predefined label of benchmark tasks as knowledge-oriented or reasoning-oriented corresponds to a reusable internal signature in five 7B–31B models. Their protocol treats whole tasks as the unit of analysis, holding out entire tasks and permuting labels across them. Probes recover an `MMLU` subject split with macro-F1 of 0.78–0.81, but the prompt text alone predicts it nearly as well: **activations add only 0.017–0.070 macro-F1, which is not significant**, and the best-performing layer shifts between task panels. They conclude that there is no transferable knowledge/reasoning signature at the sensitivity tested, and they offer the protocol as a sequence of checks for future internal monitors and intervention studies.

papers.title: When Does Evidence-Graph Structure Predict Answer Correctness? Label-Free Abstention for Structured Retrieval
papers.abstract: Retrieval systems return scored answers, but a high score does not show that an answer should be trusted. The proposed training-free abstention method applies the boundary cut to the selected evidence in an evidence graph. The signal is the weighted cut between selected and unselected candidates and requires no correctness labels or confidence-model training. On MemoryAgentBench (MAB) FactConsolidation multi-hop, with unresolved queries ranked last for every selector, it raises area under the precision-coverage curve from 0.736 for the best score baseline to 0.785 (+0.049, 95% CI [+0.008, +0.092]); under the native evaluation, where score baselines keep their unresolved values, the gap is +0.108. A zero-cut subset contains 71 of 400 queries at 100% observed precision. In this pipeline, the subset corresponds to structural closure; controlled analyses attribute much of the remaining separation to resolution status, with little benefit from continuous edge weights. Across external benchmarks, usefulness varies with graph construction, edge semantics, and relation; typed structure alone does not ensure useful confidence. A supervised gradient-boosted selector achieves 0.814 versus the boundary cut's 0.785 when the retrieval stack matches. These findings provide empirical guidance for using available evidence graphs for lightweight, auditable post-retrieval abstention without additional model inference.
papers.summary: Retrieval systems return scored answers, but a high score does not mean an answer can be trusted. The authors propose a training-free abstention signal: in an evidence graph, they compute the weighted cut between the selected evidence and the unselected candidates. This needs no correctness labels and no trained confidence model. On the `MemoryAgentBench` (`MAB`) FactConsolidation multi-hop task, it raises the area under the precision-coverage curve from 0.736 for the best score baseline to **0.785**, and a zero-cut subset of 71 of 400 queries reaches 100% observed precision. Across external benchmarks, the usefulness of the signal depends on how the graph is built, and a supervised gradient-boosted selector still does better at 0.814.

papers.title: Visual Causal-chain Bookmarking: Retrieval-Weighted Credit Assignment for Reinforcement Learning from Delayed Reward
papers.abstract: RL agents trained on a single trajectory-level return face a credit-assignment problem: when a reward arrives many steps after the decision that caused it, every action gets the same signal regardless of causal responsibility. This paper studies Visual Causal-chain Bookmarking (VCBM), which concentrates credit on the decision points that determine an episode's return, via two instantiations. The first targets a fully observed, low-dimensional MDP (a delayed-reward watch-repair task), where VCBM statistically discovers which state components the agent causally controls and estimates per-decision-point action values directly, evaluated against ground truth and RUDDER, an LSTM-based baseline. VCBM converges to 95.07% correct decisions in a mean of 1,532.3 episodes across 20 seeds, versus RUDDER's slower, more variable convergence (mean 3,327.1 episodes; p<0.001); VCBM's discovered causal structure exactly matches ground truth in all seeds. The second targets a partially observed, language-based setting: an LLM agent trained with Leave-One-Out PPO (LOOP) in AppWorld, where causal discovery is intractable and a structural heuristic (state-mutating tool calls) substitutes for it, with credit distributed via retrieval over episodic memory and blended with LOOP's advantage. Over 200 iterations on identical Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct/LoRA/FSDP2 configurations, VCBM-blended LOOP improves task success over plain LOOP (0.354 vs. 0.458), reduces final-step max importance weight, and improves token efficiency, with a small KL exception favouring LOOP. The watch-repair result supports the claim that weighting causally relevant steps is more sample-efficient than an undifferentiated baseline or a learned return-redistribution network; the AppWorld result, limited to one seed per arm by a 2-GPU budget, is a compute-limited demonstration at a harder, natural-language scale, not a statistical confirmation.
papers.summary: When a reward arrives many steps after the decision that caused it, a reinforcement learning (RL) agent trained on trajectory-level returns gives every action the same credit. `Visual Causal-chain Bookmarking` (`VCBM`) instead concentrates credit on the decision points that determine the return. In a delayed-reward watch-repair task, it discovers the true causal structure in all 20 seeds and converges in a mean of **1,532 episodes versus 3,327 for the LSTM-based `RUDDER` baseline**. In `AppWorld`, `VCBM` uses a heuristic based on state-mutating tool calls and retrieval over episodic memory, blended with Leave-One-Out PPO (`LOOP`), to train a `Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct` agent; task success rises from 0.354 to 0.458, though from only one seed per arm.

papers.title: LLM Evolution in a Simple Simulated Market
papers.abstract: Arguments that AI systems will evolve in harmful ways are largely made in the abstract. We provide a concrete empirical example. We simulate simple markets consisting of populations of twenty Large Language Model agents tasked with solving arithmetic problems. Agents differ only in their system prompt; those that go bankrupt are removed and replaced by mutated copies of the prompts of successful agents. Two market conditions select for opposite phenotypes: a market that rewards accuracy produces agents with high accuracy (94%) and high token use; a market that charges per token produces agents with low accuracy (10%) and low token use. In the second market, only tokens are incentivised yet we see a collapse in accuracy. Token use and accuracy are correlated traits such that selection on one also moves the other, and behaviour adapts along an unpriced dimension. A third neutral condition with no selection allows us to separate these effects from bias in the mutation operator. Adaptation occurs through a collective optimisation process that operates above the level of individual agents, who are never told the payment rule, do not receive feedback, and have no memory.
papers.summary: To give a concrete example of harmful AI evolution, the authors simulate markets of twenty large language model (LLM) agents that solve arithmetic problems and differ only in their system prompts. Bankrupt agents are replaced by mutated copies of successful agents' prompts. A market that rewards accuracy produces agents with 94% accuracy and heavy token use, while a market that charges per token **collapses accuracy to 10%**, even though accuracy itself is never priced. A neutral control condition separates these effects from bias in the mutation operator, and the authors show that adaptation happens at the population level, even though individual agents get no feedback and have no memory.

papers.title: Client-Aware Security Adaptive Early Exit Vision Transformers for Heterogeneous Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Federated learning (FL) trains a shared model across data-owning clients without centralizing raw data, but client data difficulty and compute budgets can differ. We study local early-exit Vision Transformer (ViT) inference, where an intermediate classifier may return a prediction before the final Transformer stage. The proposed method replaces one global acceptance threshold with a client-specific base threshold from label entropy and shallow-exit confidence, then adjusts each input using predictive entropy, confidence, top-two class margin, and exit depth. Aggregation uses only clients that updated a parameter. Security-aware routing reaches 88.70% CIFAR-10 accuracy with 32.0% depth saving and 73.7% ImageNet-1K top-1 accuracy with 30\% saving. On matched six-client non-IID CIFAR-100, full-depth accuracy is 72.28% versus 68.20--71.80% for four heterogeneous-FL baselines; robustness-aware routing reaches 70.01% with 32.55% saving.
papers.summary: In federated learning (FL), clients differ in how hard their data is and how much compute they have. This work studies early-exit Vision Transformer (ViT) inference in that setting. Instead of one global exit threshold, each client gets a base threshold derived from label entropy and shallow-exit confidence, which is then adjusted per input using entropy, confidence, top-two margin, and exit depth. Security-aware routing reaches **88.70% `CIFAR-10` accuracy with 32% depth saving** and 73.7% `ImageNet-1K` top-1 accuracy with 30% saving, and the method outperforms four heterogeneous-FL baselines on non-IID `CIFAR-100`.

papers.title: What Remains Without Test Labels? Re-evaluating a Graph-Level Anomaly Detection Benchmark
papers.abstract: Graph-level anomaly detectors are trained only on normal graphs, yet benchmarks may use test labels for model selection. We examine whether UB-GOLD results reused by later papers support label-free detection. We audit UB-GOLD and 14 GLAD code bases, re-run 21 detectors on UB-GOLD's folds under selection rules with and without test labels, and evaluate sensitivity to known structural changes. Test labels select checkpoints in UB-GOLD's shared training loop and checkpoints or hyperparameters in 8 of the 14 code bases. UB-GOLD also evaluates its kernel baselines against misaligned labels. Across nine datasets, selecting checkpoints by test AUROC adds an average of 5.12 AUROC points [3.97, 6.24] for the 12 UB-GOLD detectors relative to the final checkpoint and 4.13 [3.32, 4.79] relative to held-out normal graphs. In a post hoc permutation analysis with no truly better checkpoint, picking the best of noisy test evaluations still yields a gain more than half as large as the one observed against the final checkpoint. Configurations tuned on test labels score a further 1.53 points [0.64, 2.42] above repository defaults, a gap that mixes the value of test labels with that of tuning itself. With tuned hyperparameters and label-free checkpoint selection, the two strongest detectors retain their lead, while comparisons below them are less stable. Six of eight detectors evaluated out of sample miss size-preserving composition changes that graphlet counts detect. We recommend reporting results selected without test labels as the main comparisons and release per-run outputs that allow verification without retraining.
papers.summary: Graph-level anomaly detection (GLAD) detectors are meant to train only on normal graphs, but benchmarks may use test labels for model selection. The authors audit the `UB-GOLD` benchmark and 14 GLAD code bases, then re-run 21 detectors under selection rules with and without test labels. Test labels select checkpoints or hyperparameters in 8 of the 14 code bases, and selecting checkpoints by test AUROC inflates scores by **an average of 5.12 AUROC points** relative to the final checkpoint. Under label-free selection, the two strongest detectors keep their lead but the rankings below them become less stable, and the authors recommend reporting label-free results as the main comparison.

papers.title: The Window Is in the Reasoning: When LLM Agents Decide to Follow Prompt Injections
papers.abstract: LLM agents that read untrusted content can be hijacked by prompt injections. Runtime monitors that try to catch a hijack before the agent acts, and benchmarks that score each task with a single run, share an assumption: whether an agent follows an injection is settled when the injection is read. We test this assumption with branching rollouts that replay an episode exactly up to the step at which the agent reads an injection and then resample the rest of the episode many times, splitting the outcome variance into a part fixed at read time and a part decided afterwards. Across four AgentDojo suites, a Qwen3 agent without thinking is largely decided at read time (0.91 of the outcome variance lies between states); with thinking on, this share drops to 0.62 (95% CI of the drop [-0.38, -0.22]), in the same direction for three attack templates and two success labels. How much is fixed at read time is a property of the model that the same measurement reveals, and thinking lowers the attack success rate of Qwen3 but raises it for two other models. Resampling from reasoning prefixes shows that the decision forms gradually as the agent reasons. Zero-shot chain-of-thought monitors built on cheaper models miss much of what is already decided, whereas stronger monitors, and a lookahead monitor that judges simulated next actions, come close to what the prefix determines. Finally, single-run labels of thinking agents disagree with a rerun up to 35% of the time, so benchmarks need repeated runs per task.
papers.summary: Runtime monitors and single-run benchmarks for prompt injection assume that whether an agent follows an injection is decided at the moment it reads it. Using branching rollouts that replay an episode up to that moment and then resample the rest many times, the authors measure how much of the outcome is fixed at read time across four `AgentDojo` suites. For a `Qwen3` agent without thinking, 0.91 of the outcome variance is fixed at read time, but with thinking enabled this drops to 0.62, because the decision forms gradually during reasoning. Cheap chain-of-thought monitors miss much of what is already decided, and **single-run labels for thinking agents disagree with a rerun up to 35% of the time**, so benchmarks need repeated runs per task.

papers.title: Discuss More, Comment Less: Boosting Automated Research via Multi-Perspective Collaborative Review
papers.abstract: As automated research is increasingly adopted for writing papers, automated review has become a critical link between paper generation and quality control. However, existing methods largely rely on single-model feedback or simple review aggregation, failing to explicitly model expert responsibilities or collective deliberation in actual peer reviews, which limits effective cross-examination and reliable decision-making. Therefore, we formulate paper review as a computational modeling problem of peer review mechanisms and propose RoundtableReview, a deliberative multi-agent framework for enhancing automated research. RoundtableReview structures each paper into eight semantic slots and coordinates six academic and industry reviewers with complementary perspectives, retrieval sources, and specialized responsibilities. Through independent assessment, cross-examination, roundtable deliberation, dynamically weighted voting, and chair synthesis, the framework generates evidence-based and traceable feedback. Experiments on two automated research backbones show that the method improves paper quality in both backbones and outperforms baselines in automatic and human evaluations with fewer comments.
papers.summary: Automated review is the quality-control step for automated paper writing, but existing approaches rely on single-model feedback or simple aggregation of reviews. `RoundtableReview` is a deliberative multi-agent framework that splits each paper into eight semantic slots. It assigns six academic and industry reviewer agents distinct perspectives, retrieval sources, and responsibilities, and runs them through independent assessment, cross-examination, roundtable deliberation, weighted voting, and chair synthesis. On two automated research backbones, the method **improves final paper quality while producing fewer comments**, and it outperforms baselines in both automatic and human evaluations.

papers.title: LogicVal:A Logic-Formalized Benchmark for Constraint Satisfaction in Text-to-Image Generation
papers.abstract: Text-to-Image (T2I) generative models have made significant progress in producing high-fidelity images from natural-language prompts. Alongside this progress, numerous benchmarks have been developed to evaluate capabilities such as attribute binding, numeracy, spatial reasoning, and commonsense reasoning. In this work, we propose a new perspective on T2I evaluation by casting it as a constraint-satisfaction problem. We introduce a logical framework that formally specifies the benchmark domain, including objects, attributes, and relations, alongside the constraints that generated images must satisfy. We evaluated four state-of-the-art T2I models across 9 classes of constraints ranging from a single-object-attribute to multi-object relationships constraints involving logical operators ($\forall, \exists, count, \rightarrow$). Our results reveal a substantial gap between single-object and complex conditional multi-object relationship constraint classes, with the best-performing model achieving 98% accuracy on the former and just 53% on the latter. We assess compositional generalisation, finding that the best-performing model`s accuracy drops from 84% on single-constraint prompts to 20% when satisfying multiple constraints simultaneously. Identifying unsatisfiable constraints is also challenging, with the best model correctly recognizing only 23% of such prompts. Building on this framework, we introduce \textbf{LogicVal}, an evaluation methodology that combines neural visual detection with logical reasoning to assess constraint satisfaction in generated images. On CLEVR, LogicVal achieves ROC-AUC scores ranging from 0.88 to 0.98, indicating strong alignment with human judgments. These findings underscore the value of logic-based evaluation for characterizing T2I model capabilities and limitations.
papers.summary: The authors cast text-to-image (T2I) evaluation as a constraint-satisfaction problem, using a logical framework that formally specifies objects, attributes, relations, and constraints with operators such as for-all, exists, count, and implication. Across four state-of-the-art T2I models and nine constraint classes, the best model reaches 98% accuracy on single-object constraints but only 53% on conditional multi-object ones. Its accuracy falls **from 84% on single-constraint prompts to 20% when several constraints must hold at once**, and it recognizes only 23% of unsatisfiable prompts. The accompanying `LogicVal` evaluator combines neural detection with logical reasoning and reaches ROC-AUC between 0.88 and 0.98 against human judgments on `CLEVR`.
