The main result bounds the flux error of the network and the energy error of its feasible projection $\max\{v,g\}$ by the constitutive residual, the initial mismatch, the complementarity defect, and the PDE residual weighted by $c_F^2/\alpha$, without the coercivity and norm-equivalence constants of the first-order formulation. It extends the Apushkinskaya--Repin majorant for the heat operator to general coefficients, free multipliers and a flux bound. A penetration-consistency result shows that neural triples with arbitrarily small bound exist. Outward-rounded cellwise Taylor-model enclosures turn the bound into a finite computation valid on any adaptive partition. The flux and gradient errors of the projected output are certified below $0.27$ and $0.33$ of the solution scale for a one-dimensional Stefan problem and, after adaptive refinement, below one half for all three trained networks on a two-dimensional expanding disk. On an expanding ellipse the gradient bound stays above one half; substitution diagnostics trace the floor of the trained networks to the projected state near the free boundary, and the remaining gap to enclosure overhead. Without a closed-form solution, a validated lower bound replaces the solution norm; there the enclosure is nearly exact, but the trained networks have errors above the solution scale and no useful accuracy is certified. The bounds control a state--flux norm, not the multiplier or the free-boundary location.
papers.summary: Neural surrogates trained on residuals come with no error guarantee, which is a problem for free-boundary problems such as phase change and contact. The authors derive guaranteed error bounds for neural approximations of parabolic obstacle problems, extending the Apushkinskaya–Repin majorant, and turn them into a finite computation using outward-rounded cellwise Taylor-model enclosures on adaptive partitions. **Flux and gradient errors are certified below 0.27 and 0.33 of the solution scale** for a one-dimensional Stefan problem, and below one half on a two-dimensional expanding disk. The bounds remain loose on an expanding ellipse and certify no useful accuracy when no closed-form solution is available.

papers.title: Hidden Trajectories Don't Lie: Correcting Corruption Drift for Test-Time Adaptation
papers.abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) adapts pretrained models to distribution shifts encountered during deployment. However, most existing methods rely on the weight representations of the final layer or signals derived from the model's output probability distribution. We study hidden trajectories: the ordered sequence of intermediate representations produced across a deep neural network. We observe that clean and corrupted trajectories become more separable as corruption severity increases. We introduce Drift-TTA, which adds zero-initialized low-rank adapters to a frozen backbone and trains them to align corrupted hidden trajectories with those from cleaner inputs. The approach supports two variants: a source-dependent version trained with clean targets, and a source-free setting that learns from corrupted images at different severities. We develop an online TTA approach that freezes the backbone and adapters while updating a scalar gate to control adaptation strength. We further cast trajectory alignment as MAP inference under a Gaussian observation model and derive a KL-based transfer bound characterizing test-time trajectory misalignment in terms of offline residual error, residual dimensionality, and distribution shift between offline and test corruptions. We evaluate Drift-TTA on CIFAR-10-C, CIFAR-100-C, and ImageNet-C using supervised ViTs and CLIP models. On CIFAR-100-C at severity 5, our source-free online approach improves accuracy over no TTA by 13.3 percentage points with ViT-B/16 and 11.6 percentage points with CLIP ViT-B/16, reaching 74.9% and 47.4%, respectively. Under the same setting, prior TTA baselines yield ECEs of 18.00% for ViT and 14.70% for CLIP, while our approach reduces them to 9.53% and 5.77%, respectively. These results demonstrate that hidden trajectory alignment provides an effective signal for both offline correction and lightweight online test-time adaptation.
papers.summary: Test-time adaptation (TTA) adjusts pretrained models to distribution shifts during deployment, but most methods rely only on final-layer weights or output probabilities. `Drift-TTA` instead uses hidden trajectories, the sequence of intermediate representations across the network. It trains zero-initialized low-rank adapters on a frozen backbone to align corrupted trajectories with cleaner ones, then adapts online by updating only a scalar gate, and it comes with a KL-based transfer bound. On `CIFAR-100-C` at severity 5, the source-free online variant **improves accuracy by 13.3 percentage points with `ViT-B/16`** and 11.6 points with `CLIP ViT-B/16`, and it roughly halves calibration error compared with prior TTA baselines.

papers.title: Language Models are Lazy Poets: Creative Mode Collapse at Scale
papers.abstract: While aligned large language models (LLMs) can successfully complete many creative tasks, their outputs tend to be highly self-similar. Though solutions to this problem of "mode collapse" have been proposed, comprehensive large-scale surveys of the phenomenon in specific textual genres are still lacking. We address this gap through an extensive treatment of LLM mode collapse in poetry. Across 15 poetic forms, 248 subject matter tags, and 16 open-weight models, we generate over 1.1 million poems. To our knowledge, this constitutes the largest corpus of LLM-generated poetry to date. At million-poem scale, we find that LLM poetic vocabularies and rhyming abilities are substantial, but severely underutilized. In other words, LLMs are "lazy" poets: despite possessing large poetic inventories, LLMs over-rely on a small number of words, opening phrases, and rhymes. Further, we find that lexical homogenization differs across models and poetic forms, noting observed rhyming vocabulary is correlated with model size.
papers.summary: Aligned large language models (LLMs) produce highly self-similar creative output, a problem known as mode collapse, but large-scale studies of it in specific genres have been missing. The authors generate **over 1.1 million poems** across 15 poetic forms, 248 subject tags, and 16 open-weight models, which they describe as the largest corpus of LLM poetry to date. They find that the models have large poetic vocabularies and rhyming ability but rely heavily on a small set of words, opening phrases, and rhymes. The degree of homogenization varies by model and form, and the range of rhyming vocabulary is correlated with model size.

papers.title: Training-Free Prompt Selection for Efficient Reinforcement Learning With Partial Rollouts
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has emerged as a prominent paradigm for training reasoning models, but its computational cost makes efficient data selection increasingly important. Since training examples contribute unequally to learning, selecting a small, informative subset can offer a more efficient alternative to using the entire data pool. The training-free selection method estimates prompt value with hidden states from complete greedy rollouts. However, in our datasets, $26$--$32\%$ of these rollouts fail to terminate within the generation budget. We introduce LIFT, a training-free data selector that identifies impactful prompts using only partial reasoning rollouts. At its core, LIFT uses Partial Rollout Context Lift (PRCL), a score inspired by pointwise $\mathcal{V}$-information that accumulates token-level log-likelihood ratios between a question-conditioned context and a null context with the question removed. This enables prompt scoring from a short rollout prefix rather than a complete trajectory. Across Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-1.5B, prefixes retaining at least 90\% and 95\% of the full-rollout PRCL score, respectively, require only 26\% and 4.7\% of the tokens generated by full rollouts. Compared with SHIFT, LIFT reduces selection cost by 3.7--9.1$\times$ while achieving competitive downstream RLVR performance, with the highest six-benchmark average in three of six settings.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is expensive, so choosing a small, informative subset of training prompts can save compute. The existing training-free selector scores prompts from complete greedy rollouts, but 26–32% of those rollouts fail to finish within the generation budget. `LIFT` instead scores prompts from partial rollouts using `Partial Rollout Context Lift (PRCL)`, which accumulates token-level log-likelihood ratios between the generation conditioned on the question and the same generation with the question removed. On `Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B` and `DeepSeek-R1-Distill-1.5B`, short prefixes recover most of the full-rollout score, and LIFT **cuts selection cost by 3.7–9.1× compared with `SHIFT`** while matching its downstream RLVR performance.

papers.title: Analyzing Repetition and Interference Effects in Memory-Constrained User Simulators
papers.abstract: User simulators can help evaluate and train AI systems to interact with humans at scale. To do so, evaluation of user simulators must measure behavioral parity with people. We evaluate whether memory-constrained user simulators are sensitive to two factors known to affect human information retention: repetition of a fact and interference from competing information. We find that some simulators achieve human-like overall accuracy, and replicate the magnitude of repetition and interference effects, but none match people's accuracy on particular questions: while humans misremember facts, models forget them, leading to different error patterns. We release this data as a challenge benchmark for future work on user simulators.
papers.summary: User simulators can help evaluate and train AI systems at scale, but only if they behave like real people. The study tests whether memory-constrained simulators respond, as humans do, to repetition of a fact and to interference from competing information. Some simulators reach human-like overall accuracy and reproduce the size of both effects, but **none match people on individual questions**, because humans misremember facts while models simply forget them. The data is released as a challenge benchmark for future user simulators.

papers.title: Censored Flow Matching for Synthetic Time-to-Event Generation
papers.abstract: Generating time-to-event data is increasingly important in survival analysis, but it remains statistically challenging because event times are often censored and thus prevent flexible generative modeling. To fill this gap, we propose a novel method called censored flow matching (CFM), aiming at providing a flexible flow-based generative mechanism for synthesizing time-to-event data as well as learning their corresponding probabilistic densities. Unlike existing methods, CFM does not rely on survival likelihoods to handle censoring, but instead exploits the monotonicity property of differential flows to address censoring via pullback sampling. Under this framework, we implement an alternating procedure between pullback sampling and CFM steps, leading to a flow-based expectation--maximization (EM) algorithm tailored for time-to-event inference. Under mild distributional conditions, we establish the convergence of CFM to the true event-time distribution as the EM iterations proceed. We then apply CFM to generate time-to-event data and estimate their probabilistic densities, where the observed censoring time can be incorporated to provide truncated sampling or truncated density estimation for survival inference. Through extensive simulation studies, we demonstrate the benefits of CFM for complex and large-scale data generation. Finally, we apply CFM to analyze data from the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network (OPTN) and the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV), showcasing its benefits for synthetic and predictive survival analyses in terms of data fidelity, predictive performance, and empirical privacy characteristics.
papers.summary: Generating synthetic time-to-event data for survival analysis is difficult because event times are often censored. `Censored flow matching (CFM)` avoids survival likelihoods and instead uses the monotonicity of differential flows to handle censoring through pullback sampling, alternating these steps in a flow-based expectation–maximization (EM) algorithm. The authors **prove convergence to the true event-time distribution** under mild conditions, and simulations show benefits for complex, large-scale data. Applications to transplant data from `OPTN` and intensive-care data from `MIMIC-IV` show good data fidelity, predictive performance, and empirical privacy.

papers.title: Preserving Reasoning Diversity in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards via Adaptive Replay
papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but often reduces the diversity of their reasoning behaviors. We study this phenomenon from the perspective of finite-sample learning dynamics and show that limited on-policy rollouts can progressively suppress semantically distinct but equally rewarded reasoning modes. Once a mode becomes sufficiently under-sampled, standard on-policy RLVR rarely recovers it. Motivated by this observation, we propose TAR, a Targeted Adaptive Replay framework that preserves diverse correct reasoning behaviors already present in the base policy. TAR constructs a compact memory bank of diverse base-model solutions and selectively replays them through an adaptive mechanism that activates only when stored behaviors are being suppressed during RLVR. Across six mathematical reasoning benchmarks and two Qwen2.5 model scales, TAR consistently achieves a better balance between reasoning performance and diversity preservation than existing diversity-preserving post-training methods, while substantially reducing the forgetting of correct base-model solutions. Code is available at https://github.com/wenzhilics/tar.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) improves LLM reasoning but tends to narrow the range of reasoning strategies the model uses. The authors show that with a limited number of on-policy rollouts, distinct but equally correct reasoning modes are gradually suppressed and rarely recover once they become under-sampled. `TAR` (Targeted Adaptive Replay) keeps a compact memory bank of diverse correct solutions from the base model and replays them only when those behaviors are being suppressed. Across six math benchmarks and two `Qwen2.5` scales, TAR **balances accuracy and diversity better than existing diversity-preserving methods** and substantially reduces forgetting of correct base-model solutions.

papers.title: Encoder-Free Multimodal LLMs Learn Implicit Encoders
papers.abstract: We empirically analyze two recently proposed encoder-free multimodal LLMs, Gemma-4 12B and Inkling-Small. Unlike previous multimodal LLMs, these models do not use modality-specific encoders to extract tokenized embeddings representing audio and image input; instead, they directly feed windows of samples, pixels, or spectral features to the Transformer language model. We analyze whether the early layers of these models learn to function similarly to dedicated audio and visual encoders. We find that these early layers do in fact act as ``implicit encoders,'' encoding audio and visual inputs in a way that is largely invariant to their cross-modal context. Furthermore, when performing multimodal reasoning tasks, we show that independently encoding the modalities throughout these early model layers achieves the same accuracy as jointly encoding them from the first layer onwards. Finally, we use layer-wise probing to analyze the salient information captured by the implicit encoders and find their behavior to be similar to several popular encoder models.
papers.summary: Encoder-free multimodal LLMs such as `Gemma-4 12B` and `Inkling-Small` feed raw windows of audio samples, pixels, or spectral features directly into the Transformer, with no dedicated audio or image encoder. This analysis finds that **their early layers act as implicit encoders**, representing audio and visual inputs in a way that is largely unaffected by cross-modal context. On multimodal reasoning tasks, encoding each modality separately through these early layers gives the same accuracy as encoding them jointly from the first layer. Layer-wise probing shows the implicit encoders capture information similar to several popular dedicated encoder models.

papers.title: Extending Myerson's Optimal Auctions to Correlated Bidders via Neural Network Interpolation
papers.abstract:
We aim to design revenue-maximizing single-item auctions that are deterministic, strategy-proof, and ex post individually rational --- the quintessential fundamental model for optimal mechanism design. While Myerson's seminal work solved this model for independent bidders, straightforward extensions to correlated settings often result in non-monotonic, and therefore non-strategy-proof allocations. Critically, optimal allocation design for correlated bidders is NP-hard to approximate, rendering theoretical optimality guarantees in this domain computationally intractable.
  We establish a new standard of empirical rigor for this theoretically hard model by proposing an empirical pipeline. We synthesize neural interpolation of Myerson's greedy allocation based on marginal profits (the correlated variant of virtual valuation), formal neural verification to enforce exact strategy-proofness, and a constructive repair procedure.
  Empirically, our method is highly effective, consistently achieves near-optimal revenue across a wide range of distributions, including synthetic, adversarial, and real-world (consumer, financial, and industrial) datasets. Compared to existing manual and neural baselines, our approach shows substantial improvement, often reducing the revenue gap by an order of magnitude. Our study is also the first to introduce (unattainable) greedy revenue as a rigorous upper bound for empirical benchmarking, providing a definitive quantitative performance measure where true optima remain theoretically elusive.
  We demonstrate the generality of our approach by extending it to multi-unit auctions with unit demand and integrating our verification techniques into RegretNet to achieve exact strategy-proofness.
papers.summary: Myerson's optimal single-item auction is solved for independent bidders, but naive extensions to correlated bidders break strategy-proofness, and finding the optimal allocation in that setting is NP-hard to approximate. The proposed pipeline uses a neural network to interpolate Myerson's greedy allocation based on marginal profits, applies formal neural verification to guarantee exact strategy-proofness, and repairs any violations. Across synthetic, adversarial, and real-world distributions, it achieves near-optimal revenue and **often cuts the revenue gap to baselines by an order of magnitude**, measured against greedy revenue used as an upper bound. The approach also extends to multi-unit auctions and adds exact strategy-proofness to `RegretNet`.

papers.title: CoCoNet: Convex Conformal Network for Multi-Dimensional Uncertainty Regions
papers.abstract: Conformal prediction (CP) provides distribution-free coverage guarantees under exchangeability, but the efficiency of its prediction regions depends critically on the choice of the conformity score. This is particularly important in multivariate regression, where dependencies across output dimensions induce complex joint uncertainty structures. This paper introduces CoCoNet (Convex Conformal Network) for learning convex conformity scores that induce flexible, data-adaptive prediction regions. CoCoNet learns the score from held-out data by optimizing prediction-region efficiency while enforcing convexity with respect to the residual. CoCoNet then applies split-conformal calibration to retain finite-sample coverage guarantees. The paper presents two variants of the method: CoCoNet$_{\mathrm{Spline}}$, based on piecewise-linear scores, and CoCoNet$_{\mathrm{ICNN}}$, based on Input Convex Neural Networks. Experiments compare CoCoNet with other CP baselines over synthetic and real-world datasets with output dimensions ranging from 2 to 16. The results demonstrate the flexibility of CoCoNet in learning different response types. Across 8 models and 30 multi-dimensional regression tasks, CoCoNet$_\text{ICNN}$ and CoCoNet$_{\mathrm{Spline}\text{-}\ell_1}$ achieve the best efficiencies with average ranks of 1.45 and 2.75, respectively. In particular, CoCoNet$_\text{ICNN}$ ranks first on 22 tasks out of 30 in terms of efficiency.
papers.summary: Conformal prediction (CP) gives distribution-free coverage guarantees, but how tight its prediction regions are depends heavily on the conformity score. This is especially true in multivariate regression, where output dimensions are correlated. `CoCoNet` learns convex conformity scores from held-out data to make regions as small as possible, then uses split-conformal calibration to keep finite-sample coverage. It comes in a piecewise-linear `CoCoNet_Spline` variant and an `Input Convex Neural Network (ICNN)` variant. Across 8 models and 30 tasks with 2 to 16 output dimensions, **`CoCoNet_ICNN` produces the most efficient regions on 22 of 30 tasks**.

papers.title: Probing Ambiguity: Adversarial Intent Resolution for Robust Text-to-SQL
papers.abstract: Text-to-SQL systems typically assume a one-to-one mapping between natural-language queries and correct SQL translations. In practice, however, many queries are inherently ambiguous, admitting multiple valid interpretations that yield distinct outputs. We introduce Adversarial Intent Resolution (AIR), a multi-agent framework that actively probes and resolves such ambiguity without any task-specific training. AIR first constructs competing interpretations, verifies through SQL execution that they produce genuinely different results, and generates targeted clarification questions grounded in the observed data differences. Evaluating on leading benchmarks for ambiguous questions, AIR demonstrates strong performance, efficiency, and robust cross-benchmark transferability. On the AMBROSIA benchmark under schema-only context, a realistic production setting where exposing the full database is infeasible, AIR outperforms IntentRL, the state-of-the-art reinforcement learning model, across all metrics (e.g., F1 0.679 vs. 0.618). Crucially, AIR exhibits only ~7% performance degradation without the full database, compared to ~20% for IntentRL. On the AmbiQT benchmark, where ambiguity arises from schema design rather than linguistic structure, AIR achieves higher F1 under both context settings without any benchmark-specific adaptation.
papers.summary: Text-to-SQL systems usually assume each question has one correct SQL query, but many real questions are ambiguous. `Adversarial Intent Resolution (AIR)` is a training-free multi-agent framework that builds competing interpretations, executes their SQL to confirm they return different results, and asks clarification questions grounded in those differences. On the `AMBROSIA` benchmark with only the schema available, AIR beats the reinforcement-learning model `IntentRL` on all metrics (F1 0.679 vs. 0.618) and **degrades only about 7% without full database access, versus about 20% for `IntentRL`**. It also achieves higher F1 on `AmbiQT`, where ambiguity comes from schema design, without benchmark-specific adaptation.

papers.title: Can This LLM Annotate My Data? Estimating Zero-Shot LLM Performance
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in annotation tasks with varying success. While several studies have demonstrated the opportunities and shortcomings of LLMs for annotation, a critical question remains unanswered: is it possible to predict how well they will perform on a new dataset? To answer this and related questions, we construct two task families which induce 461 text classification datasets. We find that it is possible to predict LLM performance - to a certain degree - and that contrary to other work which highlights the usefulness of LLM verbalizations of self-confidence, internal log-probabilities are the most predictive signal.
papers.summary: LLMs are widely used to annotate data, with mixed results, which raises the question of whether their accuracy on a new dataset can be predicted in advance. The authors build two task families that yield 461 text classification datasets and test which signals predict zero-shot LLM performance. Performance turns out to be predictable to a degree, and, contrary to work that favors the model's verbalized self-confidence, **internal log-probabilities are the most predictive signal**.

papers.title: Cortex: A Fixed-Point Theory of Governed Coding Agents - Technical Report
papers.abstract: A coding agent combines a large language model (LLM) with a harness that plans, edits, and executes code. We study Cortex, a supervisory layer for pre-execution governance, requirement tracking, and iterative validation and repair. We formalize requirement closure on a finite lattice. For a fixed requirement set and a sound, monotone validation rule with persistent evidence, exhaustive iteration reaches the least fixed point with no more strict increases than there are requirements. Fair consequence scheduling reaches the same closure. A separate stochastic model bounds expected completion time under a uniform positive-progress assumption. These results depend on their stated assumptions; artifact repair, fallible validation, and finite execution budgets do not satisfy them automatically. We define Gauntlet's trajectory-similarity and build-gated scores, attack-success estimators, Wilson intervals, and case-cluster bootstrap summaries. Effective-feedback accounting counts newly certified requirements, rather than estimating their information value or utility. The five evaluation families support raw-versus-governed comparisons. We report retained benchmark observations, including rescoring of existing artifacts; constructed outcomes are excluded. Unequal observation sets and incomplete provenance prevent causal claims about governance or measured long-horizon scaling.
papers.summary: `Cortex` is a supervisory layer for LLM coding agents that adds governance before code runs, tracking of requirements, and repeated validation and repair. The report formalizes requirement completion on a finite lattice and proves that, under sound and monotone validation with persistent evidence, iteration **reaches a least fixed point in no more strict steps than there are requirements**. A separate stochastic model bounds expected completion time. It also defines the `Gauntlet` evaluation scores and statistics. The authors note that real repair, fallible validation, and finite budgets do not automatically satisfy these assumptions, and that incomplete provenance rules out causal claims about the benefits of governance.

papers.title: Dynamic Neural Optimal Transport for Subset Alignment
papers.abstract: We study optimal transport between distributions when only a subset of the target population is relevant to the source. The goal is to map the source distribution to a reweighted target distribution whose density ratio with respect to the full target lies in $[0, c]$. This constraint enables the transported distribution to select an appropriate target subpopulation while limiting how strongly any region of the target can be emphasized. We propose a dynamic neural optimal transport framework for this setting using two neural networks. The first parameterizes a time-dependent potential whose spatial gradient defines the velocity field and whose terminal value enforces the density-ratio constraint. The second parameterizes an interpolation between the source distribution and the learned terminal distribution. Unlike prior neural dynamic optimal transport methods, which typically assume a fixed terminal distribution, our formulation learns the terminal distribution within the support of the target. We demonstrate the method on positive-unlabeled learning, unpaired domain translation, and trajectory inference, where meaningful alignments exist between source and target distributions, but direct distribution matching is inappropriate because the target contains additional or irrelevant components
papers.summary: Standard optimal transport maps a whole source distribution onto a whole target, but often only part of the target population is relevant. This work maps the source onto a reweighted target whose density ratio to the full target is capped at a constant, so the transport can pick out a relevant subpopulation without overemphasizing any region. A dynamic neural framework uses one network for a time-dependent potential that defines the velocity field and enforces the constraint, and a second for the interpolation path. Unlike prior neural dynamic transport methods, it **learns the terminal distribution rather than fixing it**. The method is demonstrated on positive-unlabeled learning, unpaired domain translation, and trajectory inference.

papers.title: SLA-LENS: From Classroom Transcripts to CSLA-Informed and Evidence-Linked L2 Interaction Analytics
papers.abstract: What happens after a learner makes an error, and how does the instructor's response shape the next turn? Investigating these exchanges across classrooms requires context-sensitive annotation that is difficult to scale manually. We introduce SLA-LENS, an end-to-end LLM-assisted framework that connects classroom transcripts to structured pedagogical annotations and evidence-linked descriptive analytics. Grounded in interactionist Second Language Acquisition (SLA) theory, its annotation schema captures second language learner errors, pedagogical functions, and uptake or repair while accounting for speaker roles, conversational context, and hierarchical labels. We apply the framework to 40 authentic online L2 Spanish classroom transcripts comprising over 21,000 sentence-level instances. We evaluate proprietary and open-weight LLMs, including task-specific QLoRA adaptation, using expert-reviewed gold annotations, held-out silver data, and metrics sensitive to different types of annotation error. A deterministic reporting layer generates reproducible visualizations of participation, feedback, learner errors, uptake, and temporal interaction patterns, linked to supporting transcript evidence. By making these patterns accessible and inspectable, SLA-LENS supports systematic classroom discourse research, pedagogical reflection, and curriculum design.
papers.summary: Studying how instructors respond to second-language learners' errors, and how that shapes the next turn, requires context-sensitive annotation that is hard to do by hand at scale. `SLA-LENS` is an LLM-assisted pipeline grounded in interactionist Second Language Acquisition (SLA) theory. It annotates learner errors, pedagogical functions, and uptake or repair, then produces reproducible analytics linked to transcript evidence. It is applied to **40 online Spanish classroom transcripts with over 21,000 sentence-level instances**, evaluating proprietary and open-weight LLMs, including `QLoRA`-adapted models, against expert-reviewed annotations.

papers.title: Best of Both Worlds: Fine-Tuned Small Models Complement LLMs for Cost and Performance Benefits
papers.abstract: BERT-based models require thousands of labeled samples to train. Larger models like GPT-X require only 1-5 examples per class. However, performance, cost and time tradeoffs of such models remain under-explored. In this work, we classify survey text data into 16 classes. We focus on experimental approaches and results on performance, cost, and time taken for this problem. We compare these parameters of a trained RoBERTa-based model, and an (off-the-shelf) GPT-3.5 model for text classification. Baseline experiments show that the time taken by GPT-3.5 for generating predictions on 10,000 records is 6 hours, whereas a RoBERTa-based model takes only 12 mins on a T4 GPU. To identify the best prompting approach for GPT-3.5, we explore batch prompting. We experiment with (1) batch-size, and (2) few-shot sampling. We find the best batch size is 20 with human few-shot curation. Experiments show the F1 score of a trained RoBERTa-based model (96%) is much higher than a GPT-3.5 model (83%). In case of GPT-3.5, batch prompting is beneficial in lowering inference costs by ~70%, without hindering task performance. We find the best approach is an ensemble of a RoBERTa-based and GPT-3.5 model (F1: 97.5%) incurring only 4.4% of inference cost compared to a standalone GPT-3.5.
papers.summary: The study compares a fine-tuned `RoBERTa` classifier with off-the-shelf `GPT-3.5` on performance, cost, and time for classifying survey text into 16 classes. RoBERTa reaches 96% F1 versus 83% for GPT-3.5 and labels 10,000 records in 12 minutes on a T4 GPU instead of 6 hours. Batch prompting with 20 items and human-curated few-shot examples cuts GPT-3.5 inference cost by about 70% without hurting accuracy. The best setup is **an ensemble of both models, reaching 97.5% F1 at 4.4% of the inference cost** of GPT-3.5 alone.

papers.title: Desirability Confirmation: Relational Sycophancy in AI Intimate Roleplay
papers.abstract: Research on LLM sycophancy has largely focused on propositional agreement, in which models echo users' beliefs, preferences, or judgments. Adult intimate roleplay presents a different case because what the user seeks may be preservation of a preferred relational position within a generated scene. Using a controlled prompt-based audit of 2,016 outputs from two open-weight LLMs, we identify four recurrent relational moves: legitimating desire, presenting the user as wanted, preserving non-rejection while communicating limits, and keeping intimacy available within fantasy or roleplay frames. Bringing the sycophancy literature into dialogue with sexual script theory, we conceptualize this configuration as desirability confirmation, an output-level pattern that captures how user-pleasing can operate through relational positioning. The findings extend sycophancy research and intimate-AI evaluation beyond binary compliance or refusal by showing how outputs can differ in the ways they communicate boundaries, preserve relational acceptance, and mark intimacy as fictional.
papers.summary: Research on LLM sycophancy has mostly examined models echoing users' beliefs or judgments, but in adult intimate roleplay users may instead want to keep a preferred relational position. A controlled audit of 2,016 outputs from two open-weight LLMs identifies four recurring moves: legitimating desire, presenting the user as wanted, avoiding rejection while still stating limits, and keeping intimacy available within the fiction. Drawing on sexual script theory, the authors call this pattern **desirability confirmation**. They argue that intimate-AI evaluation should look beyond binary comply-or-refuse outcomes to how outputs communicate boundaries and frame intimacy as fictional.

papers.title: Modeling bilingual naming performance through laterally-connected SOMs
papers.abstract: Computational models have explanatory power to understand cognition in individuals, but there is usually not enough training data to build such models with traditional machine learning. However, alternative architectures that model neural and cognitive processes in more detail can be more easily fit to individuals and can lead to mechanistic insights into human behavior. BiLex is such a computational model of the bilingual lexicon, containing a shared semantic system and phonetic language systems represented through self-organizing maps. In this study, BiLex was extended further into biological realism with excitatory and inhibitory lateral connections. This extension makes it possible to account for response times as well as common errors such as those based on semantic concept familiarity, typicality, and specificity. The Boston Naming Test was simulated in Spanish and English, and model performance approximated naming accuracy and error types in Spanish-English bilinguals with varying primary and secondary language histories. The results indicated that the approach captures semantic-level processes in bilingual lexical access, thus modeling the semantic cognition of individual subjects. In the future, such models may serve as a foundation for modeling impairments and treatment options.
papers.summary: Computational models of individual cognition usually lack enough data for standard machine learning, but biologically detailed architectures can be fit to individual people. The authors extend `BiLex`, a model of the bilingual lexicon built from self-organizing maps (a shared semantic map plus separate phonetic maps for each language), with excitatory and inhibitory lateral connections. These connections let the model account for response times and for common naming errors driven by concept familiarity, typicality, and specificity. Simulating the `Boston Naming Test` in Spanish and English, the model **approximates the naming accuracy and error types of individual Spanish-English bilinguals** with different first- and second-language histories.

papers.title: Dataset Inference for Data Provenance and Privacy Auditing in Tabular Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) are increasingly deployed through black-box APIs and trained on large collections of real-world tabular datasets. As this training paradigm becomes more widely adopted, private or proprietary datasets may be incorporated into pre-training corpora, yet there are currently no dedicated methods for determining whether a given tabular dataset was used to train a TFM. As a solution, we introduce the first dataset inference method for TFMs, aiming to infer whether a suspect dataset was part of a model's pre-training data. We systematically analyze a broad collection of candidate signals that can be observed from a black-box TFM via input manipulation and find that individual signals provide only weak evidence of training data membership. However, by combining multiple complementary signals, we can infer dataset membership for several state-of-the-art TFMs trained on real tabular data, achieving up to 0.99 ROCAUC dependent on the TFM. We then study factors that influence dataset identification, including pre-training data composition, model capacity, and the use of real vs. synthetic data. Our results show that our dataset inference method is a practical auditing tool for detecting privacy leakage and the use of proprietary datasets in TFMs.
authors: Dariush Wahdany (CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security)
Franziska Boenisch (CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security)
Adam Dziedzic (CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security)
papers.summary: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) are often served through black-box APIs and pre-trained on many real-world tables, which raises the question of whether a private or proprietary dataset was used in training. The authors present what they describe as the first dataset inference method for TFMs. They probe the model through input manipulation and find that each individual signal gives only weak evidence of membership, but combining several complementary signals identifies training datasets with **up to 0.99 ROC-AUC**, depending on the model. They also study how pre-training data composition, model capacity, and real versus synthetic training data affect how easily a dataset can be identified.

papers.title: BanglaShield: A Script-Robust Safety Classifier and Benchmark for Bangla Native, Romanized, and Code-Mixed Prompts
papers.abstract: Safety classifiers for large language models (LLMs) are typically built and evaluated on standard-script text, yet Bangla, like many lower-resource languages, is routinely written in native script, in Latin-script romanization, and code-mixed with English, Hindi, or Urdu. We introduce BanglaShield, a resource and model for graded prompt-safety classification across these written forms. We consolidate 10,245 Bangla prompts from six sources under a four-level taxonomy (Safe, Offensive, Harmful, Severe) and render each prompt in three aligned forms that share labels and a group-aware split, enabling strictly paired comparisons. Benchmarking six contemporary LLMs, including a Bangla-specialized one, on 36,882 classification queries and 24,318 judged responses, we find that LLM classifiers label 47.0% of unsafe native-script prompts as Safe, rising to 63.4% under romanization, while response-level safety accuracy drops by 10.3 points. Three multilingual guard models also pass 30.3-57.3% of unsafe native-script prompts. Using a model's own classification as an input filter reduces harmful compliance by only about five points. In contrast, BanglaShield, a compact fine-tuned encoder, reaches 87.8 macro-F1 on native-script and 84.4 on romanized prompts, outperforming the best LLM on each form by 42.8-46.1 points with ~130x fewer parameters than Gemma 4 31B. We release the corpus, splits, judgments, and model.
papers.summary: Bangla is routinely written in native script, in Latin-script romanization, and code-mixed with English, Hindi, or Urdu, yet LLM safety classifiers are mostly built and tested on standard script. `BanglaShield` provides 10,245 prompts under a four-level harm taxonomy, each rendered in three aligned written forms, along with a compact fine-tuned encoder classifier. Six LLMs label 47.0% of unsafe native-script prompts as safe, rising to 63.4% under romanization, and three multilingual guard models let through 30.3–57.3% of unsafe native-script prompts. The `BanglaShield` encoder reaches **87.8 macro-F1 on native-script and 84.4 on romanized prompts**, beating the best LLM by 42.8–46.1 points with roughly 130x fewer parameters than `Gemma 4 31B`.

papers.title: Beyond Clean Accuracy: The Practical Challenges and Benefits of Pixel-Based Language Models
papers.abstract: Pixel-based language models process rendered text without relying on a fixed subword vocabulary, offering a promising approach to noisy and multilingual inputs. However, their practical value depends on whether they can be reliably adapted to downstream tasks. To this end, we systematically examine this question through fine-tuning behavior, typographical robustness, and zero-shot crosslingual transfer. Under our tested settings, pixel-based models require longer training and broader labelled-data coverage than text-based models, while delayed learning and learning-rate-dependent failures make adaptation less reliable. Our analyses further suggest that task-relevant information is less readily accessible in pretrained pixel representations, placing greater demands on fine-tuning. Once successfully adapted, however, pixel-based models lose substantially less accuracy under typographical noise and achieve higher target-language accuracy than English-pretrained text-based counterparts on two crosslingual benchmarks, despite weaker clean English performance. Together, these findings reveal a central trade-off: replacing tokenization with rendering reduces sensitivity to corrupted and unfamiliar inputs, but shifts a central bottleneck to downstream adaptation.
papers.summary: Pixel-based language models read rendered images of text instead of subword tokens, which promises robustness to noisy and multilingual input. The authors test this systematically by looking at fine-tuning behavior, robustness to typos and other typographical noise, and zero-shot cross-lingual transfer. Pixel models need longer training and more labelled data, and they fail unpredictably depending on the learning rate, apparently because task-relevant information is harder to extract from their pretrained representations. Once adapted successfully, however, they **lose much less accuracy under typographical noise and transfer better to other languages** than English-pretrained text models. The result is a trade-off: replacing tokenization with rendering moves the main bottleneck to downstream adaptation.

papers.title: An important Bottleneck in LLM Optimizers: Principle-Level Local Optima
papers.abstract: Feedback-driven LLM optimizers are increasingly used for evolutionary search, Bayesian optimization, heuristic design, and scientific discovery. Yet rapid initial gains often give way to prolonged plateaus despite substantial remaining evaluation budgets. We investigate \emph{principle-level search collapse}, where an optimizer's search becomes confined to a narrow set of design principles, even though it may continue to generate distinct candidates and achieve small improvements. We assemble a diagnostic benchmark spanning molecular optimization, network sentinel-node selection, and GPU-kernel optimization, and introduce a decision-tree protocol combining principle narrowing, prolonged performance plateaus, and gaps to attainable reference solutions. Across 161 assessable runs on the three problem domains, 78.3\% receive support for collapse, including 55.3\% with strong support. Candidate-level variation can nevertheless conceal restricted search at the principle level. We then test \emph{diversity injection}, a common response to search stagnation, such as higher t, multiple LLMs, and web search, and show that it provides limited and inconsistent benefits: among 65 molecular runs, still 73.8\% and 53.8\% receive support and strong support respectively. We finally test reference-principle interventions and find that they improve some runs, but their benefits vary across models and tasks: access to a better principle does not guarantee its effective use. Our benchmark and diagnostic protocol provide a basis for evaluating future optimizers on principle-level collapse. Our findings highlight the need for online collapse detection and better mechanisms for generating and maintaining alternative principles during optimization.
papers.summary: Feedback-driven LLM optimizers used for evolutionary search, heuristic design, and scientific discovery often make quick early gains and then plateau even when plenty of evaluation budget remains. The authors trace this to principle-level search collapse: the optimizer keeps producing distinct candidates but stays locked into a narrow set of underlying design ideas. They build a diagnostic benchmark covering molecular optimization, network sentinel-node selection, and GPU-kernel optimization, and find evidence of collapse in **78.3% of 161 runs**, with strong evidence in 55.3%. Common diversity fixes such as higher sampling temperature, using multiple LLMs, or adding web search help little and inconsistently, and giving the optimizer a better reference principle does not guarantee that it will use it well.

papers.title: Inducing Fourier Geometry: A Smoothness Prior Imposes Approximate Translation Equivariance in Multimodal Stellar Embeddings
papers.abstract: Learned representations often contain geometric structure induced by symmetries in the underlying data. We ask whether a known continuous parameter space can instead be used to \emph{induce} such structure when the corresponding symmetry is only approximate. We introduce a graph-Laplacian smoothness prior that encourages representations to vary smoothly over a physical parameter space without specifying a representation geometry; in the continuum limit it selects Laplacian eigenfunctions and therefore predicts the Fourier-like geometry associated with translation symmetry. On multimodal stellar representations spanning six astronomical surveys, the prior induces Toeplitz Gram structure and sinusoidal modes along stellar parameters, including in modalities whose native representations lack this geometry, while modality-specific residuals preserve structure outside the imposed coordinates. Of the exact-symmetry predictions, stationarity in a recoverable warped coordinate survives; diagnostics assuming exact quantization or asymptotic rates do not. The prior also improves downstream linear-probe performance and label efficiency, suggesting a general strategy: where a meaningful continuous parameter space exists, its local geometry can serve as a data-informed prior.
papers.summary: Learned representations often show geometric structure that reflects symmetries in the data. The authors ask whether a known continuous parameter space can be used to induce such structure when the symmetry holds only approximately. They add a graph-Laplacian smoothness prior that pushes representations to vary smoothly over physical parameters; in the continuum limit, this predicts the Fourier-like geometry associated with translation symmetry. On multimodal stellar embeddings spanning six astronomical surveys, the prior **induces Toeplitz Gram structure and sinusoidal modes along stellar parameters**, even in modalities that lack that geometry natively, and it improves linear-probe accuracy and label efficiency.

papers.title: Constructive Universal Approximation by Infinite-Dimensional Neural Networks via Gaussian-Weighted Ridgelet Transform
papers.abstract: Neural networks whose inputs are functions, as in operator learning, are usually shown to be universal by existence arguments, either by reduction to finite-dimensional networks or by Stone--Weierstrass-type density; these prove that approximants exist but say little about how the parameters depend on the target. We take a constructive route. We extend the ridgelet transform, an integral transform related to the Fourier, Radon, and wavelet transforms, to continuous maps on a separable infinite-dimensional Hilbert space, replacing the Lebesgue measure that is unavailable in infinite dimensions by Gaussian weights with a homogeneous mixture on the direction space. The resulting transform has a Plancherel identity and reconstruction formulas incorporating the frame operator, the correction induced by the weights, and it assigns to each target an explicit coefficient measure, one for every admissible analysis filter. From these representations we obtain uniform approximation on compact sets for all continuous non-polynomial activations of polynomial growth, including ReLU, and, by Monte Carlo sampling of the coefficient, finite-width networks with a dimension-free $O(N^{-1/2})$ error in the width $N$ for globally Lipschitz activations and coefficients with finite variation and second moments. Explicit examples include Gaussian targets and neural-operator layers. A companion Lean~4 formalization provides machine-checked proofs, with its correspondence to the manuscript documented at https://shosonoda.github.io/lean-operator-ridgelet/ .
papers.summary: Universality results for neural networks that take functions as inputs, as in operator learning, usually prove that good approximations exist without saying how the parameters depend on the target function. The authors give a constructive alternative by extending the ridgelet transform to continuous maps on a separable infinite-dimensional Hilbert space, replacing the Lebesgue measure, which does not exist there, with Gaussian weights. The resulting transform has a Plancherel identity and reconstruction formulas that assign each target an explicit coefficient measure. This yields uniform approximation for all continuous non-polynomial activations of polynomial growth, including `ReLU`, and finite-width networks with a **dimension-free O(N^-1/2) error in the width N**, with the proofs machine-checked in `Lean 4`.

papers.title: Not Every User Says It All: Training Tool-Using Agents Beyond Ideal Simulated Users
papers.abstract: Tool-using agents are trained and evaluated almost exclusively with strong simulated users who state every detail clearly, yet real users are often weaker. We construct weak users by masking sentences of a simulated user's replies, holding the task and the user's knowledge fixed, and cross-evaluate agents trained with strong and weak users on tau2-bench and ToolWOZ. Weak users lower the success of every policy, and training with them does not help: no policy trained with weak users, through fixed masks, mixtures or a curriculum, serves weak users better than the strong-trained policy beyond run-to-run noise, and prompting the agent to ask more does not help either. We propose StaGPO (State-Grouped Policy Optimization): the agent writes what the task needs, what is missing and how it is being filled, and GRPO uses this state to compare turns of different rollouts that reach the same situation, assigning step-level credit. Within the standard recipe of a small SFT cold start followed by RL, StaGPO makes weak-user training useful: on ToolWOZ, the Qwen3.5-2B policy trained with weak users reaches 76.8% with weak users, the highest of any Qwen3.5-2B policy we trained, 4.8 points above GRPO and 2.8 above the strongest baseline; it is also 5.4 points above GRPO with strong users, and generalises to an unseen mask rate; trained with strong users instead, it serves weak users at least as well as GRPO trained with weak users. On tau2-bench it scores highest with weak users for both models, by a small margin for Qwen3.5-4B.
papers.summary: Tool-using agents are trained and evaluated almost entirely against simulated users who state every detail clearly, while real users often leave things out. The authors create weaker users by masking sentences in the simulated user's replies and find that every policy does worse with them; training on weak users through fixed masks, mixtures, or a curriculum, or prompting the agent to ask more questions, does not help. They propose `StaGPO` (State-Grouped Policy Optimization), in which the agent writes down what the task needs, what is missing, and how it is filling the gaps, and `GRPO` uses that state to compare turns from different rollouts that reach the same situation and assign credit per step. On `ToolWOZ`, a `Qwen3.5-2B` policy trained this way reaches **76.8% success with weak users, 4.8 points above GRPO**, and it also scores highest with weak users on `tau2-bench`.

papers.title: Predicting CVSS and CWE from CVE Descriptions with Fine-Tuned Small Language Models
papers.abstract: Until April 2026, the National Vulnerability Database labeled nearly every published Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) entry with a Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) v3.1 vector, a severity tier, and a Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) weakness type. Now, NIST enriches only the high priority CVEs, leaving many newly published vulnerabilities unlabelled with the classifiers that security teams use for patch triage. In CVE enrichment, we predict the eight base components of CVSS v3.1 vector, base score, severity tier, and CWE from the vulnerability's textual description alone. To prevent leakage between near-duplicate descriptions, all systems are trained only on CVEs published in 2022 and 2023. Results are evaluated on all 36,325 usable 2024 CVEs in the pinned NVD snapshot. All scores are either directly predicted, or calculated from predicted vectors using the CVSS formula. A fine-tuned 3.8B-parameter model Phi-3.5-mini, trained with LoRA in 2.5 hours on a single Apple M5 Pro chip, achieves 69.9% accuracy on severity and 70.9% on CWE. It matches the official vector exactly for 48.8% of test CVEs, outperforming TF-IDF logistic regression by 2.8 to 4.7 points on all accuracy metrics based on zero-exclusion paired bootstrap intervals. When we evaluate the base model with a zero-shot prompt, it achieves 20.8% accuracy on severity in a sample of 2,000 CVEs. In this same sample, its stated scores match its own vector precisely for only 3.4% of CVEs. However, deriving scores from predicted vectors boosts the critical recall of TF-IDF logistic regression from 50.7% to 73.3% with no additional cost. And since the errors of the fine-tuned model and TF-IDF affect different CVEs, at least one system matches the correct severity tier for 75.8% of test CVEs.
papers.summary: Since April 2026 the National Vulnerability Database enriches only high-priority CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) entries, so many new vulnerabilities lack the CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) vectors, severity tiers, and CWE (Common Weakness Enumeration) types that security teams rely on for patch triage. The authors predict all of these from the text description alone, training on 2022–2023 CVEs and testing on 36,325 CVEs from 2024. A `Phi-3.5-mini` model fine-tuned with `LoRA` in 2.5 hours on a single Apple M5 Pro reaches **69.9% severity accuracy and 70.9% CWE accuracy** and matches the full official vector for 48.8% of CVEs, beating TF-IDF logistic regression by 2.8–4.7 points on every accuracy metric. By contrast, the base model prompted zero-shot gets only 20.8% of severities right, and computing scores from predicted vectors with the CVSS formula raises the critical-severity recall of the logistic-regression baseline from 50.7% to 73.3%.

papers.title: Torch-DPhys: A Torch-Native, MOOSE-Compatible Framework for Differentiable Physics Simulation and Hybrid Machine Learning Integration
papers.abstract: We present Torch-DPhys, a Torch-native framework implemented in PyTorch for differentiable physics simulation and hybrid physics-machine learning. It implements selected thermal-hydraulic modeling concepts and discretizations from MOOSE's Thermal Hydraulics Module and the System Analysis Module (SAM), with a preliminary extension to continuum mechanics. Native tensor residuals support CPU and GPU execution, compilation of selected numerical kernels, and sparse direct linear solves. Sensitivities are obtained by differentiating executed numerical operations or through discrete adjoints of converged residual equations. Verification combines analytical solutions, reference-code comparisons, and derivative checks. Demonstrations cover plane-strain elasticity, one- and two-loop thermal-hydraulic transients, and an axisymmetric molten-salt fast reactor. For the reactor, comparison with SAM-Lite gives a maximum normalized field discrepancy of 1.13 x 10^-5 over 200 adaptive time steps, demonstrating agreement between the tested discrete implementations. Selected transient sensitivities are assessed using tangent-linear calculations and finite differences on fixed time schedules. Two applications illustrate the framework's connection between simulation and optimization. A residual-adjoint parameter-identification calculation recovers nominal pump head and heating power with relative errors below 0.06% from noiseless synthetic MOOSE observations. A separate three-loop plant demonstration uses solver-in-the-loop training of a predictive controller by differentiating trajectory-level objectives through the thermal-hydraulic simulation. These examples illustrate a foundation for gradient-based inference, control, and coupled physics-machine learning models in nuclear engineering.
papers.summary: `Torch-DPhys` is a PyTorch-native framework for differentiable physics simulation that reimplements selected thermal-hydraulic models and discretizations from the `MOOSE` Thermal Hydraulics Module and the System Analysis Module (`SAM`), with an early extension to continuum mechanics. It runs on CPU and GPU and computes sensitivities either by differentiating the executed operations or through discrete adjoints of the converged equations. On an axisymmetric molten-salt fast reactor it agrees with `SAM-Lite` to a **maximum normalized discrepancy of 1.13 x 10^-5** over 200 adaptive time steps. Demonstrations include recovering pump head and heating power to within 0.06% from synthetic observations, and training a predictive controller for a three-loop plant by differentiating through the simulation.

papers.title: Muon Operates Beyond the Edge of Stability
papers.abstract: We study the Muon optimizer using sharpness and provide the first empirical evidence that the Flat Minima Hypothesis also applies to Muon. Further, we derive Muon's implicit preconditioner to analyze its potential Edge of Stability behavior. Experiments on CIFAR-10 show sharpness strongly correlates with generalization gap within each optimizer (Pearson $r = 0.45$-$0.69$, $p \leq 10^{-4}$), confirming the hypothesis holds for Muon similarly to Adam and SGD. However, Muon operates above the classical sharpness-based Adaptive Edge of Stability threshold that bounds diagonally-preconditioned optimizers like Adam and RMSprop, yet remains stable. Our findings suggest Muon operates in a fundamentally different regime than diagonally-adaptive methods. Defining the exact stability boundary for Muon remains an open question. All code is available at https://github.com/NikoCovic/DL-project.
papers.summary: The authors examine the `Muon` optimizer through the lens of loss-landscape sharpness. On `CIFAR-10`, sharpness correlates with the generalization gap for Muon (Pearson r = 0.45–0.69) much as it does for `Adam` and `SGD`, which they present as the first empirical support for the flat-minima hypothesis under Muon. They also derive Muon's implicit preconditioner and find that it **trains stably above the Adaptive Edge of Stability threshold** that bounds diagonally preconditioned optimizers such as Adam and RMSprop. This suggests Muon operates in a different regime from diagonal adaptive methods, though its exact stability boundary remains open.

papers.title: Learning Administrative Boundary-Aware Location Encoders via Reverse Geocoding
papers.abstract: Location encoders learn compact representations of latitude--longitude coordinates for downstream geospatial prediction tasks. Existing approaches are pretrained using continuous or naturally occurring supervision, such as imagery, climate variables, or species distributions, and therefore do not explicitly capture administrative boundaries or place names, despite their strong influence on many real-world geospatial phenomena. We introduce, to our knowledge, the first method for learning administrative boundary-aware location encoders, using reverse-geocoded text as a self-supervised training signal. Our approach can be applied to existing location encoder architectures and consistently improves their downstream performance. We further introduce RevGeoRQ, a custom architecture tailored to reverse-geocoding supervision, which yields additional gains and exceeds contemporary location encoders on several downstream tasks. Finally, the use of human-interpretable reverse-geocoded strings and residual-quantized semantic IDs provides a more interpretable representation of geographic location than existing approaches. Code and model weights to be released soon.
papers.summary: Location encoders turn latitude–longitude coordinates into embeddings for geospatial prediction, but existing encoders are pretrained on signals such as satellite imagery, climate variables, or species distributions and do not capture administrative boundaries or place names. The authors use reverse-geocoded text, the place names returned for a coordinate, as a self-supervised training signal, and the approach can be added to existing encoder architectures. It **consistently improves downstream performance**, and a purpose-built architecture called `RevGeoRQ` that uses residual-quantized semantic IDs adds further gains, outperforming current location encoders on several tasks while giving more interpretable representations.

papers.title: RATION: Towards Quantitative Risk-Based Access Control for AI Agents
papers.abstract: AI agents increasingly interact with external environments to complete complex user tasks. These interactions can lead to unexpected behavior and expose agents to security threats such as indirect prompt injection. Current agent security systems largely protect agents by restricting their actions, which can result in a substantial security-utility trade-off for complex, open-ended tasks. To address this, we propose a quantitative risk-based approach to access control for AI agents that regulates measurable risks accumulated during task execution. As a concrete realization of this approach, we introduce RATION, a security framework that tracks measurable risks associated with agent actions and enforces quantitative constraints throughout execution. RATION first constructs a task-specific policy by combining explicit constraints derived from the user request with implicit risks calibrated from historical executions of similar tasks. During task execution, RATION continuously tracks the accumulated risks and applies different enforcement strategies depending on the type of risk. Extensive experiments on four security benchmarks show that RATION provides strong security while maintaining high task utility across diverse models and environments.
papers.summary: AI agents that act in external environments are exposed to threats such as indirect prompt injection, and current defenses mostly restrict which actions an agent may take, which costs a lot of utility on open-ended tasks. `RATION` instead treats access control as a budget on measurable risk accumulated during execution. It builds a task-specific policy by combining explicit constraints taken from the user's request with implicit risk limits calibrated from past runs of similar tasks, then tracks accumulated risk while the agent runs and applies a different enforcement strategy for each type of risk. On four security benchmarks it **provides strong security while keeping task utility high** across a range of models and environments.

papers.title: Latent State Utilization in Probabilistic Circuits
papers.abstract: Probabilistic circuits (PCs) are generative models that support efficient probabilistic inference. Adding latent states to a PC increases its representational capacity, but yields diminishing gains in likelihood. We use mutual information to examine how the dependence represented by a trained PC changes with latent size. Experiments with Hidden Chow-Liu Trees (HCLTs) on ImageNet32 show that learned dependence grows slowly and remains well below both the latent-state upper bound and estimates of dependence in the data. To understand how learning uses these states, we examine how strongly each sample favors particular latent states and how broadly states are used across the dataset. Tracking these measurements during HCLT training distinguishes rapid early posterior concentration from the more gradual stabilization of sample-dependent state preferences. Early measurements also guide initialization selection in HCLTs and hidden Markov models (HMMs), as well as tree selection in HCLTs. The resulting choices improve the ultimate performance across the tested latent sizes, providing a practical benefit from our study of latent-state utilization.
papers.summary: Probabilistic circuits (PCs) are generative models that support efficient exact inference, and adding latent states increases their capacity but with diminishing gains in likelihood. Using mutual information on Hidden Chow-Liu Trees (`HCLTs`) trained on `ImageNet32`, the authors show that the dependence the models learn **grows slowly and stays well below** both the latent-state upper bound and estimates of the dependence actually present in the data. Tracking how sharply each sample prefers particular latent states, and how broadly states are used across the dataset, separates quick early concentration of the posterior from slower stabilization of per-sample preferences. Measurements taken early in training also help choose initializations for HCLTs and hidden Markov models and tree structures for HCLTs, which improves final performance.

papers.title: The Judge Can Debias Itself: Awareness and Self-Debiasing for Reliable LLM-as-a-Judge
papers.abstract: LLM-as-a-Judge systems are increasingly employed for automated evaluation, yet remain susceptible to systematic biases that undermine their reliability. We demonstrate that the judge can effectively debias itself without additional training. We propose two lightweight strategies: bias-aware prompting, which explicitly alerts the judge to potential target biases prior to evaluation, and self-debiasing, in which the judge critiques the initial judgment for bias influence. To broaden the evaluation scope, we introduce three novel benchmarks--authority bias (fabricated citations), confidence bias (assertive phrasing), and formatting bias (structured presentation)--and evaluate across seven bias types in total. Across three frontier models, self-debiasing improves performance in 20 out of 21 model-bias combinations with gains up to 15 percentage points, while bias-aware prompting also yields consistent improvements. The recent fine-tuned external critic, however, does not generalize as reliably to the newly-introduced bias types (degradation observed in 5 out of 9 cases). Our findings demonstrate that prompting a judge to reason about bias, either preemptively or retrospectively, is a robust and generalizable approach for enhancing evaluation integrity.
papers.summary: LLMs used as automatic judges carry systematic biases that make their evaluations less reliable. The authors test two training-free fixes: bias-aware prompting, which warns the judge about specific biases before it evaluates, and self-debiasing, in which the judge critiques its own first verdict for signs of bias. They also introduce three new benchmarks for authority bias (fabricated citations), confidence bias (assertive phrasing), and formatting bias, and evaluate seven bias types in total. Across three frontier models, **self-debiasing improves 20 of 21 model–bias combinations, by up to 15 percentage points**, while a recent fine-tuned external critic degrades in 5 of 9 cases on the new bias types.

papers.title: Morpheus-2.0: Multiscale Probabilistic Forecasting with Dual-Axis Attention
papers.abstract: A universal forecaster is trained once and applied everywhere, so it must serve tasks whose schemas, forecast horizons, and temporal resolutions all differ. The number of targets and covariates changes from dataset to dataset, horizons vary by orders of magnitude, and sampling rates range from seconds to years. Existing time-series foundation models address these only in part, since they isolate each series or visit the two grid relations in separate blocks, and they fix the horizon and resolution before training begins. We introduce Morpheus-2.0, a compact encoder-only foundation model that represents targets and covariates on a single variable-time grid. Its dual-axis attention runs both relations side by side in every layer, one across variables at a timestep and one across time within a variable; a learned gate weights the two per layer, and an axis-aware rotary encoding preserves both grid coordinates. The forecast length is sampled during training, so one set of weights spans short to long horizons at no additional inference cost. Morpheus-2.0 Multiscale extends the model to several temporal resolutions at once, weighting them according to the series being forecast. Across GIFT-Eval, which spans several domains and frequencies, the two models give complementary operating points: Morpheus-2.0 attains 0.685 relative MASE with 81M parameters, while the larger Morpheus-2.0 Multiscale attains 0.646 relative MASE and 0.455 relative CRPS, the lowest of any published system on both metrics.
papers.summary: A universal time-series forecaster has to handle datasets with different numbers of targets and covariates, horizons that differ by orders of magnitude, and sampling rates from seconds to years. `Morpheus-2.0` is a compact encoder-only foundation model that places all variables on one variable–time grid and, in every layer, attends across variables and across time in parallel, with a learned gate weighting the two. Forecast length is sampled during training so one set of weights covers short to long horizons, and a `Multiscale` variant combines several temporal resolutions, weighted according to the series being forecast. On `GIFT-Eval` the 81M-parameter base model reaches 0.685 relative MASE, and the Multiscale variant reaches **0.646 relative MASE and 0.455 relative CRPS, the best published results on both metrics**.

papers.title: PAC Learning with Query Feedback
papers.abstract: We study realizable multiclass PAC learning with query feedback, where each training example provides a single binary response indicating whether its true label belongs to a chosen subset from a fixed query family. Our main contribution is the query dimension, a combinatorial parameter that captures both the structure of the hypothesis class and the ability of the available queries to distinguish labels. This parameter generalizes the bandit DS dimension, which it recovers under singleton queries. We establish a sample-complexity lower bound of $\Omega(D/\varepsilon)$ and an upper bound of $\widetilde{O}(D^2/\varepsilon)$, suppressing factors polylogarithmic in the number of labels and the failure probability. When the available queries can split every candidate set into two parts of comparable size, we improve the upper bound to $\widetilde{O}(D/\varepsilon)$, yielding a characterization up to logarithmic factors.
papers.summary: The authors study realizable multiclass PAC learning in which each training example reveals only a single yes-or-no answer about whether its true label lies in a chosen subset from a fixed family of queries. They introduce the query dimension, a combinatorial parameter that captures both the hypothesis class and how well the available queries can tell labels apart, and that reduces to the bandit DS dimension when queries are single labels. They prove a sample-complexity lower bound of Ω(D/ε) and an upper bound of Õ(D²/ε). When the queries can always split a candidate set into two roughly equal halves, the upper bound improves to Õ(D/ε), giving **a characterization tight up to logarithmic factors**.

papers.title: Power-Law Correlations Without Apparent Temperature-Tuned Criticality in Fixed-Tree Hierarchical Languages
papers.abstract: Sampling temperature can substantially reshape autoregressive generation, but it is unclear when temperature changes in long-range correlations reflect a genuine phase transition rather than a smooth change in statistics. We study this question in a controlled analogue of temperature sampling: a finite-depth probabilistic context-free grammar on a fixed hierarchical tree, where exact next-token conditionals are computed by belief propagation and then rescaled by a softmax temperature before autoregressive sampling. We measure two-point mutual information between tokens as a function of separation. Across the tested temperatures and grammar ensembles, mutual information remains well described by a power-law envelope. Temperature changes the correlation magnitude and fitted exponent, but within the accessible system sizes we find no long-distance plateau characteristic of an ordered phase and no clear crossover to short-range exponential decay. An approximate mapping to an Ising model on a tree explains how exponential decay in tree distance becomes a power law in token distance, allowing power laws to persist without tuning to a special decoding temperature. This controlled baseline clarifies which temperature effects can arise from hierarchical structure alone, before adding training, approximation error, or neural architecture.
papers.summary: Sampling temperature visibly changes long-range correlations in autoregressive generation, and the authors ask whether this reflects a genuine phase transition or just a smooth change in statistics. They study a controlled setting: a finite-depth probabilistic context-free grammar on a fixed tree, where exact next-token probabilities are computed by belief propagation and then rescaled by temperature before sampling. Across the temperatures tested, mutual information between tokens **follows a power law in their separation**, with temperature changing only its magnitude and exponent, and shows neither an ordered-phase plateau nor a switch to exponential decay. An approximate mapping to an Ising model on a tree explains how exponential decay in tree distance becomes a power law in token distance, so power laws can appear without tuning to a special temperature.

papers.title: Uniform convergence at optimal rate and scale
papers.abstract: Uniform convergence asks how many random samples suffice for empirical averages to approximate expectations simultaneously over an entire class of functions. It is a central concept in probability and a foundation of statistical learning. For binary-valued classes, the Vapnik--Chervonenkis theorem characterizes uniform convergence by finiteness of the VC dimension. For dimension $d$, the sharp worst-case sample complexity for additive error $\varepsilon$ is of order $d/\varepsilon^2$. For real-valued functions, the analogous combinatorial parameter is the fat-shattering dimension, which depends on an approximation scale $\gamma$. The challenge is to achieve error $\gamma+\varepsilon$ with order $d/\varepsilon^2$ samples, matching the sample bound for binary classes, where $d$ is now the fat-shattering dimension at scale $\gamma$. Previous results achieved either the optimal scale or the optimal sample complexity, but not both. Our main result closes this gap, establishing the sharp sample complexity at the optimal scale. Along the way, we use several tools that may be of independent interest. The first concerns $\varepsilon$-nets with margin. A classical $\varepsilon$-net intersects every set of mass at least $\varepsilon$ in a prescribed family; we allow the net to intersect a slightly enlarged version of each such set. Remarkably, this relaxation permits bounds independent of the ambient dimension in natural geometric settings. Second, we derive improved covering bounds in both discrete and real-valued settings: we extend Haussler's covering lemma to partial concept classes and use this extension to obtain $\ell_2$ covers at the optimal scale for real-valued function classes. Third, we obtain a chaining bound at the optimal scale by aligning the covers so that successive approximations become increasingly close to one another.
papers.summary: Uniform convergence asks how many samples are needed for empirical averages to approximate expectations across an entire function class at once. For binary classes the sharp answer is of order d/ε² in the VC dimension d, but for real-valued functions, measured by the fat-shattering dimension at a scale γ, earlier results achieved either the optimal scale or the optimal sample complexity, never both. The authors **close this gap, achieving error γ + ε with order d/ε² samples at the optimal scale**. Along the way they introduce ε-nets with margin, which can give dimension-independent bounds in natural geometric settings, extend Haussler's covering lemma to partial concept classes, and develop a chaining argument at the optimal scale.

papers.title: What Matters for NVFP4 Training? A Comparative Study of Low-Precision Pretraining Recipes
papers.abstract: Training large language models directly in 4-bit floating-point (FP) formats promises substantial improvements in throughput and energy efficiency.
