While some recipe design choices have been validated at scale, many promising approaches remain untested beyond small models and short token horizons, leaving open the question of which trends will hold. We present a systematic comparison of recent NVFP4 recipes at medium model scale, evaluating dense 8B and 30B-A3B MoE models trained for up to 1T tokens, with a focus on which ingredients are necessary for accuracy recovery. We propose a final recipe grounded in the principles behind established stable NVFP4 training at scale, incorporating state-of-the-art techniques such as unbiased gradient estimation with lower quantization error than stochastic rounding. To the best of our knowledge, this is the strongest FP4 training result demonstrated at this scale to date in loss gap to BF16. Through ablation studies, we find that: (i) each technique in the optimized recipe measurably improves loss trajectory, (ii) selective high-precision layers are necessary for recovering accuracy at scale, (iii) not all tensors in the backward pass benefit equally from de-biasing, leaving room to apply complementary error-reduction techniques to the remaining tensors.
papers.summary: Pretraining LLMs directly in 4-bit floating point promises large gains in throughput and energy efficiency, but many proposed recipes have been tested only on small models over short training runs. The authors systematically compare recent `NVFP4` recipes on a dense 8B model and a 30B-A3B mixture-of-experts model trained for up to 1T tokens, and assemble a final recipe that includes unbiased gradient estimation with lower quantization error than stochastic rounding. They report **the smallest loss gap to BF16 shown for FP4 training at this scale**. Ablations show that every component of the recipe improves the loss trajectory, that keeping selected layers in high precision is necessary at scale, and that de-biasing helps some backward-pass tensors more than others.

papers.title: The Certification Exponent: Instance-Optimal Sequential Certification of Policy Improvement from History Dependent Logs
papers.abstract: Before a new policy replaces a deployed one, we often want a certificate, computed from logged episodes, that it is better. We ask how many episodes such a certificate needs when the logging policy is known but history-dependent, and the error probability must stay below $\delta$ in every environment consistent with the logs. The answer is an exponent $K^\star$: the smallest KL divergence from the logged law to a law with the same logged action probabilities under which the target does not improve. No sound certifier stops in fewer than $\log(1/\delta)/K^\star$ expected episodes, at any $\delta$, and whenever $0<K^\star<\infty$ a plug-in Kelly certifier attains this rate to first order as $\delta\to0$. Coverage, computed by one backward induction, decides whether certification is impossible ($K^\star=0$), possible at a finite rate, or possible in a constant number of episodes ($K^\star=\infty$). By convex duality, the optimal certificate bets on the importance-weighted advantage and also places fair bets on the logged actions, so doubly robust control variates act as hedges rather than estimators. As a consequence, no choice of off-policy estimator changes $K^\star$, a coverage ceiling explains the curse of memory, and structural assumptions can be priced in exponent units. A cushion certifier extends the approach to trees too large to enumerate. In experiments the plug-in's median stopping time is 1.13-1.43x the lower bound on memory tasks, 1.13-1.51x on Tiger ($H\le5$) and 1.17-1.64x on random trees. The best scalar betting baselines need up to 2.65x (memory) and 4.1x (Tiger) the plug-in's episodes; only on a few shallow random trees is a doubly robust bet faster, by at most 18%.
papers.summary: Before replacing a deployed policy, practitioners want a statistical certificate, computed from logged episodes, that the new policy is better. The setting here has a known but history-dependent logging policy, and the error probability must stay below a level δ in every environment consistent with the logs. The authors show that the minimum number of episodes is governed by a single exponent K*. This is the smallest Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence from the logged distribution to an alternative that keeps the logged action probabilities but under which the target policy does not improve. **No sound certifier can stop in fewer than log(1/δ)/K* expected episodes**, and a plug-in `Kelly` betting certifier matches this rate asymptotically. The analysis also shows that no choice of off-policy estimator changes K*, and that doubly robust control variates act as hedges rather than estimators. In experiments on memory tasks, `Tiger`, and random trees, the certifier's median stopping time was 1.13 to 1.64 times the lower bound. Scalar betting baselines needed up to 4.1 times as many episodes.

papers.title: Measuring the Task Value of Precision Upgrades in Closed-Loop Agents
papers.abstract: A low-precision agent can call its full-precision (BF16) model at selected decisions as a fallback. A learned precision router chooses where to call it from the disagreement between the two models and is judged by end-to-end success. An inserted BF16 action, however, can rescue a failing task or damage a succeeding one. We argue that a fallback's value is the number of tasks it saves minus the number it spoils, measured for the intervention that will actually run. From restored states, we run paired branches that cross which model supplies the current action with which model continues, separating replacement of one action, takeover of later execution, and both. On Qwen3 agents with simulated 4-bit weights in tau2-bench, replacing the first action where the two models differed in tool use changed many task outcomes, but rescues and damages nearly cancelled, and on held-out telecom tasks the action-only estimate was negative. Replacing both the action and the continuation had a positive net gain in two of five exploratory lower-bit stress settings. Two references changed outcomes at fixed bit width: replacing an action with that of a second 4-bit checkpoint changed about as many outcomes as replacing it with the BF16 action, and reordering tool-argument keys changed outcomes while the executed tool call stayed identical. At common states, the additional value of the BF16 action over that checkpoint remained unresolved. A frozen uncertainty trigger found more outcome changes than random selection, while its net benefit stayed within the range of random selection. We recommend evaluating each fallback by its signed task benefit under the intended continuation, against same-precision references, before attributing gains to more bits.
papers.summary: A quantized agent can fall back to its full-precision (`BF16`) model at selected decisions, but an inserted full-precision action can damage a successful task as easily as it rescues a failing one. The authors argue that a fallback should be valued by tasks saved minus tasks spoiled. They measure this with paired branches from restored states that separate replacing a single action from taking over the rest of the execution. On `Qwen3` agents with simulated 4-bit weights in `tau2-bench`, **rescues and damages from replacing a single action nearly cancelled out**, and the estimate was negative on held-out telecom tasks. Same-precision changes, such as swapping in a second 4-bit checkpoint or merely reordering tool-argument keys, changed about as many outcomes as the full-precision fallback. The authors recommend judging fallbacks against such same-precision references before attributing gains to extra bits.

papers.title: Exact Risk Certificates for Pairwise-Judged Reranking
papers.abstract: Pairwise relevance judgments constrain both the loss numerator and the ideal-ranking denominator of nDCG. We characterize the exact worst-case loss of replacing a ranking with a fixed proposal. Binary gains attain this loss and provide an inspectable witness. Threshold verification reduces to at most $K+1$ maximum-closure problems. Our exposure-flow ablation isolates denominator coupling: on shared judge trajectories, exact verification saves 2.34 comparisons per TREC-DL development query and 1.98 per confirmation query at a budget of 32. Savings transfer to BEIR and a second proposer. Predictive gates achieve higher deployment gains, while certificates expose the worst gains still permitted by accepted comparisons.
papers.summary: When a reranker relies on pairwise relevance judgments, those judgments constrain both the loss and the ideal-ranking normalizer in normalized discounted cumulative gain (`nDCG`). The authors characterize the exact worst-case `nDCG` loss of replacing a ranking with a fixed proposal. Binary gains attain this worst case, and verifying a threshold reduces to at most K+1 maximum-closure problems. Exact verification saves **2.34 comparisons per `TREC-DL` development query** at a budget of 32, and the savings carry over to `BEIR` and a second proposer. Predictive gates achieve higher deployment gains, but certificates expose the worst outcome still permitted by the accepted comparisons.

papers.title: Blackbox Performance Analysis of LLM-based Network Control
papers.abstract: LLMs are becoming an indispensable part of network control systems due to their impressive reasoning. Before such LLM-enabled systems can be deployed, it is imperative to develop tools that can audit their performance on previously unseen inputs. However, auditing these systems is challenging due to the inherent opacity of LLMs. LENS is the first step towards black-box performance analysis of LLM-enabled network control systems. It uses novel methods to extend deep reinforcement learning to guide the search for performance gaps and inputs that make LLMs struggle. LENS finds large gaps for LLM-based traffic engineering and GPU allocation systems, and even matches existing white-box analyzers designed for hand-crafted TE heuristics.
papers.summary: As large language models (LLMs) are built into network control systems, operators need ways to audit how they perform on unseen inputs, which is hard because the models are opaque. `LENS` performs black-box performance analysis by extending deep reinforcement learning to search for inputs where an LLM-based controller performs much worse than it should. It finds **large performance gaps in LLM-based traffic engineering and GPU allocation systems**. It also matches existing white-box analyzers that were designed for hand-crafted traffic engineering heuristics.

papers.title: Can Agents Keep Secrets They Were Never Told? Benchmarking Latent Privacy Risks Across Sessions with MemJoin
papers.abstract: To support sustained interactions and personalized assistance, agents use long-term memory to retain and combine user information across sessions. Reusing such memories can lead an agent to state a sensitive relation while completing an ordinary task that does not require it. The relation to protect and the combination of clues that reveal it may remain hidden at memory write time, when later records and tasks are still unknown. In this paper, we introduce MemJoin, a privacy benchmark of 288 synthetic analysis cases in which the complete history entails a sensitive relation, but every individual session is insufficient. We evaluate six memory systems with the same answer-generating model, alongside full-history and no-history controls. Each system writes and updates memories in session order and later retrieves context for an ordinary task, while target annotations remain with the evaluator. We separately check which target attribute values appear in stored records and retrieved context, and whether the final answer states the complete, person-linked relation. In a separate paired test on a prespecified subset, removing shared identifiers and other connecting clues can change complete-relation output while all checked target attribute values remain visible. These findings show why checking attribute visibility alone is insufficient to evaluate what records from different sessions reveal together.
papers.summary: Agents with long-term memory can combine clues from separate sessions and reveal a sensitive relation about a user during an ordinary task. At memory-write time, neither the relation nor the combination of clues that exposes it may be known yet. `MemJoin` is a benchmark of 288 synthetic cases in which the full history implies a sensitive relation but no single session does. It is used to evaluate six memory systems with the same answer-generating model, against full-history and no-history controls. A paired test shows that **removing shared identifiers and other linking clues can change whether the full relation is disclosed even while every checked sensitive attribute stays visible**. Checking which attributes are visible is therefore not enough to assess what memories reveal when combined.

papers.title: FlashMap: Flow Map Speculative Decoding
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model (LLM) inference by using a lightweight drafter to propose a block of tokens that the target model verifies in one parallel pass. Autoregressive drafters generate this block one token at a time, whereas block diffusion drafters such as DFlash generate it in one pass, making drafting faster. However, these diffusion drafters predict each token independently, ignoring dependencies between tokens in the block. We introduce FlashMap, a continuous flow drafter that conditions a flow map language model on the target model's hidden states and generates the whole block in one forward pass while capturing inter-token dependencies. On Qwen3-8B, FlashMap is faster than a matched DFlash baseline on every benchmark, with 7% higher average speedup and up to 6.1x lossless acceleration.
papers.summary: Speculative decoding speeds up large language model (LLM) inference by having a lightweight drafter propose tokens that the target model verifies in parallel. Block diffusion drafters such as `DFlash` draft a whole block in one pass but predict each token independently, which ignores dependencies between tokens. `FlashMap` instead uses a continuous flow map language model, conditioned on the target model's hidden states, to generate the full block in one forward pass while capturing those dependencies. On `Qwen3-8B` it is faster than a matched `DFlash` baseline on every benchmark, with 7% higher average speedup and **up to 6.1x lossless acceleration**.

papers.title: Revisiting Smoothed Online Learning: Competitive Ratio, Dynamic Regret with Switching Cost, and Best of Both Worlds
papers.abstract: We revisit smoothed online learning and develop algorithms with improved competitive ratios, optimal dynamic regret with switching cost, and best-of-both-worlds guarantees. Surprisingly, minimizing the hitting cost alone is $\max(1,\frac{2}{\alpha})$-competitive for $\alpha$-polyhedral functions under the $\ell_2$-norm switching cost and $1+\frac{4}{\lambda}$-competitive for $\lambda$-quadratic growth functions under the squared $\ell_2$-norm switching cost, significantly improving existing guarantees. The polyhedral bound is tight for this naive algorithm, and we establish a matching lower bound for $\alpha\geq1$. For convex $\lambda$-quadratic growth hitting costs, minimizing a suitably weighted sum of hitting and squared $\ell_2$-norm switching costs yields a competitive ratio of $1+\frac{2}{\sqrt{\lambda}}$. For dynamic regret with the $\ell_2$-norm switching cost, we develop Smoothed Ader (SAder), which achieves the optimal $O(\sqrt{T(1+P_T)})$ rate in the standard online convex optimization setting, where $P_T$ is the comparator's path-length. Its lookahead version removes the bounded-gradient assumption, and a matching lower bound establishes optimality in this setting. Finally, for convex hitting costs on a bounded convex domain, we develop UDNP to aggregate any two experts in the lookahead setting under both switching costs. Its additional cumulative cost is at most $O(1)$ relative to the first expert and $O(\sqrt{T\log T})$ relative to the second, yielding best-of-both-worlds guarantees without bounded gradients.
papers.summary: Smoothed online learning is revisited here: a learner pays both a per-round hitting cost and a cost for switching between decisions. The authors show that simply minimizing the hitting cost is **max(1, 2/α)-competitive for α-polyhedral functions**, which improves substantially on existing guarantees. They prove tight or matching lower bounds and give improved ratios for quadratic-growth costs. A new algorithm, `SAder`, achieves the optimal O(√(T(1+P_T))) dynamic regret with switching costs, where P_T is the comparator's path length; a lookahead variant drops the bounded-gradient assumption. A second algorithm, `UDNP`, combines any two experts in the lookahead setting and obtains best-of-both-worlds guarantees.

papers.title: Defending Against Dormant Poisoning Attacks Across Language and Multimodal Agents
papers.abstract: Recent work shows that attackers can implant dormant malicious behaviors that remain hidden at release but emerge after benign fine-tuning. As foundation models are used as agents, whether dormant poisoning extends to harmful agent actions and multimodal settings remains unclear. We show two agentic risks: (1) harmful behaviors activated by benign fine-tuning can extend to unseen actions; (2) multiple harmful behaviors can coexist and be jointly activated by benign downstream fine-tuning. Existing defenses often rely on external safe responses, which are hard to obtain for agent actions, or a trusted clean reference model. We exploit a key property of dormant poisoning: the attacker must preserve safe behavior at release to conceal poisoning, and this behavior can serve as a safety reference. Leveraging this property, we automatically construct a Safety Buffer pairing harmful inputs with the released model's responses and benign versions generated by the same model to remove harmful intent. The Safety Buffer can replace external safe responses in existing defenses, but these defenses do not distinguish updates that weaken safety from those that preserve it, often increasing over-refusal or reducing utility. To address this limitation, we introduce LookAhead Defense, which previews benign fine-tuning updates using the Safety Buffer and penalizes only updates predicted to weaken safe behavior on harmful inputs or increase the likelihood of refusals on benign versions in the Safety Buffer. Across language models, language agents, and multimodal agents, LookAhead Defense reduces harmful behavior in agents from up to 93.9% to at most 14.2% and harmful responses in language models from up to 92.5% to at most 2.0% versus vanilla fine-tuning, while maintaining competitive utility and low over-refusal. It remains effective against other poisoning methods.
papers.summary: Dormant poisoning implants malicious behavior that stays hidden at release and emerges after benign downstream fine-tuning. The authors show that in agents, the activated harm can extend to unseen actions, and several harmful behaviors can be activated together. Their defense relies on the fact that the attacker must keep the released model safe-looking. They use the released model's own responses to build a `Safety Buffer` of harmful inputs paired with safe responses, plus benign rewrites of those inputs. `LookAhead Defense` then previews each fine-tuning update and penalizes only those predicted to weaken safety or increase over-refusal. Across language models, language agents, and multimodal agents, **harmful agent behavior drops from up to 93.9% to at most 14.2%** while utility stays competitive and over-refusal stays low.

papers.title: Learning from the Right Regions: Class-Conditioned Explanation Guidance for Medical Imaging
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks can achieve strong predictive performance in medical imaging while relying on regions unrelated to the predicted finding. Explanation-guided learning can address this problem, but multi-label classification introduces a key challenge: multiple abnormalities may coexist in an image, requiring each prediction to align with its corresponding spatial evidence. We propose a class-conditioned explanation-guided learning framework that constructs a separate explanation for each positive class and penalizes evidence outside its class-specific annotated regions. We instantiate the framework using Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) and evaluate it on 14 abnormalities using EfficientNet-B1, ViT-B/16, ViT-B/32, and Swin-B. Explanation guidance substantially improves annotation alignment across all architectures: All-Saliency Precision increases from 0.140 to 0.625, 0.052 to 0.551, 0.060 to 0.403, and 0.095 to 0.570, respectively. These improvements are accompanied by smaller, architecture-dependent changes in classification performance. Our results show that class-conditioned explanation guidance can substantially improve where multi-label classifiers concentrate their explanatory evidence while largely preserving predictive performance.
papers.summary: Medical image classifiers can score well while basing predictions on regions unrelated to the finding. This is hard to correct in multi-label settings, where several abnormalities coexist in the same image. The proposed framework builds a separate Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (`Grad-CAM`) explanation for each positive class and penalizes evidence outside that class's annotated regions. Across 14 abnormalities and four architectures (`EfficientNet-B1`, `ViT-B/16`, `ViT-B/32`, `Swin-B`), **All-Saliency Precision rises sharply, for example from 0.140 to 0.625 on `EfficientNet-B1`**. Classification performance changes only modestly, and how much depends on the architecture.

papers.title: A decomposition-integration framework coupling singular spectrum analysis with a volatility-adaptive LSTM for stock price forecasting
papers.abstract: Financial time series exhibit multi-scale, high-noise, and non-stationary volatility dynamics. Decomposition--integration frameworks built on complete ensemble empirical mode decomposition with adaptive noise (CEEMDAN) have advanced this field, yet existing CEEMDAN hybrids remain unstable: high-frequency mode mixing contaminates downstream predictors, and the heterogeneous volatility of decomposed components is not matched by any volatility-adaptive mechanism. To address these gaps, this paper proposes CEEMDAN-SE-SSA-VMGL. CEEMDAN adaptively decomposes the original series, and sample-entropy-driven K-means clustering groups the intrinsic mode functions into high-, mid-, and low-frequency and residual components. Singular spectrum analysis (SSA) is then applied to the high-frequency group, whose singular-value decomposition of the trajectory matrix and principal-component reconstruction decouple intertwined pseudo-oscillatory modes and alleviate mode mixing. We further design a plug-and-play robust LSTM variant, the volatility-modulated GARCH-LSTM (VMGL), which embeds a differentiable GARCH(1,1) layer inside the LSTM cell as a risk gate; the estimated conditional volatility multiplicatively scales the forget-gate activation, letting memory decay adapt to the instantaneous volatility while remaining fully end-to-end trainable. Component predictions are linearly combined. On five US and Chinese financial series (CSI 300, CSI 500, AAPL, GOOGL, S&P 500), the proposed model is compared with eleven benchmark architectures, lowering the forecasting error by 9% to 24% relative to the best benchmark and by 60% to 70% relative to a standard LSTM. Diebold--Mariano and model-confidence-set (MCS) tests confirm the statistical significance and stability of the gains, spectral analyses verify the SSA denoising efficacy, and backtesting demonstrates the framework's economic utility.
papers.summary: Stock price forecasting has to cope with noisy, non-stationary, multi-scale volatility, and existing hybrids built on complete ensemble empirical mode decomposition with adaptive noise (`CEEMDAN`) suffer from high-frequency mode mixing. The proposed pipeline first decomposes the series with `CEEMDAN`. Sample-entropy-driven K-means clustering then groups the components by frequency, and singular spectrum analysis (`SSA`) denoises the high-frequency group. Each component is forecast with `VMGL`, an LSTM variant whose forget gate is scaled by volatility from an embedded differentiable `GARCH(1,1)` layer. On five US and Chinese series, the model **lowers forecasting error by 9% to 24% relative to the best of eleven benchmarks**, and statistical tests confirm the gains.

papers.title: Learning volatility-adaptive forgetting via GARCH-modulated LSTM for stock price forecasting
papers.abstract: Stock price forecasting is hindered by the heteroscedastic nature of financial time series, in which turbulent and tranquil regimes alternate. Although the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network is widely used for this task, its gates are oblivious to such volatility variation, so memory retention remains fixed regardless of market conditions. A common remedy is to supply volatility estimates as an additional input feature, yet this leaves the internal memory dynamics untouched. Instead, volatility can serve as a direct regulatory signal over the gate activation itself. This paper presents the Gsigmoid-LSTM model, which embeds Generalized Autoregressive Conditional Heteroscedasticity (GARCH(1,1))-derived volatility estimates into the LSTM forgetting gate through the Gsigmoid activation function, a volatility-adaptive variant of the sigmoid that combines a volatility adjustment factor with slope regulation via a learnable parameter. The model thereby automatically prioritizes recent information during turbulent periods while preserving long-term dependencies in stable markets. In the engineering application of daily stock price forecasting, extensive experiments, including activation function comparisons, baseline evaluations, and ablation studies, demonstrate that this structural gating modification effectively improves forecasting accuracy and robustness. The proposed model significantly outperforms a feature-level fusion baseline carrying the same volatility signal on all five datasets, as confirmed by Diebold-Mariano tests with all p<0.01, attains the best average rank of 1.00 in the Friedman test across nine models, and achieves the lowest MSE and MAE on all five datasets.
papers.summary: Standard LSTM gates ignore the alternation between turbulent and calm periods in financial markets, and feeding volatility in as an extra input feature leaves the internal memory dynamics unchanged. `Gsigmoid-LSTM` instead injects Generalized Autoregressive Conditional Heteroscedasticity (`GARCH(1,1)`) volatility estimates directly into the forget gate. It does this through `Gsigmoid`, a volatility-adjusted sigmoid with a learnable slope, so the model emphasizes recent data in turbulent periods and keeps long-term dependencies in stable ones. Across five daily stock datasets, it **significantly outperforms a feature-level fusion baseline that receives the same volatility signal** (Diebold-Mariano tests, p<0.01). It also ranks first among nine models.

papers.title: MSCR: Jointly Balancing Utilization Across Modalities and Discovering Synergistic Information
papers.abstract: In multimodal learning, modality imbalance often lets one modality dominate optimization and keeps the model from fully exploiting cross-modal interactions. Balance-oriented methods such as the Multimodal Competition Regularizer (MCR) perform well by alleviating this imbalance during training. These dynamic balancing methods, however, mainly adjust modality contributions and do not consider how imbalance affects the formation of synergistic information during fusion. Synergy is a major source of multimodal advantage, because it is predictive gain that cannot be recovered from unimodal evidence alone. We propose the Multimodal Synergistic Competition Regularizer (MSCR), a fusion method that jointly promotes balanced modality utilization and the discovery of synergistic information. MSCR has two complementary objectives. An anti-dominance objective suppresses excessive unimodal influence and leaves room for synergistic information, and a synergy objective encourages the fused predictor to outperform a non-synergistic unimodal reference. An adaptive gate further concentrates the regularization on samples that need stronger collaborative modeling. Experiments on five benchmarks show that MSCR consistently improves performance over MCR and strengthens synergistic capability. It raises conditional recovery, the accuracy of the fused prediction on samples that the unimodal predictors misclassify, as well as the share of the model's output that InterSHAP attributes to cross-modal interactions. Its gain in conditional recovery persists when the fusion module is Transformer-based. Code is available at https://github.com/chenxinyu991-collab/MSCR.
papers.summary: In multimodal learning, one modality often dominates training. Balancing methods such as the Multimodal Competition Regularizer (`MCR`) address this but do not encourage synergy, meaning predictive gain that no single modality provides on its own. `MSCR` combines an anti-dominance objective that curbs excessive unimodal influence with a synergy objective that pushes the fused predictor to beat a non-synergistic unimodal reference. An adaptive gate focuses this regularization on the samples that need it most. Across five benchmarks it consistently improves on `MCR` and **raises accuracy on samples that the unimodal predictors misclassify**. It also increases the share of output that `InterSHAP` attributes to cross-modal interactions, including with Transformer-based fusion.

papers.title: Prototype-Guided Optimization of Quantum Data Embeddings with Linear Cost
papers.abstract: In supervised quantum machine learning with classical data, classification performance critically depends on the geometry induced by quantum data embedding. Existing data-adaptive approaches rely on pairwise fidelity evaluations between samples, which scale as $O(B^2)$ for $B$ samples and create a computational bottleneck in iterative embedding optimization. To address this issue, we propose a prototype-guided framework for efficient data-adaptive quantum embedding. Using class-prototype separation and sample-to-prototype compactness, we derive a measurable lower certificate for class-ensemble distinguishability and construct a prototype-based objective requiring only $O(B)$ fidelity evaluations. We integrate this objective into an end-to-end pipeline that combines task-specific quantum circuit architecture optimization with continuous refinement of the data-embedding parameters. Across five benchmark datasets with up to 20 qubits, our method retains competitive quantum kernel support vector machine (SVM) performance while reducing fidelity-evaluation cost, with particularly strong gains over budget-matched pairwise optimization on T-MNIST. Geometric analyses examine how the learned embeddings relate to kernel alignment and classification margins, revealing dataset-dependent benefits and limitations. We further derive a prototype-based classifier in the reproducing kernel Hilbert space that provides an explicit witness for the SVM objective and a low-cost proxy for model selection, and extend the framework to multiple prototypes for multimodal class structures.
papers.summary: In quantum machine learning on classical data, the data embedding largely determines classification quality, but optimizing it adaptively needs pairwise fidelity evaluations whose number grows quadratically with the number of samples. The authors replace these with an objective built on class prototypes, combining prototype separation with how compactly samples cluster around their class prototype. This **cuts the cost to a linear number of fidelity evaluations** while still giving a measurable lower bound on how distinguishable the classes are. Across five datasets with up to 20 qubits, the method keeps competitive quantum kernel support vector machine (SVM) accuracy, with notable gains over budget-matched pairwise optimization on `T-MNIST`. The authors also derive a prototype-based classifier that serves as a cheap proxy for model selection.

papers.title: Long Listening Thoughts: Eliciting Open Auditory Reasoning with Deliberative Perception and Cognitive Refinement
papers.abstract: We introduce Long Listening Thoughts (LLT), a framework for constructing post-training datasets that improves audio reasoning by pairing deliberate perceptual grounding with explicit cognitive behaviors. On audio understanding and reasoning benchmarks, large audio-language models (LALMs) are limited primarily by perceptual errors, yet existing post-training datasets rely on audio descriptions of limited diversity. Through a four-stage pipeline, LLT (1) builds multi-aspect dense audio descriptions spanning semantic, acoustic, and temporal information, (2) generates more challenging questions, (3) synthesizes incorrect reasoning traces, and (4) extends short reasoning traces into long ones via a thought-continuation strategy that elicits cognitive behaviors such as verification and backtracking. Using LLT, we synthesize 1.6M reasoning traces and train Qwen2.5-Omni-7B with a two-stage pipeline of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) followed by direct preference optimization (DPO). This improves accuracy on MMAU Test-mini (71.5 to 78.2), MMAR (56.7 to 63.7), and MMSU (60.6 to 66.0).
papers.summary: Large audio-language models (LALMs) mostly fail on audio reasoning benchmarks because of perception errors, and existing post-training data relies on audio descriptions with little diversity. `Long Listening Thoughts` (`LLT`) is a four-stage data pipeline. It builds dense audio descriptions covering semantic, acoustic, and temporal aspects, generates harder questions, synthesizes incorrect reasoning traces, and extends short traces into long ones that include verification and backtracking. Training `Qwen2.5-Omni-7B` on 1.6M synthesized traces with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) followed by direct preference optimization (DPO) **improves `MMAU` Test-mini accuracy from 71.5 to 78.2**. It also brings gains on `MMAR` and `MMSU`.

papers.title: Ask Less, Ask Better: Allocating User Attention in Proactive LLM Agents with Interruption Budgets
papers.abstract: LLM agents can ask clarifying questions to complete tasks, but answering each question demands users' time and effort. Existing evaluations typically measure this burden by counting questions, treating necessary and avoidable questions equally. We propose an evaluation protocol that distinguishes how often agents ask from how well they ask. An interruption budget limits the number of questions, while a user-attention cost charges extra for questions that are hard to read or not worth asking, as rated by a human-validated LLM judge. Beyond question counts, this cost captures perceived effort: on conversation pairs with the same number of questions, human annotators agreed with the cost on which conversation required more effort 75% of the time. Across eight LLMs and four customer-service domains, limiting agents to one to three questions reduces user-attention cost by 36-73% while keeping 86-94% of the task reward they earn with unlimited questions. At the same budget, reviewing each question against the memory of users' earlier answers cuts attention cost by another 13% with little reward loss and yields more valuable questions. Models also differ sharply in how well they ask: at the same user-attention cost, the most efficient models gain more than twice as much reward from their questions as the others. These results show that asking less and asking better are distinct goals, and that evaluations of proactive agents should measure both.
papers.summary: Agents that ask clarifying questions cost users time, yet evaluations usually just count questions. The proposed protocol combines an interruption budget, which caps the number of questions, with a user-attention cost that charges extra for questions that are hard to read or not worth asking, as rated by a human-validated LLM judge. Across eight LLMs and four customer-service domains, **limiting agents to one to three questions cuts attention cost by 36-73% while keeping 86-94% of the task reward** earned with unlimited questions. Checking each question against memory of the user's earlier answers saves another 13% of attention cost. At equal attention cost, the most efficient models gain more than twice as much reward from their questions as the others.

papers.title: Cross-Dimension and Cross-Modality Relational Tensor Representation Learning for Multimodal Health Data Modeling
papers.abstract: Multimodal health data integrate information from heterogeneous clinical sources, creating substantial opportunities for data-driven decision support. Realizing these opportunities, however, requires effectively modeling complex dependencies that arise both within individual modalities and across modalities. This paper proposes Relational Tensor Representation (RTR), a unified framework that jointly learns dimension-specific tensor representations and cross-dimensional and cross-modality relationships. RTR introduces learnable relational bridge matrices that maintain relational information while preserving the structural identities of tensor dimensions and modalities. A structured fusion mechanism further integrates factor-level and relationship-level information into compact representations for downstream prediction. Experiments on simulated data and two multimodal neurophysiological datasets, covering emotion recognition and brain activity classification, demonstrate that RTR consistently outperforms representative tensor learning, multimodal fusion, and Transformer-based baselines. These results highlight the value of explicitly modeling cross-dimensional and cross-modality relationships for learning informative representations from heterogeneous multimodal tensor data. The source code is planned for public release to support reproducibility and future research.
papers.summary: Multimodal health data contains dependencies both within each modality's tensor dimensions and across modalities. Relational Tensor Representation (`RTR`) learns a representation for each tensor dimension and connects dimensions and modalities through learnable relational bridge matrices that keep their structural identities intact. A structured fusion step merges factor-level and relationship-level information into compact features for prediction. On simulated data and two multimodal neurophysiological datasets, covering emotion recognition and brain activity classification, **`RTR` consistently outperforms tensor learning, multimodal fusion, and Transformer baselines**.

papers.title: Toward a Universal Local Speech Feature Extractor Through Distillation
papers.abstract: Self-supervised speech models commonly consist of a set of convolutional neural network (CNN) layers used as a local feature extractor, followed by transformer layers. The CNN layers are computationally demanding, and are also similar across models and resemble the much simpler mel spectral features. We hypothesize that the CNN layers can be replaced by a simple, universal model. To test this hypothesis, we learn a two-layer feature extractor via distillation from one or more teacher models (HuBERT, data2vec, and WavLM). Experiments on SUPERB(-SG) benchmark tasks show that our model largely retains the performance of the teacher models and can also be used in an unseen model (wav2vec 2.0). Our feature extractor requires only 3% of the MACs of the CNNs, resulting in a $>$20% overall inference runtime reduction.
papers.summary: Self-supervised speech models typically start with computationally heavy convolutional (CNN) feature extractors that look similar across models and resemble simple mel spectral features. The authors distill a two-layer feature extractor from one or more teachers (`HuBERT`, `data2vec`, `WavLM`) to replace these layers. On `SUPERB` and `SUPERB-SG` tasks it largely retains teacher performance and even works when plugged into an unseen model, `wav2vec 2.0`. It **needs only 3% of the CNN's multiply-accumulate operations, reducing overall inference runtime by more than 20%**.

papers.title: Margin-Based Generalization for Quantum Machine Learning with Classical Data Encoding
papers.abstract: Understanding generalization is essential for assessing the practical viability of quantum machine learning. In many applications, quantum models operate on classical data that must first be encoded into quantum states, making the encoding part of the effective hypothesis class. We develop a margin-based generalization framework for this setting, covering both fixed and trainable quantum data encodings. For fixed encodings, the existing margin bound transfers unchanged. For trainable encodings, we derive a bound using a two-scale covering argument that combines the original margin-dependent term with an additive encoding-capacity term of order $\tilde O(\sqrt{L/m})$, where $L$ is the number of trainable encoding parameters and $m$ is the training-sample size. Across 19,440 simulated training runs spanning various image datasets, circuit architectures, and optimization settings, the inverse margin performs best among five baseline and two bound-derived complexity measures under conditional-independence and 90th-percentile sign-error criteria, within bootstrap uncertainty. These results provide a unified margin-based view of generalization in quantum machine learning with classical data.
papers.summary: In quantum machine learning on classical data, the encoding of data into quantum states is part of the hypothesis class, so it affects generalization. The authors build a margin-based generalization framework for both fixed and trainable encodings. Existing margin bounds carry over unchanged for fixed encodings. For trainable ones, a two-scale covering argument adds an encoding-capacity term of order √(L/m), where L is the number of trainable encoding parameters and m the number of training samples. Across 19,440 simulated training runs, **the inverse margin best predicts generalization among seven complexity measures**.

papers.title: When Opposite Premises Translate Identically: A Source-Conditioned Diagnostic for Multilingual Commonsense Items
papers.abstract: Multilingual reasoning comparisons depend on translated premises preserving the relations in their English sources. Automatic translation scores can rank source-target pairs, but an acceptance decision alone cannot certify a counterfactual benchmark field. We test a source-contrast diagnostic for ACCORD premises: reverse the English polarity, translate both arms independently, count identical target outputs, and score each arm against its own source. Across 71 matched question identities at two containing-item depths, five target languages, and three translation checkpoints, Swahili has 63, 113, and 67 exact collisions among 710 pairs per checkpoint. At a human-reference-calibrated threshold, round-trip NLI passes both arms of 3 of the 113 NLLB-3.3B collisions, while LaBSE passes 78. Each collision proves at least one unfaithful translation, but does not identify its arm. These controlled measurements do not establish screening accuracy on spontaneous translation errors or a language-by-hop reasoning effect; the study has no native equivalence labels or answer-model evaluation.
papers.summary: Multilingual reasoning benchmarks assume that translated premises keep the meaning of their English sources, but automatic translation-quality scores cannot certify that. The proposed diagnostic reverses the polarity of each English premise from the `ACCORD` benchmark, translates both versions independently, and counts cases where the two translations come out identical. Every such collision means at least one translation is unfaithful. Swahili produced up to **113 collisions out of 710 pairs** with `NLLB-3.3B`. At a calibrated threshold, round-trip natural language inference (NLI) passed both arms of only 3 of these collisions, while `LaBSE` similarity passed 78. The authors note that the method cannot tell which arm is wrong and does not measure screening accuracy on naturally occurring translation errors.

papers.title: Transport What Shares the Conduction Pathway: Normal-Anchored SPD Geometric Transport for Source-Free Patient Adaptation of Holter and Patch ECG
papers.abstract: Electrocardiogram (ECG) beat classifiers lose accuracy on new patients and devices, and source-free adaptation methods that assume class-balanced target batches fail on real recordings, whose label-free prefix is 87.9--98.6% normal beats. We propose Normal-Anchored Geometric Transport (NAGT, GA_NS), which estimates a closed-form symmetric positive-definite congruence map from label-free normal anchors in the first 5 min of each recording and applies it only to the normal and supraventricular prototypes, keeping the ventricular and fusion prototypes fixed. The score offsets and decision rules were set on MIT-BIH only; the rate-invariant RR head (relA) was adopted after the development databases (INCART, SVDB) had been opened; the frozen model was then evaluated once on Icentia11k chest-patch recordings under a pre-registered protocol. In 493 patients (973 recordings, 3,615,388 evaluated beats), NAGT reached an arrhythmia macro-$F_1$ $J = \frac{1}{2}(\text{S-}F_1 + \text{V-}F_1) = 48.7\%$ [95% CI 42.1, 54.7] versus 34.5% without adaptation ($\Delta J = +14.1$ [+8.6, +19.3] pp; 59.8% versus 43.9% in non-AF) and outperformed all five Holm-adjusted comparators, including AdaBN, Tent and T3A. In the 75-patient test subgroup of the historical split (73 analyzed), the gain was not significant (+6.1 [-8.5, +23.4] pp). Adaptation takes a median of 5.8 ms per record without back-propagation.
papers.summary: Electrocardiogram (ECG) beat classifiers lose accuracy on new patients and devices. Source-free adaptation methods that assume class-balanced batches break down on real recordings, where 87.9-98.6% of early beats are normal. Normal-Anchored Geometric Transport (`NAGT`) computes a closed-form symmetric positive-definite mapping from unlabeled normal beats in the first five minutes of a recording. It applies the mapping only to the normal and supraventricular class prototypes and leaves the ventricular and fusion prototypes fixed. In a pre-registered evaluation on 493 patients from the `Icentia11k` chest-patch dataset, **arrhythmia macro-F1 rose from 34.5% to 48.7%**, beating five comparators including `AdaBN`, `Tent`, and `T3A`. The gain was not significant on a smaller historical test subgroup.

papers.title: Transformers as Adaptive Kernel Learners across Tasks for In-Context Learning
papers.abstract: Transformers have emerged as a dominant architecture in modern machine learning, with in-context learning (ICL) enabling models to adapt to new tasks by conditioning on prompts, without any parameter updates. To understand the attention mechanism in transformer blocks, a growing line of theoretical work interprets ICL through the lens of classical statistical estimators. Recent works have established a connection between the attention mechanism and kernel methods, while the kernel function is usually assumed to be fixed. In practice, the query and key matrices in the attention mechanism are trained, which allows the attention mechanism to serve as an adaptive kernel method. In this work, we demonstrate that transformers can act as adaptive anisotropic kernel learners. Specifically, we study ICL for low-rank linear and multi-index nonlinear regressions, and conduct numerical simulations to show that the learned attention scores closely resemble the oracle kernels for these function classes. We then develop a general framework to analyze the generalization error of ICL by connecting transformers to the oracle kernel estimator for each function class. Our theory gives an explicit and constructive implementation of the oracle kernel estimators for these function classes using a wide and shallow transformer architecture, illustrating how the prediction is carried out by the interaction between the query token and the context tokens. Our work complements existing studies by providing numerical and theoretical evidence of how the attention mechanism adapts to anisotropic kernels in both linear and nonlinear settings.
papers.summary: Earlier theory links attention in transformers to kernel methods, but it usually assumes a fixed kernel, even though the query and key matrices that shape attention are trained. The authors study in-context learning (ICL) on low-rank linear and multi-index nonlinear regression, and show in simulations that the learned attention scores come to look like the oracle anisotropic kernels for each function class. They also build a framework that bounds ICL generalization error by relating transformers to these oracle kernel estimators, and give an explicit construction of the estimators using **a wide, shallow transformer**. Together, the results suggest attention works as an adaptive kernel learner rather than a fixed one.

papers.title: Near-Optimal Regret for Semi-Bandit Learning of Monotone Stochastic Problems
papers.abstract: We consider the task of learning an (approximately) optimal policy for stochastic optimization problems where the true distributions are unknown. In each period, the algorithm plays a policy for the stochastic problem and observes semi-bandit feedback, i.e., it only receives new samples from the random variables that were selected by the policy. We obtain an algorithm that works for a large class of ``monotone'' stochastic problems, including prophet inequality, Pandora's box, series testing, stochastic knapsack and stochastic matching. We obtain $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{nkT})$ regret for ``weakly'' monotone problems and $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{nT})$ regret for ``strongly'' monotone problems, where $T$ is the number of periods, $n$ is the problem dimension (number of random variables) and $k$ is the maximum support size of any random variable. This improves over previous regret bounds by a $\sqrt{n}$ factor. In fact, our dependence on $n$ and $T$ is the best-possible due the $\Omega(\sqrt{nT})$ lower bound for multi-armed-bandits. Our main technique is the use of Hellinger distance in bounding the ``error'' between the true and learned distributions, and the use of a constant-factor chain rule for the Hellinger distance of dependent random variables.
papers.summary: The setting is learning near-optimal policies for stochastic optimization problems when the underlying distributions are unknown, using semi-bandit feedback in which the algorithm only sees samples from the random variables its policy selects. The proposed algorithm covers a broad class of 'monotone' problems, including prophet inequality, Pandora's box, series testing, stochastic knapsack and stochastic matching. It achieves regret of roughly sqrt(nkT) for weakly monotone problems and sqrt(nT) for strongly monotone ones, which **improves prior bounds by a sqrt(n) factor** and matches the multi-armed bandit lower bound in n and T. The main tools are Hellinger distance for bounding distribution-estimation error and a constant-factor chain rule for the Hellinger distance of dependent variables.

papers.title: Generative Retrieval for Reverse Target Fishing with a Proteome-Scale Benchmark
papers.abstract: Reverse target fishing identifies protein targets for a query molecule and is central to drug discovery and repurposing. Discriminative approaches adapted from virtual screening face sparse, long-tailed associations and missing-not-at-random measurements: treating unrecorded pairs as negatives can suppress genuine targets. We reformulate the task as generative retrieval and introduce GenFish. Residual vector quantization converts frozen protein language model features into shared semantic identifiers. Given a molecular fingerprint, GenFish autoregressively models codes conditioned on the query and preceding code, ranking proteins by identifier likelihood without explicitly labeling unrecorded pairs as negatives. We introduce ProTargetBench, the first proteome-scale benchmark for reverse target fishing to jointly support measured-panel discrimination and full-catalogue recovery of experimentally recorded positives. Covering 20,431 UniProt-reviewed human proteins, it integrates curated bioactivity evidence and distinguishes experimental inactivity from unmeasured associations. On 198 held-out molecules, GenFish achieves higher mean performance across all three full-catalogue retrieval metrics than four discriminative neural baselines and three non-neural baselines, including ligand-based methods. A controlled positive-hiding experiment shows that targeted removal of false-negative competition improves contrastive retrieval beyond matched random masking; GenFish remains stronger under the same incomplete supervision. Pfam alignment indicates that the semantic identifiers capture biologically meaningful relationships among proteins. These results establish generative retrieval as a principled paradigm for reverse target fishing under incomplete bioactivity records.
papers.summary: Reverse target fishing means finding the protein targets of a given molecule. Discriminative methods struggle here because bioactivity records are sparse and incomplete, so unrecorded molecule-protein pairs are wrongly treated as negatives. `GenFish` recasts the task as generative retrieval: it turns frozen protein language model features into semantic identifiers using residual vector quantization, then autoregressively generates those codes from a molecular fingerprint. The authors also release `ProTargetBench`, a proteome-scale benchmark covering 20,431 human proteins that separates experimentally confirmed inactivity from pairs that were never measured. On 198 held-out molecules, **`GenFish` beats four discriminative neural baselines and three non-neural baselines on all three full-catalogue retrieval metrics**, and its identifiers line up with biologically meaningful Pfam protein-family relationships.

papers.title: Measuring Empowerment from Offline Data for Intrinsically Motivated Exploration
papers.abstract: Large, unlabeled datasets of prior experience have become increasingly available for agentic tasks in domains such as robotics and coding. A common recipe for these tasks is to train a policy using the prior data, and then further improve it with online rollouts. But while much work has studied how to use both the offline and online data for policy extraction, far less work has been done to understand how the prior data can be used to efficiently \textit{explore} during the online learning phase. Previous work has attempted to formalize this idea by defining the \textit{empowerment}, a measure of how many future states an agent can realize; states with higher empowerment require more exploration as there are more futures to explore. However, existing methods for estimating empowerment require online policy rollouts in the environment. We propose the first method for estimating empowerment from unlabeled prior data, without any environment interaction. By jointly learning an empowerment-maximizing policy together with its discounted state-occupancy measure, our estimator can be trained on unlabeled trajectories generated from any unknown policy. We demonstrate that our empowerment estimator qualitatively gives intuitive empowerment measures and show that the pretrained estimator can be used to improve exploration in the online goal-conditioned reinforcement learning setting. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/ishirgarg/offline-empowerment}.
papers.summary: Empowerment measures how many future states an agent can reach from a given state, and it can guide exploration, but existing estimators need online rollouts in the environment. The authors propose **the first method to estimate empowerment purely from unlabeled offline trajectories**, collected by any unknown policy. It works by jointly learning an empowerment-maximizing policy and that policy's discounted state-occupancy measure. The resulting estimates are qualitatively intuitive, and a pretrained estimator improves exploration in online goal-conditioned reinforcement learning.

papers.title: Which Long Documents Matter? A Controlled Study of Data Selection for Context Extension
papers.abstract: Natural long documents are widely used for context extension, but which selection pipelines are effective remains unclear. We conduct a controlled comparison on Qwen2.5-3B at 128K under matched 6B-token continued-training budgets. Random sampling of natural long documents (random-long) outperforms repacking at longer evaluation lengths. Within the same candidate pool, selecting documents with high LongPPL key-token density yields further gains, unlike the evaluated generic-quality and LLM-judge selectors. We introduce truncLongPPL to reduce scoring cost by computing key-token density over a truncated prefix. At 128K, scoring the first half of the reference span yields downstream performance close to full-span scoring with a measured $2.28\times$ end-to-end scoring speedup. Across three training seeds, truncLongPPL achieves the highest mean scores among evaluated pipelines, exceeding random-long by 4.54 points on validation HELMET and 3.28 on held-out RULER, with gains most consistent in retrieval. At a 256K target context, it gains 2.82 average RULER points over random-long on Qwen2.5-3B. In short/long mixed training across Qwen2.5-3B, Qwen3-8B, and OLMo~3-7B, it gains 1.47--7.31 average RULER points over random-long mixing, with seven-task short-context averages within 0.23 points of the corresponding baselines. After supervised fine-tuning (SFT), Qwen3-8B and OLMo~3-7B models trained with selected long documents outperform their random-long counterparts by 1.13--1.67 points on LongBench v2 and 0.62--1.44 points on MRCR.
papers.summary: This controlled study asks which long documents work best for extending a model's context window, comparing selection pipelines on `Qwen2.5-3B` at 128K tokens with a matched budget of 6B continued-training tokens. Randomly sampling naturally long documents beats repacking shorter ones at longer evaluation lengths. Selecting documents by `LongPPL` key-token density helps further, while generic quality filters and LLM-judge selectors do not. The proposed `truncLongPPL` scores only a truncated prefix of each document, which makes scoring 2.28x faster, and it **beats random selection by 4.54 points on `HELMET` and 3.28 on `RULER`**. The gains carry over to 256K context, to `Qwen3-8B` and `OLMo 3-7B`, and through supervised fine-tuning, with short-context performance essentially unchanged.

papers.title: Pluralistic Alignment in Language Models: Objectives, Human References, and Preference Representations
papers.abstract: Pluralistic alignment aims to represent meaningful variation in human preferences rather than collapse heterogeneous judgments into a single target. Yet existing work often mixes three distinct questions: what pluralistic behavior a model should exhibit, whose preferences define the reference, and what evidence is sufficient to demonstrate success. We organize the literature around a two-layer taxonomy. Layer 1 distinguishes representing a range of human-supported viewpoints (Overton Pluralism), adapting faithfully to a specified perspective or preference condition (Steerable Pluralism), and matching the response distribution observed in a target population (Distributional Pluralism). Layer 2 distinguishes aggregate populations, countries and regions, and subgroups as human references. Preference representation, implementation mechanism, modality, and evidence quality are treated as cross-cutting design choices rather than additional forms of pluralism. We synthesize a protocol-bounded corpus of 70 works on pluralistic alignment and neighboring areas, using the objective-by-human-reference matrix to map existing approaches and identify underexplored combinations. The coded literature concentrates on Steerable Pluralism and Distributional Pluralism, while eligible Overton Pluralism work appears only at the aggregate-population level under our stated protocol. We then connect each objective to the evidence needed to support it, including perspective validity, conditional fidelity, distributional fidelity, support preservation, and uncertainty in subgroup estimates. Together, the taxonomy and evaluation framework clarify what current methods establish, where their claims exceed their evidence, and how future systems can represent disagreement without mistaking variation for faithful representation.
papers.summary: Pluralistic alignment aims for models that represent real variation in human preferences instead of collapsing them into a single target. This survey argues that the field often conflates three separate questions: what behavior is wanted, whose preferences serve as the reference, and what evidence shows success. It proposes a two-layer taxonomy. The first layer covers objectives: `Overton Pluralism`, which presents a range of supported viewpoints; `Steerable Pluralism`, which adapts to a specified perspective; and `Distributional Pluralism`, which matches a population's response distribution. The second layer covers reference populations, from aggregate populations to countries and subgroups. Mapping 70 works onto this grid shows **research concentrated on steerable and distributional objectives**, and the authors connect each objective to the evidence needed to support claims about it.

papers.title: Ben-Misandry: A Bengali Dataset and Late-Fusion Transformer Framework for Detecting Anti-Male Gender Hate
papers.abstract: Gender based hate speech research in Bengali has focused almost exclusively on misogyny, leaving anti male hate, or misandry, entirely unstudied for this language and creating a systematic blind spot in moderation systems trained to catch attacks on women but not on men. We introduce Ben-Misandry, the first Bengali misandry detection dataset: 5,000 comments across six taxonomy classes, including a novel category for mocking male emotional vulnerability with no direct analogue in existing misogyny taxonomies. The corpus is taxonomy-controlled synthetic data generated with GPT-4.1, spot-checked by four human reviewers on a 500-comment sample who confirmed the large majority of assigned labels; a full inter-annotator- agreement study is left to future work. We benchmark it with a classical pipeline (seven classifiers over four text representations) and a transformer pipeline (BanglaBERT, XLM-RoBERTa, and two fusion strategies). The best classical model, a linear SVM over character-level TF-IDF, reaches 91.8% accuracy; a late fusion ensemble averaging BanglaBERT and XLM-RoBERTa softmax outputs reaches 96.6% accuracy and macro ROC-AUC above 99%, nominally ahead of every single model and early fusion, though we have not run significance testing to confirm these margins are meaningful. We relate this to classifier combination theory, under which averaging encoders with decorrelated errors is expected to reduce variance, and corroborate the decision boundary with Shapley explanations that recover the same class- discriminative vocabulary found in our exploratory analysis, while noting this cannot rule out the model partly keying on synthetic-generation artifacts. Our results indicate misandry detection in Bengali is feasible and measurable on this synthetic corpus, offered as an initial public resource pending validation on real-world data.
papers.summary: Research on gender-based hate speech in Bengali has focused almost entirely on misogyny, leaving anti-male hate (misandry) unstudied. `Ben-Misandry` is a 5,000-comment dataset with six taxonomy classes, generated synthetically with `GPT-4.1` and spot-checked by human reviewers on a 500-comment sample. In benchmarks, a linear SVM over character-level TF-IDF features reaches 91.8% accuracy, and **a late-fusion ensemble of `BanglaBERT` and `XLM-RoBERTa` reaches 96.6% accuracy**. The authors note that they ran no significance tests and that the models may partly key on artifacts of synthetic generation, so the results still need validation on real-world data.

papers.title: Private Evaluation of High-Dimensional Functions
papers.abstract:
We study differentially private black-box evaluation of arbitrary high-dimensional functions. Given a dataset $S$ and query access to a function $f$---whose sensitivity may be unknown or unbounded---the goal is to privately output an approximation to $f(S)$. The black-box evaluator can only query the value of $f$ over a down neighborhood of $S$ (i.e., those subsets of $S$ that are obtained by removing a bounded number of elements from $S$). We design generic black-box evaluators for both pure and approximate differential privacy through a reduction to high-dimensional private quasi-concave optimization (QCO).
  Our black-box evaluator enjoys a geometric notion of utility. Consider the vectors obtained by applying $f$ on sets in a down neighborhood of $S$. With high probability, the evaluator's output is guaranteed to be in the convex hull of these vectors.
  Our work generalizes the result of Linder et al. [LRSS25] for real-valued function evaluation to high dimensions. It also recovers the private center-point guarantees of Beimel et al. [BMNS19], with an explicit additive approximation to maximum Tukey depth. We also apply our evaluators to user-level quasi-concave and convex optimization, showing how they can improve upon the sample-and-aggregate baseline of Nissim et al. [NRS07] by replacing the multiplicative data overhead with an additive overhead.
  Finally, we show that our formulation of high dimensional black-box evaluation and high dimensional private QCO are equivalent up to a factor of the dimension: the hardest private evaluation instances already arise from the cases that $f$ is a (non-private) quasi-concave optimizer.
papers.summary: The goal is to privately approximate an arbitrary high-dimensional function of a dataset under differential privacy, using only black-box queries to the function on subsets that differ from the dataset by a bounded number of removed elements; the function's sensitivity may be unknown or unbounded. The authors build generic evaluators for both pure and approximate differential privacy by reducing the problem to private quasi-concave optimization. **The output lies, with high probability, in the convex hull of the function's values on those subsets.** The framework extends earlier real-valued results to high dimensions, recovers known private center-point guarantees, and improves user-level private optimization by replacing a multiplicative data overhead with an additive one.

papers.title: Beyond Recall Saturation: Scaling Hard-Negative Reranker Training for Industrial Legal Retrieval
papers.abstract: Industrial retrieval systems often improve quality by enlarging embedding candidate pools or adopting complex training pipelines. We show that, under a sufficiently large but practical candidate pool, embedding recall exhibits diminishing returns, motivating a closer examination of reranker quality. On Chinese legal retrieval benchmarks, embedding top-300 reaches a high-recall operating region, while relevant evidence may still be ranked below the output cutoff. We compare hard-negative strategies for reranker training, including embedding-mined, self-mined, and dynamic-negative variants, under aligned retrieval protocols that evaluate reranking after candidate retrieval. Among the evaluated staged configurations, an embedding-to-self-mined pipeline provides a favorable trade-off; additional dynamic stages do not improve all held-out metrics. The selected pipeline scales from a 0.6B to a 4B reranker. Relative to the native 4B reranker, the trained 4B Stage2 model improves reported metrics on the STARD and CSAID benchmarks and on an internal development set, and is preferred in 72.4\% of non-tied comparisons on 410 de-identified, reconstructed internal operational-query inputs in a latency-sensitive offline preference evaluation. These results support evaluating the retrieval and reranking stages separately when selecting an optimization target for industrial retrieval systems.
papers.summary: Industrial retrieval systems often try to improve quality by enlarging the candidate pool returned by embedding search. On Chinese legal retrieval benchmarks, however, the authors find that **recall levels off around the top 300 embedding candidates**, so the bottleneck shifts to reranking. They compare hard-negative strategies for training rerankers, including embedding-mined, self-mined and dynamic negatives, and find that an embedding-mined stage followed by a self-mined stage gives the best trade-off. Scaled to a 4B reranker, this pipeline improves on the native model on the `STARD` and `CSAID` benchmarks and is preferred in 72.4% of non-tied comparisons on internal operational queries.

papers.title: Write Once, Check Many: Reusable Ledgers for Post-Hoc Policy Compliance Auditing of Agent Trajectories
papers.abstract: Auditing LLM agents against policies is critical to ensure safety but requires rereading long trajectories once per policy. Can we instead record each trajectory once and reuse that record for policies not known in advance? We propose write once, check many, a framework in which a writer model converts each agent trajectory into a policy-independent ledger of the agent's actions and outcomes. A reader then checks each new policy against the ledger alone, without access to the original trajectory. On 900 trajectories from SHADE-Arena, $\tau$-bench, and $\tau^2$-bench, we show that a 12B reader of narrative ledgers can either match or in fact achieve higher AUC than the same 12B model reading full trajectories. On SHADE-Arena policies that combine several facts, our approach outperforms a 31B model reading the trajectory (.777 vs. .713 AUC). When checking eight SHADE-Arena policies separately, ledgers use about $5\times$ fewer tokens, including the cost of writing them. A deeper analysis shows that rule-based extraction performs better on some single-action policies, and ledgers can miss evidence in long tool outputs and message contents. Our results suggest that reusable, policy-independent records can make retrospective agent auditing more efficient and effective, and highlight important considerations in ledger design.
papers.summary: Auditing LLM agents against policies usually means rereading long trajectories once for every policy. In the proposed write-once, check-many framework, a writer model converts each trajectory into a policy-independent ledger of the agent's actions and outcomes, and a reader model later checks new policies against the ledger alone. On 900 trajectories from `SHADE-Arena`, `tau-bench` and `tau2-bench`, a 12B reader of narrative ledgers matches or beats the same model reading full trajectories, and on multi-fact policies it **outperforms a 31B model reading the raw trajectory (0.777 vs. 0.713 AUC)**. Checking eight policies costs about 5x fewer tokens, including the cost of writing the ledgers, though ledgers can miss evidence buried in long tool outputs.

papers.title: Modeling Discourse Profiles in Climate Misinformation Discourse
papers.abstract: Prior work on climate misinformation detection typically classifies individual comments or claims using text alone. This framing overlooks a key property of online climate discourse: misinformation is often produced, reinforced, and sustained through recurring rhetorical patterns that reappear across comments and threads. Using a large-scale TikTok climate discourse dataset, we construct discourse profiles by clustering climate-related comments into recurring rhetorical patterns. We then incorporate these profiles into fine-grained climate misinformation classifiers using a late-fusion architecture. Under video-disjoint evaluation across three training seeds, discourse-profile-aware models significantly improve macro-F1 over text-only baselines for bag-of-words, TF-IDF, and MPNet representations. RoBERTa-large exhibits a positive mean improvement but substantially greater variability, and the difference is not statistically significant. Beyond classification, our results show discourse profiles shape misinformation reception and propagation. Discourse-profile-conditioned language model agents exhibit misinformation acceptance patterns aligned with profile-level misinformation prevalence in ClimateDisc, and the relationship between misinformation prevalence and engagement persistence differs across dominant discourse profiles.
papers.summary: Climate misinformation detection usually classifies individual comments from their text alone, ignoring rhetorical patterns that recur across comments and threads. Working with a large TikTok climate-discourse dataset, the authors cluster comments into 'discourse profiles' and feed them into fine-grained misinformation classifiers through late fusion. On evaluations where training and test comments come from different videos, **profile-aware models significantly improve macro-F1** for bag-of-words, TF-IDF and `MPNet` representations. For `RoBERTa-large` the gain is not statistically significant. Language model agents conditioned on a discourse profile also accept misinformation at rates that track the profile's misinformation prevalence.

papers.title: Vocal-Tract Acoustics, Aerodynamics, and Overlap-and-Add Synthesis in DYNARTmo
papers.abstract: This paper presents the acoustic and aerodynamic extension of DYNARTmo, a dynamic articulatory model for visualizing and synthesizing speech production. Gestural control trajectories determine vocal-tract geometry, which is converted into an acoustic tube with nasal branching and effective lateral passages. A lumped aerodynamic network relates prescribed glottal motion and pulmonary pressure to airflow and supraglottal pressure storage. Phonatory excitation, oral friction, and glottal aspiration are synthesized as separate contributions. Frame-specific acoustic responses are combined by overlap-and-add, preserving response tails beyond individual control frames. Three German words, ``Tasse'', ``Muse'', and ``Lade'', illustrate the coordination of articulation, pressure, flow, and acoustic sources across vowels, nasals, laterals, fricatives, and plosives. The implementation has been optimized by the author primarily for sound recognizability; independent perceptual evaluation remains outstanding, and fricative-noise naturalness requires further refinement. The model provides an inspectable, articulatorily controlled production plant for future neural simulations of babbling, imitation, and early word acquisition. Further work will improve acoustic realism, reduce empirical source corrections, and extend the sensory information available to developmental learning models.
papers.summary: This work extends `DYNARTmo`, a dynamic articulatory model of speech production, with acoustics and aerodynamics. Gestural control trajectories set the vocal-tract geometry, which is converted into an acoustic tube with nasal and lateral branches and paired with a lumped airflow model. Voicing, frication and aspiration are synthesized as separate sources. Each frame's acoustic response is combined by overlap-and-add, so response tails carry over past individual control frames. Three German words demonstrate **coordinated articulation, pressure, flow and sound sources**, though no independent perceptual evaluation has yet been done.

papers.title: VBO-MI: A Differentiable Black-Box Optimization Framework via Variational Mutual Information Estimation
papers.abstract: Many real-world tasks require optimizing expensive black-box functions accessible only through noisy evaluations, a setting commonly addressed with Bayesian optimization. While Gaussian processes(GPs) and Bayesian neural networks have driven significant progress, GP-based methods scale cubically with observations, and BNN-based approaches remain burdened by expensive posterior sampling such as Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, and inner-loop acquisition optimization in high-dimensional setting. In this work, we propose VBO-MI, a fully gradient-based BO framework that requires no assumptions on a Gaussian prior or a variational posterior family over $f$. While our framework uses gradient-based updates to train the internal action and information-estimation networks, it treats the objective function $f$ as a strict black box, requiring only zeroth-order evaluations. To enable end-to-end gradient flow, we employ an actor-critic architecture consisting of an action-net to navigate the input space and a variational critic to estimate a surrogate information signal for exploration. Additionally, we design a lightweight surrogate that approximates the objective from observed data using a replay buffer, which reduces the total required real function queries to one batch per iteration. We provide theoretical analysis for our framework, establishing convergence of its training objective and surrogate estimator, and showing, that near-optimal solutions exist. We evaluate our method on a diverse suite of benchmarks, including high-dimensional synthetic function and complex real-world tasks such as Rover Trajectory planning optimization, the Lunar Lander, and Pest Control problems. Our experiments demonstrate that VBO-MI provides the same or superior optimization performance over the various baselines.
papers.summary: Bayesian optimization of expensive black-box functions usually relies on Gaussian processes, whose cost grows cubically with the number of observations, or on Bayesian neural networks, which need costly posterior sampling. `VBO-MI` is a fully gradient-based alternative. An actor network proposes query points, a variational critic estimates a mutual-information signal that drives exploration, and a lightweight surrogate trained on a replay buffer keeps real function queries to one batch per iteration; the objective itself is still treated strictly as a black box. The authors prove convergence of the training objective and surrogate, and report **performance matching or beating baselines** on high-dimensional synthetic functions, rover trajectory planning, `Lunar Lander` and pest control.

papers.title: Backend-Frontend Converter: Component-Based Conversion of .NET Computational Models to TypeScript
papers.abstract: Computational models developed in .NET often need to run locally within web applications. We present Backend--Frontend Converter, an architecture for generating TypeScript implementations of component-based models. The converter maps components, connections, aliases, and formula trees to model-specific TypeScript code. Reusable runtime libraries provide numerical integration, data access, and state handling. We evaluate stored generated implementations through four orbital scenarios and a recorded trading-strategy comparison. Orbital calculations execute in a browser and are paired with C\# results by crossing event and timestamp; trading outputs are aligned by date.
