Analytic scheduler tests and deliberately perturbed outputs assess the validation procedure. Each orbital scenario produces 91 paired events with identical timestamps. Position and velocity differences remain below $(10^{-6}\)~km$ and $(10^{-9}\)~km/s$. All 20 analytic scheduler checks pass, and the comparator detects each of three prescribed state and time perturbations. The trading comparison contains 501 aligned daily records with matching indicator values, positions, and order events. The evaluated implementations preserve the compared outputs across the C#/TypeScript boundary. Component-specific generation and reusable execution libraries provide a practical route from supported .NET computational models to TypeScript applications.
papers.summary: Computational models written in .NET often need to run locally inside web applications. The proposed converter generates model-specific TypeScript by mapping a model's components, connections, aliases and formula trees, and relies on reusable runtime libraries for numerical integration, data access and state handling. Across four orbital scenarios, the browser results match the C# originals with **position differences below 1e-6 km** and identical event timestamps. A trading-strategy comparison also matches across 501 daily records, and the validation procedure detects deliberately injected perturbations.

papers.title: CoTs remain monitorable when being unfaithful requires computation: Replicating and Extending the Necessity Effect Across Eleven Models
papers.abstract: While a LLM's chain of thought (CoT) is a promising approach to interpreting model outputs, prior work shows CoT's content does not always accurately reflect the reasoning process. Emmons et al. (2025) finds that models can follow a question hint without revealing so in its chain of thought, but when the hint is sufficiently complex the computation is forced into the CoT. This claim, however, has only been tested on Gemini models, and the datasets and code is closed source. We replicate their proxy task across eleven models from six families and find the necessity effect generalizes. Every model follows simple cues above a no-hint baseline, while concealed complex-cue following falls back near baseline for most models. We also extend the study from Emmons et al. (2025) to measure CoT-necessity and unfaithfulness across five cue families (four of them new) and three difficulty levels. The relationship between when CoT is necessary and unfaithfulness is task-specific and model-specific. For some hint types, models often verbalize their hint-following behavior even when the hint can be decoded in a single forward pass. These results support the case for CoT monitoring when unsafe behavior requires non-trivial computation, and that properties of CoT unfaithfulness are sensitive to model and setting.
papers.summary: Earlier work found that models can follow a hint in a question without mentioning it in their chain of thought (CoT), but that sufficiently complex hints force the reasoning into the CoT, where a monitor can see it. That finding was only tested on Gemini models with closed data. This replication across eleven models from six families finds that **the necessity effect generalizes**: every model follows simple cues, but concealed following of complex cues drops back near baseline for most models. An extension to five cue families and three difficulty levels shows that the link between CoT necessity and unfaithfulness depends on the task and the model. The results support CoT monitoring for unsafe behavior that requires non-trivial computation.

papers.title: TideKV: Delayed KV Eviction via Layer-Wise Chunked Prefill for Memory-Efficient Long-Context LLM Inference
papers.abstract: Long-context large language model (LLM) inference is important for modern intelligent applications but remains constrained by peak memory during prompt prefill. Existing KV cache compression reduces decoding memory but typically requires full-prompt prefill to preserve global context, retaining a high construction peak. Online chunk-level eviction lowers memory earlier but selects before each layer has observed the complete prompt, potentially degrading cache construction and decoding. We present TideKV, an on-GPU cache-construction architecture using layer-major delayed eviction. TideKV processes all prompt chunks within each Transformer layer, retains full-prompt KV only for the active layer, and evicts at layer end. This schedule preserves full-prompt-aware selection while reducing activation and temporary memory. Experiments across multiple computing platforms show that TideKV preserves the inference quality and final cache size of the evaluated compression methods. At 64K on A100, it reduces the construction-time transient footprint by 83.89%. On RTX 4090, it increases time to first token by only 1.06% at 64K and enables 128K prefill. TideKV also completes 128K on Jetson, whereas matched post-prefill compression runs out of memory on both resource-constrained platforms. These results show that delayed layer-end eviction substantially expands feasible context lengths without sacrificing cache utility.
papers.summary: Peak memory during prompt prefill limits long-context LLM inference. Existing KV-cache compression still processes the full prompt before evicting entries, while online chunk-level eviction decides what to drop before each layer has seen the whole prompt. `TideKV` processes all prompt chunks within one Transformer layer at a time, keeps the full-prompt KV cache only for the active layer, and evicts at the end of that layer, so eviction decisions still see the entire prompt. It preserves the quality and final cache size of the compression methods it wraps while **cutting construction-time transient memory by 83.89% at 64K on an A100**. On an RTX 4090 it adds only 1.06% to time to first token at 64K, and it enables 128K prefill on both the RTX 4090 and a Jetson device, where matched post-prefill compression runs out of memory.

papers.title: HiPPO Functional Memory: Coordinate-Queryable Attention for Irregular Time Series
papers.abstract: Irregular time series require models to answer temporal queries at arbitrary coordinates, yet existing approaches typically retain observation-dependent representations that must be repeatedly resolved for each query. We introduce HiPPO Functional Memory (HiPPO-FM), a functional-memory attention operator that compiles an irregular history into a reusable coordinate-addressable state. Instead of storing observation-indexed tokens or latent trajectories, HiPPO-FM writes observations into a fixed-rank functional space and performs direct coordinate evaluation through matched functional geometry. Kernel-smoothed HiPPO coordinates and Gram-based readout define a shared write/read mechanism, while observed-support self-attention enables content-dependent representations before compression. We characterize the induced finite-dimensional query space and derive an error decomposition separating functional geometry approximation from learned-memory mismatch. Across continuous-coordinate reconstruction, irregular representation learning, real-world extrapolation, and event-sequence prediction, HiPPO-FM consistently improves strong irregular time-series baselines, achieving strong reconstruction accuracy on Spiral, competitive performance across 20 UEA datasets, improved real-world extrapolation, and superior results on several irregular event benchmarks. After encoding, the compact functional state can be reused across different query sets without reprocessing the observation history.
papers.summary: Models for irregularly sampled time series have to answer queries at arbitrary time coordinates, yet most keep observation-dependent representations that must be reprocessed for each query. `HiPPO Functional Memory` (`HiPPO-FM`) compiles an irregular history into a reusable, fixed-rank functional state that can be evaluated directly at any coordinate. It uses kernel-smoothed `HiPPO` coordinates for writing and Gram-based readout for reading, with self-attention over observations before compression. The authors derive an error decomposition and report **consistent gains over strong irregular time-series baselines** in reconstruction, representation learning on 20 `UEA` datasets, extrapolation and event-sequence prediction.

papers.title: BEM: Learning Bregman Divergences for Concept Erasure in Flow Matching Models
papers.abstract: Concept erasure removes harmful, private, or copyrighted concepts from text-to-image models while preserving their other abilities. Leading models such as FLUX and Stable Diffusion 3 are trained with flow matching, and erasure methods for them fine-tune the model toward a guided teacher's velocities under a Euclidean loss. Yet the squared distance is only one member of a larger family: Bregman divergences are exactly the losses under which flow matching recovers the correct velocity field, and each member shapes differently what is erased and what is preserved. We introduce BEM (Bregman erasure matching), which is, to our knowledge, the first to learn this divergence through bi-level optimization, so that the fine-tuned model forgets the concept on unseen prompts while its unrelated generations stay unchanged. In the experiments we target the suppression of nudity, violence, real identities, and copyrighted characters. Under the evaluation protocol of GEM, BEM removes more of the concept than GEM on most settings, cutting the unsafe rate on bloody gore from 53.9% to 14.4% and the FID on nudity from 8.64 to 6.64, while retention holds on some concepts and degrades on others.
papers.summary: Concept erasure removes harmful, private or copyrighted concepts from text-to-image models such as `FLUX` and `Stable Diffusion 3`, which are trained with flow matching. Existing erasure methods fine-tune these models with a squared-Euclidean loss, but flow matching recovers the correct velocity field under any Bregman divergence, and each choice of divergence changes what gets erased and what is preserved. `BEM` (Bregman erasure matching) learns the divergence through bi-level optimization. Under the `GEM` evaluation protocol it erases more than `GEM` in most settings, for example **cutting the unsafe rate on bloody gore from 53.9% to 14.4%**, although retention of unrelated content holds for some concepts and degrades for others.

papers.title: Denoising Implicit Variational Inference
papers.abstract: Semi-implicit variational inference (SIVI) expands the representational capacity of variational families, but optimizing the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) remains challenging because the marginal score of the semi-implicit distribution is generally intractable. Unbiased Implicit Variational Inference (UIVI) and related methods address this difficulty through reparameterized ELBO gradients, but existing approaches estimate the required score indirectly through reverse-conditional sampling or approximation, which can be computationally costly and unstable. We propose Denoising Implicit Variational Inference (DIVI), which learns the marginal score directly via denoising score matching. The learned score is used as a plug-in estimator in the pathwise ELBO gradient, replacing inner reverse-conditional sampling with a score-network evaluation. We analyze DIVI as inexact stochastic gradient ascent and show, under stated assumptions, that the averaged stationarity measure is controlled by the usual optimization term and the average score-matching error. Empirically, we evaluate DIVI on both synthetic distributions and a variety of real-data Bayesian inference tasks. The results show that DIVI improves over the current UIVI baselines while reducing the cost of ELBO-gradient estimation.
papers.summary: Semi-implicit variational inference (SIVI) uses richer variational families, but optimizing the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) is hard because the marginal score of these distributions is intractable. Existing methods such as Unbiased Implicit Variational Inference (UIVI) estimate that score indirectly through costly and sometimes unstable reverse-conditional sampling. `DIVI` (Denoising Implicit Variational Inference) instead learns the marginal score directly with denoising score matching and plugs it into the pathwise ELBO gradient. The authors bound its convergence in terms of the score-matching error, and experiments show **improvements over `UIVI` baselines at lower gradient-estimation cost**.

papers.title: What "Form'' of Uncertainty Does Conformal Prediction Quantify?
papers.abstract: Conformal prediction (CP) is a post-hoc calibration method that returns prediction sets with distribution-free coverage guarantees, and the size of the output set is often interpreted as a notion of uncertainty. We show that the difference in set size between full and split CP is directly connected to Bayesian posterior variance, which is the epistemic uncertainty of the model. Essentially, this difference in set size is an aggregation of two opposite effects: (1) better model accuracy and therefore smaller set size achieved by training over extra calibration points, and (2) the "formability" of the model at test point towards every possible label. The latter effect vanishes with stronger models or more calibration data (as epistemic uncertainty is known for that behavior). It turns out that the model's formability itself (without the quantization effect of prediction sets, and through estimating the posterior variance) is a useful tool to quantify the epistemic uncertainty. In our empirical evaluation it performs on par with the state of the art in many setups.
papers.summary: Conformal prediction (CP) produces prediction sets with distribution-free coverage guarantees, and set size is often read as a measure of uncertainty. The authors show that **the gap in set size between full and split CP is tied to Bayesian posterior variance**, which corresponds to the model's epistemic uncertainty. This gap combines two opposing effects: better accuracy from training on the extra calibration points, and the model's 'formability', meaning how easily it can be pushed toward each possible label at the test point. Estimated directly, formability performs on par with state-of-the-art epistemic uncertainty measures in many setups.

papers.title: TopoCompile: Molecular Generation with Exact Global Count Constraints
papers.abstract: Molecular generation designs novel molecules with desired structures and properties. Global count constraints specify molecular size, elemental composition, and ring content without prescribing detailed structure. Property-conditioned generators steer generation toward such targets but do not guarantee exact satisfaction. We introduce TopoCompile, which combines an autoregressive component-tree generator with a dynamic-programming compiler for supported component-additive integer counts. TopoCompile represents molecules as trees of intact ring systems and individual atoms, making each supported count additive over components. At each step, an autoregressive Transformer scores component and attachment actions, while the compiler masks actions with no target-satisfying completion. Within the fixed component vocabulary and typed attachment rules, constrained decoding guarantees exact equality for supported non-negative, component-additive integer counts. Applied at inference time, these checks let the same trained generator support different targets and count combinations without retraining. Across four benchmarks, TopoCompile achieves 100% Exact-valid yield for Common and Rare four-count target groups; the strongest baseline within each dataset reaches 44.9% or less on Rare targets. In unconditional generation, it achieves the highest validity or valid-unique-novel (V.U.N.) among the compared methods across all four benchmark datasets.
papers.summary: Generators that are conditioned on molecular properties can be steered toward targets such as atom counts, elemental composition or ring content, but they do not guarantee that the output hits those targets exactly. `TopoCompile` represents each molecule as a tree of intact ring systems and individual atoms, so that each supported count becomes a sum over components. An autoregressive Transformer scores possible next components and attachments, while a dynamic-programming compiler masks out any action from which the target counts can no longer be reached. Because the check runs only at decoding time, one trained model can serve many target combinations without retraining. Across four benchmarks it reaches **100% exact-valid yield on both common and rare four-count targets**, against at most 44.9% for the strongest baseline on rare targets, and it also leads on validity or on valid-unique-novel (V.U.N.) rate in unconditional generation.

papers.title: ProbePO: Sparse Probes, Redistributed Credit for Critic-Free LLM Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards assigns one terminal reward to an entire reasoning trajectory, obscuring how individual reasoning steps contributed to the outcome. GRPO broadcasts a group-normalized advantage to every response token, while finer-grained approaches often rely on dense auxiliary rollouts or branching schemes that can also alter the data used for policy updates. We cast the missing middle as budgeted measurement: with a limited rollout budget, which partial solutions should be evaluated, and how should their value estimates refine credit? ProbePO selects partial-solution states with a reward-free uncertainty score and estimates their expected verifier rewards under a capped continuation budget. ProbePO redistributes, rather than replaces, GRPO's trajectory-level advantage across tokens while preserving each trajectory's mean token-level advantage; probe continuations serve only as measurements. Across three DeepSeekMath and Qwen-family models spanning 1.5B-7B parameters, ProbePO consistently outperforms GRPO and achieves the highest accuracy among the four evaluated methods in 16 of 18 model-benchmark comparisons. Against dense-probing VinePPO on DeepSeekMath-7B, ProbePO achieves higher accuracy on all six benchmarks with 76% less end-to-end training time.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards gives a whole reasoning trajectory a single terminal reward, so it is unclear which steps helped. `GRPO` handles this by applying the same advantage to every token, while finer-grained alternatives depend on costly dense rollouts. `ProbePO` treats credit assignment as a measurement problem on a fixed budget: it picks a few uncertain partial solutions using a reward-free uncertainty score, estimates their expected verifier reward with a capped number of continuations, and uses these estimates to redistribute the trajectory-level `GRPO` advantage across tokens while keeping its mean unchanged. On `DeepSeekMath` and `Qwen`-family models from 1.5B to 7B parameters, it is the best of four methods in 16 of 18 model-benchmark comparisons. On `DeepSeekMath-7B` it beats dense-probing `VinePPO` on all six benchmarks with **76% less end-to-end training time**.

papers.title: Axiomatic World Modeling for Physics Reasoning
papers.abstract: Recent research-level physics-reasoning benchmarks for LLMs reveal a failure mode that lies not in knowledge or execution, but in modeling the world being reasoned about. Models often silently alter given quantities, fabricate laws, or inject unstated assumptions to force a problem into familiar patterns, and then reason inside this corrupted world. We define this premise-level divergence as modeling drift: the gap between a model's internal axiomatic world model (AWM) and the true physical world specified in the problem. Although RLVR and PRM have yielded substantial gains in mathematics and code, their reward shapes do not directly supervise world modeling in axiomatic domains such as physics. We propose Reinforcement Learning with Axiomatic World Modeling (RLAWM), which optimizes the policy by penalizing divergence between its inferred axiomatic world model and the true physics world. RLAWM probes physics reasoning at two hierarchical levels (modeling and solving), each scored by a physically grounded reward. The modeling reward targets abstract knowledge formulation, evaluating whether the model captures the true axiomatic world before attempting calculation. The solving reward targets instantiated knowledge reasoning, checking whether the model's concrete derivation remains consistent with the axiomatic world. This two-level structure separates what world the model believes it is reasoning in from how it reasons within that world. The framework operates exclusively during training, with no extra cost during inference. RLAWM improves performance by up to +12.2 points on PhysReason and +5.2 on PHYSICS over the baseline. It also generalizes zero-shot across difficulty, source, and domain, with a 2.45x gain and +10 points over the strongest baseline on olympiad-level physics and math.
papers.summary: On research-level physics benchmarks, LLMs often fail because they misread the setup of the problem rather than because they lack knowledge or make calculation errors: they silently change given quantities, invent laws or add unstated assumptions, then reason correctly inside that distorted setup. The authors call this gap between the model's internal axiomatic world model (AWM) and the physics the problem actually specifies "modeling drift". They propose Reinforcement Learning with Axiomatic World Modeling (`RLAWM`), which gives two physically grounded rewards during training: one for whether the model sets up the correct axiomatic world before calculating, and one for whether its concrete derivation stays consistent with that world. The method adds no cost at inference time and improves results by **up to +12.2 points on `PhysReason`** and +5.2 on `PHYSICS`. It also generalizes zero-shot to olympiad-level physics and math problems.

papers.title: Reconstruction of Unobserved Core Electron Density in Tokamak Plasmas with a Neural Operator Transport Surrogate and Uncertainty Quantification
papers.abstract: Real-time control of tokamak plasmas requires the electron density profile. However, in a reactor-relevant device, diagnostic port access is limited and the profile can be observed only partially. In the present work we reconstruct the density profile by inferring the coefficients of a physics-based one-dimensional particle transport equation, using a Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) surrogate of the transport solver as a fast differentiable forward model. The surrogate enables realtime-compatible gradient-based reconstruction and uncertainty quantification from the reflectometry and interferometry measurements. We compare four uncertainty quantification methods - multi-seed ensembles, the Laplace approximation, Metropolis-Hastings, and a Gaussian method independent of the reconstruction fit. The resulting uncertainty is scored with CRPS and coverage calibration, separately on the observed and unobserved regions. We further demonstrate advantage of our approach over standard analytical function fit on synthetic and experimental DIII-D discharges.
papers.summary: Real-time control of a tokamak plasma requires the electron density profile, but in reactor-like devices diagnostic access is limited and only part of the profile can be measured. The authors reconstruct the full profile by inferring the coefficients of a one-dimensional particle transport equation. A `Fourier Neural Operator` (FNO) trained to mimic the transport solver serves as a fast, differentiable forward model, which makes gradient-based fitting to reflectometry and interferometry data compatible with real-time use. They compare four uncertainty quantification methods (multi-seed ensembles, the Laplace approximation, Metropolis-Hastings, and a Gaussian method independent of the fit) and score each separately on the observed and unobserved regions of the profile. On synthetic and experimental `DIII-D` discharges, the approach **outperforms standard analytical function fits**.

papers.title: Rethinking EEG Spatial Super-Resolution as Dynamic State Decomposition and Filtering
papers.abstract: EEG spatial super-resolution aims to recover high-density neural signals from sparse electrode observations. Existing methods have achieved substantial progress through spatial modeling, generative reconstruction, and temporal representation learning. However, the current EEG state contains two different sources of information: predictable evolution inherited from preceding states and newly emerging changes revealed by the current observation. Most approaches typically do not model these two components explicitly. In this work, we formulate streaming EEG spatial super-resolution as a sequential state filtering problem and propose Dynamic State Filtering (DSF). Rather than relying on a single temporal reconstruction pathway, DSF combines a history-aware dynamical branch with an innovation-filtering branch that explicitly decomposes waveform-state estimation into prediction and observation-driven correction. To infer how spatially incomplete innovations should affect missing locations, DSF routes the observed innovations across electrodes through a mask-constrained, topology-aware transition operator and incorporates them through uncertainty-aware state correction. The two complementary estimates are finally fused to reconstruct the dense EEG signal. Experiments on SEED, SEED-IV and BCI2000 demonstrate that DSF improves reconstruction fidelity and downstream utility while maintaining robustness under dynamically changing and unreliable sparse observations.
papers.summary: EEG spatial super-resolution tries to reconstruct high-density brain signals from a sparse set of electrodes. The authors argue that the current signal state mixes two parts that existing methods do not separate: a predictable evolution carried over from earlier states, and new changes revealed by the current observation. `Dynamic State Filtering` (DSF) treats streaming super-resolution as a sequential filtering problem. A history-aware branch predicts the next state, while an innovation-filtering branch passes the newly observed changes to missing electrodes through a topology-aware transition operator and applies an uncertainty-aware correction. On `SEED`, `SEED-IV` and `BCI2000`, DSF **improves reconstruction fidelity and downstream utility** and stays robust when the sparse observations change over time or become unreliable.

papers.title: Contrastive Hypergraph Source-free Domain Adaptive Object Detection in Adverse Weather Conditions--Extended Version
papers.abstract: Adverse weather conditions such as fog, rain, snow, and low illumination introduce structured visibility degradations that severely impair object detectors trained on clear-weather data. When source data are inaccessible due to privacy or trans- mission constraints, source-free domain adaptation (SFDA) becomes necessary. However, existing SFDA methods based on pairwise contrastive learning struggle to capture high-order semantics and often suffer from agreement collapse under severe corruption. We propose REUNION, a hypergraph-guided SFDA framework for object detection in adverse weather conditions. REUNION constructs a contrastive hypergraph over target-domain object proposals, encoding high-order relations through intra-image context, weather-aware grouping, prototype-based semantic anchors, and uncertainty-aware connections between reliable and low-confidence instances. To effectively exploit these structured relations, we introduce a group-wise Hyper-InfoNCE objective that optimizes representations at the hyperedge level, enabling semantic information to propagate from confident proposals to corrupted or low-contrast instances. Experiments with diverse benchmarks demonstrate that REUNION effectively mitigates domain shifts and achieves state-of-the-art performance in SFDA settings.
papers.summary: Fog, rain, snow and low light degrade object detectors trained on clear-weather images. When the original training data is unavailable, adaptation has to be source-free (SFDA), and existing SFDA methods built on pairwise contrastive learning miss higher-order relations and can collapse under heavy corruption. `REUNION` builds a contrastive hypergraph over object proposals in the target domain, linking them through intra-image context, weather-aware grouping, prototype-based anchors, and connections between confident and uncertain instances. A group-wise `Hyper-InfoNCE` loss operates at the level of these hyperedges, so semantic information flows from confident detections to degraded ones. The authors report **state-of-the-art SFDA detection performance** across several adverse-weather benchmarks.

papers.title: Structured Latent Dynamics for Long-Horizon Embodied World Models
papers.abstract: Reliable long-horizon prediction remains a central challenge for embodied world models. Although recent generative models can synthesize visually plausible action-conditioned futures, their latent dynamics are typically learned through unconstrained transition modules, which may gradually deviate from coherent physical evolution as predictions are recursively rolled forward. We investigate whether explicitly structuring latent state evolution can improve the stability and utility of such imagined trajectories. To this end, we introduce HWM, a structured dynamics framework that represents backbone latents in a learned phase space consisting of generalized coordinates and momenta. Future states are propagated through dissipative Hamiltonian dynamics and mapped back to the original latent representation through a learnable inverse interface. The resulting formulation can be integrated into existing world-model architectures without redesigning their perception or decoding components, while multi-step transition supervision encourages the structured rollout to remain aligned with the latent trajectories induced by real observations. Controlled simulation experiments show that HWM produces more accurate estimates of velocity, acceleration, and jerk and substantially reduces long-horizon energy drift relative to unstructured latent dynamics. We further evaluate the approach across three distinct embodied world-model settings, covering single-arm multi-view prediction with Ctrl-World, dual-arm single-view prediction with EVAC, and task-oriented single-arm prediction with Cosmos-Predict2.5-2B. On RoboCasa, incorporating HWM into Cosmos-Predict2.5-2B yields a 2.7% relative improvement in task success. On real-world AgiBot World trajectories, it improves nDTW by 9.7% with Ctrl-World and Logic by 8.4% with EVAC.
papers.summary: Embodied world models can generate plausible action-conditioned video, but their learned latent transitions tend to drift away from physically coherent motion over long rollouts. `HWM` maps backbone latents into a learned phase space of generalized coordinates and momenta, steps them forward with dissipative Hamiltonian dynamics, and maps them back through a learnable inverse interface. Because of this design, it can be added to existing world models without changing their perception or decoding components. In controlled simulations it estimates velocity, acceleration and jerk more accurately and **substantially reduces long-horizon energy drift**. Added to `Cosmos-Predict2.5-2B`, `Ctrl-World` and `EVAC`, it raises `RoboCasa` task success by 2.7% (relative) and improves real-world `AgiBot World` metrics by 8 to 10%.

papers.title: From Score to Diagnosis: Search-Independent Post-Diagnosis for Symbolic Regression
papers.abstract: Symbolic regression (SR) solvers employ diverse search mechanisms, yet most rely on the same low-information scalar fitness. Such scores provide little guidance on why a skeleton fails or how it should be revised. Recent methods develop new methods to address this bottleneck. Their enhanced feedback mechanisms are tightly coupled to their search processes and are difficult to reuse across diverse SR solvers. Instead, we ask whether a shared feedback mechanism can further improve diverse solvers facing the same bottleneck. To this end, we propose PostDiag, a search-independent feedback mechanism, which can be shared to different SR solvers. PostDiag introduces Patch-wise Feature Profiling (PFP) to capture local behavior through patch-wise features of level, trend, and roughness. Based on PFP, PostDiag quantifies Skeleton Expressiveness Risk by comparing the fitted candidate with the observations, and Skeleton Stability Risk by measuring variability of behavior after bootstrap refitting. The Diagnostic Risk Plane (DRP) combines two risks to determine whether a skeleton should be preserved, repaired, simplified, or rewritten, while the patch-wise discrepancies provide evidence for the intervention. An LLM editor then performs the diagnosis-guided intervention, and the validated revision is returned to the original solver through a lightweight adapter. Experiments across multiple LLM-based and GP-based SR solvers show that PostDiag consistently improves accuracy and accelerates convergence.
papers.summary: Most symbolic regression (SR) solvers guide their search with a single fitness score, which says nothing about why a candidate expression skeleton fails. Richer feedback schemes exist, but each is tied to the solver it was built for. `PostDiag` is a feedback layer that works independently of the search method. It profiles the local level, trend and roughness of a fitted candidate patch by patch, and measures two risks: whether the skeleton can express the data (expressiveness) and how much its behavior varies under bootstrap refitting (stability). A Diagnostic Risk Plane combines the two risks to decide whether to keep, repair, simplify or rewrite the skeleton, an LLM editor applies that change, and the result is returned to the original solver through a lightweight adapter. Across several LLM-based and genetic-programming (GP) solvers, PostDiag **consistently improves accuracy and speeds convergence**.

papers.title: A Multi-Step Inertial ADMM Algorithm for Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Federated learning has recently emerged as an important paradigm for large-scale distributed model training, which can be naturally formulated as a class of distributed learning problems. The alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) is a widely used approach for solving such problems. However, its practical performance is often hindered by significant communication overhead and system heterogeneity. In this paper, we propose a multi-step inertial ADMM algorithm, called MiFedADMM, for federated learning. The proposed method leverages multiple historical iterates on the server side to construct a higher-order extrapolation after each aggregation to accelerate the convergence behavior. Under mild assumptions, we establish convergence results for the single-step variant of the proposed method and derive an O(1/K) convergence rate. Numerical experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and improved performance of the proposed method compared with existing approaches.
papers.summary: The alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) is a common way to solve federated learning problems, but communication overhead and differences between client systems slow it down. `MiFedADMM` speeds up convergence by having the server extrapolate from several past iterates after each aggregation round, a multi-step inertial update. The authors prove convergence with an **O(1/K) rate for the single-step variant** under mild assumptions. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show better performance than existing approaches.

papers.title: Write Once, Query Many: Evolving Compact Reusable Memory for Long Videos
papers.abstract: Long videos often exceed the context capacity of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), while agentic search repeats costly video processing and grounding for each query. Reusable memory can amortize this cost, but must preserve information for questions unknown during construction. We propose Video-EMem, an evolvable video memory harness built on time-anchored perceptual observations. This representation combines compact free-form text with sparse images to preserve semantic content and complementary visual details across temporal scales, supporting temporal navigation without a fixed semantic schema. A Writer encodes each video once by consolidating overlapping multiscale observations, and a Reader retrieves and organizes evidence solely from the resulting memory. With the underlying models frozen, we evolve their workflows and operators using distinct feedback: query-independent source fidelity and coverage for the Writer, and QA failures in evidence localization and utilization for the Reader. Experiments support this separation for generalization beyond development queries, with our evolution strategy improving average accuracy by 7.2% over the unevolved harness. While reducing storage by about 99.86% on average relative to raw videos, Video-EMem improves Qwen3-VL-30B by an average of 2.6% across three long-video QA benchmarks over direct input of 2,048 frames. Using the same o3 answer model as the state-of-the-art agentic method, it improves average accuracy by 2.5% with lower per-query latency.
papers.summary: Long videos often exceed the context window of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), and agentic search re-processes the video for every new question. `Video-EMem` instead builds a reusable memory once per video. A Writer consolidates overlapping observations at several time scales into compact, time-anchored text plus a sparse set of images, and a Reader answers questions using only this memory. With the underlying models kept frozen, the Writer's and Reader's workflows are evolved from separate feedback signals: fidelity and coverage of the source for the Writer, and QA failures for the Reader. This evolution adds 7.2% average accuracy over the unevolved setup. The memory cuts storage by **about 99.86% relative to raw video** while improving `Qwen3-VL-30B` by 2.6% over feeding it 2,048 frames directly, and with `o3` as the answer model it beats the leading agentic method by 2.5% at lower per-query latency.

papers.title: Accelerating Finite-Sum Bilevel Optimization with Fully First-Order Oracles
papers.abstract: We study nonconvex--strongly-convex bilevel optimization with finite-sum objectives and fully first-order oracles. We propose Sampled Implicit Corrections for Bilevel Optimization (SICBO), which combines a penalty approximation with variance-reduced corrections for the lower-level variables. Under componentwise lower strong convexity, SICBO finds a point $x$ satisfying $\mathbb{E}\|\nabla\Phi(x)\|^2\le\varepsilon^2$ within $\tilde{O}(N+\sqrt{N}\kappa^{7/2}\varepsilon^{-2})$ component-gradient calls, where $N$ is the total number of components and $\kappa$ is the normalized lower-level condition number. The bound achieves square-root finite-sum dependence using only gradients and preserves the best known deterministic fully first-order condition-number exponent for smooth problems. Our improvement follows from a curvature-dependent bound for nonlinear correction errors, which permits epochs of length $\tilde{\Theta}(\sqrt{N/\kappa})$ with batches of size $\tilde{\Theta}(\sqrt{N\kappa})$. A single-level reduction shows that the dependence on $N$ and $\varepsilon$ is optimal up to logarithmic factors for fixed $\kappa$.
papers.summary: The paper studies bilevel optimization with a nonconvex upper level, a strongly convex lower level, finite-sum objectives, and access to gradients only. Sampled Implicit Corrections for Bilevel Optimization (`SICBO`) combines a penalty approximation with variance-reduced corrections for the lower-level variables. It finds an approximate stationary point in Õ(N + √N κ^{7/2} ε^{-2}) component-gradient calls, where N is the number of components and κ is the lower-level condition number. This **achieves square-root dependence on N using only first-order information** while matching the best known condition-number exponent. A reduction to single-level problems shows that the dependence on N and ε is optimal up to logarithmic factors for fixed κ.

papers.title: EGIP: An Evidence-Grounded Interaction Protocol for Clinical Agents
papers.abstract: Interactive clinical agents acquire evidence through patient dialogue and diagnostic examinations, yet their performance also depends on how the interaction environment exposes information, available actions, and examination results. When these conditions are implicit or inconsistently controlled, final-answer accuracy can conflate diagnostic reasoning with the effects of the interaction protocol. We propose the \textbf{E}vidence-\textbf{G}rounded \textbf{I}nteraction \textbf{P}rotocol (EGIP), which enforces role-specific information boundaries, exposes diagnostic actions without revealing their results, retrieves examination results from stored clinical records, and organizes acquired evidence for final decision-making. By separating evidence acquisition from terminal prediction, EGIP enables different decision strategies to operate on the same observations. We evaluate EGIP across two clinical-agent frameworks, five datasets, and six language models. EGIP improves diagnostic accuracy over native baselines across all primary comparisons. A clinician review further shows that the proportion of automatically scored correct responses jointly judged evidence-supported rises from 10.20\% to 36.55\%. These findings support the effectiveness of EGIP as a unified interaction protocol for improving clinical-agent performance through controlled evidence access and acquisition.
papers.summary: Interactive clinical agents gather evidence by talking to a simulated patient and ordering examinations. Their final-answer accuracy therefore depends partly on how the simulation environment reveals information, which can blur the measurement of actual diagnostic reasoning. The Evidence-Grounded Interaction Protocol (`EGIP`) enforces role-specific information boundaries, lists available diagnostic actions without revealing their results, retrieves examination results from stored clinical records, and organizes the collected evidence for a separate final decision step. Across two agent frameworks, five datasets and six language models, EGIP improves diagnostic accuracy in every primary comparison. In a clinician review, the share of automatically scored correct answers that were also judged evidence-supported **rose from 10.20% to 36.55%**.

papers.title: Theory-Guided Instance-Dependent Early Stopping via Second-Order Loss Dynamics
papers.abstract: Instance-dependent early stopping (IES) reduces training computation by skipping backpropagation for examples whose losses have stabilized, but the second-order loss-difference criterion used by IES lacks a theoretical justification. We develop Theory-Guided Instance-Dependent Early Stopping (TG-IES), which analyzes this criterion under explicit assumptions and derives a noise-calibrated mastery threshold and a conditional stability bound for instance exclusion. We show that second-order differencing has a favorable bias-variance trade-off over first- and third-order differences in a specific signal-to-noise regime, and that its signal contains both gradient-drift and curvature terms. TG-IES derives its stopping threshold and patience from training-run statistics rather than using the manually selected threshold of IES. Across CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, TG-IES saves 53-58% of backpropagation instances in its main convolutional settings while keeping accuracy within 0.1-0.9 percentage points of full training; in the primary ResNet-18/CIFAR-10 setting, this corresponds to 35.7% FLOP-normalized savings. The method also transfers to ViT-Tiny, where it achieves smaller savings and incurs a modest accuracy cost. These results provide a theoretical basis for second-order instance-dependent early stopping and show that theory-guided calibration can substantially reduce training computation under the assumptions and experimental settings studied.
papers.summary: Instance-dependent early stopping (IES) saves training compute by skipping backpropagation for examples whose loss has stabilized, using a second-order loss-difference criterion that has had no theoretical justification. `TG-IES` analyzes this criterion under explicit assumptions. It shows that second-order differencing has a better bias-variance trade-off than first- or third-order differences in a specific signal-to-noise regime, and it derives the stopping threshold and patience from training-run statistics instead of tuning them by hand. On `CIFAR-10` and `CIFAR-100`, it **skips 53-58% of backpropagation instances while staying within 0.1-0.9 points of full-training accuracy**, which corresponds to 35.7% FLOP-normalized savings for `ResNet-18`. On `ViT-Tiny` the savings are smaller and accuracy drops modestly.

papers.title: From Stories to Features: Scaling Concept Vectors for AI Alignment & Interpretability
papers.abstract: We study feature vectors: directions in a language model's activation space that correspond to human-interpretable concepts, such as honesty or deception. Existing unsupervised methods like sparse autoencoders attempt to recover the whole feature space, often at the cost of feature quality and interpretability. We take a more pragmatic route: focusing on concepts relevant to AI safety and alignment, we generate synthetic concept-antagonist story pairs and use the difference of their mean model activations as a feature vector. We scale this approach to 1,036 alignment-relevant concepts using 2M synthetic stories across multiple languages and genres, which we publicly release. Across six models from three model families, our feature vectors reliably generalize to detecting their corresponding concepts in chat dialogues and web text. They form an interpretable geometry shared across models and can causally steer model behavior when injected into activations. We further use these features to analyze model representations during jailbreak attacks, mathematical and agentic reasoning. Our targeted feature construction thus offers a scalable route to studying concepts in language models, potentially extending to millions of features across arbitrary domains.
papers.summary: Rather than recovering a model's entire feature space with sparse autoencoders, the authors build targeted feature vectors for concepts relevant to AI safety, such as honesty or deception. For each concept they generate synthetic story pairs that express the concept and its opposite, and take the difference of the model's mean activations on the two sets as the feature direction. They scale this to **1,036 alignment-relevant concepts using 2M synthetic stories** in multiple languages and genres, and release the data. Across six models from three families, the vectors detect their concepts in chat dialogues and web text, form an interpretable geometry shared across models, and can causally steer behavior when injected into activations. The authors also use them to analyze model representations during jailbreak attacks, mathematical reasoning and agentic reasoning.

papers.title: No-Regret Revenue Maximization in Sequential Market Making Under Inventory Constraints
papers.abstract: Market makers keep trading efficient by setting bid and ask prices for buyers and sellers. In sequential market making, trades happen independently based on price thresholds, requiring the market maker to maintain balanced, low-risk inventory over T rounds. This paper studies how to maximize revenue with unknown buyer and seller valuations using regret minimization. When the market maker only sees trade success or failure, an algorithm achieves regret and inventory bounds proportional to T to the power of 2/3. When full order book data is available for failed trades, regret and inventory limits improve significantly to the square root of T. We also establish a fundamental trade-off via a lower bound, by proving that tighter round-by-round inventory limits strictly force higher minimum regret.
papers.summary: A market maker posts bid and ask prices over T rounds, earns revenue when trades occur, and must keep its inventory balanced, all without knowing buyers' and sellers' valuations. The authors frame this as regret minimization. When the market maker only observes whether each trade succeeded, their algorithm achieves regret and inventory bounds of order T^{2/3}. With full order-book information on failed trades, both **improve to order √T**. A lower bound shows that tighter per-round inventory limits necessarily force higher minimum regret.

papers.title: Representations Have Trajectories: Characterizing Temporal Representation Dynamics in Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Recent work has shown that deep neural networks exhibit an implicit low-rank simplicity bias. In this paper, we investigate the questions that naturally arise from this observation. What are the temporal consequences of low-rank simplicity bias during optimization? How does representation geometry evolve throughout optimization rather than only at convergence? Do different neural architectures exhibit distinct geometric optimization behaviors? To answer these questions, we conduct a large-scale empirical study tracking representational geometry throughout training. We find that neural networks follow three recurring geometric trajectories: persistent high-rank, collapse-and-recovery, and persistent low-rank. We further identify Destructive Representation Collapse (DRC) as a pathological regime in which representations collapse to rank-one and fail to recover, leading to a sustained loss of representational capacity. While collapse-and-recovery is consistently associated with successful optimization in controlled settings, experiments on real-world models show that the relationship between geometric trajectories and optimization outcomes is configuration dependent. Overall, our findings suggest that representation geometry evolves dynamically during training and provide a new perspective on how deep neural networks learn.
papers.summary: Deep networks are known to have an implicit bias toward low-rank representations, but it is less clear how representation geometry changes during training. A large-scale empirical study that tracks representational rank throughout optimization finds **three recurring trajectories: persistent high rank, collapse followed by recovery, and persistent low rank**. The authors also identify Destructive Representation Collapse (DRC), a failure mode in which representations collapse to rank one and never recover, permanently reducing capacity. Collapse followed by recovery goes with successful optimization in controlled settings, but in real-world models the link between trajectory and outcome depends on the configuration.

papers.title: ASR Personalization in Pathological Voice: Accuracy, Efficiency, and Duration Effects
papers.abstract: Automatic Speech recognition (ASR) struggles with Pathological speech due to persistent speaker-specific mismatch. In clinical and accessibility scenarios, only limited target-speaker data is typically available, making full model retraining impractical. We present a component-level analysis of LoRA adaptation in Whisper, investigating how adapter placement interacts with the model size, training efficiency and utterance-duration in single-speaker settings. Our experimental comparative study shows that while scaling reduces errors, it does not eliminate mismatch. Furthermore, the full attention LoRa provides the most reliable accuracy, and the best time--accuracy trade-off. Improvements vary across utterance length, with medium-length recordings benefiting the most, while short and long utterances remain challenging. These findings highlight the importance of adaptation placement and duration-dependent evaluation, under challenging, data-scarce personalization scenarios.
papers.summary: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) performs poorly on pathological speech, and clinical or accessibility settings usually have too little data from the target speaker for full retraining. The authors study `LoRA` adaptation of `Whisper` for single speakers, varying where adapters are placed, model size, training efficiency, and utterance length. Larger models reduce errors but do not remove the speaker mismatch. **Applying LoRA to all attention layers gives the most reliable accuracy and the best time-accuracy trade-off.** Medium-length utterances benefit most from adaptation, while short and long ones remain difficult.

papers.title: DeliMF: Gated Cross-Attention Fusion of Structured Time Series and Clinical Text for Early Intensive Care Delirium Prediction
papers.abstract: Delirium affects a large fraction of intensive care unit (ICU) patients and foreshadows longer stays, lasting cognitive decline, and higher mortality. Flagging the patients who will become delirious within the first day of admission would give clinicians a window to intervene. Yet state-of-the-art predictors rely only on the structured electronic health record (EHR) of vital signs, laboratory values, and medications, while overlooking the free-text clinical notes written in the same window, which carry information the numbers cannot encode. To this end, we present DeliMF, a multimodal framework that fuses the structured time series with clinical text. It encodes the structured signals with a temporal Transformer and the time-stamped radiology reports with a clinical text encoder, and fuses the two through a gated cross-attention module. The gate learns a per-patient weight on the text; when a patient has no note the gate closes and DeliMF reduces to its structured-only form, giving robustness to missing text by construction. On an incident-only MIMIC-IV cohort, DeliMF improves significantly over the baselines, particularly on patients who carry clinical text, while losing nothing on those without. Ablation studies confirm the contribution of multimodal fusion and gated cross-attention, and a case study further shows that fusing clinical text with the structured stream recovers delirium cases that the structured data alone misses. We hope DeliMF encourages early ICU prediction to make fuller use of the overlooked clinical text and contributes to the early identification and timely intervention of delirium.
papers.summary: Delirium is common in intensive care unit (ICU) patients and predicts worse outcomes, yet current early predictors use only structured electronic health record (EHR) data and ignore the clinical notes written during the same period. `DeliMF` encodes vital signs, labs and medications with a temporal Transformer and time-stamped radiology reports with a clinical text encoder, then fuses the two through gated cross-attention. The gate learns how much weight to give the text for each patient and closes when no note exists, so the model falls back to its structured-only form. On an incident-only `MIMIC-IV` cohort, it **significantly outperforms baselines, especially for patients with clinical text**, without losing accuracy for those without notes.

papers.title: Conditional Weight of Evidence for Gradient-Boosted Credit Models: Estimation, Additivity and Its Relation to Adverse Action Reasons
papers.abstract: Traditional weight of evidence assigns a credit characteristic a value based on its association with default across a population. Credit analysis also requires an assessment of that characteristic in the context of an individual applicant's record. We study conditional weight of evidence for this purpose. It measures the change in default log odds from observing a characteristic after the remaining credit information is known. Its sign identifies whether the characteristic adds adverse or favorable information for that applicant, and its magnitude measures the strength of that information. The same characteristic value can therefore receive different assessments for applicants with different payment histories or other credit attributes. We develop estimators using gradient-boosted trees and evaluate their accuracy in a bureau-style simulation. Regressions of the full model's predicted probabilities recover conditional evidence more accurately than separate models fitted to default outcomes, provided the full model is accurate. They also recover a deliberately constructed file-age effect whose direction varies with utilization and is often missed by marginal weight of evidence. Local class-frequency estimates improve on marginal weight of evidence but remain inaccurate for some weak effects. An application to FICO HELOC data illustrates estimation when the population evidence is unknown. Conditional weight of evidence provides an applicant-specific interpretation of the information in a credit characteristic; its population summary, a conditional information value, splits the joint information in the record across blocks when averaged over orderings. Neither is an adverse action reason, which explains the fitted score difference between the applicant and chosen passing records.
papers.summary: Traditional weight of evidence scores a credit characteristic by its association with default across the whole population, without considering the rest of an applicant's record. The authors study conditional weight of evidence: the change in default log-odds from observing a characteristic once all other credit information is known. Its sign and size can therefore differ between applicants. They develop estimators based on gradient-boosted trees, and in a bureau-style simulation **regressions on the full model's predicted probabilities recover conditional evidence most accurately**, including a constructed file-age effect that marginal weight of evidence misses. An application to `FICO HELOC` data illustrates the method, and the authors distinguish this quantity from adverse action reasons.

papers.title: Training with Ciphers to Enhance In-Context Terminology Learning For Translation from Rare Languages
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning LLMs with in-context examples (IC-Train) lets translation models adapt to new parallel data at deployment, but it is unclear whether they actually learn the translations of rare terms from those examples. We formalize this capability as in-context term learning (ICTL). We show that standard IC-Train develops this capability only weakly, and propose RareCipherFT, which strengthens it without any lexical resources. RareCipherFT pairs each training target with in-context examples that share a rare term with it. It then replaces that term with a character-shuffled cipher in both the context and the reference, so the term can only be recovered by copying from context. The ciphered fraction of training data is annealed to preserve translation quality. Across seven translation directions between English and Tamil, Assamese, Mizo, Nepali and Hausa, and four models from 1B to 7B parameters, RareCipherFT raises term recall over standard IC-Train by 5-15 absolute points without lowering COMET. Probes using synonyms, nonce words and controls for shared surface context show that these gains come from linking source terms to their in-context translations rather than from shortcuts.
papers.summary: LLM translation models fine-tuned with in-context examples can, in principle, pick up the translations of rare terms from those examples at deployment time, but the authors find that standard in-context training (`IC-Train`) builds this skill only weakly. `RareCipherFT` pairs each training target with in-context examples that share a rare term, then replaces that term in both the context and the reference with a character-shuffled cipher, so the model can only produce it by copying from context. The share of ciphered training data is annealed down over training to preserve overall translation quality. Across seven directions between English and Tamil, Assamese, Mizo, Nepali and Hausa, using models from 1B to 7B parameters, it **raises term recall by 5-15 absolute points without lowering `COMET`**. Probes with synonyms and nonce words indicate that the gains come from linking source terms to their in-context translations rather than from shortcuts.

papers.title: AdamPM: Memory-Efficient LLM Optimization via Moment Pooling
papers.abstract: Adam is widely used for training large language models (LLMs) owing to its strong optimization performance and training stability, but its element-wise estimation for the first and second moments incur substantial memory overhead. Although numerous memory-efficient optimizers have been proposed, many incur additional computational overhead or require additional tuning of hyperparameters. Consequently, Adam remains a dominant and reliable choice for LLM pre-training. We propose AdamPM (Adam with Pooled Moments), a simple and memory-efficient variant of Adam that groups adjacent moment entries along the row or column dimension and represents each group by a single shared mean. AdamPM can well inherit Adam's hyperparameter settings and is readily integrated into existing Adam optimizer implementations, with less memory overhead. We systematically investigate pooling of both first and second moment estimates and identify second moment pooling as the effective design. With a group size of $s$, AdamPM reduces second moment memory to $1/s$ of the original requirement. Extensive experiments on language model pretraining, fine-tuning and multimodal learning demonstrate that AdamPM maintains model performance and training speed while substantially reducing optimizer-state memory. Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/jixiaowei95/AdamPM}.
papers.summary: `Adam` stores a first-moment and a second-moment estimate for every parameter, which takes a lot of memory when training large language models (LLMs). Many memory-saving optimizers add compute overhead or need their own hyperparameter tuning. `AdamPM` (Adam with Pooled Moments) groups neighboring moment entries along a row or column and replaces each group with its mean. It keeps Adam's hyperparameters and fits into existing Adam implementations. The authors find that pooling the second moment is the design that works: with group size s, **second-moment memory drops to 1/s while performance and training speed are maintained** across pretraining, fine-tuning, and multimodal experiments.

papers.title: Severity-Channel Conditioning: An Injection-Level Study for Consumer-Device Deblurring
papers.abstract: Motion-deblurring models lose substantial accuracy when transferred from professional cameras to smartphone-derived imagery. This paper studies whether a severity descriptor, partly derived from the paired sharp target, helps adaptation on the iPhoneBlur consumer-device benchmark. Under a shared update budget, input concatenation of a severity map is compared with global feature modulation by capture metadata, spatial feature modulation by the severity map, and a tier-contrastive output objective, together with an unconditioned spectral-loss control, all fine-tuned from the same domain-adapted latent-diffusion baseline. The primary experiment is an oracle diagnostic: target-derived information is supplied at inference. For the evaluated model pair, input concatenation improves overall peak signal-to-noise ratio from 31.23 to 31.30 dB, whereas feature modulation, the contrastive objective, and the spectral-loss control do not exceed the baseline. The gain is positive on 87.2% of test images and on 14 of 15 held-out source videos; this video-level analysis describes the evaluated checkpoint pair and does not establish robustness to retraining, and three training seeds are reported separately. The input-level gain recurs on a transformer backbone. In one exploratory run, zeroing the channel at inference retains most of the gain in peak signal-to-noise ratio but lowers structural similarity below the baseline. A normalized-step diagnostic does not support the expected larger-gradient explanation. The results characterize the evaluated configurations and do not establish injection location as the sole cause, a spatial-locality mechanism, or a reliable deployment advantage.
papers.summary: Motion-deblurring models lose accuracy when moved from professional-camera images to smartphone images. The authors test several ways of feeding a blur-severity signal into a latent-diffusion deblurring model fine-tuned on the `iPhoneBlur` benchmark: concatenating a severity map to the input, modulating features with capture metadata or the severity map, and a contrastive objective. In an oracle setting where the severity information is derived from the sharp target, only input concatenation helped, raising peak signal-to-noise ratio **from 31.23 to 31.30 dB**, and the gain also appeared on a transformer backbone. The authors state that the results do not show a reliable deployment advantage or explain why the gain occurs.

papers.title: TCMScience: An Autonomous Scientist for Traditional Chinese Medicine
papers.abstract: Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) research connects classical texts, medicinal entities, molecular assays, computational predictions, and clinical studies. An autonomous research agent must preserve the inferential boundaries between these evidence types while coordinating analysis across heterogeneous resources. We introduce TCMScience, a scientific knowledge-discovery agent that separates language-model proposals from execution and release authority. Its architecture combines a trusted kernel, a scientific compiler, and claim-support contracts: plans are compiled into typed operations, execution is bounded by explicit permissions, and candidate findings are checked against source provenance, study design, and claim scope before release. The full capability registry contains 117 public-source connectors with 444 typed operations across 29 domains and 150 native tools across 12 domains; the TCM data hub catalogs 136 databases, 76 dataset specifications, and 84,294 formula-source records. These resources support model-independent workflows through browser and local execution interfaces. In a network-pharmacology analysis of Gegen Qinlian Tang, replacing the whole-proteome background with the assayed-protein background changed the number of significant pathways from 66 to zero; incorporating inactive screening records identified nine pathways, including drug-metabolism signals retained as mechanistic hypotheses. A governance ablation over 121 constructed erroneous outputs spanning 26 classes released 121 errors without governance, 57 with the domain layer, seven with the kernel, and zero with both layers. All 10 compliant controls were retained. These results establish complementary control of known failure modes and show how explicit evidence contracts change the conclusions an agent is permitted to report.
papers.summary: `TCMScience` is an autonomous research agent for traditional Chinese medicine (TCM), which draws on classical texts, molecular assays, computational predictions, and clinical studies. Its design separates language-model proposals from execution and release: plans are compiled into typed operations, a trusted kernel enforces explicit permissions, and claim-support contracts check each candidate finding against its source provenance, study design, and claim scope before it is released. In a network-pharmacology case study, using the correct background of assayed proteins reduced the number of significant pathways from 66 to zero. In a governance ablation over 121 deliberately erroneous outputs, the combined kernel and domain layers **released zero errors, compared with 121 without governance**, and kept all 10 valid controls.

papers.title: How Much Do Activation Monitors Benefit from Original Model Computations?
papers.abstract: One powerful way to safeguard AI systems is to monitor their internal computations--where signs of undesirable behavior might be more easily detectable than from models' inputs and outputs alone. However, recent studies begin to question the premise that activations provide a unique window into model behavior. In this paper, we study how much of activation monitors' success depends on access to the original behavior-generating computations. Within a fixed choice of target model and monitoring architecture, we compare how well monitors trained and evaluated on trajectories that differ in computational context can predict the behavior of the original execution, after the transcript is changed in a controlled manner (e.g., its exact text, or chat formatting). We first find that much performance can be recovered without access to the original behavior-generating trace (in up to 4 models across 2 counterfactual monitoring tasks), but a mild yet consistent advantage to native-trained monitors remains, outperforming strongest controls by up to 0.014 AUROC. Interestingly, we find monitors trained with native access have notable uplift on original examples whose behavioral label changes under paraphrasing. We further find this a useful lens to expose limitations of baselines that use simple forms of privileged information (i.e., answer logit margins). While our results show the advantage of native monitor access is modest in aggregate, they highlight the importance of evaluations that identify if and when original model computations provide additional predictive value.
papers.summary: Activation monitors read a model's internal activations to detect undesirable behavior, but it is unclear how much they depend on access to the computation that actually produced that behavior. The authors compare monitors trained on the original activations with monitors trained on controlled variants of the transcript, such as paraphrased text or changed chat formatting, across up to 4 models and 2 tasks. Most of the monitoring performance can be recovered without the original computation, and **monitors trained on the original activations keep only a small but consistent edge of up to 0.014 AUROC** (area under the ROC curve). That edge is larger on examples whose behavioral label changes under paraphrasing, and the same comparison exposes weaknesses in baselines that use answer logit margins.

papers.title: Safety Kernel: Mechanistic Alignment for Cross-Lingual Defense in LLMs
papers.abstract: The safety capabilities of large language models (LLMs) are highly uneven across different languages, often allowing cross-lingual attacks to bypass safety guardrails. Existing alignment methods predominantly rely on external alignment signals and provide limited insight into underlying neuron-level mechanisms, making it difficult to provide a unified internal target for cross-lingual safety interventions. To address this, we analyze cross-lingual safety behavior at the neuron level and identify a compact set of safety-related neurons shared across languages, termed the safety kernel (SK). Specifically, we first utilize multilingual parallel safe and unsafe prompts to compute safety contrast with activation responsiveness (SCAR) scores, identifying language-wise safety-neuron candidates from internal activation patterns. We then intersect the resulting language-wise safety-neuron sets to obtain the SK, and validate its functional relevance to cross-lingual safety behavior through activation suppression and activation-state transfer interventions. Finally, building on the SK coordinates, we introduce SK-Masked LoRA, which constrains LoRA adaptation to the feed-forward network (FFN) output dimensions corresponding to the SK, thereby focusing safety-related changes on the cross-lingually shared neuron coordinates. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SK-Masked LoRA substantially reduces attack success rates across multiple languages, including languages excluded from SK discovery, while intervening on only a small fraction of internal neuron coordinates and producing generally limited changes in the model's general capabilities.
papers.summary: LLM safety is uneven across languages, so attacks written in lower-resource languages can get past safety guardrails. The authors score neurons with safety contrast with activation responsiveness (`SCAR`) on parallel safe and unsafe prompts in several languages, then intersect the per-language results to find a small set of shared safety neurons, which they call the safety kernel. Suppressing these neurons and transferring their activation states confirm that they matter for safety behavior. `SK-Masked LoRA` then restricts low-rank adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning to the feed-forward output dimensions of those neurons, which **substantially reduces attack success rates across languages, including languages left out of kernel discovery**, while generally causing limited changes to general capabilities.

papers.title: Uncovering Semantic Hierarchies in Text-Attributed Graphs via Variational EM-based LLM-GNN Synergy
papers.abstract: While hierarchical structures are intrinsic to organizing human knowledge, current representation learning on text-attributed graphs predominantly operates on flat semantic spaces, overlooking the rich coarse-to-fine granularity inherent in real-world data. To bridge this gap, we propose SHiFT, which synergizes the reasoning power of LLMs with the structural representation capability of GNNs within an Expectation-Maximization (EM) paradigm. In the E-step, we harness LLMs as expert taxonomists to induce an explicit semantic tree, introducing a lightweight Mapping & Diagnosis strategy that reduces inference costs by surgically updating the hierarchy only when anomalies are detected. In the M-step, we align the GNN encoder with this induced hierarchy from complementary perspectives, including clustering partition, topological skeleton, and semantic concepts. Theoretical analysis interprets SHiFT as a generalized Variational EM algorithm. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SHiFT not only achieves state-of-the-art performance but also uncovers high-quality, human-readable taxonomies. Our code can be found at https://github.com/Cloudy1225/SHiFT.
papers.summary: Representation learning on text-attributed graphs usually treats categories as a flat set and ignores their coarse-to-fine hierarchy. `SHiFT` alternates two steps in an Expectation-Maximization (EM) loop. In the E-step, an LLM builds an explicit taxonomy tree and updates it only when it detects anomalies, which keeps inference costs down. In the M-step, a graph neural network (GNN) encoder is aligned with that tree through its cluster partition, topological skeleton, and semantic concepts. The authors frame the method as a generalized variational EM algorithm and report **state-of-the-art results along with human-readable taxonomies**.

papers.title: Muse Glimmer 30B: An On-Device Agentic Model
papers.abstract: We introduce Muse Glimmer, an open-source 30B parameter causal language model with perception encoder, purpose-built for autonomous agentic tasks on consumer hardware. Muse Glimmer integrates multi-step reasoning, reliable tool use and failure recovery into a single model that runs locally on consumer devices without requiring cloud infrastructure. The model accepts text and image inputs and produces text outputs, was trained on data from over a hundred languages, and is quantized to approximately 4-bit precision for efficient single-GPU inference. Muse Glimmer achieves state-of-the-art performance for its size class on agentic benchmarks, setting a new standard compared to the models of its size: Gemma4-31B and Qwen3.6-27B on tool use, multi-step planning, and agentic task completion. We release the model under the Apache 2.0 license to foster open-source development of capable, safe, local AI agents.
papers.summary: `Muse Glimmer` is an open-source 30-billion-parameter model that takes text and image inputs and is built to run autonomous agent tasks locally on consumer hardware, without cloud infrastructure. It combines multi-step reasoning, tool use, and recovery from failures in a single model, was trained on data in over a hundred languages, and is quantized to about 4-bit precision so it runs on a single GPU. The authors claim **state-of-the-art agentic performance for its size class, ahead of `Gemma4-31B` and `Qwen3.6-27B`** on tool use, multi-step planning, and task completion. The model is released under the Apache 2.0 license.

papers.title: Modeling Uncertainty Propagation in 3D Morphable Models
papers.abstract: We study the problem of mapping parameter-space variance of a 3D Morphable Model (3DMM) to per-vertex variance. Traditionally, per-vertex variance has been used to visually interpret the learnt parameter uncertainty. However, mapping parameter-space variance to per-vertex using sampling or error propagation is computationally expensive. We address this limitation with Closed-form Local Uncertainty Estimation (CLUE), which transforms the parameter-space distribution of 3DMMs to per-vertex through a closed-form approximation. CLUE emerges from applying the law of total variance to the 3DMM formulation and is modular, computationally inexpensive, and accurate. Subsequently, we study integrating CLUE for in-the-wild human mesh recovery training and inference. We note that CLUE uses the geometry of the mesh as an inductive bias when predicting the variance, leading to improved accuracy. Through extensive qualitative and quantitative experiments, we show that when used in training, CLUE (1) outpeforms probabilistic and deterministic baselines on metrics evaluating joints, mesh and uncertainty, and (2) has the highest uncertainty-to-error spearman correlation, with applications including data mining and interpretable uncertainty. Finally, we share SAM 3D Body (CLUE) which augments the regressor with high resolution uncertainty maps. We make our code available at https://github.com/vita-epfl/CLUE
papers.summary: Showing a 3D Morphable Model's (3DMM) parameter uncertainty as variance at each mesh vertex has usually required expensive sampling or error propagation. Closed-form Local Uncertainty Estimation (`CLUE`) applies the law of total variance to the 3DMM formulation to get **a cheap closed-form approximation of per-vertex variance**, which uses the mesh geometry as an inductive bias. When used to train in-the-wild human mesh recovery models, `CLUE` beats probabilistic and deterministic baselines on joint, mesh, and uncertainty metrics. It also has the highest Spearman correlation between predicted uncertainty and actual error. The authors also release `SAM 3D Body (CLUE)`, which adds high-resolution uncertainty maps to that regressor.

papers.title: EdgeKernelBench: Unified LLM-Driven Kernel Generation for Edge Backends
papers.abstract: Recent works show that LLMs can generate kernels with strong performance on server GPUs. Edge deployment presents distinct challenges because the hardware is heterogeneous, the software stacks are fragmented, and the resource budgets are tight. LLM kernel generation across diverse edge backends has yet to be studied systematically. We introduce EdgeKernelBench, which combines a unified IR deployment framework with a hierarchical benchmark for edge workloads. The unified IR captures reusable computation, scheduling, and memory decisions and connects to each target backend through a compiler interface.
