The benchmark spans progressively larger program scopes, from individual operators to compact model graphs, across representative edge application domains. We instantiate the design with TVM as a reference compiler and validate it across heterogeneous edge backends. With a single generation attempt, the best model achieves 64.5% Correct@1 but only 25.5% Fast@1.0. This gap shows that functional correctness does not consistently translate into performance gains. We therefore introduce the Layered Edge Kernel Agent (LEKA), which organizes optimization through a layered IR. On the agent evaluation subset, LEKA achieves 43.5% Fast@1.0, compared with 13.0% for direct generation and 26.1% for Claude Code. LEKA and Claude Code use the same base model and optimization budget. Together, EdgeKernelBench and LEKA support unified evaluation and layered optimization of kernels generated by LLMs across edge backends.
papers.summary: LLMs can write fast kernels for server GPUs, but edge devices bring varied hardware, fragmented software stacks, and tight resource budgets. `EdgeKernelBench` pairs a unified intermediate representation (IR), which connects to each backend through a compiler interface (`TVM` in the reference implementation), with a benchmark that ranges from single operators to small model graphs. With one generation attempt, the best model produced correct kernels 64.5% of the time but faster-than-baseline kernels only 25.5% of the time. The proposed Layered Edge Kernel Agent (`LEKA`) organizes optimization through a layered IR and reaches **43.5% Fast@1.0, versus 13.0% for direct generation and 26.1% for `Claude Code`**, using the same base model and optimization budget.
papers.highlight_summary:
LLM kernel generators mostly target server GPUs. Edge devices are harder targets: their hardware and software stacks are fragmented, and memory budgets are tight. The approach here has the LLM write its computation, scheduling, and memory decisions in one shared IR, which deterministic `TVM`-based adapters then lower to each backend; the benchmark comes with a layered agent that optimizes one IR level at a time.

- The benchmark has **331 PyTorch tasks**, organized by complexity (single operators, composed operator graphs, compact model graphs such as `MobileNetV2` and `TinyLlama` decoder blocks) and by edge domain, and is instantiated as 650 task instances across CPU/LLVM (Snapdragon 8 Gen 3), CUDA (Jetson AGX Orin), and OpenCL (Mali-G610) backends.
- In one-shot generation against a tuned `MetaSchedule` baseline, the best model reaches **64.5% Correct@1 but only 25.5% Fast@1.0**, and the top Fast@1.0 falls from 51.0% at Level 1 to just **0–4% at Level 3**, so correct code rarely turns out faster than the compiler.
- Memory errors (**34.0%** of failures, mostly about allocation legality rather than running out of capacity) and syntax/API errors (**25.4%**) dominate, and models with strong correctness don't necessarily produce fast code: `DeepSeek-V4-Pro` hits 75.3% correctness on CPU Level 2 but only 3.2% Fast@1.0 there.
- `LEKA` gives each IR level its own agent (`Relax` graph, `TIR` schedule, then CUDA/OpenCL/LLVM code), keeps a candidate tree that records how each candidate was derived, and sends each hardware profiling result to the level that owns the relevant decision.
- On a 69-instance subset, with the same `GLM-5.3-Flash` base model and the same time budget, `LEKA` raises Fast@1.0 to **43.5%**, compared with 13.0% for one-shot generation and 26.1% for `Claude Code`, and is **3.8× faster** than `Claude Code` by geometric mean; however, the gain shrinks to 2.9× at Level 3, the agent was tested on only a small sample, and only one compiler stack (`TVM`) was evaluated.

papers.title: Good Judgment, Bad Advice: Decision-Model Controllers Raise Agent Cost Without Improving Success
papers.abstract: Agent scaffolds increasingly delegate small decisions (whether to stop, verify, or change approach) to cheaper models. We ask whether a typed decision model, Jev 1.13, consulted only at deterministic decision points, makes a Claude Sonnet 5.5 terminal agent cheaper without making it worse. In a pre-specified study on Terminal-Bench 2.1, we hold one agent loop fixed and vary only the controller: none, deterministic rules, a small LLM (Claude Haiku 5.5) answering the same questions, Jev, and a placebo that samples Jev's development-phase choice frequencies at the same moments. On 21 held-out tasks (315 trials), Jev raised cost per attempt by 19% (geometric-mean ratio 1.19, 95% CI 1.02-1.36) at an identical pass rate (73.0% vs. 73.0%). Jev was cheaper than the small-LLM controller (ratio 0.81) but 22% more expensive than the placebo, and no pass-rate difference between arms was detectable. Offline, Jev ranked finish requests better than the alternatives (AUROC 0.78 vs. 0.62 for rules and 0.60 for the small LLM) but was poorly calibrated: its mean probability that a run was complete was 0.50 when 87% of those runs passed, so it asked the agent to verify work that was already correct. No controller ever chose to abandon a run. Informative decision signals did not become useful interventions; we discuss what that would require.
papers.summary: Agent scaffolds increasingly hand small decisions, such as whether to stop, verify, or change approach, to cheaper models. In a pre-specified study on `Terminal-Bench 2.1`, the authors keep a `Claude Sonnet 5.5` terminal agent loop fixed and swap only the controller: none, deterministic rules, `Claude Haiku 5.5`, the typed decision model `Jev`, or a placebo. Over 315 held-out trials, **`Jev` raised cost per attempt by 19% with an identical 73.0% pass rate**, and no controller produced a detectable change in pass rate. Offline, `Jev` ranked finish requests better than the alternatives (AUROC 0.78), but it was poorly calibrated and repeatedly asked the agent to verify work that was already correct.

papers.title: Lightweight Machine Learning for Classifying Disaster-Related Social Media Posts
papers.abstract: Classifying disaster-related social-media posts into humanitarian information labels is challenging because individual messages are typically short and context-limited, humanitarian categories can overlap semantically, and the CrisisBench label distribution is strongly imbalanced. This study investigates whether lightweight lexical machine-learning methods can provide effective and computationally efficient classification under these conditions. Using the CrisisBench v1.0 English humanitarian task, comprising 87,455 records across predefined Train, Development and Test splits, we conduct a controlled comparison of TF-IDF representations and lightweight classifiers, with Macro-F1 as the primary model-selection metric. Beyond aggregate predictive performance, the study jointly examines per-label behaviour, directional error patterns, relative decision margins, computational requirements, and the effect of domain-specific training through a tropical-cyclone specialist model. The selected balanced LinearSVC with unigram-bigram TF-IDF and C=0.5 achieved an Accuracy of 0.8282, a Macro-F1 of 0.6578 and a Weighted-F1 of 0.8315 on the held-out Test split. Lower decision margins were substantially associated with prediction errors, while the tropical-cyclone specialist achieved modestly higher in-domain aggregate performance with substantially lower feature and fitting requirements. The study contributes a controlled, label-sensitive and resource-aware evaluation of lightweight humanitarian text classification that characterises not only aggregate performance, but also where these models fail and how their behaviour changes under domain-specific training.
papers.summary: Disaster-related social media posts are short, their humanitarian categories overlap, and the labels in `CrisisBench` are heavily imbalanced, all of which make classification hard. The authors run a controlled comparison of TF-IDF features with lightweight classifiers on the 87,455-record English humanitarian task. The selected class-balanced `LinearSVC` with unigram and bigram features reaches **0.8282 accuracy and 0.6578 macro-F1** on the test split. Predictions with small decision margins were strongly associated with errors, and a model trained only on tropical-cyclone data did slightly better in its own domain while needing fewer features and less fitting.

papers.title: Can AI agents make law? Evaluating AI legal relevance and creativity
papers.abstract: Large language models, the artificial intelligence (AI) systems behind modern chatbots, are trained on vast amounts of legal text, but can they build on it to write law for situations that text never anticipated? In this study, we analyse AI agents' ability to draft a hypothetical "Constitution" for a "community of AI agents". We design "constitutional assemblies" in which a single language model plays several characters that debate to produce a draft constitution. We find that the assemblies converge on a robust floor of legal provisions, and generate a wide variety of different proposals around it, including several AI-specific provisions with no equivalent in human law. Looking more closely at the "creativity" of these AI agents, we find different levels: most proposals combine existing concepts and themes from human constitutions with AI-specific vocabulary. We introduce a measure of this recombination, which helps identify and highlight the most novel legal material. This study reveals a ceiling on AI creativity: the agents extend familiar legal ideas to new situations, but they do not work through what those situations would change. Although current AI models can help develop new laws, they still depend on human legal reasoning.
papers.summary: The authors test whether LLMs can write law for situations their legal training text never covered by having them draft a constitution for a community of AI agents. In each simulated constitutional assembly, a single language model plays several characters who debate a draft. The assemblies agree on a stable core of provisions and propose varied additions around it, including some AI-specific provisions with no counterpart in human law. A new recombination measure shows that **most proposals restate existing human constitutional concepts in AI vocabulary**, which the authors take as a ceiling on AI legal creativity.

papers.title: What RL Brings to Reasoning: A Few Decisions the Base Model Would Not Make
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) substantially improves mathematical reasoning, but what it adds to the base model remains unclear. We investigate this through a sequence of generation-time interventions on Qwen3-4B-Base, measuring how much of its RL-trained counterpart's gain each intervention recovers on 120 AIME problems. Power sampling with the same 8,192-token output limit brings no gain beyond greedy decoding. Yet borrowing the RL model's token only where the two models' greedy choices differ, roughly 4% of generated positions, recovers 90.5% of the pass@1 gain, with similar recovery across three model pairs on MATH-500. We find that even a single opening token has a substantial effect: forcing the base model to begin with "Alright" recovers 35% of the RL gain. The opening alone is insufficient, however. Later replacements after the same opening add another 5.2 percentage points to pass@1, and the fixed rules we test for inserting reflective words such as "Wait" do not reproduce this benefit. Sparse replacement also retains much of the base model's diversity while staying close to the RL model at pass@1. At k=256, it solves 67.5% of the problems, significantly more than the RL model (61.4%) and a mixture of whole responses matched in pass@1 (61.45%). The comparison is at equal attempt counts rather than equal compute, since rl-replace consults both models at every decoding step. These results show that the opening can recover a meaningful part of the RL gain, but a larger contribution comes from later choices, which can be borrowed while retaining much of the base model's diversity. Code is available at https://github.com/CyrusZhang04/WhatRLBrings.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) improves mathematical reasoning, but it is unclear what it adds to the base model. On `Qwen3-4B-Base` and 120 `AIME` problems, the authors test generation-time interventions. Power sampling gives no gain over greedy decoding, while **borrowing the RL-trained model's token only where the two models' greedy choices differ, about 4% of positions, recovers 90.5% of the pass@1 gain**. Forcing the base model to open with "Alright" alone recovers 35%, and fixed rules for inserting words like "Wait" do not reproduce the later gains. Because sparse replacement keeps much of the base model's diversity, it solves 67.5% of problems at k=256 versus 61.4% for the RL model, though this compares equal attempt counts rather than equal compute.

papers.title: Knowledge Diversion: A Novel Paradigm for Pre-training Decomposable Image Generation Models
papers.abstract: Large-scale pre-trained models have become foundational to modern machine learning, yet conventional pre-training objectives primarily optimize source-domain performance without explicitly considering downstream requirements. Consequently, transferable and task-specific knowledge remains entangled within a shared parameter space, limiting selective knowledge reuse and efficient downstream adaptation. This limitation is particularly consequential for image-generation models, which must accommodate diverse conditions and domains. To address this challenge, we introduce Knowledge Diversion (KDiv), a condition-aware pre-training paradigm for learning inherently decomposable generative models. Before pre-training, KDiv factorizes randomly initialized weights into rank-one Knowledge Units, which are organized into learngenes and tailors. During pre-training, continuous condition-aware routing consolidates knowledge shared across conditions in learngenes while directing condition-dependent variations to tailors. This structured organization enables learngenes to capture transferable generative priors and tailors to develop condition-specific expertise, allowing the resulting model to be selectively recombined for diverse downstream conditions. Extensive experiments across class-, text-, and image-conditioned generation demonstrate that KDiv consistently matches or surpasses dense baselines at comparable pre-training cost and achieves the strongest average downstream performance with a trainable parameter budget comparable to low-rank adaptation methods.
papers.summary: Standard pre-training mixes knowledge that transfers across tasks with knowledge specific to one condition in the same weights, which makes selective reuse in image generation harder. Knowledge Diversion (`KDiv`) splits randomly initialized weights into rank-one knowledge units before training. These units form shared "learngenes" and condition-specific "tailors", and condition-aware routing directs knowledge to each during pre-training. Across class-, text-, and image-conditioned generation, `KDiv` matches or beats dense baselines at similar pre-training cost and achieves **the best average downstream performance with a trainable-parameter budget comparable to low-rank adaptation**.

papers.title: Do Conversational Agents Need Explicit Memory? A Controlled Comparison with Raw-History Retrieval
papers.abstract:
Explicit memory systems transform conversation history into persistent representations intended to improve future access, often at substantial construction cost. Yet it remains unclear whether this added complexity yields better answer accuracy than retrieving directly from raw history. This study compares six state-of-the-art explicit memory systems with raw-history RAG on LongMemEval-S and BEAM-100K under original and controlled retrieval settings. We find only localized gains for particular question types and tight run-time context budgets, with no consistent advantage over strong raw-history RAG baselines. Oracle retrieval shows that some systems fail to preserve answer-supporting information during explicit memory construction, while others preserve it but fail to retrieve it effectively, despite construction costs reaching hours per conversation.
  Our findings suggest that while many existing memory systems for AI agents emphasize increasingly elaborate explicit memory construction, they are often evaluated without strong controlled comparisons to raw-history RAG and may underemphasize retrieval. Retrieval remains a major bottleneck when useful information is preserved, suggesting that improving access to existing information may be at least as important as constructing richer explicit memory.
papers.summary: Explicit memory systems for conversational agents turn chat history into persistent structures, often at high construction cost. The authors test whether that beats retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over the raw history by comparing six state-of-the-art memory systems against raw-history RAG on `LongMemEval-S` and `BEAM-100K`, under both original and controlled retrieval settings. The memory systems showed only localized gains for certain question types and tight context budgets, with **no consistent advantage over strong raw-history RAG baselines**, even though building the memory can take hours per conversation. Oracle-retrieval experiments show that some systems lose answer-supporting information during construction and others keep it but fail to retrieve it, which points to retrieval as a major bottleneck.

papers.title: MM-LeJEPA: Correlated Gaussian Regularization for Multimodal Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures
papers.abstract: LeJEPA derives an isotropic Gaussian embedding target by minimizing, under its task assumptions, a Fisher information criterion that controls the task-averaged squared prediction bias. This enables unimodal self-supervised learning without reconstruction decoders, exponential-moving-average teachers, or contrastive negatives. However, its isotropic task prior does not account for the cross-modal structure of multimodal tasks that read shared content. We introduce MM-LeJEPA by extending LeJEPA's task assumptions to multimodal learning. Specifically, we model multimodal tasks as strength-weighted combinations of components that read independent information from the two modalities and components that read the same content from both. Under explicit gradient-moment, correspondence, and symmetry assumptions, we derive a correlated Gaussian target that minimizes a weighted Fisher information functional under a fixed total variance constraint. An analytic transform adapts Sketched Isotropic Gaussian Regularization (SIGReg) to this target, yielding a two-term objective that combines distributional regularization with local-to-global prediction. The extension adds a single scalar hyperparameter, the target cross-modal correlation, and retains the simplicity of LeJEPA. On public audio-visual classification benchmarks, our results are competitive with representative open-source methods. Code will be released.
papers.summary: `LeJEPA` trains self-supervised embeddings toward an isotropic Gaussian target, which removes the need for reconstruction decoders, exponential-moving-average teachers, or contrastive negatives. Its isotropic assumption, however, ignores the content that two modalities share. `MM-LeJEPA` models multimodal tasks as a mix of components that read independent information from each modality and components that read shared content. Under stated assumptions this yields **a correlated Gaussian target that adds only one hyperparameter, the target cross-modal correlation**, and an analytic transform adapts the `SIGReg` regularizer to that target. On public audio-visual classification benchmarks, results are competitive with representative open-source methods.

papers.title: Contrastive Adversarial Training for Robust Graph Neural Networks under Label Poisoning
papers.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are effective for modeling relational data but are vulnerable to label poisoning, where a small number of corrupted training labels can propagate errors across the graph via message passing. Despite this risk, defenses against label poisoning remain underexplored: existing methods are primarily designed for label noise and often rely on robust losses or heuristic data cleaning that fail to distinguish adversarial poisoning from naturally hard examples. In this paper, we propose CoLAT (Contrastive Label-flipping for Adversarial Training), a novel contrastive adversarial training framework tailored for robust node classification on graphs. The core of our approach is a structure-aware detection model that uses contrastive learning to identify label-structure inconsistencies. Unlike prior contrastive methods that focus on representation learning, CoLAT leverages contrastive embeddings to select high-risk nodes that guide adversarial label-flipping during training. This alternating optimization not only performs structure-aware adversarial training but also implicitly sanitizes some corrupted labels, improving robustness against diverse attacks from the literature. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks show that CoLAT consistently outperforms existing defenses under various poisoning intensities while scaling efficiently to large graphs.
papers.summary: In graph neural networks (GNNs), a few poisoned training labels can spread errors through message passing, and existing defenses built for label noise struggle to tell adversarial poisoning apart from naturally hard examples. `CoLAT` (Contrastive Label-flipping for Adversarial Training) uses a contrastive, structure-aware detector to find nodes whose labels conflict with the graph structure. It then uses those high-risk nodes to guide adversarial label flipping during training, which also implicitly cleans up some corrupted labels. Across several benchmarks, **`CoLAT` consistently outperforms existing defenses at a range of poisoning intensities** and scales efficiently to large graphs.

papers.title: Geometry-Aware Interpolation for Inverse Problems
papers.abstract: Recovering missing visual information from incomplete or degraded images remains a challenging problem, particularly when spatial variations and complex image structures affect reconstruction accuracy. Although Spatial Transformer Networks (STNs) facilitate spatial feature alignment, their reliance on conventional linear or bilinear interpolation limits their ability to capture the underlying geometric characteristics of image data. Furthermore, interpolation based on a restricted set of neighbouring pixels can introduce inconsistencies in gradient propagation, potentially affecting optimisation stability. To address these limitations, we propose a Geometry-Aware Interpolation Network (GAIN), a variational autoencoder-based framework that incorporates manifold geometry into spatial transformation and image reconstruction. Rather than estimating pixel intensities solely from fixed spatial neighbours, GAIN exploits the local tangent structure of the data manifold to construct geometry-informed intensity approximations. An entropy-based regularisation mechanism further guides the estimation of spatial transformation parameters, promoting more adaptive interpolation. In addition, a convolutional normalisation strategy is introduced to regulate the magnitude of non-zero activations and improve gradient stability during training. Extensive experiments on challenging image completion and classification benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of GAIN in improving predictive accuracy while reducing computational cost compared with existing methods.
papers.summary: Spatial Transformer Networks (STNs) align features with linear or bilinear interpolation, which ignores the geometric structure of image data and can make gradient propagation inconsistent. The Geometry-Aware Interpolation Network (`GAIN`) is a variational-autoencoder framework that estimates pixel intensities from the local tangent structure of the data manifold rather than from fixed neighboring pixels. It adds an entropy-based regularizer for the spatial transformation parameters and a convolutional normalization scheme that stabilizes gradients. On image completion and classification benchmarks, `GAIN` **improves accuracy while lowering computational cost** compared with existing methods.

papers.title: Verifying Human-Written Reasoning References
papers.abstract: Evaluating the reasoning of AI systems often relies on human-written reasoning chains as references, yet the logical support for their individual steps is rarely verified. Although prior neuro-symbolic approaches have formalized and checked reasoning, their reported evaluations do not systematically assess whether step conclusions in human-written reference derivations are entailed by their cited premise sets or investigate the sources of failures in those references. To address these limitations, we present a novel reference-centred assessment method for human-written derivations that combines entailment checking against cited premise sets, full-premise rechecking, and failure attribution to examine the reliability of these derivations and their formal representations. We evaluate it on P-FOLIO, using a large language model (LLM) to translate step conclusions into first-order logic (FOL) and the Z3 SMT solver to check entailment. Of 386 derivations examined, 202 (52.3%) meet all our checking criteria, meaning that every translated step is entailed by its stated support and the required target is established under the available FOL representations. Among 230 steps not entailed by their stated support, 191 become entailed when checked against the complete original premises, indicating that most initial failures reflect incomplete or mismatched support rather than unsupported claims. Manual analysis of the remaining 39 cases identifies 21 human reasoning errors, 11 FOL translation errors, and 7 dataset annotation errors. A separate manual audit of 50 randomly sampled steps that passed the entailment checks found 46 faithful FOL translations (92%). These findings suggest that disagreement with a human-written reasoning reference may originate in the reference or its formal representation rather than in the AI system being evaluated.
papers.summary: Benchmarks for AI reasoning often treat human-written reasoning chains as ground truth without checking whether each step actually follows from its cited premises. The authors use an LLM to translate the step conclusions in `P-FOLIO` derivations into first-order logic (FOL), check entailment with the `Z3` solver, recheck failures against the full premise set, and attribute the remaining failures to a cause. **Only 52.3% of 386 derivations passed every check.** Of 230 steps not entailed by their cited premises, 191 were entailed once all premises were included, and manual review of the remaining 39 found 21 human reasoning errors, 11 translation errors, and 7 annotation errors. The authors conclude that disagreement with a reference chain may reflect flaws in the reference rather than in the AI system being evaluated.

papers.title: Native Probability Outputs for Clinical Triage: An Evaluation of Calibration and Decision Accuracy
papers.abstract: Patient-facing triage requires an appropriate care recommendation and recognition of when information is insufficient. We evaluate whether Jev, a decision model that returns probabilities over predefined actions, supports both judgments. Using CARE-Bench, we compare Jev with four general-purpose language models and three input-independent baselines across 925 decision points from 439 public cases. On the public test subset, Jev ranks fourth of five models by macro-F1 (0.461) but has the lowest observed multiclass Brier score (0.610), an 18.7\% improvement over uniform prediction (case-bootstrap 95\% interval, 4.9--31.1\%). Noul has lower binary Brier than Choice (0.215 versus 0.276). A evaluation of 453 HealthBench conversations again gives Jev the lowest observed Brier score (0.299), but measures a distinct emergency-referral judgment. Jev combines lower probability error with missed clarification needs in the four-action task. Asking about information sufficiency separately increases recall but also produces frequent unnecessary clarification assignments.
papers.summary: Patient-facing triage requires recommending the right level of care and recognizing when more information is needed. The authors evaluate `Jev`, a decision model that outputs probabilities over predefined actions, against four general-purpose language models and three input-independent baselines on 925 decision points from `CARE-Bench`. `Jev` ranks fourth of five models by macro-F1 (0.461) but has **the lowest multiclass Brier score (0.610), an 18.7% improvement over uniform prediction**. It also has the lowest Brier score on a separate emergency-referral evaluation of 453 `HealthBench` conversations. However, it misses cases that need clarification, and asking about information sufficiency as a separate question raises recall at the cost of many unnecessary clarification requests.

papers.title: Spherical Physics-informed Neural Operator with Multi-scale Coupling for Meteorological Downscaling
papers.abstract: Meteorological downscaling is crucial for high-resolution regional climate forecasting and disaster early warning. While neural operators have emerged as a promising paradigm for modeling complex spatiotemporal mappings, existing frameworks often struggle with spherical manifold geometric distortions, inherent atmospheric multi-scale coupling mismatches, and lack of explicit atmospheric laws. We propose the Spherical Physics-informed Neural Operator, which utilizes a Spherical Laplacian Decomposition to partition atmospheric fields into hierarchical frequency components, maintaining exact point-wise correspondence across scales. To evaluate these representations at arbitrary locations, we introduce a localized spherical integral operator that approximates continuous kernel transforms via geometry-aware attention. Dynamical consistency is further enforced by embedding differentiable constraints into the learning process. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our framework attains superior accuracy and zero-shot generalization across various meteorological variables and unseen queries, representing a robust and interpretable solution for global-to-regional meteorological downscaling.
papers.summary: Neural operators used for meteorological downscaling (turning coarse global forecasts into high-resolution regional ones) have trouble with distortion on the sphere, with mismatches between atmospheric scales, and with the lack of explicit physical laws. The proposed `Spherical Physics-informed Neural Operator` uses a `Spherical Laplacian Decomposition` to split atmospheric fields into hierarchical frequency components that keep exact point-wise correspondence across scales. A localized spherical integral operator built on geometry-aware attention evaluates these components at arbitrary locations, and differentiable physical constraints enforce dynamical consistency during training. The authors report **superior accuracy and zero-shot generalization across meteorological variables and unseen query locations**.

papers.title: When Do Repetition Loops Lock? Truncation Sampling, Bounded Penalties, and a Blind Spot in DRY
papers.abstract: Language models sometimes repeat verbatim until the generation limit. We study the exit rather than the entrance: given that a span has already been repeated $n$ times, when is escape still possible? Along the loop the context is deterministic, so loop survival under any sampler can be computed exactly from one forward pass. Pure sampling leaves a positive escape probability at every step; top-$p$ with threshold $\pi>1/2$ locks a position exactly when the continuation probability reaches $\pi$. A bounded penalty can leave a position locked; a penalty that outgrows the model's preference for the loop over unseen tokens guarantees escape under top-$p$. The same analysis predicts a blind spot in the widely deployed DRY sampler: its sequence breakers cap the penalty at $\lambda b^{g-1-a}$ for loops whose longest breaker-free run has $g$ tokens. On eleven open models, 66\% of locked units with $g=6$ stay locked under DRY and 1\% with $g=8$. In free generation with llama.cpp, all 109 loops that survive DRY have $g\le 7$. We propose DRY-C, which adds a term that grows exponentially with the number of verbatim recurrences, up to its look-back window. With it, none of 720 structured-output generations looped to the length limit, and task completion stayed close to DRY's.
papers.summary: Instead of asking why language models fall into verbatim repetition loops, the authors ask when a loop that has already repeated n times can still be escaped. Because the context inside a loop is deterministic, the chance that a loop survives under any sampler can be computed exactly from one forward pass. Pure sampling always leaves some probability of escape, `top-p` sampling with a threshold above 1/2 locks a position once the continuation probability reaches that threshold, and the widely deployed `DRY` sampler has a blind spot: its sequence breakers cap the penalty for loops with short breaker-free runs, and all 109 loops that survived `DRY` in free generation with `llama.cpp` had such short runs. The proposed fix, `DRY-C`, adds a penalty that grows exponentially with the number of verbatim recurrences, and with it **none of 720 structured-output generations looped to the length limit** while task completion stayed close to `DRY`'s.

papers.title: DiffuPlan: Editable Planning State for Diffusion Language Model Agents
papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (dLLMs) are emerging as an alternative to autoregressive (AR) language models, yet dLLM agents largely inherit an interaction protocol designed for AR generation: once intermediate state is written, later observations can only be incorporated by appending more text. This is a poor match to a defining capability of dLLMs -- reconstructing earlier text conditioned on context that appears both before and after it. We ask whether this capability can support a different agent-state paradigm in which intermediate planning state is directly revisable as evidence arrives. We introduce DiffuPlan, a diffusion search agent that maintains a single editable planning state and reconstructs only the affected steps when later evidence resolves an entity or changes the search route. To support variable-length revisions, we introduce Expansion-Partition Marginalization (EPM), which marginalizes over equivalent expansion paths. We further adapt diffusion trajectory RL to multi-turn search. Across four multi-hop QA benchmarks, DiffuPlan achieves 50.24 average F1, outperforming strong AR search agents. More importantly, under identical data and training, editable planning state improves the diffusion agent by 2.44 F1 versus only 0.47 for its AR source model. These results show that dLLMs need not imitate append-only AR agents: revising committed state is a distinct agentic advantage.
papers.summary: Agents built on diffusion language models (dLLMs) usually copy the append-only protocol of autoregressive (AR) agents, which ignores the ability of dLLMs to rewrite earlier text using context on both sides of it. `DiffuPlan` is a diffusion search agent that keeps one editable planning state and regenerates only the affected steps when new evidence resolves an entity or changes the search route. It relies on `Expansion-Partition Marginalization` (`EPM`) to handle revisions of variable length, and adapts diffusion trajectory reinforcement learning to multi-turn search. Across four multi-hop QA benchmarks it reaches 50.24 average F1, beating strong AR search agents, and under identical data and training **editable planning state adds 2.44 F1 to the diffusion agent versus only 0.47 to its AR source model**.

papers.title: Neuro-Inspired Inhibitory Message Passing for Accurate and Token-Efficient Multi-Agent Reasoning
papers.abstract: Multi-agent systems promise to solve problems by bringing together information beyond the reach of any individual agent. Retrieval and tool use can distribute this information across agents, making communication essential to collaboration. A central challenge is keeping crucial evidence visible in each agent's context as messages accumulate. Repeated information can crowd out rare, decisive evidence. Models of cortical circuits suggest a principle for addressing this imbalance: inhibition can selectively suppress shared inputs while preserving sensitivity to weaker signals. We adapt this principle into inhibitory message passing, a training-free communication router that cancels redundant evidence separately for each evidence sentence and receiver. Each round, it forwards evidence sentences restated in agents' messages, delivering each at most once to receivers whose own evidence lacks it and excluding the senders' reasoning and answers. Against standard message passing, accuracy in peer groups rose by 39-77 percentage points across three benchmarks, and tokens per run fell by 10-46%. Gains held across seven open models spanning four to thirty-two billion parameters and two commercial models, in groups up to sixty-four agents, and across multi-agent architectures including peer-to-peer, orchestrator-worker, and multilevel hierarchical organizations. These findings support a scalable design pattern for more accurate and token-efficient multi-agent reasoning.
papers.summary: In multi-agent systems, information repeated across agents' messages can crowd rare but decisive evidence out of each agent's context. Taking inspiration from inhibition in cortical circuits, the authors propose `inhibitory message passing`, a training-free router that forwards each evidence sentence at most once, and only to receivers whose own evidence lacks it, while leaving out the senders' reasoning and answers. Compared with standard message passing, **accuracy in peer groups rose by 39-77 percentage points across three benchmarks** and tokens per run fell by 10-46%. The gains held across seven open models from 4B to 32B parameters, two commercial models, groups of up to 64 agents, and peer-to-peer, orchestrator-worker, and hierarchical setups.

papers.title: Tensor Network Datamodels for Training Data Attribution
papers.abstract: Datamodels predict how a model's behavior changes when different parts of its training data are included or removed. However, linear datamodels assign fixed contributions to training units and cannot represent non-additive joint effects. We introduce Tensor Network Datamodels (TNDMs), which use low-rank tensor networks to model dependencies among training units while keeping the representation compact. TNDMs learn a map from subsets of the training data to the outcome of training on those subsets, allowing them to represent interactions among several training units. We prove that complementary and redundant training groups can induce high-degree subset functions with compact low-rank representations. A single fitted TNDM can then be used for several training data questions, including predicting the effect of removing data, measuring the importance of individual training units, identifying interactions between training units, and selecting useful subsets of the training data. We evaluate TNDMs on controlled tasks designed to contain strong interactions, as well as standard fine-tuning settings for classification and reasoning. On a controlled reasoning task, TNDMs outperform every baseline while observing only half as many training subsets, and TNDM-TT reduces prediction NMSE by $89\%$ relative to the linear datamodel after observing approximately $0.0061\%$ of all possible training subsets. In factual-association fine-tuning, a single TNDM-CP raises held-out $\mathrm{R}^2$ from $0.579$ to $0.668$ over the linear datamodel. These results demonstrate that compact low-rank models improve prediction when training data effects depend on combinations of training groups.
papers.summary: Datamodels predict how a model's behavior changes when parts of its training data are added or removed, but linear datamodels give each training unit a fixed contribution and cannot capture joint effects. `Tensor Network Datamodels` (`TNDMs`) use low-rank tensor networks to map subsets of the training data to training outcomes, and the authors prove that complementary or redundant data groups produce high-degree interactions that still have compact low-rank forms. One fitted model can answer several questions: the effect of removing data, the importance of individual units, interactions between units, and subset selection. On a controlled reasoning task, **`TNDM-TT` cuts prediction error by 89% relative to the linear datamodel after seeing about 0.0061% of all possible subsets**, and in factual-association fine-tuning `TNDM-CP` raises held-out R² from 0.579 to 0.668.

papers.title: PV-Decoding: Progressive Verification Decoding with Decode Gating for Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: Discrete diffusion language models (dLLMs) offer an attractive alternative to autoregressive generation by updating multiple tokens in parallel, but their inference efficiency is still limited by the cost of safely committing tentative predictions. In particular, speculative decoding for dLLMs is challenging because speculative tokens within the same diffusion block may depend on one another, making aggressive acceptance prone to error propagation and strict verification computationally expensive. We present PV-Decoding, a confidence-driven speculative decoding framework with progressive verification for block diffusion inference. PV-Decoding partitions masked positions into directly decoded tokens, speculative tokens, and unresolved tokens using two confidence thresholds, and then verifies speculative tokens with progressively stronger policies, including single-batch, dual-batch, and multi-batch verification. This design exposes a practical accuracy--efficiency trade-off: weaker verification minimizes overhead, whereas stronger verification improves acceptance precision and robustness. Experiments on three diffusion language models across GSM8K, MBPP, and HumanEval show that PV-Decoding reduces sequential model forward passes (MFPs) by 8%--37% relative to confidence-based decoding, while keeping the largest observed accuracy drop to 1.3%. On Dream-7B-Instruct/GSM8K, PV-Decoding (1-batch) and PV-Decoding (2-batch) improve throughput by 7.0%--13.6% under the same hardware budget, whereas PV-Decoding (multi-batch) is slower under the current runtime. These results suggest that confidence-guided speculation with structured verification is a practical path toward efficient and reliable dLLM inference.
papers.summary: Speculative decoding is hard for discrete diffusion language models (dLLMs) because speculative tokens in the same block can depend on each other, so accepting them aggressively spreads errors and verifying them strictly is expensive. `PV-Decoding` uses two confidence thresholds to sort masked positions into directly decoded, speculative, and unresolved tokens, then checks the speculative ones with progressively stronger single-, dual-, or multi-batch verification. On three dLLMs across `GSM8K`, `MBPP`, and `HumanEval`, it **reduces sequential model forward passes by 8-37% relative to confidence-based decoding with at most a 1.3% accuracy drop**. On `Dream-7B-Instruct` the 1- and 2-batch variants raise throughput by 7.0-13.6%, while the multi-batch variant is slower under the current runtime.

papers.title: fxBench: Evaluating and Understanding Formula Suggestions in Spreadsheets
papers.abstract: Spreadsheets are among the most widely used tools for computations, and formulas are their core building blocks. Besides agentic spreadsheet tools, proactive formula suggestions enable significant productivity gains and are now available in popular spreadsheet software (Microsoft Excel and Google Sheets). Such suggestions pose interesting challenges: the right context must be collected and represented for a machine learning model, which must then be able to write a correct formula, in a way that is fast and cheap enough to trigger on every = (or subsequent keystrokes for auto-completion) without taking users out of their editing flow. Surprisingly, there is no public benchmark for formula suggestions on real spreadsheets. In this paper, we therefore (1) introduce fxBench as a manually curated benchmark of 503 formula suggestion tasks based on Sheetpedia, (2) break down the formula suggestion problem into four capabilities (gather context, understand context, understand intent, write formula) that a formula suggestion system requires, and (3) evaluate existing and new approaches to understand bottlenecks in these capabilities that pose interesting research directions. Specifically, we annotate each benchmark with the cells that describe intent to determine the theoretical performance limit of a given context selection strategy, we evaluate performance of small and large models on different representations of context, including a dense format with high theoretical coverage at low token counts, and we fine-tune smaller language models to show that we can learn to understand such dense formats. Additionally, we perform quantitative and qualitative analysis on failure modes to understand bottlenecks in the formula writing capability; the best configuration only achieved 58.8% correct suggestions.
papers.summary: Proactive formula suggestions now ship in Excel and Google Sheets, yet no public benchmark exists for suggesting formulas on real spreadsheets. `fxBench` provides 503 manually curated tasks drawn from `Sheetpedia` and splits the problem into four capabilities: gathering context, understanding context, understanding intent, and writing the formula. The authors annotate the cells that express intent so they can bound what each context-selection strategy could achieve, test small and large models on different context representations (including a dense, low-token format), and fine-tune small models to read that format. Failure analysis shows formula writing remains a bottleneck, with **the best configuration producing only 58.8% correct suggestions**.

papers.title: GLOSS-MT: Controllable Low-Resource Machine Translation with an Editable Dictionary
papers.abstract: Adapting a pretrained machine translation (MT) model to new terminology usually requires new parallel data and another round of fine-tuning, which is costly for low-resource languages. We ask whether controllability can be added to MT, and the fine-tuning burden reduced, without degrading the pretrained model. GLOSS-MT looks up the source's noun phrases in an offline English-Twi dictionary, replaces every phrase found by its Twi translation in place, and fine-tunes a translation model once to translate these mixed inputs. We apply the same data and pipeline to NLLB-200 (600M, 1.3B, 3.3B), OPUS-MT en-tw and TranslateGemma 4B. On a document-level English-to-Asante Twi benchmark (84 documents, four domains), every fine-tune scores above its pretrained base in chrF2 (+2.85 to +5.48), and the three NLLB fine-tunes are the best open systems (50.12-50.80). A direct controllability test on human-translated Bible passages shows that the three fine-tunes tested write 79-97% of the dictionary terms, and that replacing every dictionary entry by a different term changes the output accordingly (70-97% of the new terms appear) with no retraining. We release the models, data and code.
papers.summary: Adapting a machine translation (MT) model to new terminology usually takes new parallel data and another round of fine-tuning, which is costly for low-resource languages. `GLOSS-MT` looks up noun phrases from the English source in an offline English-Twi dictionary, swaps in their Twi translations, and fine-tunes a translation model once to handle these mixed inputs. Applied to `NLLB-200`, `OPUS-MT`, and `TranslateGemma 4B`, every fine-tune beats its pretrained base on a document-level English-to-Asante Twi benchmark, and the `NLLB` fine-tunes are the best open systems. In a controllability test, **replacing dictionary entries with different terms changes the output accordingly (70-97% of new terms appear) with no retraining**.

papers.title: How Does Muon Work in Private Deep Learning? Scalable Differentially Private Training via Orthogonalization
papers.abstract: Training deep neural networks requires optimizers that balance computational efficiency with formal data privacy. While orthogonalized update rules, such as the recently introduced Muon optimizer, have shown strong empirical performance and scalability, their behavior under Differential Privacy (DP) is not yet understood. In this paper, we propose DP-Muon, a differentially private variant of the Muon optimizer. By analyzing Muon's orthogonalized updates through the lens of a Linear Minimization Oracle (LMO), we show that the leading effect of per-example clipping is a positive rescaling of the gradient, to which the LMO is blind, so that only a small directional residual controlled by the centered gradient variance enters the optimization error. This yields an $\mathcal O(K^{-1/4})$ convergence rate, up to logarithmic factors, to a clipping-dependent neighborhood at a fixed noise scale and, with noise calibrated to a fixed $(\varepsilon,\delta)$ budget, the standard $(\sqrt d/(n\varepsilon))^{1/2}$ privacy--utility bound of DP-SGD, without assuming bounded gradients. Furthermore, we investigate the hyperparameter landscape of DP-Muon and document how the optimal learning rate, momentum, and batch size change under privacy. Empirically, on image classification DP-Muon matches or improves on DP-SGD and DP-Adam, whereas on language modeling the best optimizer depends on the batch size, with DP-Muon best at small batches and DP-Adam best near the privacy-optimal batch size.
papers.summary: How orthogonalized optimizers like `Muon` behave under Differential Privacy (DP) has not been understood, so the authors propose `DP-Muon` and analyze it through a Linear Minimization Oracle (LMO) lens. Their analysis shows that per-example clipping mainly rescales the gradient, which the LMO ignores, so only a small directional residual enters the error. This gives **the standard DP-SGD privacy-utility bound without assuming bounded gradients**, and the authors also map how the best learning rate, momentum, and batch size shift under privacy. In experiments, `DP-Muon` matches or beats `DP-SGD` and `DP-Adam` on image classification; on language modeling it is best at small batches, while `DP-Adam` wins near the privacy-optimal batch size.

papers.title: Gaussian Process Bandits with Paired Auxiliary Observations
papers.abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) is widely used for expensive black-box optimization, yet observation noise makes each evaluation less informative and slows posterior learning. Standard BO learns from costly outcomes gathered during optimization. In many applications, however, low-cost auxiliary data are available beforehand. We introduce Auxiliary-Informed Gaussian Process Bandit (AI-GPB), a variance-reduction method that combines an offline estimate of the auxiliary mean with a correction coefficient learned from paired online observations. Notably, it exploits correlation between paired observation errors without requiring the auxiliary mean to approximate the objective. We establish finite-sample GP confidence bounds and regret guarantees, including explicit cumulative and simple regret rates for Mat\'ern kernels. Numerical experiments across continuous BO benchmarks with varied landscapes and dimensions show consistent reductions in cumulative and simple regret relative to vanilla GP-UCB, even when within-pair correlation is moderate and the auxiliary mean is estimated from noisy offline data.
papers.summary: Noisy evaluations slow Bayesian optimization (BO), even though cheap auxiliary data is often available before optimization starts. `Auxiliary-Informed Gaussian Process Bandit` (`AI-GPB`) reduces variance by combining an offline estimate of the auxiliary mean with a correction coefficient learned from paired online observations, using the correlation between paired errors rather than requiring the auxiliary signal to approximate the objective. The authors prove finite-sample confidence bounds and explicit regret rates for Matérn kernels. In experiments, **`AI-GPB` consistently lowers cumulative and simple regret relative to vanilla `GP-UCB`**, even with moderate correlation and noisy offline data.

papers.title: From Overparameterised Expressions to Parsimonious Models: Fisher-Geometric Pruning for Symbolic Regression
papers.abstract:
Genetic programming symbolic regression (GPSR) often returns expressions that are larger than necessary, with dormant branches and finely tuned algebraic configurations that fit sampling noise. Existing complexity-control strategies, such as multi-objective size-accuracy search or information criteria embedded in the fitness function, act on syntactic representations during model search. We introduce Fisher-Geometric pruning (FGP), a post-hoc model-reduction framework that acts on fitted models and can complement these techniques.
  FGP combines local information geometry at the maximum-likelihood solution with explicit compatibility tests for interpretable parametric boundaries. A taxonomy of parametric directions separates local sensitivity from proximity to reducible boundaries, enabling the treatment of unidentifiable directions and reductions through zero constraints, asymptotic limits, and signed parameter identifications. Candidate reductions are realised by symbolic contraction and refitting, then accepted only when their cross-validated predictive risk remains within a prescribed tolerance.
  We evaluate FGP on controlled diagnostic problems and Pareto fronts generated by GPSR. Across both settings, FGP substantially reduces structural complexity while preserving, and often improving, out-of-sample accuracy. Comparisons with competing pruning strategies and ablations show that, by combining geometric screening, boundary compatibility, and predictive validation, FGP yields the most consistent joint gains in parsimony and generalisation.
papers.summary: Genetic programming symbolic regression (GPSR) tends to return expressions larger than needed, with dormant branches and finely tuned terms that fit noise. `Fisher-Geometric pruning` (`FGP`) is a post-hoc step that combines the local information geometry at the maximum-likelihood fit with explicit tests for interpretable reductions, such as zero constraints, asymptotic limits, and parameter identifications. Candidate simplifications are contracted symbolically, refitted, and accepted only if cross-validated predictive risk stays within a set tolerance. On diagnostic problems and GPSR Pareto fronts, **`FGP` substantially reduces structural complexity while preserving and often improving out-of-sample accuracy**, more consistently than competing pruning strategies.

papers.title: Paired-Outcome Learning for Selective Spacecraft Attitude Capture under Torque Limits
papers.abstract: Torque-limited spacecraft attitude capture requires adapting the maneuver speed to uncertain braking authority. Faster settings can reduce average tracking error while worsening individual maneuvers, making selective modification of an existing controller a baseline-relative learning problem. A paired-outcome method combines three mechanisms: physically interpretable continuation policies with different speed envelopes, separate prediction of task failure and successful-pair tracking gains, and context-dependent rejection that executes the unchanged baseline. Complete paired simulations provide labels under common plant parameters and measurement seeds; training, validation, and calibration are separated by context. Basilisk experiments use 108 development contexts, 324 labeling rollouts, and 624 evaluation episodes across 48 test contexts, including disclosed post-freeze diagnostics. The selective controller reduces aggregate integrated attitude error by 4.67% relative to the branch baseline, with 17 improvements, 31 exact ties, and no observed regressions. Always using the fast alternative achieves a 4.81% reduction but worsens 11 cases. Gains occur in principal-axis, near-axis, braking-boundary, and selected noise/drift maneuvers; general coupled cases retain the baseline. Ablations show no additional aggregate benefit from branch commitment, active querying, or score subtraction. The evidence supports a restricted empirical trade-off between average improvement and individual regression, without establishing a closed-loop safety guarantee.
papers.summary: When a spacecraft captures a target attitude under torque limits, faster maneuver settings can lower average tracking error while making some individual maneuvers worse. The proposed paired-outcome method chooses among physically interpretable continuation policies, separately predicts task failure and tracking gains, and falls back to the unchanged baseline controller when it is unsure. In `Basilisk` simulations across 48 test contexts, **the selective controller cuts aggregate attitude error by 4.67% with no observed regressions**, whereas always using the fast alternative gives 4.81% but worsens 11 cases. The authors state that the results do not establish a closed-loop safety guarantee.

papers.title: BanglaBBQ: A Bias Benchmark for Question Answering in the Bangladeshi Context
papers.abstract: This paper introduces BanglaBBQ, a question-answering bias benchmark designed to capture stereotypes grounded in the Bangladeshi context, in both Bangla and English. Following KoBBQ and PakBBQ, BanglaBBQ adapts the original Bias Benchmark for Question Answering (BBQ) by classifying its templates into three groups: directly translated (DT), modified to align target groups or contexts with Bangladesh (TM), and removed when deemed unsuitable for the Bangladeshi context (SR). This process retains 140 templates across six categories, comprising 76 DT and 64 TM templates. Five newly authored (NA) categories, based on stereotypes common in Bangladeshi society, are then added: marital status, age and political perception, regional origin, educational background, and mental-health status. Native Bangladeshi annotators judged all 466 newly authored templates, and 372 were retained because a strict majority of English annotators identified the intended target and rated the attitude as common enough. Each newly authored template is linked to a documented source and a verbatim quote from it. Each evaluated template also has a counter-stereotypical version of its disambiguated context. The dataset was evaluated using two open-weight models (Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B) and two closed models (GPT-4.1-mini and Gemini 2.5 Flash). All four lean towards the stereotyped person when the context is ambiguous, in both languages, and the effect of language differs by model, so English results do not predict behaviour in Bangla. On the adapted BBQ templates, both Qwen3 models are also less accurate when the context contradicts a stereotype than when it confirms it. On the newly authored templates, the closed models follow counter-stereotypical evidence almost perfectly, and all four models are more biased on the templates that annotators validated than on those they rejected.
papers.summary: `BanglaBBQ` adapts the Bias Benchmark for Question Answering (`BBQ`) to stereotypes in Bangladeshi society, in both Bangla and English. It keeps 140 translated or localized templates and adds 372 annotator-validated templates in five new categories, including marital status, regional origin, and mental-health status, each linked to a documented source. Testing `Qwen3-4B`, `Qwen3-8B`, `GPT-4.1-mini`, and `Gemini 2.5 Flash` shows that **all four lean toward the stereotyped person when the context is ambiguous, in both languages**, and the effect of language varies by model, so English results do not predict behavior in Bangla. The models were also more biased on templates annotators validated than on those they rejected.

papers.title: ECHO: Efficient Causal Self-Recursion Beyond Auxiliary Multi-Token Prediction
papers.abstract: Existing Multi-token prediction (MTP) methods are auxiliary by design: the multi-horizon loss mostly trains modules attached to the backbone, and each added horizon costs another module and another pass. We propose Efficient Causal Self-Recursion (ECHO), which removes both costs. The backbone's own final layer predicts every horizon, so the supervision lands on the parameters that generate the next token, and Dynamic Depth Sampling (DDS) keeps deeper horizons affordable by drawing the training depth with probabilities that decay along depth. Future prediction thus becomes part of the autoregressive objective rather than a task attached to it, and the gains follow on both sides of it. In pretraining, added depth converts into downstream accuracy where auxiliary modules saturate, concentrating on reasoning and code at half the MTP training overhead of training every depth. At inference, the pretrained model is its own drafter: it drafts beyond the depth it was trained for, and keeps its draft-target alignment on the open-ended, high-entropy generation where post-hoc drafters lose theirs. The advantage survives a doubled token budget, a repeated pretraining run, and supervised finetuning.
papers.summary: Multi-token prediction (MTP) methods usually train extra modules attached to the backbone, and each added horizon costs another module and another pass. `Efficient Causal Self-Recursion` (`ECHO`) has the backbone's own final layer predict every horizon, and uses `Dynamic Depth Sampling` (`DDS`) to sample training depths with decaying probabilities so deeper horizons stay affordable. In pretraining, **added depth keeps improving downstream accuracy, especially on reasoning and code, where auxiliary modules saturate**, at half the overhead of training every depth. At inference, the model drafts for its own speculative decoding beyond its trained depth and stays aligned with its outputs on high-entropy generation, where post-hoc drafters lose alignment.

papers.title: Evidence Field: Adaptive Covering Programs for Medical Imaging
papers.abstract: Medical image classifiers typically return predictions without a native contract for independently reconstructing their spatial decision computation. Evidence Field is a trainable spatial-program architecture that jointly produces class scores, selected covering programs and signed evidence. Its encoder combines absolute and image-relative response fields with associative spatial moments and learned characteristic sums. A typed classifier scores individual regions and parent-conditioned multiplicative groups; a covering recursion selects scale, partition and composition. We establish exact one-fold coverage, optimality within the registered grammar, a bound relating smooth training to hard inference, signed-score conservation and class-centred offset invariance. Direct contractions and their adjoint specify arithmetic and storage scaling on two- and three-dimensional grids. Native output records bind inputs, parameters, supports, types and contextual dependencies to individual and ensemble predictions. In a separately reported histopathology application, patient-separated training and evaluation across held-out centres provide empirical evidence for the architecture. Trained mechanism and corrected-loss comparisons distinguish predictive effects from implementation correctness; independent readers reconstruct descriptors, routes, scores and probability mixtures. The principal contribution is a coupled representation, decision and evidence architecture whose selected computation can be reproduced independently.
papers.summary: Medical image classifiers usually output predictions without any built-in way to independently reconstruct the spatial computation behind them. `Evidence Field` is a trainable architecture that outputs class scores together with selected covering programs over image regions and signed evidence, using a typed classifier and a covering recursion that chooses scale, partition, and composition. The authors prove properties including exact one-fold coverage, optimality within the registered grammar, and conservation of signed scores, and each prediction comes with records that bind its inputs, parameters, and dependencies. The central claim is that **independent readers can reproduce the selected computation behind each prediction**, with supporting evidence from a separately reported histopathology study across held-out centers.

papers.title: Global Convergence in Deep Networks via the Second Law of Thermodynamics
papers.abstract: Existing convergence analyses of finite-width overparameterized deep neural networks under standard parameterization often rely on parameters remaining close to their initialization and typically neglect the role of noise, despite empirical evidence that stochasticity can improve optimization and generalization. To bridge this gap, we study $L_2$-regularized continuous-time Langevin dynamics (CLD) with isotropic noise, for training feedforward networks with smooth activations. We introduce a change-of-measure inequality, inspired by the second law of thermodynamics, that enables control of key properties of the training dynamics under the time-evolving parameter distribution. Leveraging a sharpened lower bound on the minimum eigenvalue of the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) at initialization, we show that injected noise helps preserve NTK stability with high probability without confining the weights to a small neighborhood of their initialization. As a result, we derive a non-asymptotic upper bound on the expected training loss. Our analysis yields explicit conditions on width and noise temperature that guarantee convergence to a finite loss floor. Finally, we experimentally show the network Jacobian can change from initialization, departing the commonly analyzed lazy regime.
papers.summary: Convergence proofs for finite-width overparameterized networks usually assume the weights stay near initialization and ignore noise, even though stochasticity appears to help in practice. The authors study L2-regularized continuous-time Langevin dynamics and introduce a change-of-measure inequality inspired by the second law of thermodynamics to control training under the evolving parameter distribution. With a sharper lower bound on the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) at initialization, they show that **injected noise keeps the NTK stable without confining weights near initialization**, which yields a non-asymptotic bound on training loss and explicit width and temperature conditions for convergence. Experiments confirm that the network Jacobian moves away from initialization, outside the commonly analyzed lazy regime.

papers.title: Process-Aware Event Log Augmentation for Process Prediction under Labeled Data Scarcity
papers.abstract: Predictive Process Monitoring (PPM) forecasts future events of ongoing business processes based on event logs. However, deep learning PPM approaches are often limited by labeled data scarcity and the low variability of real-world logs. To address this, we introduce SiamSA-PPM, a self-supervised framework combining Siamese learning with statistically grounded data augmentation. It employs novel transformation methods that leverage control-flow semantics and frequent behavioral patterns to generate realistic, semantically valid trace variants, learning generalizable prefix representations without labeled supervision. Extensive experiments on real-world event logs with a wide range of variability, incorporating exhaustive hyperparameter tuning, demonstrate the value of this process-aware augmentation. Compared to state-of-the-art baselines, SiamSA-PPM achieves competitive or superior predictive performance in both next activity and final outcome prediction tasks. An open source implementation of our method is publicly available under https://github.com/SvStraten/SiamSA-PPM-Extension..
papers.summary: Deep learning methods for Predictive Process Monitoring (PPM), which forecast future events in business processes from event logs, are limited by scarce labels and low-variability logs. `SiamSA-PPM` combines Siamese self-supervised learning with augmentations that use control-flow semantics and frequent behavioral patterns to generate realistic, valid trace variants. On real-world event logs, **it matches or beats state-of-the-art baselines on next-activity and final-outcome prediction**, and the implementation is open source.

papers.title: Martingale Posterior Cox Processes
papers.abstract: Cox processes provide a principled Bayesian nonparametric framework for modeling event-based data through an underlying intensity function. However, existing inference methods for estimating the intensity typically rely on computationally expensive Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling or approximate inference techniques. In addition, to ensure tractability, these methods often define priors over indirect latent structures, making them challenging to interpret. In this paper, we introduce the Martingale Posterior Cox Process (MPCP), which recasts Bayesian intensity estimation as inference over unobserved events given the observed event history. This perspective avoids the need to define complex priors while retaining the flexibility of nonparametric modeling. We propose a scalable, GPU-friendly copula-based predictive update, and provide strong theoretical guarantees for the convergence of the predictive resampling algorithm. Empirically, we show that MPCP provides excellent performance in both simulations and real data at a fraction of the computational cost of competing Bayesian approaches.
papers.summary: Bayesian inference for Cox processes, which model event data through an underlying intensity function, usually depends on expensive Markov chain Monte Carlo or on priors over hard-to-interpret latent structures. The `Martingale Posterior Cox Process` (`MPCP`) instead treats intensity estimation as inference over unobserved events given the observed history, which removes the need for complex priors. It uses a GPU-friendly copula-based predictive update with convergence guarantees for its resampling algorithm, and **delivers strong performance on simulated and real data at a fraction of the computational cost** of competing Bayesian approaches.

papers.title: Information Theory of Random Composition Trees
papers.abstract: Random composition trees model the hierarchical semantic structures of meaningful texts as a statistical ensemble generated by recursively splitting texts into coherent chunks. A recent study shows that different text types can be described by random composition trees with distinct branching factors, and that the entropy rates of these trees exhibit a similar dependence across text types as the entropy rates of the actual texts. Motivated by this correspondence, we analyze information-theoretic properties of this stochastic splitting model. First, we demonstrate that the entropy of random composition trees grows linearly with the root size, and we derive an analytical expression for the entropy rate as a function of the branching factor. Second, we prove that large trees exhibit typicality: with high probability, they belong to a typical set in which each tree is approximately equally likely. Our analysis reveals that the random composition tree model shares two key information-theoretic properties of language when modeled as a stationary and ergodic stochastic process: linear entropy growth and typicality.
papers.summary: Random composition trees model the hierarchical meaning of texts by recursively splitting them into coherent chunks, and earlier work found that their entropy rates track those of real texts across text types. The authors analyze the model's information-theoretic properties and derive an analytical expression for the entropy rate as a function of the branching factor. They prove that tree entropy grows linearly with root size and that large trees exhibit typicality, so **the model shares two key properties of language modeled as a stationary ergodic process: linear entropy growth and typicality**.

papers.title: Who Gets Unmasked? Sampler-Induced Bias in Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (dLLMs) generate by gradually unmasking a canvas, so their samplers decide not only which token to write but also when to commit it. We show that this second decision changes who appears in generated text, a sampler-induced bias on top of the model's own. Common commit rules, including LLaDA's default, commit the positions whose sampled tokens are most probable; this peeking favors majority options. To separate the sampler from the model, we read the model's belief about a fork, such as a protagonist's gender, in one forward pass, and show that this belief matches exact sampling from the model. Measured against it, peeking samplers on LLaDA and Dream amplify occupational gender stereotypes and collapse opinion distributions, and confidence-based ordering shifts gender-balanced occupations toward men, more so under faster parallel decoding. We propose Fork-First Sampling, which decides the fork before anything else is written: it follows the belief or any target distribution, improves fluency, and avoids the stories that remark on the protagonist's gender, which prompt-based fixes produce, at the cost of one forward pass. Fairness evaluations of dLLMs should report the commit rule.
papers.summary: Diffusion language models (dLLMs) decide both which token to write and when to commit it, and the authors show that the commit decision alone can change who appears in generated text. Common rules, including `LLaDA`'s default, commit the most probable positions first, which favors majority options; measured against the model's own belief about a choice such as a protagonist's gender (read in one forward pass), these samplers on `LLaDA` and `Dream` **amplify occupational gender stereotypes and collapse opinion distributions**, and the effect grows with faster parallel decoding. The proposed `Fork-First Sampling` settles the choice before writing anything else, follows the model's belief or any target distribution at the cost of one forward pass, and improves fluency. The authors recommend that fairness evaluations of dLLMs report the commit rule.

papers.title: Table Serialization Determines Which Relations Language Models Preserve
papers.abstract: We study how text serialization affects table lookup in instruction-tuned language models. Our diagnostic asks the model to find the row containing a specified value under one named column, then return the value under another named column in that same row. We render the same synthetic 256-cell tables in row-major form and in column-major form with each header placed beside its values, while varying the table aspect ratio across five shapes. Across three models, the better format changes with table shape: row-major performs better on tall tables, whereas column-major performs better on wide tables. At 64 x 4, row-major leads by 42.3-54.0 percentage points; at 4 x 64, column-major leads by 35.0-59.0 points. Mapping wrong answers back to their source cells reveals a complementary error pattern: row-major tends to preserve the correct row but lose the target column, while column-major tends to preserve the correct column but lose the row. We use the term relational locality to describe this pattern: serialization keeps one relation locally available while making the other depend on positional alignment. A separate non-tabular ordering experiment supports this interpretation. Thus, apparent width-related failures in text-serialized tables depend on linearization, not table shape alone.
papers.summary: Instruction-tuned language models read tables as flattened text, and the choice of linearization turns out to decide which relationships in the table survive. Using a synthetic lookup diagnostic over 256-cell tables rendered row-major or column-major across five aspect ratios, three models showed opposite preferences depending on shape: **row-major led by 42.3 to 54.0 percentage points on a 64x4 table, while column-major led by 35.0 to 59.0 points on a 4x64 one**. Tracing wrong answers back to their source cells revealed mirrored error modes, with row-major keeping the right row but losing the target column and column-major doing the reverse, a pattern the authors call relational locality. The conclusion is that reported failures on wide tables stem from serialization rather than table shape alone.

papers.title: Is User Calibration Still Necessary for Continuous Myoelectric Control? A Closed-Loop Comparison of Calibration-Free Controllers
papers.abstract: The need for user-specific calibration remains an often-cited barrier to widespread adoption of myoelectric control. Cross-user models trained on large multi-user datasets can now recognize gestures from unseen users without calibration, but they have been evaluated almost exclusively offline, leaving open whether calibration is still needed in closed-loop control. This study compared six calibration-free controllers, trained on 306 users of the EMG-EPN-612 dataset and used without any calibration data from the test participant, against three calibrated controllers in a closed-loop Fitts' law target-acquisition task with sixteen participants. The calibrated controllers achieved higher offline balanced accuracy (90.6% against 73.1% for the best controller of each paradigm), but completion rates did not differ significantly between paradigms, and the highest completion rate was achieved by a calibration-free controller. Calibrated controllers moved faster on successful acquisitions, partly because of their individually fitted speed mappings, though not significantly after correction for multiple comparisons. However, every calibration-free controller produced more direct and stable trajectories than every calibrated controller, even after adjusting for cursor speed. Offline accuracy did not predict completion rate across controllers or within participants, and across paradigms higher offline accuracy was associated with poorer trajectory quality in 15 of 16 participants. Without any calibration data from the end user, a model trained across a large population matched calibrated control in completion rate and exceeded it in trajectory quality. The offline accuracy gained through calibration should therefore not be taken as evidence of a closed-loop benefit.
papers.summary: Myoelectric prosthesis control normally requires each user to record calibration data, and cross-user models trained on large populations have been proposed as a replacement but judged almost entirely on offline accuracy. Six calibration-free controllers trained on 306 users of the `EMG-EPN-612` dataset were compared against three calibrated controllers in a closed-loop Fitts' law target-acquisition task with sixteen participants.
