Although calibrated controllers scored far higher offline (90.6% versus 73.1% balanced accuracy), **completion rates did not differ significantly between the two paradigms and every calibration-free controller produced more direct and stable cursor trajectories**, even after adjusting for speed. Offline accuracy failed to predict completion rate either across controllers or within participants, and higher offline accuracy went with worse trajectory quality for 15 of 16 participants.

papers.title: Aptamers as a sandbox for lab-in-the-loop agentic molecular discovery
papers.abstract:
Despite breakthroughs in AI-driven molecular generation, existing discovery pipelines operate largely in silico, with wet-lab feedback reserved for validation rather than iterative improvement. Whether large language model (LLM)-based reasoning agents can accelerate de novo discovery by iterating with lab data remains unproven.
  Here we use protein-binding aptamer design as a sandbox (1-2 week cycles, \$1-\$3 per candidate) to demonstrate a wet lab in a closed loop with AI systems. We tasked agentic pipelines with developing aptamer binders against $\alpha$-thrombin and myoglobin across three design-test-improve cycles ($\sim$1,000 candidates per round; $\sim$4,400 constructs). Statistically significant, bead-corrected on-target hit rates among new candidates rose across rounds from 0.0% in Round 1 to 26.0% in Round 2 and 42.1% in Round 3 on $\alpha$-thrombin (37.1% excluding literature motif descendants), and from 10.2% in Round 1 to 3.7% in Round 2 and 33.5% in Round 3 on myoglobin. Single-clone bead-binding titrations of eight full-length $\alpha$-thrombin candidates confirmed concordance with pooled sequencing enrichment (Pearson $r = 0.90$). In these assays, literature-derived motifs engineered by the agents to reduce off-target reactivity in the pooled screen reached apparent affinities of $K_D = 24.6$--$133$ nM, whereas de novo scaffolds showed low-micromolar binding ($K_D > 1\ \mu$M).
  We also report how our pipelines used myoglobin binding data to exploit the G-quadruplex binder space, diagnose cross-reactivity as on-target specificity dropped from 75.0% to 19.1%, and recover by developing strategies that restored specificity to 72.4%. We demonstrate that empirical lab data is more valuable than existing computational proxies, showing how iterative experimental feedback enables AI agents to diagnose assay artifacts and refine molecular designs across rounds.
papers.summary: AI-driven molecular design pipelines usually run entirely in silico and treat wet-lab results as a final check rather than as feedback, leaving open whether large language model (LLM) agents can actually learn from experiments. Protein-binding aptamer design served as a fast, cheap testbed (one to two week cycles, $1-$3 per candidate) for three design-test-improve rounds against alpha-thrombin and myoglobin, covering roughly 4,400 constructs. **On-target hit rates for new candidates rose from 0.0% in round one to 42.1% by round three for alpha-thrombin**, and from 10.2% to 33.5% for myoglobin, with single-clone binding titrations tracking pooled sequencing enrichment at Pearson r = 0.90. Agents also diagnosed cross-reactivity when on-target specificity fell from 75.0% to 19.1% and recovered it to 72.4%, and literature-derived motifs they engineered bound at 24.6-133 nM while fully de novo scaffolds stayed above 1 micromolar.

papers.title: Medical Fine-Tuning Reshapes, Not Reduces, Patient-Facing AI Risk: A Rubric-Based, LLM-Judge Evaluation Framework
papers.abstract: Patient-facing medical question answering with large language models (LLMs) is moving from research demonstrations to production deployments, yet evaluation remains anchored on factual correctness. Factuality is necessary but not sufficient: a response can be factually grounded and still issue a directive that, if acted on, would harm the patient. We introduce a risk-sensitive evaluation framework that scores responses by the presence and severity of six categories of risk-bearing language (treatment directives, contraindications, dosage expressions, urgency-triage cues, high-alert medication mentions, and overconfident assertions), anchored on published clinical harm taxonomies. Severity is classified by a three-judge LLM ensemble. We apply this framework to six 7-9B instruction-tuned models, three general (Mistral-7B, Phi-3.5-mini, Llama-3.1-8B) and three medically adapted (BioMistral-7B, OpenBioLLM-Llama3-8B, Med42-Llama3-8B), on 200 real patient questions from the K-QA benchmark. Two findings emerge. First, ensemble risk-bearing language is statistically independent of factual hallucination rate (pooled Spearman $\rho = -0.065$, $n = 300$, 95% CI $[-0.18, +0.05]$; distance correlation $= 0.10$, independence test $p = 0.24$). Second, medical fine-tuning does not reduce aggregate risk but reshapes it: continued-pretraining adaptations (BioMistral, OpenBioLLM) consistently suppress high-alert medication mentions while amplifying overconfident assertions, whereas clinical instruction-tuning (Med42) suppresses dosing only, without amplifying overconfidence. Per-category Krippendorff $\alpha$ is fair to good for the four linguistically anchored categories (0.53-0.71) and low for the two clinical-judgment-dependent categories (0.19, 0.31), indicating where automatic safety evaluation is and is not yet reliable. We release the rubric, judge prompts, and evaluation code.
papers.summary: Evaluation of patient-facing medical question answering focuses on factual correctness, yet a factually accurate response can still contain a directive that would harm someone who acted on it. The proposed framework scores responses for the presence and severity of six categories of risk-bearing language — treatment directives, contraindications, dosage expressions, urgency-triage cues, high-alert medication mentions, and overconfident assertions — graded by a three-judge LLM ensemble, and was applied to six 7-9B instruction-tuned models including `Mistral-7B`, `Llama-3.1-8B`, `BioMistral-7B`, `OpenBioLLM-Llama3-8B`, and `Med42-Llama3-8B` on 200 real questions from `K-QA`. **Risk-bearing language was statistically independent of factual hallucination rate** (pooled Spearman rho = -0.065, independence test p = 0.24), and medical fine-tuning redistributed risk rather than reducing it, with continued-pretraining models suppressing high-alert medication mentions while amplifying overconfident assertions. Inter-judge agreement was fair to good for the four linguistically anchored categories and poor for the two requiring clinical judgment, marking where automated safety scoring is not yet dependable.

papers.title: Ask, Don't Guess: Targeted Clarification for Speech Recognition Errors
papers.abstract: Speech recognition in real time in far-field conversational settings still incurs significant errors. Identifying potential error spans during streaming ASR permits a recourse mechanism where the speaker can be asked to repeat the affected content under cleaner acoustic conditions. We propose PARDON, a new framework for online error localization, that identifies spans likely to benefit from this intervention. Our supervision uses clean audio to estimate how the recognizer's output might change under improved acoustic conditions. We probabilistically align noisy and clean decodes using a pair-HMM to obtain soft supervision. These soft targets train a counterfactual gain scorer by combining a suite of acoustic and language features to produce token-level scores, that are further grouped into spans for targeted recourse. An LLM uses the ASR transcript of the repetition to revise only the selected span. At a precision of 70%, PARDON achieves the highest recall by identifying up to 52% more erroneous tokens compared to the strongest baseline. Targeted repetition yields relative WER reductions of up to 24% under a budget that accounts for both interruption frequency and the lengths of re-uttered spans.
papers.summary: Streaming speech recognition in noisy far-field settings still makes errors, and one unused recourse is simply asking the speaker to repeat the specific words that went wrong. `PARDON` localizes such spans online by using clean audio to estimate how the recognizer's output would change under better acoustics, probabilistically aligning noisy and clean decodes with a pair hidden Markov model to produce soft supervision for a counterfactual gain scorer over acoustic and language features; an LLM then revises only the flagged span from the repeated audio. At 70% precision the method identifies **up to 52% more erroneous tokens than the strongest baseline**, and targeted repetition cuts word error rate by up to 24% relative under a budget that charges for both interruption frequency and the length of re-uttered text.

papers.title: Tilted Mondrian: Triage and Mitigation of Fine-grained Disparities in Conformal Prediction
papers.abstract: Fairness in conformal prediction is often pursued through Mondrian calibration, which provides finite-sample coverage guarantees separately across groups. These guarantees, however, are coarse: substantial disparities can remain within finer strata. This coarse-to-fine fairness issue raises two questions: how severe can such disparities be, and how can they be mitigated? Aggregate disparities can depend on how groups are distributed across strata. For severity assessment, we introduce propensity standardization to examine the effect of population composition, and show how group composition can induce disagreement between aggregate and finer-stratum comparisons. For mitigation, we develop Tilted Mondrian to improve fairness compared to group-Mondrian at a finer level without additional model training. Tilted Mondrian retains groupwise coverage guarantees and mitigates coverage and prediction set size disparities within finer strata. Finally, we derive a method-agnostic bound that quantifies how much reduction in finer-stratum coverage disparity can be achieved.
papers.summary: Conformal prediction is often made fair through Mondrian calibration, which guarantees coverage separately for each declared group, but those guarantees say nothing about finer subgroups inside a group. Two tools address this coarse-to-fine gap: propensity standardization, which isolates how population composition across strata can make aggregate comparisons disagree with fine-stratum ones, and `Tilted Mondrian`, a calibration scheme that reduces coverage and prediction-set-size disparities within finer strata **while retaining the original groupwise coverage guarantees and requiring no model retraining**. The authors also derive a method-agnostic bound on how much fine-stratum disparity reduction is achievable at all.

papers.title: First-Order LoRA Training with Phone NPUs
papers.abstract: On-device fine-tuning lets a large language model (LLM) learn from its user's private data without uploading it. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) reduces the trainable parameters, but each first-order training step still multiplies by the frozen base-model weights during the forward pass, activation recomputation, and input-gradient computation. A phone's neural processing unit (NPU) already holds these weights for inference; using it for training also requires computing input gradients, which its inference interface does not support. We present a system that runs all three frozen-weight products on the NPU while keeping the training graph, adapters, and optimizer on the CPU. Its input-gradient kernels reuse the resident weight tiles and the forward dequantizer, avoiding a transposed weight copy and ensuring forward and backward use the same effective weights. To preserve usable gradients, the system selects precision by gradient sensitivity and applies a per-row range guard for half-precision (FP16) outputs. Its runtime fuses the remaining CPU operators and overlaps NPU execution with adapter computation, while resumable execution and thermal pacing let training proceed as a background job. We evaluate it on two Qualcomm Snapdragon platforms using four LLMs from the Qwen and Llama families. Our workloads cover nightly personalization with labels supplied on the phone and the public LaMP-2 benchmark; comparisons include an optimized CPU trainer, a phone-GPU trainer, forward-only training, and GPU-trained references.
papers.summary: Fine-tuning a language model on a phone keeps private data local, but even low-rank adaptation (LoRA) must multiply by the frozen base weights three times per step — forward pass, activation recomputation, and input-gradient computation — and a phone's neural processing unit (NPU), which already holds those weights for inference, exposes no interface for input gradients. The described system runs all three frozen-weight products on the NPU while keeping the training graph, adapters, and optimizer on the CPU, with **input-gradient kernels that reuse the resident weight tiles and the forward dequantizer, avoiding a transposed weight copy and keeping forward and backward on identical effective weights**. Precision is chosen by gradient sensitivity with a per-row range guard for FP16 outputs, and the runtime fuses CPU operators, overlaps NPU work with adapter computation, and adds resumable execution plus thermal pacing so training runs as a background job. Evaluation covers two Qualcomm Snapdragon platforms, four `Qwen` and `Llama` models, nightly on-device personalization, and the `LaMP-2` benchmark, against CPU, phone-GPU, forward-only, and server-GPU references.

papers.title: Efficiency Measured in English: Tokeniser Coverage Bounds Small Language Models on Indic Scripts
papers.abstract: Small Language Models with quantisation and parameter-efficient adaptation are widely offered as the route to multilingual AI under compute constraints, and their efficiency is almost always reported as a single memory figure. We show that this figure is measured in English and does not transfer. Across a 131k-sentence corpus spanning eleven Indic scripts, TinyLlama-1.1B's tokeniser emits 1.34 subword tokens per Latin-script word and 22.60 per Kannada word. This is not inefficiency; it is absence. Its vocabulary contains 0% of Odia's codepoints, 1% of Telugu's and 2% of Kannada's, and for five of eleven scripts the measured fertility sits at the UTF-8 byte-fallback ceiling, on Odia at 99.6% of it, with 93.6% of emitted tokens being raw bytes. Because SentencePiece byte fallback never raises an unknown-token marker, this failure is entirely silent: TinyLlama's UNK rate is 0.0% on every script, including the one it reads as bytes. We further show that low fertility can indicate the opposite of efficiency: mBERT posts its best score anywhere (1.10 tokens/word, on Odia) while discarding 87.9% of the text as UNK. MuRIL, an Indic-vocabulary encoder with a fifth of TinyLlama's parameters, reads every script at 1.23-2.26 tokens/word with zero UNK and zero byte fallback. The binding constraint is the vocabulary, not the parameter count. The consequence is concrete: on a 2048-token context window, the same model gives an English user 1,528 words of usable context and a Kannada user 91.
papers.summary: Small quantized models are routinely pitched as the path to multilingual AI on limited compute, with efficiency reported as a single memory number measured on English text. Across a 131,000-sentence corpus in eleven Indic scripts, `TinyLlama-1.1B`'s tokenizer emits 1.34 subword tokens per Latin-script word but **22.60 per Kannada word**, because its vocabulary contains 0% of Odia's codepoints and 1-2% of Telugu's and Kannada's; for five scripts fertility sits at the UTF-8 byte-fallback ceiling, and because SentencePiece byte fallback never raises an unknown-token marker the failure is silent at a 0.0% UNK rate. Low fertility can also mean the opposite of efficiency: `mBERT` posts its best tokens-per-word score on Odia while discarding 87.9% of the text as unknown, whereas `MuRIL`, an Indic-vocabulary encoder with a fifth of TinyLlama's parameters, reads every script at 1.23-2.26 tokens per word with no UNK and no byte fallback. The practical consequence is that a 2,048-token window holds 1,528 English words but only 91 Kannada ones, making vocabulary rather than parameter count the binding constraint.

papers.title: Pair-Aware Optimization: Coordinating Exploration and Refinement for Jailbreaking LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents are vulnerable to adversarial inputs that induce attacker-specified malicious behaviors, commonly referred to as jailbreaking. Existing optimization-based jailbreak attacks primarily employ first-order (FO) methods that leverage gradient information or zeroth-order (ZO) methods that rely on function-value feedback. However, their complementarity and optimization ordering remain underexplored. We systematically investigate four strategies: pure ZO, pure FO, ZO->FO, and FO->ZO, and develop a ZO-FO framework that explores adversarial prefixes through ZO optimization and refines their corresponding suffixes through FO optimization. To coordinate the two processes, we introduce Pair-aware optimization, which retains multiple prefix candidates, conditionally refines their suffixes and selects among the resulting prefix-suffix pairs. We further investigate agent jailbreaking from a more general stochastic-generation perspective, where the same adversarial input can induce diverse reasoning trajectories and actions that a single greedy output cannot capture. Accordingly, we adopt consistent stochastic decoding during both optimization and evaluation. Experiments across malicious-instruction and malicious-environment benchmarks demonstrate that hybrid optimization improves attack effectiveness over single-optimizer methods, while optimization order substantially influences performance.
papers.summary: Adversarial inputs that steer LLM agents into attacker-specified behavior are typically searched for with either first-order methods that use gradients or zeroth-order methods that use only function values, and how the two combine has not been examined. Four orderings (pure zeroth-order, pure first-order, and both sequential combinations) are compared within a framework that explores adversarial prefixes with zeroth-order search and refines the matching suffixes with gradients, coordinated by a pair-aware procedure that keeps several prefix candidates, conditionally refines their suffixes, and selects among the resulting pairs. The work also argues for evaluating agents as stochastic generators, since one input can yield many different reasoning traces and actions that greedy decoding hides, and so uses consistent stochastic decoding during both search and evaluation. Across malicious-instruction and malicious-environment benchmarks, **hybrid optimization is more effective than either single-optimizer approach, and the order of the two stages matters substantially**.

papers.title: Compose the Horizon: Parameter-Shared Blockwise Forecasting under a Sequential-Compute Trade-off
papers.abstract: Most long-horizon forecasters emit the complete future in one pass. We ask whether a compact operator can instead be reused to emit contiguous future blocks, trading stored parameters for sequential computation. Recursive Functional Decomposition (RFD) factorizes the horizon mapping into three parameter-shared block predictions. The blocks occupy disjoint future intervals and are concatenated, not added as trend, seasonal, or residual components, and each emitted block joins the rolling context that conditions the next application. In controlled three-seed experiments, removing forward feedback hurts all four evaluated datasets while stopping gradients through it changes little, so the useful signal is the evolving forecast state itself; reapplying the shared operator helps consistently, but by less than widening it. The model uses 0.08--0.46M parameters, yet its sequential channel-wise execution is slower and more memory-intensive than an iterative baseline at high channel count. In a frozen long-context evaluation against ten strong baseline families, RFD records lower test error in 23 of 24 cells; the comparison is cross-protocol, with RFD using 512/720-step context and the baselines using 96.
papers.summary: Long-horizon time-series forecasters usually emit the whole future in a single pass, which means parameters scale with horizon length. `Recursive Functional Decomposition` instead factorizes the horizon mapping into three parameter-shared predictions of contiguous, disjoint future blocks that are concatenated rather than summed as trend or seasonal parts, with each emitted block folded into the rolling context for the next application. Controlled three-seed ablations show that removing forward feedback hurts on all four datasets while stopping gradients through it barely matters, implicating the evolving forecast state itself; reusing the shared operator helps less than simply widening it. The model uses **0.08 to 0.46 million parameters and records lower test error in 23 of 24 evaluation cells against ten baseline families**, though its sequential channel-wise execution is slower and more memory-hungry than an iterative baseline at high channel counts and the headline comparison is cross-protocol, giving the model a much longer input context than the baselines.

papers.title: Recurrent Temporal Restricted Boltzmann Machines as Unsupervised Encoders for Biomechanical Movement Sequences
papers.abstract: Biomechanical movement recordings are continuous, high-dimensional time series, and analyzing them without manually labeling them requires representations that capture how movements evolve over time. Most unsupervised representation-learning pipelines, however, treat each observation frame independently and discard this temporal structure, while energy-based models that could capture it have not extensively been adapted to biomechanical signals. So, this paper implements the Recurrent Temporal Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RTRBM), a recurrent energy-based model, into an unsupervised encoder that maps windows of movement data to fixed-length embeddings, and tests what its recurrent structure contributes. We adapt the model to continuous-valued signals, stack it into a deep architecture, and integrate it into the SIT-FUSE segmentation pipeline. We evaluate the embeddings on simulated musculoskeletal reaching and on two real gait datasets, using clustering, reconstruction, and walking-speed classification of unseen subjects, and compare them against non-recurrent and non-probabilistic baselines, including a control that removes the recurrent connection. Clustering the embeddings recovers movement structure tied to progress toward the target without any labels, which also transfers to unseen episodes. On gait data, the embeddings outperform PCA and autoencoder baselines under a nonlinear probe. However, removing the recurrent connection does not yield a measurable loss on the reaching task, and simple per-channel summary statistics classify walking speed at least as well as the embeddings. The model is therefore a working, verified encoder for SIT-FUSE, while the evidence for a benefit of recurrence is mixed, and the learned embeddings did not outperform simple summary statistics on gait.
papers.summary: Unlabeled biomechanical recordings are continuous high-dimensional time series, but most unsupervised representation pipelines treat frames independently and throw away temporal structure. The `Recurrent Temporal Restricted Boltzmann Machine`, a recurrent energy-based model, is adapted to continuous-valued signals, stacked into a deep encoder that maps movement windows to fixed-length embeddings, and integrated into the `SIT-FUSE` segmentation pipeline, then tested on simulated musculoskeletal reaching and two real gait datasets via clustering, reconstruction, and walking-speed classification of unseen subjects. Clustering recovers label-free structure tied to progress toward the reaching target and transfers to unseen episodes, and on gait the embeddings beat principal component analysis and autoencoder baselines under a nonlinear probe. **The evidence for recurrence itself is negative, however: ablating the recurrent connection costs nothing measurable on the reaching task, and simple per-channel summary statistics classify walking speed at least as well as the learned embeddings.**

papers.title: Measuring Consensus in AI Agent Networks
papers.abstract: As AI agents become increasingly connected through networks and take on tasks that require negotiation and joint decision-making, a systematic approach is needed to assess how their views converge and what information supports their decisions. We present an evaluation framework that treats consensus formation as the evolution of publicly stated positions toward a shared region, using accumulated communication history as context. The framework tracks position trajectories, group dispersion, and information expressed in public messages. Two case studies examine staffing decisions based on distributed facts and decisions requiring agents to reconcile duplicate information and a cancelled contract. Results from 1,872 completed runs associate sharing explanations with more accurate group decisions, while the second task reveals persistent disagreement despite accurate aggregate answers. Membership-change experiments provide a complementary evaluation. By separating convergence among agents from progress toward a task's full-information answer, the framework relates decision accuracy and bounded disagreement to the information available during the exchange.
papers.summary: As networked AI agents take on negotiation and joint decisions, there is no standard way to ask whether their stated views actually converge or what information drove the outcome. The proposed framework treats consensus as the movement of publicly stated positions toward a shared region given accumulated communication history, tracking position trajectories, group dispersion, and the information expressed in public messages, with membership-change experiments as a complementary probe. Two case studies — staffing decisions from facts distributed across agents, and decisions requiring agents to reconcile duplicate information and a cancelled contract — span **1,872 completed runs, in which sharing explanations was associated with more accurate group decisions** while the second task showed persistent disagreement even when the aggregate answer was right. Separating agreement among agents from progress toward the full-information answer is what lets accuracy and bounded disagreement be attributed to the information actually exchanged.

papers.title: A Statistical Viewpoint on Adam, Shampoo and Muon
papers.abstract: We provide new statistical insights into designing stochastic optimization methods. By modeling the gradient via a normal distribution, we argue that the stochastic gradient should be whitened using its covariance. We give an online method for estimating the mean and variance of the gradients based on regularized likelihood or, equivalently, through a maximum a posteriori estimate. We then show how to use structured approximations to the covariance within this same framework, which includes diagonal and Kronecker-factored approximations. The diagonal approximation results in a method that is very closely related to Adam and performs as well in practice. The Kronecker approximation results in the new MN method, which is a variant of Shampoo and KL-Shampoo. We also recover Muon by applying this same statistical framework to the gradient direction rather than the full gradient. By combining this with a whitening step, we arrive at MN-Muon, a novel preconditioned version of Muon. Our experiments on GPT-2-type models at Chinchilla scale indicate that MND, the diagonal implementation of MN, outperforms both the Distributed Shampoo and the KL-Shampoo implementations in terms of stability, final validation loss and time taken. MND-Muon, the diagonal implementation of MN-Muon, improves on Muon in 21 of 24 paired GPT-small runs and achieves a lower best validation loss on GPT-medium, where it remains stable over the six tested learning rates. However, we found that NorMuon was comparable to MND-Muon and achieved a slightly lower validation loss on GPT-medium and at GPT-small batch 512 on FineWeb.
papers.summary: Modeling the stochastic gradient as a normal random variable implies it should be whitened by its own covariance, and this one assumption reproduces several popular optimizers as special cases. An online estimator for gradient mean and covariance via regularized likelihood (equivalently a maximum a posteriori estimate) yields `Adam` under a diagonal approximation and a new method, `MN`, under a Kronecker-factored one that relates it to `Shampoo` and `KL-Shampoo`; applying the same framework to gradient direction instead of the full gradient recovers `Muon`, and adding whitening gives `MN-Muon`. On GPT-2-style models at Chinchilla scale, the diagonal variant **outperformed both Distributed Shampoo and KL-Shampoo on stability, final validation loss, and wall-clock time, and improved on `Muon` in 21 of 24 paired GPT-small runs**; the authors also report that `NorMuon` was comparable and slightly better at GPT-medium and at GPT-small batch 512 on `FineWeb`.

papers.title: An Impossibility Result for ETF Target Geometry, and an Equinorm Remedy for Imbalanced Analytic Continual Learning
papers.abstract: Analytic continual learning (ACL) methods such as ACIL and GACL fit a ridge-regression classifier head on frozen features via the Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury identity, achieving exemplar-free, exact updates. A separate line of work, Progressive Neural Collapse (ProNC), shows standard continual classifiers benefit from a progressively expanding Simplex Equiangular Tight Frame (ETF) target. It is natural to ask whether fusing the two ideas, exact analytic updates and ETF targets, would yield a better closed-form continual learner. We show this is not the case as the fusion turns out to be identical to plain one-hot ACIL. Further, Simplex ETFs are not nested across class counts, so the literal "progressively expand the ETF" construction stops yielding an ETF as new tasks arrive, and it introduces catastrophic forgetting ($4\times$ that of a classic ACIL head). We therefore separate an ETF's two defining properties, equiangularity and equinormality, and apply each on its own to the classifier weights rather than the targets, where the invariance above does not hold. Equinorm post-processing of the fitted weights recovers both tail-class and overall average accuracy across the long-tailed regime from 5:1 to 100:1 imbalance (e.g. +32.0 tail-accuracy points and +16.0 average-accuracy points at 100:1 on CIFAR-100/ViT), transferring in sign across two backbones and two datasets, at a mild cost of 5.4 average-accuracy points on CIFAR-100/ViT on near-balanced streams (below $\approx 3{:}1$). Equiangular geometry, by contrast, is exactly inert on the target side but actively harmful on the weight side, usually losing to plain one-hot. Hence, the generally useful part of Neural Collapse geometry in Analytic Continual Learning is equinorm post-processing of the weights, becoming more useful as class imbalance grows; and equiangularity is at best a no-op and induces catastrophic forgetting at worst.
papers.summary: Analytic continual learning fits a ridge-regression head on frozen features for exact, exemplar-free updates, while separate work shows continual classifiers benefit from a progressively expanding Simplex Equiangular Tight Frame (ETF) target, so combining them looks promising. **The fusion turns out to be mathematically identical to plain one-hot analytic learning, and because Simplex ETFs are not nested across class counts the literal progressive-expansion construction stops being an ETF as tasks arrive and causes four times the forgetting of a standard head.** Splitting the ETF's two properties and applying each to the classifier weights instead of the targets shows that equinorm post-processing of fitted weights recovers tail and overall accuracy under long-tailed streams (for example +32.0 tail and +16.0 average accuracy points at 100:1 imbalance on `CIFAR-100` with a `ViT` backbone), at a cost of 5.4 average points on near-balanced streams. Equiangularity is exactly inert on the target side and actively harmful on the weight side, so equinorm is the piece of neural-collapse geometry worth keeping.

papers.title: MisleadQA: Diagnosing LLM Failures under Misleading Context
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used to answer questions from retrieved or user-provided context. However, provided context can be factually true yet out-of-scope, describing a different entity, time, or location from the one the question targets, and still lead models to a wrong answer. Prior work has mainly studied factually false or irrelevant context. It remains unclear whether such out-of-scope context misleads models as much as false context, and whether adding gold context prevents models from being misled by either. We introduce **MisleadQA**, a diagnostic dataset of multiple-choice questions with an abstention option. Each question pairs gold context (G) with true but out-of-scope context (S) and false but in-scope context (F) supporting the same wrong answer. We evaluate six open-weight LLMs. On questions they answer correctly without context, providing S alone leads them to switch to this wrong answer in 29.3% of cases, and providing F alone does so in 75.4%. Adding G nearly removes the effect of S, but F still misleads models in 21.0% of cases, especially when F comes first. A context-faithful instruction reduces these errors mainly through abstention and lowers accuracy even with G. These findings suggest that evaluations should check whether context applies to the question, not only whether it is true, and should report correct, misled, and abstention rates together. Data and code are available at [https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MisleadQA](https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MisleadQA).
papers.summary: Retrieved or user-supplied context can be entirely factual yet describe a different entity, time, or place than the question asks about, a failure mode distinct from the false or irrelevant context prior work studies. `MisleadQA` is a multiple-choice diagnostic with an abstention option in which each question pairs gold context with true-but-out-of-scope context and false-but-in-scope context that both support the same wrong answer. On questions six open-weight models answer correctly with no context, out-of-scope context flips them to the wrong answer 29.3% of the time and false context 75.4% of the time; **adding gold context nearly eliminates the out-of-scope effect but false context still misleads models in 21.0% of cases, especially when it appears first**. A context-faithfulness instruction reduces errors mainly by inducing abstention and lowers accuracy even when only gold context is present, which argues for evaluations that check whether context is applicable and that report correct, misled, and abstention rates side by side.

papers.title: Learning to Program Retrievals: Composing Search Primitives via Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented language models increasingly use multi-step search to solve knowledge-intensive tasks, yet existing systems typically expose retrieval through fixed pipelines or collections of atomic tools. We introduce Retrieval Program Learning (RPL), a programmable search framework that allows a policy to compose search primitives into executable programs with local state and control flow. This enables adaptive search that can retrieve broadly, process intermediate results, and selectively construct model context without tying retrieval breadth to context consumption. However, the resulting flexibility creates a difficult exploration problem: useful programs may require several coordinated decisions, while reinforcement learning often supplies only sparse feedback. To address this challenge, we propose program mutation, a grammar-constrained and execution-verified procedure that generates local variants of suboptimal programs sampled during RL, converts them into training trajectories, and distills them back into the policy. We evaluate RPL on open-domain question answering and corpus-level reasoning tasks, comparing it with a range of retrieval and reasoning baselines. RPL consistently improves open-domain QA performance across model sizes and in- and out-of-domain benchmarks, with particularly large gains on multi-hop tasks. Notably, a 4B model trained with RPL outperforms all 8B model baselines. On corpus-level reasoning, RPL achieves the highest answer F1 and document-coverage F1 for both model sizes while substantially reducing context consumption and retrieval turns. Our results show that programmable search expands the retrieval strategies that agents can learn, while program mutation provides an effective mechanism for exploring useful program structures beyond direct on-policy sampling.
papers.summary: Retrieval-augmented models that search in multiple steps are usually limited to fixed pipelines or a flat set of atomic tools, which ties how broadly they can search to how much context they consume. `Retrieval Program Learning` lets a policy compose search primitives into executable programs with local state and control flow, so it can retrieve widely, process intermediate results, and selectively build context; because useful programs need several coordinated decisions under sparse reinforcement-learning reward, the authors add program mutation, a grammar-constrained and execution-verified procedure that turns local variants of suboptimal sampled programs into training trajectories distilled back into the policy. Gains hold across model sizes and in- and out-of-domain open-domain question answering, with the largest improvements on multi-hop tasks, and **a 4B model trained this way outperforms every 8B baseline**. On corpus-level reasoning it achieves the best answer and document-coverage F1 at both sizes while cutting context consumption and the number of retrieval turns.

papers.title: LLM-Based Evaluation Planning for Heterogeneous Optimization
papers.abstract: Heterogeneous optimization problems require an optimizer to decide not only which candidate solutions to evaluate, but also which objectives and constraints should be evaluated under different costs and fidelities. Existing SOTA methods such as MFE-NSGA-III address this setting with manually designed selection metrics, but their behavior is largely determined by predefined heuristic rules and hyperparameters. In this work, we propose REP-HO, a reasoning-based evaluation planner that replaces the rule-based mixed-fidelity selection step with a large language model (LLM) planner. The LLM receives the same primitive optimization-state information as the heuristic planner, such as surrogate predictions, uncertainties, evaluation costs, and budget status. We first show that REP-HO achieves competitive performance compared to the human-designed metric-based method (MFE-NSGA-III). We then further enhance each decision with an adaptive nearest-neighbor summary, leading to better and more stable results. We evaluate REP-HO across five heterogeneous regimes covering cost imbalance, constraint difficulty, surrogate fidelity, budget level, and objective conflict. Across these regimes, one of the two variants obtains the best mean ranking score in every regime, REP-HO(Deepseek) is first or second throughout, and the planner shows adaptive allocation behavior, such as prioritizing constraint evaluations under tighter budgets and reallocating constraint evaluation budget when surrogate reliability changes. These results suggest that LLMs can serve as flexible evaluation planners for heterogeneous optimization, offering a general alternative to fixed hand-designed metrics.
papers.summary: Heterogeneous optimization problems force an optimizer to choose not only which candidates to evaluate but which objectives and constraints to evaluate, each at different cost and fidelity — a decision that state-of-the-art methods such as `MFE-NSGA-III` make with hand-tuned heuristic rules. `REP-HO` replaces that selection step with an LLM planner given exactly the same primitive state the heuristic sees: surrogate predictions, uncertainties, evaluation costs, and remaining budget, optionally augmented with an adaptive nearest-neighbor summary of past decisions. Across five regimes spanning cost imbalance, constraint difficulty, surrogate fidelity, budget level, and objective conflict, **one of the two variants achieves the best mean ranking score in every regime**, with the `DeepSeek`-backed version always first or second. The planner also shows adaptive behavior such as prioritizing constraint evaluations when budgets tighten and reallocating them as surrogate reliability changes.

papers.title: FlowMaker: From Tasks to Cost-Efficient Generative AI Workflow Deployments
papers.abstract: Generative AI workflows execute user tasks by composing sequences of LLM calls, where each call performs a sub-task (e.g., summarization or translation), forming a workflow. Executing such workflows requires decisions over workflow structure, model assignments, and deployment configurations, which jointly determine latency, cost, and accuracy under dynamic workloads and resource constraints. Existing systems optimize these decisions in isolation or fix them early, leading to suboptimal cost and goodput. We make two key observations. First, efficient serving requires jointly exploring all combinations of workflows, model choices, and deployment configurations under dynamic cluster state. Second, reuse of deployed LLMs is critical for reducing cost, but must be performed on-the-fly, as reuse depends on current load and resource availability. Together, these make selecting a workflow-variant-a combination of workflow, models, and deployment configuration-a time-critical problem. We present FlowMaker, which exposes a task-level interface and selects workflow-variants on behalf of users. To realize this, we design a constraint-guided load-aware pruning algorithm for fast, on-the-fly decisions. FlowMaker improves goodput by up to 10.14$\times$ and reduces cost by up to 2.77$\times$ compared to state-of-the-art baselines, including Murakkab.
papers.summary: Generative AI workflows chain several LLM calls per user task, and latency, cost, and accuracy depend jointly on the workflow structure, which model handles each sub-task, and how each model is deployed — decisions existing systems either optimize separately or freeze too early. `FlowMaker` exposes a task-level interface and picks a workflow-variant (a workflow plus model assignment plus deployment configuration) on the user's behalf, on the premise that these choices must be explored together under live cluster state and that reusing already-deployed models is the main cost lever but only decidable on the fly from current load. A constraint-guided, load-aware pruning algorithm makes that selection fast enough to run per request, **improving goodput by up to 10.14 times and cutting cost by up to 2.77 times** relative to state-of-the-art baselines including `Murakkab`.

papers.title: Dual Task Vector Merging: Leveraging Emotion and ASR Knowledge for Low-Resource Alzheimer's Disease Detection
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's Disease (AD) detection from speech benefits from both paralinguistic and linguistic cues, yet model training is frequently constrained by limited data. Fine-tuning a large pretrained speech encoder can easily overfit, while a frozen probe leaves the encoder's task-relevant knowledge underutilized. Therefore, we propose Dual Task Vector Merging, a parameter-efficient method that adapts a frozen wav2vec 2.0 backbone using task knowledge learned outside the AD task. Specifically, we inject two task vectors, derived as weight deltas from emotion- and ASR-fine-tuned wav2vec 2.0 models, into each transformer layer. During AD training, only layer-wise merging coefficients and a linear classification head are optimized, updating less than 0.1% of the parameters required for full fine-tuning. Speaker-independent experiments on ADReSS and ADReSSo show that dual merging improves over frozen probes, LoRA, and full fine-tuning, in the main binary settings, and gives the best results when combined with LoRA. Evaluation on PROCESS further shows that our advantages transfer to three-class HC/MCI/dementia classification when paired with LoRA. Experiments under reduced training data (20%, 40%, and 80%) confirm reliable gains in low-resource settings.
papers.summary: Detecting Alzheimer's disease from speech draws on both acoustic and linguistic cues, but datasets are small enough that fine-tuning a large speech encoder overfits while a frozen probe leaves its knowledge unused. Dual Task Vector Merging injects two task vectors — weight deltas taken from emotion-fine-tuned and speech-recognition-fine-tuned `wav2vec 2.0` models — into each transformer layer of a frozen backbone, then trains only the layer-wise merging coefficients and a linear head, **updating under 0.1% of the parameters that full fine-tuning would touch**. Speaker-independent experiments on `ADReSS` and `ADReSSo` beat frozen probes, `LoRA`, and full fine-tuning on the binary task and do best when combined with LoRA, with the advantage carrying over to three-class healthy/mild-impairment/dementia classification on `PROCESS` and holding at 20%, 40%, and 80% of the training data.

papers.title: Bellman Language Models: Solving the Recurring Decisions of LLM Agents
papers.abstract:
A general observation in agentic workflows, especially bounded ones, is that the decision space of the LLM, when we separate a decision from generation, starts approaching saturation: the agent meets the same states again and again, and after enough conversations it stops meeting new ones. LLMs generally don't treat these decisions as an optimization problem and instead re-derive them from their context/prompt on every turn. We show that treating decision making within reasonable bounds as an optimization problem, solving it once, and reusing the solved decisions can often make an agent faster, cheaper and more reliable. Our approach, which we call Discretize, Then Decide, starts from data such as the workflow's own logs or, when none exists, runs of the LLM agent itself. It reads each conversation into discrete states and estimates the probability of each outcome and the cost of each move, until no new states appear and the probabilities stop changing. It then solves the resulting Markov decision process. The solution runs as a controller around the model, sending moves whose content is fixed in the state, such as a tool call or a templated reply, and any state it hasn't seen is sent back to the LLM. We call an LLM run this way a Bellman language model (BLM), after Richard Bellman's equation for the best move in each state.
  On $\tau^2$-bench telecom, the controller with no model solves 79% of tasks. As a BLM, Qwen3.8-27B, an open model, goes from 29% to 96% with 93% fewer model calls. For Claude Opus 5.5, which solves 96% of tasks on its own, running it as a BLM cuts model calls and cost per task by about 98% and lets it solve 2 more tasks. On InventoryBench, the solved policy with no model beats every published method. Where the hard part is writing content rather than choosing moves, such as resolving SymPy issues, few decisions can be solved in advance, and a BLM helps little.
papers.summary: In bounded agentic workflows the set of distinct decision states saturates — the agent keeps meeting states it has seen before — yet an LLM re-derives each choice from its prompt every turn. The Discretize, Then Decide approach reads workflow logs (or runs of the agent itself when no logs exist) into discrete states, estimates outcome probabilities and move costs until no new states appear and the estimates stabilize, solves the resulting Markov decision process, and runs the solution as a controller that emits the fixed content for known states such as a tool call or templated reply while forwarding unseen states to the model. On `tau^2-bench` telecom the solved controller alone handles 79% of tasks; **wrapping `Qwen3.8-27B` this way raises it from 29% to 96% with 93% fewer model calls, and wrapping `Claude Opus 5.5` cuts calls and cost per task by roughly 98%** while solving two more tasks. On `InventoryBench` the model-free solved policy beats every published method, but the benefit largely vanishes where the work is writing content rather than selecting moves, as in resolving `SymPy` issues.

papers.title: The Missing Compliance Class: LLM Graders That Collapse Jailbreak Success, and a Free Check
papers.abstract: Jailbreak papers report an attack success rate, the share of responses that deliver the harmful request, and read it as a property of the target model. We hold the target model, the prompts and the responses fixed and change only the grader. Three dense graders of 8B and 9B parameters, from three model families, move compliant responses to the neighbouring class, evasion, instead of scattering them across classes. One of them assigns the compliance label zero times in 900 responses. This class collapse also appears on new harmful requests, on a target model from a third family, and in a held-out 7B grader from a fourth family. Per-class label counts expose it at no cost and without human labels. The collapse decides how the rate behaves under a change of grader. On two corpora of 900 responses and eight graders, the compliance rate differs by a factor of 22 to 25, while the non-refusal rate differs by 18 to 23 percentage points. Without the three collapsing graders, compliance differs by a factor of 1.7 to 2.8 on all four corpora, and non-refusal still differs by 10 to 22 points. These results do not change when every grader is called once. We propose a reporting minimum that keeps the compliance rate and adds its per-class label counts and the named grader. Beside it goes the non-refusal rate, whose disagreement across graders is additive.
papers.summary: Jailbreak studies usually treat attack success rate, the share of responses that deliver the harmful request, as a property of the target model. The authors keep the target model, prompts and responses fixed and change only the LLM grader. Three dense 8B–9B graders from different model families consistently relabel compliant responses as evasion, and one never assigns the compliance label in 900 responses. Across eight graders, **the measured compliance rate varies by a factor of 22 to 25**. Counting labels per class exposes this collapse at no cost and without human labels, so the authors propose reporting per-class label counts and the grader's name alongside both the compliance rate and the non-refusal rate.

papers.title: The One-Pixel of Reasoning: One Truthful Relation Is Enough to Mislead LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Can one sentence manipulate an agent's belief by targeting a single implicit warrant linking evidence to a conclusion? In this paper, we introduce the one-relation attack (ORA), a novel cognitive attack on this inferential relation. ORA localizes a critical implicit warrant and performs a one-relation intervention using a single source-grounded sentence that qualifies this warrant and steers the agent toward an incorrect belief. Across eighteen models on biomedical inference and vulnerability detection, best-of-$10 attacks overturn initially correct answers at mean rates of 54.9% for proprietary and 80.0% for open-weight models. Attacks also transfer without victim feedback, and paired controls support the roles of targeting and qualification. Moreover, successful sentences can pass source-support checks and evade identification, and multi-agent debate raises team error from 50.0% to 59.5% in our balanced stress test. These findings establish implicit warrants as a cognitive attack surface for manipulating agents' beliefs.
papers.summary: The one-relation attack (`ORA`) manipulates an LLM agent's beliefs by targeting a single implicit warrant, the unstated link between evidence and a conclusion. It inserts one true, source-grounded sentence that qualifies this warrant and steers the agent toward a wrong answer. Across eighteen models on biomedical inference and vulnerability detection, best-of-10 attacks overturn initially correct answers **80.0% of the time for open-weight models** and 54.9% for proprietary ones. The attacks transfer without feedback from the victim, can pass source-support checks, and raise team error under multi-agent debate from 50.0% to 59.5%.

papers.title: RAFT: Redundancy-Aware Input Filtering for Temporal Graph Neural Network Training
papers.abstract: Temporal graph neural networks (TGNNs) have shown strong performance on dynamic graph learning tasks by continuously updating node memories from evolving interactions (i.e., events) and leveraging these memories for downstream predictions. As graphs grow rapidly in modern applications, training requires processing an increasing number of events; meanwhile, each event can update node memories used by later events, creating dependencies that constrain parallel execution and limit the benefits of additional computing resources. These costs motivate an upstream question: Are all events, and the dependencies they introduce, necessary for learning? We investigate this question through two roles of temporal events: prediction targets and historical events sampled as inputs. We observe that targets involving stable node memories tend to exhibit lower prediction loss, while filtering historical events associated with stable memories can retain similar training-loss trajectories in several evaluated settings. Together, these observations suggest an opportunity to identify input redundancy through changes in node memories. Building on this opportunity, we propose RAFT, a redundancy-aware input-filtering framework for TGNN training. RAFT tracks memory changes during training and uses them to guide two filters: a root-event filter removes selected prediction targets before training, and a support-event filter excludes selected historical context during sampling. Filtering inputs before their downstream preparation and processing reduces the work they trigger. Across three TGNN models and five datasets, RAFT reduces training inputs by 35.23% on average and up to 97.11%, while reducing recorded training time by up to 52.56\% with negligible changes to model precisions.
papers.summary: Training temporal graph neural networks (TGNNs) means processing ever more events whose memory updates depend on one another, which limits parallelism. The authors observe that events involving stable node memories contribute little, and they propose `RAFT`, which tracks memory changes during training to filter both prediction targets and sampled historical events. Across three TGNN models and five datasets, `RAFT` cuts training inputs by 35.23% on average and **reduces training time by up to 52.56%** with negligible change in precision.

papers.title: Sample-Efficient Reinforcement Learning with General Utilities via Neural Dual Critics
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with general utilities optimizes nonlinear functionals of policy-induced occupancy measures. We develop a natural actor-critic method for concave RLGU objectives admitting an exact variational dual representation, with explicit constructions for a broad class of separable occupancy utilities. Rather than estimating the occupancy measure and then forming the policy-gradient pseudo-reward, our method learns this pseudo-reward directly as a function of the state-action pair using a neural critic. The critic is trained by projected stochastic updates, while multilevel Monte Carlo combines outputs across training horizons to control its bias at logarithmic expected cost. Our analysis separates conditional actor bias from estimator second moments and accounts explicitly for dual optimization, critic approximation, and neural linearization errors. Under policy-transfer, dual-stability, and local critic-regularity conditions, the method achieves $\widetilde{O}(T^{-1/2})$ global convergence above policy, critic-class, and finite-width approximation errors using $\widetilde{O}(T)$ expected environment transitions and reference samples. For a fixed critic representation, this yields $\widetilde{O}(\epsilon^{-2})$ sampling complexity above the approximation floor, covering infinite state-action spaces and occupancy utilities beyond fixed finite vectors of returns.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning with general utilities (RLGU) optimizes nonlinear functions of the state-action occupancy measure a policy induces, rather than plain expected return. The authors propose a natural actor-critic method for concave objectives that have an exact variational dual. A neural critic learns the policy-gradient pseudo-reward directly instead of first estimating the occupancy measure, and multilevel Monte Carlo keeps the critic's bias in check at logarithmic cost. Under stated regularity conditions, the method reaches **roughly O(ε⁻²) sample complexity**, above an approximation floor, in infinite state-action spaces.

papers.title: Measuring Data Diversity with Embeddings: A Taxonomy and Benchmark for Diversity Measures
papers.abstract: Diversity is a critical property of text corpora, with direct implications for training data curation, test set design, and model generalization. However, its measurement remains fragmented and poorly understood. Existing embedding-based diversity measures vary widely in how they are computed and can yield substantially different diversity scores on the same data, yet no systematic comparison of their empirical behaviour exists. We make two contributions toward addressing this gap. First, we present a taxonomy of 21 embedding-based diversity measures, organizing them into four families based on their underlying computations. Second, we introduce EmbDivBench, a benchmark that evaluates these measures along three conceptually distinct components (variety, balance and disparity) on both simulated and natural text data. Although Mean Pairwise Distance is the most commonly used measure, our experiments show that it is outperformed by several alternatives on the three diversity components, with Graph Entropy being the best choice overall. Lastly, we distil these findings into practical recommendations for diversity measure selection.
papers.summary: Embedding-based measures of text-corpus diversity are widely used for data curation and test-set design, yet they often disagree and had not been compared systematically. The authors organize 21 such measures into four families and introduce `EmbDivBench`, which scores each measure on variety, balance and disparity using both simulated and natural text. The most common measure, `Mean Pairwise Distance`, is outperformed by several alternatives, with **`Graph Entropy` the best choice overall**. The paper ends with practical recommendations for choosing a measure.

papers.title: Query-Dependent Reading for Quantized Inner-Product Estimation: A Minimax Separation
papers.abstract:
We study quantization for inner-product estimation when storage and reading have separate budgets. In the static bit-probe model [Yao, 1981], an encoder stores $w$ bits about $x$ before seeing a query $y$, and a reader probes at most $r<w$ bits to estimate $x^\top y$. Both vectors lie in the $d$-dimensional Euclidean unit ball. Protocols may be randomized, and computation is unrestricted. Performance is measured by $d$ times the worst-case mean-squared error over $x,y$, averaged over protocol randomness.
  First, we show that query-independent reading cannot benefit from extra storage. Any such reader is equivalent to fully reading an $r$-bit message, even when later reads depend on previously returned bits. At fixed positive rates $W=w/d$ and $R=r/d$, the normalized minimax error converges to $1/(4^R-1)$, independent of $W$. The upper bound was already known [Ordentlich and Polyanskiy, 2025]. We prove the matching lower bound for arbitrary scalar decoders, extending the result for unbiased compressors [Safaryan et al., 2020].
  Then, we show that query-dependent reading makes extra storage useful. We construct a two-batch protocol using Gaussian projections and random thresholds, with asymptotic normalized error at most $(\pi+o(1))/[4R\log(W/R)]$ as $W/R\to\infty$. At fixed $R$, this error vanishes as storage grows, giving an unbounded advantage over query-independent reading. We also prove a finite-dimensional lower bound for arbitrary encoders, decoders, and fully branching readers. In the doubly sparse regime $W/R\to\infty$ and $R\log(W/R)\to0$, it gives normalized error at least $(1-o(1))/[2R\log(W/R)]$. Thus, our protocol is optimal within a factor of $\pi/2$ in the leading constant.
papers.summary: The paper studies quantized inner-product estimation in the bit-probe model, where an encoder stores w bits about a vector and a reader may probe only r < w bits after seeing a query. The authors prove that when the reader cannot adapt its reads to the query, extra storage gives no benefit and the normalized error converges to 1/(4^R − 1). A two-batch protocol based on Gaussian projections and random thresholds lets the reader choose bits based on the query, and its **error vanishes as storage grows at a fixed read budget**. A matching lower bound shows this protocol is optimal to within a factor of π/2 in the leading constant.

papers.title: Scalable and Adaptive Distribution Regression via Random Features
papers.abstract: Distribution regression seeks to learn mappings from probability distributions to response variables and has emerged as a unifying framework for kernel methods, multi-instance learning, and set-valued learning. Despite its success, kernel-based distribution regression remains computationally expensive and sensitive to kernel choice, motivating scalable and adaptive representations. Building on random feature approximations, we develop a finite-sample analysis of Random Feature Distribution Regression (RaDR) under two-stage sampling. Our perturbation analysis separates the effects of distribution-level sampling, finite within-bag sampling, and random feature approximation. We establish sufficient feature-budget conditions under which RaDR preserves the order of our excess-risk upper bound for exact two-stage kernel distribution regression while maintaining computational efficiency. We further propose Adaptive Random Feature Distribution Regression (A-RaDR), a unified score-guided framework that adaptively allocates random features according to downstream learning objectives. Experiments on synthetic benchmarks and 41 real-world datasets demonstrate that RaDR delivers substantial computational savings while maintaining competitive predictive performance, whereas A-RaDR further improves learning accuracy in distribution regression while retaining the computational speed up. Together, these results establish a practical and theoretically grounded framework for adaptive, scalable distribution learning
papers.summary: Kernel-based distribution regression, which maps probability distributions to responses, is expensive to compute and sensitive to the choice of kernel. The authors give a finite-sample analysis of Random Feature Distribution Regression (`RaDR`) under two-stage sampling. They identify feature budgets under which `RaDR` keeps the excess-risk rate of the exact kernel method. They also propose `A-RaDR`, which allocates random features adaptively according to the downstream objective. On synthetic benchmarks and 41 real-world datasets, `RaDR` **saves substantial computation while staying competitive in accuracy**, and `A-RaDR` improves accuracy further.

papers.title: LastWords: Boring Problems Revisited
papers.abstract: In 2022, the second author published a Last Words piece in Computational Linguistics in which he pointed out that, despite the advances in AI up to that point, there were still some problems in natural language processing that on the one hand seemed trivial and perhaps boring, but on the other were hard to solve using purely neural methods. One such problem discussed in that context was text normalization, and a particular subproblem of that, namely number name reading. The piece came out just a few months before the first release of ChatGPT, and needless to say, a lot has happened since then. Indeed, as we document here, the problem (of number name reading) has practically been solved, at least by one of the latest frontier models. However, we believe that there are still open issues for such limited domain, constrained and limited resource problems, and that in some future machine learning approach, the massive resources of the latest frontier models would not be needed to solve them.
papers.summary: In 2022, a Computational Linguistics essay argued that seemingly trivial text-normalization problems, such as reading numbers aloud as words, were still hard for purely neural methods. Revisiting the question after the arrival of ChatGPT and later frontier models, the authors find that **number name reading is now practically solved by at least one frontier model**. They argue that narrow, constrained, low-resource problems like this one remain open in the sense that solving them should not require the massive resources of frontier models.

papers.title: Peer Pressure: Execution-Verified Co-Evolution of Attacker and Defender Populations for Code Security
papers.abstract:
LLM code agents increasingly ship code with little oversight, yet defenders trained on static vulnerability datasets fall behind adapting adversaries. We co-train attacker and defender instead, and let execution decide every reward: an attacker (Red) edits a real repository and earns nothing unless its patch applies, builds, passes the tests, completes its development task and reproduces a real exploit in an isolated container, whose path also labels the entry point, the critical operation and the trace between them.
  Peer-Relative Policy Optimization (PRPO) makes both sides populations of LoRA adapters over one frozen base and credits each against same-role peers that faced an identical condition, placing the population inside the policy-gradient baseline rather than the opponent pool, with a tournament preserving diversity. Matching cancels the condition's difficulty: at equal coverage it is worth 2.3 points of balanced accuracy over a baseline computed on other conditions, and it matches a within-policy control at half the verifier spend.
  PRPO's 7B diff reviewer reaches 64.8% balanced accuracy on four unseen applications in three untrained languages, 5.5 points above supervised security fine-tuning and 4.4 above a frozen frontier reviewer (Claude Opus 4.8), which it leads by 15.8 on the application it trains on. Its 9B repository agent recovers 23 of 172 held-out VulnGym advisories, against 10 after supervised fine-tuning and 7 for the same backbone untrained under the same scaffold, and locates 17 of 43 reachable entry points against 13 for mini-swe-agent with GLM-5.2. Run unchanged on jailbreak defense, the same algorithm matches or exceeds WildGuard's static F1 at equal corpus and model size. Under a judge distinct from its training oracle it cuts attack success from 36.0% to 4.6%, against WildGuard's 8.9%.
papers.summary: Code-security defenders trained on static vulnerability datasets fall behind adversaries who adapt, so the authors co-train attacker and defender populations of LoRA adapters on a shared frozen base model. Every reward comes from execution: an attacker is rewarded only if its patch builds, passes tests, completes its development task and reproduces a real exploit inside a container. Their method, Peer-Relative Policy Optimization (`PRPO`), scores each adapter against same-role peers that faced the same condition. The resulting 7B diff reviewer reaches 64.8% balanced accuracy on unseen applications, ahead of supervised fine-tuning and a frozen `Claude Opus 4.8` reviewer. A 9B repository agent recovers 23 of 172 held-out `VulnGym` advisories, versus 10 after supervised fine-tuning, and the same algorithm applied unchanged to jailbreak defense **cuts attack success from 36.0% to 4.6%**.

papers.title: Distribution-Based Regularization for Reward Fine-Tuning Diffusion and Flow Models
papers.abstract: Reward fine-tuning is an effective way to adapt pretrained diffusion and flow-matching models to downstream objectives, but aggressive optimization often leads to mode collapse and distributional drift. Existing methods attempt to control this drift with reverse-KL regularization, implemented as an $\ell_2$ penalty on the velocity field; however, this functions by indirectly constraining sampling dynamics rather than directly acting on the generated distribution. To address this, we propose DFR (Distributional Functional Rewards), which augments the task reward with a distribution-dependent, per-sample reward that acts explicitly on the generated distribution. Formally, we generalize the KL-regularized objective from expected rewards, which are linear in the model's distribution, to convex functionals of it. The first variation of this objective defines an effective, distribution-dependent reward that directly penalizes deviation from the pretrained distribution. This formulation yields additive per-sample rewards for the Fr\'echet distance (FD), maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), and DreamSim diversity, recovering several recently proposed rewards as special cases. Across various text-to-image fine-tuning tasks, DFR matches the peak reward of KL-tuned baselines while increasing diversity by up to 29% at equal or lower drift.
papers.summary: Reward fine-tuning of diffusion and flow-matching models tends to cause mode collapse and drift away from the pretrained distribution, and the standard reverse-KL penalty constrains this only indirectly through the velocity field. Distributional Functional Rewards (`DFR`) extend the KL-regularized objective to convex functionals of the generated distribution, which yields additive per-sample rewards for Fréchet distance, maximum mean discrepancy and `DreamSim` diversity. On text-to-image fine-tuning tasks, `DFR` matches the peak reward of KL-tuned baselines while **increasing diversity by up to 29%** at equal or lower drift.

papers.title: HybridResearcher: Bridging the Structured-Unstructured Boundary for Deep Research Agents
papers.abstract: While LLM agents are increasingly capable of gathering and synthesizing evidence from a single homogeneous source, such as structured tables or unstructured data, real-world analytical questions frequently span heterogeneous sources. For example, answering one enterprise question may require both a result computed over an internal database and evidence found on the web. Recent evaluations on benchmarks like HybridDeepResearch show that even frontier agents struggle when evidence must cross this boundary. While these benchmarks have exposed the limitation, methodologies to explicitly teach cross-source reasoning remain absent. To address this, we introduce HybridResearcher, a 4B agent trained to bridge evidence across the structured and unstructured boundary. To build it, we synthesize cross-source bridge trajectories by starting with validated single-source tasks-such as existing text-to-SQL or web search queries-and fabricating the missing source around a bridge entity drawn from the seed's own output. We retain a sample only when strict construction gates confirm that neither side alone suffices, ensuring the data requires true cross-source interdependence. Finally, we train on this curated dataset using supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning. Evaluated on the existing HybridDeepResearch benchmark, HybridResearcher improves over our base model, Qwen3.5-4B, by 30.0 points pass@8 and surpasses the far larger Qwen3.5-397B-A17B by 8.3 points, while also improving over its base model on established, held-out single-source benchmarks (BrowseComp and BrowseComp-Plus), demonstrating that this complex cross-source reasoning can be taught directly to small models without triggering catastrophic forgetting.
papers.summary: Deep-research agents struggle with questions that need evidence from both structured sources, such as databases, and unstructured sources, such as the web. To produce training data, the authors start from validated single-source tasks such as text-to-SQL or web-search queries and fabricate the missing source around a bridge entity. They keep a sample only if neither source alone can answer it, then train a 4B agent with supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning. `HybridResearcher` improves on its base model `Qwen3.5-4B` by 30.0 points pass@8 on `HybridDeepResearch` and **surpasses the far larger `Qwen3.5-397B-A17B` by 8.3 points**, while also improving on the held-out `BrowseComp` and `BrowseComp-Plus` benchmarks.

papers.title: Compositional Activation Steering Across Languages and Behaviors with Contextual Gates
papers.abstract: Activation steering has emerged as an effective and precise way to influence the behaviours of language models. However, composing multiple steering directions to control several behaviours simultaneously remains challenging, particularly in multilingual settings and with training-free steering vectors. We address this challenge with contextual steering, jointly training gates that adapt the strength of fixed steering directions to the current hidden state and interactions between interventions. Across a broad range of languages, behavioural attributes, and models, our approach outperforms constant-strength steering and four strong baselines, including prompting. It also better preserves general knowledge and keeps the model's internal computation closer to that of the prompted model. Our analysis further shows how jointly trained gates adapt their contributions during composition, explaining the mechanisms underlying effective compositional steering.
papers.summary: Activation steering can control individual behaviours of a language model, but combining several steering directions at once is hard, especially across languages and with steering vectors that need no training. The authors jointly train contextual gates that adjust the strength of fixed steering directions based on the current hidden state and on how the interventions interact. Across many languages, attributes and models, the approach **outperforms constant-strength steering and four strong baselines, including prompting**. It also better preserves general knowledge and keeps the model's internal computation closer to that of the prompted model.

papers.title: A Symmetry-Matching Approach to Blind-Spot Reduction in Sparse Autoencoders
papers.abstract: Language models can treat semantically distinct inputs as interchangeable at the representation level, creating blind spots that standard sparse autoencoder (SAE) objectives do not target. In safety-critical settings such as clinical dosage extraction, legal clause interpretation, or financial amount verification, such failures can propagate silently into downstream decisions. We study this problem as one of feature-basis orientation. Building on a symmetry-matching view from algebraic error-detection theory, we add a differentiable $V_{\mathrm{Gini}}$ regularisation term to SAE training that penalises uneven perturbation response within a specified family. Across GPT-2, Gemma 2, and Qwen 2.5, a frozen multi-seed evaluation shows that $V$-regularisation raises both relative and absolute lower-tail responses while reducing response-profile imbalance, with no material general-text reconstruction degradation. JumpReLU and minimum description length (MDL) objectives remain close to the Standard SAE profile under the same protocol. Family-geometry controls show that the effect is not explained by template duplication or a single dominant perturbation family, and held-out probes plus null-calibrated separation tests evaluate how far the representation-level change carries to downstream discriminability. A zero-shot audit on out-of-distribution clinical radiology minimal pairs finds the relative weak-tail lift in all evaluated model-by-family cells, not perfectly rank-aligned with the trained statistic, and a held-out family audit finds it on family kinds never used in training. Together, the results show that perturbation-aware SAE training can reorient feature bases toward safety-relevant input changes while leaving downstream validation as a separate empirical step.
papers.summary: Language models sometimes represent semantically distinct inputs as interchangeable, for example two different clinical dosages, and standard sparse autoencoder (SAE) training does nothing to surface these blind spots. Drawing on a symmetry-matching idea from algebraic error-detection theory, the authors add a differentiable `V_Gini` regularizer that penalizes uneven responses to perturbations within a specified family of inputs. Across `GPT-2`, `Gemma 2` and `Qwen 2.5`, the regularizer **raises weak-tail responses to safety-relevant input changes without degrading reconstruction**. The lift also appears on out-of-distribution clinical radiology pairs and on held-out perturbation families never used in training.

papers.title: ATLAS: Expert-Guided Sustainable Satellite Backhaul for Off-Grid Wildlife Monitoring
papers.abstract:
Remote wildlife monitoring increasingly depends on high-fidelity cameras and sensors deployed far from grid power and terrestrial networks. Low Earth orbit satellite links can provide connectivity in these settings, but their high power draw and variable bandwidth, combined with intermittent on-site solar harvesting, make continuous backhaul infeasible. Current systems therefore filter at the edge, with motion triggers that waste limited energy and bandwidth on environmental artifacts, or fixed vision models that cannot follow evolving expert objectives.
  We present \textsc{ATLAS}, an expert-guided edge-to-cloud system that treats satellite backhaul as a scarce resource for off-grid wildlife monitoring. \textsc{ATLAS} uses foundation models to compile natural-language expert intent into semantic scoring logic, combines semantic relevance with environmental and energy state, and uses a constrained reinforcement-learning scheduler to decide which clips to upload and when. As a representative case study, we deployed \textsc{ATLAS} for over six months across 18 off-grid salmon-monitoring river sites. \textsc{ATLAS} achieves a mean clip-selection accuracy of $87.4\%$, exceeding mean baseline accuracy by $26.4$ percentage points, while maintaining near-continuous operation through low-solar periods in which baselines incur 16.0\% downtime.
papers.summary: Off-grid wildlife cameras can send data over low Earth orbit satellite links, but limited solar power and variable bandwidth rule out continuous uploads. `ATLAS` uses foundation models to compile experts' natural-language goals into semantic scoring logic, then combines those scores with environmental and energy state in a constrained reinforcement-learning scheduler that decides which clips to upload and when.
