Over six months at 18 salmon-monitoring river sites, it reached 87.4% clip-selection accuracy, **26.4 points above the baseline average**, and kept operating through low-solar periods in which baselines were down 16.0% of the time.

papers.title: A Cross-Domain Evaluation of Prompting Techniques for Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Prompt engineering has become a central mechanism for guiding the behavior of Large Language Models (LLMs) across a wide range of reasoning and language understanding tasks [1], [2]. However, existing studies frequently evaluate prompting techniques using different LLMs, datasets, or task settings, making direct comparisons across methods and domains difficult [3]. Consequently, in this paper we present a controlled cross-domain evaluation of Zero-Shot prompting, Few-Shot prompting, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), and automatic prompt optimization based on a PE2-inspired optimization pipeline [4]-[6]. All experiments were conducted with the same LLM and evaluated on six benchmark datasets covering arithmetic reasoning, logical reasoning, commonsense reasoning, and factual verification. The results show that no prompting strategy consistently outperforms the others across all domains, and pairwise statistical comparisons of the highest-performing configurations revealed no significant differences. RAG achieves the highest overall average accuracy of 78.33% when 300 examples are available for retrieval, while Few-Shot Prompting achieves comparatively high accuracies across several structured reasoning tasks. Zero-Shot Prompting remains competitive on tasks with self-contained inputs, whereas the PE2-inspired optimization approach produces stable but not systematically superior results compared to the other evaluated prompting techniques. Furthermore, increasing the number of task-specific examples does not consistently improve performance across prompting techniques, indicating strong domain and task dependency. These findings suggest that prompting techniques should be selected adaptively based on task characteristics rather than treated as universally applicable optimization strategies.
papers.summary: Prompting techniques are usually compared across different models and datasets, which makes direct comparison difficult. The authors evaluate zero-shot prompting, few-shot prompting, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and a `PE2`-inspired automatic prompt optimizer with a single LLM on six benchmarks covering arithmetic, logical and commonsense reasoning and factual verification. **No strategy wins across all domains, and the best configurations do not differ significantly**. RAG has the highest average accuracy (78.33%), and adding more task examples does not consistently help.

papers.title: Arctic-SWE: Revisiting the Long Horizon Agent Training by Modeling-System Co-Design
papers.abstract: Long-horizon agent training, including software engineering, is advancing rapidly, but the recipe and infrastructure needed for a strong reinforcement-learning baseline remain difficult to reproduce. This makes gains from new algorithms or data hard to distinguish from improvements to an under-tuned baseline. We present Arctic-SWE, a fully asynchronous RL framework that establishes such a baseline through model-system co-design, using overfitting on a small task pool as the testbed. This testbed exposes failures that early reward gains conceal and guides the integration of established components: gated reward, importance-weight control, aligned training and inference engines, and consistent state across policy updates. No single component is new, yet together they form the missing foundation. On raw R2E-Gym data, without new algorithms or data work, Arctic-SWE trains Qwen3.5-4B to 62.0% pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified. This is comparable to concurrent FrogNano (61.5%), which relies on online task synthesis, after about one-sixth as many training rollouts. Building on this foundation, we further filter and refine R2E-Gym, SWE-rebench V2, and Scale-SWE. With this curated subset, the 4B model improves from 47.4%/25.0%/37.9% to 65.0%/38.3%/59.7% on SWE-bench Verified/Pro-v1/Pro-v2, and the recipe also improves Qwen3.5-9B from 56.2%/31.9%/48.8% to 65.7%/39.6%/70.2% on Verified/Pro-v1/Pro-v2. Controlled comparisons show that both curation and test strengthening improve held-out performance, although stronger tests reduce apparent training-task mastery. Arctic-SWE provides a documented starting point for studying better algorithms, data and environments for asynchronous agent RL.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning for long-horizon software-engineering agents is hard to reproduce, so gains from new methods are hard to separate from improvements to an under-tuned baseline. `Arctic-SWE` is a fully asynchronous RL framework that combines established components: gated rewards, control of importance weights, aligned training and inference engines, and consistent state across policy updates. The authors debugged these components by deliberately overfitting a small task pool. Using raw `R2E-Gym` data, it trains `Qwen3.5-4B` to 62.0% pass@1 on `SWE-bench Verified` with about one-sixth the training rollouts of a comparable concurrent method. With curated data from `R2E-Gym`, `SWE-rebench V2` and `Scale-SWE`, the **4B model reaches 65.0% on Verified**, and `Qwen3.5-9B` reaches 70.2% on Pro-v2.

papers.title: How Well Can LLMs Verbalize Mathematical Formulas? A Multi-Domain Evaluation
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong capabilities across natural language tasks. But their ability to generate accurate written verbalizations of mathematical formulas has not been systematically evaluated. Such verbalization is important for text-to-speech systems supporting audio-based learning and visually impaired users. We evaluated five state-of-the-art LLMs across six scientific domains and constructed Read-Aloud Math, a balanced multi-domain corpus with LaTeX formulas, manually validated simple and extended transcriptions, multiple variants, textual context, domain labels, and formula complexity levels. Using multi-reference BLEU, GPT-5.2 achieved the highest score for simple transcriptions (75.9% without context, 64.9% with context), although without context it did not significantly outperform Grok 4.1 Fast or Claude Sonnet 4.5. Claude Sonnet 4.5 achieved the highest score for extended transcriptions without context (36.5%), and Grok 4.1 Fast with context (48.8%). For extended transcriptions, Statistics and Mathematics scored highest across the two context settings, while Physics scored lowest. Formula length was significantly negatively associated with BLEU for simple transcriptions without context, but not with context, whereas BLEU increased significantly with formula length for extended transcriptions in both settings. Grouping symbols were most frequently involved in transcription differences, while variable names, capitalization, and Greek letters were associated with lower BLEU scores. Overall, LLM-based formula verbalization is promising but remains sensitive to transcription type, textual context, and formula characteristics.
papers.summary: Text-to-speech for audio learning and for visually impaired users needs accurate spoken renderings of mathematical formulas, a task LLMs had not been systematically tested on. The authors build `Read-Aloud Math`, a corpus of LaTeX formulas from six scientific domains with manually validated simple and extended transcriptions, and evaluate five LLMs using multi-reference BLEU. `GPT-5.2` scores highest on simple transcriptions (**75.9% without context**), while `Claude Sonnet 4.5` and `Grok 4.1 Fast` lead on extended ones depending on whether context is given. Grouping symbols, variable names, capitalization and Greek letters cause the most errors.

papers.title: CARTA: Self-Supervised Reusable Transaction Embeddings via Heterogeneous Tokenization and Cross-Attention
papers.abstract: Acquiring fraud labels for payment transactions is expensive and inconsistent across tasks, and high-cardinality identifiers such as merchant names make one-hot feature pipelines infeasible at scale. We present CARTA, a self-supervised encoder that learns a compact 16-dim embedding from raw transactions without labels; the frozen embedding is then reused for label-efficient fraud probing and exploratory unsupervised risk stratification without retraining the encoder. CARTA uses type-specific projections with learned embedding tables for high-cardinality identifiers, trained with token excision and InfoNCE contrastive loss. On IEEE-CIS, its linear probe at 1% of labels exceeds a raw-feature probe at 100%; on IBM TabFormer (2M rows), its frozen embedding reaches GBDT AUPRC 0.508, above frequency encoding (0.411) and the merchant-dropping baseline (0.022), though fully-supervised CatBoost is stronger. CARTA is a label-free, reusable representation that complements task-specific supervised models.
papers.summary: Fraud labels for payment transactions are expensive to obtain, and identifiers with very many distinct values, such as merchant names, make one-hot feature pipelines impractical at scale. `CARTA` is a self-supervised encoder that learns a 16-dimensional transaction embedding without labels, using type-specific projections, token excision and an `InfoNCE` contrastive loss. On `IEEE-CIS`, **a linear probe trained on 1% of the labels beats a raw-feature probe trained on all of them**. On `IBM TabFormer`, the frozen embedding outperforms frequency encoding, although fully supervised `CatBoost` remains stronger.

papers.title: DF-PALM: Dynamic Fusion Prompt Learning for Audio--Language Models
papers.abstract: Few-shot audio classification requires audio--language models to distinguish variable acoustic events from limited labeled data. PALM's main formulation adapts encoded class representations without changing pretrained encoders, but its class representations remain input-independent and classification uses audio features without class-conditioned refinement. We introduce DF-PALM, a dynamic feature-space prompting framework that combines audio-conditioned class representations with asymmetric cross-attention for audio refinement. Class representations are conditioned after text encoding, held fixed across fusion layers for each input, and reused for final scoring. Both pretrained encoders remain frozen, avoiding audio-conditioned text-encoder passes. With PENGI as the frozen backbone, the main 16-shot evaluation covered 11 benchmarks and six baselines. DF-PALM achieved 80.69% mean accuracy and 80.32% macro-averaged F1, exceeding PALM by 4.11 and 4.30 percentage points, respectively. Paired benchmark-level tests supported both gains after Holm correction. Across four shot settings, DF-PALM achieved the highest mean accuracy and macro-averaged F1 among the four evaluated prompt-learning methods. The gains extended to LAION-CLAP and OpenFLAM, with significant improvements over PALM in both metrics. At 50 candidate classes, operator-counted inference floating-point operations increased by 0.39% relative to PALM. These results support instance-conditioned feature-space adaptation as an effective approach to few-shot audio classification. Our code is publicly available at GitHub https://github.com/sunyulin0421/DF-PALM.
papers.summary: Few-shot audio classification with audio–language models needs class representations that adapt to each input, which the prompt-learning method `PALM` lacks. `DF-PALM` conditions class representations on the audio input and refines audio features through asymmetric cross-attention, keeping both pretrained encoders frozen. With `PENGI` as the backbone, it reaches 80.69% mean accuracy across 11 benchmarks in the 16-shot setting, **4.11 points above `PALM`**, at only 0.39% more inference compute. The gains carry over to the `LAION-CLAP` and `OpenFLAM` backbones.

papers.title: Stable Signer V3: 4D Deformable Primitive Splatting Is All You Need for Sign Language Production
papers.abstract: We present Stable Signer V3, an interactive high-resolution sign language avatar system built on 4D Deformable Primitive Splatting. It addresses three limitations of existing avatars: restricted facial expression, inaccurate identity-specific body deformation, and loss of fine appearance details. Shared Face Primitive Splatting adds transferable superquadric primitives for richer expression control; Test-Time Body Primitive Splatting learns an identity-specific virtual muscle layer for more faithful motion; and Test-Time Tunneling Super-Resolution uses TunnelingNet to recover identity-specific high-resolution details. Both test-time modules are optimized once per signer identity; inference then runs entirely from the stored identity parameters. Together, they reduce facial geometry error by 71.4%, body-boundary error by 35.1% across ten identities, and high-resolution RGB reconstruction error by 24.2% on held-out evaluations, while retaining interactive streaming.
papers.summary: Existing sign-language avatars offer limited facial expression, deform signers' bodies inaccurately and lose fine appearance detail. `Stable Signer V3` builds on 4D deformable primitive splatting and adds three components: transferable superquadric face primitives, an identity-specific virtual muscle layer, and a super-resolution network called `TunnelingNet`. The last two are optimized once per signer. Together they **reduce facial geometry error by 71.4%**, body-boundary error by 35.1% and high-resolution reconstruction error by 24.2%, while keeping streaming interactive.

papers.title: Means-Ends Analysis Helps LLMs Plan in Continuous-State Domains
papers.abstract: LLM planning research has traditionally focused on discrete-state domains, where actions form a finite, enumerable set. Existing LLM planning frameworks largely assume actions are enumerable, modeling planning as a search process over candidate actions. However, in continuous-state domains, where actions form a continuum and cannot be enumerated, this assumption breaks down. We find a remedy in Newell and Simon's Means-Ends Analysis (MEA), a general problem-solving technique rooted in heuristics from human psychology. We develop Medaka, an MEA-inspired structured prompting framework that encourages recursive goal decomposition, algebraic derivation, and per-step state tracking. To evaluate native LLM planning abilities in continuous-state domains, we develop Liquidworld, a systematic testbed on liquid mixing. On Liquidworld, Medaka can improve performance across model families, suggesting that classical means-ends analysis elicits LLM-native reasoning abilities that are helpful for continuous-state planning.
papers.summary: Most LLM planning frameworks treat planning as a search over a finite, enumerable set of candidate actions, an assumption that breaks down in continuous-state domains where actions form a continuum. The authors draw on Newell and Simon's Means-Ends Analysis (`MEA`) to build `Medaka`, a structured prompting framework that encourages recursive goal decomposition, algebraic derivation, and step-by-step state tracking. They also introduce `Liquidworld`, a liquid-mixing testbed for measuring native LLM planning in continuous domains. On it, **`Medaka` improves performance across model families**, suggesting that classical means-ends heuristics draw out reasoning abilities LLMs already have.

papers.title: What Can't Jev Decide? Probing the Limits of One-Pass Decision Models
papers.abstract: Jev and its open replicas choose among the options a caller supplies with a single forward pass, fast enough to decide inside an agent loop. We ask what such a model cannot decide, and find a simple limit: Jev cannot make a decision that an LLM makes only by writing out intermediate steps. On a benchmark that varies one factor at a time, Jev finds and selects records without error up to 20k tokens and 64 options, but once the answer depends on two or more updates of one user, accuracy falls, to 53-80% at sixteen updates, because similar records interfere. Given a stale summary of the state, Jev follows it. On real decision items graded by how many thinking tokens a reference LLM needs, Jev answers 97.5% of the items that one forward pass of that LLM solves, but only 74% of the others. Jev also does not know its limit: its confidence flags the errors it makes itself but not those it inherits from a stale input, and neither an explicit nor a trained hand-off option catches the latter. The open models we evaluate share these limits. Checking the state such models rely on requires a model that reasons.
papers.summary: `Jev` and its open replicas pick among caller-supplied options in a single forward pass, fast enough to run inside an agent loop; the authors probe what such one-pass decision models cannot decide. On a benchmark that varies one factor at a time, `Jev` retrieves and selects records without error up to 20k tokens and 64 options, but accuracy drops to 53-80% once the answer depends on many sequential updates to the same user, because similar records interfere. On real decision items, it answers 97.5% of those a reference LLM solves in one forward pass but **only 74% of items that need intermediate reasoning steps**. It also follows stale state summaries without flagging them, and neither explicit nor trained hand-off options catch those inherited errors, a limit shared by the open models tested.

papers.title: TrustAgent-RFF: Agentic Diagnostic Planning for Reliable RF Fingerprinting under Domain Shift
papers.abstract: Radio frequency fingerprinting (RFF) models can achieve accuracy under source domain conditions but become unreliable when the receiver, distance, collection day, or environment changes. Incorrect predictions in unseen domains may receive high softmax confidence, making confidence thresholding insufficient for trustworthy deployment. We propose TrustAgent-RFF, a prediction level reliability framework for RFF that operates with a frozen in-phase and quadrature (I/Q) classifier without target domain labels. For each device prediction, the framework acquires radio frequency evidence: counterfactual stability, prototype consistency, acquisition domain similarity, and signal quality. A source calibrated trust estimator combines these diagnostics with classifier confidence, prediction margin, and evidence availability indicators. Source derived lower tail penalties and cross module interactions reduce trust when diagnostic signals indicate weak support. A large language model (LLM) based planner adaptively selects the next diagnostic action based on evidence, trust state, action costs, and remaining budget. A deterministic source calibrated decision layer updates the prediction state as Accept, Reject, or Defer. Experiments across five RFF datasets and classifier backbones reveal an average source to target accuracy drop of 38.7% and show that many incorrect target domain predictions remain highly confident.
papers.summary: Radio frequency fingerprinting (RFF) classifiers that identify wireless devices become unreliable when the receiver, distance, collection day, or environment changes, and their wrong predictions often still carry high softmax confidence. `TrustAgent-RFF` wraps a frozen in-phase and quadrature (I/Q) classifier with a per-prediction trust estimator that combines diagnostics such as counterfactual stability, prototype consistency, domain similarity, and signal quality, all calibrated on the source domain without target labels. An LLM-based planner chooses which diagnostic to run next under a cost budget, and a deterministic layer then accepts, rejects, or defers each prediction. Across five RFF datasets, the experiments show an **average source-to-target accuracy drop of 38.7%**, with many incorrect target-domain predictions remaining highly confident.

papers.title: MLFont: Machine Learning-Driven Font Subsetting and Range-Compact Unicode-Range Slicing for Low-Latency Web Typography
papers.abstract:
CSS3 @font-face rules with unicode-range descriptors partition web fonts into downloadable slices. While Latin fonts need ~20 KB in WOFF2, Pan-European (LGC) and East Asian (CJK) fonts contain 2,297-30,759 codepoints (158 KB-5.9 MB in WOFF2), where heuristic partitioning causes unused-glyph downloads, high HTTP RTT, CSS bloat, or missing-glyph fallbacks. We present MLFont, a machine learning and optimization framework that learns font slicing strategies from corpora via three stages: (1) a Zipfian High-Frequency Tier (most) isolating top-frequency codepoints; (2) a Latent Co-Occurrence Topic Tier using Online Variational Bayes LDA (Online LDA) or a Deep Neural Network Topic Model (DNNTM) with Shannon Entropy Difference Loss and Sinkhorn-Knopp normalization; and (3) a Memetic Range-Compact Genetic Algorithm (GA) with Potts-Viterbi dynamic programming and island bridging that minimizes topic discrepancy and CSS fragmentation. Across five Google Noto fonts (LGC, KR, JP, TC, SC), MLFont cuts 3G per-glyph latency by 56.7%-75.3% over single-file delivery and 46.1%-66.3% over equal-bin baselines on CJK with 100% coverage, reduces CSS intervals by 17.9%-41.7%, and achieves 1.56x-6.09x cold-cache speedups (65.4%-84.9% CJK and 44.7% LGC bandwidth savings) across 20 websites in simulator and Headless Chrome benchmarks (45/45 exact slice-set parity).
  Code: https://github.com/wq2012/mlfont
  Models: https://huggingface.co/collections/wq2012/mlfont
papers.summary: Web fonts for Pan-European and East Asian scripts contain thousands of codepoints, and the heuristic `unicode-range` slicing commonly used to split them causes wasted downloads, extra round trips, bloated CSS, or missing glyphs. `MLFont` learns slicing strategies from text corpora in three stages: a high-frequency tier of the most common codepoints, a co-occurrence topic tier built with `Online LDA` or a neural topic model, and a memetic genetic algorithm that keeps the resulting ranges compact. Across five `Google Noto` fonts, it **cuts 3G per-glyph latency by 56.7-75.3% versus single-file delivery**, shrinks CSS interval counts by 17.9-41.7%, and delivers 1.56x-6.09x cold-cache speedups across 20 websites in simulator and `Headless Chrome` benchmarks.

papers.title: T-MUON: Tensorizing Muon via t-SVD for Large Language Model Pre-training
papers.abstract: Muon has recently emerged as a strong optimizer for large language model pretraining by exploiting matrix structure through polar orthogonalization. However, it processes each parameter matrix independently, whereas recent tensor-aware extensions of Muon jointly update groups of eligible matrix parameters through matrix unfoldings. In contrast, we propose T-MUON, a t-SVD-based generalization that groups structurally related Transformer gradients into third-order tensors and defines the corresponding Muon-style update directly through the $M$-transform. We show that the exact T-MUON update is a steepest-descent direction under the $\star_M$-spectral norm and establish a convergence guarantee. Across GPT-2-style and LLaMA-style models from 51M to 1.3B parameters trained on FineWeb and FineWeb-Edu, head-wise T-MUON with the identity transform consistently achieves lower validation perplexity than AdamW, Muon, and variants using DFT, DCT, or DST transforms. These gains persist in additional experiments with longer context lengths and larger token budgets, although the preferred tensorization mode varies across settings.
papers.summary: The `Muon` optimizer speeds up LLM pretraining by orthogonalizing each parameter matrix's update, but it treats every matrix independently. `T-MUON` groups structurally related Transformer gradients, such as per-head weights, into third-order tensors and defines a Muon-style update through the tensor singular value decomposition (`t-SVD`). The authors prove the update is a steepest-descent direction under a matching spectral norm and give a convergence guarantee. On GPT-2-style and LLaMA-style models from 51M to 1.3B parameters trained on `FineWeb` and `FineWeb-Edu`, **head-wise `T-MUON` consistently reaches lower validation perplexity than `AdamW` and `Muon`**, although the best way to group matrices varies across settings.

papers.title: LowNet: Looped Wavelet Neural Networks with 24 Learnable Parameters for Solving Poisson Equations
papers.abstract: Poisson equations frequently appear in various fields, such as mathematics, physics and informatics. Solving Poisson equation, however, is challenging. Traditional methods are not data-specific, although have high certainty. They require a large number of iterations due to the CFL numerical stability. In contrast, deep learning methods are data-driven and more efficient, but require accurate training data and suffer from heavy computation. To tackle these issues, we propose a wavelet-inspired Poisson solver with 24 trainable scalars. The proposed network has several advantages. First, it is compact. It has four independent $5\times5$ kernels, each represented by six parameters, leading to 24 scalars in total. Such compact format can be deployed on most devices. Second, thanks to the loop design, it achieves higher accuracy than previous methods. A residual loop reuses the wavelet block without increasing its parameters. Numerical experiments confirm that such loop indeed improves the solving accuracy. On 10000 images, one, two, and three loops of the wavelet block lead to PSNRs of $47.27$, $74.14$, and $100.74$ dB, respectively. Third, the proposed method is computationally fast. Thanks to the wavelet transform, the proposed method has linear computation complexity, leading to high computation performance. In short, we propose a novel looped wavelet neural network with compactness, accuracy and efficiency for solving Poisson equations. Our method can be applied in various fields, such as computational fluid dynamics, image reconstruction, biomedical engineering, electromagnetic field simulation.
papers.summary: Classical Poisson-equation solvers need many iterations to stay numerically stable, while deep learning solvers require accurate training data and heavy computation. `LowNet` is a wavelet-inspired solver with only 24 trainable scalars, made of four 5x5 kernels with six parameters each, and a residual loop that reuses the same wavelet block to refine its answer without adding parameters. On 10,000 images, one, two, and three loops reach PSNRs of 47.27, 74.14, and **100.74 dB**, and the wavelet structure keeps computational cost linear in problem size.

papers.title: Epi: Towards a Persistent, Self-Improving Agent for Autonomous Research
papers.abstract: We present \'{E}pi, an autonomous research agent that sustains investigations across model sessions and evolves its methods through accumulated experience. \'{E}pi combines persistent research history, hierarchical memory, branching and independent review to maintain research continuity, learn from experiments, and explore and revisit alternative approaches. Its experiments run across session boundaries, and a fixed verifier evaluates their outputs. \'{E}pi produced 120 record-setting results, comprising 20 numerical bound records across 12 families and 100 construction records across eight families. These include an approximately 84-fold narrower interval for the $n$-queens constant and a more than 3.6-million-fold narrower rigorous interval for the quartic Feigenbaum attractor dimension. Exact dual certificates establish that the Cohn-Elkies linear-programming bound cannot be sharp in dimensions 10 and 11. Beyond numerical improvements, \'{E}pi gives a computer-assisted proof of Tuza's conjecture for split graphs with an eight-vertex clique part and at most three triangle-active neighborhood types, with arbitrary multiplicities. We extend this research process to algorithmic coding with \'{E}pi-turbo, a lightweight configuration that develops executable solvers for tasks including vehicle routing, scheduling and production planning. On 30 FrontierOR tasks, \'{E}pi-turbo achieves a 5.4% higher total benchmark score than Codex at 64% of its model cost, using the same underlying model and reasoning effort. \'{E}pi is designed to support human understanding by connecting computational results to explicit methods and mathematical arguments that researchers can examine and build upon.
papers.summary: `Épi` is an autonomous research agent built to sustain investigations across many model sessions, combining a persistent research history, hierarchical memory, branching exploration, and independent review, with a fixed verifier checking every experimental output. It produced **120 record-setting results**, including an interval for the n-queens constant roughly 84 times narrower than before, dual certificates showing the Cohn-Elkies linear-programming bound cannot be sharp in dimensions 10 and 11, and a computer-assisted proof of a case of Tuza's conjecture for split graphs. A lightweight coding configuration, `Épi-turbo`, writes solvers for operations-research tasks such as vehicle routing and scheduling, scoring 5.4% higher than `Codex` on 30 `FrontierOR` tasks at 64% of its model cost with the same underlying model.
papers.highlight_summary:
Most research agents work within a single model session, but real investigations often take far longer. `Épi` is built to carry one investigation across many sessions. It keeps a persistent research state, uses hierarchical memory and versioned branches, and gets independent review from a second model, while a fixed verifier checks every candidate result before it counts as an improvement.

- Short-term memory holds the current state and handover notes, long-term memory stores reusable lessons and documented dead ends, and every alternative method lives on a versioned branch the agent can backtrack to; all of this runs on `Breadboard` infrastructure with model weights (`GPT-5.6 Sol`, `GPT-6-Astra`) kept fixed.
- Across mathematical campaigns `Épi` set **120 records**: **20 numerical bounds across 12 families** and **100 constructions across eight families** (97 of them geometric packings), including an **~84-fold narrower interval for the n-queens constant** and a **>3.6-million-fold narrower rigorous interval for the quartic Feigenbaum attractor dimension**.
- Exact dual certificates show the `Cohn–Elkies` linear-programming bound **cannot be sharp in dimensions 10 and 11**, with lower bounds exceeding known packing upper bounds by about 0.35% and 1.92%; separately, exact certificates for 560 neighborhood profiles plus a truncation lemma give a computer-assisted proof of **Tuza's conjecture for split graphs with an eight-vertex clique part and at most three triangle-active neighborhood types**.
- The lightweight `Épi-turbo` configuration beat `Codex` on 30 `FrontierOR` operations-research tasks, using the same model and a $20 budget per task: it scored **53.96 vs. 51.21 (5.4% higher)** at **64% of the model cost** ($7.30 vs. $11.35 mean per task), with a median research time of 22 vs. 37 minutes.
- Limitations: `FrontierOR` results come from one run per task with no significance testing, and the advantage comes mostly from faster programs, since in direct comparisons on 119 instances `Codex` found the better solution 61 times versus 18 for `Épi-turbo`.

papers.title: Robust Direct Preference Optimization under Preference Label-Flip Attacks
papers.abstract: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is widely used for offline Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback. However, recent works have shown that DPO can be easily manipulated by adversarial preference label flip attacks, which are specifically designed to mislead the learner toward an attacker-chosen target policy. To address this issue, we design robust DPO methods that can defend against such attacks. Building on the property that lable flips induce parameter-independent gradient shifts in log-linear DPO, we propose Trim-$K$ Robust-DPO, which removes the $K$ highest-impact pairs, and Soft-Trim-$K$ Robust-DPO, which smoothly downweights them. We establish deterministic gradient perturbation bounds uniformly over all attack sets containing at most $K$ flips, explicitly separating defense-induced bias from surviving attack effects. Under bounded-region assumptions, these bounds yield time-uniform parameter and policy deviation guarantees. We further quantify how quadratic regularization improves curvature while introducing additional bias. Experiments on Stanford Human Preferences, HH-RLHF, and UltraFeedback-Binarized validate our analysis.
papers.summary: Direct Preference Optimization (`DPO`) can be steered toward an attacker-chosen policy by adversarially flipping preference labels in its training data. Using the fact that label flips shift the gradient by a parameter-independent amount in log-linear DPO, the authors propose `Trim-K Robust-DPO`, which removes the K highest-impact pairs, and `Soft-Trim-K Robust-DPO`, which smoothly downweights them. They prove **gradient perturbation bounds that hold for any attack of up to K flips**, separating the bias the defense introduces from the attack effect that survives, and derive time-uniform guarantees on how far the parameters and policy can drift. Experiments on `Stanford Human Preferences`, `HH-RLHF`, and `UltraFeedback-Binarized` support the analysis.

papers.title: Over-Defense in Coding Agents Begins at Silent Forks
papers.abstract: Language models behind coding agents are post-trained with outcome rewards, and recent methods concentrate credit on the turns that decide the outcome. We find that defensive actions beyond what a task requires escape both. They begin at silent forks, the turns where every next action leads to the same outcome. Such actions leave the success rate unchanged, and frontier models take the disproportionate branch there in up to 91% of decisive actions under implicit budgets. The most direct fix, a checker in the trajectory reward, reaches these forks only through fully proportionate trajectories, leaving 74% of GRPO groups with identical rewards and behavior unchanged. This motivates a rethink of where learning signals belong, namely where behavior diverges, which a behavioral checker can locate and the outcome cannot. Our method, ForkDPO, contrasts a proportionate and a disproportionate action at the same prefix, at silent forks on both sides of the required behavior. On a test set of unseen repositories, it lowers a 4B model's disproportionate behavior from 70.3% to 58.9%, against 67.7% for DPO at randomly chosen turns, establishing behavioral divergence as a learning signal for how agents act beyond whether they finish. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/Astarojth/silent-forks.
papers.summary: Coding agents often take defensive actions beyond what a task requires, and outcome-based post-training misses this behavior because it originates at silent forks: turns where every possible next action leads to the same task outcome. Frontier models choose the disproportionate branch in up to 91% of decisive actions under implicit budgets, and adding a behavior checker to the trajectory reward leaves 74% of `GRPO` groups with identical rewards, so behavior does not change. The proposed `ForkDPO` instead contrasts a proportionate and a disproportionate action from the same prefix at these forks. On unseen repositories it **lowers a 4B model's disproportionate behavior from 70.3% to 58.9%**, compared with 67.7% for `DPO` applied at randomly chosen turns.

papers.title: ControlJEPA: Principled Trajectory Regularization via Lyapunov Tube Loss
papers.abstract: Next-token prediction leaves hidden-state trajectories largely unconstrained, while existing geometric regularizers primarily control the direction rather than the magnitude of trajectory deviations. We introduce \emph{ControlJEPA}, a trajectory regularization framework based on a discrete-time Lyapunov contraction condition from practical Input-to-State Stability theory. Its Lyapunov Tube Loss penalizes violations of this condition on a normalized, scale-invariant measure of transversal deviation. When the contraction condition holds at every step, the hidden-state trajectory remains within an explicit tube around the reference secant. In the partial-ISS regime, we bound mean transversal energy, temporal variance, and average tube width using the Lyapunov loss and contraction parameters, with horizon-independent variance bounds under uniformly bounded violations. ControlJEPA requires no architectural modifications. Across six benchmarks and six model families, it consistently improves accuracy and data efficiency over standard fine-tuning and prior trajectory regularizers. The resulting smoother transversal profile also persists empirically during inference, when the regularizer is inactive. The code is publicly available at: \url{https://github.com/t-khanusa/ControlJEPA}
papers.summary: Next-token prediction places few constraints on how a model's hidden states evolve across a sequence, and existing geometric regularizers mostly control the direction of deviations rather than their size. `ControlJEPA` adds a Lyapunov Tube Loss, based on a contraction condition from Input-to-State Stability (ISS) theory, that penalizes scale-invariant sideways deviation of the hidden-state trajectory; when the condition holds at every step, the trajectory provably stays within a tube around a reference path. It needs no architectural changes, and across six benchmarks and six model families it **consistently improves accuracy and data efficiency over standard fine-tuning and prior trajectory regularizers**, with the smoother trajectories persisting at inference when the regularizer is switched off.

papers.title: CasePlay: Self-Play Reinforcement Learning from Case Reports for Medical Reasoning
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is a promising way to improve the clinical reasoning abilities of large language models (LLMs), but current pipelines often rely on expert-labeled questions or costly synthetic-data generation. Meanwhile, the medical literature offers a wealth of high-quality unlabeled documents, including clinical case reports that trace the full clinical course from initial presentation to final treatment decisions. We study whether document-grounded self-play can convert these reports into effective RL training signals. We identify two challenges that limit existing self-play methods in this setting: knowledge-point fixation}, where the proposer repeatedly asks about a narrow set of salient clues in a source report, and difficulty-quality mismatch, where appropriately difficult questions may still be poorly formed or shallow, limiting their value for reasoner training. To address these challenges, we propose CasePlay, a self-play framework with two key components: (a) a Knowledge-Conditioned Proposer, which anchors question generation to case-specific knowledge points so that questions draw on a broader range of evidence from the source report; and (b) a Rubric-Judge Reasoner, which augments answer-accuracy feedback with rubric-based quality feedback on clue integration, reasoning depth, and option quality, guiding the proposer toward reasoning-intensive questions that better support reasoner training. Extensive experiments across seven medically related benchmarks demonstrate that CasePlay outperforms existing self-play baselines and improves the SFT warm-start model by 3.1 points on average, highlighted by a 6.3-point gain on LiveClin. This approach offers an effective path toward continually improving medical reasoning ability through self-play RL.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) for clinical reasoning in LLMs usually depends on expert-labeled questions or expensive synthetic data, while unlabeled clinical case reports remain largely unused. `CasePlay` turns those reports into training signal through self-play, in which one model proposes questions and another answers them. It addresses two failure modes: proposers fixating on a few salient clues, handled by conditioning question generation on case-specific knowledge points, and well-calibrated but shallow questions, handled by rubric-based feedback on clue integration, reasoning depth, and option quality. Across seven medical benchmarks it beats existing self-play baselines and **improves the supervised fine-tuned starting model by 3.1 points on average**, including 6.3 points on `LiveClin`.

papers.title: Revealing what benchmark scores hide: Jointly measuring the breadth and reliability of LLM capabilities using accessibility profiles
papers.abstract: Language model benchmarks assign each question a single outcome from one fixed wording, even though the same underlying request can be expressed in many equivalent ways. We argue that the quantity of interest should therefore not be correctness on one wording, but the accessibility of an inquiry, which we define as the probability that a model succeeds across meaning-preserving formulations. The distribution of accessibility across inquiries reveals a structure that accuracy and existing best-, worst-, or average-case prompt scores collapse: how broadly a model's capabilities extend across inquiries and how dependably those capabilities can be elicited. Two models can have the same average performance while one succeeds across more inquiries unreliably and the other succeeds across fewer inquiries but more consistently, leading to opposite preferences depending on whether the task allows multiple retries until one success or when repeated consistent success is required. Across six benchmarks and more than twenty models, this tradeoff is common: for about half of the model pairs with nearly equal mean accessibility, which model looks better depends on whether one success across five formulations is enough or all five must succeed, quantities we call Access@5 and Reliable@5, respectively. For some pairs the two measures diverge significantly, by up to 10 points in opposite directions. Accessibility also reveals that scaling, reasoning, and prompt optimization can redistribute capability across inquiries in ways aggregate accuracy obscures, sometimes broadening the set of inquiries a model can succeed on while making success on them less repeatable. Accessibility turns formulation sensitivity from a nuisance into a measurable property of capability, distinguishing what a model can sometimes succeed on from what users can actually depend on.
papers.summary: Benchmarks grade each question on a single fixed wording, even though the same request can be phrased many equivalent ways. The authors define an inquiry's accessibility as the probability that a model succeeds across meaning-preserving rephrasings, and use its distribution to separate how broad a model's capabilities are from how reliably they can be elicited, through metrics called `Access@5` (at least one of five phrasings succeeds) and `Reliable@5` (all five succeed). Across six benchmarks and more than twenty models, **for about half of the model pairs with nearly equal average accessibility, the preferred model flips depending on which metric is used**, with gaps of up to 10 points in opposite directions. The analysis also shows that scaling, reasoning, and prompt optimization can broaden the set of solvable inquiries while making success on them less repeatable.

papers.title: CoworkEnv: Synthesizing Training Environments for Long-Horizon Cowork Agents
papers.abstract: AI coworkers must coordinate tools, communicate across turns, and act on changing workspace state while respecting workflow constraints. Constructing training experience for these capabilities requires coherent requests, service records, tool interfaces, and grading checks. We present CoworkEnv, a capability-guided framework for synthesizing executable training environments for AI coworkers. Workflow requirements guide task construction, and programmatic validation with feedback repair checks generated specifications and grading behavior. Teacher executions yield curated demonstrations for supervised fine-tuning (SFT), while student interactions provide rollouts and rewards for reinforcement learning (RL). Using these resources, we train compact PocketWorker models. For Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, SFT raises the mean score from 46.6 to 64.1 on Claw-Eval, including a 31.9-point gain on Multi-turn tasks. An SFT-only extension to ClawMark demonstrates applicability across coworker benchmarks. We further compare RL training dynamics across configurations that vary reward processing and credit assignment. Improving training rewards provide preliminary evidence that the constructed environments support policy optimization.
papers.summary: Training AI coworkers to coordinate tools, communicate across turns, and act on changing workspace state requires coherent tasks, service records, tool interfaces, and grading checks, which are costly to build by hand. `CoworkEnv` synthesizes executable training environments from workflow requirements, using programmatic validation with feedback-driven repair to check the generated specifications and graders. Teacher runs supply demonstrations for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and student runs supply rollouts and rewards for RL, producing compact `PocketWorker` models. **SFT lifts `Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct` from 46.6 to 64.1 on `Claw-Eval`**, including a 31.9-point gain on multi-turn tasks, and early RL experiments show steadily improving training rewards.

papers.title: Label-Space Mismatch Distorts Cross-Cohort Evaluation in Breast Cancer Molecular Subtyping
papers.abstract: Cross-cohort evaluation of breast cancer subtype classifiers is unreliable when source and target cohorts use different annotation standards: METABRIC labels six classes, PAM50 defines five, and a claudin-low prediction cannot be correct under a five-class standard. A classifier transferred from 1,369 METABRIC patients (train n=958) to TCGA-BRCA (n=987) and GSE21653 (n=266) separates three evaluation operations routinely conflated in cross-site comparisons. (1) Label-space restriction - an evaluation-rule change, not a retraining gain - is the dominant correction (73.76%->79.74% on TCGA-BRCA; 63.16%->68.42% on GSE21653); (2) EM prior correction on the reconciled space is an optional calibration step (Brier fidelity up, macro F1 down; to 80.65% and 74.06%); and (3) the target label space is not recoverable from unlabelled predictions (EM retains prior 0.0751 on the absent class; calibrated detectors fail), so compliance must come from cohort documentation. The protocol exposes why internal validation overstates cross-cohort value: multimodal fusion gains do not transfer (no configuration beats mRNA alone, n=694; McNemar p=0.13-1.00), and the genomic panel adds nothing to pathological complete response prediction over clinical variables (DeltaAUC = +0.0045). Clinically, without label-space compliance, cross-site accuracy comparisons misattribute annotation-standard differences to model skill; Luminal A/B and claudin-low boundary errors map to distinct treatment decisions; and subtype accuracy is a weaker portable endpoint than survival discrimination (external C-index 0.577-0.584). Reporting the cohort's allowed label set and applying label-space compliance are therefore prerequisites before any cross-cohort performance claim.
papers.summary: Breast cancer subtype classifiers are often compared across patient cohorts that use different annotation standards: `METABRIC` labels six classes while `PAM50` defines five, so predictions of the extra class can never count as correct on the other cohort. Transferring a classifier from `METABRIC` to `TCGA-BRCA` and `GSE21653`, the authors show that **restricting predictions to the target cohort's label set is the dominant correction** (73.76% to 79.74% on `TCGA-BRCA`), and that the target label space cannot be inferred from unlabeled predictions, so it must come from cohort documentation. Under this protocol, multimodal fusion gains seen in internal validation do not transfer, and the genomic panel adds essentially nothing over clinical variables for predicting treatment response.

papers.title: DeGMatch: Target-Aware Reasoning Data Selection via Deconfounded Gradient Matching
papers.abstract: Reasoning post-training on long trajectories has substantially improved the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but scaling such training to large datasets is increasingly expensive. We study target-aware reasoning data selection, where a small reference set specifies a target capability and guides the selection of training trajectories for specialization. We find that existing target-aware methods can exhibit limited target discrimination on long reasoning trajectories, while dominant population-level structure in candidate gradients can obscure finer target-dependent variation during gradient matching. To address these limitations, we introduce Deconfounded Gradient Matching (DeGMatch), which first constructs a target-relevance gate and then reranks candidates using model-specific gradients. DeGMatch centers gradients using the candidate-population mean and removes leading principal directions before target matching, reducing the influence of dominant population-level structure and improving target discrimination. Across mathematics, science, and code, DeGMatch outperforms strong heuristic, target-aware, and reasoning-specific data selection baselines, while remaining effective across selection budgets, model families, and scales. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/CHLee0801/degmatch.
papers.summary: Reasoning post-training on long trajectories is expensive at scale, which motivates selecting only the training data most relevant to a target capability specified by a small reference set. Existing target-aware selection methods struggle on long reasoning trajectories because dominant population-wide structure in the candidate gradients masks finer target-specific signal. Deconfounded Gradient Matching (`DeGMatch`) first applies a target-relevance gate, then centers gradients on the candidate-population mean and removes leading principal directions before matching them against the target. Across mathematics, science, and code, it **outperforms heuristic, target-aware, and reasoning-specific selection baselines** across selection budgets, model families, and scales.

papers.title: PRECOCIAL: Pretraining with Code Curriculums via Iterative Search for Accelerated Learning
papers.abstract: Fully synthetic pretraining data generated by symbolic programs can bootstrap downstream training on naturalistic tasks, such as language modeling, but the generating programs have so far been designed by hand. We introduce PRECOCIAL, a method for automatically optimizing programs that generate synthetic pretraining data. Starting from an initial generator program, an LLM iteratively rewrites the program, and each rewrite is scored by pretraining a randomly-initialized transformer on its data and fine-tuning it on the downstream task. Because every score requires training, PRECOCIAL keeps a single network for the entire search, continuing its pretraining for each accepted program instead of training a new network per candidate, making it significantly more efficient. On four language and code datasets, at a fixed fine-tuning budget, optimized programs reach lower perplexity than hand-designed curricula, published procedural generators, random program mutation and the program the LLM writes in the first iteration of the search, and reach the same perplexity as the hand-designed curricula with 9-33% fewer fine-tuning steps. PRECOCIAL also ends with lower perplexity than FunSearch and AlphaEvolve, which train a new network for every candidate, at the same number of evaluations and a lower cost. We also observe that an optimized program generator from one domain transfers to datasets in other domains. Additionally, optimized programs allow for better downstream performance on four different reasoning and problem-solving tasks.
papers.summary: Synthetic pretraining data generated by symbolic programs can bootstrap later training on natural language, but those generator programs have so far been written by hand. `PRECOCIAL` has an LLM iteratively rewrite a generator program, scoring each version by pretraining a transformer on its data and fine-tuning on the downstream task; to keep this affordable, it continues training a single network across accepted programs instead of training a fresh one per candidate. On four language and code datasets, optimized programs **match hand-designed curricula with 9-33% fewer fine-tuning steps** and reach lower perplexity than published procedural generators, `FunSearch`, and `AlphaEvolve` at the same number of evaluations and lower cost. Optimized generators also transfer across domains and improve performance on four reasoning tasks.

papers.title: Rubrics Carry the Standard: Shapley Attribution for Checklist-Based LLM Judges
papers.abstract: Checklist rubrics applied by large language model (LLM) judges have become a standard instrument for evaluating open-ended outputs and for rewarding them during training. Two assumptions surround this practice: that leniency or strictness is a property of the judge model, and that a rubric can be improved by asking a model to review it. We test both in a controlled grading task with planted flaws and on two human-labeled datasets, SummEdits and RAGTruth. Holding the judge and the outputs fixed, rubric content moves the pass rate of correct outputs from 2% to 100%, whereas changing the judge model or the rendering of the same checks moves it by a few points. Model self-review then drifts the rubric toward the reviser's own standard: it adds requirements the task never stated and deletes checks that human labels had taught, with three reviser models and on all three datasets. To measure and control this, we show that under all-must-pass aggregation the Shapley value of each check has an exact closed form, which yields per-check catch credit, false-fail blame and unique catches in linear time. Attribution shows that self-review deletes the checks that do unique work and keeps the checks that cause false fails. A change-control gate that combines these quantities with a provenance freeze on label-derived checks holds nearly every drifting revision chain at its starting quality, with identical decisions under three judge models.
papers.summary: Checklist rubrics applied by LLM judges are now standard for evaluating and rewarding open-ended outputs, and practitioners commonly assume that leniency is a property of the judge and that rubrics improve when a model reviews them. In a controlled grading task with planted flaws and on `SummEdits` and `RAGTruth`, **rubric content moves the pass rate of correct outputs from 2% to 100%**, while swapping the judge model shifts it by only a few points. Model self-review drifts rubrics toward the reviser's own standard, adding unstated requirements and deleting checks learned from human labels. The authors derive an exact, linear-time Shapley attribution for each check under all-must-pass aggregation and use it in a change-control gate that holds drifting revision chains at their starting quality across three judge models.

papers.title: A Measurement Perspective on Benchmarking LLM-Generated Text Detectors using Item Response Theory
papers.abstract: Benchmarking large language model (LLM)-generated text detectors commonly relies on aggregate detector-level metrics such as accuracy, F1 score, and AUC. Although useful for summarizing overall performance, these metrics provide limited insight into how benchmark composition shapes detector comparisons or which texts distinguish detectors with different response profiles. We propose a measurement-based benchmarking framework for jointly characterizing benchmark heterogeneity and detector behavior using multidimensional item response theory (IRT). By treating benchmark texts as measurement items and detectors as respondents, the framework estimates text-level discrimination and difficulty-location parameters alongside multidimensional detector abilities. We apply the framework to a benchmark of 32K human-written and machine-generated texts across four domains, evaluated by 14 detectors. The estimated IRT item-parameter space reveals distinct but overlapping human-machine distributions, with substantial variation across domains and text lengths. The human-machine label shows the strongest multivariate association with this space, while domain and text length further contribute to benchmark heterogeneity. Detector ability profiles reveal multidimensional and domain-dependent response patterns that are not fully reflected in aggregate performance rankings. As a practical application, clustering texts in the estimated IRT space yields a compact subset of 2,088 texts (6.5\% of the full 32K benchmark) that largely preserves the comparative detector-performance patterns observed on the full benchmark. Overall, the proposed framework provides a principled and interpretable methodology for benchmarking heterogeneous detection technologies while jointly characterizing the measurement properties of the texts used for their evaluation.
papers.summary: Detectors of LLM-generated text are usually compared on aggregate metrics such as accuracy, F1 score, and AUC, which say little about how benchmark composition shapes the rankings. The authors apply multidimensional item response theory (`IRT`), treating benchmark texts as test items and detectors as respondents, to a benchmark of 32K human and machine texts across four domains scored by 14 detectors. The estimated parameters show that domain and text length add substantial heterogeneity beyond the human-versus-machine label, and that detector abilities are multidimensional in ways aggregate rankings hide. Clustering texts in the IRT space yields a **subset of 2,088 texts (6.5% of the benchmark) that largely preserves the full benchmark's detector comparisons**.

papers.title: The World as Viewed by 136 Countries: An Open, Curated, Annotated, and Multilingual Dataset of 118 Million State Media Articles
papers.abstract: State media outlets often project their governments' narratives to target both domestic and foreign audiences. Because this content is plentiful and free to access, it appears widely in the web corpora that large language models (LLMs) are trained on and that retrieval systems draw from. However, the prevalence of state media in these corpora and its potential influence on LLM outputs remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we introduce WorldStateMedia, an open dataset of 118 million state media articles from 136 countries in 114 languages. We extract these articles from existing pretraining corpora and annotate each outlet with level of state control from State Media Monitor. Using WorldStateMedia to audit these corpora, we find that, in English web crawls, the share of state media pages from editorially controlled (vs. independent) outlets rose from 39% in 2013 to 93% in 2025. In several low-resource languages, state media make up a substantial share of all web data, such as 17.8% for Uyghur and 7.8% for Belarusian. To characterize the differing narratives of news outlets, we compare Russian and Ukrainian state media in English and in their native languages, revealing asymmetric topical focus and opposing framings of contested issues such as Crimea. Furthermore, in a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) experiment on territorial disputes, retrieving a country's state media shifts model answers toward that country's claims, most strongly for English-language (foreign-targeted) media. We release WorldStateMedia to support multilingual, cross-national insights on state media at https://huggingface.co/collections/manestay/worldstatemedia
papers.summary: State media content is plentiful and freely accessible, so it appears widely in LLM pretraining corpora and retrieval sources, yet its prevalence and influence have been little studied. `WorldStateMedia` extracts 118 million state media articles from 136 countries in 114 languages out of existing pretraining corpora and annotates each outlet with its level of state control. In English web crawls, **the share of state media pages coming from editorially controlled outlets rose from 39% in 2013 to 93% in 2025**, and state media make up 17.8% of all web data in Uyghur and 7.8% in Belarusian. In a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) experiment on territorial disputes, retrieving a country's state media shifts model answers toward that country's claims, most strongly for foreign-targeted English-language outlets.

papers.title: Certified Sparse Attention via Perturbed Retrieval
papers.abstract: Sparse attention speeds up long-context decoding by reading few keys of the KV cache, but existing methods do not control the error of a query, and on real KV caches their errors have heavy tails. We show that perturbing the score of every key with an independent Exp(1) variable turns threshold retrieval into sampling keys with probability proportional to their attention weights. Lowering the threshold along a geometric grid gives nested samples, a Horvitz--Thompson estimate of the output at every level, and confidence bounds that hold simultaneously over all levels, so each head stops at the first level whose certificate meets the target error $\varepsilon$. With fresh perturbations at every decoding step, each certificate fails with probability at most $\delta$ during generation. At a suitable threshold, the estimator reads $O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log(1/\delta))$ values regardless of the context length, and no adaptive method reads fewer, up to constants. A 4-bit scan with deterministic bounds, shared across a grouped-query-attention group, generates the candidates exactly but reads every key. On three LLMs and ten settings at 16K--128K tokens, no certificate is violated, and at equal keys read our 90th-percentile error is 4.6--7.9$\times$ lower than that of the best of 15 baseline families. At equal bytes, the best baselines have 0.6--1.6 times our 90th-percentile error and at least 4.9 times our largest. End to end, our method stays within one point of dense attention on tasks and within 0.1\% in PG-19 perplexity, and the strongest baselines at equal bytes score as well. On CPU, decoding steps at 32K--128K tokens run 1.1--1.4$\times$ faster than dense attention on the same 16-bit cache.
papers.summary: Sparse attention speeds up long-context decoding by reading only some keys from the KV cache, but existing methods give no per-query error control and show heavy-tailed errors on real caches. Adding independent exponential noise to every key's score turns threshold retrieval into sampling keys in proportion to their attention weights, which yields an unbiased estimate of the attention output plus confidence bounds, so each head stops reading at the first threshold whose certificate meets a target error. The number of values read is independent of context length and provably optimal up to constants. On three LLMs at 16K-128K tokens no certificate is violated, **90th-percentile error at equal keys read is 4.6-7.9x lower than the best of 15 baseline families**, accuracy stays within one point of dense attention, and decoding on CPU runs 1.1-1.4x faster than dense attention.

papers.title: When Does Better Acceptance Pay? A Controlled Study of Speculative Decoding
papers.abstract: The throughput gains of speculative decoding depend on the trade-off between acceptance length and execution latency. We ask when additional acceptance is worth the cost of obtaining it. We establish a comparison protocol spanning training, inference, and evaluation, remeasuring released checkpoints and retraining six drafter recipes on shared target-generated data across ten benchmarks and two target models. Alignment changes the picture: gaps that appear large in published comparisons shrink substantially under shared training and inference conditions. This narrowing motivates two deeper questions: how is acceptance improved at different costs, and when do these gains improve throughput? We find that acceptance can be improved through nearly free objective and context changes or more expensive token-to-token conditioning. DCore illustrates the former route as a strong baseline with little additional measured drafting overhead. The payoff is conditional: task uncertainty and serving conditions affect acceptance returns, execution costs, and the preferred drafter and budget. These findings inform future drafter design and deployment choices.
papers.summary: Speculative decoding speeds up generation by having a small drafter propose tokens that the target model then verifies. The real speedup depends on balancing how many proposed tokens get accepted against how long drafting takes. The authors re-measure released checkpoints and retrain six drafter recipes on shared target-generated data, across ten benchmarks and two target models. **Gaps that look large in published comparisons shrink substantially once training and inference conditions are aligned.** Acceptance can be improved either through nearly free changes to the training objective and context, illustrated by the strong low-overhead baseline `DCore`, or through costlier token-to-token conditioning. Whether higher acceptance actually raises throughput depends on task uncertainty and serving conditions.

papers.title: Block Recursive Transformers for Structured Parameter Sharing
papers.abstract: Recursive Transformers depend not only on how many parameters are shared, but also on how shared parameters are organized across depth. Existing static schemes adopt two extreme reuse topologies: layer-wise repetition, where each layer is reused independently, and global cyclic reuse, where the entire stack is repeatedly applied as a single shared function. We argue that sharing granularity is an important factor in recursive parameter sharing. This study proposes Block Recursive Transformers (BRT), which partition layers into contiguous blocks and recursively reuse each block before moving to the next. This intermediate topology enables local refinement within blocks while preserving depth-wise transitions, without adding routing modules, auxiliary states, or extra training objectives. Across decoder-only models up to 1.7B parameters, with additional encoder-decoder and encoder-only studies, BRT improves validation negative log-likelihood and downstream accuracy over static recursive sharing baselines. Ablations and representation analyses further show that intermediate block granularity better balances local refinement and depth-wise differentiation. Project website: https://aim-skku.github.io/BRT/
papers.summary: Recursive Transformers save parameters by reusing layers across depth, but existing schemes either repeat each layer on its own or cycle the entire stack. `Block Recursive Transformers` (`BRT`) instead split the layers into contiguous blocks and reuse each block recursively before moving on to the next. This needs no routing modules, auxiliary states, or extra training objectives. On decoder-only models up to 1.7B parameters, plus encoder-decoder and encoder-only studies, **`BRT` improves validation negative log-likelihood and downstream accuracy over static recursive sharing baselines**. Ablations suggest that intermediate block sizes best balance local refinement against differentiation across depth.

papers.title: SoK: PIAtlas: Decomposing the Unbounded Prompt Injection Attack Space
papers.abstract: Prompt injection is the dominant security risk for large-language-model (LLM) applications and agents, yet the field still lacks a coherent map of how these attacks are constructed. More than twenty public datasets describe prompt injection using incompatible vocabularies, often organized around delivery vector, attacker goal, or generation method. In this Systematization of Knowledge, we present PIAtlas, a taxonomy organized instead around how the injected instruction is constructed to subvert the underlying model. Its six classes, one per subversion mechanism, form the roots of a hierarchy of techniques and sub-techniques that researchers can use to describe attacks consistently and design more systematic evaluations. We derive the taxonomy from how LLMs are trained, prompted, and influenced by human-like framing, and compare it with historical attack data. To ground this comparison, we release PICorpus, to our knowledge the largest license-clean collection of public prompt-injection datasets, and map thousands of its records to PIAtlas under a human-verified protocol. The mapping shows that attacks usually combine several techniques drawn from only a few mechanisms. It also reveals gaps that existing labels obscure: widely used agent benchmarks test only part of the attack space, and adaptive attackers favor mechanisms that curated benchmarks underrepresent. PIAtlas thus provides a common foundation for understanding this attack space, improving benchmark coverage, and guiding red teaming and defenses.
papers.summary: Prompt injection is the leading security risk for large language model (LLM) applications and agents, but more than twenty public datasets describe it with incompatible vocabularies. This Systematization of Knowledge introduces `PIAtlas`, a taxonomy organized by how the injected instruction subverts the model. It has six root classes, one per subversion mechanism, each with a hierarchy of techniques and sub-techniques. The authors also release `PICorpus`, a large license-clean collection of public prompt-injection datasets, and map thousands of its records to the taxonomy under human verification. The mapping shows that attacks usually combine techniques from only a few mechanisms, and that **widely used agent benchmarks cover only part of the attack space while adaptive attackers favor underrepresented mechanisms**.

papers.title: UtoMe: Observation-Uncertainty-Guided Token Merging for Weather Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Weather transformers process dense reanalysis fields whose reliability varies across variables, locations, and weather regimes. Token merging can reduce computation, but feature similarity alone does not account for this heterogeneous input uncertainty. We introduce UtoMe, an observation-uncertainty-guided token merging framework that combines dynamics saliency with ensemble data assimilation spread as a relative input-reliability proxy. The resulting importance score protects selected tokens as anchors and calibrates bipartite matching between the remaining tokens. Three variants use external uncertainty at both training and inference, during training only, or neither stage. In ERA5 72-hour forecasting at two spatial resolutions, UtoMe improves Overall error over train-time ToMe at matched token budgets. At $1.40625^\circ$ and 50% token reduction, UtoMe-E lowers Overall error from 67.32 to 53.00 at the same 0.55x encoder FLOPs. Small reductions remain close to the full-token baseline; larger reductions incur measurable accuracy losses. Component ablations and spatial uncertainty controls support combining dynamics with aligned uncertainty when allocating a weather transformer's token budget.
papers.summary: Weather transformers process dense reanalysis fields whose reliability varies by variable, location, and weather regime, yet standard token merging relies only on feature similarity. `UtoMe` scores token importance by combining dynamics saliency with the spread of an ensemble data assimilation system, used as a proxy for input reliability. The score protects anchor tokens and calibrates the matching used to merge the rest. Three variants use the external uncertainty at training and inference, during training only, or not at all. In `ERA5` 72-hour forecasting at 1.40625° with 50% token reduction, **`UtoMe-E` lowers overall error from 67.32 to 53.00 versus train-time `ToMe` at the same 0.55x encoder compute**, though larger reductions still cost measurable accuracy.

papers.title: UpLoop: Upcycling Large Language Models with Gated Loop
papers.abstract: Looped large language models trade parameter storage for recurrent computation, but most are trained from scratch. In practice, pretraining with looped depth is expensive, making post-training upcycling of a pretrained non-looped LLM an attractive alternative. We introduce \textbf{UpLoop}, a post-training recipe based on \emph{layer-wise} recurrence. Instead of looping a whole model or a middle block, UpLoop loops each selected layer locally, preserving the pretrained depth hierarchy and avoiding feature-space mismatch. To make loop execution useful, we add hidden-wise gates on the attention and MLP residual branches, so later loops act as progressive refinements rather than redundant rewrites. Empirically, UpLoop breaks the commonly observed saturation at two loops ($R=2$) in prior looped models. Starting from Qwen3-4B Base and applying SFT, UpLoop improves the average accuracy across 20 benchmarks by 6.17\% at $R=3$. We use $R=3$ as the main setting for the best accuracy--cost trade-off, while both native and extrapolated $R=4$ yield further gains.
papers.summary: Looped language models trade parameter storage for repeated computation, but pretraining them from scratch is expensive. `UpLoop` is a post-training recipe that converts an existing non-looped LLM by looping each selected layer locally, rather than the whole model or a middle block, which preserves the pretrained depth hierarchy. Gates on the attention and MLP residual branches make later loops act as progressive refinements instead of redundant rewrites. The method breaks the saturation at two loops commonly seen in prior looped models. Starting from `Qwen3-4B Base` with supervised fine-tuning, **three loops improve average accuracy across 20 benchmarks by 6.17%**, and four loops give further gains.

papers.title: No Escape from the Quadratic Barrier: Adaptive Attacks on Linear $\ell_2$ Sketches
papers.abstract: Linear sketches estimate properties of high-dimensional inputs from a fixed low-dimensional projection. At constant accuracy, randomized Euclidean-norm sketches, notably the Johnson-Lindenstrauss transform, support exponentially many nonadaptive queries in sketch dimension $k$. For adaptive black-box queries, known privacy-based defenses guarantee $\widetilde{\Omega}(k^2)$ and it remained open whether stronger guarantees were possible. Prior attacks used more queries, restricted the responder, or provided weaker failure guarantees. We show that the quadratic guarantee is optimal up to logarithmic factors, even with a computationally unbounded responder that knows the matrix, attack algorithm, history, and query distributions and may change its randomized rule after every query. For every fixed hidden $A\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times n}$ with $n>40k$ and target accuracy $\alpha \in (0,1]$, our black-box attack uses $O(k+\alpha^2k^2\log(2+\alpha^2k))$ queries in $\widetilde{O}(1+\alpha^2k)$ adaptive rounds to force, with constant probability, a round in which a constant fraction of answers have $\Omega(\alpha)$ relative error. Our results clarify the limits of defending a fixed compressive linear representation by adapting the prediction rule.
papers.summary: Randomized linear sketches such as the `Johnson-Lindenstrauss` transform estimate Euclidean norms from a low-dimensional projection. They support exponentially many non-adaptive queries, but known privacy-based defenses guarantee only about k² adaptive queries for sketch dimension k. The authors give a black-box attack, valid against any fixed hidden matrix and even a computationally unbounded responder that adapts its rule after every query. The attack forces a constant fraction of answers to have large relative error using roughly α²k² log terms of queries. This shows that **the quadratic guarantee is optimal up to logarithmic factors**, settling an open question about the limits of defending fixed compressive linear representations.

papers.title: Conjugate Compilation: Self-Improving Agentic Co-Compilation for Speculative Decoding
papers.abstract: As LLM adoption surges, scaling model serving requires unlocking stranded GPU capacity alongside deploying more GPUs. Speculative decoding brings two models into the serving process: a small draft model proposes tokens that a larger target model verifies. Yet compiling these models individually leaves their shared execution outside the compiler's optimization boundary. We introduce CONJUGATE COMPILATION, which reframes speculative decoding as a cross-model compilation problem and jointly optimizes the draft and target models within their shared execution rather than treating each in isolation. Our key insight is that cross-model compilation should be informed by the measured performance of the co-located shared execution it produces: an optimization that improves a kernel in isolation need not improve the models when they execute together. To expand cross-model opportunities, we devise operand layouts that interleave blocks from both models within common tiles, co-locating GEMM and non-GEMM work while preserving their mathematics. We realize CONJUGATE COMPILATION through a self-improving agentic search system in which an LLM edits cross-model optimization plans using the compiler and GPU execution as its environment. Each proposed plan is compiled and evaluated through its co-located shared execution, whose measured score, together with kernel-level verdicts and compiler feedback, informs subsequent proposals, while Monte Carlo tree search accumulates rewards to guide exploration. Across six single-GPU speculative-decoding configurations on NVIDIA B300 and RTX 5090 GPUs, CONJUGATE COMPILATION achieves a geometric-mean per-round speedup of 1.37x over conventional execution. Interleaved kernels raise this speedup to 1.45x, reaching 1.59x in the best case. CONJUGATE COMPILATION also improves GPU utilization on average by 1.46x on RTX 5090 and 1.50x on B300.
papers.summary: In speculative decoding, a small draft model and a large target model run together, yet compilers optimize each model in isolation. `Conjugate Compilation` treats the pair as one cross-model compilation problem and introduces operand layouts that interleave blocks from both models within shared tiles. An LLM agent edits optimization plans, and each plan is compiled and scored on real GPU execution. The measured scores and compiler feedback guide later proposals, while Monte Carlo tree search steers exploration. Across six single-GPU configurations on NVIDIA `B300` and `RTX 5090`, **interleaved kernels deliver a 1.45x geometric-mean per-round speedup (up to 1.59x)** over conventional execution, and GPU utilization rises by about 1.5x.

papers.title: Latent World Models Should Plan with Distances Along the Latent Manifold
papers.abstract: Latent world models such as LeWM plan by searching for an action sequence whose predicted terminal latent is closest to the goal latent under an ambient norm, such as the Euclidean distance. Planning with such a cost assumes that proximity in the ambient latent space reflects proximity to the goal in the environment. Studying LeWM, we find that this assumption holds only in a small neighborhood around the goal, whereas farther away the L2 cost forms spurious low-cost basins that trap the planner. Yet neighborhood-based embeddings show that the latents retain the underlying physical state.
