We therefore hypothesize that the latents lie near a curved, low-dimensional manifold, and that the terminal cost should measure the distance along this latent manifold rather than through the ambient space. To estimate this manifold distance, we propose the Neighborhood Graph Cost (NGC), which computes shortest-path distances on a mutual nearest-neighbor graph constructed over training latents. NGC changes only the terminal cost and requires no retraining. This single change improves the planning success rate of LeWM across all four benchmark tasks and nearly solves TwoRoom and Reacher: even at the farthest goal offsets tested, NGC reaches 95% and 100% success, whereas the L2 cost falls to 27% and 81%. These results support the manifold hypothesis and our argument that latent world models should plan with distances along the latent manifold.
papers.summary: Latent world models such as `LeWM` plan by searching for actions whose predicted final latent state is closest to the goal latent under a Euclidean distance. The authors find this distance is meaningful only near the goal; farther away it forms spurious low-cost basins that trap the planner. They hypothesize that the latents lie near a curved low-dimensional manifold. Their proposed `Neighborhood Graph Cost` (`NGC`) estimates distance along that manifold with shortest paths on a mutual nearest-neighbor graph built over training latents, and it requires no retraining. Changing only the terminal cost improves success on all four tasks, and **at the farthest goals `NGC` reaches 95% and 100% success on `TwoRoom` and `Reacher`, versus 27% and 81% with the Euclidean cost**.

papers.title: Multifidelity Monte Carlo Estimator for High-Dimensional Quantities of Interest
papers.abstract: Multifidelity Monte Carlo (MFMC) reduces the cost of estimating the statistics of quantities of interest (QoIs) computed via expensive high-fidelity model by using cheaper low-fidelity models as control variates. We extend MFMC to vector-valued QoIs by replacing the scalar control-variate coefficients with matrices and minimizing a weighted mean-squared error. The optimal full-matrix coefficients are available in closed form, and their variance reduction is summarized by an effective correlation that takes the place of the squared Pearson correlation in the closed-form MFMC design. Restricting the coefficients to block-diagonal, diagonal, and scalar classes gives a nested hierarchy of estimators with increasing variance reduction and increasing pilot-data demand, with closed-form coefficients for compatible weightings. For a scalar QoI obtained by linearly projecting the state, correcting the full state before projecting is never worse at the population level. Experiments on a Gaussian problem, a reduced-order model of an advection--diffusion problem, and a coarse-grid two-phase flow problem show that the best class depends on the pilot size relative to the number of covariance quantities it must estimate, and that reusing the pilot samples lowers the mean-squared error.
papers.summary: Multifidelity Monte Carlo (`MFMC`) cuts the cost of estimating statistics from expensive high-fidelity simulations by using cheaper low-fidelity models as control variates. The authors extend it to vector-valued quantities of interest by replacing scalar coefficients with matrices, with closed-form optimal coefficients and an effective correlation that summarizes the variance reduction. Restricting the matrices to block-diagonal, diagonal, or scalar form gives a nested family of estimators that trade variance reduction against how much pilot data they need. Experiments on a Gaussian problem, an advection-diffusion reduced-order model, and a two-phase flow problem show that **the best estimator class depends on the pilot sample size relative to the number of covariance quantities it must estimate**.

papers.title: Decentralized Online Exp-Concave Optimization
papers.abstract: Decentralized Online Convex Optimization (D-OCO) is a fundamental framework in which a set of local agents aims to minimize a sequence of global loss functions using only local computations and communications. While recent work has established near-optimal regret guarantees for convex and strongly convex losses, the case of exp-concave losses remains an open challenge: specifically, whether logarithmic regret is achievable. In this paper, we answer this question affirmatively by proposing Decentralized Online Newton Step (D-ONS), which adapts the idea of blocking and accelerated gossip to the Online Newton Step algorithm in a non-trivial manner. Concretely, our algorithm achieves a regret bound of $O\left(Nd(1-\sigma_2)^{-1/2}\,\log^2(T) \right)$ where $N$ is the number of agents, $d$ is the dimension, $T$ is the horizon, and $1-\sigma_2$ represents the spectral gap of the network. To our knowledge, this is the first logarithmic regret bound for decentralized online exp-concave optimization. We further establish a nearly matching lower bound of $\Omega\left(Nd (1-\sigma_2)^{-1/2}\,\log(T/N) \right)$ showing the near optimality of our upper bound. Finally, we extend our algorithm to decentralized online linear regression in which the feasible domain is unbounded and features and labels are locally observed. By gossiping covariance and label-feature statistics, we also achieve logarithmic regret.
papers.summary: In decentralized online convex optimization, networked agents minimize a sequence of global losses using only local computation and communication. Whether logarithmic regret is achievable for exp-concave losses in this setting had been open. The proposed Decentralized Online Newton Step (`D-ONS`) adapts blocking and accelerated gossip to the Online Newton Step algorithm. **It achieves the first logarithmic regret bound for this setting, O(Nd(1−σ₂)^(-1/2) log²T)**, which a nearly matching lower bound shows is close to optimal. The authors also extend the method to decentralized online linear regression with an unbounded domain.

papers.title: LLM Agents as Suppliers of Physical System Models: Calibration and Acceptance in Modelica
papers.abstract: To procure a model of a device, a client hands a supplier a description, sometimes with recorded data or a target response, and accepts the model against this handover. We let LLM coding agents act as the supplier on handovers with data, building Modelica models from library components for four simulated systems and a real switching magnet, and ask what acceptance certifies. Several agents reach the noise floor, but a handover admits a set of models: the description leaves parts of the structure open, and the data narrow it only to the agreed accuracy. We therefore accept by membership in this set, not by matching one reference, and add layers above behaviour: a physical invariant exposes an energy-creating model at the noise floor. Interpretability becomes a property of the delivered model, tested on a variant, read where none exists and shaped through the handover. Most failures are fits delivered with a systematic residual on their own fitting data, where the handover left open how close is close enough. In a follow-up, stating a threshold makes the agents compare against it, and more deliveries pass. The argument applies wherever a handover underspecifies a model meant to be read, not only run.
papers.summary: LLM coding agents act as model suppliers: given a device description plus recorded data, they build `Modelica` models from library components for four simulated systems and a real switching magnet. Because a description and noisy data admit many valid models, the authors judge acceptance by membership in that admissible set rather than by matching one reference model. They add checks above behavior, such as a physical invariant that exposes an energy-creating model fitting at the noise floor. Most failures were fits that left a systematic residual on their own fitting data because the handover never said how close was close enough. **Stating an explicit accuracy threshold led the agents to check against it, and more deliveries passed.**

papers.title: Synergy-Aware Residual Flow Matching for Single-Cell Perturbation Prediction
papers.abstract: Predicting single-cell responses to genetic and chemical perturbations is important for understanding regulatory mechanisms and prioritizing therapeutic interventions. Existing methods have made progress by modeling perturbation-conditioned expression shifts with neural networks, graph priors, foundation-model representations, or distributional generative models. However, combinatorial perturbation prediction remains challenging because much of the response can be explained by additive single-perturbation effects, while the biologically informative signal often lies in a smaller non-additive residual induced by perturbation interactions. Directly generating the full post-perturbation expression profile may therefore allocate substantial capacity to the dominant additive component and underemphasize synergy-specific structure. To address this issue, we propose \textbf{SynGeneFlow}, a synergy-aware flow matching framework that anchors the source distribution at an additive prior and learns a residual flow toward the true perturbed state. SynGeneFlow further incorporates perturbation-conditioned gene interaction modeling, where a static gene-gene mask provides biological structure and a perturbation-dependent deformation bias dynamically modulates gene-gene coupling. To preserve population-level response structure, we align both endpoint distributions and biological residual distributions with MMD-based regularization. We evaluate SynGeneFlow on genetic and drug perturbation benchmarks under observed-single, held-out, and cross-modality settings. The results demonstrate that residualizing flow matching around additive perturbation effects provides a biologically grounded and robust framework for single-cell perturbation response prediction.
papers.summary: When predicting how single cells respond to combinations of genetic or chemical perturbations, most of the response is explained by adding up single-perturbation effects. The biologically informative signal often lies in a smaller non-additive residual. `SynGeneFlow` uses flow matching that starts from an additive prior and learns only a residual flow toward the true perturbed state. It adds gene-interaction modeling that combines a static gene-gene mask with a perturbation-dependent bias, plus regularization based on maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) to preserve population-level structure. On genetic and drug perturbation benchmarks in observed-single, held-out, and cross-modality settings, the authors report that **residualizing flow matching around additive effects gives robust response prediction**.

papers.title: Integrable building blocks for symplectic neural networks: learned-type layers, fiber-preserving layers, and what a single layer can do
papers.abstract: Exactly symplectic neural networks are built almost exclusively from shear maps and gain expressivity only through depth. We ask what else a single explicit symplectic layer can be. Observing that every layer in use is the exact flow of a Hamiltonian that is a function of commuting integrals, we obtain three families of layers: a learned-type layer, in which every conjugate pair is rotated, squeezed or sheared by a state-dependent amount and the type is found by training; moving-plane shears, residual symplectic maps outside the known ridge-function class; and fiber-preserving layers, which combine an unconstrained point transformation with a fiber translation at the cost of one linear solve. We characterize residual symplectic layers $x \mapsto x + J\nabla H(x)$: in one degree of freedom they are exactly the shears along a line, while from two degrees of freedom on a strictly larger class exists. Conjugating a learned-type layer by a symplectic network yields an exact one-parameter group with an exactly conserved learned Hamiltonian. In experiments on sixteen systems with one to forty degrees of freedom, against SympNets, H\'enonNets and learned-plane shear networks, layers built on nonlinear integrals are far more accurate when the Hamiltonian contains functions of those integrals. On nonlinear Schr\"odinger lattices with six to forty sites, twist layers alternating with linear symplectic maps are over a hundred times more accurate than every shear-based network, and with an on-site potential of learned form three to four orders of magnitude more accurate. On chains of Tao oscillators with the step size as an input, stretch layers are 45 to 70 times more accurate than learned-plane shears and recover the Hamiltonian to 1%. On generic non-separable systems, fiber layers improve on learned-plane shears by at most a factor of two, and widening the networks does not help any architecture.
papers.summary: Exactly symplectic neural networks, which preserve the geometric structure of Hamiltonian dynamics, are built almost entirely from shear maps and gain expressivity only through depth. Observing that every layer in use is the exact flow of a Hamiltonian built from commuting integrals, the authors derive three new layer families. They are learned-type layers that rotate, squeeze, or shear conjugate pairs; moving-plane shears; and fiber-preserving layers. Across sixteen systems compared with `SympNets`, `HénonNets`, and learned-plane shear networks, **twist layers are over a hundred times more accurate than every shear-based network on nonlinear Schrödinger lattices**, and stretch layers are 45 to 70 times more accurate on Tao oscillator chains. On generic non-separable systems the gains are at most a factor of two.

papers.title: One Head Away from Language Confusion: Single Attention Heads Across Model Families
papers.abstract: Large language models sometimes reply in an unexpected language, a failure known as language confusion. We ablate individual attention heads in 12 model checkpoints spanning seven model series, using FLORES-200 continuations in five languages and Language Confusion Benchmark (LCB) chat replies. In ten models, zeroing one head causes substantially more departures from the expected language than zeroing any other head in its layer; its LCB pass-rate drop persists, though reduced, under mean ablation. Seven heads move 8.0 to 51.5 percent of all FLORES continuations out of the prompt's language, versus at most 1.4 percent for other same-layer heads; the other three mainly affect explicitly requested languages. These seven heads matter less in base models given plain text. In two models, replacing the values a head reads at the requested-language name with another language's mean makes replies fail and shifts some into that language, unlike a random change of equal size. Replacing a head's output with another language's mean redirects 84 to 99 percent of scored non-English monolingual LCB replies into that language in five models. Yet the requested language's mean improves crosslingual replies beyond every control head only in the two Gemma models, whose baselines are low. Code and results are available in the public repository at https://github.com/christian-hoang-04/anonymous-release.
papers.summary: Language models sometimes reply in an unexpected language, a failure called language confusion. Ablating individual attention heads in 12 checkpoints from seven model series, using `FLORES-200` continuations and the `Language Confusion Benchmark` (`LCB`), the authors find that in ten models one head causes far more language departures than any other head in its layer. **Zeroing such a head moves 8.0 to 51.5% of continuations out of the prompt's language, versus at most 1.4% for other same-layer heads.** Replacing that head's output with another language's mean redirects 84 to 99% of scored non-English replies into that language in five models. However, steering toward the requested language improves crosslingual replies only in the two `Gemma` models.

papers.title: Beyond the Teacher: Understanding and Preserving Distillation Overshoot in Agentic On-Policy Distillation
papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains agents on their own trajectories using supervision from a stronger teacher. We uncover a counterintuitive phenomenon in multi-turn agentic tasks: a smaller, initially weaker student can substantially outperform its teacher during training, only to regress as distillation continues. We term this phenomenon distillation overshoot. Through decision- and task-level analyses, we trace overshoot to two competing effects of OPD: repairing weak student decisions and eroding successful student choices that the teacher disfavors. Early in training, repair outpaces erosion, allowing the student to combine the teacher's corrections with its own strengths and surpass the teacher. As training continues, erosion overtakes repair, causing these gains to vanish. Motivated by this finding, we propose Success-Preserving On-Policy Distillation (SPOD), which selectively masks conflicting teacher supervision on successful student choices and introduces a soft probability floor to counteract their erosion, while retaining teacher guidance elsewhere. SPOD requires only binary episode success and model probabilities already available during OPD. Across two model families and three agentic benchmarks, SPOD consistently outperforms ordinary OPD and evaluated variants, improving final success by up to 15.2 percentage points and surpassing the teacher by up to 20.0 points. Moreover, SPOD's final checkpoints outperform even ordinary OPD's best intermediate checkpoints in all six settings, demonstrating that beyond-teacher gains can be not only preserved but further extended. Code: https://github.com/Jike338/SPOD
papers.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains an agent on its own trajectories using supervision from a stronger teacher. In multi-turn agentic tasks, the authors observe distillation overshoot: a weaker student surpasses its teacher mid-training, then regresses. They trace this to two competing effects, where teacher feedback repairs weak student decisions but also erodes successful choices the teacher disfavors. Success-Preserving On-Policy Distillation (`SPOD`) masks conflicting teacher supervision on successful student choices and adds a soft probability floor, using only binary episode success. Across two model families and three agentic benchmarks, **`SPOD` improves final success by up to 15.2 points and surpasses the teacher by up to 20.0 points**.

papers.title: Normalizing Flow for Neural-Enhanced Track-Before-Detect
papers.abstract: Multiobject tracking (MOT) is a fundamental capability in autonomous navigation, radar and sonar systems, as well as 6G integrated sensing-and-communication (ISAC) networks. In this paper, we propose a neural-enhanced track-before-detect (TkBD) framework that operates directly on complex-valued raw signals and learns a latent representation of unmodeled propagation effects during runtime. We introduce an environment-dependent latent intensity variable that characterizes the signal power of each object in the shared propagation environment. The probability density function of this intensity variable is represented by a normalizing flow and trained online in an unsupervised manner within the sequential Bayesian inference procedure. The learning objective is derived from a variational Bayes formulation by maximizing the evidence lower bound (ELBO), thereby accounting for the uncertainties inherent in the Bayesian TkBD problem. To enable scalable inference, we make use of a recently introduced Bayesian TkBD framework that combines belief propagation, which avoids high-dimensional operations, with sequential Monte Carlo methods for efficient low-dimensional updates.
papers.summary: Multi-object tracking is central to radar, sonar, autonomous navigation, and 6G integrated sensing-and-communication networks. The authors propose a neural-enhanced track-before-detect framework that works directly on complex-valued raw signals. It models each object's signal power through an environment-dependent latent intensity variable whose density is a normalizing flow. **The flow is trained online and without supervision inside sequential Bayesian inference by maximizing the evidence lower bound (ELBO).** To keep inference scalable, it builds on a Bayesian framework that combines belief propagation with sequential Monte Carlo methods.

papers.title: PACT: NVFP4 Data-Flow LoRA Fine-Tuning on Consumer GPUs
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning language models on consumer GPUs is constrained by computation and memory. Although LoRA reduces trainable parameters and optimizer state, frozen projections remain expensive, and activations retained for backward can dominate memory usage. We present PACT, a LoRA fine-tuning system that accelerates frozen projections with native NVFP4 GEMMs while reducing quantization and dequantization overhead and limiting quantization error. To reduce activation memory, PACT reuses quantized RMSNorm outputs and saves gate/up activations in NVFP4 for backward. To limit numerical error, it preserves BF16 inputs for forward nonlinear operations and calibrates frozen weights offline using GPTQ adapted to NVFP4 scales and quantized activations. Fused nonlinear kernels and cached forward and backward weight layouts reduce quantization and dequantization overhead. Evaluations across multiple models and tasks on a 16\,GB RTX~5080 show lower memory usage and faster LoRA fine-tuning with competitive accuracy, enabling model adaptation on resource-constrained consumer hardware.
papers.summary: Fine-tuning language models on consumer GPUs is limited by compute and memory. Even with low-rank adaptation (LoRA), the frozen projections stay expensive, and activations saved for the backward pass can dominate memory. `PACT` runs the frozen projections with native `NVFP4` 4-bit matrix multiplies, stores reusable activations in `NVFP4`, and keeps BF16 inputs for nonlinear operations. It also calibrates frozen weights offline with a `GPTQ` variant adapted to `NVFP4`. Fused kernels and cached weight layouts reduce quantization overhead. **On a 16 GB `RTX 5080`, `PACT` lowers memory use and speeds up LoRA fine-tuning while keeping accuracy competitive** across multiple models and tasks.

papers.title: HCFM: Helmholtz Component Flow Matching for Time Series Anomaly Detection
papers.abstract: Flow Matching (FM) is an efficient simulation-free approach for training flow-based generative models, making it a promising foundation for scalable time-series anomaly detection (TSAD). However, standard FM learns a monolithic vector field in which nominal transport and local density-changing behavior are entangled. This creates a central challenge for TSAD; local expansion and contraction carry crucial anomaly-sensitive information, yet isolating this signal requires expensive Jacobian-trace estimation over the entire field. We propose \emph{Helmholtz Component Flow Matching} (HCFM), an unsupervised TSAD framework that parameterizes the vector field prediction network with separate transport, compression, and residual heads. The transport head is constrained to be divergence-free, so divergence estimation is restricted to the compression head, while a lightweight residual head absorbs the remaining mismatch. This structured parameterization improves scalability and detection performance by separating volume-preserving nominal transport from density-changing compression, yielding cleaner anomaly signals from distinct deviations of nominal behavior. Experiments on large-scale univariate and multivariate TSAD benchmarks show that HCFM consistently improves detection accuracy while maintaining efficient inference compared with 16 baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/TrustAIoT/HCFM__time-series-anomaly/
papers.summary: Flow matching is a promising basis for time-series anomaly detection, but a standard flow learns a single vector field in which normal transport and local density changes are entangled. Isolating the anomaly-sensitive density signal then requires expensive Jacobian-trace estimates. `Helmholtz Component Flow Matching` (`HCFM`) splits the predicted field into a divergence-free transport head, a compression head, and a lightweight residual head, so divergence only needs computing on the compression head. **On large univariate and multivariate benchmarks, `HCFM` improves detection accuracy over 16 baselines while keeping inference efficient.**

papers.title: Policy Is Not Capability: Some Safety Benchmarks Measure Which Definition of "Unsafe" You Trained On
papers.abstract: A guardrail classifier is reported as if unsafe were a property of text. It is not: it is a property of a policy, and the policy enters the model through its labels. We exploit an accident of an industrial deployment in which the same ~53k prompts were labelled twice, under two operational definitions ("is this a request for harmful content?" and "would a moderator block this?"), and used to train ten guardrail arms sharing architecture, codebase and optimiser family, at two model scales. First, the guardrail's own training corpus already contained the benchmarks: JailbreakBench-benign is 88% and OR-Bench-hard 82% present in the training pools, two over-refusal benchmarks, the kind a guardrail reports to argue it does not over-block. Everything below is decontaminated. Second, safety benchmarks stratify sharply by how much of their score is decided by the label definition rather than by the model: with architecture and optimiser fixed, the range across the ten arms is 0.99 on HarmBench-copyright and 0.043 on WildGuard-benign, a 23x spread. Third, a benchmark score can be moved across its entire range by 0.03% of the parameters. Across these arms HarmBench-copyright spans 0-100 and OR-Bench-hard over-refusal 3.4-56.4%, and the four arms whose last supervision signal carries a given policy occupy one extreme of both (exact rank p=0.005, or 0.04-0.14 at worst), at unchanged detection capability. For a distilled student the teacher's soft labels do this even when every hard label carries the other policy, so teacher provenance is an unrecorded confound in any released checkpoint. Fourth, validation accuracy on the one split that grades all twenty arms tracks agreement with the annotator's policy (rho=+0.74), not detection capability (rho=+0.34). We argue that guardrail evaluations should report contamination, a seed floor and the definition they were graded against as first-class variables.
papers.summary: In an industrial deployment, the same roughly 53k prompts were labeled under two definitions of "unsafe": whether a request seeks harmful content, and whether a moderator would block it. The authors used both label sets to train ten guardrail classifiers with shared architecture and code. They first find heavy benchmark contamination: 88% of `JailbreakBench`-benign and 82% of `OR-Bench-hard` appear in the training pools. After decontamination, **benchmark scores vary 23x more on some benchmarks than others depending on the label definition alone**. Scores such as `HarmBench`-copyright swing across their full range with unchanged detection capability, and distillation teachers can carry their policy into students. The authors argue that guardrail evaluations should report contamination, seed variance, and the policy they were graded against.

papers.title: The Optimal Sample Complexity of Pointwise Replicable Agnostic Learning
papers.abstract: Pointwise replicability asks that two independently trained predictors, using the same random seed, agree at each fixed query with high probability. We determine its optimal agnostic sample complexity on finite and countable domains. For every nonempty binary class of finite VC dimension $d\ge1$, the required number of independent examples is $\Theta\!\left(\frac{d}{\rho^2\alpha^2}+\frac{\log(1/\beta)}{\alpha^2}\right)$, uniformly over independent accuracy, failure, and disagreement parameters $\alpha,\beta,\rho\in(0,1/10)$. The learner returns one binary function, may be improper, and uses unrestricted shared randomness. Its sample budget is fixed before observing data, and the replicability guarantee includes queries of zero marginal mass. The main construction combines an ensemble of empirical-risk minimizers with a smooth, signal-dependent risk decomposition. A single shared phase selects the final binary predictor. Record times certify its weak-signal risk, while a uniform bound protects the strong-signal risk at that same selected time. A phase-comparison theorem controls the actual shared-seed execution under simultaneous changes in the marginals and risk coefficients. A rare repair step then makes the confidence cost additive. Together with matching lower bounds, this removes the remaining logarithmic overhead and parameter restrictions in the general countable-domain sample-complexity problem. This extended version also retains the earlier explicit constructions and their proofs, including proper learning for VC-one classes, the full finite-atom class, a faster realizable bound, and counterexamples that separate restrictions of particular algorithms from restrictions of the learning problem.
papers.summary: Pointwise replicability requires that two predictors trained independently with the same random seed agree at each fixed query with high probability. For every binary class of finite VC dimension d on finite or countable domains, the authors establish that **the optimal agnostic sample complexity is Θ(d/(ρ²α²) + log(1/β)/α²)**. This holds uniformly over the accuracy, failure, and disagreement parameters. The matching upper bound comes from an ensemble of empirical-risk minimizers, a shared phase-selection mechanism, and a rare repair step, which together remove earlier logarithmic overheads and parameter restrictions.

papers.title: Auto-MD-bench: Evaluating Autoresearch Agents for Real-World Medical Tasks
papers.abstract: Autonomous agents are increasingly capable of developing machine learning (ML) models end to end. In medical practice, however, strong performance on the target metric does not fully characterize how good the models are in real-world use cases. For example, medical ML models should also provide well-calibrated risk estimates and remain robust across patient populations. Yet autonomous model development is typically guided by task objectives that emphasize simple predictive discrimination (e.g. AUROC). This raises a key question: are these objectives sufficient to guide agents toward models that meet the broader requirements of real-world medical use? In this study, we introduce Auto-MD-bench, a benchmark of 15 real-world medical tasks from 10 clinical datasets, spanning survival analysis, classification and sequential prediction, with external validation across cohorts, hospitals and time periods. We evaluate four agents: AIDE, AI Scientist v2, Codex, and Autoresearch. The strongest agents achieve competitive primary scores, yet their predicted risks are less calibrated than those of the simple baseline models, which could lead to severe medical accidents. Moreover, models with nearly identical primary scores can exhibit markedly different calibration, while performance varies substantially across population shifts. These findings show that primary task performance alone is insufficient to assess autonomous clinical modeling and multiple different metrics widely used in healthcare practice need to be taken into consideration.
papers.summary: Autonomous agents that build machine learning (ML) models are usually steered by a single discrimination metric such as AUROC (area under the ROC curve), but clinical models also need well-calibrated risk estimates and robustness across patient populations. The authors introduce `Auto-MD-bench`, 15 real-world medical tasks drawn from 10 clinical datasets and covering survival analysis, classification and sequential prediction, with external validation across cohorts, hospitals and time periods. They evaluate four agents: `AIDE`, `AI Scientist v2`, `Codex` and `Autoresearch`. The strongest agents reach competitive primary scores, but **their predicted risks are less calibrated than those of simple baseline models**, models with nearly identical primary scores can differ sharply in calibration, and performance varies substantially under population shift.

papers.title: P2N: Reusing Deep Representations for Greater Effective Depth
papers.abstract: Mathematical problem solving and autonomous agents are increasingly important applications of language models, demanding stronger reasoning capabilities. Computational depth is a key resource for such reasoning, but adding model layers increases both training and inference costs, while test-time scaling incurs substantial additional inference computation. We introduce P2N (Previous to Next), which reuses the previous token's deep representations, already available during generation, to increase effective computational depth with negligible decoding overhead. Specifically, P2N adds the previous token's deep hidden state to the current token's shallow representation, allowing subsequent layers to build on previously completed deep computation. This recurrence extends effective computational depth across tokens, while introducing only a single vector addition per decoding step. We train the recurrence using parallel Jacobi updates restricted to a middle-layer core. Experiments with Qwen-style models show that, at 1.5B parameters, P2N improves GSM8K accuracy by over 10 percentage points under both zero-shot and few-shot prompting, with nearly unchanged decoding latency. The benefits also extend to language modeling and average performance on general downstream benchmarks. on general downstream benchmarks.
papers.summary: Reasoning benefits from computational depth, but adding layers raises training and inference cost, and test-time scaling adds a lot of extra inference compute. `P2N` (Previous to Next) adds the previous token's deep hidden state, which already exists during generation, to the current token's shallow representation, so later layers build on computation already finished for earlier tokens. The method costs one vector addition per decoding step, and the recurrence is trained with parallel Jacobi updates restricted to a middle-layer core. On 1.5B-parameter Qwen-style models it **improves `GSM8K` accuracy by more than 10 percentage points** under both zero-shot and few-shot prompting with nearly unchanged decoding latency, and it also improves language modeling and general downstream benchmarks.

papers.title: CoEvo-RSI: When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?
papers.abstract: Model--harness co-evolution has emerged as a prominent paradigm for recursive self-improving (RSI) agents, jointly evolving their execution scaffolds and intrinsic capabilities. We study the persistent yet often overlooked brain--body mismatch problem in this paradigm, where an evolving harness (body) demands behaviors its model (brain) has not learned or restricts capabilities it already possesses. We introduce CoEvo-RSI, a RSI framework that advances model--harness co-evolution through agent-driven, bidirectional historical inheritance. Drawing on a shared evolutionary archive and execution feedback, a meta-agent coordinates harness development from historical designs with model checkpoint selection or merging and subsequent adaptation under the selected harness, aligning inherited capabilities with evolving execution requirements to reduce brain--body mismatch. Using only supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on its own rejection-sampled trajectories, CoEvo-RSI makes Qwen3.5-9B competitive with larger models across diverse vertical applications, including multi-agent failure attribution, role-aware text-to-SQL, and smart-home instruction following. It surpasses DeepSeek-V4-Pro on TraceElephant (+14.16 agent accuracy) and GLM-5.3 on HomeBench VM (+4.90 success rate), underscoring the need for brain--body alignment and the potential of bidirectional historical inheritance to advance agent co-evolution.
papers.summary: In recursive self-improving (RSI) agents that evolve both their execution scaffold (the harness) and the underlying model, a harness can come to demand behaviors the model never learned or block capabilities it already has; the authors call this the brain–body mismatch. `CoEvo-RSI` uses a meta-agent and a shared evolutionary archive to develop new harnesses from earlier designs while selecting or merging model checkpoints and adapting them to the chosen harness. Using only supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on its own rejection-sampled trajectories, it makes `Qwen3.5-9B` competitive with much larger models on multi-agent failure attribution, role-aware text-to-SQL and smart-home instruction following. It **beats `DeepSeek-V4-Pro` on `TraceElephant` by 14.16 points of agent accuracy** and `GLM-5.3` on `HomeBench` VM by 4.90 points of success rate.
papers.highlight_summary:
Agents that co-evolve their harness (the tools, prompts and control flow around the model) and their model weights suffer from a "brain–body mismatch": the evolved harness asks for behaviors the model never learned, or blocks capabilities it already has. `CoEvo-RSI` addresses this with bidirectional historical inheritance: a meta-agent draws on a shared archive of past harnesses, model checkpoints and their outcomes, choosing which earlier harness design to build on and which earlier checkpoints to reuse or merge for it, instead of always pairing the latest model with the latest harness.

- Each round, a Curator diagnoses failures and pulls relevant history from the archive, eight independent editors each pick a historical base harness to modify, and the meta-agent either selects a single checkpoint or blends several with `TIES-Merging`, scoring candidates by task score and a new diagnostic, the Turn-level Interface Mismatch Rate (`TIMR`: the share of model turns with malformed outputs or calls to unavailable tools); the chosen pair is then refined with SFT on its own verifier-accepted trajectories.
- On failure attribution, `Qwen3.5-9B` reaches **70.78% agent accuracy on `TraceElephant` (+14.16 over `DeepSeek-V4-Pro`)** and **69.43% on `Who&When Pro`** (vs. 65.03% for `Qwen3.8-Max`), and on `Who&When Hand` it scores 68.39% at **22× lower inference cost** than `DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash`.
- In other domains it achieves the best Safe-EX on `RBAC Spider` (**80.85%**, with a 1.57% access-violation rate) and raises the `HomeBench` valid multi-device success rate from 10.91% to **75.51%**, 4.90 points above `GLM-5.3`.
- In ablations, evolving only the harness keeps TIMR above 1% in eight of ten rounds (full method: at most 0.22%), and the best `RBAC` result came from reviving a round-3 checkpoint in round 10, a pairing a latest-only approach would miss; a three-round run costs about **$2.72 in API fees and 17.5 hours**.
- Limitations: the evolved pairs are explicitly domain-specialized with no claim of cross-domain transfer, the method trails baselines on `Who&When Algo.` (62.17% vs. 68.25%) and on step-level accuracy where RL baselines win, its out-of-distribution `BIRD` Safe-EX (60.15%) lags coding-agent harnesses (about 71–75%), and TIMR captures only interface-level mismatch, not deeper capability gaps.

papers.title: Dual-Slot: From Serial Loops to Parallel Slots in Language Models
papers.abstract: Looped language models increase computational depth by repeatedly applying shared layers, offering a way to improve model quality without adding parameters. However, sequential dependencies between loop iterations increase autoregressive decoding latency. We introduce Dual-Slot, an architecture that reorganizes serial looped computation into parallel latent and prediction slots. Rather than waiting for the current token's latent computation to finish, the prediction slot combines the previous token's deep latent state with the current representation, while the latent slot produces a state for the next decoding step. This shifts the latent dependency across adjacent tokens, replacing two sequential module invocations with a single paired invocation while preserving standard autoregressive generation. To preserve token-level parallelism during training, we use a small number of Jacobi iterations to refine latent states across the sequence in parallel. Experiments on Qwen-style dense and mixture-of-experts (MoE) models show consistent improvements in language modeling and average downstream accuracy. On the 1B dense model, Dual-Slot reduces Pile validation perplexity from 7.25 to 7.00 and improves average five-shot accuracy across nine task configurations by 2.26 percentage points. After supervised fine-tuning, it improves zero-shot GSM8K accuracy by 5.83 and 3.49 percentage points for the 1B dense and A0.6B MoE models, respectively. Across the evaluated batch sizes, Dual-Slot retains 93.1-96.5% of vanilla decoding throughput for the dense model and 98.1-99.6% for the MoE model.
papers.summary: Looped language models gain depth by reapplying shared layers, but the sequential dependency between loop iterations slows autoregressive decoding. `Dual-Slot` reorganizes the serial loop into parallel latent and prediction slots: the prediction slot combines the previous token's deep latent state with the current representation, while the latent slot produces a state for the next step, so two sequential module calls become one paired call. Training stays parallel across tokens by refining latent states with a few Jacobi iterations. On a 1B dense model it lowers `Pile` validation perplexity from 7.25 to 7.00 and raises average five-shot accuracy by 2.26 points, and after supervised fine-tuning it improves zero-shot `GSM8K` accuracy by 5.83 and 3.49 points on the dense and mixture-of-experts (MoE) models, **while keeping 93.1–99.6% of vanilla decoding throughput**.

papers.title: Beyond Factual Accuracy: A Benchmark for Evaluating Perspective Alignment in LLMs
papers.abstract: Large Language Models often generate factually correct responses that fail to maintain user-requested perspectives, blending multiple perspectives and forcing users to filter through unwanted information---a perspective control failure that factual accuracy metrics cannot detect. We introduce PerspectiveBench, a benchmark quantifying perspective alignment by constructing scenarios where multiple valid reasoning paths coexist, and propose the Perspective Alignment Score (PAS) to measure adherence to specified perspectives. Experiments reveal that state-of-the-art models successfully include target content but fail to exclude non-requested perspectives. Providing documents through RAG improves factual grounding but does not resolve perspective drift, as models prioritize comprehensive coverage over strict user constraints. Code and data are available at https://github.com/sunghoon014/PerspectiveBench.
papers.summary: Language models often give factually correct answers that still fail to stay within a perspective the user asked for, mixing in other viewpoints in a way that accuracy metrics cannot detect. The authors build `PerspectiveBench`, a set of scenarios in which several valid reasoning paths coexist, and propose the Perspective Alignment Score (`PAS`) to measure how closely a response sticks to the requested perspective. State-of-the-art models reliably include the requested content but **fail to exclude perspectives the user did not ask for**. Supplying documents through retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves factual grounding but does not stop this perspective drift, because models favor broad coverage over the user's constraint.

papers.title: Conformal Prediction-Enabled Sequence-level Policy Optimization for Reasoning Language Models
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning improves the reasoning capability of large language models through verifiable rewards for mathematical and coding tasks. In token-level methods such as GRPO, clipping acts on individual token ratios while the reward and advantage apply to a complete response. Recent sequence-level methods align these units but still use fixed clipping bands, whose tail probabilities change as the score distribution evolves. We propose Conformal Prediction-Enabled Sequence-level Policy Optimization (CSPO), which adaptively calibrates sequence-level clipping bounds using recent training statistics. The resulting band targets a specified marginal tail budget and adapts to policy drift; calibration conditional on response length requires additional assumptions. We bound the probability that a fresh score falls outside the band by the target miscoverage level plus explicit CDF discrepancy and drift terms. Under additional moment conditions, this bound also controls the objective and gradient error relative to the unclipped GSPO power surrogate. Experiments with the Qwen3-1.7B series show improvements over GSPO on difficult mathematical reasoning benchmarks and ALFWorld, with clipping endpoints that adapt during training.
papers.summary: In token-level reinforcement learning methods for reasoning models, such as `GRPO`, clipping acts on individual token ratios while the reward applies to the whole response. Sequence-level methods such as `GSPO` fix that mismatch but still use fixed clipping bands, whose tail probabilities shift as the score distribution changes during training. `CSPO` uses conformal prediction to calibrate sequence-level clipping bounds adaptively from recent training statistics, targeting a specified tail budget, and the authors prove a bound on the probability that a fresh score falls outside the band, with extensions to objective and gradient error. Experiments with the `Qwen3-1.7B` series show **gains over `GSPO` on difficult mathematical reasoning benchmarks and `ALFWorld`**, with clipping endpoints that adapt over the course of training.

papers.title: Deep Fusion Memory: A Chunk-Level Parametric Memory for Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Large language models need effective ways to acquire and use external knowledge beyond what they retain from pretraining. Continued pretraining risks catastrophic forgetting, while retrieval at inference time can add substantial overhead. External parametric memory avoids online retrieval, but constructing its training data requires extensive offline search, and output-level interpolation provides only shallow fusion. We introduce Deep Fusion Memory (DFM), a parametric memory architecture that reduces this construction workload and incorporates learned memory into intermediate hidden states. A causal memory predictor learns to generate memory from the preceding context, using retrieved chunk embeddings from the corpus as supervision. The predicted memory is shared across tokens within each chunk and fused into their hidden states through gated cross-attention. Memory prediction and fusion are trained end to end with the backbone frozen, and inference requires no explicit retrieval. Compared with existing parametric memory approaches, which often construct token-level memory targets, DFM requires $32\times$ fewer retrieval queries and $2048\times$ fewer retrieved items to construct its training data. Across six QA tasks, DFM performs better over the strongest baseline by 12.71% on Mistral-7B-v0.3 and 11.19% on Qwen3-8B-Base. Beyond QA, domain adaptation yields average gains of 6.51 and 4.38 points over Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base, respectively.
papers.summary: Language models can gain new knowledge through continued pretraining, which risks catastrophic forgetting, or through retrieval at inference time, which adds overhead; existing parametric memory avoids online retrieval but needs heavy offline search to build training data and fuses memory only at the output. `Deep Fusion Memory` (`DFM`) trains a causal predictor to generate a chunk-level memory from the preceding context, supervised by retrieved chunk embeddings, and fuses it into intermediate hidden states through gated cross-attention while the backbone stays frozen. Building its training data takes **32× fewer retrieval queries and 2048× fewer retrieved items** than token-level approaches, and inference needs no retrieval. Across six QA tasks it beats the strongest baseline by 12.71% on `Mistral-7B-v0.3` and 11.19% on `Qwen3-8B-Base`, and it also improves domain adaptation.

papers.title: Non-Acceleration of the Heavy-Ball Method in 1D
papers.abstract: Despite having an asymptotically optimal rate of convergence on convex quadratics, the acceleration of Polyak's heavy-ball method and a characterization of its dynamics within more general settings have remained long standing open problems. Recently, the work of Goujaud et al. [Math. Program. (2025)] made progress regarding acceleration in the context of smooth, strongly convex minimization: for a small enough inverse condition number, either the method does not accelerate on quadratics, or there exists a smooth strongly convex function such that heavy-ball cycles over the roots of unity. The constructed functions have two variables, thus leaving the question of acceleration over univariate functions open. In this work, we use a Fourier-based analysis to i) provide a proof for the non-acceleration of the heavy-ball method over the class of univariate smooth strongly convex functions. We also ii) provide a strict enlargement of the previous root-of-unity cycling region, with insights regarding the "fractional" sets of Goujaud et al. [arXiv:2502.19916], and iii) give a higher dimensional cycling instance which is not covered by root-of-unity cycling.
papers.summary: Whether Polyak's heavy-ball method accelerates beyond convex quadratics has been a long-standing open problem; earlier work showed failure to accelerate using two-variable counterexamples, which left the one-dimensional case unresolved. Using a Fourier-based analysis, the authors **prove that heavy-ball does not accelerate on univariate smooth strongly convex functions**. They also strictly enlarge the known parameter region where the method cycles over roots of unity, clarify the related "fractional" sets from earlier work, and give a higher-dimensional cycling example not covered by root-of-unity cycling.

papers.title: Generation-Heavy Hybrid Machine Translation
papers.abstract:
The state of the art techniques in Machine Translation (MT) require large amounts of symmetric resources from source and target languages. This is true regardless of whether the approach is Transfer or Interlingua, Symbolic or Statistical. Symmetry within these approaches is necessary to ensure quality, robustness and retargetability. In reality, such symmetry, whether it is in terms of structural transfer lexicons, interlingual dictionaries or parallel corpora, is a major bottleneck in developing any MT system.
  This dissertation presents an approach to MT that addresses the lack of symmetry by exploiting symbolic and statistical target language resources in source-poor/target-rich language pairs. This approach is called Generation-Heavy Hybrid Machine Translation (GHMT). Expected source language resources include a syntactic parser and a simple one-to-many translation dictionary. No transfer rules or complex interlingual representations are used. Rich target language symbolic resources are used to overgenerate multiple structural variations from a target-glossed syntactic dependency representation of source language sentences. Statistical target-language resource are then used to select amongst the overgenerated translations. The source-target asymmetry of systems developed in this approach makes them more easily retargetable to new source languages.
papers.summary: Mainstream machine translation (MT) approaches, whether transfer-based, interlingua-based, symbolic or statistical, depend on symmetric resources such as transfer lexicons or parallel corpora, which are scarce for many language pairs. This dissertation presents Generation-Heavy Hybrid Machine Translation (`GHMT`), which needs only a source-language syntactic parser and a simple one-to-many dictionary. Rich target-language symbolic resources overgenerate many structural variants from a target-glossed dependency representation of the source sentence, and target-language statistical models then pick among them. Because **the system leans almost entirely on target-language resources**, it is easier to retarget to new source languages.

papers.title: Self-organizing reinforcement learning: a swarm approaches the explore-exploit optimum
papers.abstract: The explore/exploit trade-off is the core problem of reinforcement learning (RL). We show that a minimal foraging swarm approaches its optimum - the ideal-free / Nash allocation of a multi-agent resource-sharing game (an equilibrium, not a return maximum) - with no learner and no reward signal. Agents explore by heavy-tailed (Levy) flights, recruit neighbours to a discovery through a threshold cascade on their proximity network, and disperse as a patch crowds; this cascade cycle balances exploration and exploitation and drives foragers toward the ideal free distribution. The swarm attains the shape of this optimum (committed foragers track richness with slope 0.94) but not its exact equilibrium - it stays measurably exploitable - reaching it dynamically (~150 steps) through the coupling of recruitment to movement: remove the coupling and matching collapses (0.94 -> 0.08). The RL sits at the level of the problem and the allocation reached, not the micro-rule: no step evaluates payoff (reward-free by construction, though the crowd signal is informationally tied to payoff), and the swarm reaches the allocation without learning it (quality plateaus and re-settles after resources move, no cumulative gain). Against a trained baseline the comparison is two-sided: in an easier, disembodied game a learner is more precise, while in the same embodied environment the reward-free swarm reaches ~65% of a validated oracle ceiling at zero training and leads until trained PPO and centralised-critic (CTDE) learners overtake it (~74-75%, 16 seeds, all above the swarm mean) after ~4,000 of 15,000 training steps - its advantage is in budget, not asymptote. In this one setting we read it not as beating RL but as a strong zero-shot, reward-free operating point: a demonstration that the self-organizing physics of a minimal swarm can carry a collective close to the optimum RL seeks, with none of RL's machinery.
papers.summary: The authors show that a minimal foraging swarm, with no learner and no reward signal, approaches the ideal-free (Nash) allocation of a multi-agent resource-sharing game, which is the explore/exploit optimum of that game. Agents explore with heavy-tailed Lévy flights, recruit neighbors to discoveries through threshold cascades on their proximity network, and disperse as patches become crowded. The swarm matches the shape of the optimum (committed foragers track patch richness with slope 0.94), though it stays measurably exploitable, and **matching collapses to 0.08 when recruitment is decoupled from movement**. In an embodied comparison, the swarm reaches about 65% of an oracle ceiling with no training and leads until `PPO` and centralized-critic learners overtake it at about 74–75% after roughly 4,000 of 15,000 training steps.

papers.title: Compile Once, Run Cheap: Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents, and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds
papers.abstract: Embodied AI lacks the data-rich pretraining that gave language models their agents and skills, so new manipulation capability costs demonstrations per task or a frontier model in every episode. We study a third route: a strong general model acts only as an offline author that writes, runs, diagnoses and repairs a manipulation skill in simulation until it passes an exam on layouts drawn after freezing; the frozen skill then runs as code alone or under a cheap caller that reads only its description. We call this skill-level recursive self-improvement Skill-RSI and specify a compile protocol (isolated, audited author; hidden validation layouts; no-feedback and inherit-only controls; tamper-evident ledger) and a reuse protocol that runs the identical files with executors from another model family. On 7 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks with cluttered tables, Claude Code compiled 4 tasks into 7 frozen skills, 5 from a first draft needing only qualification, at USD 4.29-8.22 of author cost each (USD 55 per skill counting the 13 failed campaigns). The other three tasks did not compile in 18 campaigns, including five with GPT-6 and a pre-registered 150-layout run: on the hardest task every campaign scored 78-95 of 100 but had 3-16 safety aborts, failing the gate of 95% success with zero aborts; a 100-episode exam bounds an abort rate only to 3.6%. On hidden layouts, repair that inherits the previous version beat from-scratch rewriting in 8 of 8 controlled campaigns (sign test p = 0.004); an inherit-only lineage attributes most of the gap to inheritance, with development feedback adding a little (3 of 3, p = 0.125). Write-once campaigns found no detectable first-draft effect of practice (minimum detectable effect 14 points). The frozen skills kept 148/150 successes on new layouts with no model and 147/150 with a DeepSeek-flash caller at USD 0.00028-0.00054 per episode; no direct-control baseline was run.
papers.summary: New robot manipulation skills usually cost either per-task demonstrations or a frontier model in every episode. In `Skill-RSI`, a strong model works only as an offline author that writes, runs, diagnoses and repairs a manipulation skill in simulation until it passes an exam on hidden layouts; the frozen code then runs alone or under a cheap caller model. On 7 `RoboTwin 2.0` tasks, `Claude Code` compiled 4 tasks into 7 frozen skills at USD 4.29–8.22 of author cost each, while three tasks never passed the strict safety gate in 18 campaigns, including runs with `GPT-6`. Repairs that inherited the previous version beat from-scratch rewrites in 8 of 8 controlled campaigns, and **the frozen skills succeeded in 148 of 150 episodes on new layouts with no model at all**, or 147 of 150 with a `DeepSeek-flash` caller at under USD 0.001 per episode.

papers.title: Polynomial Learning of Positive ReLU Networks under Gaussian Inputs
papers.abstract: We study positive, bias-free, one-hidden-layer ReLU networks under standard Gaussian inputs. We obtain algorithms with polynomial sample and real-arithmetic complexity, without separation or conditioning assumptions on the hidden directions. When the conditional label mean is a width-$k$ network with total output weight at most one, the learner achieves squared prediction error $\varepsilon$ with output width at most $k+\min\{k,d\}$ and complexity linear in one plus the residual second moment. For arbitrary labels with bounded second moment, we obtain a positive ReLU network of width $O(k\log(2/\varepsilon))$. Its risk is bounded by the irreducible noise variance plus $Ck^3\log^{9/2}(2k/\varepsilon)$ times the squared distance of the conditional mean to the target class, plus $\varepsilon$. The proofs combine implicit Hermite moments, orthogonal tensor-train compression, and a direction decoder whose probability of returning a direction far from every atom is bounded linearly in the compression and estimation errors. Exact Gaussian localization refines the resulting direction covers. In the agnostic setting, a cone-constrained convex program with a scale-dependent penalty produces a positive network; in the conditional-mean setting, exact sparsification yields the smaller width. We also establish projective direction recovery and confidence amplification with sample complexity proportional to the logarithm of the reciprocal failure probability.
papers.summary: The authors study how to learn positive, bias-free, one-hidden-layer ReLU networks from standard Gaussian inputs, and give **algorithms with polynomial sample and arithmetic complexity that need no separation or conditioning assumptions on the hidden directions**. When the conditional label mean is itself such a width-k network, the learner reaches any target squared error with output width at most k + min(k, d); for arbitrary labels it returns a network of width O(k log(2/ε)) with an explicit agnostic risk bound. The proofs combine implicit Hermite moments, tensor-train compression, a direction decoder, and a cone-constrained convex program.

papers.title: Memory as Belief: Bayesian Evolution of Memory for Self-Evolving LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on external memory to accumulate past experiences for continual adaptation. However, effectively reusing memory requires accurately assessing its value, as retrieved experiences may become unreliable when transferred across task contexts. Despite its importance, memory valuation remains largely underexplored, with existing methods relying on historical retrieval success rates that overlook the context dependency of memory usefulness and the varying reliability of estimates under different amounts of evidence. Inspired by the Bayesian brain hypothesis, we propose BEAM (Bayesian-style Evolutionary Agentic Memory), a framework that reformulates memory value evaluation as a parameterized cognitive inference process, where memory value is represented as a context-conditioned dynamic belief rather than a passive historical statistic. Specifically, BEAM infers memory value beliefs from current task contexts and continuously calibrates them using execution feedback as empirical evidence, transforming memory from passive storage into an adaptive cognitive mechanism for continual self-evolution. Extensive experiments across reasoning and code generation benchmarks demonstrate that BEAM consistently improves memory utilization and enables continual self-evolution of LLM agents.
papers.summary: Agents that reuse past experiences from external memory need to judge how valuable each memory is, but existing methods rely on historical retrieval success rates that ignore context and how much evidence backs each estimate. `BEAM` (Bayesian-style Evolutionary Agentic Memory), inspired by the Bayesian brain hypothesis, **treats each memory's value as a context-conditioned belief** that is inferred from the current task and continually updated with execution feedback. Experiments on reasoning and code generation benchmarks show that `BEAM` consistently improves memory use and supports continual self-improvement of language model agents.

papers.title: ClinSDT: LLM-Encoded Clinical Semantic Guidance for Sepsis Treatment via Decision Transformer
papers.abstract: Offline sepsis treatment aims to learn treatment policies from retrospective ICU trajectories. Decision Transformer-based methods provide a natural sequence modeling framework for this task, but they mainly rely on raw physiological states and historical clinician actions. Such raw trajectory tokens may not explicitly capture clinical semantics that clinicians use in practice, such as patient severity, recent treatment response, and current risk priorities. To address this limitation, we propose ClinSDT, an LLM-assisted Decision Transformer framework for offline sepsis treatment. ClinSDT uses a frozen LLM as a semantic bridge rather than a treatment decision maker. It constructs three clinical semantic views from ICU trajectories, namely Profile, Context, and Advisory, and inserts their encoded representations as independent tokens into a Decision Transformer policy. To support policy refinement and rollout, ClinSDT further trains a Treatment-Response Forecaster to estimate the next physiological state, SAPS-II change, and predictive uncertainty from state-action inputs. In the second training stage, the forecaster screens local counterfactual treatment candidates, and only low-uncertainty candidates with lower predicted SAPS-II increase are distilled into the policy after semantic regeneration. During inference, ClinSDT performs closed-loop treatment rollout by refreshing semantic inputs from the currently available patient state. Experiments on MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV show that ClinSDT achieves consistent relative improvements over representative imitation learning, offline reinforcement learning, and Decision Transformer baselines under the same rollout protocol. Code and data are available at https://github.com/KAG778/ClinSDT.
papers.summary: Decision Transformer methods for learning sepsis treatment policies from past intensive care unit (ICU) records mostly see raw physiological states and clinician actions, and miss the clinical meaning doctors attach to them, such as severity and recent response to treatment. `ClinSDT` uses a frozen language model to encode three clinical semantic views (Profile, Context and Advisory) as extra tokens for the policy. It also trains a Treatment-Response Forecaster that predicts the next state, the change in the `SAPS-II` severity score, and uncertainty, and uses it to screen counterfactual treatment candidates to distill into the policy. On `MIMIC-III` and `MIMIC-IV`, it **shows consistent relative gains over imitation learning, offline reinforcement learning and Decision Transformer baselines**.

papers.title: Behave Like Experts: Fusing Data with Semantic Knowledge for Effective and Efficient Semantic Map Construction
papers.abstract: Semantic map models (SMMs) construct a graph that reflects conceptual similarity by comparing cross-lingual form-meaning mappings. Experts build such models not only by obeying the data constraint, i.e., the connectivity hypothesis, which states that conceptual nodes belonging to the same form must be connected, but also by incorporating their prior semantic knowledge. Current automatic methods ignore this knowledge, which harms both accuracy and efficiency by enlarging the search space of candidate graphs. In this paper, we fuse the distributional semantic knowledge hidden in the internal representations of language models into a top-down, data-driven algorithm. This expert-like behavior re-sorts the candidates in a huge search space, guided by conceptual semantics similarity. Experiments on a self-collected benchmark of 10 datasets and comprehensive metrics show that our method builds SMMs both effectively and efficiently.
papers.summary: Semantic map models (SMMs) are graphs of conceptual similarity built by comparing how languages map forms to meanings. Experts build them using both the connectivity hypothesis and their own semantic intuition, while automatic methods use only the data constraint and therefore search a very large space of candidate graphs. The authors inject distributional semantic knowledge from language model representations into a top-down, data-driven algorithm that reorders candidates by conceptual similarity. On a self-collected benchmark of 10 datasets, **the method builds SMMs both more accurately and more efficiently**.

papers.title: Memories That Outlive Their Reasons: Dependency-Tethered Memory for Tool-Using LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Agents now act on the Web, publishing packages, models and datasets through registry APIs, and remembering past verifications spares them the work. But a verdict rests on premises. When a signing key is revoked, everything built on it stops passing, yet the advisory names only the key, and the old verdicts of its dependents may never share a retrieval window with it. This non-locality of invalidation turns memory into a liability: in long simulated chats, an agent reading a memory of atomic facts publishes 62% of the objects whose failure lies upstream, each backed by a record that was true when written. Yet derivation is local even when invalidation is not. Tether records, at write time, the exact versions each verdict derives from, and at read time withdraws any verdict whose support has failed anywhere in the store; the agent reads the same fields as before. On Fallout, a generator of versioned worlds with hypothesis-blind simulated histories shared by every memory, Tether publishes 0.3% of upstream-failing objects across three domains when relations are stated with their verdicts, with 37% fewer verification calls than checking everything. A-Mem and Graphiti re-verify most candidates (0.83-0.86 checks per candidate), which limits their savings, yet publish 9% of upstream-failing objects; Mem0 relies on memory more and publishes 42%. Flushing every verdict on any failure is as safe as Tether but costs 32% more checks. The gain over fact memory holds with three open-weight backbones and against a whole-store window. These gains depend on capturing dependencies: when relations arrive in sessions apart from their verdicts, Tether's downstream unsafe publication rate rises to 9.4-22.1%, and a weak writer that misses edges loses safety in the same way.
papers.summary: Agents that publish packages, models and datasets cache past verification verdicts, but when an upstream premise such as a signing key is revoked, the stale verdicts of its dependents may never be retrieved alongside the advisory. In long simulated sessions, an agent with plain fact memory published 62% of objects whose failure lay upstream. `Tether` records at write time the exact versions each verdict depends on and, at read time, withdraws any verdict whose support has failed anywhere in the store. On the `Fallout` world generator, it **published only 0.3% of upstream-failing objects while making 37% fewer verification calls** than checking everything, compared with 9% for `A-Mem` and `Graphiti` and 42% for `Mem0`, though safety drops when dependency relations are captured separately from verdicts or missed by a weak writer.

papers.title: Trackable Skill Library Lifecycle Management for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Skill-augmented agentic RL has emerged as an effective approach to improving LLM agents on long-horizon tasks. Despite this progress, individual skills may follow distinct trajectories as the policy evolves, with some becoming redundant after the model internalizes their capabilities, others remaining valuable as external scaffolding, and still others turning harmful. However, existing skill library systems fail to identify each skill's true contribution due to free-riding among co-retrieved skills, difficulty confounding across tasks, and the absence of skill-specific counterfactual evidence, which prevents reliable skill lifecycle management. We propose TrackRL, an agentic RL framework where skill tracking drives skill library full lifecycle management. Specifically, within each GRPO group, we turn grouped sampling into online randomized controlled experiments. Independent random injection and within-group contrasts on the same task isolate each skill's true contribution, and reliability-weighted aggregation accumulates evidence across groups. As evidence accumulates, we continuously track skill utility, which measures the skill's causal contribution as external scaffolding, and model mastery, which reflects how far the corresponding capability has been internalized. Along this line, we formulate skill lifecycle management as an evidence-gated state-transition process that governs each skill from generation and admission through protected incubation to retention, retirement, or removal, while a soft capacity bound controls library growth. Experiments show that TrackRL outperforms recent skill-augmented RL baselines in both library-assisted and skill-free evaluation, with further analyses revealing how skill value shifts during policy learning and how evidence-driven state transitions shape skill library evolution. Our code is available at https://github.com/xizhu1022/TrackRL.
papers.summary: In skill-augmented agentic reinforcement learning, each skill in the library may become redundant, stay useful or turn harmful as the policy learns, but existing systems cannot isolate a single skill's contribution. `TrackRL` turns each `GRPO` sampling group into an online randomized controlled experiment, injecting skills independently at random and comparing outcomes within the group on the same task. The accumulated evidence tracks each skill's causal utility and how far the model has internalized it, and these drive an evidence-gated lifecycle of admission, incubation, retention, retirement or removal under a soft capacity limit. **`TrackRL` outperforms recent skill-augmented RL baselines both with and without the skill library at evaluation time**.

papers.title: MemBubble: Benchmarking How Agent Memory Shapes LLM Response Diversity
papers.abstract: Memory serves as the core component of LLM-based agents, enabling personalized responses via extracting and using user preferences from past interactions. However, its use may reduce response diversity, thereby narrowing the range of information available to users. Existing evaluations rely largely on synthetic interactions and cover few memory systems, leaving the effects of memory on response diversity insufficiently evaluated in real-world scenarios. We introduce MemBubble, a benchmark of 1000 instances built on preferences extracted from real user-assistant conversations. To measure the extent to which memory concentrates response distributions, we construct test queries in scenarios distinct from user preferences while preserving topical relevance through shared preference categories. Across multiple LLMs and memory mechanisms, entropy decreases by 34.7% on average compared with directly providing the full interaction history, highlighting the important role of memory processing in diversity loss. We also explore simple user-side interventions and changes in information availability but find that these do not effectively close the diversity gap. Our findings highlight the need to consider preserving diversity and user access to information alongside improvements in personalization when designing and using agent memory systems.
papers.summary: Agent memory lets language models personalize answers from past interactions, but it may also narrow the range of responses users see. `MemBubble` is a benchmark of 1,000 instances built from preferences extracted from real user–assistant conversations, with test queries set in scenarios that differ from those preferences but share a preference category. Across several language models and memory systems, **response entropy drops by 34.7% on average** compared with giving the model the full interaction history, which points to memory processing as a source of diversity loss. Simple user-side interventions and changes in information availability did not close the gap.

papers.title: Decision-Target Reversal under Informative Label Missingness
papers.abstract: Informative label missingness can improve classification efficiency because the pattern of label availability may itself contain information about the discriminant structure. We show that this advantage need not persist across deployment objectives: with the data-generating model and statistical experiments held fixed, informative partial classification can be favourable under one loss and unfavourable under another. We call this phenomenon decision-target reversal. For binary Gaussian discrimination, we derive a local cost-sensitive excess-risk expansion and, in one dimension, obtain explicit critical cost ratios at which the first-order risk ordering reverses. We show that the required covariance geometry arises under finite uncertainty-dependent missingness mechanisms with a fixed marginal missing-label proportion. We then extend the analysis to multiclass finite-action problems through loss-specific active-boundary curvature, yielding a general decision-target frontier. Monte Carlo experiments illustrate the predicted reversals, and a descriptive gastrointestinal-lesion application with agreement-defined label availability illustrates sensitivity to deployment costs. The results show that favourable informative missingness is a property of the statistical experiment relative to the deployment decision, rather than of the experiment alone.
papers.summary: When the pattern of which labels are missing carries information, it can make classification more efficient, but the authors show this benefit depends on the deployment objective. With the data model held fixed, informative partial labeling can help under one loss and hurt under another, a phenomenon they call **decision-target reversal**. For binary Gaussian discrimination they derive a local cost-sensitive excess-risk expansion with explicit critical cost ratios in one dimension, then extend the analysis to multiclass problems. Monte Carlo experiments and a gastrointestinal-lesion example illustrate the predicted reversals.

papers.title: Many Repairs, One Direction: Steering Code Models Toward Safer Cryptographic API Use
papers.abstract: Cryptographic API misuse in large language model-generated code can compromise software security. While many existing approaches improve code security by modifying model parameters or inputs, how representation changes associated with different cryptographic API repairs can support a shared intervention for safer code generation remains underexplored. To investigate this, we construct 48,000 matched program pairs across four programming languages and ten cryptographic API misuse categories. Each pair changes a specified API decision while preserving the programming task. Subtracting the misuse program's internal representation from its secure counterpart's gives a repair vector. Across five models, comparisons of mean repair vectors reveal stronger organization by misuse category than by language. These category-specific patterns also support a shared intervention. We introduce CrypSteer, which extracts a shared direction by normalizing repair differences and selecting a principal component aligned with repairs across misuse categories. With model weights fixed, adding one shared direction per model to its internal activations during generation improves aggregate target security rates by 5.28--15.00 percentage points over unsteered generation across languages and misuse categories. These findings connect the shared structure of cryptographic repair representations to a reusable intervention for safer code generation.
papers.summary: Code generated by language models often misuses cryptographic APIs. The authors build 48,000 matched program pairs across four programming languages and ten misuse categories, each differing only in one API decision, and define a repair vector as the difference between internal representations of the secure and insecure versions. Across five models, these vectors cluster more by misuse category than by language, and `CrypSteer` extracts a single shared direction per model by normalizing repair differences and choosing an aligned principal component. With weights unchanged, **adding this one direction to activations during generation raises target security rates by 5.28–15.00 percentage points** over unsteered generation.

papers.title: TIRE: Top-Down Formula Instantiation with Reliable Execution for Physics Problem Synthesis
papers.abstract: Advancing physics reasoning in large language models requires scalable training data that connect physical laws, concrete problem scenarios, and verifiable numerical answers. Expert-designed problems offer top-down control over physical laws, conditions, and scenarios, but require costly human effort.
