papers.summary: `EasyResearch` extends the earlier `EasyClassifier` with open-source analysis cores and a no-code Windows app for regression, time-series forecasting, and signal classification. Every task uses leakage-safe defaults: everything is learned on training data only, models keep published defaults with fixed seeds, the selected model gets a separate final score, forecasts are never scored on shuffled data, and each run writes a Methods paragraph with references. Scored against held-out data, common practices overstated results, for example **screening predictors on all rows reported R² = 0.27 on pure noise versus −0.44 on new data**. Likewise, shuffled cross-validation promised forecast errors 19% smaller than those achieved, while `EasyResearch`'s estimates stayed nearly unbiased.

papers.title: Federated Learning for Malware Image Classification under Data Heterogeneity
papers.abstract: Malware image classification (MIC), in which binary files are converted into visual representations and deep neural networks are trained to identify malware families, has recently emerged as an effective approach for malware detection. Federated learning (FL) enables malware image classifiers to be trained collaboratively by multiple clients without sharing raw data. However, a fundamental challenge in FL is data heterogeneity (non-IID), which is particularly relevant but understudied in the malware context. In this paper, we address this gap via three contributions. First, we present an empirical study of federated MIC under varying degrees of data heterogeneity across three popular malware image datasets (MalImg, Virus-MNIST, and MalNet). We show that while FL achieves strong accuracy under IID conditions, both accuracy and training stability degrade as data becomes increasingly non-IID. Second, we introduce a set of round-level statistics that characterize the data contributed by participating clients in each FL round, and demonstrate that class entropy (diversity of class labels present in a given round) exhibits strong positive correlation with global model accuracy. Third, leveraging this insight, we propose an entropy-aware client selection strategy that filters candidate client subsets based on class entropy, and show that our strategy outperforms standard random selection. Our results highlight the role of client composition in federated MIC and underscore the importance of distribution-aware classifier training under data heterogeneity.
papers.summary: Malware image classification converts binaries into images and trains neural networks to recognize malware families. Federated learning lets organizations train such classifiers jointly without sharing raw data, but how it handles non-IID data in this setting is understudied. An empirical study on `MalImg`, `Virus-MNIST`, and `MalNet` shows accuracy and training stability degrade as client data grows more heterogeneous. The authors find that **the class entropy of each round's participating clients correlates strongly with global model accuracy**, and an entropy-aware client-selection strategy based on this beats random selection.

papers.title: SPARC: Spoken Profile Authorship Recognition Corpus
papers.abstract: Speech anonymization has focused on the acoustic signal, leaving open how much speaker information the transcribed words themselves retain. In this work, we study pairwise speaker and demographic-attribute verification from transcribed speech. We introduce SPARC (Spoken Profile Authorship Recognition Corpus), a benchmark built from two podcast corpora comprising over 12,500 speakers, 1.5M quality-filtered utterances, and speaker-level inferred or source-provided labels for sex, age, and accent, and evaluate five attribution models and three LLMs on identity- and attribute-verification trials with episode- and metadata-based topic proxies. LLM adversaries distinguish same-speaker pairs from text alone. Attribute-label agreement is harder to verify, but LLMs perform sex- and accent-label verification above chance. Finally, releasing only short probe texts (50 words) degrades the strongest adversaries the most, offering a partial reduction in observed linkage.
papers.summary: Speech anonymization usually targets the audio signal, leaving open how much speaker information the transcribed words alone reveal. `SPARC` is a benchmark built from two podcast corpora with over 12,500 speakers and 1.5M utterances, labeled for sex, age, and accent. It is used to evaluate five authorship-attribution models and three LLMs on speaker- and attribute-verification trials. **LLM adversaries can tell same-speaker pairs apart from text alone** and verify sex and accent above chance. Releasing only short 50-word probe texts weakens the strongest adversaries the most, but only partially reduces linkage.

papers.title: EG-GRPO: Evidence-Guided Step-level Credit Assignment for Deep Search Agents
papers.abstract: LLM-based search agents demonstrate strong capabilities in long-horizon information seeking and reasoning, typically trained via reinforcement learning. However, existing approaches predominantly rely on trajectory-level outcome rewards, providing limited supervision for complex search and reasoning processes. Although step-level credit assignment offers a promising solution, obtaining reliable and task-grounded supervision for open-ended search remains challenging. In this paper, we propose Evidence-Guided Group Relative Policy Optimization (EG-GRPO), a framework that derives step-level supervision from the evidence annotations available in synthetic deep search data. EG-GRPO identifies the first supporting citation for each required evidence claim and uses the newly acquired evidence to construct step-level process rewards. By representing the accumulated evidence as an evolving knowledge state, EG-GRPO further performs state-conditioned relative advantage estimation and combines the resulting step-level signal with the standard trajectory-level outcome advantage. Experiments on five challenging deep search benchmarks show that EG-GRPO generally outperforms standard GRPO and existing reward-enhanced and step-level RL baselines across different model scales. These results demonstrate that task-grounded evidence annotations can provide effective process supervision for credit assignment in deep search RL.
papers.summary: LLM search agents trained with reinforcement learning usually receive only a trajectory-level outcome reward, which gives weak supervision for long multi-step search. `EG-GRPO` (Evidence-Guided Group Relative Policy Optimization) uses the evidence annotations already present in synthetic deep-search data to build step-level process rewards from the first supporting citation of each required evidence claim. It treats accumulated evidence as an evolving knowledge state, estimates advantages relative to that state, and combines this step-level signal with the standard outcome advantage. On five deep-search benchmarks it **generally outperforms standard `GRPO` and existing step-level and reward-enhanced RL baselines** across model scales.

papers.title: Bridging Concepts: Multi-Agent Reasoning over Scientific Concept Graphs for High-Impact Research Prediction
papers.abstract: Within a research community, new topics often emerge when previously unconnected concepts are first studied together. We construct scientific concept graphs (SCGs)--domain knowledge graphs whose nodes are fine-grained research concepts extracted from paper text by LLMs and whose edges capture their co-occurrence in papers--and study the task of forecasting high-impact concept pairs, i.e., discovering concept pairs that are currently unconnected but will have high impact when connected. To this end, we introduce new benchmark datasets constructed from CIKM, KDD, and SIGIR conference papers, with varied prediction settings, including impact forecasting for emerging concepts unseen during training. We propose MiroGraph, a Multi-agent reasoning framework with scientific concept Graphs, in which a feature designer agent designs predictive features for a given concept pair from structural, semantic, and trend perspectives, and then three LLM agents compute the actual feature values from the enclosing subgraph of the concept pair. Using these feature values, a classifier designer agent constructs a classifier that predicts the final impact labels. MiroGraph outperforms various impact forecasting and temporal link prediction methods.
papers.summary: New research topics often emerge when previously unconnected concepts are first studied together. The authors frame this as forecasting which unconnected concept pairs in a scientific concept graph will be high-impact once linked, and release benchmarks built from `CIKM`, `KDD`, and `SIGIR` papers. Their framework, `MiroGraph`, has a feature-designer agent propose structural, semantic, and trend features for each concept pair. Three LLM agents compute those features from the pair's enclosing subgraph, and a classifier-designer agent builds the final predictor. It **outperforms impact-forecasting and temporal link-prediction baselines**, including for emerging concepts unseen during training.

papers.title: Data-driven forecasting of tropical cloud forest phenology: A dynamical systems and machine learning hybrid approach
papers.abstract:
Forecasting how species and ecosystems respond to climate change is a critical challenge in ecology, particularly in hyper-diverse tropical biomes. While traditional phenological models often rely on preconceived functional forms, this study introduces a data-driven hybrid approach that integrates dynamical systems theory with machine learning to forecast flowering and fruiting cycles.
  Using a robust 35-year dataset from a Venezuelan tropical cloud forest, we reconstruct the system's state-space using delay vectors inspired by Takens' theorem, incorporating climate forcing variables such as temperature and precipitation. The model was trained using Gaussian Process Regression, providing both point predictors and explicit uncertainty estimates.
  Our results clearly suggest that the synergy between dynamical systems and machine learning effectively captures the non-linear complexities of ecological time series. Specifically, the model achieved higher predictive accuracy for flowering and fruiting. This hybrid framework offers a scalable tool for anticipating phenological mismatches and informing conservation strategies in the face of global environmental change.
papers.summary: Forecasting when tropical plants flower and fruit is hard because most phenological models assume a fixed functional form. The authors take a data-driven route on a 35-year record from a Venezuelan tropical cloud forest. They rebuild the system's state space from time-delay vectors, following Takens' theorem, add temperature and precipitation as climate forcing, and train a `Gaussian Process Regression` model that gives both point forecasts and uncertainty estimates. They report that the hybrid of dynamical systems and machine learning **achieved higher predictive accuracy for both flowering and fruiting**, and present it as a scalable way to anticipate phenological mismatches.

papers.title: A discrete-continuous-time stochastic framework for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder-related symptom modeling and pharmacological intervention via methylphenidate
papers.abstract: This paper presents an original mathematical and computational framework for modeling the efficacy of methylphenidate as an optimal control policy acting on the nonlinear dynamics of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. Neural processes in ADHD are conceptualized as stochastic processes with trajectories that inherently converge towards stable, yet dysfunctional patterns associated with clinical symptoms. The pharmacological intervention is mathematically formalized as an external control signal that reassesses the system's drift and redirects these trajectories towards neurotypical regimes. To bridge these theoretical stochastic models with empirical clinical data, latent representations are inferred using a novel deterministic hybrid deep learning architecture, combining a one-dimensional convolutional neural network and a Vision Transformer, trained on preprocessed functional magnetic resonance imaging data.
papers.summary: The authors propose a mathematical framework that treats methylphenidate as an optimal control policy acting on the nonlinear dynamics of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Neural processes are modeled as stochastic trajectories that settle into stable but dysfunctional patterns linked to symptoms. The drug is formalized as an external control signal that alters the system's drift and **steers trajectories back toward neurotypical regimes**. To connect the model to clinical data, latent representations are inferred from preprocessed functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) with a hybrid deep network that combines a one-dimensional convolutional neural network and a `Vision Transformer`.

papers.title: The Explainability Illusion: Must ViTs Exhibit Patch-Decoding Interpretability?
papers.abstract: Transformers are widely assumed to exhibit token-decoding explainability. In particular, in vision transformer (ViT) classifiers, decoding individual patch tokens has become a common diagnostic tool due to its tendency to yield human-interpretable outputs. In light of the increasing popularity of this approach, an important question is whether token-decoding explainability is an inherent property of transformers that should be expected to hold across architectures, scales, and training objectives, or merely an artifact of some implicit bias. In this paper we systematically study token-decoding explainability across diverse ViT settings, spanning architectures, scales, and training objectives, using both controlled experiments and real-world models. We find that while some models indeed exhibit aligned and interpretable token decodings, others exhibit either inverted explainability maps or a complete lack of correlation with the image semantics. As we show, these tendencies toward different explainability behaviors are not intrinsic to the architecture and can vary arbitrarily with changes in the optimization landscape. We provide theoretical support for these observations by demonstrating a setting where a single fixed toy transformer architecture can provably implement the optimal classification rule in multiple ways, which differ in their patch-decoding explainability patterns. Our results show that token-decoding explainability is not an inherent property of trained transformers, but rather an outcome contingent on the problem setting and thus should not be a-priori assumed to hold. Code can be found in https://ronensc.github.io/Explainability-Illusion/ .
papers.summary: Decoding individual patch tokens in vision transformer (ViT) classifiers is a common diagnostic because it often produces human-interpretable maps. The authors test whether this property holds in general, using controlled experiments and real-world models across architectures, scales, and training objectives. Some models give aligned, interpretable decodings, while others give inverted maps or maps unrelated to image semantics, and which behavior appears can shift arbitrarily with the optimization landscape. A toy transformer that provably implements the optimal classifier in several ways with different decoding patterns supports the conclusion that **token-decoding explainability is not an inherent property of trained transformers** and should not be assumed.

papers.title: World Model Interpretability: From Decoding Representations to Understanding Latent Worlds
papers.abstract: Emerging Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) are moving beyond representation learning towards latent world models that support prediction, planning, and control. Yet their latent worlds naturally lack a human-interpretable interface. In this Perspective, we argue that as JEPA latents become internal states for prediction and action, interpretability must move beyond what they encode to how latent variables interact, evolve, and causally drive prediction. To this end, we envision a four-stage research agenda, involving Ground, Structure, Verify, and Act, to guide this shift toward actionable latent-world understanding. Within our framework, existing JEPA interpretability efforts provide early evidence for Ground, while systematic analysis of latent structure, causal verification, and intervention remains largely unexplored. Overall, this Perspective aims to call for a broader latent-world interpretability agenda that shifts attention from decoding representations toward understanding, validating, and acting on latent worlds.
papers.summary: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) are evolving from representation learners into latent world models used for prediction, planning, and control, but their latent spaces have no human-interpretable interface. This Perspective argues that interpretability must move from asking what latents encode to asking how latent variables interact, evolve, and causally drive prediction. It proposes **a four-stage research agenda of Ground, Structure, Verify, and Act**. The authors find that existing `JEPA` interpretability work mostly addresses the first stage, while analysis of latent structure, causal verification, and intervention remains largely unexplored.

papers.title: Aligning Language Models with Indigenous Community Cosmovision through Constitutional AI
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are predominantly trained on corpora that reflect Western, anglophone worldviews. This asymmetry is not neutral: when a model answers questions about territory, community authority, or the relationship with nature, it does so from assumptions that may be alien to the communities using the system. This paper presents a system for aligning language models with the ethical principles of Indigenous communities in Latin America. Drawing on interviews with five Indigenous leaders and defenders, we built an operational cultural constitution grounded in an Indigenous cosmovision, with 12 principles. On this basis, we implemented a Constitutional AI (CAI) pipeline in two phases: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and direct preference optimization (DPO). The base models were Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct. With only 24 preference pairs, improvements were modest but detectable in intergenerational transmission, linguistic caution, and consultation and consent. Qualitative analysis reveals that the SFT phase was responsible for the primary shift in alignment, while DPO refined specific categories. The system was deployed in a conversational interface with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) that allows communities to feed the knowledge base, turning alignment into a participatory cycle. We argue the architecture is functional and will scale qualitatively once the corpus is expanded and computing constraints are resolved. The work constitutes a first iteration of an epistemic justice mechanism for value alignment in the Global South.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) mostly reflect Western, anglophone worldviews, which can clash with the values of Indigenous communities on topics such as territory, authority, and nature. Based on interviews with five Indigenous leaders in Latin America, the authors write a 12-principle cultural constitution. They apply it through a Constitutional AI (CAI) pipeline of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) followed by direct preference optimization (DPO) on `Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct` and `Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct`. With only 24 preference pairs, gains were modest but detectable in areas such as linguistic caution and consultation and consent, with **SFT driving most of the alignment shift** and DPO refining specific categories. The system is deployed with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) so communities can add to its knowledge base themselves.

papers.title: Learning When to Abort in Transformer Planning: A Mechanistic Study
papers.abstract: Planning does not by itself imply the ability to recognise errors, but recognising errors can improve planning capacity. In this paper, we study this phenomenon in Transformer planning. To analyze the inner mechanism, we follow the approach of Wang et al. (2024) and abstract planning as path-finding in graphs. In this setting, we train the model to detect the error of invalid transitions, i.e., after the model generates a next node that is not adjacent with the current node, the model should then generate a special abort token x. For expressiveness, we construct a Transformer with feed-forward width $O(|V|)$ for any fixed graph with node set $V$. It can detect all possible invalid transitions, and select a valid next node if the prefix is valid. We then propose a worst-case lower bound on feed-forward width, which makes the detector's linear width near-optimal up to logarithmic factors. In trained models, we demonstrate that invalid-transition detection increases previous-node attention, and most of the valid--invalid separation locates in the feed-forward network's output. This accords with our theoretical insights. Finally, we use this error detection to improve the model's performance: at inference, generating the abort token x will directly cause an external procedure to discard the attempt and restart from the original prompt. Experiments show that error detection combined with retry improves model's planning reliability on graphs, Countdown, and mazes.
papers.summary: The authors study whether Transformers can learn to recognize their own planning errors, framing planning as path-finding in graphs where the model must emit a special abort token after generating an invalid transition to a non-adjacent node. They construct a Transformer with feed-forward width linear in the number of nodes that detects all invalid transitions, and prove a lower bound showing this width is near-optimal up to logarithmic factors. In trained models, error detection raises attention to the previous node, and most of the separation between valid and invalid transitions sits in the feed-forward output. Restarting from the prompt whenever the abort token appears **improves planning reliability on graphs, `Countdown`, and mazes**.

papers.title: Atoms, Not Knowledge: What Production-Scale Addressed-Memory Writes Deposit
papers.abstract: Deterministic hash-addressed conditional memory permits local post-hoc knowledge injection. Extending arXiv:2610.21553's bounded-feasibility audit rejecting under-specified generality claims with repaired probes and training-dose/capacity axes, we give, to our knowledge, the first production-scale write-content verdict. We test 124M-7B self-trained/publicly pretrained beds, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP8 (176.95B; 320,001,536 FP8 rows), and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. Write coverage requires a sufficiently trained backbone prior, full-width readout, trainable gates; undertrained-bed intervention confirms a threshold, not a slope. At fixed budget, coverage falls from 98% (50 facts) to 12.7% (1,000); table size is not binding. Two-hop composition does not exceed the independent single-hop baseline (26% observed vs 25% expected; 15% lexical-distortion floor). Synergy remains absent across dose/load in two independent bed families. A 28-percentage-point in-context gap (given vs recalled intermediates) localizes failure to retrieval-for-reasoning, not gate access. Writes are independently retrievable, precisely addressable, reversible atoms, not composable into reasoning. A layered protocol, the first, to our knowledge, to cover compositionality in behavioral memory evaluation, separates baseline, synergy and distortion floor. Any addressed/key-value memory must report coverage, synergy ratio and distortion rate before deployment claims. Composition must be system-orchestrated; multi-constraint queries should explicitly chain written atoms. In-context controls show given intermediate entities are exploited at twice the implicit rate. Production load fits exponential interference ($R^2=0.98$); its mechanism, between budget dilution and write interference, remains open. All numbers are recomputed from archived raw logs/JSON; a fresh 52-target production rerun gives 52/52, exactly matching archived baselines.
papers.summary: The authors audit what knowledge written into deterministic hash-addressed conditional memory actually provides, testing models from 124M to 7B parameters as well as production-scale `Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP8` and `DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash`. Writes only take hold with a sufficiently trained backbone, full-width readout, and trainable gates. At a fixed budget, coverage drops from 98% at 50 facts to 12.7% at 1,000. Most notably, **two-hop composition of written facts is no better than chance combination of single hops (26% observed vs 25% expected)**: writes behave as independently retrievable, reversible atoms that the model cannot compose into reasoning. The authors argue that any key-value memory system should report coverage, synergy ratio, and distortion rate before making deployment claims, and that multi-step queries should chain written facts explicitly at the system level.

papers.title: Where and Why Search-Augmented LLMs Fail When Reasoning over Rapidly Evolving Knowledge
papers.abstract: As the world changes, new information is published while older records remain online. This complicates reasoning for large language models (LLMs), which must retrieve evidence and resolve conflicts to determine which information remains valid. Existing evaluations treat information seeking as a black box, revealing little about where and why LLMs fail. To address this gap, we introduce TREK, a suite of three components: TREKTRACE is a plug-and-play framework that attributes failures to specific stages of retrieval and reasoning. We apply it to TREKBENCH-WILD, a meta-benchmark of real-world questions that require complex reasoning over rapidly evolving knowledge. Surprisingly, the main bottleneck is post-retrieval reasoning rather than retrieval: frontier models are often misled by conflicting evidence even after retrieving all the information needed to answer. To study this bottleneck, we build TREKBENCH-CTRL, a controlled benchmark with distractors spanning temporality, relevance, and trustworthiness, and show that benchmarks dominated by outdated distractors substantially underestimate task difficulty. Together, TREK provides a testbed for diagnosing and improving reasoning over rapidly evolving knowledge.
papers.summary: Search-augmented large language models (LLMs) must work out which retrieved information is still valid when outdated records stay online, yet existing evaluations treat this process as a black box. `TREK` has three parts: `TREKTRACE`, a plug-and-play framework that attributes failures to specific retrieval and reasoning stages; `TREKBENCH-WILD`, a meta-benchmark of real-world questions over rapidly evolving knowledge; and `TREKBENCH-CTRL`, a controlled benchmark with distractors that vary in temporality, relevance, and trustworthiness. The main finding is that **the bottleneck is post-retrieval reasoning rather than retrieval**: frontier models are often misled by conflicting evidence even after retrieving everything needed to answer. Benchmarks dominated by outdated distractors also substantially underestimate task difficulty.

papers.title: Where Groups Split: A Probe Prior for Nonzero Within-Group Variance in RL Post-Training
papers.abstract: Group relative policy optimization learns from a prompt only when the rewards in the sampled group disagree. With a binary verifier, a group that is entirely correct or entirely incorrect has within-group variance zero and a zero advantage. Uniform sampling continues to spend rollouts on prompts that are unanimous now and stay unanimous as training goes on. Pass rate is a weak forecast of that future. Two prompts at the same pass rate can move apart: one into the range where a finite group splits, and one toward a ceiling where the group becomes unanimous again. Aperture estimates the later pass rate from a short probe. A small subset of the pool is trained with the same recipe, every prompt is scored on the base model and on the probe model, and the two pass rates are plugged into the probability that a group of the training size is all wrong or split. The resulting weight is a static prior. It can be used alone or multiplied by an online scheduler, and the GRPO update is left as it is. On mathematical and logical reasoning with 1.7B and 4B models, the prior improves greedy accuracy over uniform GRPO and raises the fraction of groups with a nonzero advantage. The same prior still helps when it is combined with dynamic sampling or with selective rollouts.
papers.summary: In group relative policy optimization (`GRPO`) with a binary verifier, prompts whose sampled group is all correct or all wrong yield zero advantage and waste rollouts, and the current pass rate is a poor predictor of which prompts will produce mixed groups later. `Aperture` trains a short probe on a small subset of prompts, scores every prompt on both the base and probe models, and converts the two pass rates into the probability that a training-size group will split. The result is a static sampling prior that can be used alone or multiplied with an online scheduler, leaving the `GRPO` update unchanged. On mathematical and logical reasoning with 1.7B and 4B models, it **improves greedy accuracy over uniform `GRPO`** and increases the share of groups with nonzero advantage, including when combined with dynamic sampling or selective rollouts.

papers.title: Follow the Mixed Groups: Ridge-Tracking Gaussian Sampling for Zero-Variance Web Rollouts
papers.abstract: Group relative policy optimization learns from a question only when the sampled responses disagree. A group that is entirely correct or entirely incorrect has zero reward variance and a zero advantage. On the Web, that group has already spent its searches and page fetches. Gaussian curricula aim the next batch at pass rates where a finite group can still mix. A Gaussian on the latest empirical rate treats every all-fail history as the same point, and a center stepped by the average signed change of those rates is pushed by prompts already stuck at 0 or 1. RIDGE keeps the Gaussian curriculum and changes the coordinate, the center, and the width. Each prompt carries a Beta posterior. The sampling weight is the marginal of a Gaussian target under a Gaussian approximation of that posterior, divided by a prediction of tool-call cost. The center and the width are an exponential smooth of the posterior means of groups that just came back mixed. All-correct and all-incorrect groups refresh the posterior and do not move the center. The GRPO update itself is unchanged. On two math backbones and a retrieval-augmented question answerer, RIDGE raises average accuracy by 3.4 and 2.9 points over GRPO and average exact match by 3.7 points, at 29.6\% fewer math rollouts and 32.7\% fewer tool calls than dynamic sampling.
papers.summary: When group relative policy optimization (`GRPO`) is used for web agents, groups that are all correct or all incorrect waste both learning signal and costly searches and page fetches. Existing Gaussian curricula also mishandle prompts that are stuck at 0% or 100% pass rates. `RIDGE` gives each prompt a Beta posterior over its pass rate and sets its sampling weight from a Gaussian target, divided by its predicted tool-call cost. The target's center and width track only the groups that just came back mixed, and the `GRPO` update itself is unchanged. On two math backbones and a retrieval-augmented question answerer, it **raises average accuracy by 3.4 and 2.9 points and exact match by 3.7 points** over `GRPO`, while using 29.6% fewer math rollouts and 32.7% fewer tool calls than dynamic sampling.

papers.title: A Distribution-Free Separation Between Learned and Fixed Features
papers.abstract:
The success of neural networks is largely attributed to their ability to learn useful representations from training data. However, known results that prove a computational advantage of learned features over fixed ones are restricted to specific input distributions. We settle the COLT open question of Feldman, Kamath, and Srebro (2026) by showing that this advantage can persist in the distribution-free setting.
  We construct a family of hypothesis classes that can be efficiently learned by a natural gradient-based algorithm on a two-layer ReLU network, but cannot be represented by linear predictors over any fixed feature map with polynomial dimension (and runtime). Specifically, for any sufficiently small error and any sufficiently large runtime budget R (depending on the error), there exists a hypothesis class that the neural network learns under any input distribution to the desired expected classification error in time at most R, while the dimension complexity (governing the dimension needed by linear predictors) is superpolynomial in R.
papers.summary: Prior proofs that neural networks gain a computational advantage by learning features, rather than using fixed ones, held only for specific input distributions. The authors resolve a COLT open question of Feldman, Kamath, and Srebro by constructing hypothesis classes that a natural gradient-based algorithm on a two-layer ReLU network learns efficiently under any input distribution. These same classes cannot be represented by linear predictors over any fixed feature map of polynomial dimension. **The dimension complexity needed by fixed features is superpolynomial in the network's runtime budget**, establishing a distribution-free separation between learned and fixed features.

papers.title: Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention
papers.abstract: Multi-head attention is a central component of the transformer architecture, yet how its expressivity depends on the number of heads remains poorly understood. We study a one-layer, attention-only transformer with additive positional embeddings and define the head complexity $H^\ast(f)$ of a Boolean function $f$ as the minimum number of attention heads required to represent it. We derive an exact linear-fractional normal form for head complexity, prove a general threshold-degree lower bound, and give an explicit ten-bit function for which this bound is strict. For symmetric Boolean functions, we independently show that head complexity equals the number of times the function changes value between consecutive Hamming-weight levels, even when positional embeddings are allowed. This agrees with the concurrent characterization of Hsu and Xu (arXiv:2608.04243) in a model without positional embeddings. The symmetric lower bound combines our general threshold-degree bound with the classical result of Aspnes et al. (1994). These results were discovered and formalized by a frontier model through conjecture generation, theorem proving, and machine verification, while human researchers asked the high-level questions and reviewed the generated theorems. We make the Lean formalization and research traces publicly available to support agent-assisted theorem proving and formal verification in mechanistic interpretability. This work provides a proof of concept for using the capabilities of frontier models, grounded by formal verification, to develop an understanding of transformer architectures.
papers.summary: The authors analyze how the expressivity of multi-head attention depends on the number of heads, defining head complexity as the minimum number of heads a one-layer, attention-only transformer needs to represent a Boolean function. They derive an exact normal form, prove a general threshold-degree lower bound that is strict for an explicit ten-bit function, and show that for symmetric functions head complexity equals the number of value changes across Hamming-weight levels. **These results were discovered and machine-verified in `Lean` by a frontier model** through conjecture generation and theorem proving, while humans posed the high-level questions and reviewed the theorems. The formalization and research traces are released as a proof of concept for agent-assisted theorem proving in mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: Predicted Class Correction: Conformal Thresholds for Classes with No Calibration Data
papers.abstract: Class-conditional conformal prediction calibrates a separate score threshold for every class and therefore requires labelled calibration examples of every class. In long-tailed deployments these are exactly what is missing: rare classes are left with few or no held-out examples, and existing methods are either undefined for them or fall back to the shared marginal threshold. We ask whether the per-class correction can instead be predicted from descriptors of the class that require no labels at all. We propose Predicted Class Correction (PCC), which regresses the offset between the per-class and the marginal conformal quantile on geometric descriptors of the classifier head, shrinks the prediction by a scalar selected on the labelled classes, and refits a single marginal offset. The descriptors depend only on the model's weights, so a class with zero calibration examples still receives its own threshold, and since only one scalar is calibrated, split conformal's marginal guarantee is retained. On ImageNet, PCC improves worst-class coverage on such classes by 0.058 [0.006, 0.110] at matched average set size, 42% of an oracle that sees the test labels. Of eight baselines on the same splits, six change the statistic by exactly zero and the best reaches 0.016 with an interval containing zero, so PCC is the only one distinguishable from no improvement; the gain persists with only 100 labelled classes out of 1000. A second finding concerns evaluation: worst-class coverage becomes unmeasurable before it becomes unachievable. Below roughly 35 test examples per class no improvement can be shown even for an oracle, so a null result there reflects the evaluation set, not the method. Restricting evaluation above this depth recovers a significant improvement on Pl@ntNet-300K, where the effect had appeared absent.
papers.summary: Class-conditional conformal prediction needs labelled calibration examples for every class, which long-tailed deployments lack for their rare classes. `Predicted Class Correction` (`PCC`) predicts each class's threshold offset from label-free geometric descriptors of the classifier head, shrinks the prediction by one calibrated scalar, and so keeps split conformal's marginal guarantee. On `ImageNet`, it **improves worst-class coverage on classes with no calibration data by 0.058**, 42% of what an oracle achieves, while six of eight baselines produce no change at all. The authors also show that below roughly 35 test examples per class, worst-class coverage cannot be measured reliably. Restricting evaluation above that depth recovers a significant gain on `Pl@ntNet-300K` that had previously looked absent.

papers.title: CHSM8: A Chess Transformer that Follows Natural-Language Style Prompts
papers.abstract: We present CHSM8, a 210M-parameter chess transformer that plays moves conditioned on a free-text description of a playing style, e.g. "go for the Sicilian Defense", "solid, safe, risk-free chess" or "You are Magnus Carlsen in his prime". The model is pretrained without search on 1.07B filtered Lichess games, using a factorized move representation and legal-move masking. It reaches 1837 Elo against a strength-limited Stockfish and, in 1,000-game matches, beat every other public model we tested that was likewise trained without preference tuning, rewards or search, including one with 13 times as many parameters. We then fine-tune it to follow text on a synthetic dataset: Gemma-4-31B describes the playing style of 3M game sides, a 1B Gemma-3 model distilled from the 2.4M of those descriptions that contradict nothing on the board labels the rest, and every one of 30M selected game sides gets five descriptions. Supervised fine-tuning attaches a frozen text encoder through gated cross-attention, and direct preference optimization (DPO) uses the same moves under a mismatched description as the rejected sample. After DPO, style adherence rises on every prompt we test (for example, queens traded early 53% -> 67%, pawn moves 29% -> 32% of all moves, queenside castling 97.3% -> 99.7%), and strength without a prompt stays within noise of SFT (1792 vs. 1797 Elo). Design choices at every stage were made by fixed-budget automated search loops on top of standard architectures and training recipes. We document the full pipeline and the decisions behind it, report the ablations that failed, and evaluate the models across many style prompts and kinds of games, with 1,000 games per setting. The work is fully open source and reproducible: weights, datasets with all training labels, prompts, configurations, inference code and playable demos are public and free to build on.
papers.summary: `CHSM8` is a 210M-parameter chess transformer that plays moves conditioned on free-text style prompts such as opening choices, risk preferences, or imitating a specific player. Pretrained without search on 1.07B `Lichess` games, it reaches 1837 Elo and beats every other public search-free model tested, including one 13 times larger. Style-following comes from synthetic style descriptions generated by `Gemma` models, supervised fine-tuning through gated cross-attention to a frozen text encoder, and direct preference optimization (DPO) that uses mismatched descriptions as rejected samples. After DPO, **style adherence rises on every tested prompt while unprompted strength stays within noise (1792 vs 1797 Elo)**. Design choices at every stage were made by automated search loops, and weights, datasets, training labels, code, and demos are all released.

papers.title: CD-OPD: Contextual Digest for On-Policy Distillation
papers.abstract: Teacher takeover in on-policy distillation (OPD) can produce incorrect responses even when the student and teacher independently answer the same problem correctly, a failure we quantify using Collaboration Failure Rate (CFR). To address it, we propose Contextual Digest for On-Policy Distillation (CD-OPD). CD-OPD structures the earlier context of teacher guidance through a teacher-generated dependency graph, curating the required problem conditions and preceding reasoning as node summaries alongside the unchanged guidance in a Contextual Digest before student continuation. We further develop online meta-reweighting, which compares Digest segment gradients with a task gradient from independent student responses to improve student-only performance, favoring updates predicted to reduce task loss. Across eight benchmarks, CD-OPD improves average accuracy by 1.32--7.05 percentage points over representative existing OPD methods. It also reduces CFR by 27.4\%--56.4\% relative to existing takeover-based OPD methods.
papers.summary: In on-policy distillation (OPD), letting the teacher take over partway through can produce wrong answers even when the student and teacher each solve the problem correctly on their own, a failure the authors measure as Collaboration Failure Rate (CFR). `CD-OPD` adds a Contextual Digest before the student continues: a teacher-generated dependency graph that summarizes the required problem conditions and the preceding reasoning. An online meta-reweighting step favors updates whose gradients align with the student's own task performance. Across eight benchmarks, it **improves average accuracy by 1.32 to 7.05 percentage points** over existing OPD methods and cuts CFR by 27.4% to 56.4% relative to takeover-based approaches.

papers.title: Operator-Mismatch Contrastive Learning for World-Relative Trajectory Coherence
papers.abstract: World models are increasingly judged by how well they rank plausible futures, yet plausibility alone is the wrong target. The same scene can evolve under many latent rules, and a future that is smooth and physically valid under one rule can be incoherent under the rule actually in force. We formalize the resulting failure, operator-blindness, and show that it is systematically hidden by standard evaluation: a scorer can attain near-perfect generic ranking while separating current-world from other-world futures no better than chance. We introduce Operator-Mismatch Contrastive (OMC) learning, whose semantic hard negatives are valid-but-wrong-operator trajectories, and a matching protocol that measures world-relative coherence directly. On a controlled synthetic benchmark with in- and out-of-distribution operator parameters, across two trajectory-scoring backbones, and on feature-level external validation with CoPhy ballsCF, OMC raises operator-sensitive scoring far above a chance baseline that nonetheless achieves 0.99 generic top-1. We prove that the wrong-operator negative is necessary both for the protocol to detect the failure and for the objective to fix it, and position OMC as an auxiliary coherence signal (a trajectory-coherence scorer, not a generative model, planner, or control agent) that can be attached to existing world-model representations.
papers.summary: World models are usually judged by how well they rank plausible futures, but a future that is physically valid under one latent rule can be incoherent under the rule actually in force. The authors call this failure operator-blindness and show that standard evaluation hides it: **a scorer can reach 0.99 generic top-1 ranking while telling current-world from other-world futures no better than chance**. `Operator-Mismatch Contrastive` (`OMC`) learning uses valid trajectories generated under the wrong operator as hard negatives, together with a protocol that measures this world-relative coherence directly. It substantially improves operator-sensitive scoring on a synthetic benchmark across two backbones and in feature-level validation on `CoPhy` ballsCF, and the authors prove the wrong-operator negatives are necessary.

papers.title: Aligning Cultural Behaviors in Arabic Language Models via Preferences
papers.abstract: Arabic LLMs have improved rapidly, but aligning them with country-specific cultural behavioral preferences remains underexplored. Previous work has focused primarily on instruction-tuning for factual knowledge, overlooking nuanced cultural behaviors. We propose ArabPref, which to our knowledge is the first large-scale pan-Arab preference data set for the alignment of cultural behavior conditioned on the country. Our contribution includes two resources in English and Modern Standard Arabic: a culturally grounded preference dataset for training and evaluation, and a multiple-choice benchmark designed to assess culturally aligned behavior across nations. All test data are validated by native speakers to ensure authenticity. To optimize cultural alignment, we experiment with post-training methods across multilingual and Arabic-centric language models, evaluating performance on both generation tasks and our cultural multiple-choice benchmark. By releasing an evaluation benchmark, we provide a foundation for systematically studying and improving culturally aligned behavior in language models.
papers.summary: Work on Arabic large language models (LLMs) has focused on instruction-tuning for factual knowledge, leaving country-specific cultural behavior largely unaddressed. The authors introduce `ArabPref`, which they describe as **the first large-scale pan-Arab, country-conditioned preference dataset for cultural behavior alignment**, released in English and Modern Standard Arabic. It comes with a multiple-choice benchmark of culturally aligned behavior across nations, and all test data is validated by native speakers. They evaluate post-training methods on multilingual and Arabic-centric models using both generation tasks and the benchmark.

papers.title: GreenNIDS: A Benchmark Workflow and Analysis Dataset for NetFlow Intrusion Detection Experiments
papers.abstract: Comparing the predictive performance and computational cost of flow-based intrusion detection experiments requires both quantities to be available for each run. GreenNIDS connects benchmark execution on public NetFlow datasets to a reusable analysis dataset. Model implementations write a common set of outputs, which are ingested into a run-level table with companion tables for model configuration, feature importance, and training history. The run-level table combines predictive metrics with timing, throughput, memory use, and energy estimates based on thermal design power. A CPU-only demonstration comprises 216 runs across four dataset families, three versions, and binary and multiclass tasks. Ingestion produces a 216 x 96 analysis table with no duplicate run identifiers and complete Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) and F1 coverage. Multiclass ROC-AUC is missing for 36 PyTorch runs, making metric availability an explicit part of subsequent comparisons. The stored records support grouped performance and training-time plots, as well as resource screening after execution. Combining task-specific MCC thresholds with limits on training time, peak RAM, and estimated training energy retains 25.0% of the full run collection. These results establish compatibility within the evaluated collection and support comparisons after execution, subject to the recorded preprocessing, execution profile, and approximate energy accounting.
papers.summary: Comparing flow-based network intrusion detection experiments requires both predictive performance and computational cost for every run. `GreenNIDS` connects benchmark execution on public NetFlow datasets to a run-level analysis table that combines predictive metrics with timing, throughput, memory use, and energy estimates based on thermal design power. A CPU-only demonstration of 216 runs across four dataset families yields a 216 by 96 table with complete Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) and F1 coverage. Filtering by task-specific MCC thresholds plus limits on training time, peak RAM, and estimated energy **retains 25.0% of runs**, showing how the data supports resource-aware model screening after the experiments have run.

papers.title: Multi-site Learning for Forecasting Day-Ahead Wind-Power Production for Onshore Wind Farms in Great Britain with Deep Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Accurate day-ahead wind-power production forecasting is increasingly important for energy system operations, market activity and balancing Great Britain's grid as wind generation grows. In this study, we train multi-site deep neural networks (DNNs) using pooled historical production and reanalysis weather data from 88 onshore wind Balancing Mechanism Units (BMUs). Forecasts are produced at 09:00 UK time for the following midnight-to-midnight delivery day, matching NESO's operational day-ahead forecasting schedule. We use reanalysis weather as future covariates during training and numerical weather prediction (NWP) forecasts during inference, extending training beyond the available historical NWP archive. Our multi-site recurrent neural network outperforms site-specific RNNs and a multi-site XGBoost model, while processing the full future-weather trajectory for the forecast horizon further improves accuracy relative to hour-aligned approaches. Our best model, an RNN with a bidirectional weather encoder (BiRNN) for NWP trajectory processing, reduces MW mean absolute error and root mean squared error relative to NESO by 17.94% and 12.51%, respectively, across 638,246 matched BMU-hour observations under conditions approximating unconstrained wind farm operations. In 40 leave-one-out trials, the BiRNN achieves lower MAE than NESO at 32 excluded sites, indicating transferable forecasting ability despite reduced accuracy when sites are omitted from training. Our capacity-estimation, data-cleaning and reanalysis-based training approach provides a basis for scaling NWP-aware multi-site forecasting to additional wind farms, longer production histories, and increased forecast accuracy beyond that seen in this study.
papers.summary: The authors forecast day-ahead output for 88 onshore wind farms in Great Britain with multi-site deep neural networks trained on pooled production and reanalysis weather data. Training uses reanalysis weather and inference uses numerical weather prediction (NWP) forecasts, matching the operational schedule of the grid operator NESO. A multi-site recurrent network outperforms site-specific networks and multi-site `XGBoost`, and the best model, an RNN with a bidirectional weather encoder (`BiRNN`), **reduces mean absolute error by 17.94% and root mean squared error by 12.51% relative to NESO**. In leave-one-out trials, it still beats NESO at 32 of 40 sites excluded from training.

papers.title: Whistle and Wrong Lyrics: Synthetic Queries Are Not Enough for Real-World Query-by-Melody
papers.abstract: People look up a song by humming it, but also by whistling it or singing it with the wrong words. Published query-by-humming systems and benchmarks focus on hums and sung queries, and no public dataset pairs whistles or wrong-lyrics singing with song recordings. We study both query types with a melody-only retrieval system: a key-normalized pitch track embedded by a 5.2M-parameter contour encoder, with a spectral-peak tracker for whistles. First, a physics-grounded generator renders synthetic whistles and nonsense-syllable singing from the vocal melodies of 11,083 songs. Training on them raises top-1 retrieval of held-out synthetic queries against an 11,050-song gallery from 0.180 to 0.251 for whistles and from 0.193 to 0.264 for wrong-lyrics singing, but the gain does not transfer: on the MLEnd test performers the best synthetic-only model gets 210 of 339 real whistles right at top-1, against 214 for the baseline. Second, a closed-set fine-tune on real MLEnd whistles with performer-disjoint splits raises whistle-to-hum top-1 from 0.631 (95% CI 0.581-0.681) to 0.673 (0.622-0.723), on known songs only. Third, two further generations of synthetic queries also fail to transfer: melody-conditioned whistles and la-la singing from a commercial neural music model leave real-whistle top-1 at 0.631, and an open-source pipeline (YingMusic-Singer-Plus singing with partly wrong, mumbled or nonsense lyrics, a DDSP whistle synthesizer, and a melody-error model fitted on real performers) gives at best 0.619 (paired difference -0.012, 95% CI -0.038 to +0.015). Across physics-based, commercial neural and open-source neural synthetic data, nothing transferred to real whistles, which points to collecting real queries as the missing step. Code is public; models and data will be released.
papers.summary: Query-by-melody systems and benchmarks focus on humming and sung queries, and no public dataset pairs whistles or wrong-lyrics singing with song recordings. Using a melody-only retrieval system built on a 5.2M-parameter pitch-contour encoder, the authors train on synthetic queries from three sources: physics-based rendering, a commercial neural music model, and an open-source neural pipeline. Synthetic training improves retrieval of held-out synthetic queries, but **none of the three synthetic data sources improves retrieval of real whistles**. Only fine-tuning on real `MLEnd` whistles helped, raising top-1 accuracy from 0.631 to 0.673 on known songs, which points to collecting real queries as the missing step.

papers.title: MemDerive: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Agent Memory over Evolving Data
papers.abstract: Long-running agents rely on memory of their past interactions for task state, such as what has been completed and which conditions still hold. Such state is usually a derived state. No record states it, and it must be computed by rules from multiple records of an evolving history. Existing memory benchmarks score only the final answer, with no reference for the intermediate states behind it. A wrong answer therefore cannot be traced to the state that was missed, and a state that silently became outdated goes undetected. We present MemDerive, a diagnostic benchmark for agent memory over evolving data. It specifies each scenario symbolically, derives exact gold answers with Datalog, records the gold derivation DAG and the supporting events of every query, and renders the history in natural language with fictional entities and distractors. Its 10 scenarios contain 4,692 events and 1,503 queries whose difficulty varies along access, evolution, and composition. On this ground truth, MemDerive evaluates answer reliability, diagnoses failures by probing the nodes of the gold derivation DAG, and tracks whether answers stay correct as events arrive. Our evaluation of four memory systems reveals failures that final-answer benchmarks hide. On derived state, every memory system falls behind simple BM25 retrieval, although the same answer model reaches 96.01% when given the supporting events. Most failures are ungathered, as a system holds the missing intermediate state but does not retrieve it for the question that needs it. Memory systems also rarely propagate implicit changes, which no new record states. These results suggest three principles for memory design. Gather inputs along the derivation, store rules with their versions, and maintain derived states through recorded dependencies.
papers.summary: Long-running agents depend on derived state, such as what has been finished or which conditions still hold. No single record states these facts; they have to be computed from many events in an evolving history, yet existing memory benchmarks score only the final answer. `MemDerive` specifies 10 scenarios symbolically and computes exact gold answers with `Datalog`, along with the derivation graph and supporting events for each of 1,503 queries over 4,692 events. This makes it possible to trace a wrong answer to the intermediate state that was missed. Across four memory systems, **every system falls behind simple `BM25` retrieval on derived state, even though the same answer model reaches 96.01% when given the supporting events**. Most failures happen because the system holds the needed intermediate state but never retrieves it, and implicit changes are rarely propagated.

papers.title: Mining the Self-Rewriting System: A Vision for Data Mining on AI-Native Infrastructure
papers.abstract: Classical data mining treats data as generated outside the learner. Emerging AI-native infrastructure invalidates this assumption: as agents observe system state, act, update retrieval stores and models, and promote new artifacts into the serving path, their own decisions reshape the future logs, traces, corpora, and evaluation records used for later training and release. We call this new research object a self-rewriting system and the resulting system-induced distribution shift endogenous drift. Our central, falsifiable claim is that cross-surface causes are not identifiable in general from marginal per-surface monitoring: different coupled failures can produce the same individual signals while differing in their joint behavior, requiring joint analysis for reliable attribution. This agenda comprises four foundational research problems: fusing heterogeneous drift signals into calibrated gating and attribution (C1); mining agent traces whose activity alphabet evolves (C2); maintaining knowledge fabrics through online reindexing, faithfulness, and compression decisions (C3); and safely promoting concurrent learning streams through one shared evaluation gate (C4). These remain fragmented across concept drift, performative prediction, process mining, streaming retrieval-augmented generation, and MLOps, without a unified data-mining agenda. We outline public benchmarks and evaluation criteria, using AI-native telecom only as a motivating exemplar with analogues in finance, software CI/CD, and clinical decision support.
papers.summary: A position paper arguing that classical data mining assumes data is generated outside the learner, an assumption that breaks on AI-native infrastructure. There, agents' own actions reshape the logs, traces, corpora, and evaluation records later used for training. The authors call such a setup a self-rewriting system and the shift it causes endogenous drift. Their central falsifiable claim is that **cross-surface failure causes cannot in general be identified from per-surface monitoring alone**, so attribution requires joint analysis. They lay out four research problems, covering drift-signal fusion, mining agent traces with evolving activity alphabets, maintaining knowledge stores, and safely promoting concurrent learning streams, and they sketch benchmarks using telecom as a motivating example.

papers.title: TILDE: Teacher-in-the-Loop Distillation from Embodied Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Large-scale action pretraining equips Embodied Foundation Models (EFMs) with strong manipulation capabilities, with particular strengths in generalization and closed-loop robustness, but reproducing such pretraining requires substantial robot data and computation. To transfer these capabilities from pretrained EFMs to policies without action pretraining, we introduce TILDE (Teacher-In-the-Loop Distillation from EFMs), which synergizes on-policy distillation at student-induced states with learning from teacher-executed recovery trajectories. We further propose AutoDAgger, an autonomous data aggregation pipeline in which a robotic reward model is utilized to monitor task progress and trigger teacher intervention, thereby collecting recovery experience without human monitoring or manual control. AutoDAgger accelerates recovery-trajectory collection by more than $2\times$ compared with the human-in-the-loop method. By unifying learning from demonstrations, on-policy teacher supervision, and teacher's corrective behavior, TILDE improves task performance by up to $4.1\times$ over behavior cloning across three real-world tasks and supports effective cross-architecture distillation.
papers.summary: Embodied Foundation Models (EFMs) get strong manipulation skills from large-scale action pretraining, which is expensive to reproduce. `TILDE` transfers these skills into policies without action pretraining by combining on-policy distillation at states the student visits with learning from recovery trajectories executed by the teacher. Its `AutoDAgger` pipeline uses a robotic reward model to monitor task progress and trigger teacher intervention without human supervision, collecting recovery data more than 2x faster than human-in-the-loop collection. Across three real-world tasks, `TILDE` improves performance by **up to 4.1x over behavior cloning** and supports distillation across different architectures.

papers.title: Simulating Infant Senses with Age-Tuned Networks
papers.abstract: What a newborn sees, hears and feels, and how this changes month by month, has been measured sense by sense, with different methods and in different units. We bring these measurements together for the first two years of life and ask whether small neural networks tuned to a given age can turn them into a quick, inspectable simulation of sensory perception. Each sense's immaturity is written as a fixed, age-indexed filter on the input, and a small prediction network learns behind it over the first year. The filters alone reproduce the order in which the senses mature, by construction. The networks add what filters cannot: in vision they extract far less than their input allows at early stages (at the newborn stage a toy's position cannot be read out, $R^2 = 0.00$, against 0.57 for a network trained directly on the same input), and a critical period and perceptual narrowing emerge without being built in; in hearing they track what their input allows. The same filters drive the Baby Senses Lab, a free website that shows a user's own images and sounds as a baby of a chosen age might sense them. It is a research and teaching tool, not a diagnostic test.
papers.summary: Measurements of how infant vision, hearing, and touch mature over the first two years are combined into age-indexed filters on sensory input, with a small prediction network trained behind each filter. The filters alone reproduce the order in which the senses mature, by construction. The networks add effects the filters cannot produce: at the newborn stage, a toy's position cannot be read out of the vision network (**R² = 0.00 versus 0.57 for a network trained directly on the same input**), and a critical period and perceptual narrowing emerge without being built in. The same filters power the `Baby Senses Lab` website, which renders a user's own images and sounds as a baby of a chosen age might perceive them.

papers.title: Outcome-Anchored Credit Reallocation for Agentic Knowledge Graph Question Answering
papers.abstract: Agentic knowledge graph question answering (KGQA) requires large language models (LLMs) to solve complex questions through multi-turn interactions with a knowledge graph (KG). Outcome-supervised reinforcement learning derives verifiable outcome rewards from final answers but uniformly assigns each rollout's outcome-level advantage to all policy-generated tokens, creating a trajectory-to-operation mismatch since KG operations within a rollout can have varying effects on the search process and final answer. To address this, we propose Outcome-Anchored Credit Reallocation (OACR), which employs a training-only KG-state outcome model to estimate outcome-reward changes between adjacent KG search states and converts them into operation credit, from which token-wise weights are derived. These multiplicative weights reallocate token-level update magnitudes while preserving the sign of the outcome-level advantage at every generated token. Across three benchmarks, OACR achieves stronger overall performance than existing KGQA methods while using fewer inference-time LLM calls and tokens.
papers.summary: In agentic knowledge graph question answering (KGQA), large language models (LLMs) answer questions through multi-turn interactions with a knowledge graph. Outcome-supervised reinforcement learning gives every token in a rollout the same final-answer advantage, even though individual graph operations contribute unequally. Outcome-Anchored Credit Reallocation (`OACR`) trains an auxiliary model, used only during training, that estimates how the expected outcome reward changes between successive search states. It turns those changes into per-operation credit and token-level weights that rescale updates without flipping the advantage's sign. Across three benchmarks, `OACR` **outperforms existing KGQA methods while using fewer inference-time LLM calls and tokens**.

papers.title: Structured Relevance Determination and Channel Additive Gaussian Processes for Image Data
papers.abstract: We introduce radial basis function (RBF) kernels for Gaussian processes that use structured hyperparameter sharing for image-valued inputs. For high-dimensional inputs such as images, a fully anisotropic RBF kernel assigns a separate lengthscale to each input dimension, which can introduce many hyperparameters and may lead to overfitting and poorly calibrated predictive uncertainty when data are limited. We propose structured relevance determination by tying lengthscales across groups of adjacent pixels and within each colour channel. This yields patch-wise and channel-wise constrained anisotropic RBF parametrisations that reduce the number of independently learned lengthscales. We further introduce channel-additive Gaussian processes for multi-channel images and combine them with structured relevance determination, resulting in a parameter-efficient decomposition of the latent function into components defined on channel subsets, enabling some non-local generalisation. The proposed kernels are evaluated on MNIST and a compact binary aircraft-detection dataset of low-resolution RGB satellite image chips. We also show how channel-wise structured relevance determination can be incorporated into convolutional Gaussian processes. We observe improved predictive performance compared to isotropic and fully anisotropic RBF baselines.
papers.summary: Gaussian processes with fully anisotropic radial basis function (RBF) kernels assign one lengthscale per pixel, which can overfit and miscalibrate uncertainty when image data is limited. The authors propose structured relevance determination, which ties lengthscales across patches of adjacent pixels and within colour channels. They also introduce channel-additive Gaussian processes, which decompose the latent function into components defined on subsets of channels, and they show how the scheme fits into convolutional Gaussian processes. On `MNIST` and a small RGB satellite aircraft-detection dataset, the structured kernels **improve predictive performance over isotropic and fully anisotropic RBF baselines**.

papers.title: The Hidden Look-Ahead: Point-in-Time Leakage in Electricity Market Data
papers.abstract: Empirical studies of electricity prices routinely state that their models use only information available at the time of the trading decision. For weather-driven forecasts drawn from commercial archives, this condition is harder to meet than it appears, and whether it holds can change over time. We identify three timing pitfalls. A forecast run is labelled by the issue time of its weather model, but becomes available hours later and keeps changing after publication. Auction gates follow local clock time, while archives use UTC. Outturn series are revised after publication without earlier values being kept. Using the timestamps of 128,656 forecast runs from ten weather-model configurations, matched to the day-ahead and first intraday auction gates in Great Britain over 2022-2026, we find that selecting "the latest run issued before the gate" picks a run not yet published at the gate on more than 99% of delivery days for six of the ten configurations at one of the two gates. For GFS at the day-ahead gate, the share is 0.6% in winter and 99.8% in summer. The exposure also shifts as publication delays drift, and an action margin of a few minutes can cost a full six-hour forecast cycle. The wrongly selected inputs differ materially from those available at the gate, but their apparent accuracy gain ranges from -9% to +24% across variables, models, gates and seasons, so its effect cannot be assumed and must be measured. We argue that point-in-time correctness is a dynamic property of the data pipeline, and propose a protocol that audits it from timestamps before any model is fitted.
papers.summary: Electricity price studies typically claim to use only information available at decision time, but weather forecasts from commercial archives make this hard to guarantee. Archives label forecast runs by issue time rather than publication time, mix UTC with local auction clocks, and overwrite revised outturn data. Using timestamps from 128,656 forecast runs matched to Great Britain's auction gates over 2022-2026, the authors find that picking the latest run issued before the gate **selects a run not yet published on more than 99% of delivery days for six of ten model configurations at one of the two gates**. The resulting change in apparent accuracy ranges from -9% to +24%, so the bias has to be measured rather than assumed. The authors propose a timestamp-based audit protocol to run before any model is fitted.

papers.title: Paloma: Phase-Conditioned Residual Modulation for Time Series Forecasting
papers.abstract: Explicitly modeling periodicity has proven to be an efficient approach for time series forecasting, where the residual, obtained after removing the periodic component from the time series, is typically treated as unstructured noise. However, in this work, we show that such residuals still exhibit structured, \textit{phase-dependent} deviations, as supported by both empirical observations and theoretical analysis. This suggests that residuals should not be treated merely as unstructured noise, but instead as \textit{phase-conditioned signals} whose variations arise in both direction and magnitude. Motivated by this perspective and inspired by phase and amplitude modulation in classical signal processing, we propose \textit{Paloma}, a simple yet effective framework for modeling residual deviations. Specifically, Paloma comprises two complementary modules: \textit{a Phase Rotation module}, which performs phase-conditioned rotations to capture directional changes in the feature space, and \textit{an Amplitude Scaling module}, which applies phase-conditioned affine transformations to model magnitude variations. We further abstract the two modules into a general-purpose plugin, termed the \textit{Paloma technique}, which can be readily integrated into existing forecasting architectures to modulate input sequences in a phase-aware manner, enabling backbone models to capture phase-dependent variations in both direction and magnitude. Extensive experiments on twelve datasets demonstrate that Paloma achieves state-of-the-art and robust forecasting performance. Additional results show that the Paloma technique consistently improves a wide range of baseline models, validating its effectiveness as a general-purpose component. Our Code is available at \url{https://github.com/TSTS13/Paloma}.
papers.summary: Time series forecasters often remove a periodic component and treat the residual as unstructured noise. Empirical observations and theoretical analysis here show that these residuals still contain **structured, phase-dependent deviations in both direction and magnitude**. Drawing on phase and amplitude modulation from signal processing, `Paloma` adds a Phase Rotation module, which applies phase-conditioned rotations in feature space, and an Amplitude Scaling module, which applies phase-conditioned affine transforms. Packaged as a plug-in, it achieves state-of-the-art results on twelve datasets and consistently improves a range of existing forecasting backbones.

papers.title: From Unverifiable Domain Text to Cross-Lingual RLVR via Code-Switched Task Synthesis
papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) can improve reasoning in large language models, but specialized non-English domains expose a data mismatch. Raw English domain text is often available, while target-language RLVR tasks with verifiable rewards are scarce. We introduce code-switched task synthesis for cross-lingual RLVR, a data-centric approach that derives target-language and code-switched RLVR task variants from otherwise unverifiable English domain text. Using fill-in-the-middle multiple-choice QA as a seed task format, we synthesize automatically verifiable tasks from domain passages and reshape them into cross-lingual variants. These variants preserve the same evidence-answer relation but change how English and target-language evidence are presented during RLVR. On Korean medical benchmarks and cybersecurity benchmarks across four target languages, code-switched training outperforms matched monolingual and bilingual-mixture baselines on average target-language performance while maintaining comparable English performance. Additional analyses provide evidence of better target-language input understanding and stronger cross-lingual alignment in both model outputs and internal representations. These results suggest that code-switched training helps target-language inputs access domain reasoning learned more strongly in English.
papers.summary: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) needs tasks whose answers can be checked automatically, and such tasks are scarce in specialized non-English domains, even when raw English domain text is plentiful. The authors synthesize fill-in-the-middle multiple-choice questions from English passages and reshape them into target-language and code-switched variants that preserve the same evidence-answer relation. On Korean medical benchmarks and cybersecurity benchmarks in four target languages, **code-switched training beats matched monolingual and bilingual-mixture baselines on average target-language performance while keeping English performance comparable**. Further analyses point to stronger cross-lingual alignment in both model outputs and internal representations.

papers.title: Towards Figurative Language Understanding in Moroccan Darija: An Evaluation of Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Figurative language remains a major challenge for Machine Translation (MT) systems, as the intended meaning of such expressions often goes beyond literal translation. Although recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) improved the translation of Arabic dialects, benchmark resources for evaluating figurative language translation in Moroccan Darija remain scarce. To this end, we introduce the Moroccan Darija Figurative Language Corpus (MDFC), a benchmark dataset for MT and multiple-choice question (MCQ) selection covering idioms, metaphors, and proverbs. Using MDFC, we evaluate 19 open- and closed-weight language models and MT systems at both the expression and contextual levels under zero-shot and six-shot settings. We also conduct layer-wise similarity-based probing to determine how model representations distinguish figurative from literal meanings. Our findings reveal that closed-weight models achieve the strongest translation performance, while the benefits of contextual information vary across models and tasks. Differences between translation performance and MCQ accuracy highlight the distinction between generating an appropriate figurative translation and recognizing the intended meaning among candidate translations.
papers.summary: Machine translation (MT) of figurative language in Moroccan Darija lacks benchmark resources. The Moroccan Darija Figurative Language Corpus (`MDFC`) covers idioms, metaphors, and proverbs for both translation and multiple-choice question (MCQ) selection. The authors evaluate 19 open- and closed-weight language models and MT systems, at the expression and contextual levels, under zero-shot and six-shot settings, and they also probe layer-wise representations. **Closed-weight models translate best**, the benefit of added context varies across models and tasks, and gaps between translation scores and MCQ accuracy show that producing a good figurative translation differs from recognizing the intended meaning.

papers.title: Mixture-of-Memories: Low-Overhead Language Modeling with Modular Knowledge Injection
papers.abstract: Large language models store substantial factual knowledge in their parameters, yet this knowledge is difficult to control, update, and reliably elicit at inference time. Existing memory-augmented approaches typically rely on a single auxiliary mechanism, such as retrieval, parameter updates, or neural memory, and therefore apply the same form of correction to tokens with very different knowledge demands. We propose Mixture-of-Memories (MoM), a memory-augmented language modeling framework that separates routed neural memory from writable factual memory. MoM combines a frozen base LM with two neural memory experts: a latent memory that provides low-latency hidden-state corrections and a lexical memory that provides a token-space knowledge pathway. A lightweight Budget Router sets per-token mixture weights from uncertainty and disagreement features, replacing the fixed interpolation of prior memory modules.
