For post-hoc updates, an external explicit memory stays outside the router, because a router trained before facts are written learns to down-weight it; new facts are appended without retraining any component and used only when an answer-level gate accepts the retrieved fact. Experiments across language modeling, factual QA, update analysis, and efficiency show that MoM improves both predictive accuracy and updateability while retaining low inference overhead.
papers.summary: Factual knowledge stored in language model parameters is hard to control and update, and existing memory-augmented methods apply a single correction mechanism to every token. Mixture-of-Memories (`MoM`) keeps the base model frozen and adds two neural memory experts: a latent memory that makes low-latency hidden-state corrections and a lexical memory that works in token space. A lightweight Budget Router mixes them per token based on uncertainty and disagreement features. New facts go into a separate explicit memory that sits outside the router and is used only when an answer-level gate accepts the retrieved fact. Across language modeling, factual QA, and update experiments, `MoM` **improves both accuracy and updateability while adding little inference overhead**.

papers.title: MOSAIC: Multi-Objective Search for Allocating Inference Cache Across LLM Decoder Layers
papers.abstract: The Key-Value (KV) cache is the main memory bottleneck of long-context LLM inference. Token eviction methods such as SnapKV, H2O, AdaKV and L2Norm shrink it, but they give every transformer layer the same budget, although layers differ in which tokens they need. We present MOSAIC, a multi-objective neural architecture search that learns per-layer KV-cache budgets for any eviction method. One search maps the trade-off between average budget and task score; its best allocation transfers to every target budget without further search, and an optional budget-constrained search refines it. Across four eviction methods on Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2, MOSAIC beats uniform allocation in 146 of 154 (task, method, budget) settings, by up to +48 points on RULER and +11.9 on LongBench (LCC). On both models, it reaches the score of uniform allocation with up to 4x less KV cache (75% smaller). Against EvolKV, MOSAIC explores a ~10^40 x larger search space with 4x fewer evaluations and 18% fewer GPU-hours per budget, and scores higher in 5 of 6 settings. The learned allocations consistently favour a small set of middle layers.
papers.summary: Token-eviction methods such as `SnapKV`, `H2O`, `AdaKV`, and `L2Norm` shrink the Key-Value (KV) cache in long-context inference but give every layer the same budget. `MOSAIC` uses multi-objective neural architecture search to learn per-layer budgets for any eviction method, and a single search yields an allocation that transfers across target budgets. On `Llama-3-8B-Instruct` and `Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2`, it beats uniform allocation in 146 of 154 settings, by up to +48 points on `RULER`, and **matches uniform allocation's score with up to 4x less KV cache**. The learned allocations consistently favour a small set of middle layers.

papers.title: RARE: Reinforcement Learning with Adaptive Rubric Evolution for Open-Ended Generation
papers.abstract: Verifiable rewards have advanced reinforcement learning in mathematics and code. However, many valuable open-ended tasks share three properties: no automatic verifier of overall quality, multiple requirements to satisfy jointly, and multiple valid responses to each query. Training therefore needs feedback on requirement satisfaction across different valid responses. Rubric-based reinforcement learning provides this feedback by aggregating scores from explicit criteria. As learning progresses unevenly, some criteria become fully satisfied and lose discrimination while others remain informative. Dynamic methods revise shared rubrics or select evolving criteria to restore discrimination, but may also change useful criteria. To address this, we propose Reinforcement Learning with Adaptive Rubric Evolution (RARE). The core idea is to use current policy feedback to guide both which criteria change and what their replacements assess. Sample-level updates replace criteria fully satisfied across current outputs with checks of remaining quality differences, retaining all other criteria and scores. Within this rule, we compare rewarding desirable qualities with penalizing observed flaws. Video script generation exemplifies these properties and supports content production. Its demands for coherent, executable narratives under constraints make it a challenging testbed. Targeting flaws performs best across three video types with a mean gain of 3.82 points over matched static rubrics. Model and human preferences support these gains. Improvements also extend to writing and general generation benchmarks.
papers.summary: Open-ended generation tasks have no automatic verifier and many valid answers, so reinforcement learning on them often relies on rubrics of explicit criteria. Those criteria stop discriminating between outputs once the policy satisfies them all. Reinforcement Learning with Adaptive Rubric Evolution (`RARE`) uses the current policy's outputs to replace only the fully satisfied criteria with checks of the quality differences that remain, leaving all other criteria and their scores intact. In video script generation, replacement criteria that penalize observed flaws work best, with **a mean gain of 3.82 points over matched static rubrics** across three video types. The gains are supported by model and human preferences and extend to writing and general generation benchmarks.

papers.title: Design Considerations in Low-Resource Archival OCR: A Case Study in Lakota
papers.abstract: Building and expanding access to digital archives supports language reclamation and creates lasting resources for community revitalization. Designing effective tools to support these efforts requires taking into account the community-, language-, and document-specific context. We investigate how small ($\leq$3B) vision-language models (VLMs) can be adapted as optical character recognition (OCR) tools for Lakota, a North American Indigenous language. In addition to benchmarking modeling approaches, we inspect four practical facets of low-resource archival OCR that arise in previous work and conversations with community members: constrained training budgets, segmentation noise, scan degradation, and orthographic variance. We demonstrate that fine-tuning VLMs for OCR post-correction on 35 pages of transcribed data decreases character error rate (CER) from 17.1 to 3.9\% on a bilingual corpus, and find that training only with nine pages increases CER by only 1.1\% over this. However, evaluating under realistic automatic segmentation nearly doubles the CER of the best-performing models, stressing the importance of taking realistic use cases into account. We hope this work encourages future research on developing language technologies grounded in the workflows and constraints of ongoing revitalization efforts.
papers.summary: The authors adapt small vision-language models (VLMs) of up to 3B parameters as optical character recognition (OCR) tools for archival documents in Lakota, a North American Indigenous language. They also study practical constraints raised in earlier work and in conversations with community members: small training budgets, segmentation noise, scan degradation, and orthographic variation. Fine-tuning for OCR post-correction on 35 transcribed pages cuts character error rate (CER) from 17.1% to 3.9%, and training on only nine pages raises CER by just 1.1 points over that. However, **realistic automatic segmentation nearly doubles the CER of the best models**.

papers.title: Enhanced Masked Diffusion Unlearning
papers.abstract: Masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) generate text by iteratively unmasking tokens with bidirectional context. As these models reach real-world deployment, machine unlearning becomes essential. This process aims to remove the influence of a designated "forget set" without retraining from scratch, so that sensitive, copyrighted, or restricted content can no longer be elicited while preserving retained capabilities. Masked Diffusion Unlearning (MDU) is the first publicly available unlearning method customized for these models: it tunes the model $p_\theta$ to match a frozen prompt-masked anchor $p_{\mathrm{anchor}}$ on the forget set by minimizing the anchor-last divergence $\mathrm{KL}(p_\theta \Vert p_{\mathrm{anchor}})$. We identify two failure modes of MDU. First, random answer masking can leave key forget tokens visible to the anchor even when the question is fully masked. Second, at a memorized (near-one-hot) prediction, the anchor-last logit gradient vanishes while the anchor-first divergence $\mathrm{KL}(p_{\mathrm{anchor}} \Vert p_\theta)$ logit gradient does not. As a result, MDU training stalls on the tokens we most need to forget. Backed by theoretical and empirical analyses, we propose Enhanced Masked Diffusion Unlearning (EMDU): anchor-first KL divergence toward a frozen anchor whose entire answer span is masked. On TOFU and RWKU benchmarks using LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B, our EMDU matches or exceeds the forgetting of MDU and adapted AR baselines, while better preserving retain utility.
papers.summary: Masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) need unlearning methods that remove a designated forget set, and the existing method, Masked Diffusion Unlearning (`MDU`), trains the model to match a frozen anchor model whose prompt is masked. The authors identify two failure modes in `MDU`: random masking can leave key answer tokens visible to the anchor, and the KL-divergence direction it uses has **vanishing gradients on memorized tokens, so training stalls exactly where forgetting is needed**. Their fix, `EMDU`, masks the anchor's entire answer span and reverses the KL direction. On `TOFU` and `RWKU` with `LLaDA-8B` and `Dream-7B`, it matches or exceeds the forgetting of `MDU` and adapted autoregressive baselines while better preserving the abilities that should be retained.

papers.title: Semi-supervised learning on singular data sets
papers.abstract: We propose to model singular data clouds by subanalytic sets, and develop an approach to semi-supervised learning in this setting. It relies on a Morrey-type embedding for Sobolev spaces relative to globally subanalytic measures with possibly singular support. As an illustration, we present a greedy method based on a Monte Carlo approximation of the Sobolev norm of the candidate solutions. We report numerical experiments on point clouds sampled from real algebraic varieties, as well as a test on a classification problem based on MNIST images downsampled into $7\times7$.
papers.summary: Data clouds with singularities are modeled as subanalytic sets, and a semi-supervised learning approach is built on a Morrey-type embedding for Sobolev spaces relative to measures whose support may be singular. As an illustration, the authors give a greedy method that approximates the Sobolev norm of candidate solutions by Monte Carlo sampling. Experiments cover point clouds sampled from real algebraic varieties and **a classification test on `MNIST` images downsampled to 7x7**.

papers.title: System X: An LLM Decision Model That Replies from Its Own KV Cache
papers.abstract: Decision models return probabilities over supplied options, but a deployed agent may also need to reply in words. The present study introduces System X, a large language model (LLM) decision model that adds a text-reply option to the LLM-as-Jev readout. When this option wins, or confidence is low, the same model continues from the decision's key-value (KV) cache, avoiding a repeated prompt prefill. Qwen3-0.6B has been fine-tuned with LoRA on Reason-9k and Bitext reply rows. JevBench accuracy shows no statistically significant change (55.4% to 54.5%, p=0.87), while expected calibration error falls from 0.292 to 0.169. Held-out Bitext routing accuracy reaches 98.3%. Cache reuse saves 15-37% of latency on an Apple M4 Pro, with token-identical replies in the FP32 demonstration cases. Scoring options on copies of the prompt cache matches full-sequence scoring to within 1.4e-6 in probability. Adding dialogue, industry and complaint data (System X+) improves support-task results but lowers IFEval accuracy from 55.5% to 45.0%. System X v4 uses Qwen3-1.7B, rebalanced data and teacher-rewritten reply targets. Against its base LLM, JevBench accuracy rises from 55.0% to 61.0% (p=0.04), with no statistically significant IFEval change (p=0.71). A matched latency test on unadapted Qwen3-1.7B saves 17-39%. One LLM judge prefers v4 replies to an unadapted 1.7B second call (31 to 11 pairs, p=0.003); the other's preference is not significant. These reply comparisons also differ in prompts and generation limits. State conflicts and unsupported reply details remain failure modes. Further studies with several seeds, human raters and real support data are recommended.
papers.summary: LLM decision models return probabilities over a fixed set of options, but deployed agents sometimes need to reply in words instead. `System X` adds a text-reply option, and when that option wins or confidence is low, the same model continues generating from the decision step's key-value (KV) cache instead of re-processing the prompt. A LoRA fine-tune of `Qwen3-0.6B` keeps `JevBench` accuracy statistically unchanged, lowers calibration error from 0.292 to 0.169, and **saves 15-37% of latency on an Apple M4 Pro through cache reuse**. A `Qwen3-1.7B` version raises `JevBench` accuracy from 55.0% to 61.0% without a significant `IFEval` change, although state conflicts and unsupported reply details remain failure modes.

papers.title: Quality-Controlled Reply and Summary Data for Post-Training Small Language Models in AI Call-Screening Agents
papers.abstract: Small language models have improved to the point where a phone can plausibly screen its own calls, answering on an absent owner's behalf without sending call content off the device, a privacy-respecting alternative to cloud call handling. Realizing that promise takes a model that can do two things well: reply within the owner's authority during the call, and afterward tell the owner what happened and what needs attention. Released small models do neither reliably - they raise unwarranted alarms about ordinary callers and write summaries that drop material conditions or report a caller's claims as fact - and real calls supply no reference replies or summaries to learn from. We construct supervision for both tasks from synthetic calls under an information-boundary constraint: a caller writer works from a private scenario brief, a reply writer sees only the conversation up to the current turn, and a summary writer sees the completed transcript. Separate model-based reviews of the full dialogue and the summary decide which calls enter training, yielding a corpus of 3,395 calls with 15,102 targets (11,707 reply, 3,395 summary). Training a single shared LoRA adapter on both tasks, we evaluate six models (0.6-4B parameters) before and after adaptation on 192 held-out calls. Reply qualification rises from 21-54% to 94-97% and summary qualification from 0-6% to 43-72%; all twelve paired gains (six models x two tasks) have bootstrap intervals above zero, and the summary gains hold in every source family. Because one model both screened the training data and scored the outputs, these rates measure agreement with that evaluator's standard rather than human acceptance, which a planned human study will test. After adaptation, coherence and naturalness failures nearly vanish, leaving grounding and usefulness - faithfully tracking who said what, under which conditions - as the remaining challenge.
papers.summary: On-device call screening needs a small model that replies within the owner's authority during a call and then summarizes it faithfully, but released small models raise false alarms and write unreliable summaries. The authors generate synthetic calls under an information-boundary constraint: the caller, reply, and summary writers each see only what they should. Model-based reviews filter the results into 3,395 calls with 15,102 training targets. A shared LoRA adapter on six models of 0.6-4B parameters **raises reply qualification from 21-54% to 94-97% and summary qualification from 0-6% to 43-72%**. These rates reflect agreement with the same model that filtered the training data rather than human judgment, and grounding (tracking who said what, under which conditions) remains the main weakness.

papers.title: BiDex-100: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation Across 100+ Simulation Tasks
papers.abstract: Bimanual manipulation with dexterous hands has attracted growing attention in research on robotic action models. However, few studies have developed benchmarks specifically tailored for dexterous manipulation, leaving the dexterous manipulation capabilities of existing models insufficiently characterized. In this paper, we present BiDex-100, a simulation benchmark for bimanual dexterous manipulation that combines broad task coverage, multi-dimensional evaluation, and high-DoF hand embodiments. Concretely, the benchmark comprises 106 tasks organized along five capability axes: generalization, instruction following, limited demonstrations, long horizon, and memory. Each task is paired with an out-of-domain variant featuring controlled visual and spatial changes, allowing systematic assessment of robustness. In addition, the benchmark supports two embodiments and provides 8,080 success-validated teleoperated demonstrations, totaling 6.25 million frames. We evaluate seven recent Vision-Language-Action models under a unified protocol, establishing baselines for capability-specific performance, robustness, and data efficiency. The website is available at https://BiDex-100.github.io/BiDex-100/.
papers.summary: Benchmarks built specifically for dexterous manipulation are rare, so the capabilities of robotic action models on such tasks are poorly characterized. `BiDex-100` is a simulation benchmark of **106 bimanual dexterous tasks organized along five capability axes**: generalization, instruction following, limited demonstrations, long horizon, and memory. Each task has an out-of-domain variant with controlled visual and spatial changes for robustness testing. The benchmark supports two high-DoF hand embodiments and ships 8,080 validated teleoperated demonstrations totaling 6.25 million frames. Seven recent Vision-Language-Action models are evaluated under a unified protocol to set baselines.

papers.title: Reliability-Preserving Compression for Deployable Medical Image Segmentation
papers.abstract: Post-training compression of pretrained medical segmentation models commonly uses quantization, pruning, or distillation to reduce model size and computational cost. Existing medical segmentation quantization studies mainly evaluate Dice, model size, memory, and latency, but this is incomplete for safety-critical use because compressed models should also preserve uncertainty signals that indicate unreliable predictions. We study this problem in compressed MRI/CT segmentation and formalize why Dice can remain stable while uncertainty changes. Motivated by this failure mode, we propose score-guided aggregate-validated mixed precision (SGAV-MP), a post-training compression framework that selects layer precisions under reliability constraints. SGAV-MP ranks quantization actions with a compact benefit-risk score and accepts them only after full-model reliability validation on a calibration set. Across five 2D backbones and three 3D benchmarks, SGAV-MP preserves FP32-level Dice and high uncertainty-map agreement, achieving $3.59\times$--$7.8\times$ compression in 2D and $4.73\times$--$7.82\times$ in 3D. We also report backend-supported TensorRT deployment measurements separately to distinguish runtime execution from reliability-preserving storage compression.
papers.summary: Studies of compressed medical segmentation models usually report Dice score, size, and latency, but safety-critical use also requires preserving the uncertainty signals that flag unreliable predictions. The authors formalize why Dice can stay stable while uncertainty shifts. They then propose score-guided aggregate-validated mixed precision (`SGAV-MP`), which ranks per-layer quantization actions by a benefit-risk score and accepts each one only after validating reliability on the full model. Across five 2D backbones and three 3D benchmarks, it **preserves FP32-level Dice and uncertainty-map agreement while achieving 3.59x-7.8x compression in 2D and 4.73x-7.82x in 3D**.

papers.title: DiaLong: Benchmarking Reminiscence in Long-Context Dialogues
papers.abstract: How well can transformer-based Large Language Models (LLMs) retain and recall memories in long contexts of dialogue? LLMs are known to forget long-range factual information in their context, yet the field lacks a comprehensive benchmark to quantitatively assess these shortcomings. We present DiaLong, a long-context dialogue dataset and accompanying memory task that standardizes evaluation in this space. It consists of 100 unique conversations created by humans and then augmented with LLMs, extending beyond lengths found in existing datasets. Our selected memory task is fact recall: classify 40 candidate facts about a dialogue as true or false. This task directly probes the model's ability to actively retain and retrieve information, serving as a critical measure of memory within extended conversational contexts. In testing both the latest LLMs and proposed memory enhancements on DiaLong, we demonstrate that more work needs to be done to enable LLMs with better memory performance. By enhancing memory capabilities, LLMs can improve in maintaining coherence, relevance, and human-like interaction over extended conversation. Improving these capabilities will help LLMs fulfill diverse user needs and expectations in various conversational scenarios.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are known to forget facts from far back in their context, but there is no standard way to measure how much they forget over long conversations. `DiaLong` is a benchmark of 100 human-written conversations, extended with LLMs to be longer than those in existing datasets. Each conversation comes with a fact-recall task: label 40 candidate facts about the dialogue as true or false. Tests of recent LLMs and of proposed memory enhancements show that **current models still fall short on long-range conversational memory**.

papers.title: On Reasoning Correctness Directions
papers.abstract: We present experimental evidence suggesting that information about whether a model's reasoning is on the right track can be linearly decodable without defining a causally useful direction for steering. To study this, we introduce ChainSearch, a controlled arithmetic reasoning task that extends Countdown with explicit search and backtracking. We train a 3-million-parameter model to solve this task. Its compact size allows us to study internal model correctness directions in detail using linear probes, mean activation differences, and direct optimisation, as part of a rigorous search for internal reasoning-correctness directions. We find that while the model contains statistically significant internal directions of reasoning correctness, none of the resulting directions consistently improves reasoning under causal intervention. This calls into question whether the linear representation hypothesis is sufficient for identifying causally useful directions in the context of reasoning. Our code is made available together with this work.
papers.summary: The authors test whether a model's internal signal that its reasoning is on track can also be used to steer that reasoning. They introduce `ChainSearch`, an arithmetic task that extends `Countdown` with explicit search and backtracking, and train a 3-million-parameter model on it. They search for correctness directions using linear probes, mean activation differences and direct optimisation. The model does contain statistically significant correctness directions, yet **none of them consistently improves reasoning when used for causal intervention**, which suggests the linear representation hypothesis is not enough to find steering directions for reasoning.

papers.title: Near-Optimal Last-Iterate Convergence of SGD in the Smooth Interpolation Regime
papers.abstract: We study the last iterate of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with a constant stepsize on smooth convex objectives in the low-noise and interpolation regimes, where the variance $\sigma_\star^2$ of the stochastic gradients at the optimum is small or zero. We establish that after $T$ steps of SGD on $\beta$-smooth convex losses with any constant stepsize $0<\eta<2/\beta$, the last iterate attains expected excess risk $\widetilde O\bigl(\tfrac{1}{\eta(2-\beta\eta)^3T}+\tfrac{\eta}{(2-\beta\eta)^4}\sigma_\star^2\bigr)$, which gives the rate $\smash{\widetilde O(1/T)}$ for every constant stepsize in the interpolation regime ($\sigma_\star=0$), matching the $\Omega(1/T)$ lower bound up to logarithmic factors and improving upon the $O(1/\sqrt T)$ rate of Attia et al. (2026) for $\eta=1/\beta$. Our analysis is based on a new technique, which compares the second moments of the stochastic gradients along the SGD trajectory across only logarithmically many time scales. For quadratic losses in the interpolation regime, an adaptation of this technique gives an $O(1/T)$ rate for every constant stepsize, extending the recent optimal rate for the randomized Kaczmarz method of Derezinski and Dong (2026) to stepsizes above the greedy stepsize with an arguably simpler proof.
papers.summary: The authors analyze the final iterate of constant-stepsize stochastic gradient descent (`SGD`) on smooth convex losses in the low-noise and interpolation regimes, where gradient noise at the optimum is small or zero. They show that for any constant stepsize below 2 divided by the smoothness constant, the last iterate reaches **an excess-risk rate of about 1/T in the interpolation regime**. This matches the known lower bound up to logarithmic factors and improves on the previous 1/√T rate. The proof uses a new technique that compares second moments of stochastic gradients across only logarithmically many time scales, and it also gives an optimal rate for quadratics that extends recent results for the randomized `Kaczmarz` method.

papers.title: A failure of Imagination: VLMs fail to use visual representations for text, but self-distillation can help
papers.abstract: Vision-language (VL) models are typically built by fine-tuning a language model to attend to visual features in service of a Visual Question-Answering objective. We ask whether this alignment changes how language models represent text---especially on tasks where visualization would help, like geometry questions posed in words. We distinguish weak multimodality (the model can answer questions about an input image) from strong multimodality (the model's text representations themselves become vision-aligned, improving performance on text-only tasks with latent visual structure). To test for strong multimodality, we construct a task of shape-counting problems with paired equivalent text and image specifications. This task is trivial when the image is provided, but requires visualization when specified in text as line coordinates. We compare instruction-tuned Qwen-2.5 and Mistral models against their vision-aligned counterparts on the text variant of the task. We find that the multimodal models do no better in this setting, despite strong performance on the image version of the task. Probing experiments corroborate this: vision-aligned decoder embeddings carry no more visual structure than their text-only counterparts. Finally, we provide an optimization objective that distills in-context visual embeddings into text embeddings. This alignment induces gains on the text variant of the task without explicit task supervision, even on samples more complex than seen during alignment. This suggests that VQA-style alignment leaves available cross-modal transfer untapped.
papers.summary: The authors ask whether training a language model to see images also changes how it represents text, for instance by helping it picture geometry problems described in words. They build a shape-counting task where each problem comes in two equivalent forms, an image or a text list of line coordinates, and compare instruction-tuned `Qwen-2.5` and `Mistral` models with their vision-language versions. **The vision-aligned models do no better on the text version** even though they handle the image version well, and probes find no extra visual structure in their text embeddings. A self-distillation objective that transfers in-context visual embeddings into text embeddings improves text-only performance without task supervision, including on problems harder than those seen during alignment.

papers.title: Consistent LLM Call Handling Across Java Frameworks: A Reference Implementation and Benchmark
papers.abstract: Java applications reach large language models (LLMs) through an integration framework, and rely on it to handle a failing provider: to retry what can be retried and nothing else, to wait as long as the provider asks, never to present a truncated answer as complete, and to record each failure in the application's metrics. We state these expectations as a six-clause reliability contract and measure Spring AI 2.0.1 and LangChain4j 1.21.0 against it with a scripted OpenAI-compatible provider: fifteen failure scenarios, synchronous and streaming, three repetitions. LangChain4j meets it in 47 of 77 applicable cases with its defaults and in 51 of 83 when configured explicitly, Spring AI in 72 of 77 and 76 of 83; both deliver a stream that ended without its terminator as a complete answer. We then place one implementation of the contract beneath both frameworks, at the HTTP boundary - an OkHttp interceptor for Spring AI, an HttpClient for LangChain4j, and a java.net.http transport for code without a framework - sharing a 725-line core that depends only on the JDK and the Micrometer Observation API. With it, all three clients behave identically and meet the contract in 90 of 91 cases; the remaining case is a policy trade-off between retrying a hung provider and waiting for a slow first token. Against a local model server the layer rejected none of 700 calls, and it adds a median of 32-217 microseconds to a call.
papers.summary: Java applications call large language models (LLMs) through integration frameworks, which are expected to handle provider failures correctly: retry only what can be retried, respect the provider's wait instructions, never pass off a truncated answer as complete, and record failures in metrics. The authors write these expectations as a six-clause reliability contract and test `Spring AI` and `LangChain4j` against a scripted provider across fifteen failure scenarios. `LangChain4j` meets the contract in 47 of 77 applicable cases with defaults and `Spring AI` in 72 of 77, and both return a stream that ended without its terminator as a complete answer. A shared 725-line implementation placed at the HTTP layer beneath both frameworks makes all clients behave identically and **meet the contract in 90 of 91 cases**, adding a median of 32–217 microseconds per call.

papers.title: Probabilistic Limit Order Book Forecasting with Conditional Diffusion Models
papers.abstract: Modeling limit order book (LOB) dynamics is central to market forecasting and execution-strategy evaluation. While diffusion models achieve strong empirical performance, existing LOB snapshot models typically lack a learned recurrent encoder and formal statistical guarantees. We introduce LOBGrad, a conditional DDPM framework for probabilistic LOB forecasting that combines an autoregressive RNN encoder with a diffusion-based generator. In particular, we establish an excess-risk oracle inequality for the one-step DDPM noise-prediction objective under exponential mixing and regularity assumptions. We further show that, under contractive dynamics, the dependence on the conditioning-window length can be reduced to a dependence on the latent-state dimension. Experiments on BTC/USDT, GOOGL, and META show that LOBGrad improves on its encoder-free diffusion ablation across all reported queue metrics and obtains competitive results against other baselines. It also reproduces the key stylized facts of LOB microstructure, and yields reasonably calibrated queue-based predictive intervals. A stylized downstream task illustrates the potential value of the generated forecasts.
papers.summary: A limit order book (LOB) records outstanding buy and sell orders, and modeling how it evolves matters for market forecasting and for evaluating execution strategies. Existing diffusion models of LOB snapshots typically lack a learned recurrent encoder and formal statistical guarantees. `LOBGrad` pairs an autoregressive recurrent encoder with a conditional denoising diffusion probabilistic model (`DDPM`) generator and comes with an excess-risk oracle inequality for its training objective. On `BTC/USDT`, `GOOGL` and `META` data it **improves on its encoder-free ablation across all reported queue metrics**, is competitive with other baselines, reproduces the key stylized facts of LOB microstructure and gives reasonably calibrated prediction intervals.

papers.title: Self-Distillation for Supervised Fine-Tuning
papers.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning treats the expert demonstration or gold response as a one-hot target, suppressing valid alternative continuations that the model would otherwise assign probability to. We propose Gold-Conditioned Distillation (GCD), a method that turns expert demonstrations into model-native supervision. GCD uses one model as both teacher and student: the teacher conditions on a prompt containing the gold response in context, the student conditions on the original prompt as at inference, and the student is trained to minimize the forward KL divergence to the teacher's next-token distribution at each gold response token. This lets the model use its prior knowledge to teach itself the new task: correctness is anchored by the gold response, while the soft target preserves plausible alternatives. Across various training tasks on Qwen and Llama models, GCD improves new-task accuracy over SFT and generally reduces degradation on general benchmarks.
papers.summary: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) treats the gold response as a one-hot target, which suppresses valid alternative continuations the model would otherwise consider. `Gold-Conditioned Distillation` (`GCD`) uses one model as both teacher and student: the teacher sees the gold response in its prompt, the student sees only the original prompt, and the student is trained to match the teacher's next-token distribution at each gold token. The gold answer anchors correctness while the soft targets keep plausible alternatives. Across several tasks on `Qwen` and `Llama` models, **`GCD` improves new-task accuracy over SFT and generally reduces degradation on general benchmarks**.

papers.title: Steered Not Stirred: Effective Reward Tilting using Surrogate Reward Mixing
papers.abstract: Continuous-time generative models, from diffusion models, flow matching, and now flow maps, owe their practical value to high-fidelity generation and steerability. In many applications, a ground-truth latent ``oracle'' reward $R^*$ is unavailable or expensive to evaluate, e.g., human judgments or experimental measurements. Although the oracle reward is not directly observable, it can often be approximated through multiple cheaper surrogates that, individually, provide incomplete characterizations but collectively reveal substantial information about the downstream task. In this paper, we present a method for composing such surrogates to steer a pretrained model toward the distribution tilted by an unavailable $R^*$. Given a small feedback set of oracle rankings or numerical rewards, we introduce Mixing And Reward Tilting for INference-time Improvement (MARTINI), which learns a surrogate composition for plug-and-play use with standard inference-time steering methods. Our theory characterizes surrogate information limits and relates population recovery error to ideal-target KL at small tilt strength. For preferences, the bound additionally accounts for an irreducible mismatch between the Plackett-Luce population target and the conditional mean. Experiments demonstrate improved oracle-tilt fidelity in language generation and ImageNet alignment, and improved joint pose accuracy and validity in protein-ligand cofolding, without inference-time oracle queries.
papers.summary: The goal is to steer pretrained diffusion, flow-matching and flow-map models toward outputs favored by a true reward, such as human judgment or a lab measurement, that is too expensive to query during generation. `MARTINI` (`Mixing And Reward Tilting for INference-time Improvement`) uses a small set of oracle rankings or reward values to learn how to combine several cheaper surrogate rewards, and the combination plugs into standard inference-time steering methods. The accompanying theory bounds how much information the surrogates can carry and how far the recovered target can be from the ideal one. Experiments show **better fidelity to the oracle-tilted distribution with no oracle queries at inference time**, across language generation, `ImageNet` alignment and protein-ligand cofolding.

papers.title: From Seeing to Reporting: A Theory of Reliable Visual Set Generation in Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are asked to report what they see: to count objects, box them, parse a screen or pick a click target (GUI grounding). We argue that reporting is part of the visual task, not merely its formatting. In a dense scene with 173 shapes, GPT-6.1 lists 173 records that match every shape, yet the counts it states in the same response sum to 188. From Seeing to Reporting (FSR) is a theory of visual reporting and a set of inference-time procedures that improve the reports of frozen VLMs. It models reporting as a chain from responses to decoded records, constructed sets and task answers, linked by task-compatible matching. The chain gives exact relations for deleting records, averaging their coordinates and switching readouts, and it splits the error of one answer chosen among several calls into missing candidates, lost representatives and wrong choices. These relations guide procedures for counting, detection, document layout, screen parsing and GUI grounding that use the task specification and a shipped configuration, without requiring labels from the target task. On 50 dense synthetic scenes, a one-call reporting-and-decoding protocol cuts per-type count error by 85.2% for GPT-6.1 and 98.8% for Claude Sonnet 5.5. On 600 ScreenSpot-Pro items, a GUI-grounding tier that combines three models lowers the miss rate from 13.67% for GPT-6.1's two-stage zoom to 9.33%, against 12.67% for three such zooms combined by a cluster vote at about the same cost. A plain vote over the same three models misses 12.33%: the other models supply the candidates, and selecting among them turns those candidates into fewer misses. We release the protocols, the stored responses and the analysis code.
papers.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) often see a scene correctly but report it inconsistently: in one dense scene, `GPT-6.1` listed all 173 shapes correctly, yet the counts it gave in the same response added up to 188. `From Seeing to Reporting` (`FSR`) models reporting as a chain from raw responses to decoded records, constructed sets and task answers. The theory guides label-free inference-time procedures for frozen VLMs on counting, detection, document layout, screen parsing and GUI grounding (finding the screen element to click). A one-call reporting protocol **cuts per-type count error by 85.2% for `GPT-6.1` and 98.8% for `Claude Sonnet 5.5`**, and on `ScreenSpot-Pro` a three-model grounding tier lowers the miss rate from 13.67% to 9.33% at roughly the same cost as weaker alternatives.

papers.title: Where Are Language-Specific Features Represented in Multilingual LLMs? Everywhere
papers.abstract: Previous work has argued that multilingual LLMs encode language-specific features most strongly in their initial and final layers, implying that intermediate layers support language-agnostic representations. This paper reconsiders this finding by performing four different experiments: three that undertake a fine-grained analysis of representations of Portuguese and Spanish, two closely related languages, and one large-scale language identification experiment that covers over 200 languages. The results of these experiments challenge the strict separation between language-specific and language-agnostic layers in multilingual LLMs, using Llama 3.2 1B as a test case. By analyzing and manipulating contextual sentence embeddings, we demonstrate that language identity remains strongly recoverable throughout the model rather than being restricted to initial and final layers. Moreover, we find that the model tends to classify ambiguous strings as closer to Spanish than to Portuguese, revealing a skew in model behavior that differs from human judgments.
papers.summary: Earlier work argued that multilingual large language models (LLMs) encode language-specific features mainly in their first and last layers, leaving the middle layers language-agnostic. Using `Llama 3.2 1B`, the authors test this with three fine-grained experiments on the closely related Portuguese and Spanish and one language-identification experiment covering more than 200 languages. They find that **language identity stays strongly recoverable from sentence embeddings at every layer**, which challenges the strict layer separation. The model also tends to classify ambiguous strings as closer to Spanish than to Portuguese, a skew that differs from human judgments.

papers.title: KPI-Aware Multimodal Anomaly Detection for 5G and Open RAN Telemetry
papers.abstract: Reliable anomaly detection is a deployment bottleneck for 5G/Open RAN observability and emerging self-optimizing 6G systems, where hundreds of heterogeneous KPIs, severe class imbalance, and strict alert budgets make purely numerical scores brittle. We present KAC, a deployment-oriented KPI-aware multimodal anomaly-detection framework that uses KPI-level residual-text alignment to turn compact operator-style summaries into a learnable feedback signal over full-KPI temporal evidence. This gives the detector broad numerical coverage like modern time-series models, while retaining the sparse KPI-specific reasoning that makes operator feedback sustainable in a future operator-facing workflow. Across public telecom telemetry, enterprise-scale Open RAN observability data, and a Nokia benchmark built from real 5G RAN production packet traces with realism-hardened injected anomalies, KAC achieves strong threshold-based detection performance while remaining competitive on threshold-free ranking metrics. On TelecomTS, at a fixed 2.5 percent false-positive-rate operating point, KAC achieves the highest recall among the evaluated residual-based methods while maintaining comparable precision; across the evaluated benchmarks, it remains robust under substantial class imbalance. KAC is integrated in pre-production shadow mode with Nokia's GKE-based KPI construction pipeline, where it continuously scores telemetry windows alongside an internal packet-level anomaly detector for operational evaluation.
papers.summary: Anomaly detection on 5G and Open RAN (radio access network) telemetry is hard because there are hundreds of different key performance indicators (KPIs), anomalies are rare and alert budgets are strict. `KAC` aligns per-KPI residuals with compact operator-style text summaries, turning those summaries into a learnable feedback signal over the full KPI time series. Across public telecom data, enterprise Open RAN data and a `Nokia` benchmark built from real 5G production traces, **`KAC` achieves the highest recall among residual-based methods on `TelecomTS` at a fixed 2.5% false-positive rate** and holds up under heavy class imbalance. It is running in pre-production shadow mode inside `Nokia`'s KPI pipeline.

papers.title: Dynamics-Aligned Representation Learning under Induced Partial Observability
papers.abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) has enabled sample-efficient learning of continuous control policies from high-dimensional observations through learned latent dynamics models. These models are typically trained with observation reconstruction objectives, which provide strong supervision but can bias representations toward visual fidelity leading to an undertrained prior and unreliable long-horizon predictions. We propose a stochastic gating mechanism that induces controlled partial observability during training by sampling a spatial binary mask from a Beta--Bernoulli random field and applying it to the raw observation. The gate probability is resampled at each time step, exposing the encoder to conditions ranging from near-total occlusion to near-full visibility. Integration of our method requires minimal architectural changes from existing dynamics models: the gated observation and the binary mask are channel-wise concatenated and passed to the encoder as a single augmented input, with no modifications to the broader training pipeline. We evaluate the proposed approach on a set of pixel-based continuous control tasks selected from the DeepMind Control Suite. Using model predictive control for evaluation, which relies solely on open-loop model rollouts, we show that stochastic gating improves planning performance and data efficiency across tasks. Further analysis demonstrates that performance is robust to the spatial scale of the mask, and a balanced observability during training outperforms configurations biased toward either sparser or denser observations.
papers.summary: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) agents usually train their latent dynamics models by reconstructing observations, which can push representations toward visual detail at the expense of reliable long-horizon prediction. The proposed method applies a random spatial binary mask, drawn from a Beta–Bernoulli random field, to each raw observation during training, with the visibility level resampled every time step. The masked observation and the mask are concatenated and fed to the encoder, so the rest of the pipeline is unchanged. On pixel-based `DeepMind Control Suite` tasks evaluated with model predictive control, **stochastic gating improves planning performance and data efficiency**, and balanced visibility during training outperforms settings skewed toward sparser or denser observations.

papers.title: ATEST: Adaptive Resource-Aware Test-Time Scaling for LLM Inference
papers.abstract: Test-time scaling (TTS) improves large language model (LLM) reasoning by sampling multiple answers, but fixed sampling budgets ignore both query difficulty and the changing energy cost of inference under GPU contention. We measure up to a 4.1-fold increase in energy for the same four-sample query as GPU load rises. We present ATEST, a resource-aware TTS framework that jointly considers the expected value of additional samples and their current GPU cost. ATEST-Online, its default mode, requires no offline calibration: it incrementally generates samples, estimates the stability of the plurality answer, monitors live GPU conditions, and learns step energy cost online to decide when to stop. ATEST-Calibrated instead selects a per-query budget using offline accuracy and cost models, favoring deployments with stable loads. We evaluate both modes on four reasoning and question-answering datasets using Phi-3-mini on an NVIDIA A100 under controlled varying load, and test transfer to an NVIDIA L40S and Qwen2.5-3B. Across the four A100 datasets, ATEST-Online answers every query without exceeding the energy budget, while achieving the highest or statistically tied accuracy and reducing sampling as load increases. On GSM8K at high load, it achieves 60.0% accuracy with no deferrals, versus 44.0% accuracy and 42.4% deferrals for ATEST-Calibrated. Ablations show that online cost learning drives adaptation to load. Including offline profiling, ATEST-Online uses 42 times less GPU time and 48 times less energy than ATEST-Calibrated for the evaluated workload. Online control trades higher tail latency and lower throughput on short tasks for robustness under varying load; offline calibration remains competitive under stable conditions.
papers.summary: Test-time scaling (TTS) samples several answers from a large language model (LLM) to improve reasoning, but fixed sample budgets ignore both how hard a query is and how much energy each sample costs as GPU load changes. The authors measured up to a 4.1-fold energy increase for the same query under contention. `ATEST-Online` generates samples one at a time, tracks how stable the plurality answer is, monitors live GPU conditions and learns energy cost online to decide when to stop, while `ATEST-Calibrated` picks per-query budgets from offline models. With `Phi-3-mini` on an A100, `ATEST-Online` stays within the energy budget on all four datasets and on `GSM8K` under high load reaches **60.0% accuracy with no deferrals, versus 44.0% accuracy and 42.4% deferrals for the calibrated mode**, at the cost of higher tail latency on short tasks.

papers.title: FracTS: Hierarchical and Autoregressive Time Series Generation
papers.abstract: Time series are ubiquitous across different domains, and the growing use of synthetic data for privacy-preserving sharing, data augmentation, and stress testing makes time series generation increasingly important. Early generative approaches are predominantly autoregressive, which can suffer from low sample diversity, error accumulation, and difficulty modeling long-range dependencies. In this paper, we introduce FracTS, a hierarchical, coarse-to-fine autoregressive model for multivariate time series generation. Inspired by fractal generative modeling developed for images, FracTS adapts the paradigm from 2D to 1D sequences by learning a multi-scale representation that captures global trajectory structure at coarse scales and local dynamics at fine scales while following the autoregressive nature of time series. In contrast to unstructured images, time series are structured, allowing easy automated or designated temporal feature processing optimized for the model, and global (static) feature extraction describing the instances that generate the corresponding time series in the collection. We incorporate them in the generation process to further improve the generation quality. The design naturally handles multivariate dependencies and improves long-horizon temporal coherence without requiring fixed-length inputs. Experiments on five datasets (two conditional, three unconditional) conducted against seven baselines show that FracTS consistently outperforms baselines across marginal distribution and predictive ML utility, and correlation preservation in the unconditional setting. In particular, the predictive ML utility is averagely improved by 100.0% and 75.0-81.0% for unconditional and conditional time series datasets compared to the best baseline (relative error computed on dataset-averaged raw values). Code is available at: https://github.com/BetterdataLabs/fracts.
papers.summary: Synthetic time series are useful for privacy-preserving data sharing, data augmentation and stress testing, but autoregressive generators can suffer from low diversity, accumulating errors and weak long-range structure. `FracTS` adapts fractal generative modeling from images to 1D sequences as a coarse-to-fine autoregressive model: coarse scales capture the global trajectory and fine scales capture local dynamics. It also conditions on engineered temporal features and static per-instance features. Across five datasets and seven baselines it consistently performs best on marginal distribution and predictive utility, and **improves predictive ML utility by an average of 100% on unconditional datasets and 75–81% on conditional ones** relative to the best baseline.

papers.title: Breaking the 1/3 Barrier for Approximate Nash Equilibria in Symmetric Bimatrix Games
papers.abstract: We give the first unconditional family of polynomial-time algorithms that breaks the $1/3$ approximation barrier for symmetric bimatrix games. For every fixed $\delta>0$, an algorithm in this family computes a symmetric $(1-1/\sqrt{2}+\delta)$-approximate Nash equilibrium, improving on the previous best guarantee of $(1/3+\delta)$ due to Kontogiannis and Spirakis [2011].
papers.summary: Computing approximate Nash equilibria in two-player (bimatrix) games is a central problem in algorithmic game theory, and for symmetric games the best polynomial-time guarantee had stood at 1/3 since 2011. The authors give the first unconditional family of polynomial-time algorithms that breaks this barrier. For every fixed δ > 0, an algorithm in the family computes **a symmetric (1 − 1/√2 + δ)-approximate Nash equilibrium**, which is about 0.293.

papers.title: From Clinical Risk Prediction to Operational Decisions: An Uncertainty-Aware Framework for ICU Staffing
papers.abstract:
Advances in electronic health records (EHR) and large-scale critical care databases have enabled the development of machine learning models for the early detection of patient deterioration. While these models often achieve strong predictive performance for outcomes such as sepsis and mortality, most studies evaluate them purely on discrimination metrics. This leaves a critical gap: how to systematically translate probabilistic clinical risk estimates into downstream operational decisions under real-world constraints, such as shift rigidity and hiring delays.
  This study proposes an uncertainty-aware anticipatory staffing framework that bridges short-term patient risk prediction and staff planning without altering the upstream predictive model. Instead of relying on naive deterministic aggregation or fixed safety buffers, the framework explicitly models dynamic predictive uncertainty and evaluates extreme shortage exposure using Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR). These aggregated, risk-calibrated demand signals are then embedded into an hourly rolling-horizon scheduling policy to generate delay-constrained staffing decisions.
  Evaluated on realistic trajectories from the MIMIC-IV database, the proposed framework demonstrates a favorable cost-shortage trade-off compared to deterministic and purely reactive baselines. Pareto frontier analysis illustrates how uncertainty-aware demand construction changes resource allocation under varying safety preferences, while stress testing confirms the framework's operational robustness even when subjected to systematic predictive bias in the form of calibration drift. By formalizing this translation layer, this work provides a principled, transparent pathway for safely integrating probabilistic AI outputs into high-stakes healthcare operational systems.
papers.summary: Machine learning models that predict patient deterioration in intensive care are usually judged only on how well they rank risk, not on how their outputs feed real decisions such as staffing. The proposed framework leaves the predictive model unchanged and turns its risk estimates into staffing plans. It models predictive uncertainty explicitly, measures exposure to extreme shortages with Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR), and feeds the resulting demand signals into an hourly rolling-horizon scheduler that respects hiring delays. On trajectories from `MIMIC-IV`, it achieves **a better cost-shortage trade-off than deterministic and purely reactive baselines** and stays robust under calibration drift.

papers.title: Auditing Tool Traces in Agentic LLMs: Source Localization and Counterfactual Dependence Testing
papers.abstract: Agentic LLMs increasingly support scientific prediction by grounding decisions in external evidence. In biology, they promise accurate, interpretable predictions for important problems by integrating complex experimental and computational evidence. However, serialized tool results can contain hidden label shortcuts, such as dataset identifiers or template artifacts, that create apparent success without biological reasoning. To address this risk, we introduce a two-stage audit. Stage 1, Per-Tool TF-IDF Decomposition (PT2D), localizes label-predictive patterns to individual tool results while avoiding signal dilution in the concatenated tool trace. Stage 2, Token-Class Redaction, counterfactually tests whether the frozen LLM depends on the localized shortcut. We apply this audit to TCR-pMHC binding, where tool augmentation substantially outperforms a no-evidence baseline. At face value, this suggests that the LLM has learned to use scientific evidence. The audit overturns this interpretation: PT2D localizes the strongest signal to identifiers in one tool result, and redacting them reduces performance to chance. These findings show how hidden label shortcuts can masquerade as scientific reasoning or discovery, motivating source-level audits before benchmark gains are trusted.
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents that ground scientific predictions in tool outputs can appear to reason well when they are in fact exploiting hidden label shortcuts, such as dataset identifiers, in those outputs. The authors propose a two-stage audit. `Per-Tool TF-IDF Decomposition` (`PT2D`) locates label-predictive patterns in individual tool results, and `Token-Class Redaction` tests whether the frozen LLM actually depends on them. On TCR-pMHC binding prediction, where tool augmentation far outperforms a no-evidence baseline, the audit traces the strongest signal to identifiers in one tool's output, and **redacting them drops performance to chance**.

papers.title: Reinforcement learning on the EPRI AI-ccelerating Unit Commitment benchmark: diagnosing over-commitment and guiding MILP with learned policies
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is increasingly proposed as a fast solver for unit commitment (UC), but standalone agents remain far more expensive than mixed-integer linear programming (MILP). In the first study of RL on the 51-generator, 72-hour benchmark of the Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI) AI-ccelerating Unit Commitment competition, we trace this gap to the agents' own exploration, close most of it, and show that the resulting policy can accelerate an exact solver. In every configuration tested, Proximal Policy Optimisation (PPO) and an action-branching Deep Q-Network (DQN) trained from scratch committed about twice the units of a thermal-only MILP optimum, at 39-64% higher cost, whereas a merit-order rule came within 1.6-7% (10-24% when unserved energy is priced). When each unit's decision is sampled independently, spare units insure against random de-commitments. Consistent with this, injecting exploration noise during fine-tuning enlarged a lean policy's fleet, a reward without shaping terms did not remove the over-commitment, and under their training noise the agents outperformed the rule subjected to comparable noise. Imitating the MILP solutions and fine-tuning conservatively brought PPO within 2.6% of the optimum, and these policies had the lowest penalised cost of any evaluated (about 5%). Fixing the fine-tuned policy's confident decisions made the MILP 3.8-8.5 times faster within 0.10-0.25% of the best solution, with a smaller worst case than an imitation-only policy fixing as many variables (1.1% against 8.9%). Because dispatch method and benchmark scope alone shift the reported optimality ratio by up to 3.6% and 9%, we propose a reporting protocol.
papers.summary: Unit commitment (UC) is the problem of deciding which power generators to run and when, and reinforcement learning (RL) agents for it have remained far more costly than mixed-integer linear programming (`MILP`) solutions. On the 51-generator, 72-hour `EPRI` benchmark, `PPO` and an action-branching `DQN` trained from scratch committed about twice the units of the `MILP` optimum, at 39–64% higher cost. The authors trace this to exploration: when each unit's decision is sampled independently, spare units insure against random shutdowns. Imitating `MILP` solutions and then fine-tuning conservatively brought `PPO` within 2.6% of the optimum, and **fixing the policy's confident decisions made the `MILP` solver 3.8–8.5 times faster within 0.10–0.25% of the best solution**; the authors also propose a reporting protocol.

papers.title: Beyond the record: evaluating probabilistic AI weather forecasts deep in the tail
papers.abstract: Can probabilistic artificial intelligence (AI) weather forecasts retain skill beyond their training domain? We compare four state-of-the-art AI models (ArchesWeatherGen, U-Cast, WeatherNext2 and GenCast-mini) with the physics-based IFS-ENS over land in 2022, at 1.5{\deg} resolution and lead times of 2--10 days. Monthly ERA5 records from 1979--2021 define common historical boundaries, and we characterize new records set in 2022 by their depth, i.e., the exceedance margin relative to local historical variability. Two proper scores, record-threshold weighted CRPS and Brier score, assess the magnitude and probability of record exceedances across all eligible cases, retaining both missed extremes and false alarms. Verified against ERA5, AI models outperform IFS-ENS for heat and cold records at almost every lead and depth. For heat, the advantage strengthens with depth, partly because IFS-ENS over-forecasts deep records, and largely persists for deeper records under HRES-fc0 verification. For wind, gains erode for deeper records and longer leads. Better tail scores can nevertheless coexist with aggregate probability deficits or surpluses, and some improvements arise chiefly on non-exceedances. Increasing underprediction on progressively more extreme observed subsets can also arise through outcome selection, even for an ideal conditional-mean forecast. These findings establish that native probabilistic AI ensembles retain, and for heat increase, their advantage over IFS-ENS as thresholds move beyond local records, although all advantages narrow with lead time. They caution against generalizing the extrapolation failure reported for deterministic AI forecasts to probabilistic systems, and motivate common verification conventions that separate comparative tail skill, performance on realized extremes, and probabilistic calibration.
papers.summary: The question is whether probabilistic AI weather models keep their skill on extremes that exceed anything in their training data. Four AI ensembles (`ArchesWeatherGen`, `U-Cast`, `WeatherNext2` and `GenCast-mini`) are compared with the physics-based `IFS-ENS` on land temperature and wind records set in 2022, scored with record-threshold weighted `CRPS` and `Brier` scores at 2–10 day lead times. Verified against `ERA5`, **the AI models beat `IFS-ENS` for heat and cold records at almost every lead time and record depth, with the heat advantage growing for deeper records**, while gains for wind erode for deeper records and longer leads. The authors caution against carrying the extrapolation failures reported for deterministic AI forecasts over to probabilistic systems, and call for common verification conventions.

papers.title: EmotiQ: A Quantum Residual Specialist Framework for Text Emotion Classification
papers.abstract: Emotion classification from text is challenging because many affective states are distinguished by subtle linguistic signals and semantically overlapping boundaries. We investigate whether compact quantum modules can serve as targeted residual specialists that assist traditional classifiers on difficult emotion decisions. We introduce EmotiQ, a residual specialist framework for text emotion classification using a frozen transformer classifier as the primary decision maker, identifies challenging emotion boundaries from validation behavior, and trains boundary specialists, including quantum encodings, data re-uploading specialists, prototype and fidelity specialists, and kernel-based specialists. Specialists are permitted to intervene only when they satisfy validation-based admission criteria. We evaluate the framework across six text emotion classification datasets and establish traditional model baselines. Experimental results show that the admitted EmotiQ policy improves mean macro-F1 metrics over the baseline, and achieves positive gains on five of six datasets. Among the quantum components, ZZ interaction feature maps are the most consistently effective, yielding a mean macro-F1 improvement of +0.0030 and positive gains on four datasets. These findings suggest that current quantum NLP methods can be deployed as residual specialists that provide localized improvements under strong classical supervision.
papers.summary: Some emotions in text are hard to tell apart because they differ only in subtle wording. `EmotiQ` keeps a frozen transformer classifier as the main decision maker, finds hard emotion boundaries from its validation behavior and trains specialist modules for them, including quantum encodings, data re-uploading, fidelity and kernel-based specialists. A specialist may intervene only if it passes validation-based admission criteria. Across six datasets the admitted policy raises mean macro-F1 and gains on five of them, while the best quantum component, `ZZ` interaction feature maps, adds **a mean macro-F1 improvement of only +0.0030**.

papers.title: Narrow Decision Models: A System-1 Architecture for Calibrated, Typed Decisions
papers.abstract: System One models, introduced with TypeSafe's Jev, answer typed questions about a state with calibrated probabilities instead of generated text: choosing among options described in natural language (Choice), placing the state on an ordered scale (Score), or judging a yes/no statement (Noul). Jev is general-purpose: one set of weights, served as an API and adapted to a domain only through the request. We study the other end of the design space. A Narrow Decision Model (NDM) offers the same interface but is trained for the decisions of one organization, is small enough to run on its own infrastructure, and has an open architecture whose properties can be stated and tested. The state can be any text or structured record about which decisions are made; our running case is the routing of court communications. The architecture serializes a request as a prefix tree (the state, then each question, then each option) and runs a bidirectional encoder under a block attention mask with logical positions, so that each answer is, by construction, invariant to the order of its options and independent of the other questions asked. Routing through an organization chart is a composition of Choice decisions with an explicit "none of these" option. We describe training with proper scoring rules through a curriculum, calibration and abstention, decisions composed by rubrics, and a protocol that accepts or rejects the mechanism before held-out data is opened. A minimal validation on public and fictitious data shows that the invariances hold to rounding in a trained model, that a small instance routes on organization charts it has never seen well above lexical retrieval, and that, at equal compute, the block architecture reaches a lower loss than a pairwise cross-encoder. A first instance trained on real legal documents agrees with the LLM classifier in production on 91% of held-out documents.
papers.summary: A `Narrow Decision Model` (NDM) answers typed questions about a state with calibrated probabilities instead of generated text: picking among options (Choice), placing the state on an ordered scale (Score), or judging a yes/no statement. Unlike general-purpose API models such as `Jev`, an NDM is trained for one organization's decisions and is small enough to run on that organization's own infrastructure. The request is serialized as a prefix tree and processed by a bidirectional encoder under a block attention mask. By construction, each answer is therefore unaffected by the order of its options and independent of the other questions asked. On court-communication routing, a small model routes on organization charts it has never seen well above lexical retrieval and beats a pairwise cross-encoder at equal compute, and a first instance trained on real legal documents **agrees with the production LLM classifier on 91% of held-out documents**.

papers.title: FTFM: Factorized Tabular Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) are becoming a powerful alternative to conventional tabular learning, adapting to new datasets in context without task-specific training. Current architectures, however, face a trade-off: models that preserve cell-level representations are expensive because they repeatedly attend across rows and columns, while faster models collapse each row into a fixed embedding and lose this fine-grained state. We introduce Factorized Tabular Foundation Models (FTFM), which preserve cell representations while factorizing their computation through one contextual latent per row and one per column. Cells no longer attend to one another directly; instead, each cell is updated through the interaction of its row and column latents, reducing repeated attention while retaining feature-specific information. FTFM achieves competitive predictive performance in tabular classification on major benchmarks such as TabArena and BeyondArena.
papers.summary: Tabular foundation models adapt to new datasets in context, but current designs face a trade-off. Some keep a representation for every cell and pay heavily for repeated attention across rows and columns; others are faster but collapse each row into a single embedding and lose fine-grained detail. `FTFM` keeps cell-level representations but factorizes the computation through one contextual latent per row and one per column, so cells are updated through their row and column latents rather than by attending to each other directly. This **reduces repeated attention while keeping feature-specific information**, and the model reaches competitive classification performance on `TabArena` and `BeyondArena`.

papers.title: Concurrent two-scale topology optimization of printable bone scaffolds via rectified-flow generation and exact latent-space refinement
papers.abstract: Bone scaffolds must reconcile a macroscale mechanical response with microscale geometric feasibility, yet conventional approaches to their design restrict attainable constitutive properties. This work presents a concurrent two-scale topology optimization framework; a conditional rectified flow generates periodic lattice microstructures, which are then refined in latent space by exact finite-element homogenization sensitivities. The resulting unit-cell geometries and their spatial assignments are jointly optimized under mechanical and feature-size constraints. In a distal rabbit femur benchmark, all eight flow-started refinements produce printable cells with maximum relative errors under 1\% across six prescribed engineering moduli. Constructing the implant from a single tiled cell reproduces intact whole-femur compliance within 0.1\% and regional strain energy within 0.35\% under four loading conditions. In human femoral reconstruction, multiscale concurrent optimization produces a cortical mid-shaft scaffold with porosity 63\% while satisfying the compliance constraint within 2\% under walking and stair-climbing loads. It achieves an 84\% porosity on a proximal cancellous scaffold with strain-energy deviations below 0.25\% under the same loads. Analysis of the learned representations reveals distinct architectural families in latent space. Further, the attention heads of the rectified-flow transformer specialize for spatial shifts -- learning the analogue of a finite-difference stencil -- and coordinate symmetries, with ablations showing their influence on generated topologies. These results establish a route to printable, mechanically constrained scaffold designs. The framework is general enough for extending to many other multiscale structural design applications including topology-microstructure co-design in metal additive manufacturing.
papers.summary: Bone scaffolds must match a required large-scale mechanical response while keeping their microscale geometry printable. The proposed framework designs both scales at once: a conditional rectified-flow model generates periodic lattice unit cells, which are then refined in latent space using exact finite-element homogenization sensitivities. In a rabbit femur benchmark, all refined cells were printable and **matched six prescribed engineering moduli to within 1% maximum relative error**. A human femoral reconstruction reached 63% porosity in a mid-shaft scaffold and 84% in a cancellous scaffold while meeting the stiffness (compliance) constraints. Analysis of the trained model shows that its attention heads specialize in spatial shifts, effectively learning a finite-difference stencil, and in coordinate symmetries.

papers.title: Flattening Fantasies: Analyzing Stereotypes in Pornographic Discourse
papers.abstract:
This study presents a large-scale quantitative analysis of 5.4 million video
  titles from xHamster, the world's fourth most visited pornography platform, to
  examine linguistic patterns used to describe different dimensions of
  identities (e.g., race and gender). Specifically, we investigate how
  nationalities, ethnic groups, and gender identities are portrayed in
  pornographic discourse, focusing on stereotypes and deviations from implicit
  norms of pornography. The results show the dominance of American pornography
  over other groups, which acts as the de facto norm for the adult industry. We
  identify persistent ethnic stereotypes reflecting colonial power dynamics,
  religious fetishization, and the sexualization of cultural taboos. The
  analysis reveals gendered representational differences across cultures, with a
  prevalent Madonna-Whore dichotomy in the portrayal of women and stereotypical
  depictions of men in physically dominant roles.
papers.summary: A quantitative linguistic analysis of 5.4 million video titles from `xHamster` examines how nationalities, ethnic groups, and gender identities are described in pornographic discourse. The study finds that **American pornography acts as the de facto norm** against which other groups are marked. It also finds persistent ethnic stereotypes reflecting colonial power dynamics, religious fetishization, and the sexualization of cultural taboos, and across cultures women are commonly portrayed through a Madonna-Whore dichotomy while men appear in physically dominant roles.

papers.title: Representations in Motion: Layer-wise Rotation and Trajectory Divergence in LLMs
papers.abstract: Recent work suggests that activation dynamics--how representations change during inference--might be more revealing about language model behavior than static readouts from individual layers. In this work, we investigate the layer-wise evolution of representations of factuality, using true and false statements when the model is prompted to either lie or to be honest. We report a geometric phenomenon in which the factuality directions extracted from the lying and honest conditions appear to rotate away from each other across layers. We find that such layer-wise rotation also occurs in a task that requires the model to take different visual perspectives in the 3D world, suggesting that the rotation phenomenon might be indicative of manipulating conceptual spaces in general, rather than unique to factuality. We then investigate the "real time" transformation of conceptual representations on a trial-to-trial basis. We show that it is possible to make strong predictions about the model's target task and behavior from trajectories alone. In addition, diverging points in single-trial trajectories correspond to the onset of rotation in aggregated-trial analysis. Finally, we show that both rotation and divergent trajectories occur in more naturalistic settings in which models are not overtly prompted to "lie" but rather report false statements in the course of completing a different task.
papers.summary: This study tracks how factuality representations change across layers when an LLM is prompted to lie or to be honest about true and false statements. The factuality directions extracted under the lying and honest conditions **rotate away from each other across layers**. The same rotation appears in a 3D visual perspective-taking task, which suggests it reflects a general manipulation of conceptual spaces rather than something specific to deception. Single-trial activation trajectories alone predict the model's target task and behavior well, their divergence points line up with where the rotation begins, and both effects also appear in naturalistic settings where models state falsehoods without being told to lie.

papers.title: Benchmark for Structured Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Perovskite Photovoltaics
papers.abstract: While retrieval-augmented language models increasingly serve as literature assistants in the physical sciences, existing benchmarks evaluate them primarily on qualitative text overlap or through model-based scoring rather than against verified experimental ground truth. In experimental materials disciplines such as perovskite photovoltaics, however, the most critical inquiries are inherently quantitative and aggregate measurements across dozens or hundreds of papers. Here, we present a quantitative question-answering benchmark where all 755 ground-truth answers are computed directly from 45,441 measured device records (40,889 human-curated records through 2021 and 4,552 records extracted from 2022-2026 literature). Benchmarking six retrieval architectures over 158,274 passages from 25,662 papers using an open 14B model on a single 24 GB GPU, standard passage retrieval tops out at 16-23% accuracy (compared to 1.6-6.5% zero-shot). In contrast, equipping the language model with read-only SQL execution over the structured device table elevates accuracy to 51.5% on historical and 50.8% on prospective literature -- a 33.01.8 percentage-point advantage over hybrid text retrieval. Aggregate queries spanning extrema, distributions, and filtered record counts prove virtually unsolvable via text retrieval alone, demonstrating that systematic table extraction is an operational prerequisite for literature-scale quantitative inquiry.
papers.summary: A new benchmark for retrieval-augmented language models in perovskite photovoltaics contains 755 quantitative questions. Every ground-truth answer is computed from 45,441 measured device records rather than judged by text overlap or another model. Six retrieval designs were tested over 158,274 passages using an open 14B model on a single 24 GB GPU, and standard passage retrieval reached only 16-23% accuracy. Giving the model read-only SQL access to the structured device table raised accuracy to **about 51% on both historical and newer literature, roughly 33 percentage points above hybrid text retrieval**.
