Aggregate queries such as extrema, distributions, and filtered counts were nearly unsolvable through text retrieval alone.

papers.title: Finite Interaction Lens: Structured Precision Sharing for Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Identifying which visual interventions interact in a vision-language model requires comparing their joint and separate effects. The resulting four-output difference can be small enough for rounding error to obscure it. We introduce the Finite Interaction Lens (FIL), a mixed-precision method for evaluating finite intervention families. At each selected linear projection, FIL decomposes each candidate's input into a native state, two single-intervention components, and a full-dimensional mixed residual. It projects the single-intervention components at higher precision and reuses the same numerical contributions in the joint candidates, while retaining every mixed residual and nonlinear trajectory. We derive a local cancellation identity and a conditional bound on error propagation through a smooth nonlinearity. In one MLP of Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct, FIL reduces final interaction MSE by 94.4% on 16 synthetic families and by 99.85% and 99.35% in two separate four-image COCO studies, relative to a control that has the same nominal BF16-product budget and higher-precision single interventions but projects each joint candidate independently. One image accounts for most of the absolute gain in each COCO study. Higher-accuracy multi-product BF16 arithmetic on all candidates gives lower aggregate error at similar total query times. Single-product BF16 already recovers the reference choices in both candidate-selection tasks we tested. On these development inputs, FIL improves interaction fidelity at a fixed nominal precision budget. Its practical value depends on a task that needs the extra fidelity.
papers.summary: Measuring whether two visual interventions interact in a vision-language model requires comparing their joint and separate effects, and the resulting difference can be small enough for rounding error to hide it. The `Finite Interaction Lens` (FIL) is a mixed-precision method that splits each projection input into a native state, single-intervention components, and a mixed residual. It computes the single-intervention components at higher precision and reuses those results across the joint candidates. In one MLP of `Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct`, FIL **cut interaction mean squared error by 94.4% on synthetic families and by over 99% in two `COCO` studies** relative to a budget-matched control. However, ordinary single-product BF16 arithmetic already recovered the correct choices in the candidate-selection tasks tested, so the extra fidelity matters only for tasks that need it.

papers.title: CVTA: Cross-Variable Temporal Attention for Multivariate Irregular Time Series Prediction
papers.abstract: Irregularly sampled multivariate time series arise in many real-world domains such as healthcare, climate science, and large-scale monitoring systems. Characterized by asynchronous observations and heterogeneity across variables, such time series pose significant challenges for forecasting. In this work, we introduce Cross-Variable Temporal Attention (CVTA), a short-term, continuous-time forecasting framework that learns prediction functions from its compact, interpretable state summarizing recent temporal dynamics across variables. CVTA uses Variable-Conditioned Embeddings to project heterogeneous variables into variable-specific latent spaces, and applies temporal attention to capture cross-variable dependencies from this state. Furthermore, we demonstrate that CVTA can be integrated as an auxiliary module into existing state-of-the-art prediction models through a dynamic meta-decision model. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world benchmarks show that CVTA achieves strong short-term predictive accuracy, supports efficient online inference, improves existing prediction models when used as an auxiliary module, and learns attention patterns that align well with domain knowledge.
papers.summary: Multivariate time series in healthcare, climate science, and monitoring are often sampled irregularly, with observations arriving at different times for different variables. `Cross-Variable Temporal Attention` (CVTA) is a short-term, continuous-time forecasting framework that projects each variable into its own latent space using variable-conditioned embeddings. It then applies temporal attention over a compact summary of recent dynamics to capture dependencies between variables. On real-world benchmarks CVTA delivers strong short-term accuracy and efficient online inference, and it also **improves existing state-of-the-art forecasters when added as an auxiliary module** through a dynamic meta-decision model.

papers.title: Assertion and Belief: Moore's Paradox in Language Models
papers.abstract: Moore's paradox \citep{moore1942} concerns sentences such as ``It is raining, but I don't believe that it is,'' which may well be true yet cannot be sensibly asserted. The absurdity lies not in the content but in the act, since to assert is to vouch for one's own belief. This makes the paradox a test of whether language models take the speech act into account when computing meaning. We present the first test of Moore's paradox in LLMs, evaluating 12 models on a curated set of Moorean sentences in varied contexts. We find that models largely recognize the infelicity of Moorean sentences, and that the judgement is not tied to a memorized form and tracks the speech act. Using the Rational Speech Act framework (RSA; \citealt{goodmanfrank2016}), we then test whether these judgements arise from a listener reasoning about a speaker. We find the models' own listeners do not reason about their own speakers, and their reasoning traces suggest that they instead recall knowledge about the paradox and apply rules therein. The models thus appear to have learned the paradox as a fact about sentences, not as a requirement on speakers.
papers.summary: Moore's paradox concerns sentences like "It is raining, but I don't believe that it is," which can be true but cannot sensibly be asserted, so it tests whether language models account for the speech act when computing meaning. Twelve LLMs largely recognize these sentences as infelicitous, and their judgments are not tied to a memorized surface form. Tests based on the `Rational Speech Act` (RSA) framework, however, show that the models' listeners do not reason about their own speakers, and their reasoning traces instead recall and apply knowledge about the paradox. The authors conclude that **models learned the paradox as a fact about sentences rather than as a requirement on speakers**.

papers.title: Divergence based Ranked Preference Alignment for LLMs
papers.abstract: Alignment of large language models typically relies on pairwise preference feedback, though ranked feedback can capture more comprehensive information across multiple responses within a single annotation. However, ranked-preference alignment is underexplored in practice compared to simpler pairwise approaches, potentially resulting in suboptimal behavior. Concurrently, recent research has conceptualized large language model alignment objectives as divergence estimators between aligned (preferred) and unaligned (less-preferred) response distributions, resulting in a family of objectives with an interpretable theoretical foundation and strong empirical performance. This work unifies these perspectives by introducing $f$-RPO, a $f$-divergence objective for ranked preference optimization that extends divergence-based alignment to ranked feedback and recovers pairwise preference alignment as a special case. Our theoretical analysis establishes rank-order consistency, showing that $f$-RPO preserves the underlying preference ordering at convergence. Empirical results indicate that total-variation and reverse-KL variants of the proposed objective consistently outperform ranked-alignment baselines in both ranking and generation quality across Qwen, Llama, & Gemma models ranging from 0.5B to 8B parameters.
papers.summary: LLM alignment usually relies on pairwise preferences, even though ranked feedback over several responses carries more information. `f-RPO` extends divergence-based alignment objectives to ranked preferences using f-divergences, and it recovers pairwise preference alignment as a special case. Theory shows that it preserves the underlying preference order at convergence. Experiments on `Qwen`, `Llama`, and `Gemma` models from 0.5B to 8B parameters show that its **total-variation and reverse-KL variants consistently beat ranked-alignment baselines** in both ranking and generation quality.

papers.title: Distributionally-Robust Policy Learning with Observational Data
papers.abstract: Policy learning from observational data is fundamental to applications ranging from personalized medicine to welfare-program targeting, but standard approaches optimize empirical performance and may fail when the deployment distribution differs from the training distribution. We study \emph{distributionally-robust policy learning}: given observational data, we seek a policy $\pi \in \Pi$ that maximizes the worst-case policy value over an $f$-divergence ball of radius $\rho$ around the data-generating distribution. We propose an estimator built on cross-fitted doubly-robust scores for the conditional treatment effect, paired with a DRO solver that handles \texttt{KL}, $\chi^2$, and \texttt{CVaR} ambiguity sets. We establish two convergence guarantees. First, the estimated policy attains the standard $\widetilde{O}(n^{-1/2})$ rate on its DRO regret, and inherits the doubly-robust property -- the rate continues to hold whenever either the outcome model or the propensity model is consistently estimated, even at slow nonparametric rates. We then propose a sample-splitting bias-correction algorithm derived from the Lagrangian dual, and show that under a Tsybakov-style margin condition on the treatment-effect, the estimator attains a fast rate of $\widetilde{O}(n^{-(1+\alpha)/(2+\alpha)})$ , interpolating between $\widetilde{O}(1/\sqrt{n})$ and $\widetilde{O}(1/n)$ as the margin parameter $\alpha$ ranges over $[0,\infty)$. To our knowledge, this is the first work to incorporate a margin condition into the analysis of distributionally-robust policy learning, and the first to obtain fast rates in this setting. Empirically, on synthetic and semi-synthetic experiments calibrated to a welfare-to-work program, distributional robustness yields meaningful improvements over empirical welfare maximization when training and test distributions differ.
papers.summary: Policies learned from observational data, for example in personalized medicine or welfare targeting, can fail when the deployment distribution differs from the training distribution. This work learns policies that maximize worst-case value over an f-divergence ball around the data distribution. It combines cross-fitted doubly-robust treatment-effect scores with a distributionally robust optimization (DRO) solver supporting KL, chi-squared, and CVaR ambiguity sets. The estimator achieves the standard root-n regret rate and keeps the doubly-robust property, and a bias-corrected variant under a margin condition reaches **the first fast rates for distributionally robust policy learning**. Experiments calibrated to a welfare-to-work program show gains over empirical welfare maximization under distribution shift.

papers.title: Cognitive Map in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: It has long been proposed that animals construct cognitive maps to support flexible behavior in novel environments. We tested whether large language models form similar representations using relational reasoning tasks and causal "mosaic experiments" that manipulate internal activations in open-weight language models. Models beyond the ten-billion-parameter scale successfully inferred unstated relationships between entities and generalized to synthetic entity names. Across model and task families, models generated abstract representations of relational structure and combined them additively with representations of entity identity, binding entities to roles within that structure. Models stored observed relationships as pairwise links that they composed retrospectively when queried, rather than prospectively positioning each entity in a global coordinate system. Binding was mediated by a sparse, distributed set of key--value pairs; by perturbing these pairs, we implanted "false memories" that altered model behavior in predictable ways. Overall, our findings reveal an internal organization analogous to a cognitive map that explains how language models reason with limited information.
papers.summary: Relational reasoning tasks and causal "mosaic experiments" that edit internal activations were used to test whether open-weight LLMs build something like the cognitive maps animals use. Models above roughly ten billion parameters inferred unstated relationships and generalized to synthetic entity names. They did this by encoding abstract relational structure additively with entity identity, binding each entity to a role within the structure. Rather than placing entities in a global coordinate system, the models **store pairwise links and compose them only when queried**. This binding runs through a sparse set of key-value pairs, and perturbing those pairs implanted predictable "false memories."

papers.title: Text Dominance in Paralinguistic Conflict: Tracing Suppression Through Audio LLM Circuits
papers.abstract: Audio LLMs deployed in settings such as crisis hotlines and customer support are only useful beyond speech-to-text pipelines if they use acoustic cues rather than the transcript alone. We test whether they prioritise transcript content over paralinguistic cues (emotion, speaker identity, sarcasm) and trace the mechanism when they do. Across six audio LLMs under LISTEN-style conflict conditions, the mean text-dominance rate on mismatched text+audio items is 0.78 (0.86 excluding sarcasm). In the most text-dominant screened model, probing shows speaker identity remains linearly decodable at ceiling at the language model's input, so the failure is not perceptual. Back-patching, reported to repair lexical text dominance, has no measurable effect here; but it also fails on its own source task in our replication (n=300), so we treat its null as uninformative rather than as evidence of non-transfer. Attention knockout partially restores audio-grounded output by blocking the claim from propagating through intermediate tokens during open-ended generation, whereas blocking the answer position's direct connection to the conflicting claim has no effect. The claim's influence therefore travels through an intermediate relay rather than a single severable edge. The effect appears only in free-form generation and not in closed-set multiple choice, suggesting that benchmarks relying on that format may be systematically blind to interventions of this kind. Code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/AdvayRoongta/audio-llm-mech-interp.
papers.summary: Audio LLMs used in settings like crisis hotlines are valuable only if they use acoustic cues and not just the transcript. Across six models given text and audio that conflict on emotion, speaker identity, or sarcasm, **the mean text-dominance rate was 0.78**, meaning the models mostly followed the transcript. In the most text-dominant model, speaker identity was still linearly decodable at the language model's input, so the failure is not perceptual. Attention knockout showed that the conflicting claim's influence travels through intermediate tokens rather than a single direct connection. Because this effect appeared only in free-form generation and not in multiple choice, benchmarks that use the multiple-choice format may miss it entirely.

papers.title: Adversarial Post-Training of Foundation Models for High-Frequency Trading
papers.abstract: While autoregressive foundation models trained on limit order book (LOB) data show state-of-the-art performance for market simulation, pre-training with cross-entropy neither penalizes the compounding of sampling errors over free-running rollouts nor targets desired market properties. We introduce a post-training method for LOB foundation models using a Wasserstein generative adversarial network (GAN) objective. A critic, trained online on rollouts through the true, non-differentiable matching engine, guides updates from evolution strategies over rank-4 LoRA perturbations of the pre-trained generator, under a KL trust region. For efficiency, we use EGGROLL (Evolution Guided GeneRal Optimisation via Low-rank Learning), a memory-efficient variant of evolution strategies. On a held-out panel, adversarial post-training improves LOB-Bench realism by 17.6% (WS-21) and 17.0% (Mean-$L_1$), while selection-matched random-perturbation and compute-matched continued-pre-training controls yield no improvement. Post-training is thus a necessary stage that more pre-training does not replace. Per-position divergence measurements show that it slows error accumulation over 500-message rollouts from $3.1\times$ to $2.3\times$. Adversarial post-training is also inexpensive, requiring under 50M training tokens and 12 GPU-hours per seed, three orders of magnitude below the 48B-token pre-training budget. Ablations over critic inputs, optimizers, and the population-rollout trade-off, together with an analysis of reward hacking, yield practical design guidelines for adversarial post-training.
papers.summary: Autoregressive foundation models trained on limit order book (LOB) data simulate markets well, but cross-entropy pre-training does not penalize errors that compound during long free-running generation. The proposed post-training uses a Wasserstein GAN critic trained on rollouts through the real, non-differentiable matching engine. That critic guides `EGGROLL`, a memory-efficient evolution-strategies method, over low-rank LoRA perturbations of the generator. This **improves `LOB-Bench` realism by about 17%**, whereas compute-matched continued pre-training and random-perturbation controls bring no gain, and it costs under 50M tokens and 12 GPU-hours per seed. Error accumulation over 500-message rollouts also slows, from 3.1x to 2.3x.

papers.title: PRISM: Prior Relational Information for Self-supervised Modeling to Enhance Solubility OOD Generalization
papers.abstract: Solubility depends on intermolecular interactions between solutes and solvents, and is central to drug discovery, chemical and materials process engineering. Its prediction requires out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization to unseen solutes, solvents, and solvent mixtures, where supervised methods suffer from data scarcity, and existing self-supervised methods do not explicitly learn chemically meaningful relations. Learning chemically meaningful relational information without labels can alleviate data scarcity and improve OOD generalization, but remains challenging. We introduce Prior Relational Information for Self-supervised Modeling (PRISM) and apply it to solubility OOD generalization. PRISM is a label-free pretraining framework that converts expert-defined chemical priors into relational teachers. For solubility prediction, it trains four encoders to preserve the population-level relational information from priors capturing hydrophobic, electrostatic, polarizability, and substructural effects, using Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence to match distance-based neighborhood distributions during pretraining. Across scaffold, solute, and solvent OOD settings, PRISM matches or surpasses supervised and self-supervised baselines. Under mixed-solvent OOD, freezing the four PRISM encoders and training a lightweight fusion-and-composition head outperforms strong baselines and substantially reduces run-to-run variation. Ablations and control studies confirm that gains stem from chemically meaningful relational structures baked into the encoders by PRISM. We expect this strategy of turning relational priors into self-supervision signals to extend beyond solubility prediction to domains where chemically or biologically meaningful relational priors are available.
papers.summary: Predicting solubility requires generalizing to unseen solutes, solvents, and solvent mixtures, where labeled data is scarce. `PRISM` is a label-free pretraining framework that turns expert chemical priors into teachers. It trains four encoders to preserve the neighborhood relationships implied by hydrophobic, electrostatic, polarizability, and substructural priors, matching distance-based neighborhood distributions with KL divergence. PRISM matches or beats supervised and self-supervised baselines across scaffold, solute, and solvent out-of-distribution splits. On mixed solvents, a lightweight head on the frozen encoders **outperforms strong baselines while substantially reducing run-to-run variance**.

papers.title: Safety Offset Learning: When Benign Fine-Tuning Misaligns LLMs
papers.abstract: Safety risks from fine-tuning are commonly characterized by the harmfulness of the training data:harmful fine-tuning is considered dangerous, while benign fine-tuning is often assumed to preservealignment. We argue that this view misses a more fundamental factor-the behavioral transition inducedby supervision. Harmful fine-tuning and safety-degrading benign fine-tuning can both be understoodas learning the same refusal-to-compliance transition, but on different data distributions. We studywhether such a transition learned on benign inputs can generalize to harmful requests. We constructbenign examples that an aligned model initially tends to refuse and pair them with their originalharmless responses, creating a discrepancy between the model's initial refusal and the supervisedanswer. Fine-tuning on these examples increases harmful compliance, but only when two conditionshold together: the discrepancy is large enough, and it cannot be resolved through a narrow surface-levelshortcut. With the induced discrepancy matched, varying only whether it is localized changes harmfulcompliance by an order of magnitude; raising the discrepancy does not help while a shortcut remainsavailable, and removing the shortcut does not help while the discrepancy is small. Building on thisobservation, we introduce SAFEOFF, a dataset of benign instructions rewritten to raise the alignedmodel's refusal likelihood and paired with their original answers. Across three aligned LLMs and threesafety benchmarks, SAFEOFF substantially weakens safety alignment despite containing no explicitharmful supervision, suggesting that fine-tuning safety depends not only on what data a model sees, butalso on which behavioral boundary the supervision moves.
papers.summary: Fine-tuning on benign data can erode safety alignment, and the authors argue that what matters is the behavioral transition the supervision induces rather than how harmful the data is. They build benign examples that an aligned model tends to refuse and pair them with their original harmless answers. Fine-tuning on these examples raises harmful compliance, but only when the gap between the model's refusal and the supervised answer is large and cannot be closed by a narrow surface-level shortcut. The resulting `SAFEOFF` dataset **substantially weakens safety alignment across three aligned LLMs and three safety benchmarks despite containing no harmful supervision**.

papers.title: Curriculum Learning Teaches LLMs Long-Horizon Implicit Reasoning, Up To A Limit
papers.abstract: LLMs "reason" by externalizing intermediate steps as tokens through chain-of-thought (CoT), yet even frontier reasoning models hit abrupt performance cliffs on long-horizon tasks. Implicit reasoning (reasoning within a single forward pass) is useful during CoT generation, as the model can "search ahead" to decide the correct next move without explicit search. Models with weak implicit reasoning are more likely to commit to wrong paths and must attempt to recover via backtracking, while models with strong implicit reasoning identify the correct proof strategy directly, shortening the CoT. However, prior work shows LLMs struggle to reason implicitly beyond shallow depths, with no relief from scale. We investigate whether curriculum learning can extend this depth by fine-tuning on examples with progressively increasing vocabulary size and lookahead (the number of steps a model must search ahead to identify the correct next move). At matched compute, curriculum-trained models achieve lookaheads where no-curriculum training fails. Qwen3-0.6B reaches 98% accuracy on problems with lookahead up to 256 with curriculum, compared to 45% without. However, progress slows as fine-tuning continues, following a saturating exponential that suggests a maximum intrinsic lookahead to which models can learn to reason implicitly. Larger models reach higher fitted ceilings, fine-tuning pretrained models far outpaces training from scratch, and curriculum step sizes that are too large stall progression. Finally, the capability acquired on synthetic data transfers to natural language reasoning, with curriculum-trained models outperforming models trained without curriculum at matched compute on 11 natural language reasoning benchmarks.
papers.summary: LLMs struggle to reason implicitly within a single forward pass beyond shallow depths, and scale alone does not fix this. Fine-tuning with a curriculum that gradually increases vocabulary size and lookahead (how many steps ahead the model must search to choose the correct next move) extends that depth: **`Qwen3-0.6B` reaches 98% accuracy at lookahead up to 256 versus 45% without a curriculum** at matched compute. Gains follow a saturating exponential, which points to a maximum intrinsic lookahead; larger models reach higher ceilings, and curriculum steps that are too large stall progress. The skill learned on synthetic data transfers to 11 natural-language reasoning benchmarks.

papers.title: CheXFuse: Guided Differential Joint Attention Fusion for Robust Multimodal Chest X-Ray Classification in Data-Scarce Medical Settings
papers.abstract: A central challenge in multimodal learning is how to fuse modalities that differ substantially in predictive strength. When one modality provides a much stronger representation than another, indiscriminate cross-modal interaction can introduce weak, redundant, or unstable signals, limiting or even degrading performance relative to the strongest unimodal representation. To address this problem, we propose CheXFuse, a multimodal fusion framework based on Guided Differential Joint Attention (GuDJA). CheXFuse combines image and text token representations within a joint multimodal sequence, where learned token guidance emphasizes informative representations and differential attention reduces less useful attention responses. We evaluate CheXFuse on the Indiana University (IU) Chest X-ray dataset, using binary (normal vs. abnormal) classification as the downstream task. Experiments are conducted under both original-report and masked-report settings, with the latter serving as a controlled stress test under reduced textual informativeness. CheXFuse with GuDJA achieves the strongest mean overall performance across the evaluated baselines and ablations, reaching 95.73% accuracy, 95.79% F1-score, 96.54% recall, and 95.28% sensitivity at 95% specificity (Sens@95Spec) with original reports, and 95.58%, 95.60%, 95.60%, and 94.34%, respectively, under masked reports. These results suggest that GuDJA provides a promising fusion strategy under asymmetric or partially reduced modality informativeness.
papers.summary: When one modality is much more informative than another, unrestricted cross-modal fusion can inject noise and even underperform the stronger modality alone. `CheXFuse` fuses chest X-ray images and report text in a joint token sequence using `Guided Differential Joint Attention` (GuDJA), where learned token guidance emphasizes informative tokens and differential attention suppresses less useful attention responses. On normal-versus-abnormal classification on the `IU Chest X-ray` dataset, it **reaches 95.73% accuracy with original reports and 95.58% with masked reports**, the best mean performance among the evaluated baselines and ablations.

papers.title: Weighted State Souping for Efficient Long-Context Retrieval
papers.abstract: State space models (SSMs) combine fast inference and fixed state size with competitive language-modeling performance. Recently, state souping has been proposed as a procedure whereby an SSM independently encodes chunks of tokens like documents, tool definitions, or memory records. The resulting state encodings may be cached and recombined to cheaply construct a context for downstream queries. However, both state souping and vanilla SSMs deteriorate on long, crowded contexts, limiting their utility for long-horizon domains. To address this issue, we propose weighted state souping, a simple method that learns query-dependent weights for composing cached states. The resulting models improve long-context performance substantially across both single- and multi-hop document question answering, needle-in-a-haystack retrieval, variable tracking, and tool use. Our method can be further adapted into an efficient sparse variant, yielding near-constant encoding cost with respect to context length while preserving (and sometimes improving) performance. We also present simple theoretical arguments that illustrate why souping works and when it may fail, and discuss informally the advantages of weighted souping. Weighted state souping thus combines reusable context representations with selective retrieval, offering an efficient approach to language modeling over large collections of documents, tools, and other forms of structured context that increasingly dominate modern agentic workloads.
papers.summary: State space models (SSMs) can encode chunks such as documents, tool definitions, or memory records separately, then cache and recombine those states in a procedure called state souping, but performance degrades on long, crowded contexts. Weighted state souping learns query-dependent weights for combining the cached states, which **substantially improves long-context performance** on single- and multi-hop question answering, needle-in-a-haystack retrieval, variable tracking, and tool use. A sparse variant keeps encoding cost nearly constant as context grows while preserving or sometimes improving accuracy. The authors present the approach as an efficient way to handle large collections of documents and tools in agentic workloads.

papers.title: Zephyrus-R1: Agentic Reinforcement Learning for Weather Reporting
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a key method for training AI models in scientific applications, but RL remains difficult when outputs cannot easily be verified against a known ground-truth answer. Natural-language weather forecast reports are one such domain: they translate atmospheric data into assessments of weather evolution, hazards, and uncertainty for both the general public and key decision-makers. Unlike numerical weather-analysis questions, they admit many valid outputs, which limits deterministic verification. To address this, we develop Zephyrus-R1, a practical framework for RL on scientific weather forecast reporting. We focus on three key components of the agentic RL pipeline: reward design, curriculum learning, and an analysis of human-expert alignment. To encourage both report legibility and factual accuracy, we design a reward function that combines a meteorological rubric with bidirectional claim entailment, both evaluated against National Weather Service reference reports. Our framework optimizes this reward in a simulated tool-calling environment, enabling vision-language agents to gather and analyze forecast evidence across regions and lead times before producing a report. We use annotations from three meteorologists to audit the claim labels produced by our LLM judges. Finally, a curriculum helps small models first develop tool use and scientific reasoning through RL on verifiable weather-analysis questions, then optimize the open-ended report reward. After training Qwen3.5-4B with Zephyrus-R1, we improve the mean across six judge-metric scores by 26% over the base model and achieve results competitive with frontier open-weight models. For Qwen3.8-27B, we improve the same mean by 13% over the base model, by 6.7% over Kimi-K3, and by 2.7% over GPT-5.6-Luna.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning is hard to apply to natural-language weather forecast reports because many different outputs can be valid, so they cannot be checked against a single known answer. `Zephyrus-R1` addresses this with a reward that combines a meteorological rubric with bidirectional claim entailment against National Weather Service reports. Vision-language agents are trained in a simulated tool-calling environment, and a curriculum first builds tool use on verifiable weather-analysis questions before moving to the open-ended reports. Three meteorologists audited the LLM judges' claim labels. Training **improves `Qwen3.5-4B` by 26% over its base model** across six judge metrics, and the trained `Qwen3.8-27B` edges out `Kimi-K3` and `GPT-5.6-Luna`.

papers.title: MapSteal: Map-based Autonomous Knowledge Stealing Attack Against Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Knowledge acquisition from black-box large language models (LLMs) offers a practical approach to adapting smaller student models. However, many existing methods rely on predefined queries or student feedback to guide acquisition, leaving autonomous expansion of knowledge targets an important challenge. We propose \textbf{MapSteal}, a student-independent framework for structured recursive knowledge acquisition. Starting from a small set of initial roots, MapSteal represents acquisition targets using structured states and recursively expands them through teacher-proposed directions. Question realization, proposal admission, and deduplication constrain the acquisition process, while root-aware scheduling organizes exploration under a fixed QA budget. The resulting question--answer pairs are used to adapt student models without requiring student feedback during acquisition. Experiments with Qwen3.5 students at 2B, 4B, and 9B scales show competitive downstream performance across six medical and cybersecurity benchmarks. On the 4B medical evaluation, Full MapSteal improves average accuracy by 1.17 percentage points over a simplified recursive acquisition variant. Cross-domain evaluations show that gains depend on the domain and evaluation panel. These results demonstrate the feasibility of structured, student-independent recursive acquisition while highlighting the distinction between generating acquisition targets and obtaining useful training supervision. Our code is available at \href{https://github.com/LabRAI/Mapsteal} {https://github.com/LabRAI/Mapsteal}.
papers.summary: Pulling knowledge out of a black-box large language model (LLM) to adapt a smaller student model usually depends on a fixed set of queries or on feedback from the student. `MapSteal` needs neither. It starts from a few seed topics, stores what to ask about as structured states, and has the teacher model propose new directions to expand them recursively, with filters for turning targets into questions, admitting proposals, and removing duplicates, plus a scheduler that spreads a fixed question-answer budget across the seed topics. Students from `Qwen3.5` at 2B, 4B, and 9B parameters trained on the collected pairs perform competitively on six medical and cybersecurity benchmarks. However, the full method beats a simplified recursive variant by only **1.17 percentage points** on the 4B medical evaluation, and gains in other domains depend on the domain and the evaluation set.

papers.title: Conditional Average Treatment Effect Distillation for Hypothetical State-Intervention Targeting Under Budget Constraints
papers.abstract: Personalized public-health targeting must capture heterogeneous intervention benefits while remaining interpretable under resource constraints. Flexible causal-effect models can be hard to operationalize, while coarse subgroup policies may lose individualized effect information. We study budget-constrained hypothetical state interventions in observational data without a logged historical decision policy. For obesity, elevated glucose, and lifetime smoking-history states, causal-structure-informed pretreatment covariates are prespecified, with capacity capped at 70% of those observed in the adverse state. We evaluate causal distillation where Causal Forest and Bayesian Causal Forest teachers estimate conditional average treatment effects (CATEs), which decision tree and random forest students approximate. We compare individualized policies with unsupervised K-means subgroup policies and supervised causal-tree policies with leaf counts matched to K-means cluster counts. Observational policies are assessed on held-out data using a doubly robust estimator, bootstrap uncertainty, and decision-focused teacher-student fidelity measures. Across PIMA obesity and glucose and NHANES smoking-history experiments, each distilled student was within 0.011 absolute utility of its teacher, with allocation Jaccard similarities of 0.738-0.937. K-means and causal-tree policies were also competitive, with the highest point-estimate policy varying by application. Prespecified paired comparisons were nonsignificant after Holm adjustment, while near-budget-boundary agreement was less stable than global fidelity for some teacher-student pairs. Findings support causal distillation for translating flexible effect models into simpler budgeted targeting rules, although observational estimates depend on causal-identification assumptions and require longitudinal or prospective validation.
papers.summary: The authors study how to target public-health interventions under a budget using observational data, where flexible causal models are hard to put into practice and coarse subgroup rules lose individual detail. `Causal Forest` and `Bayesian Causal Forest` teachers estimate conditional average treatment effects (CATEs), and decision-tree and random-forest students are trained to copy them. These distilled policies are compared with `K-means` subgroup policies and causal-tree policies on obesity, glucose, and smoking-history targets from `PIMA` and `NHANES`, with capacity capped at 70% of the people in the adverse state. Each distilled student came within **0.011 absolute utility of its teacher**, with allocation Jaccard similarities of 0.738 to 0.937. The simpler subgroup policies were also competitive, and no prespecified paired comparison stayed significant after Holm correction.

papers.title: Clean Forcing: Drift-Resistant Autoregressive Video Diffusion with a Frozen Base
papers.abstract: Autoregressive (AR) video diffusion models generate streaming video of arbitrary length by conditioning each new chunk of frames on those already generated. However, they suffer from exposure bias, where a model trained on clean context must continue from its own imperfect outputs, and errors compound until quality collapses within seconds (drift). Existing methods either require cluster-scale base retraining, apply training-free inference corrections with inconsistent results, or train frozen-base correctors for sampling and cache errors. We instead find that drift is largely deterministic and therefore learnable, as holding the noisy state fixed while varying only the history reveals a counterfactual velocity gap that is ~95% systematic across noise seeds. Based on this observation, we introduce Clean Forcing, which trains a 5.9M-parameter LoRA corrector on the frozen base model to regress this gap, with a closed-loop stage that adds DAgger-style aggregation and a drift-contraction objective to expose the corrector to its own rollouts. Because the clean histories can be the base model's own single-shot generations, training needs no real videos, and the merged corrector adds no inference cost. In 50 s text-to-video generation, Clean Forcing reduces {\Delta}-drift from +11.3 to +1.65 without real video and to -0.16 with 40 real clips, improving on the best published result of +3.57 with over 150x less data. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Clean Forcing outperforms prior methods in aesthetic quality and data efficiency with reduced drift for long-horizon video generation.
papers.summary: Autoregressive video diffusion models generate long videos chunk by chunk, but because they are trained on clean context and must continue from their own imperfect output, errors compound and quality drifts within seconds. The authors find that this drift is largely deterministic: the velocity gap caused by a degraded history is about 95% systematic across noise seeds, which means a model can learn to correct it. `Clean Forcing` trains a 5.9M-parameter `LoRA` corrector on a frozen base model to predict this gap, with a closed-loop stage that uses `DAgger`-style aggregation and a drift-contraction objective. The corrector can learn from the base model's own generations and adds no inference cost once merged. On 50-second text-to-video generation it cuts Δ-drift from +11.3 to +1.65 with no real video and to **-0.16 with 40 real clips**, beating the best published +3.57 with over 150x less data.

papers.title: Uncertainty-Gated SHAP-Dirichlet Refinement for MRI-Based Depression Classification
papers.abstract: Structural MRI-based classification of major depressive disorder (MDD) remains challenging due to subtle, heterogeneous anatomical changes. We propose uncertainty-gated SHAP-Dirichlet refinement, a post-hoc reliability layer that improves predictions without retraining the classifier. The method retrieves similar labeled SHAP explanations, constructs Dirichlet class evidence, and selectively refines uncertain predictions through probabilistic fusion, while allowing unreliable cases to be deferred for expert review. We evaluate five classifiers on 504 SRPBS subjects (252 controls and 252 MDD patients) using 159 anatomical features and repeated nested cross-validation. Refinement improved accuracy across all 8 repetitions for TabM and ResNet, yielding mean gains of 1.04 and 0.45 percentage points (sign test p=0.008), while modifying at most 8.3% of predictions. Gains were concentrated among low-confidence cases, with significant improvements in calibration. The method also benefited an RBF support vector machine but not logistic regression or random forests. Ablations confirmed the importance of uncertainty gating and soft fusion. Dirichlet evidence identified baseline errors (AUROC 0.62), while deferring 50% of cases increased retained-case accuracy to approximately 75%. These findings support selective explanation-guided refinement as a practical approach to improving prediction reliability and facilitating expert triage in MDD classification.
papers.summary: Classifying major depressive disorder (MDD) from structural MRI is hard because the anatomical changes are subtle and vary between patients. The proposed post-hoc layer leaves the trained classifier unchanged. For each case it retrieves labeled cases with similar `SHAP` explanations, builds Dirichlet class evidence from them, and revises only uncertain predictions through soft probabilistic fusion, while unreliable cases can be sent to an expert. On 504 `SRPBS` subjects, refinement raised accuracy in all 8 repetitions for `TabM` and `ResNet`, with mean gains of **1.04 and 0.45 percentage points**, while changing at most 8.3% of predictions and improving calibration. It did not help logistic regression or random forests.

papers.title: Sampling of Signals on Multigraphs: From Removable and Uniqueness sets to Spectral Proxies
papers.abstract: In this paper, we study the sampling of bandlimited signals on multigraphs, where several graphs with different shift operators are defined on the same set of nodes. Since the shift operators do not commute in general, they admit only a joint block diagonalization, and the frequencies of the multigraph signal model are matrices rather than scalars. Relying on a formal algebraic convolutional signal model, we introduce a notion of frequency and bandwidth for multigraph signals that does not depend on any individual layer, and we extend the notions of removable and uniqueness sets to multigraphs. We prove that the optimality of a sampling set is determined exclusively by the common Fourier basis and its invariant subspaces, and not by any individual layer, although the individual layers provide computable sufficient conditions that certify a sampling set as a uniqueness set. Since identifying which layers provide reliable certificates requires spectral information, we propose an aggregate operator that pools the information of all the layers, is computable directly from the shift operators, and certifies uniqueness without any assumption on the individual layers. This operator leads to a greedy sampling algorithm that does not require computing the joint block diagonalization. Numerical experiments on multigraphs whose layers order the frequencies inconsistently show that the proposed algorithm selects better-conditioned sampling sets and attains lower reconstruction errors than single-layer methods.
papers.summary: The authors extend graph signal sampling to multigraphs, where several graphs with non-commuting shift operators share one set of nodes, so frequencies become matrices rather than scalars. Using an algebraic convolutional signal model, they define frequency, bandwidth, and removable and uniqueness sets for multigraph signals. They prove that whether a sampling set is optimal depends **only on the common Fourier basis and its invariant subspaces**, not on any single layer. They then propose an aggregate operator, computable directly from the shift operators, that certifies uniqueness and supports a greedy sampling algorithm without joint block diagonalization. In experiments it picks better-conditioned sampling sets and achieves lower reconstruction error than single-layer methods.

papers.title: Spherical Fixed-Point Reasoners: Adaptive Loop Halting on the Hypersphere
papers.abstract: Looped (weight-tied) transformers enable adaptive computation by allocating more iterations to harder inputs. Fixed-Point Reasoners (FPRM) achieve this with a damped fixed-point solver, but operate in an unbounded Euclidean residual space with coupled rescaling and relative-norm halting. We introduce Spherical Fixed-Point Reasoners (SFPRM), which perform the same computation on the unit hypersphere of normalized transformers (nGPT). Input injection, damping, and halting become geodesic operations, yielding boundedness by construction and eliminating coefficient coupling. We prove fixed-point existence, local convergence under an explicit step-size condition, and global convergence under strong injection. On Sudoku-Extreme, Maze-Hard, and Mini-ARC, SFPRM achieves 96.6%, 87.9%, and 59.1% test accuracy, respectively, outperforming FPRM and other baselines while allocating test-time compute more effectively. Its converged geometry is also interpretable: token-input angles capture puzzle structure and predict correctness.
papers.summary: Looped (weight-tied) transformers can spend more iterations on harder inputs. The earlier Fixed-Point Reasoners (`FPRM`) do this with a damped fixed-point solver in an unbounded Euclidean space, where rescaling and halting decisions are coupled. `SFPRM` moves the same computation onto the unit hypersphere of normalized transformers (`nGPT`), so input injection, damping, and halting become geodesic operations that are bounded by construction. The authors prove that a fixed point exists, that the iteration converges locally under an explicit step-size condition, and that it converges globally under strong injection. `SFPRM` reaches **96.6% on `Sudoku-Extreme`**, 87.9% on `Maze-Hard`, and 59.1% on `Mini-ARC`, beating `FPRM` and other baselines while using test-time compute more effectively.

papers.title: Consistency Training Suppresses Cue Following Without Teaching Cue Selectivity
papers.abstract: Language models often change answers because of a cue, a hint such as "I believe the answer is B" that gives no valid evidence. Consistency training (CT) trains a model to answer the same with and without the cue. Four CT methods apply this idea to output tokens (BCT), residual activations (ACT), attention patterns (AttCT) and sampled-answer rates (RMCT). Prior work suggests some learn different solutions. We train all four on Gemma-2-2B-it and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with the same data. We test predictions written in advance and inspect the models with a known circuit that carries cues to the answer. All four make the trained cue less effective, and their fixes share three properties. First, correct cues lose about as much influence as wrong ones. Second, the fix is usually large for cues before the answer options, as in training, and much smaller after them. Llama RMCT depends least on position. Third, the circuit heads still carry most remaining cue-induced errors. Making BCT targets depend on the cue's correctness mostly weakens the fix. CT thus weakens the trained cue without teaching models when a cue is right. Evaluations with only wrong cues at the trained position miss the first two properties.
papers.summary: Language models often switch answers because of a cue that offers no real evidence, such as "I believe the answer is B." Consistency training (CT) tries to fix this by training the model to answer the same way with and without the cue. The authors train four CT variants, acting on output tokens (`BCT`), residual activations (`ACT`), attention patterns (`AttCT`), and sampled-answer rates (`RMCT`), on `Gemma-2-2B-it` and `Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct`, and test predictions registered in advance against a known cue-carrying circuit. All four weaken the trained cue in similar ways: **correct cues lose about as much influence as wrong ones**, the effect is much smaller when the cue appears after the answer options instead of before them, and the same circuit heads still carry most of the remaining errors. CT therefore suppresses cue following without teaching the model when a cue is right, and evaluations that use only wrong cues in the trained position miss this.

papers.title: OPDArena: Understanding Learning and Forgetting in On-Policy Distillation
papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) is increasingly used for language model post-training, yet how teacher supervision shapes learning and forgetting remains unclear. We present OPDArena, a framework comparing supervised fine-tuning (SFT), reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), and OPD across five pretrained models and diverse teacher sources. It jointly evaluates mathematical learning, general capability retention, and predictive distribution changes. Teacher choice strongly shapes retention: students of RLVR-trained teachers improve on the target task while retaining prior capabilities, whereas students of SFT-trained teachers incur greater capability loss. Across post-training methods, out-of-domain (OOD) distribution change shows a more consistent positive association with forgetting than in-domain change. To understand how teacher choice affects these changes, we examine the additional information teachers provide relative to the student's pretrained model. Controlled teacher comparisons show that the task-specific preferences teachers acquire through post-training make student updates more concentrated in-domain.
papers.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) is increasingly used to post-train language models, but it is unclear how the teacher's supervision affects what the student learns and what it forgets. `OPDArena` compares supervised fine-tuning (SFT), reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), and OPD across five pretrained models and several teacher sources, measuring math learning, retention of general capabilities, and shifts in the predictive distribution. Teacher choice matters most: **students of RLVR-trained teachers improve on the target task while keeping prior capabilities**, whereas students of SFT-trained teachers lose more. Across all methods, distribution change on out-of-domain data tracks forgetting more consistently than in-domain change. Controlled comparisons suggest that task-specific preferences teachers pick up during post-training keep student updates concentrated in-domain.

papers.title: A "feature ODE" describing the learning behavior of shallow MLPs on simple functions
papers.abstract: We study the gradient flow training dynamics of two-layer multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) on anisotropic Gaussian data. Even in this simple setting, solving the dynamics in full is notoriously difficult, so we try something different. We propose a "feature ODE" that might be intuitively expected to describe the learning dynamics of a shallow MLP. We find that MLPs trained to learn simple target functions (low-order Hermite polynomials and staircase functions) actually roughly follow the loss trajectories from this feature ODE. This agreement is a surprise because of the size of the simplification and the fact that it does not come from a rigorous chain of approximations. We discuss this surprise and speculate on its reasons and uses.
papers.summary: Solving the gradient-flow training dynamics of two-layer multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) exactly is notoriously hard, even on anisotropic Gaussian data. Instead, the authors write down a heuristic "feature ODE" that one might intuitively expect to describe how a shallow MLP learns. MLPs trained on simple targets, namely low-order Hermite polynomials and staircase functions, **roughly follow the loss trajectories the feature ODE predicts**. The agreement is unexpected because the ODE is a large simplification and is not derived through a rigorous chain of approximations, and the authors speculate on why it works and how it might be used.

papers.title: Knowledge Manifold Optimization for Scientific Discovery
papers.abstract: The rapid expansion and specialization of scientific literature make it increasingly difficult to identify not only what is known, but where new and still supportable knowledge may emerge. We introduce Knowledge Manifold Optimization (KMO), a discovery-oriented extension of the Knowledge Manifold framework that treats scientific discovery as a multiobjective search over a continuous, literature-derived knowledge space. Candidate locations are evaluated using four complementary objectives: persistent knowledge-regime boundary strength, band-pass white-space novelty, semanticgradient magnitude, and evidential support. Rather than collapsing these criteria into a single weighted score, KMO identifies Pareto-optimal Supported Knowledge Gaps, defined as corpus-relative unoccupied regions that remain sufficiently supported by surrounding literature. The method is demonstrated on a 99-paper corpus in aerodynamics and aerodynamic design. On a 21 x 21 grid, exact Pareto analysis produced 19 non-dominated points, of which 16 formed the practical front after excluding points with zero white-space score. These solutions exhibited distinct discovery modes, including methodology bridges, aero-structural topology/FSI integration, functional aerodynamic-device integration, and rear-wake/vehicle flow-control integration. A distance-maximization baseline preferentially selected extrapolative regions with substantially lower support and reliability, demonstrating why emptiness alone is insufficient. Representative Pareto locations were converted into auditable evidence packages and then verbalized by a constrained large language model into candidate research hypotheses. The results show that scientific discovery can be formulated as structured multi-objective search in an explicit knowledge space, while keeping novelty corpus-relative and separating numerical discovery from downstream language generation.
papers.summary: As the scientific literature grows, it gets harder to see where new findings could still be supported by existing work. Knowledge Manifold Optimization (`KMO`) treats discovery as a multi-objective search over a continuous knowledge space built from a corpus. It scores candidate locations on knowledge-regime boundary strength, white-space novelty, semantic-gradient magnitude, and evidential support, and keeps the Pareto-optimal "supported knowledge gaps" instead of collapsing the objectives into a single weighted score. On a 99-paper aerodynamics corpus, exact Pareto analysis of a 21 x 21 grid gave **16 practical front points** in distinct discovery modes, while a baseline that simply maximizes distance chose extrapolative regions with much less support. Selected points are turned into auditable evidence packages, which a constrained LLM then phrases as candidate research hypotheses.

papers.title: Can Metadata Fix the Gauge? Calibration Turns Sparse Multi-Source Learning from Sparse PCA into Sparse Mean Recovery
papers.abstract:
Source labels tell us where a sample came from, but not how that source oriented its coordinates. In a sparse Gaussian multi-source model with source-specific sign gauges, that distinction changes the learning problem. Without calibration, pooling across sources erases the mean signal, and the source-labelled experiment reduces to sparse PCA. With task-independent relative-gauge metadata, synchronization aligns sources and the same observations become a sparse mean problem. We formalize the value of metadata through AlignedMass, which quantifies how much first-order signal a metadata-induced alignment restores. Source labels create only limited AlignedMass, whereas valid calibration can create AlignedMass proportional to the full sample size. This yields a statistical separation in micro-source regimes and, under standard sparse-PCA hardness assumptions, a computational separation as well. Synthetic experiments check the predicted scaling; controlled real-feature
  and physical sensor studies examine sign cancellation, separately
  acquired calibration, and reuse across tasks.
papers.summary: When samples come from multiple sources that each flip the signs of their coordinates differently, a source label alone does not say how to align the data. In a sparse Gaussian model with source-specific sign gauges, pooling uncalibrated sources cancels the mean signal and the problem reduces to sparse PCA. With relative-gauge calibration metadata, synchronizing the sources turns the same observations into the easier problem of sparse mean recovery. The authors quantify the value of metadata with a measure called `AlignedMass` and show that **valid calibration can restore first-order signal proportional to the full sample size**, while source labels alone restore much less. This yields a statistical separation, and a computational one under standard sparse-PCA hardness assumptions, which they check on synthetic, real-feature, and physical sensor data.

papers.title: Arbitrage-Free Implied Volatility Surface Reconstruction via Additive Martingales
papers.abstract: This work focuses on reconstructing a continuous implied volatility (IV) surface from a small number of option quotes, a fundamental task for option pricing and risk management. We propose Additive Martingale (AddMart), a few-shot IV surface reconstruction framework that satisfies static no-arbitrage conditions by construction. Rather than predicting IVs directly, AddMart maps sparse quotes to non-negative increment densities of an exponential additive martingale, from which valid risk-neutral marginals and IVs are recovered. By incorporating the no-arbitrage structure directly into its architecture, rather than enforcing it through regularization in the learning objective, AddMart produces IV surfaces that satisfy static no-arbitrage conditions throughout the domain. Extensive experiments on ten real-option datasets demonstrate that AddMart achieves competitive reconstruction accuracy with no material static arbitrage violations, while directly enabling the estimation of VaR, CVaR, and crash probabilities.
papers.summary: Option pricing and risk management need a continuous implied volatility (IV) surface reconstructed from a few option quotes, and that surface should be free of static arbitrage. `AddMart` does not predict volatilities directly. Instead it maps the sparse quotes to non-negative increment densities of an exponential additive martingale, then recovers valid risk-neutral marginals and implied volatilities from them. Because the no-arbitrage structure is part of the architecture rather than a penalty in the training loss, the surfaces **satisfy static no-arbitrage conditions everywhere in the domain**. On ten real option datasets the method matches competing reconstruction accuracy with no material violations, and it can directly estimate VaR, CVaR, and crash probabilities.

papers.title: Cross-Pollination Retrieval: Finding Transferable Ideas Across Fields in Scientific Literature
papers.abstract: Many scientific advances come from cross-pollination, carrying an idea from one field over to a problem in another. Yet retrieving papers across fields remains underexplored, with existing benchmarks confined to a narrow range of fields. We study cross-pollination retrieval, the problem of identifying transferable ideas across research fields, and introduce CPR-Dataset, a large-scale dataset constructed by mining cross-topic citations. Its evaluation split CPR-eval has 1,300 queries in 26 fields, and its training split CPR-train has 10,573 pairs. On CPR-eval, the best of eleven existing retrievers reaches a Recall@10 of only 0.26, whereas an LLM reranker reaches 0.81. Standard contrastive fine-tuning on CPR-train raises Recall@10 to as high as 0.70. The gain carries over to domains held out from training and to analogy and reasoning-intensive retrieval. On AnaloBench, it raises nDCG@10 by up to 33% over the untrained retriever, whereas training on three existing retrieval datasets lowers it. On BRIGHT, it raises nDCG@10 by up to 70%, more than twice the gain from those datasets. CPR-Dataset is available at https://huggingface.co/CPR-Dataset, and the code at https://github.com/SeokwonJung-Jay/Cross-Pollination-Retrieval.
papers.summary: Many scientific advances come from carrying an idea from one field into another, yet existing retrieval benchmarks cover only a narrow range of fields. The authors build `CPR-Dataset` by mining citations that cross topics. Its evaluation split, `CPR-eval`, has 1,300 queries across 26 fields, and its training split, `CPR-train`, has 10,573 pairs. The best of eleven existing retrievers reaches a Recall@10 of only 0.26 on `CPR-eval` versus 0.81 for an LLM reranker, and standard contrastive fine-tuning on `CPR-train` raises retriever Recall@10 to as high as 0.70. The gains carry over to held-out domains and to other benchmarks, improving nDCG@10 by up to 33% on `AnaloBench` and **up to 70% on `BRIGHT`**, whereas training on three existing retrieval datasets helped much less or hurt.

papers.title: LOOP: Recovery-Aligned Iterative Layer Pruning via On-Policy Distillation
papers.abstract: Layer-level pruning is attractive for large language model (LLM) deployment as it reduces the model size while preserving a dense architecture that can be efficiently executed on standard hardware. Current methods typically follow a one-shot paradigm, which first removes selected layers to reach a target model size and then performs additional training to recover model capabilities. However, pruning directly to the target size can substantially degrade reasoning capabilities, making subsequent recovery more difficult under a limited training budget. Moreover, this paradigm separates layer selection from recovery, limiting the use of recovery information to guide selection and potentially hindering the recovery of reasoning capabilities. To address these limitations, we propose LOOP, a Layer-level Recovery-Oriented On-Policy Pruning framework that interleaves pruning and recovery across multiple shots. In each shot, LOOP removes a single layer and performs short on-policy distillation, mitigating the abrupt degradation in reasoning capabilities associated with one-shot pruning. To guide layer selection in subsequent shots, LOOP reuses on-policy trajectories and optimization signals from recovery to jointly assess each remaining layer's reasoning contribution and recovery sensitivity, thereby making layer selection recovery-aware. Evaluations on several benchmarks show that LOOP consistently outperforms one-shot baselines in average accuracy across different model scales and pruning ratios.
papers.summary: Removing whole layers shrinks a large language model (LLM) while keeping a dense architecture that runs efficiently on standard hardware. Current methods, however, prune straight to the target size and then retrain, which can badly damage reasoning and makes recovery hard on a limited budget. `LOOP` instead removes one layer at a time, each followed by a short round of on-policy distillation. It reuses the trajectories and optimization signals from each recovery round to judge which remaining layer contributes least to reasoning and recovers most easily, so layer selection takes recovery into account. Across several benchmarks, model scales, and pruning ratios, `LOOP` **consistently beats one-shot pruning baselines in average accuracy**.

papers.title: MT-CC: Multi-Group Temperature Scaling for Asymmetric Calibration Behavior in Class-Incremental Learning
papers.abstract: As deep neural networks are required to continuously adapt to evolving data, class-incremental learning (CIL) has become an active research area. However, most existing works primarily focus on improving accuracy while overlooking confidence calibration, which measures the trustworthiness of the model's predictions. Although temperature scaling (TS) is effective for static calibration, it has rarely been explored in continual settings where data distributions evolve over time. In this paper, we introduce Multi-Group Temperature Scaling for Continual Calibration (MT-CC), a novel post-hoc calibration framework that addresses the asymmetric calibration behavior in CIL, where the rate of confidence changes does not align with the rate of accuracy degradation across tasks, leading to different levels of miscalibration. Our key contribution is to design multiple temperature parameters through a lightweight grouping network that separates samples by confidence statistics and task-aware signals in CIL. Furthermore, a Groupwise Difference-between-Confidence-and-Accuracy (GDCA) regularization is incorporated to promote intra-group consistency. Experiments demonstrate that MT-CC significantly improves calibration performance while maintaining accuracy, offering a principled framework for reliable continual learning.
papers.summary: Research on class-incremental learning (CIL) mostly targets accuracy and pays little attention to confidence calibration. In CIL, a model's confidence changes at a different rate than its accuracy degrades across tasks, so miscalibration differs from task to task. `MT-CC` is a post-hoc method that learns several temperature parameters, using a lightweight grouping network that sorts samples by confidence statistics and task-aware signals. A groupwise regularizer that penalizes the gap between confidence and accuracy (`GDCA`) keeps each group consistent. Experiments show **significantly better calibration while maintaining accuracy**.

papers.title: Progress-Guided Preference Generation for Aligning Generative Control Policies
papers.abstract: Generative policies have achieved strong performance in imitation learning tasks, but their success is often constrained by the limited availability of expert demonstrations. Although preference-based fine-tuning can leverage suboptimal rollouts to improve performance, existing approaches heavily rely on expensive human annotations. In this work, we introduce Progress-Guided Preference Generation (PGPG), an unsupervised preference alignment framework that eliminates the need for human-in-the-loop supervision. Our method leverages ordered coverage alignment to measure sequential progress relative to a small set of expert demonstrations, enabling the automatic extraction of pseudo-preference labels from autonomously collected rollouts. Furthermore, we introduce key enhancements to improve the reliability of these progress-guided preferences, enabling effective fine-tuning of pretrained generative policies without requiring manually designed reward functions. Extensive experiments across a suite of challenging long-horizon manipulation tasks demonstrate that PGPG outperforms standard supervised fine-tuning baselines. Moreover, our conceptually simple framework is broadly applicable across multiple classes of generative policies, demonstrating strong versatility when integrated with both diffusion and flow-matching policies.
papers.summary: Generative robot control policies learned by imitation are limited by how few expert demonstrations are available. Preference-based fine-tuning on suboptimal rollouts can help, but it normally needs costly human labels. `PGPG` generates preference labels without human supervision: it measures how far each autonomously collected rollout has progressed through the task by aligning it in order with a small set of expert demonstrations, then uses these pseudo-labels to fine-tune the pretrained policy without a hand-designed reward function. On challenging long-horizon manipulation tasks, it **outperforms standard supervised fine-tuning baselines** and works with both diffusion and flow-matching policies.

papers.title: Stochastic Tracking of Drifting Affine Fixed Points
papers.abstract: Linear stochastic approximation (SA) is widely used to estimate fixed points from noisy observations, but most finite-time analyses assume that the underlying operator remains fixed. We study linear SA with time-varying affine operators, where the fixed points change over time and the observation noise may be correlated across rounds. For constant-stepsize updates, we establish a bound on the cumulative expected squared distance between the iterates and the corresponding fixed points. The bound accounts for the initial error, observation noise, and changes in the fixed points over time. We also establish lower bounds for scalar Gaussian models, showing that, under specified conditions, a suitably chosen constant stepsize achieves the smallest possible worst-case cumulative error up to constant factors, even compared with estimators that use future observations. These results further quantify the effect of temporal correlation on estimation accuracy. Since choosing an appropriate stepsize generally requires knowledge of the noise level and how much the fixed points change, we develop an adaptive method that uses an additional bounded, unbiased observation of the fixed point to achieve an almost optimal algorithm without needing the knowledge of the noise level and the fixed point variation over time. Finally, we apply our results to value-function estimation using synchronous tabular temporal-difference learning in changing environments, assuming generative-model access and a common invariant distribution.
papers.summary: Finite-time analyses of linear stochastic approximation (SA) usually assume the operator stays fixed. The authors instead study time-varying affine operators whose fixed points drift, with observation noise that may be correlated across rounds. For constant step sizes they bound the cumulative squared tracking error in terms of initial error, noise, and fixed-point drift. Lower bounds for scalar Gaussian models show that a well-chosen constant step size is **worst-case optimal up to constant factors, even against estimators that use future observations**. They also give an adaptive, nearly optimal method that needs no prior knowledge of the noise level or drift, and they apply the results to tabular temporal-difference learning in changing environments.

papers.title: Predictive Bandit Curriculum Reinforcement Learning via Gradient-Based Sample Group Discovery
papers.abstract: Curriculum learning, which organizes training samples according to their learning priority, has been widely adopted in reinforcement learning to improve training efficiency. However, existing methods commonly construct curriculum units using predefined data properties and estimate their utility by simply aggregating a single proxy signal from recent training history.Such designs may group samples with different optimization effects and fail to anticipate how their utility evolves in relation to the policy. We propose Predictive Gradient-based Bandit (PGB) Curriculum, which first discovers optimization-aware learning units by clustering projected sample-level gradients. PGB then employs a lightweight temporal predictor to forecast the future utility of each unit and converts the predictions into a Boltzmann sampling distribution for adaptive data allocation. Experiments across multiple model scales and reasoning benchmarks show that PGB consistently outperforms standard GRPO, difficulty-based curricula, and history-based scheduling strategies, demonstrating improved data utilization and training efficiency.
papers.summary: Curriculum methods in reinforcement learning usually group training samples by predefined properties such as difficulty and score each group from recent training history. Such groups can mix samples with very different effects on optimization. The `PGB` curriculum instead forms learning units by clustering projected per-sample gradients, uses a lightweight temporal predictor to forecast each unit's future usefulness, and samples units from the resulting Boltzmann distribution. Across several model scales and reasoning benchmarks, it **consistently outperforms standard `GRPO`**, difficulty-based curricula, and history-based scheduling, using data and training compute more efficiently.

papers.title: Whose Credential Is It? How Owner Attribution in Agent MemoryShapes Cross-User Account Misuse
papers.abstract: Shared long-term memory lets an LLM agent serving one user inadvertently retrieve another user's credentials, but it is unclear when such exposure leads to actual harm. We introduce a three-stage audit that separates three events: a foreign credential reaches the prompt (exposure), the agent acts with it (behavior), and the other user's account changes (state). In AppWorld, a store that mixes 763 past logins from all users retrieves another user's credential for 84.7 percent of required apps, yet agents rarely act on it. Misuse appears in a stress test where memory lacks the user's own credential and presents a single foreign one as the user's record: seven agents then use it in 80 to 94 percent of runs and change the victim's account in up to 43 percent, sometimes passing the official check. Naming the owner before or inside each credential line prevents most of this: with all else fixed, misuse falls from 92 to 1 of 305 paired runs, also with name-free usernames, though owner-bound notes cost 3 to 5 successful tasks per model on clean memory. A wrongly written owner largely restores misuse; trailing owner tags and added safety instructions help only some models. Agent memory should consistently record whose credential it stores, and evaluations should measure behavior, not only exposure.
papers.summary: When an LLM agent's long-term memory is shared across users, it can retrieve another user's credentials, and a three-stage audit separates exposure (the credential reaches the prompt), behavior (the agent uses it), and state (the other user's account changes). In `AppWorld`, a memory store mixing 763 past logins retrieves a foreign credential for 84.7% of required apps, yet agents rarely act on it. In a stress test where the user's own credential is missing and a single foreign one is presented as the user's record, seven agents use it in 80 to 94% of runs and change the victim's account in up to 43%. Naming the owner before or inside each credential line **cuts misuse from 92 to 1 of 305 paired runs**, at a cost of 3 to 5 successful tasks per model on clean memory. A wrongly recorded owner largely brings misuse back, and owner tags placed at the end of the line or added safety instructions help only some models.

papers.title: Evidence Sufficiency and Model Comparisons in MexRegQA: An Item-Level Audit of Mexican-Spanish Regulatory QA
papers.abstract: Similarity-gated coverage does not establish that retrieved evidence contains the facts needed to answer a question. We audit Mexican-Spanish financial-regulatory QA and find that 35 of 135 covered items lack some or all load-bearing facts. On the post-hoc full-evidence slice (n=98), eleven prompt-matched models score 95-98/98 and none differs significantly from the anchor; this does not establish equivalence. Removing evidence-defective items changes the nominal significance status of 14 of 55 pairwise comparisons. On 56 zero-evidence items, accuracy spans 33.9%-89.3%. Removing evidence from the audited items under an abstention-permitting prompt reduces accuracy by 63-81 percentage points in all ten tested legs, with no recovered items. Building on sufficient-context research, we contribute MexRegQA v1.0: 192 items with provenance and evidence-status labels, frozen retrieval evidence for 191 evaluated items, predictions, judge outputs and offline checks. The audit was outcome-aware, the later model/panel sweep reused the same questions, and all reported scores and labels rely on machine evaluation without independent human validation. We propose releasing evidence-status labels alongside grounded QA benchmarks so that model comparisons can be examined separately from evidence availability.
papers.summary: Retrieval coverage judged by similarity does not guarantee that the retrieved evidence contains the facts needed to answer a question. An item-level audit of Mexican-Spanish financial-regulatory QA finds that **35 of 135 covered items lack some or all of the facts their answers depend on**. On the 98 items with full evidence, eleven models score 95 to 98 and none differs significantly from the reference model, while dropping the evidence-defective items changes the significance status of 14 of 55 pairwise comparisons. The authors release `MexRegQA` v1.0, with 192 items carrying provenance and evidence-status labels plus frozen retrieval evidence, and recommend publishing evidence-status labels with grounded QA benchmarks. All scores rely on machine evaluation without independent human validation.

papers.title: Corrected Block Sparse Spectral Optimization: Exact Models, Finite Identification, and Local Dynamics
papers.abstract: The block generalized-power method pairs threshold-based support selection with inexpensive Stiefel updates, but the standard block formulation conflates two nonequivalent objectives and leaves inactive components, threshold ties, and post-selection refitting ill-specified. We rebuild the model from the primal.
