Eliminating each loading column from the normalized loading-ball problem gives a sum of soft-thresholded Euclidean norms (A-SUM); the squared-threshold objective in common use arises from a quadratic lift (A-SQ). We prove both identities, exhibit a two-component instance whose maximizers disagree, and specify explicit conventions for zero-response columns, ties, rank deficiency, and mask-before-refit. For A-SQ we separate the historical full-polar iteration from a safeguarded Riemannian ascent and prove, for the latter, whole-sequence convergence via a sufficient-ascent lemma, a relative-error lemma, and the Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz property, which applies because the soft-threshold objective and the Stiefel constraint are semi-algebraic. A strict threshold margin then forces finite identification of the support and sign pattern. The post-identification map is ordinary power iteration on the active covariance for a rank-one hard threshold, and the Frechet derivative of a coupled polar map for component-specific supports; a radius-based safe-screening rule follows from the same local analysis. Planted-spike experiments match the predicted identification time and local rates. On modern-AI panels (GPT-2 residual stream, ViT CLS stream, Pitprops) the thresholded block-sparse components match dense PCA on reconstruction and improve on it in monosemanticity and class specialisation. On three native-label scRNA datasets (Zheng17 FACS-sorted PBMCs, 68k donor-A with FACS-correlated labels, Tabula Muris) A-SQ beats dense PCA on cluster-recovery AMI by +0.023 to +0.044 at matched sparsity.
papers.summary: The block generalized-power method for sparse principal component analysis mixes two objectives that are not equivalent, and it leaves inactive components, threshold ties and post-selection refitting poorly specified. The authors derive two exact formulations from the primal problem, a sum of soft-thresholded norms (`A-SUM`) and a squared-threshold quadratic lift (`A-SQ`), and show with a two-component example that their maximizers can differ. For a safeguarded Riemannian ascent on `A-SQ`, they prove whole-sequence convergence and **finite identification of the support and sign pattern under a strict threshold margin**, which also yields a radius-based safe-screening rule. In experiments on `GPT-2` residual streams, `ViT` CLS tokens and `Pitprops`, the sparse components match dense PCA on reconstruction and are more monosemantic. On three single-cell RNA datasets they improve cluster-recovery AMI over dense PCA by 0.023 to 0.044.

papers.title: Learning to Couple: Context-Adaptive Joint Denoising for Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: Diffusion language models accelerate generation by predicting multiple tokens in parallel, but factorized denoisers treat simultaneous predictions as conditionally independent. Decoding heuristics reduce the resulting errors by controlling which tokens are committed, but leave the underlying distribution factorized. Joint modeling addresses the source of the problem, yet existing methods attach separately learned layers to frozen denoisers, leaving the backbone unadapted to the joint objective and the coupling parameters fixed across contexts. We propose Codpula, a context-parameterized denoiser combining a Transformer with a tractable probabilistic inference layer. Given a partially masked input, the Transformer produces token potentials that shape per-position predictions and compact gates that modulate the layer's coupling parameters, yielding a context-dependent joint distribution while retaining exact conditional inference. We jointly optimize both components under a conditional denoising objective using a dual-flow multiplicative update that preserves valid probabilistic parameters. At inference, Codpula supports standard heuristics and uses conditional queries to adapt commitments to dependencies among proposed tokens without extra Transformer evaluations within a step. Codpula sets new state-of-the-art results across a broad suite of reasoning benchmarks while advancing the accuracy-latency Pareto frontier in mathematical reasoning and code generation.
papers.summary: Diffusion language models speed up generation by predicting many tokens in parallel, but they treat those simultaneous predictions as conditionally independent, which causes errors. `Codpula` pairs a Transformer with a tractable probabilistic inference layer: the Transformer outputs token potentials plus gates that adjust the layer's coupling parameters, so the joint distribution changes with context while exact conditional inference is preserved. The two components are trained together with a dual-flow multiplicative update, and at inference conditional queries decide which tokens to commit without extra Transformer passes within a step. The authors report **state-of-the-art results across reasoning benchmarks** and a better accuracy-latency trade-off on math reasoning and code generation.

papers.title: Inside the Scorer: Mechanistic Evidence on Rubric Control in LLM-Based Automated Essay Scoring from 25 Base Models
papers.abstract: Automated essay scoring (AES) using large language models (LLMs) offers promising use cases for language assessment, yet high-stakes testing requires scores that are both controllable and verifiable, which current LLM-based scorers lack. Given that, we investigate whether LLM-based scorers form distinct internal representations for individual scoring rubrics and whether these representations can be independently controlled. Probing and steering 25 open-weight base LLMs (0.13B-10.31B parameters; 14 families) on human-scored BESTEP English writing tasks, we find that holistic scores are decodable from model activations for the longer tasks (Parts 2 and 3) and only weakly for the shortest (Part 1). Furthermore, scoring rubrics have partly separable directions in representation space for the longer tasks, though not for short responses (Part 1). However, causal steering reveals a critical limitation: applying a matching intervention (e.g., steering "grammar" on a grammar-degraded response) yields only a negligible advantage (about 2% of the effect) over a mismatched intervention (e.g., steering "vocabulary"), and none that is detectable in any of the 10 testable comparisons across reliably measured rubrics. Rather than controlling distinct evaluative dimensions, the rubric directions share a dominant lever whose rubric-specific parts are not selective, which may mirror the halo structure of human ratings. Our contributions are two-fold. First, we show that analytic scoring rubrics designed for human raters do not behave as independent controls in base LLMs, even among the seven models whose scores agree best with human raters ($r \geq 0.6$). Second, we establish a methodology that shows that score agreement and decodability do not imply rubric-level control in LLM-based assessment.
papers.summary: High-stakes language testing needs essay scores that can be controlled and verified, so this study asks whether LLM-based scorers form separate internal representations for each scoring rubric. The authors probe and steer 25 open-weight base models (0.13B to 10.31B parameters, 14 families) on human-scored `BESTEP` English writing tasks. Holistic scores can be decoded from activations for the longer tasks, and rubric directions are partly separable there. However, steering with the matching rubric (for example grammar on a grammar-degraded essay) gives **only about 2% of the effect as an advantage over a mismatched rubric**, which suggests the directions share one dominant lever, similar to the halo effect in human ratings. The authors conclude that agreement with human scores and decodability do not imply rubric-level control.

papers.title: Anatomy of Off-Policy Policy Gradient: Importance Sampling, KL Regularization, and Baselines
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning has become a central tool for large language model (LLM) post-training, where policy gradient methods are routinely deployed off-policy, even though vanilla policy gradient assumes on-policy sampling. We study when such off-policy deployment is justified, and what roles its core ingredients, including importance sampling, KL regularization, and baselines, play in handling the resulting distribution shift. We show that for a general class of off-policy policy gradient updates, consistency, in the sense that the optimal policy remains a stationary point, requires one of two structures at the optimal policy: trajectory-level importance weighting, which suffers from the well-known curse of horizon, or KL regularization with a baseline equal to the optimal soft value, instantiated by the grouped mean. Focusing on the KL route, we identify it with the group-relative policy gradient (GRPG) update, establish an equivalence to a trajectory-level Bellman residual minimization objective, and obtain a finite-sample regret bound under all-policy coverage. This also gives a theoretical account of a variant of the empirically successful GRPO objective. We further uncover a hidden role of baselines in the off-policy setting: a constant shift in the baseline implements pessimism, the standard remedy in offline RL for partial data coverage. We instantiate this via the asymmetric REINFORCE objective, and connect it to the game-theoretic offline RL framework, showing a regret bound with single-policy coverage. Together, these results offer a unified theoretical view of off-policy policy gradient in LLM post-training and connect it to classical ideas in offline RL.
papers.summary: Policy gradient methods for LLM post-training are often run off-policy even though vanilla policy gradient assumes on-policy sampling, and this work asks when that is justified. The authors prove that keeping the optimal policy a stationary point requires either trajectory-level importance weighting, which suffers from the curse of horizon, or **KL regularization with a baseline equal to the optimal soft value, which the grouped mean provides**. They identify the second route with the group-relative policy gradient update, connect it to Bellman residual minimization, and derive a regret bound that gives a theoretical account of a `GRPO` variant. They also show that shifting the baseline by a constant implements pessimism, and they instantiate this as asymmetric `REINFORCE` with a regret bound that needs only single-policy coverage.

papers.title: No Matter Who You Are: Addressivity and Sycophancy in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Sycophancy, where an LLM becomes overly agreeable, deferential, or flattering toward the user, has been identified as a major failure mode. While post-training has been implicated as a cause, how it internally gives rise to sycophantic behavior remains insufficiently understood. Post-training transforms the model's output from text completion into utterances directed toward an addressee, thereby giving the output \textit{addressivity}. We hypothesize that the accompanying pressure to follow the addressee's instructions and align with their preferences links this addressivity to sycophancy. To test this, we use Sparse Autoencoders to extract addressivity directions from pre-trained and post-trained models and examine their relationship with sycophancy. Steering models with addressivity directions can amplify or suppress sycophancy, and this effect is observed only in post-trained models. Furthermore, comparing the internal mechanisms of both model types confirms that the association between addressivity and sycophancy is strengthened through post-training. Finally, through a controlled post-training experiment, we find that models are sycophantic not toward a specific addressee but toward any recognized addressee, suggesting that the presence of an addressee, rather than the addressee's identity, is what elicits sycophancy.
papers.summary: The authors hypothesize that LLM sycophancy comes from addressivity: post-training turns text completion into utterances aimed at an addressee, along with pressure to please that addressee. Using sparse autoencoders, they extract addressivity directions from pre-trained and post-trained models and find that steering along them can amplify or suppress sycophancy, **but only in post-trained models**. Comparing internal mechanisms shows that post-training strengthens the link between addressivity and sycophancy. A controlled post-training experiment suggests that models defer to any recognized addressee, so sycophancy is triggered by the presence of an addressee rather than by who that addressee is.

papers.title: Neural Video Coding under Limited Delay: Theoretical Optimality and System Design
papers.abstract: Traditional neural video compression (NVC) methods predominantly follow strictly causal predictive-coding paradigm, treating zero-frame delay as a fixed constraint rather than delay as an explicit design parameter. From an information-theoretic perspective, allowing limited frame delay enables a codec to exploit correlations with future frames within the delay window, thereby reducing uncertainty that is inaccessible to strictly causal prediction and potentially improving the rate-distortion tradeoff. In this work, we formalize this intuition through a rigorous rate-distortion analysis builds on the clique factorization of Markov networks, and propose Graph-Factored Sequential Coding (GFSC), a principled framework for sequential video coding under limited delay. To our knowledge, we provide the first theoretical result showing that, for general $K$-order Markov sources with positive distributions, a $K$-frame delay is sufficient to attain joint-coding rate-distortion optimality over a nontrivial distortion region, a guarantee unavailable to zero-delay causal coding in general. In practice, we instantiate GFSC through lightweight neural modules, allowing existing causal predictive codecs to be augmented without modifying their core architectures. Experiments across multiple NVC models and datasets show that GFSC consistently improves rate-distortion performance over the corresponding causal counterparts. Under matched delay budgets, GFSC also achieves competitive performance compared with representative bidirectional codecs.
papers.summary: Neural video compression usually follows strictly causal predictive coding, which treats zero frame delay as fixed rather than as a design choice. Using a rate-distortion analysis based on clique factorization of Markov networks, the authors prove that **for K-order Markov sources, a K-frame delay is enough to reach joint-coding rate-distortion optimality** over a nontrivial distortion region, which zero-delay coding cannot guarantee in general. Their framework, `Graph-Factored Sequential Coding` (`GFSC`), adds lightweight neural modules to existing causal codecs without changing their core architectures. Experiments show consistent rate-distortion gains over the causal versions and results competitive with bidirectional codecs at the same delay budget.

papers.title: Does Unlearning Survive Collaboration? Robust Unlearning for Shared-Model LLM Teams
papers.abstract: LLM unlearning is essential for removing sensitive or unwanted knowledge while preserving useful capabilities. As LLM teams are increasingly used to solve complex problems, forgetting must remain effective during collaboration. Despite advances in forgetting effectiveness, efficiency, and robustness to relearning, team deployment remains underexplored. We find that collaboration weakens forgetting: final-answer evaluations miss recoverable evidence in team messages, including complementary clues supporting joint recovery. We establish theoretically and confirm empirically that controlling final answers or individual messages does not ensure low recovery from their combination. To address this challenge, we propose Aggregation-Conditioned Unlearning (ACU). ACU trains a shared model using reconstruction feedback from individual and pooled messages, prioritizes views with higher recovery risk, and uses replacement-based credit assignment while protecting direct and collaborative utility. TOFU evaluates trajectory-level recovery, while WMDP-bio tests native forgetting and retained utility. On TOFU, ACU lowers full-trajectory recovery from 41.8% to 19.3% in ROUGE-L recall and factual recovery from 34.2% to 18.7% versus output-supervised training, with comparable retained-task performance. These results demonstrate that ACU curbs information leakage in LLM teams and generalizes across team sizes and readers.
papers.summary: LLM unlearning is normally evaluated on a single model's final answers, but in teams of LLMs that collaborate, the messages they exchange can leak supposedly forgotten knowledge, including complementary clues that together allow the knowledge to be recovered. The authors show theoretically and empirically that controlling final answers or individual messages does not prevent recovery from their combination. They propose `Aggregation-Conditioned Unlearning` (`ACU`), which trains a shared model with reconstruction feedback from individual and pooled messages, prioritizes the riskiest views and uses replacement-based credit assignment. On `TOFU`, `ACU` **cuts full-trajectory recovery from 41.8% to 19.3%** in ROUGE-L recall while keeping retained-task performance comparable, and it is also tested on `WMDP-bio`.

papers.title: A Calibrated Instrument for Detecting Disposition Drift in Language Models
papers.abstract: Before language models are released, they are tested for harmful traits such as willingness to carry out dangerous requests, deception, power seeking, and sycophancy. The safe behavior these tests certify may degrade as models are modified, by topical fine-tuning, new training data, or changes to settings such as the depth of their reasoning. Most work reports such drift as single summary rates scored by another AI model, without the error analysis needed to interpret them. We adapt a calibrated measurement methodology recently developed for assessing how inference optimizations affect the quality of model outputs. Applying it to several misalignment dimensions in two open-weight models, we first establish the instrument's precision, showing that shifts of a few percentage points can be reliably detected. We then induce drift deliberately by fine-tuning on correct and on subtly harmful medical and financial advice; harmful advice induces a far greater shift than correct advice. Most strikingly, a model that reasons before answering can conceal the shift almost entirely in its answers, even though a direct reading of its internal state shows that its disposition has moved. With reasoning switched off, the same model shifts steadily as the share of harmful advice in its training grows. These results demonstrate the importance of testing safety with reasoning turned both on and off.
papers.summary: Safety behaviour certified before release, such as refusing dangerous requests or avoiding deception and sycophancy, can drift when a model is later fine-tuned or its settings change, and such drift is usually reported as AI-judged rates without error analysis. The authors adapt a calibrated measurement method to several misalignment dimensions in two open-weight models and show it can reliably detect shifts of a few percentage points. Fine-tuning on subtly harmful medical and financial advice causes much larger drift than fine-tuning on correct advice. Notably, **a model that reasons before answering can almost entirely hide the shift in its answers even though probes of its internal state show the disposition has changed**, while with reasoning disabled the drift grows steadily with the share of harmful training data.

papers.title: How Much Does One Wrong Answer Cost? Error Propagation in Constraint Pruning with Noisy LLM Oracles
papers.abstract: Constraint pruning saves queries to a large language model (LLM) or another noisy oracle by skipping each yes/no question implied by answers accepted earlier, for example through transitivity. Entity-resolution systems and LLM-based rankers use this idea. However, their analyses typically assume a correct oracle. We argue that pruning should be judged by its risk when the oracle errs, since an accepted wrong answer spreads to every question it implies. When each answer is wrong independently with small probability $\varepsilon$, the first-order risk is set by how many facts one wrong answer corrupts on average. We consider two kinds of constraints. For implication rules, as in taxonomies, pruning in a random order adds no first-order risk: a wrong answer that would change $k$ facts is accepted with probability $1/k$, so it costs one fact on average. Rules with $s$ premises break this balance: a wrong answer at a premise shared by $r$ rules can cost order $r^{1-1/s}$ facts. For entity resolution with $m$ records of one entity, the first-order risk equals $\varepsilon$ times the Wiener index (the total pairwise distance) of the spanning tree built by the query order. Pivot orders, which first compare one record with all others, amplify errors by less than 2 and are optimal; random orders by order $m^{1/3}$; the common most-similar-first order is the worst in one dimension and, for large $m$, worse than random in two. With several entities, the cost of wrongly merging two does not depend on how many others exist. Simulations agree with every predicted constant within sampling error.
papers.summary: Constraint pruning saves queries to an LLM or another noisy oracle by skipping yes/no questions that earlier answers already imply, for example through transitivity, but existing analyses assume the oracle is always correct. The authors measure the first-order risk as the number of facts a single wrong answer corrupts. For simple implication rules, pruning in random order adds no first-order risk, but rules with several premises can amplify errors. For entity resolution, the risk equals the error rate times the Wiener index of the spanning tree built by the query order: **pivot orders are optimal and amplify errors by less than 2**, while the common most-similar-first order is among the worst. Simulations match every predicted constant within sampling error.

papers.title: Fundamental Limits of Information-Theoretic Secure Aggregation with User Dropouts in Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Secure aggregation enables a server to compute the sum of users' gradients or model updates without revealing individual values. With user dropouts, correlated random keys protect local gradients while allowing recovery of the desired gradient sum. We consider three phases: key distribution, masked-gradient upload, and mask elimination. Users establish correlated keys, upload masked gradients, and provide additional messages to eliminate residual aggregate masks. Existing information-theoretic schemes typically design mask-elimination communication for a prescribed dropout threshold and evaluate its cost under worst-case dropouts across the masked-gradient upload and mask-elimination phases. Such designs cannot adjust communication to actual dropout scenarios. Moreover, the randomness and communication costs of establishing correlated keys remain largely unexplored. To address these limitations, we formulate an adaptive secure aggregation framework under the T-colluding security constraint and construct a single scheme that supports all feasible dropout scenarios by adapting its communication to the actual number of dropouts. We establish converse bounds on four resources: key randomness, key-distribution communication, masked-gradient communication, and mask-elimination communication. The latter two bounds are characterized for each realized dropout set in the masked-gradient upload phase. The proposed scheme achieves the optimal masked-gradient communication rate for every feasible dropout scenario and the optimal mask-elimination communication rate in almost all feasible regimes. Its key rate and key-distribution communication rate are each optimal or within a factor of two of their respective information-theoretic optima. These results characterize the fundamental randomness and communication costs of secure aggregation with user dropouts.
papers.summary: Secure aggregation lets a federated learning server compute the sum of users' gradients without seeing any individual one, and correlated random keys keep this working when users drop out. Existing information-theoretic schemes are designed for a fixed dropout threshold and worst-case costs, and the cost of setting up the keys has received little attention. The authors build an adaptive scheme under a T-colluding security constraint whose communication adjusts to the number of dropouts that actually occur, and they prove lower bounds on four resources: key randomness, key-distribution communication, masked-gradient communication and mask-elimination communication. The scheme **achieves the optimal masked-gradient rate in every feasible dropout scenario**, the optimal mask-elimination rate in almost all regimes, and key costs that are optimal or within a factor of two.

papers.title: Bayesian Model Discovery with Language Models: Closing the Loop between Hypotheses and Experiments
papers.abstract: Scientific model discovery requires proposing candidate models of an unknown system and designing experiments that discriminate among them. However, LLM-based approaches typically rely on in-context learning to predict outcomes and select experiments, lacking explicit model evaluation to systematically guide hypothesis search, while Bayesian approaches enable principled model comparison but are confined to a predefined candidate set which results in limited search spaces. To this end, we introduce BMD, which closes the loop between LLM-driven hypothesis generation and Bayesian experimental design. Specifically, an LLM proposes model families, while a numerical engine fits their parameters, weighs them by model evidence, and averages their predictions. Then, BMD chooses the next experimental conditions by maximizing the joint expected information gain over families and their parameters, while feeding the updated beliefs and residual diagnostics back to the LLM to guide its next proposals. Across four scientific discovery benchmarks, BMD achieves lowest final prediction error than in-context learning and LLM-based scientific agents while recovering exact functional forms more often, with ablations supporting numerical feedback and the joint objective.
papers.summary: LLM-based scientific discovery usually relies on in-context learning without explicit model evaluation, while Bayesian methods compare models rigorously but only within a fixed candidate set. `BMD` connects the two: an LLM proposes model families, a numerical engine fits their parameters, weights them by model evidence and averages their predictions, and the next experiment is chosen by maximizing joint expected information gain over families and parameters. The updated beliefs and residual diagnostics are then fed back to the LLM to guide its next proposals. Across four scientific discovery benchmarks, `BMD` **achieves lower final prediction error than in-context learning and LLM-based scientific agents** and recovers exact functional forms more often.

papers.title: Cognitively Decoupled Meta-Induction for Out-of-Distribution Generalization
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) tackles downstream tasks conditioned on demonstrations. This paradigm relies heavily on neighbor-based matching between queries and demonstrations, limiting out-of-distribution (OOD) performance. For better generalization, rule-based inductive reasoning derives task-level regularities, which we term task-level inductive representations (TIR), before directly answering. However, existing methods lack generalizable inductive ability across diverse tasks. Inspired by meta-learning, we propose Cognitive-Decoupling meta-Induction (CoDI) for TIR-based inductive reasoning on general tasks. CoDI comprises a Cognitive-Decoupling Framework for query-blind TIR induction, and a Dual-Loop Meta-Inductive Learning method for cross-task inducer optimization. Empirically, CoDI achieves substantial performance gains on five ID and OOD benchmarks, and preserves OOD gains without explicit induction at inference. Code is available at https://github.com/Yuqian-Wang2277/codi-meta-induction.
papers.summary: In-context learning depends heavily on matching queries to similar demonstrations, which limits generalization out of distribution. `CoDI` (`Cognitive-Decoupling meta-Induction`) has the model first induce task-level rules from demonstrations without seeing the query, then answer using those rules. A dual-loop meta-learning procedure trains this inducer across many tasks. The method reports **substantial gains on five in-distribution and out-of-distribution benchmarks**, and the out-of-distribution gains persist even when explicit induction is skipped at inference.

papers.title: NADS: Navigator-Guided Data Selection for Mitigating Catastrophic Forgetting in Fine-Tuning
papers.abstract: Catastrophic forgetting is a central obstacle in single-stage fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) on a new task, especially when the original pretraining data are unavailable. Synthetic data offers a practical mitigation path, but candidate pools are often noisy and redundant, making effective selection essential. Existing methods often rely on indirect proxy signals whose alignment with actual training benefit can be limited, while utility--diversity selection over large candidate pools remains computationally demanding. To address these challenges, we propose NAvigator-guided Data Selection (NADS), a fine-tuning framework for LLMs. NADS first follows the target fine-tuning recipe without preservation regularization to obtain a navigator model, whose deviation from the pretrained model exposes recipe-induced capability drift. It then uses the predictive divergence between the navigator and the pretrained model to score forgetting-aware utility for each synthetic candidate, and constructs a constraint set through an efficient utility--diversity selection strategy. Finally, NADS fine-tunes on the new-task data while distilling pretrained behavior on the selected constraints to preserve general capabilities. Experiments show that NADS delivers a stronger balance between new-task performance and general capability preservation, while reducing utility--diversity selection overhead. Code at: https://github.com/zjh-vinky/NADS.
papers.summary: Fine-tuning an LLM on a new task often causes catastrophic forgetting, and synthetic data can help preserve old capabilities when the original pretraining data is unavailable, but candidate pools are noisy and costly to select from. `NADS` (`NAvigator-guided Data Selection`) first fine-tunes a navigator model without any preservation regularization, then scores each synthetic candidate by how much the navigator's predictions diverge from the pretrained model's. An efficient selection step balances this utility against diversity, and the final fine-tune distills the pretrained model's behaviour on the selected examples. The method **achieves a better balance between new-task performance and preserved general capability** while reducing selection overhead.

papers.title: Which Answers Agree? Evaluating Self-Consistency from Incomplete Logs
papers.abstract: Self-consistency answers a question by generating multiple responses and selecting the most frequent answer. Its evaluation requires both correctness labels and information about which responses agree; correctness labels alone generally determine neither voting accuracy nor the benefit of additional votes. For tasks in which all correct responses map to the same normalized answer, we derive sharp accuracy bounds using classical stochastic majorization, refined by abstention counts and answer-category limits. We also derive sharp bounds on accuracy changes across voting budgets that share a response pool. When answer-category counts are available, we introduce Plurality-U, a count-based dynamic program that exactly averages voting accuracy over all fixed-size subsets, eliminating finite-pool Monte Carlo error. On 1,403,520 stored outputs from recent reasoning models in Scorio Lite and Scorio Trace, recording abstention counts and answer options cuts the width of SuperGPQA accuracy intervals by more than half. For moving from 9 to 17 votes, our bounds reduce interval width by a median of 77.7% on SuperGPQA and 72.3% on 14 GPQA and Adaptive-Consistency pools, compared with a baseline that combines separate accuracy bounds. Exact computation has lower paired median runtime than 2,000-subset Monte Carlo in 14 of 15 tested pool-budget settings. These results clarify what incomplete logs can establish and provide an exact evaluation procedure when answer counts are retained.
papers.summary: Evaluating self-consistency (majority voting over multiple samples) requires knowing which responses agree, but stored logs often keep only correctness labels. For tasks where all correct responses normalize to the same answer, the authors use stochastic majorization to derive sharp bounds on voting accuracy and on how accuracy changes with more votes. When answer-category counts are available, they introduce `Plurality-U`, a dynamic program that computes accuracy exactly over all fixed-size subsets of a response pool and removes Monte Carlo error. On 1.4 million stored outputs from recent reasoning models, recording abstentions and answer options **more than halves the width of `SuperGPQA` accuracy intervals**, and exact computation is usually faster than 2,000-subset Monte Carlo.

papers.title: Remember Less, Adapt Longer: Bounded-State In-Context Reinforcement Learning with Recurrent Summary Memory
papers.abstract: In-context reinforcement learning (ICRL) enables agents to adapt to new tasks without parameter updates, relying on memory to retain what they learn from experience. For agents operating continually, existing approaches using memory trade off bounded cost against access to past experience. Approaches using growing memories, such as full-history attention and accumulating summaries, incur storage and per-decision costs that increase with task length. Fixed-size memories bound storage but restrict access: sliding windows discard older steps, while recurrent networks compress even recent interactions into a hidden state. We introduce Recurrent Summary Memory (RSM), a Transformer policy that attends exactly to a short working buffer of recent interactions and carries a fixed-capacity summary of earlier experience. When the buffer fills, RSM rewrites the summary from its previous contents and the buffer, then clears the buffer, so deployment memory and per-decision cost stay $O(1)$ in task length. On long-running partially observable tasks, frozen RSM policies sustain their adapted performance for eight times the training horizon with about 1% of full-history memory, ending ahead of every evaluated baseline while growing memories deteriorate. When the task configuration changes mid-run, RSM re-adapts better than growing and recurrent memories. Clearing the summary or blocking the policy's access to it removes its benefit, while swapping in another task's summary steers behaviour towards that task. Together, these results show that our fixed-capacity summary can sustain in-context adaptation far beyond the training horizon.
papers.summary: In-context reinforcement learning lets agents adapt to new tasks without weight updates, but growing memories become expensive over long tasks, while fixed-size memories either discard old experience or compress even recent steps. `Recurrent Summary Memory` (`RSM`) is a Transformer policy that attends exactly to a short buffer of recent interactions and keeps a fixed-capacity summary of earlier experience, rewriting the summary whenever the buffer fills, so memory and per-decision cost stay constant in task length. On long-running partially observable tasks, frozen `RSM` policies **sustain their adapted performance for eight times the training horizon with about 1% of full-history memory** and finish ahead of every baseline. They also re-adapt better when the task changes mid-run, and swapping in another task's summary steers behaviour toward that task.

papers.title: Computation, Not Memory: Chain-of-Thought and State Tracking in LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Language-model agents often reason before they act, and the value of monitoring that reasoning depends on how it relates to their actions. We ask how an agent's actions depend on its reasoning when the correct action depends on a changing state. In a small file-system task, background events announce which file's lock has been toggled but not its new value. The agent therefore has to reconstruct the current locks from its history before it can move files safely. With Qwen3-8B and Qwen3.5-9B, we separate two roles of reasoning: generating it before each action, and retaining earlier reasoning in the prompt. Most of the reduction in lock-violating commands comes from reasoning written at the moment of action. Retaining earlier reasoning adds little to rule-following, although it helps one model complete the task. The benefit depends on what the reasoning says. Filler text, reasoning written for another history and an accurate table of the state do not reproduce it. When we give the agent reasoning written for a history that differs in one lock value, the agent acts on that reasoning even against its own history. Without reasoning, linear probes recover the state from the model's activations about as well as a text classifier recovers it from the transcript. However, decoding accuracy does not predict which interventions change the agent's actions. In this setting, the benefit of reasoning for rule-following comes mainly from generating it at each step. The state that can be decoded without reasoning is a limited guide to how the agent acts.
papers.summary: To judge how useful it is to monitor an agent's chain of thought, the authors study how actions depend on reasoning in a small file-system task where the agent must reconstruct changing file-lock states from its history. With `Qwen3-8B` and `Qwen3.5-9B`, they find that **most of the reduction in lock-violating commands comes from reasoning generated at the moment of action**, while keeping earlier reasoning in the prompt adds little. Filler text, reasoning written for another history, or an accurate state table do not reproduce the benefit, and agents follow injected reasoning even when it contradicts their own history. Linear probes can decode the state without reasoning, but decoding accuracy does not predict which interventions change the agent's actions.

papers.title: Truncated Reasoning Under a Budget: Evaluating System-1 Models as Decision-makers
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often generate more reasoning tokens than needed. Limiting the reasoning budget reduces cost, but forcing an answer from an incomplete trace can hurt accuracy. System-1 decision models select among candidate options without producing a reasoning response. We evaluate Jev as a decision reader of truncated reasoning across seven LLM reasoners and five multiple-choice benchmarks (35 pairs). Jev achieves higher mean accuracy than forced answering at tested budgets from 500 to 16,000 tokens, including the estimated costs of reasoning and answering. At a 1,500-token budget, it improves accuracy by 4.1 pp overall and 8.6 pp on truncated questions, with significant gains in 17 pairs under Holm-corrected bootstrap tests. Offline replay estimates 34.5% of the full-run cost, with a 1.13 pp accuracy loss. A policy selected on training folds saves 71.3% of the estimated full-run cost on held-out folds, with a 0.58 pp accuracy loss. We also find that Jev shows strong question-only accuracy, exceeding 500-token forced answering on average (68.0% vs. 65.5%), although this advantage varies by benchmark. These findings suggest that System-1 decision models can complement LLM reasoning and reduce the need for costly reasoning completion.
papers.summary: Capping an LLM's reasoning budget saves cost, but forcing an answer from an incomplete reasoning trace can hurt accuracy. The authors use `Jev`, a System-1 decision model that picks among candidate options without generating text, to read truncated traces, and evaluate it across seven reasoners and five multiple-choice benchmarks. `Jev` beats forced answering at every budget tested from 500 to 16,000 tokens; at a 1,500-token budget it gains **4.1 percentage points overall and 8.6 on truncated questions**. A budget policy chosen on training folds saves 71.3% of estimated full-run cost on held-out folds with a 0.58-point accuracy loss.

papers.title: Standing on the Shoulders of Giants: Enhancing LLM Agents for Automated Fact-Checking with Human Expert Skills
papers.abstract: Automated fact-checking (AFC) systems powered by large language model (LLM) agents still face challenges in evidence retrieval and claim verification. Existing approaches improve their capabilities through computationally costly post-training or human-in-the-loop feedback that is difficult to scale. To transfer professional fact-checking expertise to LLM agents efficiently, we distill publicly available guidelines published by Agence France-Presse (AFP) Fact Check into a reusable, modular Professional Fact-Checking Skill (PFC-Skill). We then present SkillCheck, the first AFC system that gives LLM agents dynamic access to PFC-Skill to guide evidence retrieval and claim verification at inference time. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SkillCheck improves upon skill-free DEFAME baselines across multiple LLM backbones, with gains of 2.2--4.8 pp. in Accuracy and 1.5--6.3 pp. in Macro-F1 on the AVeriTeC benchmark. Notably, SkillCheck with GPT-4o-Mini exceeds DEFAME with GPT-4o by 3.4 pp. in Accuracy while cutting inference cost by roughly 61%. The performance gains also extend to open-web retrieval. Ablations show that incorporating the skill during evidence retrieval provides most of the gains, while incorporation into both stages yields the best overall performance. Case studies show that PFC-Skill enables more targeted search and closer scrutiny of evidence. To conclude, our work shows that LLM agents can "stand on the shoulders of giants" by drawing on the best practices of professional fact-checkers, substantially enhancing AFC performance without extra training or continuous human supervision.
papers.summary: Automated fact-checking agents built on LLMs still struggle with evidence retrieval and claim verification, and improving them usually requires costly post-training or human feedback. The authors distill public Agence France-Presse (AFP) fact-checking guidelines into a reusable, modular `Professional Fact-Checking Skill` (`PFC-Skill`) and build `SkillCheck`, which lets agents draw on that skill at inference time. On `AVeriTeC`, it improves on `DEFAME` baselines by 2.2 to 4.8 accuracy points across several LLM backbones, and **`SkillCheck` with `GPT-4o-Mini` beats `DEFAME` with `GPT-4o` by 3.4 points while cutting inference cost by about 61%**. Ablations show that most of the gain comes from using the skill during evidence retrieval.

papers.title: Detection Augmented Learning In Non-Stationary Bandit Environments
papers.abstract: We study the problem of non-stationary bandits without knowledge of the environmental changes. We propose Detection Augmented Learning (DAL) a black-box paradigm that comprises three modular components: a bandit algorithm, a change detector, and a forced exploration schedule. This modular design enables its applicability across a broad spectrum of bandit problems, from classical to highly structured settings. First, we provide theoretical insights into DAL's strong empirical performance: a single regret bound shows that DAL transfers the regret of its stationary input to the piecewise stationary setting, attaining or improving the best known bounds in every setting considered. We further identify conditions under which DAL performs well in drifting environments. Then, we showcase DAL's practical performance and versatility through extensive experimentation in which DAL consistently surpasses all state-of-the-art methods, both prior-free and prior-based, across diverse non-stationary scenarios in nine bandit settings. Finally, we investigate the effectiveness of the forced exploration and show that a bandit-driven strategy improves performance and shortens detection delay.
papers.summary: In non-stationary bandit problems the reward environment changes without warning. `Detection Augmented Learning` (`DAL`) is a black-box framework that combines any stationary bandit algorithm with a change detector and a forced exploration schedule. A single regret bound shows that `DAL` **carries the stationary algorithm's regret over to the piecewise-stationary setting**, matching or improving the best known bounds in every setting considered, and the authors identify conditions under which it also handles gradual drift. In experiments across nine bandit settings it consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, and exploration driven by the bandit algorithm shortens detection delay.

papers.title: CoMem: Learning to Anticipate Failures from Retrieved Experience
papers.abstract: Reflection lets LLM agents improve from their own attempts, but the memory it builds is local to a single task, so an agent reflecting on its own tends to revisit the same explanation for failure. Cross-task reflective memory addresses this in two forms: retrieved memory keeps past experience explicit and looks up related cases, which is specific but bounded by the bank, and parametric memory internalizes experience into parameters, which generalizes but is grounded in nothing beyond the task description. When both are used, existing agents combine them additively, feeding their outputs to the solver side by side, so retrieved experience never changes what the learned memory produces. We introduce CoMem (Compounding Memory), which makes retrieved experience an input to the learned memory itself, at training and at inference. The agent builds a bank of its own successful and failed reflections, learns from retrieved cases to write failure hypotheses, candidate explanations of how an attempt is likely to go wrong, and at test time reasons from newly retrieved cases to guide each attempt. Varying the retrieved cases gives the memory different perspectives, yielding reflective diversity that is not merely sampled but also grounded in retrieved experience. Across two backbones and five benchmarks in math, code, and multi-hop QA, CoMem achieves strong overall performance. Additional evaluations show that it generalizes to out-of-distribution tasks and enables smaller models to provide effective guidance to stronger solvers.
papers.summary: LLM agents that reflect only on their own attempts tend to repeat the same explanation for failure, and existing cross-task memories combine retrieved cases and learned memory side by side, so retrieved experience never changes what the learned memory produces. `CoMem` (`Compounding Memory`) instead feeds retrieved past reflections, both successes and failures, into a learned memory that writes failure hypotheses: candidate explanations of how the next attempt might go wrong. Varying which cases are retrieved yields varied reflections that stay grounded in real experience. Across two backbones and five benchmarks in math, code and multi-hop question answering, `CoMem` performs strongly overall, generalizes to out-of-distribution tasks and **lets smaller models give effective guidance to stronger solvers**.

papers.title: SAR: Learning Global Item-Space Matching and Geometry-Aware Placement Ranking for Buffered Online 3D Bin Packing
papers.abstract: Online 3D bin packing with a bounded buffer requires irreversible item-selection and placement decisions under limited knowledge of future arrivals. Feasibility alone is insufficient, as feasible actions can produce different residual-space structures and subsequent packing opportunities. A central architectural question is how to allocate spatial reasoning between item selection and placement evaluation. We propose Spatial Affordance Retrieval (SAR), a novel learning-based framework that coordinates global item-space matching with geometry-aware placement ranking. A voxel-token spatial encoder represents 3D container occupancy, enabling a picker to match buffered items to the residual space without requiring item-specific placement proposals as inputs. After item selection, a loader ranks feasible rotation-position candidates using candidate geometry, local geometric features (LGF), and inter-candidate comparison, without directly accessing global spatial tokens. The feasible candidate set connects the two stages, which are jointly optimized under a shared long-horizon packing return. On the Random, JD, and SF datasets, the best SAR variants improve utilization over the strongest evaluated online baselines by 0.96-4.20 percentage points under the no-buffer setting (K=1). With a buffer (K=5), the best utilization rates across SAR variants reach 93.55%, 91.04%, and 90.41%, respectively. Ablations support the complementary roles of global item-space matching and geometry-aware placement evaluation, counterfactual analysis suggests that learned item selection favors greater future packing potential, and experiments demonstrate compatibility with multiple candidate generators.
papers.summary: Online 3D bin packing with a small lookahead buffer forces irreversible choices about which item to pack next and where to put it, and a placement that fits now can still leave awkward leftover space for later items. `Spatial Affordance Retrieval` (`SAR`) splits the decision into two learned stages. First, a picker uses a voxel-token encoder of the container to match buffered items to the remaining space. Then a loader ranks feasible rotation and position candidates using candidate geometry, local geometric features (`LGF`) and comparison between candidates, and both stages are trained jointly on a shared long-horizon packing return. On the `Random`, `JD` and `SF` datasets, `SAR` beats the strongest online baselines by 0.96 to 4.20 percentage points of utilization with no buffer, and with a five-item buffer it reaches **up to 93.55% utilization**.

papers.title: Fair Regression under Approximate Demographic Parity
papers.abstract:
Exact demographic parity requires the same prediction distribution across sensitive groups. In regression, this can be too restrictive and reduce predictive accuracy. We instead bound every pairwise Wasserstein distance between group-specific prediction distributions by a chosen tolerance, allowing the groups to differ while keeping fairness tunable.
  On the real line, the prediction and constrained transport problems have the same infimum. If the transport problem attains this value and suitable Monge maps exist, a deterministic transport-form predictor realizes it. Under a standard one-dimensional condition, the problem becomes a bounded quantile optimization that is convex when the conditional expected loss is convex in prediction. Under squared loss with two positively weighted groups, the $W_1$, $W_2$, and $W_\infty$ constraints yield soft-thresholding, shrinkage, and clipping. Under the stated conditions, we establish rates for the known-cost plug-in estimator. When the cost is unavailable, we describe an observed-loss computational proxy. Synthetic and California 2018 ACS studies illustrate the tunable fairness-accuracy trade-off and distinguish calibration feasibility from held-out fairness and accuracy.
papers.summary: Exact demographic parity, which requires identical prediction distributions across sensitive groups, can be too costly to accuracy in regression. The authors relax it by capping the Wasserstein distance between every pair of group-specific prediction distributions at a tunable tolerance. They show that on the real line the constrained prediction problem matches a constrained optimal-transport problem and, under standard one-dimensional conditions, reduces to a bounded quantile optimization that is convex for suitable losses. With squared loss and two groups, the `W1`, `W2` and `W∞` constraints give **closed-form soft-thresholding, shrinkage and clipping**. Estimation rates and experiments on synthetic data and the California 2018 `ACS` data illustrate the fairness-accuracy trade-off.

papers.title: Sector-Ring Linear Reservoirs: Sector-Wise Decay-Timescale Allocation With State Reuse Across Candidate Settings
papers.abstract: In reservoir computing, performance depends on whether the fixed dynamics of the reservoir suit the task, and the appropriate memory length and frequency response differ across tasks. The reservoir settings are found by a search on each task, and driving the reservoir with the input and collecting its states for every candidate setting dominates the cost of the search. In a reservoir with a linear recurrence, the dynamics decompose into modes, one per eigenvalue, and the eigenvalue distribution becomes a design variable. We propose the Sector-Ring Linear Reservoir (SRLR), in which the eigenvalue angles are fixed at evenly spaced positions around a circle and one decay timescale, chosen from a few values, is assigned to each sector of consecutive angles. To keep the scale of each mode's state equal across candidates, the input weights are scaled using the power spectrum of the training input. To reduce the cost of the search, the states of the modes for each decay-timescale value are computed once and reused across candidates. On prediction and reconstruction benchmarks built from chaotic systems, the SRLR achieved, in all eight cases, a lower mean test error than a reference model in which all modes share one decay timescale, and was competitive with nonlinear echo state network and leaky-integrator echo state network baselines. The selected decay-timescale profiles changed with the prediction target and horizon. The state reuse reduced the number of computed mode trajectories in the search by 99.8% relative to per-candidate recomputation.
papers.summary: In reservoir computing, a reservoir's fixed dynamics have to suit each task, and tuning them is expensive because every candidate setting requires re-running the reservoir on the input. The `Sector-Ring Linear Reservoir` (`SRLR`) is a linear reservoir whose eigenvalue angles are fixed evenly around a circle, with one decay timescale, chosen from a small set, assigned to each sector of consecutive angles. Input weights are normalized using the training input's power spectrum, and mode states for each timescale are computed once and reused across candidates. On chaotic-system prediction and reconstruction benchmarks, `SRLR` beat a single-timescale linear reservoir in all eight cases, was competitive with nonlinear echo state network baselines, and **cut the number of computed mode trajectories in the search by 99.8%**.

papers.title: Communication-Efficient Federated Domain Generalization in Edge Networks via Dynamic Prototype Regulation
papers.abstract: Federated learning (FL) is a distributed paradigm for Internet of Things (IoT) edge networks. However, deploying Vision-Language Models (VLMs) over wireless edge networks presents distinct challenges: large model parameters increase uplink transmission latency over bandwidth-constrained fading channels, and non-independent and identically distributed (Non-IID) data exacerbates client drift. Existing feature alignment solutions often introduce auxiliary computations that consume time slots allocated for wireless parameter transmission, increasing the likelihood of straggler dropouts under system delay constraints. To address these issues, we propose DPGR-GCAM, a communication-efficient federated domain generalization framework. By employing a dual-parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) architecture, we design a channel-aware tiered transmission mechanism that adaptively truncates payloads to maximize node survival rates under fading conditions. To mitigate client drift, we introduce the Gradient-Conflict Aware Modulation (GCAM) mechanism. GCAM operates within the low-dimensional feature manifold to dynamically resolve multi-objective optimization conflicts with minimal edge computation latency, thereby reducing computation-induced network outages. Experiments demonstrate that DPGR-GCAM improves cross-domain generalization and sustains convergence under network fading scenarios with a 10\% client participation rate.
papers.summary: Federated learning (FL) of vision-language models (VLMs) over wireless Internet of Things (IoT) edge networks suffers from slow uploads of large parameter sets and from client drift caused by non-independent and identically distributed (Non-IID) data. `DPGR-GCAM` uses a dual parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) architecture with a channel-aware tiered transmission scheme that truncates uploads adaptively so more clients finish within delay limits. It also adds `Gradient-Conflict Aware Modulation` (`GCAM`), which resolves conflicting optimization objectives in a low-dimensional feature space at little compute cost. Experiments report better cross-domain generalization and **stable convergence under fading channels with only 10% client participation**.

papers.title: Is it RL or Data? A Controlled Comparison of GRPO and Rejection-Sampling Fine-Tuning
papers.abstract: Bauer et al. (2026) showed that in low-data reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, training GRPO on mixed-difficulty prompts gives up to 5x the sample efficiency of easy-only prompts. They did not test whether this benefit is specific to GRPO, or whether another post-training method given the same data would obtain it too. We test this on their procedural counting task with Qwen3-4B-Base and LoRA, comparing GRPO to rejection-sampling fine-tuning (RFT) on the same prompts, verifier and token cap. Six primary arms cross the two methods with three prompt sets (Easy, Mixed, and a Curated subset of prompts the base model sometimes solves, which makes GRPO's implicit filter explicit). We use three seeds per arm. Hypotheses and falsifiers were registered before training. To rule out a poorly tuned baseline, RFT receives a 27-run hyperparameter sweep, while GRPO uses Bauer et al.'s recipe unchanged. GRPO outperforms RFT at every prompt set: by 10.9 points on held-out test problems with curated prompts, and, in post hoc comparisons with matched rollout budgets, by 8.4 and 9.2 points on the easy and mixed prompts. On test the advantage survives the least favorable treatment of truncated completions; out of distribution, truncation prevents a conclusion. Curating prompts does not help RFT (-2.7 points). Mixed-difficulty data helps RFT (+3.7 points), while for GRPO the evidence is inconclusive. A secondary iterated-RFT arm, which resamples from the current policy, recovers 3.2 of the 10.9-point gap (about 30%). These are controlled measurements on one synthetic task family and one base model with three seeds per arm.
papers.summary: Earlier work found that training `GRPO` on mixed-difficulty prompts is far more sample-efficient than training on easy prompts only, but it left open whether that benefit comes from the reinforcement learning (RL) method or from the data. In a pre-registered study on a procedural counting task with `Qwen3-4B-Base` and `LoRA`, the authors compare `GRPO` against rejection-sampling fine-tuning (`RFT`) on identical prompts, verifier and token cap, and give `RFT` a 27-run hyperparameter sweep so the baseline is well tuned. **`GRPO` outperforms `RFT` on every prompt set, by 10.9 points on held-out problems with curated prompts.** Curating prompts does not help `RFT`, mixed-difficulty data helps it by 3.7 points, and an iterated `RFT` variant that resamples from the current policy closes about 30% of the gap.

papers.title: Modal Sense Disambiguation in Language Models: The Role of Context, Training Domain, and Input Frequency
papers.abstract: Modals such as may and must can take on different senses depending on discourse context, alternating between root interpretations (e.g., permission, obligation) and epistemic interpretations (e.g., knowledge, belief). While modals are known to be notoriously difficult for children to acquire, limited research exists on whether language models (LMs) can reliably distinguish between different modal senses. We evaluate seven LMs that vary in architecture, size, and training data type using vector-based similarity and surprisal measures across four datasets. Specifically, we investigate whether LMs can leverage contextual information to disambiguate modal senses and whether their performance reflects the distribution of modal senses in their training data. We show that larger LMs trained on diverse text successfully leverage additional contextual information when available. In the absence of context, they tend to favor the dominant sense based on corpus statistics. Smaller developmentally plausible LMs, including those trained on child-directed language (CDL), fail to show consistent sensitivity to modal sense distinctions and do not benefit from context to the same degree.
papers.summary: Modal verbs such as "may" and "must" switch between root senses (permission, obligation) and epistemic senses (knowledge, belief) depending on context, and children are known to find them hard to learn. The authors test seven language models of different architectures, sizes and training data on four datasets, using vector similarity and surprisal measures. **Larger models trained on diverse text use available context to pick the right sense**, and without context they fall back on the sense that is most frequent in corpora. Smaller developmentally plausible models, including ones trained on child-directed language, show little consistent sensitivity to modal senses and gain less from context.

papers.title: When Retrieval Partially Conflicts with Skills: Understanding Procedural Hallucination in Language Models
papers.abstract: Language models increasingly use skills that provide reusable instructions and procedures for task execution. After a relevant skill has been selected, the model may need to apply its governing procedure together with retrieved task context. When the retrieved context is useful but contains cues that violate the skill, the model must retain compatible information while rejecting the conflicting cues. We study failures in which the model adopts such cues and produces a retrieval-supported but skill-invalid answer, which we call procedural hallucination. We introduce SourceClash, a matched benchmark with 1,271 bundles and 6,355 prompts across ten procedural domains. Each bundle fixes the task, skill specification, and answer space while varying the relation between the skill and retrieval. Across nine models, valid-answer rates average 25.7% under conflicting retrieval, compared with 78.2% and 72.8% under two supportive retrieval settings. Mechanistic analysis of open-weight models shows that the answer-preference difference typically reaches its maximum shortly after generation begins. Residual replacement moves the model toward valid answers, while attention decomposition attributes most of the repair to value vectors. Intervention at the identified value pathway also improves final answer validity. These results characterize how partly conflicting retrieval changes skill-guided generation.
papers.summary: Language models increasingly follow reusable "skills" (procedural instructions) alongside retrieved context. When the retrieved context is useful but contains cues that contradict the skill, models often adopt those cues, which the authors call procedural hallucination. The `SourceClash` benchmark (1,271 matched bundles, 6,355 prompts across ten domains) measures this. Across nine models, **valid-answer rates fall to 25.7% under conflicting retrieval, compared with 78.2% and 72.8% under supportive retrieval**. Mechanistic analysis of open-weight models places the shift in answer preference early in generation and attributes most of it to attention value vectors, and intervening on that pathway improves answer validity.

papers.title: Diffusion Language Models Change Speed Across Tasks and Languages
papers.abstract: Diffusion language models can write several tokens in one forward pass, and they decide during generation how many passes to spend. Two outputs of the same token length can therefore vary a lot in cost. To understand the underlying factors of this cost variation, we analyze two diffusion models across 10 tasks. We find that the number of forward passes per token depends heavily on the task. Text copied or lightly edited from the input is cheap, while open-ended writing is costly. In DiffusionGemma, generating a token for story writing requires more than three times as many forward passes as for grammar correction. Two output properties explain much of this gap: how much of it is new relative to the input, and how rare its words are within the task. The same holds within a single response when thinking is involved. The final answer is cheap when it repeats the model's reasoning trace and costly when it adds something new. In multilingual generation, we find that highly tokenized languages also require more passes per token, adding to the cost they already pay with more tokens. Finally, cost tracks correctness: on the same math problem, wrong answers take more passes per token than correct ones, and weighting candidate answers by decoding speed beats majority voting by up to 4.2 points at no extra cost. Taken together, our results show that diffusion's computational advantage depends on how much of the output is already determined, while its decoding effort offers a practical signal for making inference more efficient and reliable.
papers.summary: Diffusion language models can produce several tokens per forward pass and decide during generation how many passes to spend, so two outputs of the same length can differ widely in cost. Across two models and 10 tasks, the authors find that passes per token depend mostly on how much of the output is new relative to the input and how rare its words are. For example, story writing in `DiffusionGemma` needs over three times as many passes per token as grammar correction, and heavily tokenized languages also cost more passes per token. Cost also tracks correctness: wrong math answers take more passes per token, and **weighting candidate answers by decoding speed beats majority voting by up to 4.2 points at no extra cost**.

papers.title: Where RL Breaks: Localizing and Repairing Failures via Targeted Continued Pretraining
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is widely used to improve reasoning in language models, yet growing evidence suggests that it mostly sharpens what the base model can already do. This raises a practical question: when RL fails, what is the base model missing? We look inside the RL policy's own rollouts and find that failures are localized: whether a rollout fails is strongly predicted by a small set of characteristic n-grams, ranging from reflection phrases such as "let's recheck" to specific operations such as "the inverse of A". These failures persist throughout RL training, although they are not beyond the model's reach: other sampled answers to the same question are often correct. Building on this observation, we use the failure $n$-grams to retrieve text from the pretraining corpus and continue pretraining the base model on it before RL. The resulting corpus has only 35M tokens, 3--4 orders of magnitude smaller than typical mid-training. We evaluate this approach on OLMo2 and Qwen3 models trained with RL on (1) GSM8K; (2) a mixture of math, commonsense, and knowledge questions; and (3) general math and science reasoning. Despite its size, the corpus yields consistent gains: our approach outperforms continued pretraining on the same amount of text sampled from the pretraining corpus across 10 out of 11 settings, including by $2.0$ points on GSM8K when inserted before mid-training. The retrieved text also transfers across model families: text retrieved for OLMo2-1B's failures improves Qwen3-4B on the mixture by $1.9$ points over the same baseline. Together, our results suggest that where RL fails is a cheap and effective signal for selecting pretraining data.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) mostly sharpens abilities a base model already has, which raises the question of what the base model is missing when RL fails. Inspecting RL rollouts, the authors find that failures are predicted by a small set of characteristic n-grams, such as "let's recheck" or "the inverse of A", and that these failures persist throughout training. They use those n-grams to retrieve a 35M-token slice of the pretraining corpus and continue pretraining the base model on it before RL. On `OLMo2` and `Qwen3`, this **beats continued pretraining on the same amount of randomly sampled text in 10 of 11 settings**, and text retrieved for one model family also improves the other.

papers.title: SWIFT: Self-guided Weak-to-strong dIFfusion models via Target extrapolation
papers.abstract: Training high-quality diffusion models is computationally expensive, and inference-time guidance often adds further sampling cost. In this work, we introduce Swift, a simple yet effective self-guided training method that uses a frozen weak denoiser to improve a stronger model without adding inference overhead. For each noisy input, Swift extrapolates the clean regression target away from the weak denoiser's prediction, amplifying components that remain underfit. The weak guide can be an early training checkpoint, requires no backpropagation during main-model training, and is discarded afterward. The resulting model retains the original sampler and supports both conditional and unconditional generation without label dropout or an unconditional branch. We explain this mechanism through a spectral analysis of finite-time population gradient flow in an RKHS. With an early-stopped weak guide, we prove that a nonempty range of extrapolation strengths yields strictly lower posterior-mean error than matched standard training, despite shifting the regression target away from the posterior mean. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-256 demonstrate improvements across model scales and representations. In one ImageNet-256 configuration, Swift surpasses the baseline's best FID using roughly half the total training compute, including guide preparation and training overhead. On RAEv2, it achieves FID 1.15 without inference-time guidance and 0.99 with guidance. These results establish target extrapolation as an effective approach to weak-to-strong diffusion training with efficient single-model inference.
papers.summary: Training diffusion models is expensive, and inference-time guidance adds further sampling cost. `Swift` trains a stronger model by shifting each clean regression target away from the prediction of a frozen weak denoiser, such as an early training checkpoint, which amplifies the components that are still underfit; the weak model is discarded after training, so inference cost does not change. A spectral analysis proves that a range of extrapolation strengths gives strictly lower error than standard training. On `CIFAR-10` and `ImageNet-256`, `Swift` improves models across scales, in one configuration matches the baseline's best FID (Fréchet Inception Distance) with roughly half the compute, and on `RAEv2` **reaches FID 1.15 without inference-time guidance**.
papers.highlight_summary:
Diffusion models are expensive to train, and inference-time guidance such as autoguidance improves samples only by running extra model evaluations at every sampling step. `SWIFT` moves that weak-to-strong correction into training: it pushes each clean regression target further away from what a frozen weak denoiser predicts. The final model is a single denoiser that uses the original sampler.

- The training target becomes `y = x0 + α(x0 − D_weak(x_t))`, where `D_weak` is a frozen, smaller or earlier-checkpoint denoiser that runs without gradients; this costs about **9% extra FLOPs** per step plus roughly 10 baseline-equivalent epochs to pretrain the guide, and the guide is discarded after training.
- A spectral analysis of finite-time kernel gradient flow in an RKHS proves that, with an early-stopped guide, some nonempty range of positive α gives strictly lower posterior-mean error than standard training run for the same time, even though the shifted target is itself biased.
- On ImageNet-256 with `RAEv2/DINOv3-L`, unguided FID drops from **1.56 to 1.15** and guided FID from **1.04 to 0.99**, while the best internal-guidance scale falls from 1.78 to 1.20, which suggests training has absorbed part of the guidance correction.
- One fixed recipe (α = 0.4) lowers unguided FID in all **18 `DiffusionBench` configurations**, covering VAE, representation-autoencoder, end-to-end latent, and pixel-space models, by **16.3–49.4% (median 31.3%)**, and guided FID also improves in every configuration.
- On `DINOv2-B`, `SWIFT` reaches FID 1.50 at epoch 120, beating the baseline's best of 1.53 through 320 epochs with about **0.45× the training FLOPs** even after counting guide costs; limitations are that the theory covers denoising MSE rather than FID, performance is U-shaped in α with a model-dependent optimum, and guides that are too small or undertrained degrade results quickly.

papers.title: Measurement Validity and Representation Dynamics of Confidence Signals in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Whether a language model "knows what it knows" matters for trustworthy deployment and for deciding when it should abstain. Prior work usually measures this through one channel: verbalized confidence, a linear probe on hidden states, or agreement among sampled answers (semantic entropy), and often treats these as interchangeable. We compare all three in a pre-registered audit of five Qwen2.5 models (0.5B-7B, including a base/instruct pair at 7B) on factual retrieval (PopQA, SimpleQA) and multi-step reasoning (GSM8K, MATH). First, probes trained on prefill states to predict whether sampled answers will disagree become informative earlier for retrieval (about 7% of layer depth on average) than for reasoning (about 28%). The pre-registered five-layer test supported this only marginally; a finer 21-layer follow-up, designed after those results, supports it more clearly. In most retrieval cells, however, a prompt-only TF-IDF classifier matches the probe, so the early signal may reflect surface features of the question. Second, verbalized confidence is unstable: slightly different prompt templates yield scores that barely correlate. Third, Expected Calibration Error is misleading: verbal confidence looks well calibrated because it clusters near the base rate while discriminating poorly, whereas sampling agreement has worse ECE but about twice the resolution. Of five pre-registered hypotheses, two were falsified, one was partly supported, one was not supported, and one could not be tested because the base model's verbal confidence was degenerate.
papers.summary: Whether a language model "knows what it knows" is usually measured with a single confidence signal, either verbalized confidence, a linear probe on hidden states, or agreement among sampled answers (semantic entropy), as if these were interchangeable. A pre-registered audit of five `Qwen2.5` models on `PopQA`, `SimpleQA`, `GSM8K` and `MATH` compares all three. Probe signals appear earlier in the network for retrieval than for reasoning, but a prompt-only `TF-IDF` classifier often matches the probe, which suggests the early signal reflects surface features of the question. Verbalized confidence changes a lot with small prompt-template changes, and **Expected Calibration Error makes verbalized confidence look well calibrated even though it discriminates poorly, while sampling agreement has about twice the resolution**. Of the five pre-registered hypotheses, two were falsified.

papers.title: ACE-Trader: Adversarial Co-Evolution for Generator-Critic Trading Systems
papers.abstract: Generator--critic trading systems pair an LLM-based trader that makes trading decisions with a red team agent that evaluates these decisions and provides feedback for revision. However, improving individual trading decisions does not ensure that both agents learn from experience and improve together over time. This raises an important question: how can the trader and red-Team select useful experience and learn from each other's evolving behavior? On one hand, experience that benefits decisions under one market condition may become ineffective or harmful under another. On the other hand, trading outcomes reflect both agents' actions, making it difficult to derive appropriate experience for each role. In this work, we propose ACE-Trader, an adversarial co-evolution trading framework. Specifically, we first develop separate context-dependent memory selectors that learn to identify useful experience for the current trading decision. Both selectors receive shared feedback from net-return differences between complete memory-assisted and memory-free trading pipelines, with online updates emphasizing recent outcomes. We further design a co-evolution mechanism that links role-specific memories through shared trading records. We use these records to evaluate the Red-Team's risk assessments and the effects of the Trader's revisions against realized market outcomes, then derive experience for their respective memories. By linking this experience to the corresponding records, we enable the Trader to improve its proposals based on prior critiques and the Red-Team to adjust its review focus as the Trader's behavior changes. Experiments on U.S. stock trading show that ACE-Trader outperforms all 22 active baselines in cumulative return and achieves the highest Sharpe ratio and lowest maximum drawdown across both active methods and passive benchmarks.
papers.summary: Some LLM trading systems pair a trader agent that makes decisions with a red-team agent that critiques them, but the two agents do not reliably learn from experience together. `ACE-Trader` gives each role a context-dependent memory selector, trained online from the difference in net return between pipelines run with and without memory. It also adds a co-evolution mechanism that links the two roles' memories through shared trading records, so the trader can learn from earlier critiques and the red team can shift its focus as the trader changes. On U.S. stock trading, `ACE-Trader` **beats all 22 active baselines in cumulative return** and has the highest Sharpe ratio and lowest maximum drawdown of all methods compared.

papers.title: Rubrics Beyond Evaluation: Exploiting Rubric Structure in Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Rubrics are widely used to evaluate open-ended question answering by breaking overall quality into explicit criteria. These explicit criteria make rubrics a rich source of learning guidance, yet their potential for guiding the training process has been largely overlooked. Existing methods use rubrics mainly as direct feedback signals, without explicitly modeling the capabilities behind their criteria.
