This leaves their capability structure largely unused in guiding the training process. We introduce Rubric-Structured Reinforcement Learning (RSRL), an RL framework that unlocks the full potential of rubrics by exploiting their structure throughout the training process, rather than treating them simply as direct reward signals. At its core, RSRL builds on three key designs: (1) Rubric-to-Capability Structuring first recovers the capability structure hidden in rubric criteria, (2) Self-Sufficient Capability Learning then uses this structure to bootstrap underdeveloped capabilities into effective learning, (3) Capability-Residual Credit Routing finally preserves capability-specific gains during optimization. Experiments show that RSRL consistently improves both overall performance and underdeveloped capabilities, boosting downstream scientific question-answering performance by up to 7.43 over the initial policy and 7.60 over non-rubric structured RL baselines, showing that reinforcement learning can substantially benefit from the capability structure encoded in rubrics.
papers.summary: Rubrics split answer quality into explicit criteria, but reinforcement learning (RL) methods usually treat them only as reward signals. `Rubric-Structured Reinforcement Learning` (`RSRL`) first recovers the underlying capabilities that rubric criteria measure. It then uses that structure to bootstrap learning for weak capabilities, and routes credit during optimization so gains on each capability are preserved. On scientific question answering, `RSRL` improves overall performance and underdeveloped capabilities, with gains of **up to 7.43 points over the initial policy and 7.60 over RL baselines without rubric structure**.

papers.title: Arabic Financial NLP
papers.abstract: Financial communication connects numerical accounts of economic activity with explanations of performance, responsibility and future expectations. Arabic financial natural language processing offers methods for studying these connections across corporate reports, market disclosures, journalism and banking interactions. Its contribution to digital humanities depends on retaining the relationship between a computational representation and the document from which it was made. This chapter follows that relationship from source collection and Arabic text processing to the analysis of vocabulary, evaluation, entities, causal attribution and multilingual reporting. It then examines what financial summaries and retrieval-grounded answers preserve or lose, and how dialectal intent detection changes the perspective from institutions speaking to institutions listening. Published Arabic resources are discussed in relation to the questions they were designed to answer, with a distinction between financial pretraining corpora, annotated datasets and evaluation benchmarks. A running constructed example connects the methodological discussion without presenting illustrative analysis as empirical findings. The chapter argues for an account of Arabic financial NLP in which linguistic context, documentary provenance and interpretive judgement remain part of the evidence throughout the analytical process.
papers.summary: This book chapter surveys Arabic financial natural language processing (NLP) from a digital-humanities perspective, covering corporate reports, market disclosures, journalism and banking interactions. It follows the pipeline from collecting sources and processing Arabic text through vocabulary, sentiment, entity, causal-attribution and multilingual analysis, then looks at what summaries, retrieval-grounded answers and dialectal intent detection preserve or lose. Existing Arabic resources are sorted into pretraining corpora, annotated datasets and evaluation benchmarks. The chapter argues that **linguistic context, document provenance and interpretive judgement should remain part of the evidence** throughout the analysis.

papers.title: Statistical Learning Theory for Direct Preference Optimization
papers.abstract: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) learns from pairwise preferences through a logistic objective whose score-difference parameterization follows the Bradley--Terry model. We study how failure of this modeling assumption limits DPO, distinguishing structural misspecification from limited model capacity and finite-sample estimation. Our main contribution is a characterization of structural approximation error through the triangle-curl of the preference log-odds, which vanishes exactly when preferences admit a Bradley--Terry representation. We upper bound the achievable excess logistic risk by a score-class approximation term and a triangle-curl term, and establish a lower bound proportional to triangle-curl under additional boundedness assumptions. For ReLU score models, including clipped models, we derive explicit approximation rates showing that increasing capacity can eliminate the score-approximation term while leaving the structural obstruction unchanged. We further establish finite-sample bounds for clipped empirical risk minimizers that separate network approximation, structural misspecification, and estimation error. We place these results within a surrogate-risk framework by identifying contextual preference accuracy (CPA) as a natural measure of agreement between preference judgments and changes in pairwise probability ratios relative to the reference policy. Standard logistic consistency and calibration results connect DPO's objective to this policy property and transfer our excess-risk upper bounds to CPA, without treating CPA as a complete measure of generated-response quality.
papers.summary: Direct Preference Optimization (`DPO`) assumes preferences follow the Bradley-Terry model, and this analysis separates the error that comes from violating that assumption from the error due to limited model capacity and finite samples. The structural error is characterized by the triangle-curl of the preference log-odds, which is zero exactly when preferences admit a Bradley-Terry representation, and the authors give matching upper and lower bounds in terms of it. For ReLU score models, **adding capacity removes the approximation error but leaves the structural triangle-curl error unchanged**. Finite-sample bounds and a link to a policy-level measure called contextual preference accuracy complete the framework.

papers.title: Are Self-Evolving Agents Continual Learners?
papers.abstract: Large language model agents are often deployed in environments where new knowledge, tools, and workflows keep arriving. Such an agent is therefore expected to adapt continually, learning new tasks as they arrive without forgetting earlier ones. This resembles the continual learning problem, but at a pace that conventional gradient updates cannot sustain. Nonparametric self-evolving agents are a natural alternative: they adapt by rewriting their own harness, such as prompts, memory, and skills, from task feedback while the model weights stay frozen. We study whether such agents are effective continual learners across four drifting task streams that shift in topic, workflow, or domain (built from BIRD, BFCL, and ScienceWorld). Evaluating three representative methods spanning experience retrieval and self-modification (ReasoningBank, GEPA, and Meta-Harness), we find that although self-evolution improves aggregate performance on most streams, higher plasticity consistently comes at the cost of stability. Specifically, self-modifying methods apply global edits to a shared prompt or workspace, interfering with unseen tasks and overwriting earlier knowledge as the stream shifts. Conversely, similarity-based memory retrieval localizes updates across distant domains, but still retrieves foreign memories on unseen tasks and suffers from retrieval collision when similar queries require conflicting workflows. These findings show that current self-evolving agents remain incomplete continual learners.
papers.summary: LLM agents deployed over time need to pick up new tasks without forgetting old ones, and nonparametric self-evolving agents attempt this by rewriting their prompts, memory and skills while keeping model weights frozen. The authors evaluate three such methods, `ReasoningBank`, `GEPA` and `Meta-Harness`, on four drifting task streams built from `BIRD`, `BFCL` and `ScienceWorld`. Self-evolution improves aggregate performance on most streams, but **greater adaptability consistently comes at the cost of forgetting**. Self-modifying methods make global edits that interfere with unseen tasks and overwrite earlier knowledge, while memory retrieval keeps updates local but retrieves irrelevant memories and gets confused when similar queries need conflicting workflows.

papers.title: Adaptive Decoding Methods for Token-Efficient Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Rollout decoding affects both which trajectories are used for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) and how many completion tokens are spent collecting them. We study whether candidate-token support should remain fixed or widen during training in the context of rollout sampling efficiency. Our main schedule moves from top-K=10 to K=20 and then to full support as the attempted-token budget increases. In a 4B code-RLVR setting, the schedule has a higher interpolated 150M-token validation value than its matched fixed-K=10 continuation in all three runs, with a mean gain of $1.80{\pm}0.42$ points. The schedule also performs comparably to a separately trained fixed-K=20 baseline, the strongest fixed-support setting in our sweep. Follow-up experiments suggest that late widening to full support is the most promising variant, although the evidence remains noisy, and mixed-reward-group diagnostics do not clearly explain the gain. An exploratory single-run test replay yields identical point estimates for the schedule and fixed $K=10$. Overall, our results show that rollout support is an important control for sampling efficiency in RLVR and motivate further study of adaptive support schedules.
papers.summary: In reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), the decoding settings used for rollouts determine both which trajectories are collected and how many tokens they cost. The authors test widening the candidate-token support during training, moving from top-K=10 to K=20 and then to full sampling as the token budget grows. In a 4B-parameter code RLVR setting, the schedule beats a matched fixed K=10 continuation in all three runs, with a **mean gain of 1.80 ± 0.42 points**, and performs comparably to the best fixed K=20 baseline. Follow-up results are noisy, and the authors present rollout support as a control worth further study rather than a settled recipe.

papers.title: CODA: Cohort- and Drift-aware Foundation Model for Multimodal Clinical Reasoning
papers.abstract: Recent advances in multimodal foundation models have demonstrated strong performance across diverse clinical tasks. However, existing approaches predominantly operate at the individual sample level and fail to model the interplay between population-level cohort patterns and patient-specific variation that underlie real-world clinical reasoning. In practice, clinicians routinely reason through patient cohorts sharing similar demographic, physiological, or pathological characteristics, while accounting for patient-specific deviations from the group prototype. Motivated by this gap, we propose CODA, a cohort- and drift-aware foundation model for multimodal clinical reasoning. CODA explicitly integrates cohort structure into the modeling pipeline through two complementary mechanisms: cohort-aware population stratification and drift-aware individual adaptation. In particular, we leverage reinforcement learning to discover clinically meaningful patient cohorts, and further model each patient's deviation from cohort prototypes as a structured drift signal encoding fine-grained individual heterogeneity. These cohort- and drift-aware representations are incorporated into the foundation model to enable reasoning that is simultaneously informed by population-level patterns and sensitive to individual-level variation. Extensive experiments on real-world electronic health record (EHR) benchmarks demonstrate that CODA achieves consistent effectiveness and strong generalizability across diverse clinical tasks, including closed-QA, open-QA, and report generation.
papers.summary: Multimodal clinical foundation models usually reason about one patient at a time, whereas clinicians compare a patient with similar patients and note how that patient differs. `CODA` uses reinforcement learning to discover clinically meaningful patient cohorts and represents each patient's deviation from the cohort prototype as a structured drift signal. Both signals are fed into the foundation model. On real-world electronic health record (EHR) benchmarks, `CODA` shows **consistent gains across closed-ended QA, open-ended QA and report generation**.

papers.title: Residual-Guided Adaptive Tucker Rank Allocation for Parameter-Efficient MCI Conversion Prediction
papers.abstract: Allocating limited trainable capacity across convolutional layers is a central challenge in parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) of pretrained three-dimensional (3D) networks. We propose Residual-Guided Adaptive Tucker Rank Allocation, which jointly selects input- and output-channel ranks under a fixed adapter-parameter budget while preserving the spatial kernel modes. To guide rank selection, we learn task-specific proxy updates from downstream training data and approximate them using candidate Tucker rank pairs. A perturbation analysis bounds the output discrepancy between the fixed proxy network and its Tucker approximation in terms of layerwise reconstruction residuals, motivating residual-based allocation. We normalize each squared residual by the corresponding proxy-update energy to compare relative approximation errors across layers. Dynamic programming minimizes their sum under a global budget constraint that accounts for both channel factors and the Tucker core. This yields a globally optimal allocation over the specified candidate rank pairs. We evaluate the method on the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) cohort for predicting conversion from mild cognitive impairment to Alzheimer's disease within 36 months, using hippocampal segmentation pretraining. Across five random seeds, the proposed method achieves a mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.7706, compared with 0.7239 for fixed-ratio Tucker adaptation and 0.7430 for full fine-tuning. The total number of trainable parameters is limited to approximately 0.618 million, accounting for only 1.45% of the full model. Adaptive Tucker rank allocation thus provides an effective approach to parameter-efficient transfer learning in 3D medical imaging.
papers.summary: When fine-tuning pretrained 3D convolutional networks with a limited parameter budget, a key question is how much trainable capacity each layer should get. The proposed method learns task-specific proxy updates, measures how well candidate Tucker-decomposition rank pairs approximate them, and uses dynamic programming to choose the rank allocation that minimizes total normalized residual error under a global budget. On the `ADNI` cohort, predicting conversion from mild cognitive impairment to Alzheimer's disease within 36 months, it reaches a **mean AUC of 0.7706, compared with 0.7239 for fixed-ratio Tucker adaptation and 0.7430 for full fine-tuning**, while training only 1.45% of the model's parameters.

papers.title: Learning to Reason Efficiently with Interventional Step Credit
papers.abstract: Large reasoning models often produce lengthy chain-of-thought (CoT) traces mixing useful intermediate steps with unnecessary ones. Recent methods explore step-level signals such as attention mass and step entropy to identify and suppress unnecessary steps. Despite their effectiveness, such signals reflect the model's behavior at a step rather than that step's contribution to the answer. To address this, we propose the interventional step credit (ISC), which takes a causal-intervention view and assesses step importance to the reasoning through targeted parameter-level interventions. Building on ISC, we further propose IGPO, which uses ISC to guide fine-grained advantage rescaling in reinforcement learning, reducing redundant steps while preserving the important ones. Experiments across two model scales and nine benchmarks show that IGPO achieves up to 62% average token reduction and better overall performance among compared methods.
papers.summary: Large reasoning models write long chain-of-thought (CoT) traces that mix useful steps with unnecessary ones, and existing signals for pruning them, such as attention mass or step entropy, describe the model's behavior at a step rather than the step's effect on the answer. Interventional step credit (`ISC`) estimates each step's importance through targeted parameter-level interventions. `IGPO` then uses `ISC` to rescale reinforcement-learning advantages at the step level, discouraging redundant steps while keeping important ones. Across two model scales and nine benchmarks, `IGPO` achieves **up to 62% average token reduction** and the best overall performance among the methods compared.

papers.title: DeltaTrace: Efficient Signed Attribution for Reasoning Language Models
papers.abstract: We study how words in the context support or oppose a language model's response and present DeltaTrace, a novel attribution framework that explains the effect of input tokens on a fixed model response. DeltaTrace measures how the response's log-probability changes when the context tokens being explained are masked. To distribute this difference among source tokens, it constructs operator-specific local rules for finite changes and composes them backward through the computational graph using effective secant slopes. Each token is assigned a signed attribution as the inner product of its embedding displacement and the corresponding backward-propagated slope. Local conservation makes these contributions sum to the measured score difference and preserves their meaning when aggregated over sentences or passages. DeltaTrace supports both attention and linear-attention models, with auxiliary memory growing linearly with sequence length at fixed model dimensions and chunk size. On the evaluated attention model, DeltaTrace achieves the lowest deletion-faithfulness scores (RISE and MAS) on most retrieval and reasoning tasks and the highest needle-in-a-haystack Recall, exceeding FlashTrace by 5.67-24.33 percentage points. On the evaluated hybrid attention and linear-attention model, DeltaTrace lowers RISE on 9 tasks and MAS on 12 relative to FlashTrace.
papers.summary: Explains how each context token supports or opposes a language model's fixed response by measuring how the response's log-probability changes when chosen context tokens are masked. `DeltaTrace` splits that change among source tokens using operator-specific local rules for finite changes, which it composes backward through the computational graph using effective secant slopes. Because contributions are locally conserved, the signed per-token attributions sum exactly to the measured score difference, and they still hold when aggregated over sentences or passages. It works on both attention and linear-attention models with auxiliary memory that grows linearly with sequence length, and on an attention model it beats `FlashTrace` on needle-in-a-haystack recall by **5.67 to 24.33 percentage points** while achieving the best `RISE` and `MAS` deletion-faithfulness scores on most retrieval and reasoning tasks.

papers.title: Asynchronous On-Policy Self-Distillation
papers.abstract: Unlike on-policy distillation (OPD), which depends on a separate teacher model, on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) leverages a single language model acting simultaneously as the student and the teacher, with the teacher conditioned on privileged information. Despite this architectural simplicity, synchronous rollout generation dominates overall training time, creating a severe systems bottleneck when scaling OPSD. To address this, we introduce Asynchronous On-Policy Self-Distillation (AsyncOPSD), a framework that decouples rollout generation from learner updates to improve training throughput. Since the teacher and student share parameters, AsyncOPSD eliminates the multi-model coordination overhead inherent to OPD architectures in asynchronous training. As the student policy evolves, buffered trajectories generated by older policies become stale, potentially degrading performance. To mitigate this, we introduce a distillation objective based on staleness-aware policy control and token-level entropy weighting. Across three model sizes and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, AsyncOPSD improves the training throughput by $1.96$--$2.25\times$ over synchronous OPSD while increasing average benchmark accuracy.
papers.summary: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) uses one language model as both student and teacher, with the teacher given privileged information, but synchronous rollout generation takes up most of the training time. `AsyncOPSD` separates rollout generation from learner updates, and because teacher and student share parameters, it avoids the multi-model coordination that asynchronous on-policy distillation with a separate teacher would require. To handle stale trajectories produced by older policies, it adds a distillation objective with staleness-aware policy control and token-level entropy weighting. Across three model sizes on mathematical reasoning benchmarks, it delivers **1.96 to 2.25 times higher training throughput** than synchronous OPSD while also raising average accuracy.

papers.title: Learn the Interface, Not the Implementation: Output Representation Dominates Training Regime in LLM-Based RTL Generation
papers.abstract: Large-language-model register-transfer-level (RTL) generation has concentrated on how to train the model: fine-tuning, continued pre-training, and reinforcement learning from a verifier. We argue this is the second-order question. On a bounded, formally specifiable task of generating single-error-correcting, double-error-detecting (SECDED) ECC memory wrappers, we hold the task, data, and correctness oracle fixed and vary two axes independently: the training regime (seven settings) and the output representation (four levels, from fully expanded flat Verilog to an eight-field configuration expanded by a deterministic generator). Because a reference generator exists, correctness is decided by formal equivalence over a design space of approximately ten million points, rather than sampled from a hand-written testbench. Two results follow. First, representation dominates: every representation close to raw RTL reaches a pass rate of at most 0.17, while the configuration reaches 0.83 with no training at all. Once the model emits the configuration, every training regime achieves a pass rate between 0.89 and 1.00. Second, raw RTL hits a hard output-length limit: a 512-bit design requires 44,237 tokens of flat Verilog compared with just 69 tokens for the configuration. Consequently, raw generation becomes infeasible above 32-bit data words rather than merely inaccurate. A model trained from scratch with fewer than 50 million parameters, combined with the verified generator, achieves 0.89 formal equivalence, compared with 1.00 for a 32-billion-parameter fine-tuned model, while using approximately 1600 times less inference energy per correct design. Inference energy also dominates amortized training energy. The lesson is to learn the interface, not the implementation.
papers.summary: Research on using LLMs to generate register-transfer-level (RTL) hardware code has focused on training methods, and this work tests whether the output representation matters more. On one formally specifiable task, generating single-error-correcting, double-error-detecting (SECDED) ECC memory wrappers, it varies seven training regimes and four output representations, ranging from flat `Verilog` to an eight-field configuration that a deterministic generator expands, and checks correctness by formal equivalence. Representations close to raw RTL reach a pass rate of at most 0.17, while **the configuration format reaches 0.83 with no training** and 0.89 to 1.00 under every training regime. Raw RTL also hits a hard length limit (44,237 tokens versus 69 for a 512-bit design), and a model under 50 million parameters paired with the generator reaches 0.89 equivalence while using about 1600 times less inference energy per correct design than a fine-tuned 32-billion-parameter model.

papers.title: Motor compound fault diagnosis using an attention-based cross-talk architecture
papers.abstract: As physical AI increasingly relies on sensing to understand physical systems, reliable condition monitoring of industrial machinery has become more important. Motors are ubiquitous in industrial systems, and increasing system complexity raises the likelihood of simultaneous faults. Accordingly, compound fault diagnosis that identifies multiple fault components and their severities is increasingly required. Because different fault components jointly affect the same vibration signal, their severity classification can be formulated as related tasks, making multi-task learning (MTL) suitable for exploiting shared information. However, conventional shared-trunk architectures force tasks to share a common representation, potentially causing negative transfer because fault components are characterized by different time-frequency regions. To address this issue, this study proposes a Residual Neural Dimension Reductor with Time-Frequency Channel Attention (RNDR-TFCA), an attention-enhanced cross-talk architecture for multi-output compound fault diagnosis. RNDR-TFCA preserves task-specific feature extractors while selectively exchanging information across tasks. Time-frequency attention emphasizes informative intra-task regions, while channel attention enhances useful inter-task information after nonlinear feature fusion. Experiments on a rotor-bearing system with inner-race fault, outer-race fault, misalignment, and unbalance showed that RNDR-TFCA achieved a macro F1 score of 0.898, outperforming single-task, multi-class, shared-trunk, and cross-talk baselines. Ablation experiments confirmed the benefit of jointly applying both attention mechanisms. RNDR-TFCA required 713 K parameters and 170.42 MMACs, only slightly higher than RNDR. Channel-expanded baselines still underperformed RNDR-TFCA, indicating that the gain was not simply attributable to increased model capacity.
papers.summary: Targets compound fault diagnosis in motors, where several simultaneous faults and their severities must be identified from the same vibration signal. Shared-trunk multi-task learning (MTL) can cause negative transfer because each fault shows up in different time-frequency regions, so the proposed `RNDR-TFCA` keeps a feature extractor per task and exchanges information selectively between tasks through time-frequency and channel attention. On a rotor-bearing system with inner-race, outer-race, misalignment, and unbalance faults, it reaches a **macro F1 of 0.898**, beating single-task, multi-class, shared-trunk, and cross-talk baselines with only 713K parameters. Ablations show that both attention mechanisms contribute, and channel-expanded baselines confirm the gain is not simply due to added capacity.

papers.title: Budgeted Attack Scheduling for LLM Red-Teaming: The Roles of Static Priors, Semantic Guidance, and Online Feedback
papers.abstract: As jailbreak attacks against large language models (LLMs) become increasingly diverse, red-teaming has come to rely on large libraries of jailbreak prompts and attack strategies to evaluate the robustness of victim models and their defense settings. However, attack effectiveness is highly condition-dependent: an attack that succeeds under one victim-defense setting may fail under another, while exhaustively evaluating the full attack library for each setting incurs substantial token and monetary costs. This motivates studying how jailbreak attacks should be prioritized under a limited attempt budget for efficient robustness evaluation. In this work, we formalize this problem as budgeted attack scheduling over a fixed attack library and investigate three complementary signals under a fixed victim-defense condition: (1) static historical attack success rate (ASR) priors; (2) semantic guidance from LLMs; and (3) online feedback from earlier queries. Building on these signals, we design four scheduling strategies and evaluate them across three victim models and three defense settings on GPT-5.2. Extensive experiments clearly characterize the conditions under which each signal is most effective. Historical ASR provides a strong initialization, but its reliability degrades under defense-induced distribution shifts. Semantic guidance consistently improves or matches static prior-based scheduling in the cold-start regime, while online feedback becomes particularly valuable when transferred priors become stale. Semantic guidance and online feedback can also partially compensate for missing historical priors. Taken together, these findings characterize budgeted red-teaming as an attack scheduling problem in which historical priors, semantic guidance, and online feedback play complementary roles.
papers.summary: Frames LLM red-teaming as budgeted attack scheduling: given a fixed library of jailbreak attacks and a limited number of attempts, decide which attacks to try first against a specific victim model and defense setting. The study compares three signals, namely static historical attack success rate (ASR) priors, semantic guidance from an LLM, and online feedback from earlier queries, through four scheduling strategies across three victim models and three defense settings. Historical ASR gives a strong starting point but **becomes unreliable when defenses shift the distribution**. Semantic guidance matches or improves on static priors from a cold start, online feedback matters most when transferred priors go stale, and the latter two can partly make up for missing historical data.

papers.title: SWE-Residual: Evaluating Starting-State Robustness of Coding Agents
papers.abstract: Software engineering (SWE) benchmarks are the primary way to measure the capabilities of coding agents: an agent is placed in a code repository or machine environment, given a request, and judged by hidden tests. These benchmarks almost always start the agent from a clean state that contains no earlier work on the task. In practice, however, agents often continue work that a developer or another agent has already done and reported as complete, with no indication of what remains incorrect or missing. We introduce SWE-Residual, a benchmark for Starting-State Robustness: the ability to maintain performance on a task when the starting state already contains earlier work on that task. SWE-Residual contains 198 Residual States drawn from 111 tasks in DeepSWE and Terminal-Bench, where the earlier work modifies a code repository or a whole machine environment. Each Residual State is the state a predecessor agent left behind after submitting its work as complete, although the hidden tests still fail. The evaluated agent receives only the original request and this state, without the predecessor's trajectory or any sign that the attempt failed; because the request and hidden tests are unchanged, the starting state is the only difference from the source benchmark. Across five frontier agents, success drops by 20.6--53.5 percentage points on DeepSWE and 20.6--34.9 points on Terminal-Bench relative to a Clean Start, and agent rankings on DeepSWE reverse. Failed continuations show a pattern we call acceptance bias: agents treat the inherited work as the definition of what remains to be done instead of checking it against the request. On DeepSWE, in 58.9--88.2% of failed runs, they submit with exactly the same tests failing, although they pass most of these tests from a Clean Start. SWE-Residual thus exposes a capability gap that clean-start evaluation does not capture.
papers.summary: Coding-agent benchmarks almost always start from a clean repository, but in practice agents often pick up work that a developer or another agent left behind and reported as complete. `SWE-Residual` contains 198 such residual states drawn from 111 tasks in `DeepSWE` and `Terminal-Bench`; in each one a predecessor agent submitted its work while the hidden tests still failed, and the evaluated agent gets only the original request and that state. Across five frontier agents, success drops by **20.6 to 53.5 percentage points on DeepSWE** and 20.6 to 34.9 on Terminal-Bench compared with a clean start, and agent rankings on DeepSWE reverse. The authors identify an acceptance bias: in 58.9 to 88.2 percent of failed DeepSWE runs, agents submit with exactly the same tests still failing, even though they pass most of those tests when starting clean.

papers.title: Out-of-Distribution Detection in Continual Learning
papers.abstract: Out-of-distribution detection in continual learning (OOD-CL) is highly challenging, as it requires (i) learning a sequence of tasks without catastrophic forgetting, and (ii) identifying unknown samples (OOD) without access to known (in-distribution (ID)) data from past tasks, where standard confidence-based OOD scores tend to degrade. Existing methods largely rely on a rehearsal buffer of past data or assume closed-world settings, limiting their scalability and reliability in real-world scenarios. In this paper, we propose a novel OOD detection framework for rehearsal-free continual learning, inspired by Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KAN), which mitigate catastrophic forgetting via their inherent local neuroplasticity. To better leverage KAN in OOD-CL, we introduce a task-adaptive classifier architecture, TA-KAN, which mitigates recency bias and enhances ID--OOD separability through task-specific control of activation locality. Furthermore, we propose a geometry-guided OOD score that complements TA-KAN classifier confidence without relying on past ID data. Our method significantly improves OOD detection while maintaining strong ID classification performance, achieving state-of-the-art results in OOD-CL.
papers.summary: Tackles out-of-distribution detection in continual learning (OOD-CL), where a model must learn a sequence of tasks without catastrophic forgetting and also flag unknown inputs without access to in-distribution data from past tasks. Building on Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KAN), whose local plasticity limits forgetting, the authors propose `TA-KAN`, a task-adaptive classifier that controls activation locality per task to reduce recency bias and better separate in-distribution from out-of-distribution inputs. They pair it with a geometry-guided OOD score that complements classifier confidence and requires no rehearsal buffer. The method reports **state-of-the-art OOD-CL results** while keeping in-distribution classification strong.

papers.title: An Analysis of Semantic and Spatio-Temporal Co-evolution for Edge Classification on Dynamic Text-Attributed Graphs
papers.abstract: Dynamic edge classification on text-attributed Web graphs, such as review networks, community forums, and news-derived knowledge graphs, requires high quality, adaptive semantic representations in the context of network evolution. Existing dynamic graph architectures typically initialize text feature vectors with pretrained language models and hold them static during training to preserve their semantic structure, forgoing the potential benefits of allowing them to co-evolve with network topology. In this work, we investigate the effects of enabling such co-evolution with a unified text-graph alignment framework that integrates a lightweight Transformer adapter to update token-level text representations via spatio-temporal gradients from a contrastive pretraining objective. To prevent detrimental semantic distortion, a language model maintenance objective anchors the evolving text embeddings to their original semantic structure. Evaluations on the Dynamic Text-Attributed Graph Benchmark demonstrate that this anchored text-graph co-evolution consistently improves upon the edge classification performance of frozen-text baselines across diverse Web-related domains. Representational analyses reveal that the framework reduces anisotropy, improving the linear separability of text embeddings, and effectively encodes structural and temporal information into the semantic space. A computational efficiency analysis confirms that this beneficial semantic and spatio-temporal co-evolution is achieved without incurring the prohibitive computational overhead typical of end-to-end joint training.
papers.summary: Dynamic graph models for edge classification on text-attributed Web graphs usually freeze the text embeddings produced by a pretrained language model. This work lets those embeddings co-evolve with the graph: a lightweight Transformer adapter updates token-level text representations using spatio-temporal gradients from a contrastive pretraining objective, while a language-model maintenance objective keeps them close to their original semantics. On the `Dynamic Text-Attributed Graph Benchmark`, this anchored co-evolution **consistently beats frozen-text baselines** across Web domains. Analyses show it reduces embedding anisotropy, improves linear separability, and encodes structural and temporal information, without the heavy cost of end-to-end joint training.

papers.title: CALM: Consistency-Aware Logit Masking in Decoding Space for Mitigating Overthinking of Large Reasoning Models
papers.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) have achieved strong performance on challenging mathematical and scientific tasks through long chain-of-thought reasoning, but they often suffer from overthinking with unnecessary reasoning steps. Existing truncation-based methods typically detect consecutive trial-answer agreement and force early exit, yet such local stopping signals do not necessarily indicate final-answer stability and can disrupt useful subsequent reflection or verification, potentially leading to performance degradation. We propose consistency-aware logit masking (CALM), a training-free decoding intervention for mitigating overthinking in LRMs. CALM first monitors trial answers at step boundaries and then applies logit masking to action transition point (ATP) tokens such as "Wait", "Alternatively", and "Hmm", suppressing redundant transitional reasoning while allowing the model to continue its thought process more naturally. Experiments across four advanced LRMs and five benchmarks show that CALM reduces token consumption by 18.6%-25.0% compared with full CoT reasoning while maintaining performance, and can even improve accuracy by 0.07%-1.48% by reducing redundant reasoning. LLM-as-a-Judge results also demonstrate that CALM provides more coherent and concise results.
papers.summary: Large reasoning models (LRMs) often overthink, and existing methods that force an early exit once consecutive trial answers agree can cut off useful verification. `CALM` (consistency-aware logit masking) is a training-free decoding intervention that monitors trial answers at step boundaries and then masks the logits of action-transition tokens such as 'Wait', 'Alternatively', and 'Hmm', which suppresses redundant detours while letting the model finish its reasoning naturally. Across four LRMs and five benchmarks, it **reduces token use by 18.6 to 25.0 percent** compared with full chain-of-thought while maintaining accuracy, and sometimes improves it by up to 1.48 percent. LLM-as-a-judge evaluations also rate its outputs as more coherent and concise.

papers.title: FisherEdit: Fisher Information Guided Knowledge Editing for Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Sequential knowledge editing in Large Language Models (LLMs) often leads to a degradation of general capabilities due to cumulative parameter interference. In this paper, we revisit prominent projection-based methods like AlphaEdit and reveal a surprising mismatch: their robustness is primarily driven by update regularization rather than the intended null-space projection. Based on this insight, we propose FisherEdit, a theoretically grounded method built on Fisher geometry, which replaces coarse activation-space projections with importance-aware regularization in parameter space. It penalizes changes to sensitive parameters more strongly while retaining flexibility for new facts, and admits an efficient row-wise closed-form solution. Experiments on Llama-3, Qwen2.5, and Olmo-3 across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that FisherEdit achieves state-of-the-art performance while better preserving model stability and downstream task accuracy.
papers.summary: Sequential knowledge editing gradually degrades an LLM's general capabilities, and the authors find that the robustness of projection-based editors such as `AlphaEdit` **comes mainly from update regularization rather than null-space projection**. Building on this, `FisherEdit` replaces activation-space projection with Fisher-information-weighted regularization in parameter space, penalizing changes to sensitive parameters more heavily while leaving room for new facts. It admits an efficient row-wise closed-form solution. Experiments on `Llama-3`, `Qwen2.5`, and `Olmo-3` report state-of-the-art editing performance with better preservation of model stability and downstream accuracy.

papers.title: LEAPS: Long-context Evaluation of Adaptive Pattern Learning and State Tracking
papers.abstract: Long-context language models (LCLMs) power agents that act over long trajectories, from improving a codebase to running research experiments to forecasters that condition on lengthy histories. These applications draw on three distinct long-context capabilities: recall, where the answer is a fact present in the context; state tracking, where the outcome can be computed by performing a series of transformations to a specified state; and pattern learning, where the goal is to make a prediction by sampling from a distribution inferred from many observations. Existing benchmarks primarily focus on the first capability. In this work, we introduce LEAPS (Long-context Evaluation of Adaptive Pattern learning and State tracking), a collection of 12 novel datasets, spanning agentic workflows, behavioral modeling, and forecasting of market and world events. By construction, LEAPS is resistant to data contamination, extends to millions of input tokens, and uses reliable metrics. We evaluate 30 API and open models from 8K to 512K input tokens. LEAPS distinguishes models that perform near perfectly on recall tasks, finding that such models' state tracking and pattern learning abilities can vary significantly and degrade much more dramatically with increasing input lengths--even for pattern learning, where more observations should make learning a theoretically easier task. Moreover, thinking models often underperform their base counterparts, exhausting their generation budget or oversimplifying the task. We hope LEAPS can guide the development of the next generation of LCLMs.
papers.summary: Long-context benchmarks mostly test recall, but agents and forecasters also need state tracking, which means applying a series of transformations to a known state, and pattern learning, which means inferring a distribution from many observations. `LEAPS` provides 12 contamination-resistant datasets covering agentic workflows, behavioral modeling, and market and world-event forecasting, scaling to millions of tokens. Evaluating 30 API and open models from 8K to 512K input tokens shows that models near-perfect at recall vary widely on the other two capabilities and **degrade much more sharply as inputs grow**, even on pattern learning, where more observations should make the task easier. Thinking models often underperform their base versions, either exhausting their generation budget or oversimplifying the task.

papers.title: Maestro: Agentic Formal Proof Development by Coordination
papers.abstract: Lean is increasingly used to verify mathematical proofs and software produced by LLM agents, but writing formal proofs remains hard. Existing prover systems take a divide-and-conquer approach that recursively decomposes hard proof obligations into easier lemmas and splits again any lemma that resists proof. However, a lemma can resist proof for different reasons, including insufficient guidance, a false statement, or a flaw in the decomposition that produced it. Existing systems cannot tell these apart as a failed attempt reports little beyond its failure, and responses are confined to the failing node without considering the rest of the proof or revising the plan above it. The system may thus keep decomposing obligations along a flawed proof direction until the budget runs out, causing the whole proof attempt to fail. We introduce Maestro, a Lean prover harness that handles failures through global coordination. Provers report why they failed, not just that they failed, and a coordinator that sees the whole proof chooses an appropriate response, such as guiding a stuck prover, correcting a false lemma, or retracting a flawed subtree and replanning it. The same harness extends to verified code synthesis, where a checked counterexample sends the code back for repair. We evaluate Maestro with four frontier LLMs on seven mathematics and three software verification benchmarks. It proves more targets than each model's native coding agent (Claude Code or Codex) on every benchmark the agent has not already saturated, with the largest gains on research-level mathematics. With Claude Opus 5, it discovers its own proofs of 34 of the 48 theorems in the June 2026 release of arXivLean, against 19 for the native agent. It also outperforms all published prover systems on every benchmark they share, solving 669/672 PutnamBench, 59/60 Lean-IMO-Bench, and 6/6 IMO 2026.
papers.summary: Existing Lean provers recursively split hard proof obligations into lemmas but cannot tell whether a lemma failed for lack of guidance, because it is false, or because the decomposition above it is flawed. `Maestro` has provers report why they failed, and a global coordinator responds by guiding a stuck prover, correcting a false lemma, or retracting and replanning a flawed subtree; the same harness handles verified code synthesis by sending checked counterexamples back for repair. Across four frontier LLMs and ten math and software-verification benchmarks, it beats each model's native coding agent (`Claude Code` or `Codex`) on every unsaturated benchmark, and with `Claude Opus 5` it proves 34 of 48 `arXivLean` theorems compared with 19 for the native agent. It also outperforms all published provers on every shared benchmark, **solving 669 of 672 PutnamBench problems and all 6 IMO 2026 problems**.

papers.title: UtilityBench: Measuring Language Model Utility When Errors Have Different Costs
papers.abstract: As language models are increasingly deployed in real-world scenarios with important outcomes, the impact of their mistakes often extends far beyond what correctness can capture. In domains like medicine, a single error can lead to serious consequences and put patient safety at risk. However, mainstream evaluation protocols still treat all errors as equal, overlooking the spectrum of real-world costs. To address this, we propose a utility-based evaluation paradigm that explicitly incorporates the varying consequences of errors. Guided by this principle, we develop UtilityBench, a large-scale benchmark of 15,000 instances with verifiable answers, quantifying error severity using Best-Worst Scaling to elicit meaningful, data-driven cost estimates. These quantified utilities shape when a model should answer or abstain, guiding it to make decisions that align with the true importance of each scenario. As another merit, we introduce UtilityAUC, a metric that measures the area under the utility curve determined by a model's response ordering, thereby enabling utility preference alignment beyond error frequency. Our theoretical analysis demonstrates that UtilityAUC can distinguish between models where standard accuracy and AURC fall short. Empirically, evaluating 20 state-of-the-art models, we find that greater accuracy or more advanced architectures do not reliably translate to higher UtilityAUC, highlighting a gap between problem-solving ability and responsible decision-making in language model evaluation.
papers.summary: Standard LLM evaluation treats all errors as equally costly, which misrepresents high-stakes settings such as medicine. `UtilityBench` contains 15,000 instances with verifiable answers and assigns each error a severity estimated through Best-Worst Scaling, so the resulting utilities determine when a model should answer and when it should abstain. The authors also introduce `UtilityAUC`, which measures the area under the utility curve induced by a model's response ordering, and show theoretically that it can separate models that accuracy and the area under the risk-coverage curve (AURC) cannot. Across 20 state-of-the-art models, **higher accuracy or more advanced architectures do not reliably lead to higher UtilityAUC**.

papers.title: EvoSkill v2: Fully Agentic Skill Evolution from Benchmark Adaptation to a Stateful Evolver
papers.abstract: EvoSkill v2 is a three-agent system that edits the instructions (skills) an agent is given, leaving its model and harness intact. The user starts a run by describing a benchmark and supplying a grader, which a benchmark adaptor turns into a benchmark-specific plugin. A solver attempts the tasks, and an evolver reads the solver's training rollouts and rewrites the skills at each epoch. We implement the evolver as one stateful coding agent with a bash tool for the whole run, unlike the two most common designs among the skill optimizers we surveyed: a sequence of single model calls, as in SkillOpt, and an agent that starts afresh each round, as in SkillBoost. We also measure how much the solver's rollouts vary from one attempt to the next, give the evolver several attempts per training task, and accept every epoch's skills instead of selecting among them on noisy scores. With fine-grained ground truth, EvoSkill v2's skills raised the held-out pass rate above the stronger of SkillOpt and SkillBoost by 7.7 percentage points on SpreadsheetBench v2 and by 5.4 on $\tau^3$-bench banking. In both benchmarks and both feedback settings, EvoSkill v2's evolver cost less per percentage point of held-out pass rate gained than either baseline's optimizer. EvoSkill v2 also enables a less capable model to improve its own skills, demonstrated by a gain of up to 21.5 percentage points in the $\tau^3$-bench banking experiment where Claude Haiku 5.5 powers both solver and evolver.
papers.summary: `EvoSkill v2` improves an agent by rewriting its skill instructions while leaving the model and harness unchanged, using three agents: one adapts a user-described benchmark and grader into a plugin, a solver attempts the tasks, and an evolver rewrites the skills after reading the solver's rollouts. Unlike `SkillOpt`, which uses a sequence of single model calls, and `SkillBoost`, which restarts its agent each round, the evolver is one stateful coding agent with a bash tool for the whole run; it also gets several attempts per training task and accepts every epoch's skills rather than selecting among them on noisy scores. With fine-grained ground truth, it raises held-out pass rates over the stronger baseline by **7.7 points on SpreadsheetBench v2** and 5.4 points on `tau^3-bench` banking, at a lower cost per point gained. It also lets `Claude Haiku 5.5` improve its own skills, gaining up to 21.5 points when that model powers both the solver and the evolver.

papers.title: Keep the Lineages Alive: Diversity-Preserving SMC for Diffusion LLM Decoding
papers.abstract: Inference-time sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) decoding can improve the reasoning accuracy of masked diffusion language models (diffusion LLMs) without post-training by resampling a population of partial generations according to a reward. Its effectiveness therefore depends on the resampling step, which must concentrate computation on promising candidates while retaining enough diversity to explore alternative reasoning paths. The reward can be internal, the decoder's own confidence on the committed prefix, or external, a process reward model scoring that prefix. Under either reward, multinomial resampling can disrupt this balance by duplicating high-weight particles and discarding lineages that may still reach a correct solution. The effective sample size (ESS) does not register this loss: multinomial resampling resets it to its maximum even as distinct lineages disappear. To retain such lineages, we introduce lineage-preserving SMC (LP-SMC), which combines Chopthin resampling with an input weight floor. Instead of equalizing weights, Chopthin bounds the ratio between the largest and smallest weights it returns and carries the unequal weights forward. The floor limits how far below the maximum a weight may fall before resampling so that lineages with low early weight keep a chance to recover. Across mathematical-reasoning and code-generation benchmarks on two base models, LP-SMC raises oracle coverage, the fraction of problems with at least one correct particle, in every setting, by 1.8 to 25.6 points, and raises end-to-end accuracy under a common reward-model selector in eleven of twelve settings, by up to 7.9 points on LLaDA-1.5 and 18.3 on Dream-7B. The coverage gain persists under the external reward model, which suggests that diversity-preserving resampling and the guidance signal contribute separately to inference-time search.
papers.summary: Inference-time sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) decoding improves reasoning in masked diffusion language models by resampling a population of partial generations according to a reward, but standard multinomial resampling duplicates high-weight particles and discards lineages that might still reach a correct answer. The effective sample size (ESS) does not reflect this loss, because resampling resets it to its maximum. `LP-SMC` combines Chopthin resampling, which bounds the ratio between the largest and smallest weights instead of equalizing them, with a floor on input weights so that lineages that start with low weight can recover. On math and code benchmarks it **raises oracle coverage in every setting by 1.8 to 25.6 points** and improves end-to-end accuracy in 11 of 12 settings, by up to 7.9 points on `LLaDA-1.5` and 18.3 on `Dream-7B`.

papers.title: The KV-Surgeon: Compensation-Aware Offline KV-Cache Compaction
papers.abstract: Offline compaction of the key--value cache (KV-cache) reduces the cost of repeatedly querying a fixed context by constructing a smaller cache once and reusing it subsequently. The central challenge of compaction is deciding which cache entries to delete and which to retain. Existing methods score each candidate for deletion on its own, with the rest of the cache being held fixed. However, softmax renormalization of the attention operation couples these decisions in a nonlinear manner: removing one entry changes the attention weights of every remaining one. In this work, we introduce KV-Surgeon, which uses calibration data to take interactions into account in a tractable way. We derive a quadratic surrogate that admits closed-form expressions for jointly making the optimal greedy removal decision as well as compensation within the remaining entries. On QuALITY, LongHealth, and Long Code Arena, and at every evaluated compaction ratio, KV-Surgeon substantially advances the cost--accuracy Pareto frontier of dense and mixture-of-experts models from 4B to 30B parameters. At $50\times$ compaction, KV-Surgeon improves question-answering accuracy by up to four points over attention matching (Zweiger et al., 2026), the state of the art, at comparable cost. Lastly, we introduce an even faster variant, which also exceeds the state of the art while requiring only two fifths of its cost.
papers.summary: Offline key-value cache (KV-cache) compaction builds a smaller cache once so that a fixed context can be queried repeatedly at lower cost, but existing methods score each entry for deletion independently even though softmax renormalization couples those decisions. `KV-Surgeon` uses calibration data and a quadratic surrogate with closed-form expressions that jointly choose the best greedy removal and compensate the remaining entries. On `QuALITY`, `LongHealth`, and `Long Code Arena`, it advances the cost-accuracy Pareto frontier at every compaction ratio for dense and mixture-of-experts models from 4B to 30B parameters, and at **50 times compaction it gains up to four points of question-answering accuracy** over attention matching at comparable cost. A faster variant also beats the prior state of the art at two-fifths of its cost.

papers.title: MITRA-lexicon: Lexica of attested translations from Sanskrit into English, Tibetan and Chinese
papers.abstract: The standard Sanskrit lexica are monumental and indispensable, but they cite their attestations as abbreviated references to editions, without links to the digitized texts now widely available and without a translation of the passage, and they naturally do not reflect translations made after them. To address these gaps, we present MITRA-lexicon, a family of corpus-grounded lexica based on span annotations of translation equivalents with Sanskrit as the pivot: Sanskrit-English, derived from the Mitrasamgraha corpus, as well as Sanskrit-Tibetan and Sanskrit-Chinese, derived from the MITRA-parallel corpus of Buddhist literature. In total, the resource comprises 2.18 million headword entries in six directional lexica. Headwords are lemmas and compounds from silver annotations that follow the Digital Corpus of Sanskrit (DCS). Senses are ranked by frequency, and each of the 10.4 million attestations includes its sentence pair, with character offsets of the word and its equivalent. We propose a multi-step pipeline based on grammatical annotation models, fine-tuned large language models, and a teacher-student setup to produce the alignments. We evaluate the lexica against reference dictionaries and manually corrected gold alignments. We release the lexica and the fine-tuned span annotation model, together with a web interface for looking up headwords and their attested senses.
papers.summary: Standard Sanskrit dictionaries cite attestations as abbreviated references to editions, without links to digitized texts or translations of the passages. `MITRA-lexicon` builds corpus-grounded lexica from span-annotated translation equivalents with Sanskrit as the pivot: Sanskrit-English from the `Mitrasamgraha` corpus, and Sanskrit-Tibetan and Sanskrit-Chinese from the `MITRA-parallel` Buddhist corpus. The resource holds **2.18 million headword entries across six directional lexica and 10.4 million attestations**, each linked to its sentence pair with character offsets. Alignments come from a pipeline of grammatical annotation models, fine-tuned LLMs, and a teacher-student setup, and are evaluated against reference dictionaries and gold alignments.

papers.title: Speech LLMs That Breathe: Modeling Non-Verbal Vocalizations in Dialogue
papers.abstract: The user experience of speech interaction models has improved, benefiting from the modeling of paralinguistic attributes and advances in speech reconstruction paradigms. However, human communication follows extensive norms regarding non-verbal vocalizations (NVVs) spanning respiratory, affective, and discourse. The omission of these events imposes inherent limitations on the naturalness of current approaches. In this work, we cover 13 major types of NVVs and construct a natural dialogue dataset that conforms to human conversational norms through an automated synthesis pipeline. We enhance the ability of speech interaction models to generate contextually appropriate NVV events through multi-stage fine-tuning and NVV-aware GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization). Based on distinct modeling paradigms, we substantially improve the expressiveness of VocalNet and VITA-Qinyu in empathy interactions and role-play dialogues, and further discuss the architectural necessity for achieving high-quality natural speech generation.
papers.summary: Spoken dialogue models rarely produce non-verbal vocalizations (NVVs) such as breaths, laughs, and discourse sounds, which limits how natural they sound. The authors cover 13 NVV types, build a natural dialogue dataset through an automated synthesis pipeline, and train models with multi-stage fine-tuning followed by NVV-aware Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Applied to two speech interaction models with different architectures, `VocalNet` and `VITA-Qinyu`, the approach **substantially improves expressiveness in empathetic and role-play dialogue**. The paper also discusses which architectural choices are needed for high-quality natural speech generation.

papers.title: OrderGPT: Generation Order as a Learnable Modeling Choice
papers.abstract: Generative modeling of discrete data has two popular paradigms: autoregressive models such as GPT, which factorize a sequence in a left-to-right (L2R) order, and masked diffusion models, which are essentially any-order autoregressive modeling. Rather than competing methods, these are the two extreme points of a single axis -- the generation order. For structured discrete domains without a natural traversal, both extremes may be suboptimal, yet the intermediate choice -- a single well-adapted order -- remains largely unexplored. We introduce OrderGPT, which builds on Any-Order GPT to learn a task-level generation order without canonical-order supervision. Our key observation is that predicting variables from randomly sampled reveal prefixes produces recurring attention patterns in the backbone that provide a model-dependent signal of predictive dependencies. We aggregate this signal into a reciprocal dependency graph and use a spectral teacher to derive continuous generation priorities. A lightweight OrderMLP integrated into the GPT backbone learns to predict these priorities from attention, incorporating order learning into the architecture within a single training run. Training gradually shifts toward the learned order, which is then frozen for subsequent autoregressive training and generation. The same mechanism adapts across modalities: adaptively it recovers near-L2R dependency structure in language, learns anatomically organized factorizations on human pose, and discovers a factorization on tabular data that places statistically and semantically related fields nearby, while improving downstream modeling metrics across all domains. The code is available at https://github.com/Chenhe-yang/OrderGPT/.
papers.summary: Autoregressive left-to-right models and masked diffusion models, which amount to any-order generation, sit at opposite ends of a single axis, namely generation order, and for structured data without a natural ordering both extremes may be suboptimal. `OrderGPT` builds on `Any-Order GPT` and turns recurring attention patterns, which emerge when variables are predicted from randomly revealed prefixes, into a dependency graph; a spectral teacher converts that graph into generation priorities, and a lightweight `OrderMLP` learns to predict them within a single training run. The learned order is then frozen for autoregressive training and generation. It **recovers near left-to-right structure in language**, learns anatomically organized orders for human pose and groups related fields in tabular data, and improves downstream metrics in all three domains.

papers.title: AdaExploreBench: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Proactive Exploration and Test-time Adaptation in Evolving Environments
papers.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in unfamiliar and evolving environments, requiring them to proactively explore, understand, and adapt to environmental dynamics. However, existing benchmarks rarely test whether agents can proactively discover how an environment works and adapt as it evolves. To address this gap, we introduce AdaExploreBench, a benchmark for proactive exploration and test-time adaptation in evolving environments. By instantiating environmental dynamics as hidden rules, AdaExploreBench requires agents to actively acquire evidence and infer the rules. Under implicit rule drift, the latent rule changes without announcement, requiring agents to detect from degraded performance that prior knowledge is stale and re-explore. Experiments on eight leading LLMs show that proactive and adaptive exploration remain challenging: GPT-6 Sol achieves only 61.9% calibrated accuracy, while providing sufficient evidence or removing rule drift improves average performance significantly by close to 10%. These results reveal a critical bottleneck in current LLM agents: they can often reason effectively from informative evidence once it is available, but struggle to actively acquire the right evidence and recognize when previously acquired evidence is no longer valid.
papers.summary: `AdaExploreBench` tests whether LLM agents can work out how an unfamiliar environment operates and adapt as it changes. Environment dynamics are encoded as hidden rules that agents must infer by actively gathering evidence, and under implicit rule drift these rules change without announcement, so agents must notice from declining performance that their knowledge is stale and explore again. Across eight leading LLMs, even `GPT-6 Sol` **reaches only 61.9 percent calibrated accuracy**, and supplying sufficient evidence or removing rule drift raises average performance by close to 10 points. The results suggest that agents reason well once they have informative evidence but struggle to collect the right evidence and to recognize when it has become invalid.

papers.title: Productive State-Space Exploration for Multi-turn RL in LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) for Large Language Model (LLM) agents in multi-turn, long-horizon environments remains challenging due to inefficient action selection and repetitive behavioral patterns. In particular, agents often become trapped in high-confidence yet unproductive behaviors, repeatedly executing invalid actions or entering action loops that hinder task completion. We observe that these frequently violate environment preconditions, revealing a mismatch between the agent's representation of the internal state and the dynamics of the underlying environment. In addition, repetitive high-confidence actions lead to cyclical behaviors that provide little to no progress towards the goal. We argue that addressing these challenges requires more productive task-aligned exploration to improve the agent's understanding of environment dynamics. Motivated by intrinsic curiosity-driven exploration, we propose a conditional state-space exploration framework that balances task completion with intrinsic information-seeking behavior. Specifically, we introduce an intrinsic reward that penalizes actions whose observation duplicates prior state memory. This provides the benefit of reducing redundant behaviors and encouraging state-space coverage without relying on a general information-theoretic measure. Strong experimental results demonstrate that our approach substantially improves policy learning in multi-turn environments, mitigating invalid actions and repetitive loops.
papers.summary: LLM agents trained with reinforcement learning (RL) in long, multi-turn environments often get stuck repeating confident but useless behavior, such as invalid actions that break environment preconditions or loops that make no progress. Drawing on curiosity-driven exploration, the authors propose a conditional state-space exploration framework that balances task reward against information-seeking. Its core is an intrinsic reward that **penalizes actions whose resulting observation duplicates one already in the agent's state memory**, which pushes the agent toward broader state coverage without needing a general information-theoretic measure. Experiments show substantially better policy learning in multi-turn environments, with fewer invalid actions and repetitive loops.

papers.title: Token-Set Choice Confounds POPE: A Systematic Audit of Yes/No Extraction in VLM Hallucination Evaluation
papers.abstract: We set out to reproduce a recent hallucination-mitigation result on the POPE benchmark. The LLaVA-1.5-7B baseline we measured, 82.21 F1 on the adversarial split, sat 1.21 to 8.67 points above the adversarial baselines we planned to compare against (81.00, 79.30, and 73.54). We looked at the evaluation code and found a readout choice that moves F1 on its own. A two-token logit readout decides yes versus no by comparing two vocabulary IDs, 3582 ("yes") and 1217 ("no"). Across 9,000 greedy-decode questions spanning all three splits, neither ID is generated even once. The model emits " Yes" (token 3869) and " No" (token 1939), because SentencePiece prepends a space byte after the prompt suffix "ASSISTANT:". Read with an eight-token lookup that covers the space-prefixed surface forms, LLaVA-1.5-7B scores F1 0.8221, 0.8498, and 0.8713 on the adversarial, popular, and random splits. That 6.13-point adversarial shift exceeds the adversarial gain reported by five of the six papers we surveyed. None of them states its readout, and our reference ran under 4-bit NF4 quantization, so we cannot say how much of any reported gain a matched evaluation would keep. That comparison stays unresolved until readout and precision are matched. On the fixed baseline we run nine inference-time corrections of our own (none beat it) and dissect why the adversarial split resists logit-level intervention. In a 3,000-question probe, wrong predictions draw more image attention than correct ones (Cohen's $d=-0.46$, $p=1.4\times10^{-24}$), the opposite of what grounding-based corrections assume. A four-readout audit across four further VLMs from three tokenizer families confirms the confound is protocol-level, not model-specific: porting the LLaVA-1.5 IDs verbatim drops F1 to 0.00 on the two disjoint-vocabulary models, whereas a tokenizer-derived readout holds between 0.80 and 0.92.
papers.summary: While trying to reproduce a hallucination-mitigation result on the `POPE` benchmark, the authors traced inflated and inconsistent baselines to how yes/no answers are read from model logits. A common two-token readout compares token IDs that `LLaVA-1.5-7B` never actually generates, because the SentencePiece tokenizer emits space-prefixed " Yes"/" No" tokens instead. Fixing the readout shifts adversarial-split F1 by **6.13 points, more than the gain reported by five of six surveyed mitigation papers**, none of which state their readout. Further experiments find that nine inference-time corrections fail to beat the fixed baseline, that wrong predictions draw more image attention than correct ones, and that the confound appears across four other vision-language models (VLMs) from three tokenizer families.

papers.title: GLOBE: Geometry-Led Online Behavioral Early Exit via Unit-Sphere Trajectories
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning can improve problem solving, but models often keep generating after the correct answer is already reachable; the extra steps raise serving costs and may replace a correct intermediate result with an incorrect one. We propose GLOBE (Geometry-Led Online Behavioral Early Exit), an online, training-free algorithm that terminates the model's CoT process early. GLOBE embeds each completed reasoning segment as a point on a unit sphere and reads the shape of the resulting semantic trajectory. GLOBE first applies a trial phase that generates short trial answers in a separate branch, stopping the main stream on an accepted trial after checking confidence against a threshold. If generation continues, a trajectory phase stops the stream once this path repeatedly reverses direction with little net progress. On five benchmarks including mathematical reasoning, tool calling, and agent memory, GLOBE cuts output tokens by 49.7% and active end-to-end wall time (E2E) by 51.0% across two models, and achieves a five-task average of 80.58%, comparable to Full CoT.
papers.summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning models often keep generating after the correct answer is already within reach, which raises serving costs and can overwrite a correct intermediate result. `GLOBE` is a training-free online method that embeds each completed reasoning segment as a point on a unit sphere and stops generation based on the shape of that trajectory. It first tries short trial answers in a side branch and accepts one if its confidence passes a threshold; otherwise it halts once the trajectory repeatedly reverses direction with little net progress. Across five benchmarks covering math, tool calling, and agent memory, it **cuts output tokens by 49.7% and end-to-end wall time by 51.0%** while matching full-CoT accuracy (80.58% average).

papers.title: Correctness-Dependent Asymmetric Target Distributions for Self-Distillation Policy Optimization
papers.abstract: Self-distillation policy optimization provides dense token-level supervision for LLM post-training through feedback-conditioned self-teachers. However, directly matching the self-teacher can disrupt successful behaviors on correct rollouts while providing insufficient correction on incorrect ones. We propose Asymmetric Policy Optimization via Self-Distillation (APSD), which constructs correctness-dependent targets by mixing student and self-teacher distributions: interpolation preserves successful behaviors on correct rollouts, while extrapolation beyond the self-teacher strengthens correction on incorrect ones. We analyze APSD through divergence decomposition, reverse-KL barycentric geometry, and gradient analysis, highlighting the importance of gradient flow through student-dependent targets. Experiments under reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards and rich feedback show that APSD achieves strong overall performance against reinforcement-learning and self-distillation baselines and matches SDPO performance with 2.6x fewer training steps on average across Qwen3 model scales.
papers.summary: Self-distillation policy optimization gives LLMs dense token-level training signals from a feedback-conditioned copy of themselves acting as teacher, but matching that teacher directly can damage behavior on correct rollouts and under-correct incorrect ones. `APSD` (Asymmetric Policy Optimization via Self-Distillation) builds correctness-dependent targets instead: it interpolates between student and teacher on correct rollouts and extrapolates beyond the teacher on incorrect ones. The authors analyze the method through divergence decomposition, reverse-KL geometry, and gradient analysis, stressing the role of gradients flowing through student-dependent targets. In reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards and with rich feedback, `APSD` beats RL and self-distillation baselines and **matches `SDPO` with 2.6x fewer training steps on average** across `Qwen3` model sizes.

papers.title: NIOCIS: Typed-Decision Next-Hop Routing with Node-Conditioned Option Spaces for Tool-Use Agents
papers.abstract: Tool-use agents pay per decision: at each hop a language model re-reads the state and thinks for seconds, though its actions are finite and decisions recur. We present NIOCIS, a routing layer that folds execution logs into a loop-collapsed action graph (forward transitions plus recovery back-edges) answering one typed question: which declared option at a state, plus stop, does the fleet take next? A small model reads a calibrated distribution over them in one pass, emitting no text. On 1,615 production security-operations episodes we measure what the layer replaces, returns and is bounded by. Replaces: the typed encoder matches the logged next hop on 32.2% of the 3,875 held-out decisions (34.9% within the declared options) in 10 ms of encoder time (19.5 ms for the typed-choice form), against 2.2 s per LLM hop; two feature readouts reach 32.8% and 32.3%, an ordering the paired test does not resolve, so the typed layer is chosen for cost, not a separated lead. Tuning: jpt-4b reaches 9.9% zero-shot and 31.9% fine-tuned, a gap an exact paired test does not resolve (p=0.68), at 244 ms. Returns little: the realised hop falls outside the declared options for 7.9% of decisions and outside the model's top twenty for 9.3%; the most confident 15% holds 91.9% accuracy. Bounded: a cross-trace leave-one-out test puts the released state's ceiling at 25.6--44.9% as the state key grows more specific, i.e. repeated states disagree more often than they agree; the option-space ablation attributes the gain to per-node candidate restriction (+3.5 points over a flat catalog) rather than graph traversal (zero within its interval); a gated self-evolution loop lifts every arm above its anchor yet ends below full supervision; a confidence-gated cascade loses agreement when the escalation arm is the zero-shot stand-in; and agreement past a third of the fleet needs a state carrying the plan and the observation.
papers.summary: Tool-use agents pay for an LLM call at every step, even though their action choices are finite and recur often. `NIOCIS` turns execution logs into an action graph with loops collapsed and trains a small model to output, in a single pass with no generated text, a calibrated distribution over the declared options (plus stop) at each state. On 1,615 production security-operations episodes, it matches the logged next step **32.2% of the time in about 10 ms, against 2.2 s per LLM step**, and reaches 91.9% accuracy on its most confident 15% of decisions. The authors also report its limits in detail: repeated states often disagree on the next step, capping achievable agreement at roughly 25–45%, and most of the gain comes from restricting candidates per node rather than from graph traversal.

papers.title: Graph-to-Table Interfaces Control Relational Generalisation
papers.abstract: Graph-to-table systems combine three design choices: an encoder that maps relational evidence to feature rows, a context constructor that selects labelled examples, and a tabular decoder. We investigate whether these components can be evaluated independently through matched comparisons that change one component while holding the rest of the pipeline and the evaluation constant. Across logistic regression, CATBOOST, and TABPFN-3 on CLUTRR, 57 GraphLog worlds, and 57 knowledge graphs, we show that conclusions about one component can change when the others change. On CLUTRR, absolute positional encodings maintain all distinctions among the evaluated queries and fit the short-path setting nearly perfectly; yet, they generalise worse than relation-count features because the supported prefix acts as a shortcut that breaks down on longer paths. On GraphLog, encoder preference depends on the decoder, while the relation-count representation degrades as CatBoost tree depth increases.
