Across different knowledge graphs, adding the frozen ULTRA score to local features is consistently useful, whereas adding local features to the score has a smaller and less stable effect. A pointwise TABPFN-3 readout using the full encoder underperforms native ULTRA on 48 of 57 datasets. These results show that encoder assessment depends jointly on context and decoder, while panel-level conclusions can also depend on evaluation and aggregation protocols.
papers.summary: Graph-to-table pipelines combine an encoder that turns relational evidence into feature rows, a context constructor that picks labelled examples, and a tabular decoder. The authors test whether these parts can be judged separately, using matched comparisons with `logistic regression`, `CatBoost`, and `TabPFN-3` on `CLUTRR`, 57 `GraphLog` worlds, and 57 knowledge graphs. They find that **conclusions about one component change when the others change**: positional encodings fit short paths almost perfectly but generalize worse than relation-count features, and the best encoder depends on the decoder. A pointwise `TabPFN-3` readout also underperforms native `ULTRA` on 48 of 57 datasets.

papers.title: Federated Community Detection in Bipartite Networks
papers.abstract: We study federated spectral estimation when a large matrix is horizontally partitioned across servers that cannot share raw data. We propose FLICKER, a target-specific gradient-based power iteration that recovers a singular direction associated with a prescribed spectral target using only matrix-vector products on local blocks. Different target directions can be recovered independently and in parallel. We establish non-asymptotic convergence guarantees and provide a recursive grid-search procedure for spectral target selection. Building on FLICKER, we develop BiFLICKER for federated community detection in bipartite networks, together with a sequential projected variant for nearby or repeated singular directions. Under a sparse bipartite stochastic block model, we show that properly rescaled leading singular values from a reference server provide valid global targets, and that Sequential BiFLICKER achieves a vanishing misclustering rate and exact recovery under stronger sparsity conditions. Simulations show that BiFLICKER remains close to centralized spectral clustering and is more robust than existing federated spectral baselines when local sample sizes are small. On a LastFM user-artist network naturally partitioned by country, Sequential BiFLICKER attains an overall ARI of 0.94 against centralized clustering while revealing cross-country communities with distinct listening profiles.
papers.summary: The setting is spectral estimation when a large matrix is split by rows across servers that cannot share raw data. `FLICKER` is a gradient-based power iteration that recovers the singular direction for a chosen spectral target using only local matrix-vector products, so different directions can be recovered in parallel; it comes with non-asymptotic convergence guarantees. The extension `BiFLICKER` performs federated community detection in bipartite networks and, under a sparse bipartite stochastic block model, provably achieves vanishing misclustering and exact recovery under stronger sparsity conditions. On a `LastFM` user-artist network split by country, it reaches an **adjusted Rand index (ARI) of 0.94 against centralized clustering**.

papers.title: Internalizing Chain-of-thought into Looped Transformers
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) enables constant-bit-size transformers to perform general-purpose computation through generated tokens (Li and Wang, 2025a), whereas looped transformers carry out the same computation by recurrence in hidden states (latent thought). We construct a family of constant-bit-size looped transformers that interpolates between CoT and latent thought. For a prescribed loop count $L=L(n)$ and a fixed integer $k\ge1$ satisfying $s(n)^{1/k}=\Omega(L)$, our transformer simulates a time-$t(n)$, space-$s(n)$ Turing machine using a context window of $O(s(n)/L)$ and $O(t(n)s(n)^{1/k}/L)$ generated tokens, reducing both resources by a factor of $L$ relative to the corresponding unlooped queue-machine simulation. The construction also holds with softmax attention at constant bit-size, under the finite-precision kernel specified in this paper.
papers.summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) lets constant-bit-size transformers perform general computation through generated tokens, while looped transformers do it through recurrence in hidden states. The authors construct a family of constant-bit-size looped transformers that interpolates between these two modes. With L loops, the construction simulates a Turing machine while **reducing both the context window and the number of generated tokens by a factor of L** compared with the unlooped simulation. The result also holds with softmax attention at constant bit-size, under a finite-precision kernel the paper specifies.

papers.title: TempoMoE: Identifying and Steering Fast-Slow Thinking Experts for Efficient Multimodal Reasoning
papers.abstract: Multimodal Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) reasoning models rely on long chain-of-thought (CoT) for complex tasks, yet often overthink easy inputs, increasing token cost and latency, and sometimes degrading accuracy. Existing methods optimize reasoning length during training or impose external control at inference, but leave the underlying reasoning mechanism a black box. We find that fast and slow thinking exhibit distinct expert-routing patterns: holding the input fixed and varying only the prompted reasoning tempo produces stable routing shifts. Suppressing slow-thinking experts shortens the reasoning chain, whereas suppressing fast-thinking experts lengthens it, providing causal evidence that these experts influence reasoning depth. Based on this finding, we propose TempoMoE, a training-free, two-stage framework. It identifies fast- and slow-thinking experts via tempo-contrastive routing analysis and redistributes routing weights within the original top-k set according to sample difficulty. It amplifies fast-thinking experts and suppresses slow-thinking experts on easy inputs and reverses this adjustment on hard ones, enabling difficulty-adaptive control over reasoning depth. We evaluate TempoMoE on Kimi-VL, Qwen3-VL, and ERNIE-4.5-VL across six benchmarks. Compared with Vanilla, TempoMoE consistently improves accuracy while reducing output tokens, with accuracy gains of up to 2.6 points and token reductions of up to 35.4%.
papers.summary: Multimodal Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) reasoning models often overthink easy inputs, wasting tokens and sometimes losing accuracy. The authors find that fast and slow thinking use distinct expert-routing patterns, and that suppressing slow-thinking experts causally shortens reasoning chains while suppressing fast-thinking experts lengthens them. `TempoMoE` is a training-free method that identifies these experts by contrasting routing under different prompted reasoning tempos. It then reweights routing within the original top-k experts according to input difficulty. On `Kimi-VL`, `Qwen3-VL`, and `ERNIE-4.5-VL` across six benchmarks, it improves accuracy by up to 2.6 points while **cutting output tokens by up to 35.4%**.

papers.title: PnP-CF: A Consensus Flow-Matching Solver for General Inverse Problems
papers.abstract: Plug-and-Play (PnP) methods using continuous-time deep generative models as learned data distribution priors enable synthesizing high-quality solutions of model-based inverse problems. The quality of the solutions depends critically on the interplay and consensus between the inverse problem solver and the generative model sampler. We revisit a recently introduced flow-based PnP framework, which we refer to as PnP-CF (Consensus Flow), and extend its application to nonlinear inverse problems, including those with learned neural-network forward operators. PnP-CF combines a flow-matching denoiser with (i) ADMM-like dual variable updates and (ii) a time-adaptive pullback onto the intermediate flow probability path that combines a stochastic and a deterministic component. We discuss how these two features stabilize the algorithm and promote consensus, and demonstrate on a set of experiments that PnP-CF not only solves standard linear inverse problems with quality at least comparable to state-of-the-art baselines, but also extends gracefully to nonlinear inverse problems, including forward operators realized by pretrained neural networks, for which existing methods produce unsatisfactory results or fail completely.
papers.summary: Plug-and-Play (PnP) methods use generative models as learned priors for solving inverse problems, and their output quality depends on how well the solver and the sampler agree. The authors revisit a flow-based PnP framework they call `PnP-CF` (Consensus Flow), which combines a flow-matching denoiser with dual-variable updates similar to the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) and a time-adaptive pullback onto the flow's intermediate probability path. They show it matches state-of-the-art baselines on standard linear problems and **extends to nonlinear inverse problems, including forward operators that are pretrained neural networks, where existing methods do poorly or fail completely**.

papers.title: SPLASH: Contrastive Audit Pressure for Detecting and Localizing Security Hallucinations in Generated Code
papers.abstract: Code generated by large language models often passes every functional test while remaining insecure. These security hallucinations are common, written with high confidence, and repeated across samples, so neither the generator's own uncertainty nor static analyzers reliably catch them. We introduce SPLASH, which is guided by a new measure called audit pressure. It contrasts teacher-forced log-probabilities for the generated program under a security review and a style review. Aggregated to statements and programs, and grounded in a probabilistic model of competing edits, audit pressure allows SPLASH to choose the secure program among a model's candidate programs and locate the vulnerable statement, with no model training, CWE-specific rules, or internal access to the generating model. On 63,684 programs generated by 12 models for 899 tasks, SPLASH picks secure code in 74% of cases, places the vulnerable statement first in 58% of insecure programs, and chooses better than a frontier LLM judge.
papers.summary: LLM-generated code often passes every functional test while still containing security flaws, and these "security hallucinations" are produced confidently and repeatedly, so neither the model's own uncertainty nor static analyzers reliably catch them. `SPLASH` uses a measure called audit pressure, which compares a model's teacher-forced log-probabilities for the generated program under a security-review prompt versus a style-review prompt. Aggregated per statement and per program, the signal is used to pick the secure candidate and locate the vulnerable line, without training, rules for specific Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) categories, or access to the generating model's internals. On 63,684 programs from 12 models, **`SPLASH` picks secure code in 74% of cases, ranks the vulnerable statement first in 58% of insecure programs**, and outperforms a frontier LLM judge.

papers.title: Scenario Generalization and Sector Transfer in Real Surface Irrigation Surrogate Modelling with Tabular Models
papers.abstract: Surface irrigation planning requires screening many operating conditions and spatial configurations, while high-fidelity shallow-water-equation (SWE) simulations are expensive. We study tabular surrogate models for predicting maximum water height from drone-derived field morphology, terrain, hydrological, spatial, and scenario descriptors, where each row represents a spatial cell under one irrigation scenario. To assess deployment feasibility, we evaluate gradient-boosted trees, neural tabular models, AutoML, and tabular foundation models (TFMs) under two regimes: same-sector generalization, where a model predicts unseen scenarios after observing a limited set of configurations in the same sector, and sector-out transfer, where knowledge learned from source sectors is transferred to an unseen sector. The main findings are twofold: a) under the evaluated fixed 8/32 same-sector split, surrogates achieve strong performance, especially with raw spatial coordinates; b) sector-out transfer is substantially harder because the target sector has different coordinates and geometry. Sector-frame normalization of spatial coordinates improves transfer across similarly structured sectors, but does not solve cross-shape generalization. Overall, tabular surrogates appear useful for same-sector scenario screening under this fixed split, while robust transfer to unseen sectors remains open.
papers.summary: Planning surface irrigation means screening many scenarios, but high-fidelity shallow-water-equation (SWE) simulations are expensive. The authors test tabular surrogate models that predict maximum water height from drone-derived terrain and scenario features, comparing gradient-boosted trees, neural tabular models, AutoML, and tabular foundation models. **Surrogates perform well on unseen scenarios within the same field sector**, especially when given raw spatial coordinates. Transfer to an unseen sector is much harder, and normalizing coordinates to the sector's frame helps only between similarly shaped sectors.

papers.title: Scaling Synthetic Pre-training Data and Evaluation for Indic LLMs
papers.abstract: Building capable language models for India requires scalable multilingual data and robust evaluation. We introduce Nemotron-Pretraining-Indic-v1, a synthetic pretraining corpus of approximately 2.83 trillion tokens covering all 22 scheduled Indian languages in native script and twelve in romanized form. It is the largest openly released Indic pretraining corpus. Using our GPU-accelerated pipeline, we translate curated English documents, assess translation quality, and repair low-quality outputs while preserving technical content and document structure and maintaining source traceability. Through continued-pretraining experiments across twelve languages, we show that combining our synthetic corpus with natural Indic text improves knowledge and reasoning over a public-corpus baseline. Additional experiments show how data volume, script coverage, and Indic training share affect English performance. We also introduce the Indic-LLM-Eval-Suite, a multilingual benchmark suite for evaluating Indic language models across chat, instruction following, reasoning, knowledge, code, and translation. The suite combines existing Indic benchmarks with task-aware translations of English benchmarks, using automated quality assessment, targeted correction, and native-speaker review in a human-in-the-loop pipeline. We use the suite to comprehensively benchmark contemporary open-weight Indic and multilingual models across capabilities and languages, revealing substantial variation across tasks and languages. Together, these resources provide a scalable foundation for developing and evaluating more capable Indic language models.
papers.summary: `Nemotron-Pretraining-Indic-v1` is a synthetic pretraining corpus of about **2.83 trillion tokens covering all 22 scheduled Indian languages**, described as the largest openly released Indic pretraining corpus. A GPU-accelerated pipeline builds it by translating curated English documents, scoring translation quality, and repairing poor outputs. Continued-pretraining experiments across twelve languages show that mixing it with natural Indic text improves knowledge and reasoning over a public-corpus baseline, and further experiments measure how data volume, script coverage, and Indic share affect English performance. The authors also release `Indic-LLM-Eval-Suite`, a human-reviewed multilingual benchmark suite, and use it to compare current open-weight models.

papers.title: Accelerated Drift of Scientific Prose in the LLM Era: Evidence from an Interrupted Time-Series Analysis
papers.abstract: Every scientific text is embedded in the writing norms of its time: it reflects earlier publications while also shaping the texts that follow. The growing use of LLM-based writing tools introduces a new factor in this evolving system, but the linguistic changes coinciding with their emergence remain insufficiently understood. We investigate whether the trajectories of scientific-preprint writing changed in rate or direction after conversational LLMs became publicly accessible, using the release of ChatGPT in November 2022 as the observational breakpoint. We compare pre- and post-2022 trajectories across vocabulary, punctuation, readability, and syntax in abstracts from arXiv's artificial intelligence, statistics, and quantitative biology categories and from medRxiv. Using interrupted time-series regression, we find substantial post-2022 changes across multiple feature families and research domains, including increases in average word length, reduced formula-based readability, and declines in maximum dependency-tree depth and sentence-level depth variation. Individual features follow different dynamics: some lexical markers accelerate persistently, while others rise and then recede. Our findings show that isolated marker frequencies capture only part of the shift: changes in the rate, direction, and structure of linguistic trajectories provide complementary evidence of broader post-2022 change in scientific-preprint writing. More broadly, these findings motivate monitoring scientific writing as a multidimensional, evolving system rather than through a fixed set of LLM-associated markers.
papers.summary: Using ChatGPT's November 2022 release as a breakpoint, the authors apply interrupted time-series regression to preprint abstracts from arXiv's AI, statistics, and quantitative biology categories and from medRxiv. They track how vocabulary, punctuation, readability, and syntax changed over time. They find **substantial post-2022 shifts across multiple feature families and fields**, including longer average words, lower formula-based readability, and shallower, less varied sentence structure. Individual markers behave differently, with some accelerating persistently and others rising then receding, which suggests monitoring writing as a multidimensional system rather than through a fixed list of LLM-associated words.

papers.title: ProtGlycanDock: Towards Accurate Protein-Glycan Docking with Tailored Dataset, Benchmark and Model
papers.abstract: Performing accurate protein-glycan docking is critical to understanding protein-glycan interactions which govern many biological processes. However, this important task is hampered by the lack of tailored datasets, benchmarks and models for protein-glycan docking. To fill this blank, we first curate a standard benchmark ProtGlycanDock for training and evaluating protein-glycan docking models under both protein and glycan generalization settings. On this benchmark, we evaluate ten models in three categories, physics-based docking methods, machine-learning-based docking models and molecular structure prediction models. To obtain more precise binding poses, we further propose two finetuning techniques to inject the knowledge of glycan conformations into a general-purpose molecular structure prediction model. These two techniques respectively augment model inputs with glycan topological features and refine glycan binding pose with a glycan energy loss. Benchmark results show the superiority of AlphaFold 3 among existing methods, and the two proposed finetuning techniques can be well combined to achieve a state-of-the-art model for protein-glycan docking. Also, we perform stratified benchmark analysis and case studies to better understand the strengths and weaknesses of current models, providing insights for future model improvements. We maintain datasets at https://huggingface.co/datasets/ProtGlycanDock/ProtGlycanDock and source codes at https://github.com/kasawa1234/ProtGlycanDock
papers.summary: Accurate protein-glycan docking matters for understanding many biological processes but has lacked dedicated datasets, benchmarks, and models. The authors curate the `ProtGlycanDock` benchmark with protein- and glycan-generalization splits and use it to evaluate ten physics-based, machine-learning, and structure-prediction methods, with **`AlphaFold 3` performing best among existing approaches**. They also propose two fine-tuning techniques for a general structure-prediction model: adding glycan topological features to the inputs and refining poses with a glycan energy loss. Combined, the two techniques produce a state-of-the-art docking model.

papers.title: Understanding When Reflective Prompt and Skill Optimization Helps on Locally Served Reasoning Models: A Two-Model Study of GEPA and SkillOpt
papers.abstract: Reflective text-space optimizers such as GEPA and SkillOpt have reported large gains on frontier and mid-size models. We test replication across two reasoning-native target-serving configurations: DeepSeek V4 Flash through DwarfStar and Qwen3.8-27B through LM Studio. For each target, we evaluate the same held-out tasks and four conditions - minimal baseline, GEPA prompt, SkillOpt skill, and manually engineered prompt - on HotpotQA (n=500 per condition) and MATH-500 (n=250). In the primary Qwen v2 rerun under the same frozen protocol, GEPA selects the HotpotQA seed and exactly reproduces baseline behavior, whereas SkillOpt's validation gain reverses into held-out degradation. On MATH-500, GEPA raises exact match from 0.828 to 0.904 while reducing latency but increasing token consumption, so lower response time does not imply lower token cost. DeepSeek likewise shows its strongest GEPA effect on MATH-500 (0.852 to 0.908). Across both targets, GEPA's strongest gains occur on MATH-500, while neither optimizer improves the HotpotQA baseline. Optimization is therefore task- and method-dependent, and validation gains may reverse on held-out evaluation. An earlier Qwen run is retained as serving-sensitivity evidence. These results suggest that textual headroom for a model-task pair and the observed effect of a text-space optimizer are more informative when decomposed into content/reasoning, answer-realization/evaluator alignment, and serving-completion/reliability. The cross-benchmark pattern further suggests that optimization may benefit from low-ambiguity, actionable evaluation signals.
papers.summary: Reflective text-space optimizers such as `GEPA` (for prompts) and `SkillOpt` (for skills) have reported large gains on frontier models. The authors test whether those gains replicate on locally served reasoning models, using `DeepSeek V4 Flash` via DwarfStar and `Qwen3.8-27B` via LM Studio on `HotpotQA` and `MATH-500`. **`GEPA` helps on `MATH-500` (0.828 to 0.904 on Qwen, 0.852 to 0.908 on DeepSeek), but neither optimizer improves `HotpotQA`**, and `SkillOpt`'s validation gains reverse into held-out degradation. The authors conclude that the benefit depends on the task and method, that lower latency does not imply lower token cost, and that optimizers work best when the evaluation signal is low-ambiguity and actionable.

papers.title: Towards instance-dependent regret optimality in Episodic MDPs with Posterior Sampling
papers.abstract: We study regret minimization in finite-horizon episodic Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). While minimax-optimal algorithms are known, tractable approaches to instance-dependent optimality are still lacking. Motivated by this gap, we introduce $\pi_0$-PSRL, a variant of PSRL that uses posterior samples to decide when exploration is needed, while following a fixed reference policy $\pi_0$ during exploration episodes. This decouples the test for exploration, triggered when the sampled and empirical MDPs have different optimal policies, from the choice of the policy used to gather information. The resulting design addresses a limitation of standard PSRL, where the sampled optimal policy may not be the optimal choice for exploration. We prove instance-dependent regret bounds for $\pi_0$-PSRL, identifying the logarithmic exploration cost induced by $\pi_0$ and taking a step toward matching asymptotic lower bounds for episodic RL. Our proof techniques showcase a novel proof structure to derive problem-dependent regret bounds in episodic MDPs, and concentration results for Dirichlet random variables, that may be of independent interest.
papers.summary: Minimax-optimal algorithms for regret minimization in finite-horizon episodic Markov decision processes (MDPs) exist, but tractable instance-dependent optimal methods do not. `π0-PSRL` is a variant of posterior sampling for RL (`PSRL`) that uses posterior samples only to decide whether exploration is needed, and follows a fixed reference policy π0 when it explores. This separates the decision to explore from the choice of exploration policy. The authors **prove instance-dependent regret bounds** that move toward the asymptotic lower bounds, along with new concentration results for Dirichlet random variables.

papers.title: Truncate or Not? A Scaling Study of Looped Transformers with Truncated Backpropagation
papers.abstract: Looped transformers reuse a shared block of layers to increase computational depth without increasing the number of trainable parameters. They are trained with backpropagation through time (BPTT). To save training compute, BPTT is often truncated to the last few loops, but truncation yields biased gradients that may weaken the benefit of looping. In this work, we study the value of truncation in looped transformer training in a systematic way: we jointly vary model size, training tokens, and forward and backward loop counts across nearly 600 training runs and fit a unified scaling law that captures the effects of looping and truncation through effective parameters. Despite the training-compute savings of truncation, our fitted law favors full BPTT when forward and backward loop counts are jointly optimized. In matched-compute runs, full BPTT through fewer loops consistently outperforms truncated settings of the same compute. The law further shows that at fixed model size, the compute-optimal loop count and training-token budget both grow with compute. When model size is also free, the law identifies two fully trained loops as the best looped setting. Experimentally, this setting achieves lower validation loss than the compute-optimal non-looped model with about 27% fewer non-embedding parameters and only 8% more training compute.
papers.summary: Looped transformers reuse a shared block of layers to gain depth without adding parameters, and training often truncates backpropagation through time (BPTT) to save compute at the cost of biased gradients. Across nearly 600 training runs varying model size, tokens, and forward and backward loop counts, the authors fit a unified scaling law. The law **favors full BPTT over truncation**, and at matched compute, full BPTT through fewer loops consistently wins. With model size also free, two fully trained loops is the best looped setting, reaching lower validation loss than the compute-optimal non-looped model with about 27% fewer non-embedding parameters and 8% more training compute.

papers.title: Decision4Rec: A Jev-Inspired Framework of Decision Models on Knowledge and Active Graphs for Multi-Agent Recommender Systems
papers.abstract: Decision models, such as the commercial Jev, are language models that return one probability for each option of a question instead of generating text. We present Decision4Rec, an open and modular framework that makes decision models useful for recommendation. A knowledge graph writes the logs of each recommendation scenario as short statements on a defined scale, such as "sold: top 10%". A pool of agents, proposes candidates, and a residual ranker keeps the best 30. A decision model, trained once on real choices of three scenarios, reads them through one interface of typed questions, and a fusion step combines its answers with the score of the ranker. Any model with this interface can be used, and we run the commercial Jev, the released open Kev and Kev models trained by us on recommendation requests. The framework with a trained 4B decision model is 25 to 36% above the best trained baseline in NDCG@10 in three sparse Amazon catalogues, one of them never used to train the decision model, and almost tie with baselines on the dense Steam dataset. Most of the gain comes from the pool, and with a trained recommender it comes from what the agents know about its candidates rather than from new candidates. The 27B decision model adds to the pool 5 to 6% above the 0.8B model in three of four domains. A trained 0.8B open model beats the released Jev in eleven of fifteen settings and is never worse. On MovieLens-1M, a dense domain never seen in training, the gain is 5 to 7%. Code, configurations and trained models are available at https://github.com/marcopoli/decision4rec and https://huggingface.co/m-polignano.
papers.summary: Decision models are language models that return one probability per option of a question instead of generating text. `Decision4Rec` is an open, modular recommendation framework built around them: a knowledge graph turns logs into short scaled statements, a pool of agents proposes candidates, a ranker keeps the top 30, and a decision model's answers are fused with the ranker's scores. With a trained 4B decision model, it **beats the best trained baseline by 25–36% in NDCG@10 on three sparse Amazon catalogues** and roughly ties on the dense `Steam` dataset. Most of the gain comes from the agent pool, and a trained 0.8B open model outperforms the commercial `Jev` in eleven of fifteen settings.

papers.title: FinHopper: A Progressive Multi-Hop Benchmark for Complex Financial Agents with Step-wise Evaluation
papers.abstract: Financial agents are expected to answer factual investment queries through open search, but financial multi-hop retrieval differs from general multi-hop QA in a crucial way: each intermediate answer is an exact typed constraint, such as an entity, date, event, or numerical indicator, that determines the next query. This strict answer-conditioned dependency makes small intermediate errors cascade into plausible but wrong search trajectories. We introduce FinHopper, a benchmark for complex financial agents with controlled reasoning depth from 1 to 6 hops, covering stocks, funds, and macroeconomic facts, with gold intermediate answers for process-level evaluation. To construct FinHopper at scale, we design a state-transition-based synthesis framework that composes verified atomic financial QA patterns into dependency-preserving chains, followed by targeted in-synthesis verification, model-ensemble checking, and public-search validation by financial experts. Experiments with 20 LLM-agent configurations show that public search tools are necessary but insufficient: performance drops sharply as hop depth increases, the best model remains far below human experts, and process-aware scoring reveals partial reasoning progress hidden by final-answer-only evaluation. The benchmark is available at https://github.com/justajustin/FinHopper/.
papers.summary: In financial multi-hop retrieval, each intermediate answer, such as an entity, date, event, or number, determines the next query, so small early errors cascade into plausible but wrong search paths. `FinHopper` is a benchmark with controlled reasoning depth from 1 to 6 hops over stocks, funds, and macroeconomic facts, and it includes gold intermediate answers for step-by-step evaluation. It is built by composing verified atomic financial question-answer patterns into chains, then checked with model ensembles and by financial experts. Across 20 LLM-agent configurations, **accuracy drops sharply as hop depth increases and the best model remains far below human experts**, while step-wise scoring reveals partial progress that final-answer evaluation misses.

papers.title: Balance-Aware Pivot Selection for Parallel Diffusion LLM Decoding
papers.abstract: Diffusion language models enable parallel token generation, offering a promising alternative to sequential autoregressive decoding. Existing acceleration methods use predictive confidence to enable parallel token commitment while preserving generation quality. However, confidence-based selection prioritizes reliable token predictions without explicitly considering how token positions shape the remaining decoding schedule. Moreover, such ordering does not always reflect inter-token dependencies, suggesting that confidence need not be the sole criterion for token selection. Motivated by this limitation, we propose Balance-Aware Pivot Decoding (BPD), which favors central pivots within contiguous masked intervals and decodes the selected positions in parallel. Balanced pivots yield logarithmic decoding depth in the interval length. Our practical method accounts for model uncertainty by combining confidence-based prefilling with confidence-thresholded center selection. We evaluate the resulting quality-efficiency tradeoff on LLaDA and Dream across five mathematical reasoning, code generation, and instruction-following benchmarks. Our implementation is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DLM_random_pivot-EE62/
papers.summary: Diffusion language models can generate many tokens in parallel, but existing speedups choose which tokens to commit based only on model confidence, which ignores how the chosen positions shape the rest of the decoding schedule. `Balance-Aware Pivot Decoding` (`BPD`) instead favors central pivot positions within contiguous masked spans and decodes them in parallel, which gives **decoding depth logarithmic in the span length**. The practical version handles model uncertainty by first filling in confident tokens and then picking centers above a confidence threshold. It is evaluated for its quality-efficiency tradeoff on `LLaDA` and `Dream` across five math reasoning, code generation, and instruction-following benchmarks.

papers.title: Honeyed Words, Hidden Daggers: Benchmarking and Training LLMs to See Through Mock Politeness
papers.abstract: The Chinese idiom "kou mi fu jian" ("honeyed words, hidden daggers") names speech that is polite in form but hostile in function. We present ZhenhuanBench, a 1,592-item benchmark built from expert commentary on Empresses in the Palace, covering speaker intent, emotion-language mismatch, and per-listener uptake. Text-only evaluation covers 34 LLMs. GPT-6 Astra leads the leaderboard at 73.48% overall, while its listener-reaction score is 58.37%. The annotations also supply supervised traces and string-verifiable training rewards. With 338 gold traces, an 8B model outperforms teacher distillation on identical items. Subsequent RL saturates, and chance correction reduces the estimated recoverable performance gap by a factor of 7.5. Our CPR-GRPO loop (Compress-Probe-Replenish) uses this estimate to weight gold supervision, reaching 67.0 on public multiple-choice tasks and 74.5 under the training-matched hidden protocol. Without target-task training, CPR outperforms Base, SFT, and GRPO across six Chinese and English pragmatic and sarcasm evaluations. On three external datasets, training with CPR yields higher mean Macro-F1 than SFT and GRPO.
papers.summary: Mock politeness is speech that is courteous in form but hostile in intent, and it is hard for language models to detect. The authors build `ZhenhuanBench`, a 1,592-item benchmark drawn from expert commentary on the drama Empresses in the Palace, which tests speaker intent, mismatch between emotion and wording, and how each listener reacts. Among 34 LLMs the leader, `GPT-6 Astra`, scores **73.48% overall but only 58.37% on listener reactions**. The authors also propose `CPR-GRPO` (Compress-Probe-Replenish), a training loop that weights gold supervision by an estimate of how much performance is recoverable. It lets an 8B model beat `SFT` and `GRPO` baselines on six Chinese and English pragmatics and sarcasm evaluations.

papers.title: LeakBench: Auditing Reward Hacking through Prediction-Time Leakage in Clinical Modeling Agents
papers.abstract: Autonomous clinical-modeling agents can optimize predictive performance while violating conditions that make a model usable. We introduce LeakBench, an executable, guideline-derived audit suite that tests agent decisions for prediction-time leakage, calibration, site-level evaluation, support awareness, and decision-curve net benefit. LeakBench combines a synthetic task with known failure structure and two real-data settings: MIMIC-IV (430k admissions) and governed multi-hospital inpatient record front-page (MHFP) data. Our primary analysis uses reward hacking descriptively, without attributing intent: an agent selects prediction-time-invalid inputs because they improve its validation reward. A deterministic optimizer and every evaluated unconstrained local-model configuration select a fatal leaking feature. In fully logged September 2026 A/B runs, DeepSeek Flash and GPT-6-astra each leak in 10/10 unconstrained runs and 0/10 runs with an explicit admission-time constraint. This contrast is version-sensitive: a blinded Claude/Fable-5.1 chat run does not leak in either condition, while explicit-constraint violations appear only in a historical August 2026 slice lacking raw trajectories. Replacing AUROC with AUPRC does not remove leakage selection. Renaming or disguising the leaking inputs changes neither selection nor provenance-based detection; a name-based filter fails. A deterministic provenance verifier-in-loop removes the leak, making the LLM repair loop defense-in-depth. Specific verifier feedback clears fatal leakage in a hosted agent, and a three-seed ablation finds principle-only feedback clears decision-level defects, though these mitigation results are limited. LeakBench treats trustworthy clinical prediction as a property of an agent's modeling process, not merely its score; it is an audit testbed with known-failure controls, not yet an expert-validated benchmark.
papers.summary: `LeakBench` is an executable audit suite that checks whether autonomous clinical-modeling agents use input features that would not actually be available at prediction time, along with calibration, site-level evaluation, and net-benefit checks. It combines a synthetic task with known failure modes and real data from `MIMIC-IV` and a multi-hospital inpatient dataset. Without constraints, `DeepSeek Flash` and `GPT-6-astra` **selected a fatal leaking feature in 10/10 runs**, and they never did when given an explicit admission-time constraint. Renaming the leaking inputs did not change this and defeated name-based filters, while a deterministic provenance verifier placed in the agent loop removed the leak.

papers.title: Multilingual Voicemail and Answering Machine Detection via Pretrained Audio Embeddings and Gradient Boosting Machines
papers.abstract: Answering machine detection (AMD) is a fundamental task in telephony that classifies whether an answered call is picked up by a human or a voicemail (machine). Despite its widespread use across cloud communication platforms, existing approaches rely on proprietary systems with undisclosed architectures, or require computationally expensive models that cannot operate in real time. We propose a lightweight AMD system that combines pretrained audio embeddings with gradient boosting machines, trained to prioritize the correct detection of human-answered calls. We evaluate seven models across two datasets: three models that we propose, a proprietary industry model, two prior academic approaches, and a large language model baseline that relies on automatic speech recognition. Furthermore, we release OpenAMD, the first publicly available AMD dataset comprising of more than 500 recordings in 7 languages. Our best model achieves the highest precision across both datasets while maintaining low inference latency. We assess the robustness of models to additive noise and packet loss, and perform tests of statistical significance to discover per-language and per-gender model performance. Finally, we evaluate our model on an out-of-domain task of detecting robocalls, where it achieves 94.34% recall without any additional training, which is comparable to the industry standard.
papers.summary: Answering machine detection decides whether a phone call was picked up by a person or by voicemail, and current systems are either proprietary or too slow to run in real time. The proposed lightweight system feeds pretrained audio embeddings into gradient boosting machines and is tuned to prioritize correctly detecting human-answered calls. It is compared against an industry model, prior academic methods, and an LLM baseline that relies on speech recognition, and it achieves the highest precision on both datasets with low latency. The authors release `OpenAMD`, a dataset of over 500 recordings in 7 languages, and report **94.34% recall on robocall detection** with no extra training.

papers.title: Provable Adversarial Detection: Prime Quantization meets Gromov--Wasserstein
papers.abstract: Adversarial vulnerability persists across modern vision architectures from CNNs to vision language models (VLMs), yet existing detection methods rely on heuristics without theoretical guarantees. We address the fundamental question of when adversarial perturbations can be provably detected from a geometric perspective. Our key insight is that adversarial perturbations cannot simultaneously preserve geometric structure across spaces with fundamentally different properties. Accordingly, we construct two such complementary metric spaces. First, we use a standard CNN embedding space $Z$, where adversarial samples exhibit significant displacement patterns. Second, we build a novel prime-quantized space $P$, that absorbs small perturbations through number-theoretic discretization, resulting in minimal displacement, while preserving discriminability. We then leverage the geometric discrepancies across spaces $Z$ and $P$ to detect adversarial samples. To the best of our knowledge, we establish the first rigorous separation theory for adversarial detection, proving that adversarial samples create unavoidable geometric inconsistencies across both spaces. Our framework provides theoretical guarantees including pixel-level absorption bounds, neighborhood diameter concentration, Gromov-Wasserstein (GW) separation theorems, and practical risk control. Extensive experiments validate our theoretical predictions and achieve consistently strong detection performance across a wide range of attack types and model families.
papers.summary: Existing methods for detecting adversarial inputs to vision models rely on heuristics with no guarantees. The proposed approach compares two metric spaces: a standard CNN embedding space where adversarial samples move substantially, and a new prime-quantized space that absorbs small perturbations through number-theoretic discretization. Adversarial samples are flagged by the geometric inconsistency between the two spaces, measured with `Gromov-Wasserstein` distance. The authors claim **the first rigorous separation theory for adversarial detection**, with absorption bounds and risk control, and report strong detection across many attack types and model families.

papers.title: Learning from a Bandit Learner
papers.abstract: Classical inverse bandit methods typically aim to recover true reward parameters. In contrast, we infer a demonstrator's subjective beliefs, specifically its internal estimates of suboptimality gaps. We consider no-regret demonstrators that follow randomized policies, such as Thompson sampling, and characterize a family of algorithms for which per-step inversion is possible. This enables gap estimates to be recovered directly from the arm-selection distribution. Our analysis identifies an inherent stability-coverage trade-off: inversion becomes ill-conditioned as the demonstrator concentrates its probability mass on a single arm, while the number of informative rounds depends on the rate at which its policy converges. We establish conditions under which inversion is reliable and provide theoretical guarantees on the resulting estimation error. Experiments on simulated data support the analysis and illustrate how these conditions affect gap recovery in practice.
papers.summary: Classical inverse bandit methods try to recover an environment's true rewards, but this work instead infers a demonstrating learner's own subjective estimates of how much worse each arm is than the best one. For no-regret demonstrators using randomized policies such as `Thompson sampling`, the authors characterize a family of algorithms whose gap estimates can be recovered at each step directly from the arm-selection probabilities. The analysis identifies a **stability-coverage trade-off**: inversion becomes ill-conditioned as the demonstrator concentrates on one arm, while the number of informative rounds depends on how fast its policy converges. Error guarantees are supported by simulations.

papers.title: Declarative Explanations for Graph Neural Networks: A Demonstration
papers.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have proven effective for graph analytical tasks, yet their "black-box" nature complicates the understanding of their layer-wise behavior and hinders their application to large graphs. We demonstrate SliceGXQ, an end-to-end declarative and interactive system for querying and exploring layer-wise explanations for GNNs over large-scale graphs. In particular, SliceGXQ provides (1) an interactive graphical user interface for dataset, model, and explanation configuration; (2) a lightweight SPARQL-like parser that allows users to specify target nodes, layers, explanation modes, and constraints; and (3) an integrated execution and visualization workflow that invokes SliceGX as its underlying explanation engine. We demonstrate how users can diagnose a misclassified node, identify problematic layers and influential messages, and perform targeted model debugging, together with large-scale graph interpretation and fraud-detection analysis. Our demonstration video and source code are available at https://github.com/jinzhaoqet/SliceGXQ.
papers.summary: `SliceGXQ` is an interactive system for querying layer-by-layer explanations of graph neural networks (GNNs) on large graphs. It combines a graphical interface for configuring datasets and models, a lightweight `SPARQL`-like query language for specifying target nodes, layers, explanation modes, and constraints, and an execution and visualization workflow built on the `SliceGX` explanation engine. The demonstration shows users **diagnosing a misclassified node by locating problematic layers and influential messages**, as well as interpreting large graphs and analyzing fraud detection.

papers.title: From Retrieval to Recognition:Knowledge-Enhanced Post-training of Time Series Foundation Models for Classification
papers.abstract: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) have achieved notable progress in classification tasks through large-scale pretraining. However, their post-training practice mainly focuses on implicit parameter fine-tuning, where task-relevant information is entangled with abundant irrelevant knowledge in vast parameter spaces. This may hinder TSFMs from precisely activating useful knowledge for downstream classification. To this end, we propose Retrieval-to-Recognition (R2R), a plug-and-play post-training paradigm that adapts pretrained TSFMs to time series classification. Rather than pretraining a new foundation model, R2R improves how existing TSFMs are post-trained: it introduces a decoupled query encoder to extract discriminative patterns and retrieve instance-level numerical knowledge from a constructed knowledge base. The retrieved explicit knowledge is then fused with the TSFM's implicit parametric embeddings, enabling joint knowledge transfer at both the parameter and feature levels. In this way, R2R allows TSFMs to recall task-relevant patterns learned during pretraining, improving the efficiency of knowledge utilization in downstream classification transfer. Experiments on 158 time series datasets show that R2R consistently improves the classification performance of state-of-the-art TSFMs. Ablation and knowledge-enhanced studies further validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework.
papers.summary: Time series foundation models are usually adapted to classification by fine-tuning their parameters, where task-relevant knowledge is entangled with a lot of irrelevant information. `Retrieval-to-Recognition` (`R2R`) is a plug-and-play post-training method that adds a separate query encoder to retrieve instance-level numerical examples from a constructed knowledge base, then fuses this retrieved knowledge with the model's own embeddings. Across **158 time series datasets**, `R2R` consistently improves the classification accuracy of state-of-the-art foundation models, and ablations support each component.

papers.title: Variance-Aware Non-Stationary Bandits:All-Budget Regret Bounds and Adaptation Costs
papers.summary: In non-stationary multi-armed bandits, low reward variance makes estimation cheaper, but a learner still has to keep checking arms that may have improved while unobserved. The authors characterize the minimax dynamic regret as a function of the number of arms, the horizon, a budget on how much arm means can change, and a budget on reward variance, and they match it **to within a single logarithmic factor for every admissible budget pair**. The algorithm uses a safe calibration phase and clipped observations to lower restart costs. Matching lower bounds come from fixed constructions, and the authors also show that a single policy competing with all budget-specific oracle rates must pay a polynomial adaptation cost.

papers.title: Optimal Multi-Kernel Combination for Online Multi-Label Classification
papers.abstract: Multi-label classification is particularly challenging in streaming scenarios, where data arrives sequentially. Online kernel methods offer a promising solution. However, prevailing methods rely on a single preselected kernel, making them prone to suboptimal choices since the global data distribution is unknown in advance in online settings. Although the recent method, Online Kernel Selection for Online Multi-label Classification (OKS-OMC), enables data-driven kernel selection, it fails to fully harness the complementary information from multiple kernels and encounters the curse of kernelization. To address these limitations, this paper introduces a novel online multi-kernel combination method for large-scale multi-label classification. First, an efficient and robust online single-kernel multi-label method is designed. Second, learning an optimal convex combination of multiple multi-label kernel classifiers is formalized as a structural risk minimization problem. An improved alternating optimization procedure is developed, in which the combination coefficients are updated by directly minimizing the objective function, while each kernel classifier is updated by minimizing a surrogate upper bound. This procedure decouples the learning of kernel classifiers from combination coefficients, allowing independent classifier updates via our single-kernel method and accelerating convergence to high-quality solutions. Our multi-kernel method is proven to asymptotically converge to the optimal fixed convex combination of the best fixed single-kernel models chosen in hindsight. Ablation studies confirm that our method's components outperform their counterparts in OKS-OMC. Comprehensive evaluations across 11 datasets and seven metrics demonstrate our method's overall superiority over existing online multi-label methods.
papers.summary: Online multi-label classification on streaming data usually relies on one kernel chosen in advance, and the existing kernel-selection method `OKS-OMC` neither combines information across kernels nor avoids the cost of growing kernel models. The proposed method learns a convex combination of several multi-label kernel classifiers using an alternating optimization that updates combination weights and the individual classifiers separately, which speeds convergence. It is proven to **asymptotically converge to the best fixed convex combination** of single-kernel models chosen in hindsight. Across 11 datasets and seven metrics it outperforms existing online multi-label methods.

papers.title: Nash-MOPD: Optimizing Task Trade-offs in Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
papers.abstract: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) aggregates the capabilities of multiple domain-expert teachers into a single student model. However, all domains in MOPD share the student's finite budget of optimization steps and rollouts. Fixed uses constant domain sampling ratios based on corpus sizes; by contrast, D$^3$-MOPD adjusts the ratios using the teacher-student reverse-KL divergence and its recent decrease. However, favoring large recent decreases can direct more training toward domains that already improve quickly, while domains that improve more slowly may receive too few examples. To address inflexible allocation and the risk of giving insufficient training to domains that improve more slowly, we propose Nash-MOPD, an adaptive domain scheduler based on a local minimax game using existing reverse-KL statistics. The equilibrium maximizes the smallest predicted proportional reduction under the local model and gives more prompts to domains that need more examples for comparable improvement. Consequently, Nash-MOPD responds to changing learning progress and supports domains that improve more slowly without extra teacher queries or rollouts. At step 100, Nash-MOPD exceeds both baselines' final mathematics and code checkpoint scores on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B and reaches Fixed's on Qwen3-8B-Base. Furthermore, it leads eight of nine reported metrics and is best or tied best on all six mathematics and code accuracy metrics, respectively.
papers.summary: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation trains one student model from several domain-expert teachers, but every domain shares the same limited budget of training steps and rollouts. Existing schedulers either use fixed ratios based on corpus size or favor domains whose divergence from the teacher is dropping fastest, which can starve domains that learn slowly. `Nash-MOPD` sets domain sampling ratios by solving a local minimax game over existing reverse-KL statistics, giving more prompts to slower-improving domains at no extra teacher or rollout cost. At step 100 it **exceeds both baselines' final math and code scores** on `DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B` and matches the fixed baseline on `Qwen3-8B-Base`.

papers.title: Reinforcement Learning Controllers for Fusion Scenario Development
papers.abstract: Scenario development, the design of the waveforms that take a tokamak discharge from breakdown to flat-top, is still an iterative, labour-intensive process. Every candidate scenario has to be simulated with a controller in the loop, and the classical shape and current controllers need low-level actuator references. So the process is iterative and includes a number of trial-and-error steps. We propose to replace the per-scenario controller tuning by a single goal-conditioned reinforcement-learning controller trained once, in advance, against a free-boundary equilibrium and transport simulator. A scenario is then specified only by the target waveforms of the physical quantities of interest (plasma current, line-averaged electron density, LCFS shape, x-point positions), and the controller produces the coil-current and fueling commands that realize them. We demonstrate the approach on an EAST plasma-current ramp-up: the controller takes over a small limited plasma, ramps the current and the density, grows the cross-section, forms two x-points and holds a double-null diverted configuration against sampled shape targets for the rest of a 1.2 s episode. The neural network controller is trained using TQC algorithm. On 1024 test scenarios sampled from a low-discrepancy scrambled Sobol sequence in 11-dimensional target space, the controller forms the divertor in 86% of the cases, holds it for more than 0.5 s in 67% and reaches the end of the episode in a diverted state in 58%, with flat-top tracking errors of a few kA in plasma current, $\sim 0.15\times10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$ in density, $\sim 2$ cm in position and $\sim 8$ cm in x-point location; the failures concentrate at the high-current density ($J$) region which is believed to be physically or from engineering perspective not feasible within ohmic mode.
papers.summary: Designing tokamak fusion scenarios currently requires tuning a controller and running trial-and-error simulations for every candidate scenario. The authors replace this with a single goal-conditioned reinforcement learning controller, trained once with the `TQC` algorithm against a free-boundary equilibrium and transport simulator, that turns target waveforms for plasma current, density, and shape into coil and fueling commands. On an `EAST` current ramp-up across 1,024 sampled test scenarios, the controller **forms a divertor configuration in 86% of cases** and ends the episode diverted in 58%, with small tracking errors. Most failures fall in a high-current-density region believed to be infeasible in ohmic operation.

papers.title: FLMNet: Self-Ensemble Distillation from Masks to Seeds for Single-Tower CTR Prediction
papers.abstract: Click-through rate (CTR) prediction underpins recommender systems and online advertising, where high-dimensional categorical features interact in combinatorially many ways. Several recent CTR models, such as FinalNet and QNN, report higher accuracy when a network also learns from its own averaged predictions, for example by running the same network under different dropout patterns and training each run toward the average. Why this self-distillation helps, and whether its random sampling is needed, remains unclear. This work shows that as the number of dropout patterns grows without bound, the objective reduces exactly to the label loss of the logit-averaged prediction plus a penalty on how much the dropout copies of the network disagree. When dropout does not affect how a network gates its features, this penalty can be approximated in closed form, and FLMNet is designed on this principle and trains without sampling. Networks trained from different seeds disagree in the same form, and distilling several of them into one network recovers part of their ensemble gain. On five benchmarks against seventeen baselines, the resulting models take the top two places in accuracy with a single network at inference, and the gains of the penalty and of distillation, where measurable, largely add up.
papers.summary: Some click-through rate (CTR) prediction models improve accuracy by training a network toward its own averaged predictions across dropout patterns, but why this helps has been unclear. The authors show that with unlimited dropout patterns, the objective reduces exactly to the label loss of the logit-averaged prediction plus a penalty on disagreement between dropout copies. When dropout does not affect feature gating this penalty has a closed form, and `FLMNet` uses it to train without sampling. Distilling several differently seeded networks into one recovers part of the ensemble gain, and across five benchmarks and seventeen baselines the resulting **single-network models take the top two accuracy spots**.

papers.title: Physics-Driven Framework for QoS-Constrained Satellite System with Non-Linear PA Distortion
papers.abstract: This work develops a physics-driven self-supervised graph learning framework that directly optimizes the distortion-aware precoder under nonlinear correlated power amplifier (PA) distortion, without relying on expensive optimizer-generated labels for a user-centric satellite system. We minimize nonlinear PA consumption subject to user quality-of-service (QoS) constraints under PA nonlinearity for a downlink multi-input-single-output (MISO) satellite system. Our pipeline jointly designs the precoder and admission control that minimize nonlinear PA consumed power. In particular, a graph neural network (GNN) for the design of a distortion-aware precoder is optimized end-to-end in a self-supervised manner using a differentiable It\^o-Hermite model of the true modified Rapp amplifier model. The precoder output by the GNN is used to initialize a low-complexity distortion-aware signal-to-interference-distortion (SINDR) tracking algorithm that jointly optimizes for power and admission control. Our proposed physics-based pipeline closely tracks a successive convex approximation (SCA) based solution in consumed power performance with the advantage of faster runtime and a wide operating range covered during training.
papers.summary: Satellite downlinks must meet each user's quality-of-service requirements while power amplifiers introduce nonlinear distortion that wastes power. The authors train a graph neural network to design a distortion-aware precoder in a self-supervised way, using a differentiable `Itô-Hermite` model of the amplifier instead of labels produced by an expensive optimizer. The network's output initializes a low-complexity algorithm that jointly handles power and admission control. The pipeline **closely tracks a successive convex approximation solution in consumed power** while running faster and working across a wide operating range.

papers.title: DeepSEA: A Multilingual Evaluation Benchmark for Southeast Asia
papers.abstract: While language models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities, their performance remains disproportionately skewed towards high-resource languages. This disparity is particularly acute for the 700 million inhabitants of Southeast Asia, where vast linguistic diversity remains under-represented in existing benchmarks, often suffering from limited language coverage or narrow task scopes. To address this, we introduce DeepSEA, a comprehensive benchmark constructed from established datasets through professional human translation into 12 Southeast Asian languages, spanning both high-resource (e.g., Indonesian, Thai, Vietnamese) and low-resource (e.g., Burmese, Khmer, Lao) tiers across five distinct tasks: mathematical reasoning, scientific reasoning, question answering, abstractive summarization, and machine translation. Extensive evaluation of frontier proprietary and open-weights models reveals that while frontier models like Gemini-3.7-Flash maintain robustness across resource tiers, smaller models face severe performance degradation on low-resource languages. Crucially, models perform better in reasoning and summarization when pivoted through English rather than target languages, exposing a critical dependency on English representations, especially for low-resource languages. Beyond these observations, we provide a cross-lingual error analysis and a cross-script tokenizer fertility analysis. We hope these findings shed light on the development of next-generation inclusive multilingual models.
papers.summary: Language model benchmarks underrepresent Southeast Asia's many languages. `DeepSEA` professionally translates established datasets into 12 Southeast Asian languages, ranging from higher-resource ones such as Thai and Vietnamese to low-resource ones such as Burmese, Khmer, and Lao, and covers math and science reasoning, question answering, summarization, and translation. Frontier models such as `Gemini-3.7-Flash` hold up across resource tiers, but smaller models degrade sharply on low-resource languages. Models also **reason and summarize better when routed through English** than when working directly in the target language, which points to a dependence on English representations.

papers.title: Dynamical Batching: How Class-Cycling Training Shapes the Internal Structure of Neural Networks
papers.abstract: We investigate whether cyclically varying the class composition of training batches can modify both the performance and the internal organization of neural networks. Motivated by nonequilibrium systems, in which cycling between related sub-goals can make switching between their solutions increasingly efficient, we introduce Dynamical Batching (DB), a sampling protocol that periodically emphasizes each class while leaving the loss and the optimizer unchanged, and compare it with Uniform Batching (UB), in which every mini-batch has equal class proportions. In the regime where standard training fails, DB changes the outcome: on a three-arm spiral, a capacity-limited MLP that plateaus far below perfect accuracy under UB fits the training data under DB. Tracking individual weights, we find that under DB the change between class-specialized states is carried by a smaller set of weights than under UB, and that this set is markedly more persistent from cycle to cycle, on every synthetic dataset we test and in a wider network that fits the data under both protocols. This organization is a signature of the protocol rather than a predictor of its benefit: it appears equally where DB leaves accuracy unchanged. On CIFAR-10, the same protocol modestly improves the test accuracy of a channel-narrowed ResNet-10, a standard residual architecture, and of a second capacity-limited convolutional network. These results show that how class emphasis is distributed in time can shape both the solution a network reaches and the internal structure of the network.
papers.summary: `Dynamical Batching` is a sampling protocol that cyclically emphasizes each class in turn within training batches, leaving the loss and optimizer unchanged, and is compared against batches with uniform class proportions. On a three-arm spiral, a capacity-limited MLP that plateaus under uniform batching **fits the training data under cyclic batching**. Weight tracking shows that switching between class-specialized states is carried by a smaller and more persistent set of weights, though this pattern appears even where accuracy does not improve. On `CIFAR-10` the protocol gives modest test-accuracy gains for narrowed convolutional networks, including a `ResNet-10`.

papers.title: VISAGENT: An Agent-Based End-to-End Voice Interaction System
papers.abstract: Voice-based public services have evolved from manual switchboards to intelligent platforms to meet modern user needs. However, current systems remain constrained by rigid menu-driven interaction, fragmented vertical services, and limited extensibility. To address these issues, we present VISAGENT, an agent-based end-to-end voice interaction system for large-scale public services that integrates end-to-end speech interaction, hierarchical agent routing, a scalable voice-agent marketplace, and user memory support. The system replaces menu-driven workflows with natural speech and dynamically dispatches user requests to either a general conversational model or specialized domain agents via a two-level routing paradigm that achieves sub-second intent-to-agent selection over hundreds of agents. User memory informs preference-aware agent selection and supplies relevant preferences and context to selected agents, supporting personalized task execution and reducing the need for users to repeat previously provided information. A voice-agent registration mechanism converts task agents into conversational entities, enabling dynamic onboarding and ecosystem-level extensibility. We validate VISAGENT through a real-world deployment in China's 114 hotline across multiple service domains. Experimental results demonstrate low-latency full-duplex interaction, robust routing scalability, and competitive speech naturalness. More broadly, this work advocates a shift from isolated voice assistants toward agent-centric conversational infrastructures, providing a general blueprint for building extensible voice-agent systems in public services and beyond.
papers.summary: Voice-based public service hotlines are limited by rigid menus, fragmented services, and poor extensibility. `VISAGENT` replaces menus with end-to-end speech interaction and a two-level routing scheme that sends each request to a general conversational model or to one of hundreds of specialized domain agents, with **sub-second intent-to-agent selection**. User memory supports preference-aware routing and spares users from repeating information, and a registration mechanism lets new task agents be added as conversational agents. The system is deployed on China's 114 hotline, where it shows low-latency full-duplex interaction and scalable routing.

papers.title: Conditional information Retrieval for Longitudinal Survey Harmonisation
papers.abstract: Identifying conceptually equivalent questions across different surveys is a challenging information retrieval task where surface-level textual similarity is insufficient. Two questions may be lexically similar yet assess entirely different sociological sub-concepts, or lexically different yet conceptually equivalent. We introduce a conditional information retrieval framework that addresses this by decomposing the task into two steps: concept extraction, which identifies the underlying sociological concept of a survey question using a fine-tuned generative model, and concept-aware retrieval, which augments question representations with the extracted concept as an explicit conditioning signal for finer-grained alignment. To reflect the realistic data scarcity conditions of specialised social science annotation, we use CLOSER as a case study. Our framework consistently outperforms baselines by 2-3 points in both MAP and Recall. We further analyse fine-tuning strategies including SFT, DPO, and dynamic DPO, finding that SFT delivers the most stable gains while dynamic DPO interacts differently with instruction-tuned versus distilled reasoning backbones. Finally, we demonstrate that a model fine-tuned on a general social science thesaurus (ELSST) transfers robustly to task-specific survey data, offering a practical solution under data scarcity.
papers.summary: Matching conceptually equivalent questions across social surveys is hard because similar wording can measure different concepts and different wording can measure the same one. The proposed framework first uses a fine-tuned generative model to extract each question's underlying sociological concept, then adds that concept to the question representation to guide retrieval. On the `CLOSER` survey data it **beats baselines by 2-3 points in MAP and recall**. Among fine-tuning strategies, `SFT` gives the most stable gains, and a model trained on the `ELSST` social science thesaurus transfers well to the survey data when labels are scarce.

papers.title: Reading Time Modeling with Pixel-Based Language Models
papers.abstract: Tokenization-free, pixel-based language models (PLMs) have recently been proposed as an alternative to conventional token-based language models (TLMs), typically motivated by practical considerations, e.g., the flexibility to support new languages or vocabularies. Nevertheless, PLMs also have the potential to serve as infrastructure for computational (psycho)linguistics, where tokenization has been a source of bias in estimating information-theoretic values, such as surprisal, and has pushed the bottom-up visual orthographic features outside the scope. In this study, we first integrate PLMs into the modeling of naturalistic human reading and, in particular, examine their use to estimate next-word predictability, which can also integrate orthographic and parafoveal information. Our results demonstrate that next-word prediction difficulty, computed in pixel space, has strong predictive power for gaze duration and word skipping behavior across various languages. In particular, their advantage is complementary to existing token-level surprisal and entropy estimates. Cross-lingual analyses with script variations also clarify their distinctive visual processing biases, facilitating research into how bottom-up visual information is incrementally integrated into expectation-based reading.
papers.summary: Pixel-based language models read text as rendered images instead of tokens, which avoids tokenization biases and keeps visual spelling information that matters in psycholinguistics. The authors use them to estimate next-word predictability for modeling eye movements during natural reading across several languages. Prediction difficulty computed in pixel space **strongly predicts gaze duration and word skipping**, and it adds information beyond standard token-level surprisal and entropy. Comparisons across writing systems reveal distinctive visual processing biases in these models.

papers.title: VEILED-SH: Vulnerability Expression through Indirect Language Evaluation Dataset (Self-Harm)
papers.abstract: AI systems may miss indirect, culturally situated distress or provide support mismatched to the application context. Existing benchmarks do not jointly address cultural variation, application context, and practitioner disagreement. We introduce VEILED-SH, a benchmark and construction methodology for evaluating single-turn responses to indirect expressions of suicide, self-harm, and distress. Its 10,003 prompts span counselor chat, forum posts, platform search, and triage, drawing on Singapore-grounded sources and public datasets. An expert-validated multi-label taxonomy distinguishes intent, communicative function, and response behavior. Six automated profiles, individually calibrated to three peer-support practitioners and three clinicians, retain separate reference policies for proxy-alignment scoring. Evaluating five systems on a coverage-enriched sample reveals variation in proxy alignment across profile-generated reference policies, even for the same system responses.
papers.summary: AI systems can miss indirect or culturally specific expressions of distress, or respond in ways that do not fit the setting. `VEILED-SH` is a benchmark of 10,003 single-turn prompts with indirect expressions of suicide, self-harm, and distress, drawn from counselor chats, forum posts, platform search, and triage, with sources grounded in Singapore. An expert-validated taxonomy labels intent, communicative function, and response behavior, and six automated scoring profiles are each calibrated to an individual peer-support practitioner or clinician. Evaluating five systems shows that **the same responses score differently depending on which practitioner's reference policy is used**.

papers.title: TaQFormer: A Treatment-as-Query Transformer with Data-Fusion for Multidimensional Treatment Modeling in Coupon Allocation
papers.abstract: We study coupon allocation on an online marketplace offering multiple service categories. Issuing coupons requires choosing a vector of category-specific discounts, accounting for both their direct effects and cross-category demand shifts. We present TaQFormer, a treatment-as-query Transformer for this multidimensional treatment setting. Each treatment coordinate is represented as a query token, allowing cross-attention to estimate the response to the full treatment vector. To combine large but policy-biased observational logs with a smaller stream of randomized controlled trial data, we use a two-stage pipeline: observational pretraining learns general outcome patterns, followed by LoRA fine-tuning on RCT data with a request-specific fusion gate. We evaluate the resulting system through the checks required for production, including offline uplift metrics, treatment-parallel serving, latency monitoring, and a 14-day online A/B test. At essentially the same subsidy cost rate, \model increases business value per user by 1.26\% over the production baseline and significantly outperforms both the production baseline and the RCT-only model, while meeting the latency budget. It was subsequently rolled out to all marketplace traffic and has operated at full scale for several months as of October 2026. The deployment illustrates how multidimensional treatment modeling and observational pretraining, combined with adaptation using RCT data, can support effective joint discount decisions in production.
papers.summary: An online marketplace with several service categories must choose a vector of category-specific coupon discounts for each user, accounting for both direct effects and demand that shifts across categories. `TaQFormer` represents each treatment coordinate as a query token, so cross-attention can estimate the response to the full discount vector. It is trained in two stages: pretraining on large but policy-biased observational logs, then `LoRA` fine-tuning on a smaller stream of randomized controlled trial (RCT) data with a per-request fusion gate. In a 14-day online A/B test at essentially the same subsidy cost, it raised business value per user by **1.26% over the production baseline** while meeting the latency budget, and it has since been rolled out to all marketplace traffic.

papers.title: OceanTensorCube and ST-MMT: A Multimodal Data and Transformer System for Seven-Day Forecasting of Pyropia Bleaching
papers.abstract: Bleaching of cultured Pyropia (laver) causes losses in Korean seaweed farming. We present a system that forecasts bleaching seven days ahead for farm clusters. OceanTensorCube aligns 32 channels from public marine, meteorological, ocean-model and satellite sources on a 30 m grid, and ST-MMT, a 9.2-million-parameter spatiotemporal transformer with hub-style multi-head cross-attention between variable groups, maps a 14-day input window to a seven-day-ahead bleaching probability. On the validation set, a six-seed ensemble detects every reported positive at a false-alarm rate of at most 3.5%, an upper bound because the report-based labels are positive-unlabeled. A same-date control on separately trained models indicates that the architecture discriminates between clusters when the calendar is held fixed. We also report the system's weaknesses: skill falls steeply as the quarterly nutrient survey ages (ROC-AUC 0.94 at 30 days, 0.53 at 129 days), and a single LSTM on cluster-average series outperforms a single ST-MMT, with only the ensemble leading at the operating point. We describe the labeling procedure, the evaluation protocol and the operational gate that withholds forecasts when inputs are stale. The forecasting service is operated at https://oceantensor.ai.kr.
papers.summary: Bleaching of cultured Pyropia (laver) causes losses in Korean seaweed farming, and the authors build a system that forecasts it seven days ahead for farm clusters. `OceanTensorCube` aligns 32 channels of public marine, weather, ocean-model and satellite data on a 30 m grid, and `ST-MMT`, a 9.2-million-parameter spatiotemporal transformer with cross-attention between variable groups, maps a 14-day input window to a bleaching probability. A six-seed ensemble detects every reported positive on the validation set at a false-alarm rate of at most 3.5%. The authors also report weaknesses: skill drops sharply as the quarterly nutrient survey ages (**ROC-AUC falls from 0.94 at 30 days to 0.53 at 129 days**), and a single `LSTM` outperforms a single `ST-MMT`.

papers.title: Rethinking BPE: Merge Selection as Model Selection
