papers.abstract: Subword tokenization methods such as Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) are a core component of modern language models; yet, tokenizer capacity remains typically determined by a fixed merge budget, chosen heuristically. Since larger vocabularies increase memory usage and computational cost, selecting compact and effective token inventories is essential for efficient language modeling. We study the optimization of a BPE merge budget as a statistical model selection problem and investigate information-theoretic criteria for \emph{computing optimal merge sets} directly from corpus statistics. To further improve the merge selection in limited data conditions, we augment the BPE training corpora with synthetic texts generated from the original data, providing estimates for the unigram and bigram distributions. Experiments across multiple corpora and downstream tasks show that using a principled vocabulary selection technique reduces model size, with little degradation in performance. We further observe that synthetic data can yield better tokenizers, especially in low-resource settings.
papers.summary: The number of merges in Byte-Pair Encoding (`BPE`) tokenizers, which sets vocabulary size, is usually picked by heuristic, even though larger vocabularies cost more memory and compute. The authors treat choosing the merge budget as a statistical model selection problem and use information-theoretic criteria to compute optimal merge sets directly from corpus statistics. When data is limited, they add synthetic text generated from the original corpus to better estimate unigram and bigram distributions. Across several corpora and downstream tasks, principled vocabulary selection **reduces model size with little loss in performance**, and synthetic data can produce better tokenizers, especially in low-resource settings.

papers.title: Heartbeat Thinking: Speculative Reasoning and Tool Execution While Listening in Realtime Voice Agents
papers.abstract: Tool-using voice agents often leave users waiting after speech ends, even when actionable information arrives earlier in the request. Speculative approaches begin work during speech, but chunk-bounded or interrupt-on-update generation can truncate a tool call before its arguments are complete. This couples computation time to speech updates, limiting useful work completed in advance. We introduce Heartbeat Thinking, which handles updated input through new Thinker invocations while allowing ongoing invocations and dispatched tools to finish. Periodic invocations read the latest partial transcript and a shared record of completed reasoning and tool results. These results help resolve missing arguments and initiate dependent calls, allowing preparation to progress across speech updates. Across SpeechFCEval, FDBench v3, and AudioCRAG, Heartbeat improves aggregate speculative tool coverage or retrieval reuse over a SHANKS-style windowed baseline, with benchmark-dependent effects on final task quality. On FDBench v3, it increases tool coverage by 16 percentage points and reduces mean final-response latency by 36.4\%. The results show that heartbeat thinking paradigm preserving ongoing computation during speech can turn listening time into reusable preparation for faster and more capable voice-agent responses.
papers.summary: Tool-using voice agents often leave users waiting after they stop speaking, and existing speculative approaches that start work during speech can cut off a tool call before its arguments are complete. `Heartbeat Thinking` periodically launches new reasoning calls on the latest partial transcript while letting earlier calls and dispatched tools run to completion, with all of them sharing a record of finished reasoning and tool results. This shared record helps fill in missing arguments and trigger dependent calls, so preparation keeps progressing as the transcript updates. Across `SpeechFCEval`, `FDBench v3` and `AudioCRAG` it improves speculative tool coverage or retrieval reuse over a `SHANKS`-style windowed baseline, and on `FDBench v3` it raises tool coverage by 16 percentage points and **cuts mean final-response latency by 36.4%**; effects on final task quality vary by benchmark.

papers.title: Shaping the Document, Not the Model: Optimized Suffixes for Context Following
papers.abstract: When a user supplies a document and wants the answer drawn from it, a language model is expected to follow it even when it contradicts its parametric knowledge. Prior work has focused on making the model rely on context by steering activations, contrasting logits during decoding, or instructing it in plain language. We ask whether the document alone, with no instruction written into it and no access to the model at inference time, is enough. We optimize a document suffix by discrete token search, starting from the answer to a single question and extending the objective to a set of passages, to multi-hop questions that follow from the planted fact, and to later turns of a conversation. On counterfactual passages that contradict parametric knowledge of the model, the suffix flips nearly all items the model resists across three instruction-tuned model families, in most settings outperforms the decoding baseline and the strongest instruction we could write, and matches activation steering. Controls show that the suffix largely acts through the passage rather than injecting the answer, and a single suffix per model transfers to unseen passages. Each extended objective carries the effect to its target, so the objective, not only the document, sets how far the effect reaches.
papers.summary: When a user supplies a document, a language model should answer from it even when the document contradicts what the model learned in training. Instead of steering activations, changing decoding, or adding instructions, the authors optimize a suffix appended to the document through discrete token search, extending the objective from single questions to sets of passages, multi-hop questions and later conversation turns. On counterfactual passages, the suffix **flips nearly all the items the model otherwise resists** across three instruction-tuned model families, usually beats contrastive decoding and the strongest hand-written instruction, and matches activation steering. Control experiments show the suffix mostly works through the passage rather than by injecting the answer, and a single suffix per model transfers to unseen passages.

papers.title: Machina Pauliana: A neuro-symbolic approach to the actio pauliana in Dutch insolvency law
papers.abstract: Applying a legal provision frequently requires both structured rule-based reasoning and sensitivity to open-textured terms developed in case law. The actio pauliana of Article 42 of the Dutch Bankruptcy Act (Faillissementswet, Fw), which allows an insolvency practitioner to avoid transactions that prejudice creditors, requires both. We present a neuro-symbolic model of Article 42 Fw. Its symbolic core is written in Catala in a literate style that keeps statute and formalisation aligned and was developed through pair programming, with open-textured terms represented as boolean inputs where neural components couple to the symbolic solver. A neural routine structures a case's natural-language facts into boolean and date inputs. Neural subroutines resolve the open-textured terms through case-based reasoning over Dutch civil judgments, retrieved through a pipeline that filters on the requirement being resolved and expands along the procedural chain of a case. Segmenting and labelling those judgments attains high precision and recall against a manually annotated gold standard of 100 judgments. On ten hand-annotated cases the neuro-symbolic model handles most criteria reasonably but struggles with the knowledge requirement. Retrieval depth shows no clear quantitative effect, although retrieved judgments provide explicit grounding in prior case law.
papers.summary: Applying Article 42 of the Dutch Bankruptcy Act, which lets an insolvency practitioner undo transactions that harm creditors, takes both structured rule-based reasoning and judgment about open-textured terms shaped by case law. The authors build a neuro-symbolic model whose symbolic core is written in `Catala`, with the open-textured terms left as boolean inputs that neural components fill in. A neural routine converts a case's natural-language facts into structured inputs, and neural subroutines resolve open terms through case-based reasoning over retrieved Dutch civil judgments. Segmenting and labelling judgments achieves high precision and recall on 100 annotated judgments, and on ten hand-annotated cases the model **handles most criteria reasonably but struggles with the knowledge requirement**.

papers.title: RECAP: Reciprocal Sparse Attention and Hierarchical Caching for Efficient Video Diffusion
papers.abstract: Diffusion transformers generate high-quality videos but remain computationally expensive. Sparse attention and temporal caching reduce computation within and across denoising steps, respectively, offering a natural composition. However, predictions produced with sparse attention become sources for temporal reuse, coupling their errors along the sampling trajectory. We observe that improving the accuracy of these sources recovers fidelity without changing the reuse schedule, and that sparsification errors remain directionally aligned across nearby steps, suggesting that correction information can be shared rather than recomputed. These observations motivate RECAP, a training-free method that couples sparse attention with hierarchical caching through reciprocal correction, adaptively coordinated by online error feedback. Cached dense refinement corrects omitted interactions in current sparse estimates, while fresh sparse statistics track input changes and regulate the aging correction. The resulting predictions then renew the sources for whole-step prediction reuse, allowing prediction history to advance between dense refreshes. We evaluate RECAP on multiple video diffusion models against sparse-attention methods, caching methods, and their direct compositions. On HunyuanVideo at 720p 5-second generation, RECAP achieves a 3.05x speedup and outperforms all tested direct compositions in both fidelity and inference speed.
papers.summary: Video diffusion transformers are expensive, and the two standard speedups, sparse attention within a denoising step and caching across steps, interact badly: errors from sparse attention get reused and compound along the sampling trajectory. The authors observe that improving the accuracy of these reused predictions restores fidelity, and that sparsification errors point in similar directions across nearby steps, so a correction can be shared rather than recomputed. `RECAP` is a training-free method that pairs sparse attention with hierarchical caching: cached dense refinements correct the current sparse estimates, fresh sparse statistics track input changes, and online error feedback coordinates the two. On `HunyuanVideo` 720p 5-second generation it achieves a **3.05x speedup** and beats every tested direct combination of sparse-attention and caching methods in both fidelity and speed.

papers.title: SEAM: Spectral Embedding Alignment and Merging for Low-Resource TTS
papers.abstract: Expanding the vocabulary of conditional text-to-speech (TTS) models typically requires extensive fine-tuning with paired audio, creating a major bottleneck for low-resource and cross-lingual adaptation. To address this, we introduce SEAM, a zero-audio initialization method that constructs embeddings for unseen tokens from known subtokens. Unlike standard pooling strategies that ignore sequential structure, SEAM applies a spectral filter to preserve temporal phonetic order and uses closed-form ridge regression to align the new embeddings with the pretrained conditioning manifold. Across three languages and two TTS architectures, SEAM approaches or matches baseline performance using up to four times less training data, reducing sample complexity by 75\% compared to random initialization and mean pooling. Our approach provides a lightweight, reproducible, and theoretically grounded solution for vocabulary expansion in low-resource speech synthesis.
papers.summary: Adding new tokens to a conditional text-to-speech (TTS) model usually means fine-tuning on paired audio, which is a bottleneck for low-resource and cross-lingual adaptation. `SEAM` builds embeddings for unseen tokens from known subtokens without any audio, using a spectral filter to preserve the phonetic order of the subtokens and closed-form ridge regression to align the new embeddings with the pretrained conditioning space. Across three languages and two TTS architectures, it approaches or matches baseline performance with up to four times less training data, **reducing sample complexity by 75%** compared with random initialization and mean pooling.

papers.title: AudioScorer: Learning Question-Aware Token Relevance for Large Audio Language Models
papers.abstract: Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) reason over speech, environmental sounds, music, and other acoustic information. However, their audio encoders produce dense token sequences that make long-form audio costly to process. Existing audio pruning methods reduce this cost using heuristics such as attention, representation similarity, or temporal sampling, but do not explicitly learn which tokens are most useful for a given question. We propose AudioScorer, a lightweight model that scores audio tokens according to the user question. It is trained by distilling the ranking of audio tokens under the frozen LALM's answer-gradient saliency, together with downstream answer supervision. Compared with other pruning methods, AudioScorer achieves the best or tied-best result at 10% token retention on 7 of 10 semantic and acoustic tasks, including speech recognition, emotion recognition, and audio-scene classification.
papers.summary: Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) process dense sequences of audio tokens, which makes long recordings costly, and existing pruning methods choose which tokens to keep with heuristics rather than with regard to the question being asked. `AudioScorer` is a lightweight model that scores audio tokens by their relevance to the user's question. It is trained by distilling the token ranking given by the frozen LALM's answer-gradient saliency, combined with supervision from downstream answers. Keeping only 10% of tokens, it achieves the **best or tied-best result on 7 of 10 tasks**, including speech recognition, emotion recognition and audio-scene classification.

papers.title: A Pitfall in the Evaluation of Gene Perturbation Models
papers.abstract: Gene perturbation models aim to predict transcriptional responses to unseen genetic interventions, but comparisons rely on heterogeneous evaluation metrics and differentially-expressed (DE) gene subsets. We investigate the consequences of these choices using eight methods across six single-gene perturbation datasets under a unified evaluation protocol. Varying the number of top DE genes reveals substantial instability in Precision-based rankings, with the winning method changing $86.7\%$ of the time, while rankings based on the rest of the metrics remain comparatively stable. Investigating this discrepancy exposes that repeating a single predicted expression profile across cell-level rows, a standard practice for many methods, can inflate significance estimates and produce excessively large predicted significant-DE sets. Specifically we found that $67.1\%$ of tested perturbation--gene pairs pass the significance threshold despite some of them having minuscule effects. We derive an inflation factor showing that replicated predictions can amplify the standardized Mann--Whitney statistic even after correction for tied ranks, without adding independent information. This artifact changes Precision mainly as the number of DE genes increases because for smaller cutoffs, most of the genes are already significant due to the effect-based ordering. Taking this pitfall into account in our benchmark comparison, we find that a random forest using Gene Ontology features achieves the best overall results.
papers.summary: Gene perturbation models predict how cells' gene expression responds to unseen genetic interventions, but papers compare them using inconsistent metrics and subsets of differentially expressed (DE) genes. Benchmarking eight methods on six single-gene perturbation datasets under one protocol, the authors find that Precision-based rankings are unstable, with **the winning method changing 86.7% of the time** as the number of top DE genes varies. They trace this to a common practice of repeating one predicted expression profile across cell-level rows, which inflates significance estimates so that 67.1% of tested perturbation-gene pairs pass the threshold. They derive an inflation factor for the Mann-Whitney statistic, and once the artifact is accounted for, a random forest using Gene Ontology features performs best overall.

papers.title: Trust Your Targets: Is Target Propagation Block-Diagonal Gauss-Newton?
papers.abstract: Target propagation (TP) is a backpropagation alternative in which local targets carry the global learning signal. Prior works claim that TP performs Gauss-Newton (GN) optimisation on these targets, but the correspondence has only been established under unrealistic assumptions where hitting them exactly is trivial. Practical variants instead descend on a least-squares problem via a single gradient step. In this paper, we rederive TP from a trust region under an implicit, previously unexamined norm, and introduce CGTP (Conjugate Gradient Target Propagation), which uses conjugate gradients to solve the layer-local subproblems in parallel. A single adaptive parameter jointly controls this trust region and a matching bound on the weight update; KFAC emerges exactly as the special case where the per-sample Jacobians are replaced by their batch mean, giving its factored damping a variational grounding. On MNIST and Fashion-MNIST MLPs, CGTP matches the accuracy of ADAM and KFAC while needing orders of magnitude fewer outer iterations than ADAM (about 10x fewer backward-pass-equivalents overall), while remaining stable across depth.
papers.summary: Target propagation (TP) is an alternative to backpropagation in which per-layer targets carry the global learning signal, and earlier work claimed it performs Gauss-Newton (GN) optimization, but only under assumptions where hitting the targets exactly is trivial. The authors rederive TP from a trust region under a previously unexamined implicit norm and introduce `CGTP` (Conjugate Gradient Target Propagation), which solves the layer-local subproblems in parallel with conjugate gradients. A single adaptive parameter controls both the trust region and a matching bound on the weight update, and `KFAC` falls out exactly as the special case where per-sample Jacobians are replaced by their batch mean. On `MNIST` and `Fashion-MNIST` multilayer perceptrons, `CGTP` matches the accuracy of `Adam` and `KFAC` while using **about 10x fewer backward-pass-equivalents than Adam** and remaining stable as depth grows.

papers.title: Learning SOCP Solver Dynamics with Graph Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Second-order cone programs (SOCPs) are a fundamental class of convex optimization problems widely applied across engineering domains. Classical interior-point methods are robust and accurate, but their iterative nature can be costly in real-time or repeated-solve settings. This has motivated learning-based solvers that approximate optimizer solutions with neural networks. Recent work has increasingly studied graph neural networks (GNNs) for linear, quadratic, and second-order cone optimization, leveraging their ability to model sparse relational structure among variables, constraints, and objective functions. Most existing GNN-based solvers compress the optimization process into a single forward pass, predicting the optimizer directly without using the intermediate trajectory produced by classical solvers. We introduce SOCPNet, a recursive GNN framework that uses solver trajectories to learn an iterative SOCP solution procedure. A shared GNN model is applied repeatedly, refining the current iterate at each step and enabling inference for a variable number of iterations. Rather than predicting the solution in a single pass, SOCPNet learns from intermediate iterates to progressively refine its estimates using a trajectory-regularized training procedure. We evaluate SOCPNet on multiple datasets spanning standard SOCP problem classes and show that it consistently reduces the final solution error relative to a SOCP-GNN baseline. Finally, we demonstrate how trained SOCPNet models can be used in a hybrid optimization pipeline by warm-starting a classical interior-point solver, reducing solver iterations without loss of accuracy.
papers.summary: Second-order cone programs (SOCPs) are widely used convex optimization problems, but classical interior-point solvers can be too slow when problems must be solved in real time or repeatedly. Most graph neural network (GNN) solvers predict the solution in a single forward pass, whereas `SOCPNet` applies a shared GNN repeatedly to refine the current iterate, trained on intermediate iterates from classical solver trajectories with a trajectory-regularized objective. Across several standard SOCP problem classes it **consistently reduces final solution error** compared with a `SOCP-GNN` baseline. Used to warm-start a classical interior-point solver, it reduces solver iterations without losing accuracy.

papers.title: Toward Online Robust Zero-Sum Markov Games with Function Approximation
papers.abstract: Online robust zero-sum Markov games pose a coupled operator-learning and game-solving problem: from nominal interaction data, the learner must recover a worst-case minimax Bellman operator while maintaining strategic coverage and controlling stage-game approximation error. Existing robust reinforcement-learning theory does not yet provide such an operator-learning perspective beyond specialized multi-agent settings. We develop an optimistic dual robust Bellman framework that combines dual robust Bellman fitting, optimistic minimax planning, backward-validated confidence sets, and exploiter-mix data collection. Our analysis is organized around the robust Bellman residuals induced by the candidate value class and yields a regret reduction that separates exploration complexity, robust operator-estimation error, stage-game solution error, and misspecification. Under explicit interpretable assumptions, we obtain conditional theorem interfaces for general and projected function approximation, together with closed results in several structured regimes, including tabular, epochwise cross-fit linear, self-normalized pure-online linear / finite-rank kernel, and projected RKHS truncation. Small-scale numerical experiments illustrate robustness calibration, strategic coverage, and the return-gap trade-off predicted by the framework.
papers.summary: In online robust zero-sum Markov games, a learner must use data from the nominal environment to recover the worst-case minimax Bellman operator while also exploring strategically and solving each stage game approximately. The authors propose an optimistic dual robust Bellman framework that combines dual robust Bellman fitting, optimistic minimax planning, backward-validated confidence sets and exploiter-mix data collection. Their analysis yields a **regret decomposition that separates exploration complexity, robust operator-estimation error, stage-game solution error and misspecification**, with conditional theorems for general and projected function approximation. They obtain closed-form results for tabular, linear, finite-rank kernel and projected RKHS settings, and small numerical experiments illustrate the predicted trade-offs.

papers.title: Answering While You Type: Optimizing Time-to-Answer with Streaming Generation
papers.abstract: Work on efficient large-language-model inference has concentrated almost entirely on reducing the cost of decoding once a request is complete. The quantity a user experiences, however, is the interval between submitting a request and receiving a usable response, and that interval can be shortened without making decoding itself faster. While a request is being composed it is already partially specified, yet conventional deployments begin no computation until submission. We propose and study streaming generation, a decoding regime in which the model begins producing a response from an incomplete request and revises it as the remaining input arrives, so that only a small residue of the answer remains to be computed once the request is submitted. We evaluate the regime on autoregressive and diffusion language models, characterise the conditions under which it reduces user-visible latency, and analyse the mechanism responsible.
papers.summary: Work on efficient large language model inference mostly speeds up decoding after a request is complete, but users experience the time from submitting a request to getting a usable answer. The authors study streaming generation, in which the model **starts producing a response from the incomplete request while it is still being typed** and revises it as more input arrives, leaving only a small part of the answer to compute after submission. They evaluate this on both autoregressive and diffusion language models, characterize the conditions under which it reduces user-visible latency, and analyze the mechanism behind the gains.

papers.title: CAST: Cast-Admissible Generative Design and Shape Optimization with Paired Depth Images
papers.abstract: Deep generative design can produce complex geometries, but unconstrained representations may create undercuts that prevent release from a two-part mold. We present CAST, which reformulates three-dimensional shape generation under a selected mold-opening constraint as a two-dimensional image generation problem using paired top and bottom depth images. Each valid depth pair defines one material interval along a selected mold-opening direction, so reconstructions exclude undercuts in that direction by construction. Diffusion models generate candidate shapes in this representation, and a finite element analysis (FEA) guided optimizer refines the same two boundaries. We evaluate diffusion-based generation with limited training data comprising 211 SimJEB bracket designs. On SimJEB brackets, FEA-guided refinement with a volume penalty reduced compliance in 193 of 200 generated candidates. The median reduction across all candidates was 36.8 percent in the optimization FEA model. Reconstruction of existing brackets revealed a mass--stiffness trade-off: filling occluded regions increased material volume and reduced displacement under the evaluated loads. Paired depth images thus connect generative exploration and structural refinement in a shared design space that preserves the selected pull-direction restriction.
papers.summary: Generative design can produce complex shapes, but many of them have undercuts that stop the part from being released from a two-part mold. `CAST` turns 3D shape generation under a chosen mold-opening direction into 2D image generation of paired top and bottom depth images, which rules out undercuts in that direction by construction. Diffusion models generate candidate shapes in this representation, and an optimizer guided by finite element analysis (FEA) then refines the two boundaries. Trained on only 211 `SimJEB` bracket designs, FEA-guided refinement reduced compliance in 193 of 200 generated candidates, with a **median reduction of 36.8%**.

papers.title: The Scheduler Is a Hidden Retriever: How Asynchrony Shapes Evidence Acquisition in Search Agents
papers.abstract: Language-model agents increasingly solve complex tasks through parallel reasoning and asynchronous information gathering. Controlled replay across two model families and three benchmarks shows that delivery timing redirects search decisions made before all results arrive, despite identical initial evidence. Acquisition disagreement reaches up to 24 percentage points above same-order repeat variation. This dependence persists after all initial evidence arrives and through a second search, turning temporary differences in what agents have seen into lasting differences in what they acquire. An acquisition-regret bound with a matching construction shows that invariance at a fixed early arrival count can limit the use of evidence already received. We introduce Confluent Evidence Acquisition (CEA), which instead releases local reasoning when each subquestion's evidence is complete and allocates shared search independently of completion order. For a fixed plan and stable conditional response law, we prove joint invariance of decisions, acquisitions, and answers. With question-only plans across three benchmarks, CEA brings acquisition disagreement to within 1.0 percentage point of repeat variation and achieves accuracy comparable to complete-input controls, improving over early commitment by up to 12.6 percentage points. Replacing CEA's fixed allocation with first-ready allocation under contention adds 21.6 percentage points of acquisition disagreement, while local query-target disagreement remains near repeat variation. Timed comparisons show that CEA reaches decisions earlier and responds faster than the same program waiting for all initial evidence.
papers.summary: Search agents that gather information in parallel and asynchronously can make different decisions depending on the order in which results arrive. In controlled replays across two model families and three benchmarks, delivery timing alone shifts what agents go on to search for by up to 24 percentage points beyond normal run-to-run variation, and these differences persist after all evidence has arrived. The authors introduce Confluent Evidence Acquisition (`CEA`), which runs each subquestion's reasoning only once its evidence is complete and allocates shared search regardless of completion order, and they prove that decisions, acquisitions and answers become order-invariant under stated conditions. Empirically, `CEA` **brings acquisition disagreement to within 1.0 percentage point of repeat variation**, matches the accuracy of waiting for all evidence, improves over early commitment by up to 12.6 points, and responds faster than waiting for all initial evidence.

papers.title: TriScore: Post-Hoc Out-of-Distribution Detection with Energy, Boundary Probes, and Transform Consistency
papers.abstract: Post-hoc out-of-distribution detection usually relies on a single signal extracted from a frozen classifier, such as confidence, energy, features, or gradients. This dependence becomes fragile under classifier-level adversarial shift, where the shift can preserve the detector's chosen cue while changing the model's decision behavior. We investigate whether this failure mode can be mitigated by combining complementary detection criteria instead of selecting a single score. We introduce TriScore, a post-hoc OOD detector that combines three ID-calibrated signals from the same frozen backbone: an energy prior, a boundary-fragility score, and a transform-consistency score. These signals are standardized on ID validation data and fused by an input-dependent ID-residual gate, requiring no OOD labels, auxiliary model, training, or stored feature bank. Across four ImageNet-scale backbones, TriScore achieves the best mean AUROC among 15 post-hoc baselines under a non-adaptive adversarial-shift protocol, while remaining competitive on standard OOD benchmarks. Ablations show that the gains come from combining complementary cues rather than optimizing a single detector signal. These results support multi-criterion post-hoc detection as a practical route toward more robust OOD detection under classifier-level shift. The source code is publicly available at github.com/gursoyege/TriScore.
papers.summary: Post-hoc out-of-distribution (OOD) detectors usually rely on a single signal from a frozen classifier, which can fail under adversarial shifts that keep that signal intact while changing the model's decisions. `TriScore` combines three signals from the same backbone, an energy prior, a boundary-fragility score and a transform-consistency score, standardizes them on in-distribution validation data, and fuses them with an input-dependent gate. It needs no OOD labels, auxiliary model, training or stored feature bank. Across four ImageNet-scale backbones it achieves the **best mean AUROC among 15 post-hoc baselines** under a non-adaptive adversarial-shift protocol and stays competitive on standard OOD benchmarks, with ablations showing the gains come from combining the signals.

papers.title: The Control Layer Behind Rule-Following Agents Trading Across Market Conditions
papers.abstract: Trading discipline often fails people. Our study tested whether four AI trading agents followed their strategies and risk rules. Offering traders the evidence and an agent evaluation toolkit to separate luck from following the rules, before giving agents meaningful autonomy or capital. Our study analysed 2,627 closed positions from 12 February to 27 August 2026 across the same asset universe and execution conditions. Most positions were simulated against live prices with a 0.09% round-trip fee; 18% involved real Hyperliquid orders. Each position declared a strategy, stop and target, with a limit of five open positions per agent. The fleet finished net positive after fees. Rule adherence was high across all four agents, including the unprofitable one. Profitability tracked how often agents won relative to their break-even win rates. Institutional-style controls ran by default and contained losses through a 29% market drawdown and recovery, with documented exceptions. The discipline held for all four agents. Agents kept 97.5% of gross loss within declared stops, and typical losses closed at declared levels. Declared risk remained stable after losses and broadly stable across calm and volatile months. Twenty-three of 24 runs respected the position limit; logs identify the exception's size and duration. The same live data produced different results across assigned strategies. The trade-log tests can be rerun from the published trade snapshot; regime tests also require the published Bitcoin prices and regime labels. Section 3.5 specifies the stop-breach tolerance. These trade-level results are not account-level returns or proof of a lasting edge. Our study provides an evaluation toolkit to help traders distinguish rule-following from luck before committing capital. For anyone considering allocating capital to agents to trade, discipline should be the entry test, not the only test.
papers.summary: The authors test whether four AI trading agents actually followed their declared strategies and risk rules, analysing 2,627 closed positions from February to August 2026. Most positions were simulated against live prices with fees, and 18% were real `Hyperliquid` orders. The fleet finished net positive after fees, rule adherence was high for all four agents including the unprofitable one, and **97.5% of gross loss stayed within declared stops**, with controls containing losses through a 29% market drawdown. They release an evaluation toolkit and trade data so traders can tell rule-following from luck, and they caution that these trade-level results do not prove a lasting edge.

papers.title: Typed Decision Models under Prevalence Shift: Decision Training, Calibration, and Implicit Priors
papers.abstract: Typed decision models (TDMs) return a probability over caller-defined options, and Jev is described by its vendor as calibrated. But in deployment class frequencies change, so calibration measured on a fixed test set need not hold where thresholds are applied. Existing evaluations leave two gaps: the gains of vendor decision training have not been separated from those of the backbone under an identical readout, and TDMs have been tested only at the test set's class distribution. We ask whether decision training improves a model over its own backbone, and whether a TDM's calibration and thresholds withstand prevalence (label) shift as well as a fine-tuned classifier's. We compare three TDMs (Jev, Tev1-4B, Nimble-9B), their base models and two trained classifiers on identical decisions from five public datasets under simulated shift, with 35 paired tests fixed before any test was computed. First, decision training is not uniformly beneficial: Nimble-9B, which differs from Qwen3.5-9B only by a LoRA adapter, is better calibrated on intent tasks but 12.0 Macro-F1 points worse on financial sentiment. Second, under moderate shift Jev's expected calibration error (ECE) and threshold risk grow significantly more than a fine-tuned DeBERTa's only on financial sentiment, by 1.7 and 2.5 percentage points; averaged over 2,000 shift scenarios (exploratory), the gap is at most one point on every dataset. Third, EM prior correction with the model's mean development prediction as its prior needs no labels and lowers Jev's ECE under shift by 2.7 and 1.8 points on the two datasets where it is highest, although labelled recalibration lowers it far more. The three TDMs we tested are neither uniformly better than their backbones nor uniquely fragile under shift; for calibration, their main weakness is the miscalibration they already have without shift. We release all inputs, code and outputs.
papers.summary: Typed decision models (TDMs) return a probability over caller-defined options, but calibration measured on a fixed test set may not hold once class frequencies change in deployment. The authors compare three TDMs (`Jev`, `Tev1-4B`, `Nimble-9B`), their base models and two fine-tuned classifiers on five public datasets under simulated prevalence shift, with 35 paired tests fixed in advance. Decision training is not uniformly beneficial: `Nimble-9B`, which differs from `Qwen3.5-9B` only by a `LoRA` adapter, is better calibrated on intent tasks but **12.0 Macro-F1 points worse on financial sentiment**. `Jev` degrades more than a fine-tuned `DeBERTa` under shift only on financial sentiment, and a label-free expectation-maximization (EM) prior correction modestly lowers its calibration error, though labelled recalibration helps far more.

papers.title: CIS-Transolver: A Cross-Layer Incremental-State Neural Operator for Fine-Scale Automotive Aerodynamic Flow Prediction
papers.abstract: Neural operators offer an efficient data-driven approach to rapid prediction of complex automotive aerodynamic flows. However, spectral bias and other factors limit accurate reconstruction of fine-scale flow variations near complex geometries. Existing studies improve the representation and fitting of fine-scale information mainly through information extraction and training objectives. Further study is needed to determine how extracted local details can be used continually in subsequent operator computations and contribute effectively to the overall flow-field representation. We propose CIS-Transolver, a cross-layer incremental-state neural operator that extends fine-scale modeling from local information extraction to its use across layers. The method extracts fine-scale information through local multiscale analysis and encodes it as geometric moment states that are propagated and updated across layers. By combining information from previous layers with feedback to the value representations in Physics-Attention, the method allows local details to contribute continually to subsequent modeling of global physical correlations. We systematically evaluate CIS-Transolver on three public automotive aerodynamics benchmarks, ShapeNet-Car, AhmedML, and DrivAerNet++, covering surface pressure fields and volumetric pressure and velocity fields. CIS-Transolver achieves the lowest mean relative L2 error among the evaluated methods for all five prediction metrics across the three benchmarks. The relative error reductions average 8.72% across the five metrics compared with the best baseline for each metric, reaching 16.38% for ShapeNet-Car pressure prediction and 15.60% for AhmedML velocity prediction. These results provide a new approach to fine-scale flow prediction for complex geometries.
papers.summary: Neural operators can quickly predict car aerodynamics, but they struggle to reconstruct fine-scale flow details near complex geometry. `CIS-Transolver` extracts fine-scale information with local multiscale analysis, encodes it as geometric moment states that are propagated and updated across layers, and feeds it back into the value representations of `Transolver`'s Physics-Attention. On the `ShapeNet-Car`, `AhmedML` and `DrivAerNet++` benchmarks, it achieves the lowest mean relative L2 error of all evaluated methods on all five prediction metrics. Errors fall by **8.72% on average** relative to the best baseline for each metric, and by up to 16.38% for `ShapeNet-Car` pressure.

papers.title: Large-Scale Biomedical RAG: Corpus Scaling, Document Representation, and Efficiency Trade-offs
papers.abstract: We present a controlled, large-scale evaluation of how corpus scale, document representation, and reranking affect the effectiveness and efficiency of biomedical Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems. Retrieval collections were progressively expanded while retaining the relevant source documents, enabling consistent comparisons across corpus sizes. We compared abstract, flat full-text, and hierarchical full-text representations across first-stage retrieval, reranking, and end-to-end multiple-choice question answering. Configurations selected on development data were evaluated on five external biomedical benchmarks and a held-out test set, while retrieval latency and index storage were measured to quantify operational cost. Performance patterns observed with small or controlled collections did not consistently persist as collections grew, and the usefulness of reranking depended on the corpus and retrieval setting. RAG improved three of four model configurations across the external benchmarks, with mean gains of up to 9.6 percentage points, and improved all four configurations on the held-out test set by 10.2-30.3 points. Abstract retrieval performed best when reference evidence was abstract-aligned, whereas full-text representations were generally more effective when richer evidence was needed. Hierarchical representation matched or outperformed flat full-text retrieval in most end-to-end comparisons while requiring 67% fewer indexed units and 44-56% less storage. These findings show that corpus scale should be treated as an explicit evaluation variable in biomedical RAG, and that the most appropriate design depends on evidence format, model behavior, and operational constraints.
papers.summary: Studies how corpus size, the way documents are represented, and reranking affect the quality and cost of biomedical Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). The authors expand the retrieval collections step by step while keeping the relevant source documents, then compare abstracts, flat full text, and hierarchical full text across retrieval, reranking, and end-to-end multiple-choice question answering on five external benchmarks and a held-out test set. Patterns seen on small collections often did not hold as the corpus grew, and whether reranking helped depended on the setting. RAG improved all four model configurations on the held-out test set by 10.2 to 30.3 points, and the hierarchical representation matched or beat flat full text while using **67% fewer indexed units and 44-56% less storage**.

papers.title: VibeTraining-Bench: Data-Trainer-Harness Co-Design for Iterative System Improvement
papers.abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) requires agents to diagnose system bottlenecks and coordinate improvements across training and inference. We refer to the agents' capability to jointly optimize training data, the trainer, and the inference harness as cross-component co-design. We introduce VibeTraining-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating this capability across tasks spanning terminal operation, software engineering, multi-turn tool use, and mathematical reasoning. Within each task, research agents start from an identical initial agent system under a fixed resource budget. Guided by validation feedback, they iteratively refine data, trainers, and inference harnesses, then select and submit a final agent system for evaluation on the test set. To prevent reward hacking, we enforce three safeguards: test data isolation, separate research and grading containers, and network restrictions for research agents. Our evaluation results show that frontier research agents substantially improve target agent systems. For example, on SWE-bench Verified, GPT-6-Astra raises the target agent system's performance from 32.9% to 53.7%, comparable to the human-developed instruct model's 55.4%. However, there is still room to improve their ability to co-design and iteratively refine data, trainer, and harness to achieve cumulative performance gains. We hope that VibeTraining-Bench will serve as a unified platform for advancing RSI, deepening our understanding of cross-component optimization for agent systems. Code and data are available at https://github.com/D2I-ai/VibeTraining-Bench.
papers.summary: Introduces `VibeTraining-Bench`, a benchmark that tests whether research agents can improve an agent system by jointly changing its training data, its trainer, and its inference harness. Agents start from the same initial system under a fixed resource budget, refine it using validation feedback across terminal, software engineering, multi-turn tool use, and math tasks, and then submit a final system for evaluation on a held-out test set. Isolated test data, separate research and grading containers, and network restrictions guard against reward hacking. Frontier agents make large gains: on `SWE-bench Verified`, `GPT-6-Astra` lifts the target system **from 32.9% to 53.7%**, close to the 55.4% of the human-developed instruct model, but the agents still struggle to combine improvements across components over many iterations.

papers.title: Logit Averaging During Training Sets a New State of the Art for Non-Invasive Speech BCI
papers.abstract: Non-invasive brain-computer interfaces are in practice limited by signal-to-noise ratio, and recent state-of-the-art methods address this limitation by aggregating over repeated trials of the same stimulus. Yet multi-trial aggregation has been treated inconsistently across the literature: some work averages brain signals at the model's input, other work averages predictions at the model's output, and neither treats aggregation as an architectural choice in its own right. We provide the first systematic comparison of aggregation strategies for non-invasive neural decoding, evaluating six paradigms (including logit averaging during training and three attention-based variants we introduce) across three datasets, four tasks, and two group sizes. We find that aggregation choice matters substantially: training-time logit averaging, the simplest method we propose, outperforms all others in 6 of 7 settings. On the phoneme classification setting of the 2025 PNPL competition, it sets a new state of the art, significantly outperforming the competition winner by 17.4 absolute percentage points in balanced accuracy. We further draw a theoretical connection between logit averaging and joint ensemble training, which has been shown to underperform independent ensembling in the deep learning literature; our results call into question recent explanations of why joint ensemble training fails. Together, these findings establish multi-trial aggregation as a key design choice for non-invasive neural decoding and identify training-time logit averaging as a simple, effective default.
papers.summary: Non-invasive brain-computer interfaces have a low signal-to-noise ratio, so recent methods aggregate over repeated trials of the same stimulus, but past work has done this inconsistently. The authors systematically compare six aggregation strategies, including training-time logit averaging and three new attention-based variants, across three datasets, four tasks, and two group sizes. Training-time logit averaging, the simplest of these, wins in 6 of 7 settings and beats the winner of the 2025 `PNPL` phoneme classification competition by **17.4 percentage points in balanced accuracy**. The paper also links logit averaging to joint ensemble training and argues that its results contradict recent explanations of why joint ensembles underperform.

papers.title: PhyPro-FM: A Physics and Prompt-Guided Graph Foundation Model for Contingency Analysis
papers.abstract: The continuous evolution of next-generation power systems, characterized by the high penetration of renewable energy resources and dynamic topology variations, poses formidable challenges to traditional N-1/N-2 contingency analysis in terms of computational efficiency and scalability. While deep learning-based methods offer accelerated inference, existing studies predominantly treat contingency analysis as a pure regression problem, often overlooking the physical essence of grid operation and engineering requirements of real-world scenarios. To bridge this gap, this paper proposes a physics and prompt-guided graph foundation model (PhyPro-FM) for generalizable and engineering-viable contingency analysis. The proposed architecture integrates graph neural networks with a learnable global query mechanism and, notably, introduces a prompt-guided learning paradigm. By leveraging historical snapshots as few-shot prompts, the model dynamically captures correlations between target and historical operating conditions, significantly enhancing generalization capabilities under unseen topologies. Furthermore, we design a physics-informed training mechanism that prioritizes branch power flow errors over nodal voltage errors, aligning the optimization objective with critical grid security constraints. To ensure engineering applicability, a physics-informed inference mechanism is also developed, incorporating a residual-based correction module and a specialized post-processing strategy for singular branches to circumvent numerical instability. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that PhyPro-FM outperforms state-of-the-art methods in accuracy and generalization, validating its superior physical consistency and robustness for practical engineering applications.
papers.summary: Proposes `PhyPro-FM`, a graph foundation model for N-1/N-2 contingency analysis in power grids with many renewables and frequently changing topology. The model combines graph neural networks with a learnable global query, and it uses historical grid snapshots as few-shot prompts so it can generalize to unseen topologies. Training weights branch power-flow errors above nodal voltage errors, and at inference a residual correction module plus special handling of singular branches keep results numerically stable. Experiments show **better accuracy and generalization than state-of-the-art methods**, along with stronger physical consistency.

papers.title: An Empirical Study of Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Mixture-of-Experts LLMs
papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods are critical for adapting large models under resource-constrained settings. However, as mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures, which offer efficient inference at massive parameter scales, gain increasing prevalence in the community, a critical gap arising from the lack of systematic recipes for applying PEFT to MoE models. To narrow this gap, we conduct a large-scale systematic study that investigates a set of essential design recipes, including which modules should be adapted, which granularity should be used to adapt MoE modules, which PEFT method to use, and to what extent should the load-balancing objective be used, across three MoE backbones on downstream tasks and general knowledge tasks. Our experiments yield several key insights. First, adapting MoE experts alone achieves the highest downstream performance with competitive general capability retention under a comparable parameter budget. Second, native expert-weight updates offer a better downstream--retention trade-off than adapters that bypass experts or entire MoE modules. Third, LoRA and DoRA together define the strongest operating region for high downstream accuracy among the evaluated PEFT methods. Fourth, no nonzero load-balancing coefficient Pareto-dominates the zero baseline. We finally evaluate a weight-level redesign of MoE$^2$-LoRA on Qwen3. Moving its module-level bypass pool into native expert weights improves all four upstream endpoints by 2.4 to 17.9 points with 17% fewer trainable parameters and a 3.2-point average downstream cost.
papers.summary: Large-scale study of how to apply parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) to mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models, varying which modules are adapted, at what granularity, with which PEFT method, and how much load-balancing loss is used, across three MoE backbones. The main recipe is that **adapting only the experts gives the best downstream performance while competitively retaining general capability**, and updating native expert weights beats adapters that bypass the experts. `LoRA` and `DoRA` were the strongest methods tested, and no nonzero load-balancing coefficient Pareto-dominated using none. A weight-level redesign of `MoE²-LoRA` on `Qwen3` improves upstream metrics by 2.4 to 17.9 points with 17% fewer trainable parameters, at a 3.2-point average downstream cost.

papers.title: CTLite: Lightweight Irregular Multivariate Time Series Forecasting with Reusable Continuous-Time Summaries
papers.abstract: Irregular multivariate time series forecasting (IMTSF) requires capturing temporal dynamics and cross-variable dependencies from sparse, asynchronous observations. Existing methods often rely on learned temporal encoders, coupling historical representation construction with model optimisation and repeatedly processing the same observations. We propose CTLite, a lightweight forecasting framework that decouples historical summarisation from learned prediction. Specifically, a parameter-free continuous-time moment encoder summarises local levels and trends at multiple temporal scales while suppressing poorly supported slope estimates. A compact readout combines damped local extrapolation with a low-rank cross-variable correction that accounts for observation freshness, target availability, and forecast horizon. Since the historical summaries are independent of trainable parameters and forecast queries, they can be reused across optimisation steps and repeated predictions for an unchanged history without altering predictions or parameter gradients. Experiments on four real-world benchmarks show that CTLite achieves the best or second-best mean MSE and MAE among the evaluated methods with only 88-2,537 trainable parameters. Under matched GPU workloads at batch size 32, CTLite reduces inference latency by 18.6-87.3% compared with the latest models, including the cost of historical encoding. Reusing summaries further reduces total runtime by approximately 52% over 16 forecast calls on the same history compared with recomputing the encoder for every call, including the initial encoding cost. The code is at: https://github.com/SSMa913/NICLab-CTLite.
papers.summary: Presents `CTLite`, a lightweight forecaster for irregular multivariate time series that separates summarizing the history from the learned prediction step. A parameter-free continuous-time moment encoder summarizes local levels and trends at several time scales, and a compact readout combines damped extrapolation with a low-rank cross-variable correction. Because the summaries do not depend on trainable parameters, they can be reused across training steps and repeated forecasts. On four benchmarks it ranks best or second-best in mean MSE and MAE **with only 88 to 2,537 trainable parameters**, cuts inference latency by 18.6-87.3% compared with recent models, and reusing summaries saves about 52% of runtime over 16 forecast calls on the same history.

papers.title: Selecting the Best Few with Human Evaluators: Adaptively Combining Ratings and Pairwise Comparisons
papers.abstract: This paper considers a decision-maker tasked with identifying the $k$ best items from a large pool of candidates, such as job applicants, LLMs, award nominees, or new product ideas. The decision-maker learns about the items' quality by soliciting human evaluations. Each evaluation can be costly, so the decision-maker aims to use the limited evaluation budget efficiently by allocating evaluations adaptively. A key consideration is the form of evaluation to solicit, which should be something evaluators are comfortable providing. Two popular forms are ratings and pairwise comparisons, and we allow for both, as they may be especially useful in combination given the limited budget. Ratings can be used early on to get a coarse picture of which items are good and which are not. As that picture forms, comparisons can refine the ordering of the good items, narrowing in on the ultimate top-$k$ selection. To solve the allocation problem, we develop an adaptive algorithm built from two allocation policies. The first, our primary contribution, is based on a surrogate objective that is naturally forward-looking, valuing evaluations that help inform what to evaluate in future rounds, not just those that directly improve the selection decision. The decision rule is interpretable, and we prove that it is asymptotically consistent. Late in the evaluation process, when being forward-looking is less productive, we construct a myopic policy and a criterion for switching to it. In simulation, the method gives insight into how to combine these two types of evaluations, and beats the (limited) existing benchmarks.
papers.summary: Addresses picking the top k items, such as job applicants, LLMs, or award nominees, from a large pool when each human evaluation is costly and can be either a rating or a pairwise comparison. The proposed adaptive algorithm first uses a forward-looking policy, based on a surrogate objective, that values evaluations for what they reveal about which items to evaluate next; later it switches to a myopic policy according to a defined criterion. The forward-looking rule is interpretable and **proven asymptotically consistent**. In simulations it beats the few existing benchmarks and shows how ratings for coarse screening can be combined with comparisons for fine ranking.

papers.title: ForagerSim: Evaluating Embodied Map-Based Reasoning in Large-Scale Dynamic Worlds
papers.abstract: Animals build cognitive maps of vast environments, use them to perform map-based navigation, and might even be reusing the same circuitry used in spatial reasoning for creating and using maps of arbitrary task-spaces. In contrast, current embodied AI systems either rely on hand-engineered mapping pipelines, which break in the presence of unmodeled dynamics and are restricted to metric space, or on learned policies that rarely form map-like representations at all. Developing architectures that could learn to build and use map-like representations as flexibly as animals is, however, difficult because few embodied AI benchmarks actually require map-based reasoning. To address this, we present ForagerSim --- an interdisciplinary research platform and simulation environment focused on embodied tasks that require map-based reasoning, with scenarios ranging from mobile-robot search and rescue to animal foraging in both complex mazes and vast, potentially infinite open areas. ForagerSim is highly modular and allows modifying independent axes of difficulty related to perception (abstract 2D sensing to full RGB or LiDAR), scale (room-scale to multi-km scale), topology (open-fields to complex mazes), dynamics (smoke, debris, sensorimotor failures and others) and tasks (from simple 2D coverage to foraging-inspired well-alternation tasks). We compare reinforcement learning baselines with a simple engineered robotics stack and a human player on 8 example worlds which show how different difficulty axes affect existing methods. Our results show that, when sensing is simplified to 2D, learned policies can perform multi-object search and well-alternation tasks surprisingly well in simple topologies, but they fall short of human performance in larger or more complex-topology environments where map-based baselines perform well, suggesting that map-based reasoning is the bottleneck in these scenarios.
papers.summary: Introduces `ForagerSim`, a simulation platform for embodied tasks that require map-based reasoning, ranging from robot search-and-rescue to animal-style foraging in mazes and very large or unbounded open areas. Difficulty can be tuned independently along perception (abstract 2D sensing up to RGB or LiDAR), scale (room-sized to multiple kilometers), topology, dynamics such as smoke, debris, and sensor failures, and task type. Reinforcement learning baselines, a simple engineered robotics stack, and a human player are compared on eight example worlds. With simplified 2D sensing, learned policies do well in simple layouts but **fall short of humans in large or complex-topology worlds where map-based baselines succeed**, which points to map-based reasoning as the bottleneck.

papers.title: Bridged Self-Distillation for On-Policy Learning
papers.abstract: On-policy distillation can transfer the reasoning capabilities of a strong teacher to a smaller student. However, distillation from a stronger teacher model faces two mismatches: its solutions may be difficult for a smaller student to imitate, and its token-level probabilities may be incompatible with, or even unavailable to, the student. Existing methods handle these settings through different forms of supervision. To this end, we propose Bridged Self-Distillation (BSD), a unified framework for distilling from any teacher that provides reasoning traces. The model to be distilled from, termed the external teacher, first provides a reasoning trace as privileged context, which can be generated in an offline fashion. The student generates rollouts without this context, while a copy of the student conditioned on it, serving as the self-teacher, scores the same rollouts in the student's own token space. BSD uses the resulting token-level guidance to adjust updates on unsuccessful rollouts, with a verifier providing the outcome signal. As the external teacher is queried only to produce text, the same training procedure applies to all teacher scenarios: shared-tokenizer, cross-tokenizer, and closed API teachers. Across these scenarios, BSD improves over the base model and outperforms baselines tailored to each scenario, offering a novel and unified pathway for distillation. Code is available: https://github.com/TUMLegalTech/Bridged-Self-Distillation
papers.summary: On-policy distillation from a strong teacher to a smaller student is hampered when the teacher's solutions are hard to imitate or its token probabilities are incompatible with, or unavailable to, the student. `Bridged Self-Distillation` (`BSD`) uses the external teacher only to produce a reasoning trace, which can be generated offline. A copy of the student that sees this trace acts as a self-teacher, scoring the student's own rollouts in the student's token space, and this guidance adjusts updates on failed rollouts while a verifier supplies the outcome signal. Because the teacher only has to emit text, **one procedure covers shared-tokenizer, cross-tokenizer, and closed-API teachers**, and it beats baselines designed for each of these cases.

papers.title: How Benchmark Graph Construction Shapes Multi-Hop KG Navigation: A Controlled Audit of PathQuestion and PathQuestion-Large
papers.abstract: Multi-hop knowledge-graph question answering (KGQA) benchmarks are often treated as fixed language-and-reasoning tasks, but for navigation-based methods, difficulty also depends on the graph in which those tasks are instantiated. This makes graph construction a consequential but often entangled part of the navigation task. To isolate this effect, we audit PathQuestion (PQ) and PathQuestion-Large (PQL) as graph-navigation benchmarks under a controlled intervention: we hold questions, topic entities, released answers, released path annotations, and family-level splits fixed while replacing each released task-filtered graph with the larger source KG distributed with the benchmark. Source restoration expands the effective navigation search space and graph-consistent answer and path multiplicity while sharply reducing unguided reachability to released answers. We evaluate whether these structural changes persist across navigation policies using structural references, frozen small-language-model navigation policies, and trained MINERVA policies. Across both frozen and trained policies, restoration substantially reduces released-answer accuracy and trajectory fidelity, while graph-consistent evaluation recovers only part of the loss. These results show that benchmark graph construction is part of the navigation task specification rather than merely an implementation detail and can materially shape measured behavior even when the released QA task is held fixed.
papers.summary: Audits the multi-hop knowledge-graph question answering (KGQA) benchmarks `PathQuestion` and `PathQuestion-Large` to measure how the construction of the underlying graph affects navigation-based methods. Questions, answers, path annotations, and splits are held fixed while the task-filtered graphs are swapped for the larger source knowledge graph distributed with the benchmark, which enlarges the search space and the number of valid answers and paths. Across frozen small-language-model navigators and trained `MINERVA` policies, this restoration **substantially lowers released-answer accuracy and trajectory fidelity**, and graph-consistent evaluation recovers only part of the loss. The authors conclude that graph construction is part of the task specification rather than an implementation detail.

papers.title: LaMER: Language-Conditioned Multi-Expert Routing for Weakly Supervised Referring Expression Comprehension
papers.abstract: Referring Expression Comprehension (REC) localizes the image region described by a natural language expression, underpinning applications such as autonomous navigation, human-robot interaction, and medical image analysis. Under weak supervision, REC is challenged by the visual-linguistic semantic gap and the difficulty of inferring region-text correspondences from coarse image-level signals alone. Moreover, no single visual encoder captures all complementary properties---semantic alignment, fine-grained texture, and boundary awareness---while naively fusing multiple pretrained encoders yields heterogeneous, hard-to-reconcile representations. We propose LaMER, a weakly supervised REC framework that dynamically aggregates four frozen expert encoders through a language-conditioned Cross-Modal Routing Fusion module, adapting expert selection to each referring expression without instance-level bounding-box supervision. A Cell-Text Matching Head with Negative Anchor Augmentation, trained with a multi-objective loss combining contrastive, reconstruction, alignment, and load-balancing terms, further stabilizes optimization. LaMER achieves 77.67\%, 62.81\%, and 69.49\% Acc@IoU\(\geq 0.5\) on RefCOCO, RefCOCO+, and RefCOCOg, surpassing DViN and WeakMCN by up to 16.49 and 14.49 points, with ablations validating each component.
papers.summary: Referring Expression Comprehension (REC) locates the image region described by a phrase, and doing it with weak supervision (no box labels) is hard because no single visual encoder captures all the needed cues. `LaMER` routes among four frozen expert encoders with a language-conditioned Cross-Modal Routing Fusion module, so expert selection adapts to each expression. A Cell-Text Matching Head with negative anchor augmentation, trained on a combined contrastive, reconstruction, alignment, and load-balancing loss, stabilizes optimization. It reaches 77.67%, 62.81%, and 69.49% Acc@IoU≥0.5 on `RefCOCO`, `RefCOCO+`, and `RefCOCOg`, **up to 16.49 points above prior weakly supervised methods**.

papers.title: Expert L2 English Speech Evaluation on a Gaming PC: Accuracy, Fluency, and Prosody with XLS-R, XEUS, and PhoneticXeus
papers.abstract: oollim is a locally executable system for evaluating L2 English pronunciation accuracy, fluency, and prosody on a consumer computer. The system combines pretrained XLS-R, XEUS, and PhoneticXeus representations with reference-text features and ridge regressions trained on SpeechOcean762, the Korean Learners' L2 Speech Corpus (English), J-AESOP, and their combinations. On 305 independently held-out recordings assessed by three expert raters, several ridge configurations substantially outperform archived Azure API scores obtained in January 2026 in both Spearman correlation and quadratic weighted kappa across all three constructs. These results support expert speech evaluation on consumer hardware using pretrained representations and construct-specific regressions, without neural-model fine-tuning or calibration on the private evaluation data.
authors: Richard Rose (Hankuk University of Foreign Studies)
papers.summary: Describes `oollim`, a system that runs locally on a consumer gaming PC and scores the accuracy, fluency, and prosody of English spoken by second-language learners. It combines pretrained `XLS-R`, `XEUS`, and `PhoneticXeus` speech representations with reference-text features and ridge regressions trained on `SpeechOcean762`, a Korean learners' corpus, `J-AESOP`, and combinations of them, with no neural fine-tuning. On 305 held-out recordings scored by three expert raters, several configurations **outperform archived Azure API scores on all three measures** in both Spearman correlation and quadratic weighted kappa.

papers.title: A Simple and General Approach to top-$k$ Selection
papers.abstract: This paper considers the Bayesian top-$k$ identification problem, wherein a decision maker is tasked with selecting $k$ items from a pool of items of unknown quality. To assess the items, the decision maker adaptively allocates a fixed sampling budget, where each sample of an item yields a noisy observation of its quality, with the objective of minimizing the expected opportunity cost of the selected set. We propose an approach that allocates each batch of samples by minimizing a surrogate objective derived from an upper bound on the expected opportunity cost. The approach is general: samples can be allocated in batches, the selection size $k$ is arbitrary, and it applies to many sampling distributions. It is also simple and intuitive. We prove that the method's posterior expected opportunity cost decays at an exponential rate of at least half the best rate achievable by any sampling rule. In simulations across a wide range of settings, the method is competitive with, and often improves upon, the best existing algorithm in each setting.
papers.summary: Tackles Bayesian top-k identification: spending a fixed sampling budget on items of unknown quality, where each sample is a noisy observation, so as to minimize the expected opportunity cost of the k items chosen. Each batch of samples is allocated by minimizing a surrogate objective derived from an upper bound on that cost, and the method works for arbitrary k, batched sampling, and many sampling distributions. The authors prove that its posterior expected opportunity cost **decays exponentially at no less than half the best achievable rate**. In simulations it is competitive with, and often better than, the best existing algorithm for each setting.

papers.title: Where Does Rhetorical Distortion Live? A Multi-Platform, Multi-Language Measurement of Influencer Content
papers.abstract: Much of the manipulation in online influencer content is not false but disproportionate: an accurate fact is framed as historic, urgent, or catastrophic. Fact-checking and clickbait detection are not designed to capture such framing, and little is known about where it originates: with the creator, the topic, the platform, or the audience that replies. We operationalize rhetorical distortion through five literature-grounded dimensions (Significance Inflation, Anxiety Manufacturing, Novelty Claims, Loaded Language, and Temporal Distortion) and measure it with a three-tier pipeline in which bilingual lexical rules propose candidates, negative filters cancel known false-positive contexts, and an LLM verifies or relabels the candidates. Applying the pipeline to 13,060 posts from 330 accounts on six platforms (RSS/newsletters, YouTube, Bluesky, Reddit, Weibo, and X/Twitter), we find that platform is far more strongly associated with account-level distortion than content category (Kruskal-Wallis $\varepsilon^2=0.33$; two-way ANOVA $\eta_p^2=0.49$ for platform vs. $0.09$ for category). X/Twitter scores highest (DI 7.74 vs. 0.78 for RSS). Classifying tweets and their replies separately shows where this comes from: the reply layer readers see under a post (its top-5 replies) carries 3.5x the distortion of the tweet it answers (7.65 vs. 2.17, $p<10^{-6}$, 36 of 43 accounts), driven by Loaded Language. At equal text length the gap shrinks to 1.5x but remains significant, and creator tweets alone are statistically indistinguishable from YouTube and Bluesky. Two independent human annotators confirm the reply gap, and the platform ordering and the reply gap replicate with GPT-4o as a second classifier. On threaded platforms, measured distortion thus lives largely in the audience layer, which motivates measurement that separates creator and reply text.
papers.summary: Measures "rhetorical distortion", meaning accurate facts framed as historic, urgent, or catastrophic, along five dimensions such as Significance Inflation and Loaded Language. The pipeline uses bilingual lexical rules to propose candidates, negative filters to drop known false positives, and an LLM to verify them, and it is applied to 13,060 posts from 330 accounts on six platforms. Platform is far more strongly associated with distortion than content category, with X/Twitter the highest. On X, **the top-5 replies carry 3.5 times the distortion of the tweet they answer**, mostly through loaded language; the gap shrinks to 1.5 times at equal text length but stays significant, and it is confirmed by human annotators and by `GPT-4o` as a second classifier.

papers.title: Co-Evolving Policy and Reward for Code Generation: A Mechanistic Study of Single-Adapter Drift
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is particularly well suited to code generation because generated programs can be objectively evaluated through execution. Execution also provides behavioral information that can be reused as additional supervision. The Synergistic Policy and Reward Co-Evolving Framework (SPARK), originally proposed for reasoning tasks, exploits this idea by recycling training rollouts and their evaluation results to train a model not only to generate solutions but also to evaluate and improve them. We investigate whether this policy-reward co-evolution approach transfers effectively to code generation and whether execution-grounded reflection provides an additional source of self-improvement. We compare SPARK-style rollout recycling with execution-only Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) using Qwen2.5-Coder-3B-Instruct. Our results do not support either hypothesis under the configuration tested. Although co-evolution improves training performance, these gains do not generalize to held-out problems. Compared at the same stage of training, rollout recycling produces roughly 34x greater KL divergence from the reference policy than execution-only GRPO. Over training, trained tokens per GRPO sequence fall from 185 to 86 as training pass rate increases, while held-out performance declines or fails to sustain early gains. We characterize these patterns as single-adapter policy drift: the shared trainable parameters increasingly depart from pretrained code-generation behavior without corresponding gains in generalization. The results show that higher training reward alone is not evidence of generalizable code self-improvement and highlight the importance of held-out evaluation and drift diagnostics.
papers.summary: Tests whether `SPARK`, a framework that reuses reinforcement learning rollouts and their evaluations to train a model to both generate and judge solutions, transfers to code generation with verifiable execution rewards. Using `Qwen2.5-Coder-3B-Instruct`, it compares SPARK-style rollout recycling with execution-only Group Relative Policy Optimization (`GRPO`). Co-evolution raises training performance, but the gains do not carry over to held-out problems, and **rollout recycling yields about 34 times more KL divergence from the reference policy**. The authors call this single-adapter policy drift and argue that higher training reward alone is not evidence of generalizable self-improvement, so held-out evaluation and drift diagnostics are needed.

papers.title: Local data augmentation for imbalanced binary classification
papers.abstract: Facing imbalanced binary classification, we aim at maximizing the recall while limiting the proportion of false detections in the minority class. For doing that, the present work studies the effect of several rebalancing strategies, from the uniform subsampling of the observations from the minority class, to a more involved local data augmentation scheme. To be more specific, we establish that only rebalancing class proportions cannot modify the classification performance, whereas local data augmentation is proved to have an impact on the final results. The local augmentation scheme is introduced by means of a two-step procedure. The first step randomly subsamples anchor points among the training observations. These anchor points are used in the second step, for drawing new augmentation data following an ''augmentation kernel'' to be specified. This enables us to decouple the impact of the anchor points subsampling from the one of drawing augmentation data accounting (or not) for the local geometry of the support. The experiments on synthetic data illustrate the practical performance of several strategies for subsampling anchor points combined with either a Gaussian or a diffusion-based augmentation kernel. Compared to SMOTE-like data augmentation procedures, a better performance is achieved when subsampling in the close neighborhood to the classification boundary combined with a Gaussian augmentation kernel. Furthermore in specific settings where the geometric structure of the support matters, the experimental results show that using a diffusion-based augmentation kernel outperforms the Gaussian one.
papers.summary: Studies imbalanced binary classification where the goal is to maximize recall on the minority class while limiting false detections. The authors prove that simply rebalancing class proportions cannot change classification performance, whereas **local data augmentation provably can**.
