The network learns how similarity changes across design space, while the resulting kernel defines the design-to-pose operator, its posterior uncertainty, and a criterion for sequential simulator acquisition. We represent backbone position and rotational strain with spatial kernels and reconstruct orientation directly on SO(3), preserving valid material frames and tendon geometry. We use ASkotch with Nystrom preconditioning for scalable kernel operator solves and a separate Nystrom approximation for posterior covariance. Experiments show that kernel-coverage acquisition reduces mean trajectory error by approximately 15% relative to IID sampling, while posterior variance increases for increasingly unsupported designs. Compared with prior neural-operator TDCR models, the method is 30-50% more accurate using approximately 5x fewer training designs while additionally providing posterior uncertainty estimates.
papers.summary: The authors build a surrogate model for tendon-driven continuum robots (TDCRs) that predicts the full equilibrium shape across both robot designs and actuation inputs, along with an uncertainty estimate. It is a Gaussian-process (GP) operator whose nonstationary kernel metric is learned by a shallow neural network from mechanics-aware design coordinates. Orientation is reconstructed directly on SO(3) so that material frames stay valid, and `ASkotch` with Nyström preconditioning keeps the kernel solves scalable. Compared with prior neural-operator TDCR models, it is **30–50% more accurate using about 5x fewer training designs**, and choosing which simulations to run by kernel coverage cuts trajectory error by about 15% relative to random sampling.

papers.title: Degree Bounds for Separating Polynomial and Neural Invariants for Point Clouds
papers.abstract: Neural networks that respect the symmetries of point clouds commonly compute high-order representations of the rotation group to improve their expressivity. Such models are known to be universal, and thus able to separate any pair of point clouds, when using representations of sufficiently high order, yet no precise bound on this order, as a function of the number of points, was previously known. We establish the first quadratic lower and upper degree bounds for polynomials that separate point clouds of n points up to rotations and permutations. By showing Tensor Field Networks and MACE can express all invariant polynomials of a given degree with sufficient representation order, we additionally derive the first explicit, quadratic bound on the representation order sufficient for these architectures to be complete, replacing previous existence results with concrete guarantees. We further show that, under local regularity assumptions, point cloud separation can be achieved with a message-passing-based model using invariants whose degree depends only on the size of a local neighborhood, rather than on the size of the full point cloud. Finally, we provide counterexamples showing MACE must compute high order irreducible representations to separate locally regular point clouds.
papers.summary: Rotation-equivariant point-cloud networks become universal once they use sufficiently high-order representations, but no explicit bound on that order was known. The authors prove **the first quadratic lower and upper degree bounds** for polynomials that separate point clouds of n points up to rotations and permutations. Because `Tensor Field Networks` and `MACE` can express all invariant polynomials of a given degree, this gives the first explicit bound on the representation order these architectures need to be complete. They also show that, under local regularity assumptions, a message-passing model separates point clouds with invariants whose degree depends only on neighborhood size, and give counterexamples showing `MACE` still needs high-order representations in that setting.

papers.title: Conducting Reliable Keyword Estimation with Unreliable ASR in Police Audio Data
papers.abstract: Extracting insights from large audio data sets using human transcription is expensive and time-consuming. Off-the-shelf Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems offer an easy-to-use scalable alternative, but systematic transcription errors, especially in domain-specific settings, can bias downstream analyses and lead to unreliable conclusions. We investigate whether imperfect ASR transcripts can still be used to obtain statistically valid keyword frequency estimates by combining model outputs with a small set of human-labeled examples, following Prediction Powered Inference and Design-based Supervised Learning frameworks. We evaluate this approach on police radio communications from Baltimore and Chicago, a domain in which keyword distributions could provide valuable insights into police activity, but off-the-shelf ASR systems exhibit systematic errors on operationally important terminology. Using bootstrap-based confidence interval coverage as our evaluation metric, we find that our approach substantially increases the number of domain-specific keywords that can be analyzed with statistically valid confidence intervals, from 43.0% using ASR alone and 27.2% using only a small set of human-labeled transcriptions to 56.2% in the Baltimore dataset, with similar improvements observed in Chicago data. Our results demonstrate that post-hoc error correction can improve statistical validity of downstream analyses even for poor-quality transcriptions, offering an avenue for better leveraging off-the-shelf ASR models for large-scale speech analysis.
papers.summary: Off-the-shelf automatic speech recognition (ASR) makes large audio collections analyzable, but systematic transcription errors on domain-specific vocabulary can bias downstream statistics. The authors combine imperfect ASR transcripts with a small set of human-labeled examples using `Prediction Powered Inference` and `Design-based Supervised Learning` to estimate keyword frequencies in police radio traffic from Baltimore and Chicago. On the Baltimore data, the combined approach raises the share of keywords with statistically valid confidence intervals to **56.2%, up from 43.0% using ASR alone and 27.2% using human labels alone**, and the Chicago data shows similar gains.

papers.title: Global Time-Aware Conditioning (GTC): A Mechanism for Time-Aware Pediatric Sleep Representation Learning
papers.abstract: Sleep physiology evolves throughout the night, with changes in sleep cycles, respiratory stability, and cardiovascular dynamics. However, self-supervised learning (SSL) methods for sleep typically process short, fixed-duration windows without explicitly modeling where each window occurs within the full sleep session. We introduce Global Time-Aware Conditioning (GTC), a mechanism that complements local positional encodings by conditioning latent representations on the global time-of-sleep of each input window. We integrate GTC into three representative SSL frameworks and evaluate them on five clinically relevant tasks with extreme class imbalance across two independent pediatric cohorts. GTC generally improves F1 and AUPRC across architectures and tasks, with gains persisting under cross-cohort transfer, highlighting the value of global temporal context for sleep representation learning.
papers.summary: Self-supervised learning (SSL) methods for sleep data usually process short fixed windows without knowing where in the night each window falls, even though sleep physiology changes over the course of a session. `Global Time-Aware Conditioning` (`GTC`) conditions each window's latent representation on its global time-of-sleep, complementing local positional encodings. Added to three SSL frameworks and evaluated on five heavily imbalanced clinical tasks across two pediatric cohorts, `GTC` **generally improves F1 and AUPRC**, and the gains persist when transferring between cohorts.

papers.title: SleepPairNet: Learning Multimodal Pediatric Sleep Representations with Random-Pair Cross-Attention
papers.abstract: Analyzing physiological sleep signals is important for assessing sleep quality and detecting sleep-related disorders. Learning inter-modal relationships across physiological signals can provide richer representations for downstream sleep analysis. We introduce SleepPairNet, a multimodal self-supervised learning (SSL) framework that learns pairwise interactions between physiological signals through cross-attention. We propose a random modality-pair selection strategy that exposes the model to diverse signal pairs during pretraining, enabling flexibility across modality combinations at test time. Pretrained on the NCH dataset, SleepPairNet outperforms the evaluated SSL baselines on all respiratory tasks while remaining competitive on EEG-related tasks, and shows even stronger results when transferred to the external CHAT dataset.
papers.summary: `SleepPairNet` is a multimodal self-supervised learning (SSL) framework that learns relationships between physiological sleep signals through pairwise cross-attention. During pretraining it samples random pairs of signals, so the model can work with whichever combination of signals is available at test time. Pretrained on the `NCH` pediatric dataset, it **outperforms the evaluated SSL baselines on all respiratory tasks** while staying competitive on EEG tasks, and it performs even better when transferred to the external `CHAT` dataset.

papers.title: VaDar: Implicit Goal Conditioning via Value Disaggregation
papers.abstract:
Long-horizon tasks are important for modern AI and robotics, yet pose a challenge for reinforcement learning. Historically, a popular approach has been to decompose a task into subgoals, and learn a subgoal-conditioned policy to execute each subtask in sequence.
  We introduce an alternative called Value Disaggregation (VaDar), which trains a single subgoal-independent policy to maximize a linear combination of per-subgoal critic values. Because subgoal information is needed only at training-time, VaDar removes the need for possibly costly or cumbersome subgoal-selection during policy deployment. Moreover, through careful experiments, we show that VaDar (1) is always competitive with, and frequently outperforms, natural baselines like goal-conditioning and (2) succeeds on tasks with non-sequential goal structure and multiple optimization objectives. In particular, VaDar is the first algorithm to solve challenging, long-horizon tasks in the RoboCasa suite, even when starting from a policy pretrained from behavior cloning with near-zero initial task success. Taken together, VaDar's successes suggest that subgoal information benefits actor-critic reinforcement learning by enhancing the efficacy of critic learning, whereas policy goal-conditioning is often unnecessary.
papers.summary: Long-horizon reinforcement learning tasks are often split into subgoals and solved with a subgoal-conditioned policy, which then needs a way to choose subgoals at deployment. `Value Disaggregation` (`VaDar`) instead trains one subgoal-independent policy to maximize a linear combination of per-subgoal critic values, so subgoal information is needed only during training. In experiments, it is always competitive with goal-conditioning baselines and often beats them. It handles tasks with non-sequential goal structure and multiple objectives, and it is **the first algorithm to solve challenging long-horizon tasks in the `RoboCasa` suite**, even starting from a behavior-cloned policy with near-zero success. The authors argue that subgoal information helps mainly by improving critic learning, and that conditioning the policy on goals is often unnecessary.

papers.title: When the harness decides success: state that cannot be re-observed
papers.abstract: Agent harnesses decide what a language model sees across turns: they drop old turns, summarize them, or replay the model's own earlier reasoning. We ask when these choices change whether an agent succeeds, not only what it costs, and report three findings. First, in a pre-registered synthetic probe, truncating the context window costs a low-cost reasoning model nothing in success when a needed fact can be looked up again (it looks the fact up instead), but drops its success to chance when the fact cannot be re-observed: the two penalties differ by 92.5 percentage points (90% CI [89.5, 95.5]). A pre-registered replication on one model from a second provider showed the same contrast. Once the fact was lost, that model chose no answer rather than guessing. Second, on ARC-AGI-3, where the benchmark's Standard harness trails its Provider Adapter harness by a wide margin, we decompose that gap one component at a time, for one model on four games. Summarizing old turns instead of dropping them, while keeping the Standard harness's invitation to take notes, recovers 86% of a 63-point gap without replaying the model's reasoning. The same harness without the invitation recovers 43%, and adding the provider's native replay of the model's reasoning recovers the remaining 57%. These are point estimates from one counted run per configuration and game, and the replay share depends on a single run. Third, in the benchmark's published runs and in ours, the Adapter's advantage in the probability of clearing a level it has reached is larger at deep levels than at early ones. This largely restates where runs stopped and does not separate a growing advantage from a constant one.
papers.summary: Agent harnesses decide what a language model sees across turns: they drop old turns, summarize them, or replay the model's earlier reasoning. The authors ask when these choices change whether an agent succeeds, not just what it costs. In a pre-registered synthetic probe, truncating context costs nothing when a lost fact can be looked up again but drops success to chance when it cannot, **a 92.5-percentage-point difference**, and a replication with a model from a second provider showed the same contrast. On `ARC-AGI-3`, testing one model on four games, summarizing old turns instead of dropping them while keeping an invitation to take notes recovers 86% of the 63-point gap between the benchmark's Standard and Provider Adapter harnesses. Without the note-taking invitation it recovers 43%, and replaying the model's native reasoning recovers the remaining 57%, though the authors caution that these are point estimates from single runs.

papers.title: From Outcomes to Components: A Counterfactual Evaluation Framework for LLM-Proposed Repairs
papers.abstract: A repair action proposed by a large language model (LLM) specifies which records to change and how to change their values. A failed action may still contain a useful choice of records or a useful update, depending on how the two are paired. We introduce a counterfactual evaluation framework that separates selected records (targets) from the applied change (an update). Four executions combine proposed and reference targets and updates to measure the effects of correcting or retaining each component and their interaction. We evaluate the framework on two tasks: traffic assignment, where affected demand must be identified from road counts, and database repair, where affected rows must be identified from aggregate reports. An injected fault supplies a reference action that reverses it, and the recovery rate measures an action's loss reduction relative to that reference. For sparse-target actions in the traffic experiments, retaining the proposed update on reference targets achieves 79.4% of the reference loss reduction, compared with 43.7% from tuning update strength on the proposed targets. In the database experiments, update replacement worsens 17 of 108 actions, all selecting unaffected records, with sharply different frequencies across models. The value of a proposed update depends on the targets it is paired with. Missed targets hide useful updates, while excess targets can make a milder update better than the reference correction. In a component-reuse study, testing new target-update pairings from two proposals raises mean held-out recovery rate to 0.616, compared with 0.580 when selecting between the original proposals.
papers.summary: A repair action proposed by a large language model (LLM) chooses which records to change (targets) and how to change them (an update), and a failed action may still contain one useful component. The authors' counterfactual framework runs all four combinations of proposed and reference targets and updates, scoring each by how much of a known injected fault it recovers. In traffic-assignment and database-repair tasks, for actions that select few targets, applying the proposed update to the correct targets **recovers 79.4% of the reference loss reduction, versus 43.7% from tuning update strength** on the proposed targets. Recombining targets and updates from two proposals raises mean held-out recovery from 0.580 to 0.616.

papers.title: The Effectiveness and Durability of Pretraining Data Filtering in Protein Language Models
papers.abstract: Pretraining filtering is one of the most common safeguards for open-weight language models. Here we study its effectiveness, durability and scalability using the ESM-2 family of protein language models. We find that filtering viral proteins from the pretraining data meaningfully degrades masked language modelling, mutation effect prediction and long-range contact prediction on viral proteins, while largely preserving performance on non-viral proteins. These effects are concentrated among proteins from human-infecting viruses, and grow as we scale models from 8M to 3B parameters. As models increase in size, we find that stringent filtering becomes more effective. However, fine-tuning on sequences from the removed viral families restores the lost performance. Although the cost to recover performance increases with model scale, even for the largest models it costs about 80 USD of H100 time. This work establishes pretraining filtering as moderately effective at selectively degrading performance on viral proteins, but not durable against fine-tuning with modest computational resources and access to relevant data.
papers.summary: Removing hazardous data before pretraining is a common safeguard for open-weight models, and the authors test how effective and durable it is using the `ESM-2` family of protein language models. Filtering viral proteins out of pretraining degrades masked language modeling, mutation-effect prediction, and contact prediction on viral proteins, especially those from human-infecting viruses, while largely preserving non-viral performance. The effect grows from 8M to 3B parameters. However, fine-tuning on the removed viral families restores the lost performance, at **about 80 USD of H100 time even for the largest model**, so filtering is moderately effective but not durable against modest fine-tuning.

papers.title: The Development of Sycophancy in Language Models: Tracing Vulnerabilities from Pretraining to Post-Training
papers.abstract: Language models can change a committed answer to accommodate a user's opinion or pushback without new evidence. However, when this behaviour develops during training and what a released model inherits from earlier stages remain unclear. We follow 741 checkpoints of 30 open model lineages, from early pretraining to released models. We plant initial verdicts on moral scenarios and measure how far a model follows a user's stated opinion or abandons its verdict under pressure. In most lineages the behaviour is present before post-training, and its average strength changes in either direction, at different stages across lineages. A clearer pattern emerges at the level of individual questions. Beyond responses without pressure, pretraining behaviour predicts little of which questions a released model yields on. That pattern forms during post-training: on routes with supervised fine-tuning, the fine-tuning checkpoint predicts part of it and the preference-optimization checkpoint most of it. A sibling trained from the same base along another route predicts far less: for T\"ulu-3 8B, its own preference-stage checkpoint removes 85% of the remaining prediction error, a sibling 19%. Internal states add predictive information without changing this ranking. Similar average scores conceal different vulnerabilities, and training history matters for auditing a released model.
papers.summary: Sycophancy, where a model abandons a committed answer under user pushback without new evidence, is traced across 741 checkpoints from 30 open model lineages, from early pretraining to release. The authors plant initial verdicts on moral scenarios and measure how far models follow a user's stated opinion or give in under pressure. In most lineages the behavior is already present before post-training, but which specific questions a released model yields on is shaped mostly during supervised fine-tuning and especially preference optimization. For `Tülu-3 8B`, **its own preference-stage checkpoint removes 85% of the remaining prediction error, while a sibling trained from the same base removes only 19%**. The authors conclude that similar average scores can hide different vulnerabilities, so auditing a model should account for its training history.

papers.title: SpatialScout: Can VLM Agents Actively Explore and Map 3D Scenes?
papers.abstract: Spatial intelligence requires agents to actively acquire visual evidence and integrate observations into a coherent representation of the three-dimensional world. Yet spatial question answering offers limited evidence of whether models can construct accurate metric maps through autonomous exploration. We introduce SpatialScout, a benchmark for evaluating vision-language model (VLM) agents on active object-level 3D mapping. SpatialScout comprises 80 diverse indoor scenes containing 3,140 target objects. Given an object inventory, RGB observations, camera calibration, and camera poses, agents control a camera to explore each scene and estimate object centers in a shared coordinate frame. The task requires coordinating viewpoint selection, cross-view association, geometric estimation, and map revision under bounded interaction budgets. Evaluation jointly measures localization accuracy and target coverage through object-scale overlap scores that penalize missing predictions. Experiments with frontier VLMs reveal substantial limitations: the strongest evaluated model, Claude Opus 5.5, achieves a mean overlap score of 41.71%, with 47.23% of targets exceeding an intersection-over-union (IoU) threshold of 0.5 and only 3.25% exceeding 0.9. These results reveal a substantial gap between recovering coarse object layouts and constructing complete, precise metric maps. SpatialScout provides a quantitative testbed for developing agents that build reliable 3D spatial representations through active perception. Code is available at https://github.com/JesseZZZZZ/SpatialScout.
papers.summary: Spatial question answering says little about whether vision-language model (VLM) agents can actively explore a scene and build an accurate metric map. `SpatialScout` evaluates this on 80 indoor scenes with 3,140 target objects. Given an object inventory, RGB views, and camera poses, an agent controls the camera under a bounded interaction budget to estimate object centers in a shared coordinate frame, scored jointly on localization accuracy and coverage. The strongest model tested, `Claude Opus 5.5`, reaches a mean overlap score of 41.71%, with 47.23% of targets above an intersection-over-union (IoU) of 0.5 but **only 3.25% above 0.9**, showing that current agents recover coarse layouts but not precise, complete maps.

papers.title: Nested Shared-Operator Recursion on ARC-AGI-1: An Empirical Study of HRM, TRM and URM
papers.abstract: Recursive reasoning models refine persistent internal states by repeatedly applying learned operators. We investigate whether adding a persistent intermediate state that integrates repeated updates of a faster state through the same operator improves predictive performance relative to each model family's baseline at matched parameter counts. We define this organisation operationally and implement it within three architectures: the Hierarchical Reasoning Model (HRM), Tiny Recursive Model (TRM) and Universal Reasoning Model (URM). Using the official codebases on ARC-AGI-1, we compare each baseline with its parameter-matched nested variant. We evaluate held-out queries from tasks whose demonstrations were available during training. The experiments use a single-GPU budget far below the published training protocols. Under the tested conditions, nested variants show no consistent advantage in token accuracy, predictive loss or exact solving, which remains near zero for all configurations. The results therefore leave the hypothesis open. We specify a confirmatory comparison, with an informative baseline, multiple seeds, controls that isolate nesting and predefined criteria, to determine whether this organisation merits further development.
papers.summary: The study tests whether recursive reasoning models get better at matched parameter counts when given an extra persistent intermediate state that integrates repeated updates of a faster state through the same shared operator. The authors implement this nested organisation in the `Hierarchical Reasoning Model (HRM)`, the `Tiny Recursive Model (TRM)` and the `Universal Reasoning Model (URM)` using their official codebases. They compare each nested variant against its parameter-matched baseline on `ARC-AGI-1`, training on a single GPU with far less compute than the published protocols. Under these conditions **the nested variants show no consistent advantage**, and exact solving stays near zero for every configuration, so the authors set out a confirmatory design with multiple seeds and predefined criteria to settle the question.

papers.title: PACT: Plan-Augmented Coordination via Trace-Graphs for Dynamic Multi-Agent Combinatorial Optimization
papers.abstract: Multi-agent approaches have been investigated recently as a means of improving the scalability of reinforcement learning for neural combinatorial optimization. Existing methods assume that all problem instance information is known upfront. However, real-world problems are often dynamic: relevant information is progressively revealed as the agents take actions (e.g., arriving at an edge in a routing problem only to discover it is untraversable). In such cases, existing methods fail to coordinate agents to explore and exploit the progressively revealed information. To address the arising coordination challenge, we introduce PACT (Plan-Augmented Coordination via Trace-graphs). PACT augments the environment graph with auxiliary nodes representing the plans of agents, which are connected to the resource nodes to indicate future dependencies. The proposed message-passing scheme over the augmented graph grounds inter-agent coordination in the environment and enables proactive, rather than reactive, conflict resolution. We show that PACT improves solution quality in dynamic problems relative to baselines and exhibits the best transfer to larger instances on which, remarkably, it outperforms centralized oracles with privileged access to instance uncertainty.
papers.summary: Multi-agent reinforcement learning for neural combinatorial optimization usually assumes the whole problem instance is known in advance. In real routing-style problems, information appears only as agents act, for example when an agent discovers that an edge cannot be traversed. `PACT` (Plan-Augmented Coordination via Trace-graphs) adds auxiliary nodes for each agent's plan to the environment graph and links them to the resource nodes those plans will use. Message passing over this augmented graph lets agents resolve conflicts before they happen rather than after. `PACT` improves solution quality on dynamic problems and transfers best to larger instances, where **it outperforms centralized oracles that have privileged access to instance uncertainty**.

papers.title: Which Model for Which Role? Cost-Efficient Pareto Recommendation for LLM Agentic Workflows
papers.abstract: LLM agentic workflows increasingly employ different models for specialized roles. Users may prefer different trade-offs between task quality and deployment cost, sometimes also considering latency. Finding good assignments incurs a separate search cost from evaluating multiple candidates. We introduce Cost-Coupled Gittins (CC-Gittins), a multi-objective extension of single-objective cost-aware Gittins search for Pareto recommendation. It exploits the coupling between evaluation and deployment costs: assignments that cost more to deploy also cost more to evaluate. The search alternates between seeking higher quality and lower deployment cost, reusing each evaluation to inform both searches. After each batch, CC-Gittins recommends assignments that are nondominated under uncertainty-adjusted estimates of quality and deployment cost. We evaluate CC-Gittins on eight quality--cost matrices from workflows with two to five roles and up to 1,681 candidate assignments. We also evaluate the method with latency as a third objective. Across the eight benchmarks, CC-Gittins recovers a substantial fraction of the true Pareto frontier at roughly 10% of the exhaustive-evaluation cost, and recovers most of the frontier with few false positives by 30%.
papers.summary: LLM agentic workflows often assign a different model to each role, and finding assignments that balance task quality against deployment cost is expensive because every candidate has to be evaluated. `Cost-Coupled Gittins (CC-Gittins)` extends cost-aware Gittins search to the multi-objective case. It relies on the fact that assignments that are expensive to deploy are also expensive to evaluate, alternates between searching for higher quality and for lower cost, and reuses each evaluation for both searches. After each batch, it recommends the assignments that are nondominated under uncertainty-adjusted estimates. On eight workflows with two to five roles and up to 1,681 candidate assignments, **it recovers a substantial fraction of the true Pareto frontier at roughly 10% of the cost of exhaustive evaluation**, and most of the frontier with few false positives by 30%; it also handles latency as a third objective.

papers.title: Intra-Rubric Reward Divergence: Mitigating Rubric Hacking through Latent Dimension Recovery and Balancing
papers.abstract: Rubric hacking limits both performance and training robustness in rubric-based reinforcement learning. By decomposing rubrics into sub-dimensions, we reveal the Intra-Rubric Reward Divergence: as the total rubric score increases, certain sub-dimension scores systematically decrease, suggesting the model sacrifices specific quality aspects to optimize the aggregated objective. From the sub-dimension perspective, we observe two phenomena: (1) dimension imbalance, causing the policy to favor heavily covered dimensions; (2) dimension absence, leading to a systematic gap between rewards and true quality. To mitigate these issues, we propose Fair-Race Dimension Aggregation (FRDA), which has generations compete within each dimension separately to mitigate rubric imbalance, and Residual Semantic Dimension Completion (RSDC), which mines evaluation dimensions implicitly encoded in a holistic preference signal to complete rubric coverage. Experiments in chat, science, and medical domains indicate that FRDA mitigates rubric hacking with more stable improvements, while RSDC outperforms both single-reward training and naive multi-reward aggregation, yielding generally higher-quality responses.
papers.summary: In reinforcement learning with rubric-based rewards, policies can game the aggregated score. Splitting rubrics into sub-dimensions exposes this as an **Intra-Rubric Reward Divergence: some sub-dimension scores systematically fall as the total score rises**. The authors trace the problem to dimension imbalance, where heavily covered dimensions dominate, and dimension absence, where the rubric misses aspects of true quality. `Fair-Race Dimension Aggregation (FRDA)` makes generations compete within each dimension separately, and `Residual Semantic Dimension Completion (RSDC)` mines missing dimensions from a holistic preference signal. Across chat, science and medical tasks, `FRDA` gives more stable gains and `RSDC` beats both single-reward training and naive multi-reward aggregation.

papers.title: Parallel Language Models via Variational Decoding
papers.abstract: Autoregressive language models emit one token per forward pass. This causes high inference latency, in particular as models are scaled up for quality. In this paper, we introduce Parallel Language Models (PLMs), which generate mutually consistent tokens in one forward pass by routing dependencies through latent auxiliary variables. PLMs are trained using a variational bound that reduces to an autoregressive loss plus a parallel decoding loss. Empirically, PLMs are on a faster and better Pareto frontier than autoregressive and discrete diffusion baselines. Pretrained PLMs achieve near-autoregressive pretraining loss on model scales of 80M to 3B parameters, and speedup follows a power law in model size. When post-trained, our 1.3B model matches or exceeds an identically trained autoregressive model on math, coding, and instruction-following benchmarks, speeding up inference $2.3\text{-}5.7\times$. Together, we show that parallel generation can be trained from a single training objective at autoregressive quality. We will make our code available at https://github.com/mandt-lab/plm.
papers.summary: Autoregressive language models emit one token per forward pass, which makes inference slow, especially for large models. `Parallel Language Models (PLMs)` generate several mutually consistent tokens in a single forward pass by routing dependencies between them through latent auxiliary variables. They are trained with a variational bound that reduces to an autoregressive loss plus a parallel decoding loss. Pretrained `PLMs` from 80M to 3B parameters come close to autoregressive pretraining loss, and their speedup grows as a power law with model size. After post-training, a 1.3B `PLM` matches or exceeds an identically trained autoregressive model on math, coding and instruction-following benchmarks while **decoding 2.3–5.7× faster**.

papers.title: Hierarchical Token Merging with Recursive Autoencoders for Unsupervised Grammar Induction
papers.abstract: Hierarchical abstraction is a fundamental principle across many data modalities, enabling complex sequences to be represented compositionally at multiple levels. Learning such hierarchies directly from data, without explicit structural supervision, remains a central challenge in representation learning. We investigate whether meaningful hierarchical structure can emerge from compression alone. While autoencoders learn compressed representations through reconstruction, this objective does not necessarily favour meaningful compositional structure. We study this challenge through unsupervised grammar induction, where the underlying hierarchy can be evaluated explicitly. We introduce a hierarchical token-merging autoencoder that recursively combines adjacent tokens into increasingly abstract representations, compressing entire sequences through a variational information bottleneck. The model jointly learns representations and hierarchical structure by marginalising over possible binary trees using dynamic programming. To address training instability, we combine independently trained models through unsupervised consensus and distillation. Experiments on a synthetic, ambiguous grammar demonstrate the emergence of meaningful hierarchical structure without structural supervision. The resulting model achieves 93% grammatical parse-validity and 93% exact reconstruction on held-out sequences, compared with 42% parse-validity for the strongest trivial baseline. These findings establish a proof of concept for hierarchical token merging as a mechanism for unsupervised structure discovery and abstraction learning.
papers.summary: The authors ask whether meaningful hierarchical structure can emerge from compression alone, and use unsupervised grammar induction as a setting where the learned hierarchy can be checked directly. Their hierarchical token-merging autoencoder recursively combines adjacent tokens into more abstract representations and compresses whole sequences through a variational information bottleneck. It marginalises over binary trees with dynamic programming, and it addresses training instability by combining independently trained models through unsupervised consensus and distillation. On a synthetic, ambiguous grammar, the model reaches **93% grammatical parse-validity** and 93% exact reconstruction on held-out sequences, compared with 42% parse-validity for the strongest trivial baseline.

papers.title: GeoSplit: Selective Edge--Server Map Acquisition for Cross-User Travel-Mode Recognition
papers.abstract: Networked mobility sensing couples local trajectory inference with remote geospatial context, making communication decisions part of the prediction system. We present GeoSplit, an edge--server framework for travel-mode recognition that separates the utility of map evidence, its training-time transfer, and its selective acquisition at runtime. On GeoLife with 10% labels, we evaluate these components under user-day and user-disjoint grouping. For unseen users, aligned full-map context raises macro-F1 from 0.7154 to 0.7864, while map-informed distillation yields a motion-only student at 0.7225. Through a compact query interface, entropy gating achieves 0.7729 macro-F1 versus 0.7738 for all queries, querying 39.5% of trajectories and reducing application payload by 60.5%. Under user-day grouping, selective and all-query scores are similarly close at a 21.6% query rate. Learned value estimation and probability fusion offer no consistent improvement. These results illustrate communication-efficient edge--server inference for an intelligent transportation sensing task.
papers.summary: `GeoSplit` is an edge–server framework for recognising travel mode from trajectories. It treats three things separately: how useful remote map context is, how that context can be transferred during training, and when the device should query the server for it at runtime. On `GeoLife` with 10% labels and users not seen during training, full map context raises macro-F1 from 0.7154 to 0.7864, and map-informed distillation produces a motion-only student that scores 0.7225. With entropy gating, **querying only 39.5% of trajectories gives 0.7729 macro-F1, against 0.7738 when every trajectory is queried, and cuts application payload by 60.5%**. Learned value estimation and probability fusion bring no consistent improvement.

papers.title: Doubly Robust Learning of Heterogeneous Survival Treatment Effects under Time-Varying Treatments
papers.abstract: Estimating heterogeneous survival treatment effects (HSTEs) from time-to-event data under time-varying treatments is important in fields such as medicine (e.g., to decide which sequence of treatments is better in terms of survival probability). However, this task is challenging because treatment decisions, patient characteristics, and censoring probability often evolve together, requiring sequential adjustment for both treatments and censoring. Existing survival learners mostly consider a single baseline treatment assignment, while longitudinal treatment-effect learners typically assume uncensored outcomes. In this paper, we introduce a novel doubly robust learner for heterogeneous survival treatment effects under time-varying treatments and history-dependent censoring. Our framework separates the intervention window from the survival horizon, with treatment prescribed for a finite period, after which care follows its natural course. We further establish the favorable theoretical properties of Neyman-orthogonality, rate double robustness and quasi-oracle efficiency. The framework accommodates flexible machine learning models for nuisance estimation and treatment-effect regression. We evaluate our learners through several numerical experiments, demonstrating their effectiveness.
papers.summary: Estimating heterogeneous survival treatment effects (HSTEs) under time-varying treatments is hard because treatment decisions, patient characteristics and censoring evolve together. Existing survival learners mostly handle a single baseline treatment, while longitudinal treatment-effect learners usually assume there is no censoring. The authors propose a **doubly robust learner for time-varying treatments with history-dependent censoring**. It separates a finite intervention window from the longer survival horizon and lets any flexible machine-learning model estimate the nuisance quantities. They prove Neyman-orthogonality, rate double robustness and quasi-oracle efficiency, and show that the learner works well in numerical experiments.

papers.title: HoloCosm: Beyond Single-Metric Benchmark Compression Across Multiple Metrics
papers.abstract: Benchmark compression reduces evaluation cost by selecting a small set of samples. Existing methods typically guide selection using a single metric, although benchmarks often assess models along multiple dimensions. We find that model rankings are often weakly correlated across metrics, indicating that different metrics capture distinct aspects of model performance. Samples selected for one metric do not reliably preserve scores and rankings on others when used for compressed evaluation. At 80\% compression, each of the five single-metric baselines yields higher reconstruction error than equal-size random sampling in over 70\% of cross-metric comparisons. To address this challenge, we present HoloCosm, which jointly minimizes normalized score-reconstruction error across source models and metrics while constraining ranking distortion. We evaluate HoloCosm across multiple compression rates on 15 language, multimodal, VLA, and agent benchmark configurations with 85 component metrics. With 80\% compression, HoloCosm outperforms Random, the strongest baseline overall: average NMAE drops by 35.3\% to 0.236, worst-component NMAE drops by 39.5\% to 0.330, and average Spearman correlation rises from 0.884 to 0.915. In addition, HoloCosm remains competitive with existing baselines in single-metric evaluation. We will release our code and experimental results.
papers.summary: Benchmark compression cuts evaluation cost by scoring models on a small subset of samples, but existing methods choose that subset using a single metric. Model rankings are often only weakly correlated across metrics, and at 80% compression, five single-metric selection methods each do worse than equal-size random sampling in over 70% of cross-metric comparisons. `HoloCosm` chooses samples by jointly minimising normalised score-reconstruction error across source models and metrics, subject to a limit on ranking distortion. Across 15 language, multimodal, vision-language-action and agent benchmark configurations with 85 component metrics, at 80% compression it **reduces average normalised mean absolute error by 35.3% compared with random sampling**, the strongest baseline, and raises average Spearman correlation from 0.884 to 0.915.

papers.title: Deep Pontryagin Learning for Continuous-Time Stochastic Control with Jumps
papers.abstract: We develop a deep Pontryagin learning framework for high-dimensional continuous-time stochastic control problems that naturally accommodates jump-diffusions. In contrast to direct policy optimization, which repeatedly differentiates the objective through the entire time-discretized dynamics, our method separates adjoint learning from policy improvement by explicitly incorporating state-sensitivity information from the Pontryagin stochastic maximum principle. For a fixed Markov control, we first compute pathwise adjoint labels by backpropagating the reward through time along simulated state trajectories, and project these labels onto the Markov state through a supervised regression step. The control is then updated by enforcing the pointwise Hamiltonian stationarity condition. We prove that the resulting projected adjoint process satisfies a discrete-time Pontryagin principle and converges, as the time step tends to zero, to the solution of the corresponding continuous-time adjoint backward stochastic differential equation. Numerical experiments illustrate the accuracy, stability, and scalability of the approach.
papers.summary: The framework targets high-dimensional continuous-time stochastic control problems, including those with jump-diffusions. Direct policy optimization differentiates through the entire time-discretized dynamics; this method instead uses the Pontryagin stochastic maximum principle to separate learning the adjoint (state-sensitivity) process from improving the policy. Pathwise adjoint labels are obtained by backpropagating reward along simulated trajectories, projected onto the state by regression, and then used to update the control through the Hamiltonian stationarity condition. The authors **prove that the projected adjoint satisfies a discrete-time Pontryagin principle and converges to the continuous-time adjoint backward stochastic differential equation as the time step shrinks**, and their experiments show accuracy, stability and scalability.

papers.title: Copying Under Repetition: From Prefix Matching to Position Hashing
papers.abstract: Frontier LLMs can copy random text almost flawlessly, yet they often overrun or truncate long blocks of repeated characters. In repeated strings, matching local content no longer reliably identifies where copying should continue or when it should stop. Nevertheless, we show that a two-layer transformer with $O(\log\log N)$-bit precision and $O(\log N/\log\log N)$ width can copy every string up to a chosen design horizon $N$ and terminate correctly under arbitrary repetition. We use RoPE-style rotations of attention values and outputs (VO-rotations) with small prime periods to encode distances from delimiter anchors modulo those primes. By the Chinese Remainder Theorem, these periodic encodings jointly distinguish all required distances, allowing one retrieval rule to select either the next source token or the end marker. In contrast, we prove a width-independent impossibility result for copying under sequential finite-precision softmax accumulation. It applies to transformers whose only positional input is an additive attention bias that eventually becomes constant, including NoPE and a recursive implementation of ALiBi. Once an identical-token run exceeds the resulting saturation threshold, further repetitions leave the logits unchanged. If this threshold grows sublinearly with $N$, these models cannot both complete a long all-identical copy and stop correctly, a pattern resembling the termination errors of frontier LLMs. In synthetic copying experiments, baseline transformer models fail on long repeated strings even within the training range. Trained VO models, by contrast, generalize beyond the training lengths with near-perfect accuracy up to length $\approx 5005$, the selected primes' period product.
papers.summary: Frontier LLMs copy random text almost perfectly but often overrun or truncate long runs of repeated characters, because matching local content no longer shows where copying should continue or stop. The authors build a two-layer transformer that copies every string up to a chosen length and terminates correctly, using RoPE-style rotations of attention values and outputs (`VO-rotations`) with small prime periods. By the Chinese Remainder Theorem, these periodic encodings together distinguish every required distance from a delimiter. They also prove a width-independent impossibility result for models whose only positional signal is an additive attention bias that eventually becomes constant, such as `NoPE` and a recursive `ALiBi`: once a run of identical tokens is long enough, further repetitions leave the logits unchanged. In experiments, standard transformers fail on long repeats even within the training range, while **trained `VO` models generalise beyond the training lengths with near-perfect accuracy up to length ≈5005**.

papers.title: Injection of Space Radiation Errors on Low-power NVM using Generative Deep Learning
papers.abstract: We develop an error model for a Non-Volatile Memory (NVM) device that represents the effects of physical faults experienced in a CubeSat mission in Low Earth Orbit (LEO). The CubeSat carries an off-the-shelf low-power Ferroelectric RAM (FRAM) chip and runs repeated read/write tests according to a predefined pattern. We compare every memory snapshot received from the satellite with a reference bitmap to identify bit errors. We visually analyze erroneous values distributions in the memory snapshots and we understand that they are frequently distributed according to regular spatial patterns. We define a generative deep learning technique to automatically learn these spatial patterns and to synthetically generate additional error patterns mimicking the observed ones. The model is capable at producing memory errors for general application-level experimentation. Our preliminary validation indicates that when comparing the model output with the data we collect, 0.92 of the generated bit flips correspond to bit flips in the memory snapshots and the model captures 0.91 of the observed bit flips. A comparison of the spatial distribution of bit flips in 10,000 generated error patterns also provides a Wasserstein distance of 0.073, indicating that the two distributions differ by roughly 7% of the maximum possible displacement of their probability masses.
papers.summary: The authors model radiation-induced bit errors in an off-the-shelf low-power Ferroelectric RAM (FRAM) chip flown on a CubeSat in Low Earth Orbit. They compare memory snapshots sent down from the satellite against a reference bitmap and find that errors often follow regular spatial patterns. They then train a generative deep learning model to produce synthetic error patterns for application-level fault-injection experiments. **0.92 of the generated bit flips match real ones**, the model captures 0.91 of the observed flips, and across 10,000 generated patterns the spatial distribution is within a Wasserstein distance of 0.073 of the observed data.

papers.title: EpiLens: Lightweight RAG for Epidemiological Knowledge Acquisition
papers.abstract: To prepare for future outbreaks, researchers need to know what studies have been done and what data they use. Mapping a large literature by hand is slow, while large language models alone can misstate or conflate sources. We present EpiLens, a lightweight, open-source retrieval-augmented generation package that applies a fixed retrieval template and output schema to every paper in a corpus and links outputs to source passages. We build a corpus of 2,297 papers from the sources of a multi-pathogen parameter study and evaluate EpiLens's paper-classification workflow against 214 manually labelled papers. Without task-specific training data, the classifier matches or exceeds the tested supervised and zero-shot baselines across four tasks. The study's early extraction sheets cite published sources for 327 estimates. We link each estimate to a cited document or to corpus studies included by a review. Then, we use the classifier's labels to compare the papers associated with different parameters and pathogens. EpiLens labels more papers linked to reproduction numbers than fatality risks as model-based (54% versus 22%, compared with 62% versus 24% in the manual labels). The gap is consistent with the frequent use of transmission models to estimate reproduction numbers and persists within each of five pathogens compared. Beyond the contrast between parameters, the model-based share of papers linked to incubation-period estimates differs by pathogen: 55% for SARS-CoV-2 versus 6% for mpox.
papers.summary: `EpiLens` is a lightweight, open-source retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) package for mapping epidemiological literature. It applies the same retrieval template and output schema to every paper in a corpus and links each output to the source passages it came from. On a 2,297-paper corpus from a multi-pathogen parameter study, the classifier, trained without task-specific data, **matches or exceeds the supervised and zero-shot baselines tested on all four tasks** when checked against 214 hand-labelled papers. Its labels reproduce trends found in the manual labels: papers linked to reproduction numbers are more often model-based than those linked to fatality risks, and the model-based share of incubation-period papers differs sharply between `SARS-CoV-2` and mpox.

papers.title: Cross-Fitting for Neural Posterior Estimation
papers.abstract: Neural Posterior Estimation (NPE) fits an amortized conditional density estimator to a simulated training set of complete-data realizations. NPE's training objective, log-likelihood, favors posterior approximations that assign arbitrarily high density to the training points, and typical families of amortized conditional density estimators (e.g., normalizing flows, Gaussian encoders) are flexible enough to oblige. The resulting policy of extreme overconfidence translates poorly to held-out data. Early stopping and other regularizers can prevent this degeneracy, but they are limited to selecting posterior approximations along an unfavorable optimization trajectory set by in-sample residuals, where the posterior mean is underfit while the posterior variance is overfit. To avoid this trade-off, we propose Cross-Fitting NPE (CF-NPE), which uses sample splitting to separate conditional-mean estimation from the estimation of the posterior's higher moments. Using $K$-fold cross-fitting, CF-NPE fits $K$ posterior-mean regressors and then fits a conditional density estimator to the resulting out-of-fold residuals. In experiments with synthetic data and in a cosmological application, CF-NPE achieves higher held-out log-likelihood than standard NPE and typically improves calibration. CF-NPE is most useful in high-dimensional, simulation-limited settings.
papers.summary: Neural Posterior Estimation (NPE) trains an amortized conditional density estimator by maximising likelihood on simulated data. Flexible estimators can respond by placing arbitrarily high density on the training points, which makes them badly overconfident on held-out data, and early stopping only trades an underfit posterior mean against an overfit posterior variance. `Cross-Fitting NPE (CF-NPE)` uses K-fold sample splitting: it fits K posterior-mean regressors and then fits a conditional density estimator to the out-of-fold residuals. On synthetic data and a cosmology application, **`CF-NPE` achieves higher held-out log-likelihood than standard NPE** and usually improves calibration, with the largest benefit in high-dimensional settings with few simulations.

papers.title: CAVA: Complementary-Label-Aware Data Valuation
papers.abstract: Complementary-label learning (CLL) trains a classifier from labels that name a class an instance does not belong to. Such labels are cheap to collect from crowdworkers or vision-language models (VLMs), making them attractive for large-scale annotation. However, both sources can mistakenly assign the true class as the complementary label. Such annotation errors are particularly harmful in CLL because the model is explicitly trained to suppress the correct answer. Optimal transport (OT) data valuation identifies harmful samples by comparing training data with a clean validation set, but transferring it directly to CLL creates a semantic mismatch: label $c$ means not class $c$ in the training but class $c$ in the validation. We show that this makes the OT label groups noisy mixtures whose behavior depends on the noise rate. The transferred score is informative only at sufficiently high noise, becomes uninformative at the crossover rate $1/M$ for $M$ classes, and reverses below it, where practical CLL annotation typically operates. We propose CAVA, which introduces a complementary label cost and a label margin that isolates the contribution of each complementary label to the transport potential. The margin keeps a consistent direction across noise rates, detects diagonal noise with a parameter-free threshold of closed-form precision, and allows detected samples to be recycled as ordinary-label supervision. On synthetic and human-annotated benchmarks, CAVA separates diagonal noise almost perfectly where directly transferred OT valuation performs worse than random. With only a fraction of the clean validation data, it also improves every CLL objective we evaluate, showing that OT-based valuation becomes reliable once the semantics of complementary supervision are modeled explicitly.
papers.summary: Complementary-label learning (CLL) trains classifiers from labels that name a class an instance does not belong to. These labels are cheap to collect from crowdworkers or vision-language models, but they become harmful when the annotator mistakenly names the true class. The authors show that directly reusing optimal-transport data valuation for CLL is informative only at high noise, becomes uninformative at a noise rate of 1/M for M classes, and reverses below that rate, which is where practical annotation usually operates. `CAVA` adds a complementary-label cost and a label margin that detects these errors with a parameter-free threshold and lets the detected samples be reused as ordinary labels. On synthetic and human-annotated benchmarks, **`CAVA` separates this noise almost perfectly where the transferred valuation does worse than random**, and it improves every CLL objective evaluated while using only part of the clean validation set.

papers.title: Polar Switch: Fast Muon Orthogonalization with Polynomial Circuits
papers.abstract: Muon, a 2024-born optimizer for language models, differs from the 2015-born spectral gradient descent mainly in its fast, GPU-friendly Newton--Schulz polynomial for orthogonalizing the gradient matrix. Accordingly, a line of research proposes faster polynomial iterations for gradient orthogonalization, such as Polar Express and Gram Newton--Schulz, both built on quintic polynomials. In this paper, we introduce Polar Switch, a new approach to polynomial gradient orthogonalization. Using simple polynomial circuits, Polar Switch reaches a given high polynomial degree at a lower FLOP cost than quintic iterations. We define a circuit as a short sequence of symmetric matrix products on a few square buffers, and circuits with $k$ products form a restricted family of odd polynomials of degree up to $2^{k+1}+1$. We choose the sequence of products in each circuit, their coefficients, and how the circuits are composed by numerically minimizing a worst-case bound on the polar approximation error. This minimization is subject to a FLOP budget that accounts for symmetric matrix multiplication kernels and a rounding constraint for numerical stability in half precision. Our two recommended Polar Switch methods have 15.5--18.7\% lower runtime than Polar Express on square matrices and 8.6--16.2\% lower runtime than Gram Newton--Schulz on rectangular matrices with aspect ratios 3.25, 3.5, and 8, with comparable approximation accuracy. In pretraining Modded-NanoGPT \#91, Qwen3-0.6B, and Gemma 3-1B, Polar Switch reaches final validation losses similar to those of established orthogonalization methods. Across the more than 14 million matrices that each of the two recommended methods orthogonalized in these runs, the estimated output spectral norms never exceed the designed bounds by more than 3\%, demonstrating their numerical stability.
papers.summary: The `Muon` optimizer orthogonalizes gradient matrices with fast polynomial iterations, and recent methods such as `Polar Express` and `Gram Newton–Schulz` use quintic polynomials for this. `Polar Switch` instead builds short circuits of symmetric matrix products that reach high polynomial degree with fewer FLOPs. Its coefficients and composition come from numerically minimising a worst-case polar-approximation error under a FLOP budget and a rounding constraint for half-precision stability. The two recommended variants run **15.5–18.7% faster than `Polar Express` on square matrices** and 8.6–16.2% faster than `Gram Newton–Schulz` on rectangular ones, with comparable accuracy. In pretraining `Modded-NanoGPT`, `Qwen3-0.6B` and `Gemma 3-1B`, they reach similar final validation losses and stay stable across more than 14 million orthogonalized matrices.

papers.title: recAMPLIFY: Large-Scale Pretraining of Recursive Protein Language Models
papers.abstract: Protein language models (pLMs) are powerful tools for protein annotation and mutation-effect prediction, but progress has largely depended on scaling model size and data, making them expensive and prone to memorization. Test-time scaling offers a complementary path, but methods developed for autoregressive LLMs do not transfer directly: masked encoders lack a generation loop, and amino acids do not verbalize in a reasoning language. Instead, we adapt recursive pretraining to masked pLMs, where a weight-tied Transformer core refines residue-aligned hidden states over an adjustable number of cycles. We instantiate this recipe as recAMPLIFY, a pLM with 155M unique parameters trained on the same 2T tokens as AMPLIFY-350M. Despite 56% fewer parameters, it improves CASP contact recovery and three out of four supervised tasks, notably raising fold accuracy by 22.5%. Because optimal depth for recAMPLIFY varies across tasks and assays, we then introduce Gated Mixture Recurrence (GMR), a framework that decodes each protein from a probability-weighted mixture of hidden states visited during recursion. GMR employs a learned residual gate at scalar, low-rank, or per-dimension resolution to control how much of each cycle's proposed update is accepted into the state. This unifies halting and gating into a single adaptive computation objective while recovering PonderNet-style halting as a special case without gates. Layered on top of recAMPLIFY, GMR further reduces expected layer depth by up to 37%, although the accuracy trade-off varies by task. Mechanistic analyses show that residual gating controls recurrence stability beyond the trained depth and that halt depth tracks biological properties.
papers.summary: Protein language models (pLMs) have improved mostly through scaling model size and data, and test-time scaling methods from autoregressive LLMs do not carry over to masked encoders. `recAMPLIFY` applies recursive pretraining to masked pLMs: a weight-tied Transformer core refines residue-aligned hidden states over an adjustable number of cycles. It has 155M unique parameters and is trained on the same 2T tokens as `AMPLIFY-350M`. Despite 56% fewer parameters, it improves CASP contact recovery and three of four supervised tasks, **raising fold accuracy by 22.5%**. A gated mixture-recurrence scheme (`GMR`) that adaptively weights the states visited during recursion further cuts expected depth by up to 37%, though the accuracy trade-off varies by task.

papers.title: Gradient descent reaches arbitrary accuracy in a fixed number of large steps on multiclass logistic regression
papers.abstract:
We show that gradient descent (GD) with step size $\eta$ can achieve $\varepsilon$ optimality gap on the multiclass logistic regression loss in a number of iterations $T$ that is independent of $\varepsilon$. To do so, the step size $\eta$ must be chosen large enough as a function of $\varepsilon$ (and properties of the linearly separable dataset), while $T$ is a constant that only depends on the data. The relevant properties of the data include the number of points and their margin (for $T$), and one additional quantity (for $\eta$) that turns out to be necessary in dimension $d \geq 3$. The proofs build on the known fact that, as $\eta \to \infty$, suitably rescaled GD becomes the perceptron algorithm, and the latter finds a perfect classifier in $T$ iterations. A similar claim was shown for two classes in dimension $d = 2$ using other proof techniques.
  This result adds to previous works that showed GD on the logistic regression loss can be accelerated by taking large step sizes. Those provoke a wild, oscillatory initial phase, followed by a stable phase. We provide results of this (qualitatively different) nature, too.
papers.summary: The authors prove that on linearly separable data, **gradient descent can reach any target optimality gap on multiclass logistic regression in a fixed number of iterations that does not depend on the target accuracy**, provided the step size is large enough. The iteration count depends only on the number of data points and the margin, while the required step size also depends on one more data property, which they show is necessary in three or more dimensions. The proof uses the fact that, as the step size goes to infinity, suitably rescaled gradient descent becomes the perceptron algorithm, which finds a perfect classifier in a bounded number of steps. This extends a previous result for two classes in two dimensions. The authors also give results for the regime in which large steps cause an oscillatory initial phase followed by a stable phase.

papers.title: Trajectory Replay: Continuous-Time Mixture Transport for Lifelong Generative Models
papers.abstract: Adapting pre-trained continuous-time generative models to sequentially incoming data without forgetting earlier tasks is a central challenge in lifelong learning. A leading strategy, generative replay, uses a generative model trained on historical tasks to augment its own continual update with synthetic samples from experience. However, it requires full trajectory simulations at every training step, which accumulate discretization errors and can degrade the replayed historical distribution. Here, we propose trajectory replay, which bypasses sample generation by training an updated velocity field to match both a frozen historical velocity along its trajectories and the incoming task's velocity field, weighted by a stability-plasticity coefficient. Through the lens of continuous-time transport, we show the resulting optimum averages the two task velocities by their respective densities and generates the mixture of their probability paths. Combined with mean velocity distillation, trajectory replay accesses historical trajectories using only a few network evaluations per continual update. Empirically, it outperforms generative replay and distillation baselines on class-incremental image generation. In two biological case studies, trajectory replay extends generative perturbation models to new contexts and experimental batches across two data modalities while preserving treatment-effect prediction.
papers.summary: Lifelong generative models must learn new tasks without forgetting earlier ones. Generative replay does this by sampling synthetic data from earlier tasks, which requires full trajectory simulations at every training step and accumulates discretization error. Trajectory replay skips sampling: it trains the updated velocity field to match a frozen historical velocity field along its trajectories and the new task's velocity field, with a coefficient that balances stability against plasticity. The authors show that the optimum **produces the mixture of the two tasks' probability paths**, and mean velocity distillation reduces each update to a few network evaluations. The method beats generative-replay and distillation baselines on class-incremental image generation and, in two biological case studies, extends perturbation models to new contexts while preserving treatment-effect prediction.

papers.title: TokenGate: Adapting LLMs for Fast and Memory-Efficient Prefill with Learned Token Pruning
papers.abstract: Expert human readers process large inputs (e.g., code repositories and long documents) by skimming to closely read only what matters. On the other hand, language models process all input tokens through each model layer, resulting in significant processing costs for long-context inputs. We introduce TokenGate, a small, drop-in component that extends existing trained models to enable end-to-end learnable token pruning over long-context inputs for fast and memory-efficient prefill. To enable end-to-end learning despite the non-differentiable top-K operator for token pruning, we introduce token-gated attention, a mechanism inspired by Mixture-of-Experts that re-weights attention logits using token importance scores. Across diverse tasks, TokenGate achieves $1.4$-$11.3\times$ faster time-to-first token (TTFT) and $1.5$-$3.4\times$ lower peak memory at no accuracy degradation for prefill in transformers. Compared to the best-performing prior methods for token-pruning, TokenGate gives up to $6.4\times$ faster prefill and $2\times$ lower peak memory. TokenGate natively extends both standard transformers (e.g., Qwen3) and hybrid-attention models (e.g., Qwen3.5) with simple lightweight adaptation comparable to standard parameter-efficient fine-tuning. We make our code available at: https://github.com/tokengate-models/TokenGate.
papers.summary: Language models run every input token through every layer, so the prefill stage of long-context inputs such as code repositories is slow and uses a lot of memory. `TokenGate` is a small drop-in component that adds end-to-end learnable token pruning to existing trained models. To make top-K pruning trainable, it uses token-gated attention, a mechanism inspired by Mixture-of-Experts that re-weights attention logits by learned token-importance scores. Across diverse tasks it delivers **1.4–11.3× faster time-to-first-token and 1.5–3.4× lower peak memory with no loss in accuracy**, and up to 6.4× faster prefill than the best previous token-pruning methods. It extends both standard transformers such as `Qwen3` and hybrid-attention models such as `Qwen3.5`, with adaptation cost comparable to parameter-efficient fine-tuning.

papers.title: Simulation Priors for Rapid Adaptation in Model-Based RL for Autonomous Racing
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning enables learning high-performance control policies, but its reliance on extensive interaction limits deployment on physical systems where data collection is costly, and failures are unsafe. We introduce Prior-Informed Adaptation (PIA), an offline-to-online model-based RL framework that uses structured simulation priors for rapid adaptation. PIA pretrains a world model on heterogeneous low- and high-fidelity simulated trajectories, then adapts it with limited target-domain interaction using uncertainty-regularized planning. Rather than requiring an accurate simulator for policy transfer, PIA treats simulated trajectories as biased priors whose residual mismatch is corrected during online adaptation. We evaluate PIA in autonomous racing using high-fidelity simulation and on a real full-size autonomous race car. In simulation, PIA adapts faster across track and surface shifts than strong baselines, achieving lower lap times and fewer failures. On hardware, PIA achieves reliable few-shot adaptation with less than one hour of on-vehicle interaction.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning on physical systems is held back by how much costly and potentially unsafe real-world interaction it needs. `Prior-Informed Adaptation` (`PIA`) is a model-based framework that first trains a world model offline on a mix of low- and high-fidelity simulated trajectories. It then adapts online with limited target-domain data, using uncertainty-regularized planning. The simulator data is treated as a biased prior whose mismatch is corrected during adaptation, so an accurate simulator is not required. In high-fidelity racing simulation, `PIA` adapts faster than strong baselines across track and surface changes, and on a real full-size autonomous race car it achieves reliable few-shot adaptation with **less than one hour of on-vehicle interaction**.

papers.title: HarnessPro: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement with Pareto Optimization for Performance-Cost Trade-offs
papers.abstract: Harness development plays a crucial role in building capable AI agents. Recent approaches improve harnesses through recursive self-improvement (RSI), but their performance gains often come with higher execution costs. We introduce HarnessPro, a label-free method for evolving harnesses to improve task performance while reducing execution cost. In this setting, candidate harnesses are evaluated using LLM-generated tests without access to ground-truth solutions or official tests. Specialized agents diagnose execution trajectories, plan updates with different performance-cost priorities, and implement them as candidate harnesses. Rather than returning a single harness, HarnessPro uses normalized weighted squared-distance selection to provide cost-focused (lite), balanced (medium), and performance-focused (heavy) harnesses for different deployment budgets. Selected harnesses enter the next iteration, where execution feedback guides further updates. Our experiments cover Terminal-Bench 2, SWE-Bench Pro, and ProgramBench, using GPT-5.5 with Codex and GLM-5.2 with Claude Code. Across these benchmarks using GPT-5.5 with Codex, the heavy mode of HarnessPro achieves an average pass-rate gain of 2.0 percentage points and an average per-task cost reduction of 26.1% relative to RHO. This advantage also holds when using GLM-5.2 with Claude Code. Code is available at https://github.com/pzs19/HarnessPro
papers.summary: Recursive self-improvement of agent harnesses (the scaffolding around a model that runs tools and manages the task) tends to raise performance at the price of higher execution cost. `HarnessPro` evolves harnesses without labels, scoring candidates on LLM-generated tests. Specialized agents diagnose execution trajectories, plan updates with different performance-cost priorities, and implement them. Each iteration returns lite, medium, and heavy harnesses for different budgets, chosen by normalized weighted squared-distance selection. On `Terminal-Bench 2`, `SWE-Bench Pro`, and `ProgramBench` with `GPT-5.5` and `Codex`, the heavy mode gains 2.0 percentage points in average pass rate while **cutting per-task cost by 26.1%** relative to `RHO`, and the advantage also holds with `GLM-5.2` and `Claude Code`.

papers.title: Monsoon: Scalable Spontaneous Speech Collection for Low-Resource ASR in 50 Languages
papers.abstract: For most languages, automatic speech recognition (ASR) is limited less by model architecture than by a lack of accurately transcribed spontaneous speech. We present Monsoon, a framework for collecting such data at scale. It elicits unscripted conversations between paired contributors, screens recordings with automated classifiers, corrects transcripts over five levels of human review, and selects segments for lexical and acoustic coverage. It has collected speech in 50 languages; we analyse seven 3,500-hour corpora. At equal volume, its quality stages reduce semantic word error rate (WER) by 10-39% relative to a conventional protocol. Compared with an architecture-matched baseline trained on public corpora, Whisper fine-tuned on Monsoon performs comparably on the baseline's own test sets and reduces semantic WER by 20-44 points on conversational benchmarks. The gains transfer to a second architecture and grow with data volume. We release the framework, its quality-control models, and the fine-tuned models.
papers.summary: For most languages, automatic speech recognition (ASR) is limited mainly by a shortage of accurately transcribed spontaneous speech, not by model architecture. `Monsoon` is a data-collection framework that records unscripted conversations between paired contributors, filters recordings with automated classifiers, corrects transcripts over five levels of human review, and selects segments for lexical and acoustic coverage. It has gathered speech in 50 languages, and the authors analyze seven 3,500-hour corpora. At equal data volume, the quality stages lower semantic word error rate (WER) by 10-39% relative to a conventional protocol. `Whisper` fine-tuned on `Monsoon` matches a public-corpus baseline on that baseline's own test sets and **reduces semantic WER by 20-44 points on conversational benchmarks**.

papers.title: Topological Sheaves of Irreducibility: A Theoretical Framework for Multi-Agent Task Obstructions
papers.abstract: Multi-agent systems can differ under identical agents and communication budgets when they support different forms of joint interaction. We introduce Topological Sheaves of Irreducibility (TSI), a sheaf-theoretic framework separating task-level compatibility obstructions from system capability. A task is represented by an interaction complex $K$ and a capacity sheaf $\mathcal{F}$; nonzero $H^n(K;\mathcal{F})$ defines a structural signature, while registered interventions test capability. For cocycle data, cochain realization is solvable exactly when the represented cohomology class vanishes. Examples show that the signature is sheaf-relative, and the degree-1 reduction yields cycle-space witnesses and observation requirements. We evaluate two finite one-round models. Across 15,625 degree-1 inputs, an all-agent additive primitive solves decision and repair exactly; the optimal pairwise system reaches 88.80% on decision, one input above the 88.79% majority-class baseline, and 26.63% on repair. On a degree-2 tetrahedral-boundary task over 531,441 inputs, the same-2-skeleton system retains all four three-agent primitives yet matches the pairwise-only optimum throughout the registered separation window, whereas adding the class-filling four-agent primitive makes both tasks exact. Status-preserving robustness checks retain exact performance but are not cost-matched to the class-restoring ablation. Conditional on the registered primitives and cost models, TSI provides task-relative, falsifiable tests of higher-order interaction.
papers.summary: Multi-agent systems with identical agents and communication budgets can still differ in what they can solve, depending on which forms of joint interaction they support. `Topological Sheaves of Irreducibility` (`TSI`) uses sheaf theory to separate task-level obstructions from system capability. A task is modeled as an interaction complex with a capacity sheaf, where nonzero cohomology marks the need for higher-order interaction. In finite one-round models, pairwise-only systems barely beat a majority-class baseline on degree-1 tasks (88.80% vs 88.79%), whereas **adding the class-filling higher-order primitive makes the tasks solvable exactly**, giving falsifiable tests of when higher-order interaction is required.

papers.title: Game of Phones: Harnessing Game Theory and LLMs in 'Bot Wars' to Counteract Phone Scams
papers.abstract: Phone scams impose substantial and growing costs on individuals and financial systems worldwide, yet existing countermeasures impose no resource cost on perpetrators. Strategic scam-baiting, in which automated agents engage scammers to deplete their operational capacity, offers a proactive alternative but requires dynamic strategy adaptation that static systems cannot provide. We introduce a game-theoretic framework enabling LLMs to learn effective counter-strategies through in-context experience without fine-tuning.
