The framework models scammer-baiter interactions as a two-player game with empirically grounded strategies and utility functions, using Nash equilibrium as a formal benchmark for evaluating learned behaviour. Across 300 simulated dialogues and three LLM architectures, adaptive strategy selection achieves 28.9-79.7% closer alignment to Nash equilibrium than non-adaptive baselines. The code and an annotated dataset of 300 dialogues with turn-level strategy labels and utility scores are released at https://github.com/nardinebasta/GameofPhones_/ .
papers.summary: Existing phone-scam countermeasures cost scammers nothing, so this work studies scam-baiting, where automated agents engage scammers to use up their time and capacity. The framework models scammer-baiter interactions as a two-player game with empirically grounded strategies and utility functions, and uses Nash equilibrium as the yardstick for learned behavior. LLMs learn counter-strategies from in-context experience without fine-tuning. Across 300 simulated dialogues and three LLM architectures, adaptive strategy selection comes **28.9-79.7% closer to Nash equilibrium** than non-adaptive baselines, and the annotated dialogue dataset is released.

papers.title: RESIN: Multi-Chain Reasoning with Entity-Structured Indexing
papers.abstract: Multi-chain reasoning is a challenging task not only because the multi-chain evidence is dispersed, but also because different parts of reasoning may require distinct, interacting chains of support. Flat retrieval can flood a model with loosely related text, whereas early selection of a single reasoning path can discard evidence that becomes useful only after other facts are considered. We introduce RESIN (Reasoning with Entity Structured Indexing), which uses structure to locate evidence while keeping the original source as the basis for reasoning. RESIN decomposes a question into focused one-hop needs, retrieves a small set of source-grounded units for each hop, and places only this relevant evidence in a compact reasoning buffer. The buffer preserves alternative supports until final composition, making intermediate decisions explicit without forcing a brittle path. On the full HolisQA benchmark, RESIN achieves 82.92 context recall and 76.70 answer relevancy over all questions, with higher reported CR and AR across five domains and higher F1 in four domains than the published baselines. Ablations show that both typed evidence diversity and hop-wise decomposition are essential, supporting a clear conclusion: Precise evidence organization and delayed commitment make multi-chain reasoning effective and auditable. Our code is available at https://github.com/RamonMeng/RESIN.
papers.summary: Answering multi-chain questions requires combining scattered evidence across several interacting reasoning chains, which flat retrieval floods with noise and single-path selection can prune too early. `RESIN` (Reasoning with Entity Structured Indexing) splits a question into focused one-hop needs and retrieves a few source-grounded units for each. It keeps alternative supports in a compact reasoning buffer until final composition. On the full `HolisQA` benchmark it reaches **82.92 context recall and 76.70 answer relevancy**, beating published baselines across five domains. Ablations show that typed evidence diversity and hop-wise decomposition are both essential.

papers.title: Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Market Making on Prediction-Market Order Books
papers.abstract: A market maker provides liquidity by quoting prices to buy and sell an asset, earning the spread while managing inventory risk. We study market makers trained with multi-agent reinforcement learning on prediction markets, specifically Polymarket, whose thin order books pose distinct challenges. Three challenges underpin this research: adverse selection may cause a policy trained on real data to stop quoting; the consequences of a quote can arrive many steps after the action; and prediction-market L2 data does not identify individual orders needed for simulation. We address these challenges by reconstructing order-level LOBSTER-format data from Polymarket and training agents in JaxMARL-HFT on 417 real markets. We enrich the baseline market maker's observation space with the book and recent flow, redesign its actions and inventory controls, and propose a cooperative multi-agent decomposition into a quoter and a risk manager trained using recurrent Independent Proximal Policy Optimisation (IPPO) with RNN policies. We investigate reward shaping, particularly reward blending and post-fill markout, to mitigate credit-assignment difficulties between the agents. Our redesigned single-agent market maker quotes more frequently and incurs smaller held-out losses than the retrained JaxMARL-HFT baseline, although the contributions of jointly changed observations, actions and risk constraints are not separately identified. Decomposition alone performs poorly; careful reward design substantially improves the desk relative to the unshaped split and yields our best result. Models are evaluated on realised end-of-episode portfolio value on held-out markets. None establishes positive average portfolio value in periodic held-out evaluation, and each configuration was trained with one seed. The environment, data and protocol lay a foundation for makers that quote many linked markets at once.
papers.summary: Market makers trained with multi-agent reinforcement learning are studied on the thin order books of `Polymarket` prediction markets. The authors reconstruct order-level `LOBSTER`-format data from 417 real markets and train in `JaxMARL-HFT`. They split the market maker into a cooperating quoter and risk manager trained with recurrent Independent Proximal Policy Optimisation (`IPPO`), and use reward blending and post-fill markout to ease credit assignment between the two agents. A redesigned single agent quotes more often and loses less than the retrained baseline, and careful reward shaping makes the decomposed setup the best result. However, **no configuration achieves positive average portfolio value on held-out markets**, and each configuration was trained with a single seed.

papers.title: Training with ML-labeled Data via Stochastic First- and Zeroth-Order Optimization
papers.abstract: Training a machine learning (ML) model is an optimization process that typically requires a set of examples with ground-truth labels beforehand. Obtaining these ground truths usually requires laborious human effort and can be costly. The scalability of human labeling becomes a concern when there are a large number of data points that need to be labeled. To address this practical issue, we consider an optimization setting where a subset of samples has ground-truth labels, while the remaining data points were labeled by an ML predictor, which could potentially assign incorrect labels to those points. We propose both first-order and zeroth-order stochastic optimization methods for training on datasets consisting of a mix of true-labeled and ML-labeled samples. We further conduct comprehensive empirical studies from training a linear regression model to fine-tuning a large language model (LLM) to showcase the effectiveness of the proposed algorithms for training with ML-labeled data.
papers.summary: Human labeling is expensive at scale, so this work studies training on datasets where only a subset has ground-truth labels and the rest is labeled by a possibly inaccurate ML predictor. The authors propose both first-order and zeroth-order stochastic optimization methods designed for this mix of true-labeled and ML-labeled samples. Experiments range from linear regression to **fine-tuning a large language model (LLM)**, and the authors report that the proposed algorithms are effective for training with ML-labeled data.

papers.title: On Data Scaling in Tabular ML: More Data, Better Generalization?
papers.abstract: Recent work in tabular machine learning has emphasized the importance of diverse and realistic evaluation settings. The niche of large-scale (1M+) data, however, remains under-explored. To study training-data scaling, we assemble eight real-world tabular datasets with up to around ten million training examples, retaining the natural distribution shifts of the tasks and using random-split evaluation as a control. We find that GBDTs and MLP-based models show broadly similar scaling trends, with gains from both additional training data and algorithmic improvements. Tabular foundation models show more varied scaling behavior, with recent versions benefiting more consistently from larger contexts even under distribution shift. However, scaling training data under distribution shift introduces new challenges: in-distribution and out-of-distribution performance mostly improve together at smaller scales but can diverge at larger scales. We examine this through MLP capacity sweeps and comparisons of the validation distributions used for tuning and early stopping in MLPs and GBDTs. We also compare common practices of using validation data, contrasting its use for model selection in MLP pipelines with using it for in-context fitting in tabular foundation model pipelines. Under stronger shifts, MLPs selected using validation representative of the evaluation conditions generally maintain or improve performance as training data grows. In contrast, including such examples in context improves foundation-model performance, but does not prevent deterioration with increasing training size in our experiments.
papers.summary: Large-scale tabular learning with more than a million examples is under-explored, so the authors assemble eight real-world datasets with up to about ten million training examples that keep their natural distribution shifts. Gradient-boosted decision trees (`GBDT`s) and MLP-based models scale similarly, while tabular foundation models vary more, with recent versions benefiting more consistently from larger contexts. A key finding is that **in-distribution and out-of-distribution performance improve together at small scales but can diverge at larger scales**. Choosing validation data that matches evaluation conditions helps MLPs keep improving as data grows, but putting such examples in context does not stop foundation-model performance from deteriorating with more training data.

papers.title: Two hidden layer suffice: the caterpillar net
papers.abstract: Every continuous piecewise linear (CPWL) function is a finite signed sum of maxima of affine functions, making maximum representation a central problem in the study of the expressiveness of ReLU networks. A now-disproved conjecture predicted logarithmic depth for maxima. Inspired by the proof by Brunck et al. (2026) that two hidden layers suffice for general CPWL functions, we give the Caterpillar Net, a nonrecursive construction for the maximum of $N$ inputs with two hidden layers of widths $O(N^2)$ and $2^{O(N\log N)}$. The construction has a direct geometric interpretation.
papers.summary: Representing the maximum of many inputs is central to understanding how expressive ReLU networks are, since every continuous piecewise linear (CPWL) function is a signed sum of maxima of affine functions. Building on a recent proof that two hidden layers suffice for general CPWL functions, the authors present the `Caterpillar Net`, a nonrecursive construction with a direct geometric interpretation. It computes **the maximum of N inputs with only two hidden layers**, of widths O(N^2) and 2^{O(N log N)}.

papers.title: Teacher Supervision, Fixed Representations and Calibration: Exact Risk Calculations for Candidate-Scoring Decision Models
papers.abstract: Candidate-scoring decision models return a probability distribution over a presented set of answers. Public documentation of one such system, Jev, and of an open counterpart, JevAny, describes three training ingredients that determine what these probabilities estimate: soft targets from larger models, a frozen pretrained backbone and temperature calibration. We analyze each ingredient in Gaussian surrogates where the finite-sample risk can be computed exactly. A student trained on teacher targets inherits the teacher's bias, which more student data does not remove and agreement with the teacher does not reveal. A fixed representation lowers the risk only below an explicit sample-size threshold. In a probit model the exact recalibration map is a temperature scaling, which removes all excess risk only when the teacher's coefficient has the correct direction and otherwise leaves a residual that calibration diagnostics do not detect. Under Luce's choice axiom, candidate scores are coherent across refinements of an event if and only if they aggregate by log-sum-exp. On 231,521 credit card complaints from the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, where the decision is whether a complaint ends in monetary relief, a student trained on a logistic teacher's probabilities ends at the teacher's decision cost while a student trained on outcomes goes 8% below it, a 30B model read zero-shot remains worse than the teacher after recalibration, and that model departs from the coherence condition by 17.5 decibans. Pretrained representations reduce the labeled data required and calibration corrects the scale of the probabilities, but neither corrects a biased teacher, so the probabilities have to be checked against realized outcomes.
papers.summary: Candidate-scoring decision models such as `Jev` and `JevAny` output a probability distribution over a set of presented answers. They are built from three ingredients: soft targets from larger teacher models, a frozen pretrained backbone, and temperature calibration. Exact finite-sample risk calculations in Gaussian surrogates show that **a student inherits its teacher's bias**, and that neither more data nor calibration removes it. A fixed representation helps only below an explicit sample-size threshold, and candidate scores stay coherent across refinements of an event only if they aggregate by log-sum-exp. On 231,521 `CFPB` credit card complaints, a student trained on actual outcomes beats the teacher-trained student by 8% in decision cost, and a zero-shot 30B model remains worse than the teacher even after recalibration.

papers.title: Learning to Refer: Inference-Time Collaboration in Decentralized Federated Learning
papers.abstract: In decentralized federated learning, heterogeneous clients may develop complementary expertise, yet each query is typically evaluated only by the client where it arrives. To exploit this distributed expertise without global coordination, we formulate inference-time collaboration as budgeted local expert referral, a graph-constrained routing process in which a query can move only between neighboring clients and only visited clients contribute to its final prediction. EdgeDRM implements this framework by learning a density-based routing potential for each client: differences between neighboring potentials provide the comparisons used to select successive referrals, while local task models generate predictions that are aggregated along the resulting route. Both training and inference are decentralized, using only neighbor-local information without a central router or graph-wide client scoring. We establish estimation guarantees for the learned comparisons and characterize how local improvement and graph structure govern prior-weighted density gains from referral. Experiments on benchmark and real-world medical data show that EdgeDRM outperforms graph-matched decentralized baselines in most settings, with the clearest benefits under sparse connectivity.
papers.summary: In decentralized federated learning, clients may develop complementary expertise, but a query is usually answered only by the client where it arrives. `EdgeDRM` frames inference-time collaboration as budgeted expert referral, in which a query can move only between neighboring clients. Each client learns a density-based routing potential, and comparing neighbors' potentials guides each referral. Predictions are aggregated along the route without any central router. The authors give estimation guarantees, and on benchmark and real-world medical data `EdgeDRM` beats graph-matched decentralized baselines in most settings, **with the clearest gains under sparse connectivity**.

papers.title: Scaling Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Brain Encoding
papers.abstract: Brain encoding models aim to predict neural responses to stimuli. The most widely used approach fits readouts from frozen pretrained backbones. Using neural data to train large models from scratch or fully fine-tune them after task-pretraining has proven difficult because neural data is costly and limited. We show that parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) enables us to effectively adapt very large pretrained backbones for brain encoding with a small number of trainable parameters. To make it computationally practical, we exploit the backbone's causal structure to predict multiple timepoints in a single pass instead of using sliding windows, significantly reducing feature-extraction cost. This enables efficient fine-tuning of multimodal backbones with up to 104B parameters, the largest model adapted for brain encoding to our knowledge. Trained with a low-rank adapter (LoRA) and a lightweight readout, our approach consistently improves brain encoding performance across nine diverse multimodal backbones. On the same Qwen3-Omni backbone as the prior state-of-the-art (SoTA), our method BrainLoRA achieves the best published performance on the Algonauts 2025 Challenge. We also show the adapted multimodal backbones remain interpretable: modality attribution recovers the canonical sensory topography that prior work often obtains by construction from separate unimodal encoders, and neural adaptation increases the contribution of audio inputs and cross-modal mixing within the backbone. To scale out the number of adapted models, we develop a multi-LoRA kernel that accelerates joint training of multiple LoRAs on a shared backbone. This enables an ensemble of 200+ adapted models that ranks first on the public Algonauts post-challenge leaderboard at the time of writing. Together, our results highlight PEFT as an efficient and powerful paradigm for brain encoding.
papers.summary: Brain encoding models, which predict neural responses to stimuli, usually fit readouts on frozen backbones because neural data is too scarce for full fine-tuning. `BrainLoRA` applies parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) with low-rank adapters (`LoRA`) and a lightweight readout to multimodal backbones of up to 104B parameters. A causal multi-timepoint prediction trick reduces feature-extraction cost compared with sliding windows. On `Qwen3-Omni`, the same backbone as the prior state of the art, it achieves the best published result on the `Algonauts 2025` Challenge. A multi-LoRA kernel enables an **ensemble of 200+ adapted models that ranks first on the public post-challenge leaderboard**, and the adapted backbones still recover canonical sensory topography.

papers.title: Safety Mid-Training: Internalizing LLM Safety as a Foundational Capability
papers.abstract: Safety alignment for large language models (LLMs) is primarily performed during post-training, while recent work has also begun incorporating safety data into pre-training. Yet safety can degrade when later training no longer includes safety data, and gains in safety often come at the cost of general capability. This tension suggests that safety and general reasoning should not be treated as separate training goals. We instead view safety as an LLM capability that can be learned through a reasoning structure shared with general tasks. Both require the model to understand intent or task goals, apply relevant knowledge, and reason about potential consequences. We introduce safety mid-training, a stage between pre-training and post-training that jointly develops safety and general reasoning through this shared structure. Given safety and utility prompts, the base model generates structured documents and reasoning traces that are then used for mid-training. Safety mid-training reduces average attack success rate (ASR) by 72% to 81% relative to Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B base models, while also improving general capability. The benefits persist through subsequent post-training. After general-only SFT, mid-trained models largely retain their safety, achieving lower ASR than the baselines without sacrificing general capability. They also retain safety under general-only GRPO without safety rewards, while subsequent RL reaches a better safety-utility frontier when initialized from the mid-trained models. Together, these results suggest that learning safety and general reasoning within a shared mid-training stage can reduce the safety-utility trade-off and make safety more robust to subsequent training.
papers.summary: LLM safety alignment done in post-training tends to erode during later training and often costs general capability. Safety mid-training is a stage between pre-training and post-training that treats safety as a reasoning capability sharing structure with general tasks. For it, the base model generates structured documents and reasoning traces from both safety and utility prompts. On `Qwen3` 1.7B, 4B, and 8B base models, this **reduces average attack success rate (ASR) by 72-81% while also improving general capability**. Safety largely survives later general-only supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and `GRPO`, and subsequent RL reaches a better safety-utility frontier when started from mid-trained models.

papers.title: Next Best Action: Causal Constrained Offline RL for Business Action Targeting
papers.abstract: Next Best Action (NBA) systems must select among customer interventions (e.g., discounts, promotions, and lifecycle actions), maximize long-term economic value, satisfy complex operational constraints, and remain causally grounded. Existing approaches lack a rigorous framework for meeting these requirements jointly. We address this gap by formulating NBA as a Constrained Markov Decision Process (CMDP). We then integrate off-policy causal correction of the estimated customer dynamics directly into the Linear Programming (LP) formulation of the CMDP. The resulting policy selects actions based on customer states to maximize long-term value while explicitly enforcing business guardrails. Furthermore, the LP formulation yields shadow prices that quantify the economic trade-offs of operational constraints (e.g., fairness and user welfare), enhancing policy interpretability. We validate our proposed offline Reinforcement Learning (RL) framework on an industry case study involving rideshare coupon targeting, where customer states are defined by Recency, Frequency, and Monetary (RFM) stages. We evaluate performance using model-based off-policy evaluation, with causal dynamics estimated from a temporal holdout. Under the observed coupon budget and RFM state representation, our optimized policy improves customer lifetime value (LTV) by 19% over the estimated behavior policy and 8% over a myopic baseline. Although the demonstrated action space is binary, the proposed framework is action-agnostic, yielding a general-purpose decision module for targeting systems that manage multiple interventions.
papers.summary: Next Best Action (NBA) systems must choose customer interventions such as coupons in ways that maximize long-term value, respect business constraints, and stay causally grounded. The authors formulate NBA as a Constrained Markov Decision Process (CMDP) and build off-policy causal correction of customer dynamics into its linear-programming (LP) formulation. The LP also yields shadow prices that put an economic cost on constraints such as fairness. In a rideshare coupon-targeting case study with Recency, Frequency, and Monetary (RFM) customer states, the optimized policy **improves customer lifetime value by 19%** over the behavior policy and 8% over a myopic baseline, as estimated by model-based off-policy evaluation.

papers.title: ASTOR: Benchmarking and Improving Autoformulation for Soft-Constraint Optimization with a Formal Grammar
papers.abstract: Real-world decision problems combine two qualitatively different kinds of constraints: requirements that must be satisfied, called hard constraints, and preferences that can be violated, called soft constraints. Because these problems are often posed to decision-makers in natural language, large language models offer a natural tool for assisting with their solution. This has given rise to autoformulation, which focuses on using LLMs to translate natural-language descriptions of decision problems into executable mathematical optimization models. However, this research often neglects soft constraints like those proposed by consumers, managers, and planners, despite the fact that many practical problems require modeling them explicitly. We introduce ASTOR, an inference-time framework that maps a natural-language decision problem to a grammar-guided abstract syntax tree (AST) before deterministically compiling the resulting representation into executable optimization code. We also introduce SoftOR, a unified benchmark of natural language problems which focuses on soft constraint formulations. On SoftOR, ASTOR achieves the best aggregate accuracy among comparable single-request and multi-agent LLM methods while remaining competitive on standard autoformulation benchmarks that include only hard constraints. Code and data are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/astor-softor-iclr-E34C/README.md.
papers.summary: Autoformulation uses LLMs to turn natural-language decision problems into executable optimization models, but existing work largely ignores soft constraints, meaning preferences that may be violated. `ASTOR` maps a problem description to a grammar-guided abstract syntax tree (AST) at inference time and then deterministically compiles it into optimization code. The authors also release `SoftOR`, a benchmark focused on soft-constraint formulations. On `SoftOR`, `ASTOR` achieves **the best aggregate accuracy among comparable single-request and multi-agent LLM methods**, while remaining competitive on standard hard-constraint autoformulation benchmarks.

papers.title: AfriBED: a Speech Recognition Bias Evaluation Dataset for Low Resource African Languages
papers.abstract: Despite advancements in automatic speech recognition systems (ASR), current systems exhibit speaker-attribute bias, i.e., their speech recognition performance is biased against certain speakers based on their demographic attributes such as gender, accents, and speaker type. However, accurately assessing speaker attribute bias in a given ASR system requires the availability of a bias evaluation dataset with comparable speech across subgroups of a speaker attribute. In this paper, we introduce African speech Bias Evaluation Dataset (AfriBED), a novel speech recognition bias evaluation dataset for two low resource African languages, Bemba and Nyanja, to detect and estimate gender and speaker-type bias for ASR systems. The dataset comprises 9 hours of speech with 3928 utterances recorded by 80 speakers for Bemba, while the Nyanja set includes 6260 utterances with approximately 18 hours of speech recorded by 127 speakers. The results of our baseline experiments demonstrate that the datasets are useful for examining gender and speaker-type attribute bias in the target languages.
papers.summary: Measuring speaker-attribute bias in automatic speech recognition (ASR) requires comparable speech across demographic subgroups, which barely exists for low-resource languages. `AfriBED` (African speech Bias Evaluation Dataset) provides such data for Bemba (9 hours, 3,928 utterances, 80 speakers) and Nyanja (about 18 hours, 6,260 utterances, 127 speakers). It is designed to detect gender and speaker-type bias. Baseline experiments indicate that **the datasets are useful for examining these biases** in ASR systems for the two languages.

papers.title: SpecMRL: Redesign Matryoshka Representation Learning within Parametric Spectrum
papers.abstract: Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL) is designed to support flexible representation sizes by jointly optimizing nested prefixes. While effective, this design lacks an explicit constraint to ensure that the leading portion provides a suitable compact encoding. To address this, we propose SpecMRL, which reorganizes the feature space to enable more effective prefix readout. Specifically, we extend MRL with a parameter-derived spectral basis organized with feature importance. SpecMRL otherwise follows standard MRL, with prefix readout performed in the learned spectral space. Experiments on MTEB show that SpecMRL outperforms MRL at all evaluated reduced dimensions, with larger gains under more aggressive compression. These results suggest that the learned spectral basis better prioritizes informative directions, enabling more effective representation compression. Notably, SpecMRL extends the performance frontier of MRL, surpassing full-dimensional MRL with only half the embedding dimensions.
papers.summary: Matryoshka Representation Learning (`MRL`) trains nested embedding prefixes so that representations can be truncated to smaller sizes, but nothing explicitly ensures that the leading dimensions form a good compact encoding. `SpecMRL` reorganizes the feature space into a spectral basis derived from the parameters and ordered by feature importance, then reads prefixes in that space while otherwise following standard `MRL`. On `MTEB` it outperforms `MRL` at every reduced dimension, with larger gains under heavier compression, and **surpasses full-dimensional `MRL` using only half the embedding dimensions**.

papers.title: MemT-1.0: Towards Memory-Native Evolution
papers.abstract: Memory-native evolution requires making memory an intrinsic capability of foundation models, enabling them to continuously accumulate and utilize information. To this end, we introduce MemT-1.0, a new architecture of memory foundation models that internalize memory as part of model computation. Building on Metis, MemT-1.0 employs Gated DeltaNet-2 with a stable token-level memory update mechanism within each turn. We further introduce Mixture-of-Storage to scale native memory capacity. Following a deliberate backbone preparation, we develop a two-stage training pipeline consisting of continued pre-training and post-training, supported by 34B tokens of training data and efficient training and inference infrastructure. We release a model family comprising MemT-1.0-Nano and MemT-1.0-Flash, and conduct a comprehensive evaluation of memory and general capabilities. The results show that they outperform the parametric memory baselines on average and remain competitive with retrieval-augmented methods, while largely preserving general capabilities. At a history length of 128K tokens, MemT-1.0-Nano achieves approximately $1.86\times$ end-to-end inference speedup and a $66\times$ reduction in persistent storage relative to full context KV cache. By internalizing retrieved procedural experience, MemT-1.0 improves task success on agentic tasks, providing a practical step toward memory-native evolution.
papers.summary: `MemT-1.0` is a family of foundation models that build memory into the model's own computation, so they can keep accumulating and using information over time. Built on `Metis`, it uses `Gated DeltaNet-2` with a stable token-level memory update and a `Mixture-of-Storage` design to scale memory capacity. It is trained through continued pre-training and post-training on 34B tokens and released as `MemT-1.0-Nano` and `MemT-1.0-Flash`. The models beat parametric memory baselines on average, stay competitive with retrieval-augmented methods, and largely keep their general capabilities. At 128K tokens of history, `MemT-1.0-Nano` delivers about a **1.86x end-to-end inference speedup and a 66x reduction in persistent storage** compared with a full-context KV cache, and internalizing procedural experience improves success on agentic tasks.

papers.title: RefCraft: Benchmarking Visual-Reference-Conditioned Agentic Generation through Web Development
papers.abstract: Beyond basic tool use and coding skills, effectively incorporating visual references into agentic generation is equally essential for applying AI agents to real-world productivity tasks. We study this crucial capability through webpage development, a practical and readily evaluable setting in which existing benchmarks remain largely idealized: they typically focus on reconstructing visual targets or generating webpages from textual instructions alone, overlooking the more common workflow of developing from visual examples. Specifically, we introduce RefCraft, a benchmark comprising 300 realistic multimodal webpage-development tasks that combine natural-language instructions with screenshots from one to five reference webpages. Agents must selectively interpret and utilize these references while rendering, visually inspecting, and iteratively refining their outputs. We evaluate the resulting open-ended artifacts using independently verifiable keypoints and complementary programmatic and VLM judges. Across nine frontier (M)LLMs, the strongest system achieves an overall score of only 52.12 out of 100, revealing that visual-reference-conditioned agentic generation remains a substantial challenge for current models in practical webpage-development settings.
papers.summary: Real-world agentic work often means building from visual examples, which existing webpage benchmarks overlook in favor of reconstructing a target or working from text alone. `RefCraft` provides 300 realistic web-development tasks that pair natural-language instructions with screenshots of one to five reference webpages. Agents must selectively use the references while rendering, visually inspecting, and iteratively refining their output. Results are scored against verifiable keypoints using programmatic and vision-language-model (VLM) judges. Across nine frontier (multimodal) LLMs, **the best system scores only 52.12 out of 100**, showing that visual-reference-conditioned agentic generation remains hard.

papers.title: KEEP-Bench: Evaluating Evidence Preservation in Context Compression
papers.abstract: Context compression improves long-context efficiency but may introduce faithfulness issues through an information bottleneck. Existing evaluations rely on QA metrics, but a reader can still answer correctly from an unfaithful compression, so these metrics underestimate such loss. To bridge this gap, we introduce KEEP-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark that directly assesses compression faithfulness with 4,102 cases across three challenging settings that require keeping evidence for plausible reference resolutions, explicit qualifiers, and minority perspectives. Experiments show that even with tailored prompting, the strongest models remain unreliable: despite context windows exceeding 100K tokens and inputs averaging only 3.1K tokens, the best open-weight model (31B) preserves all required evidence in only 66.8% of cases, and the best proprietary model in only 61.6%. Performance also varies sharply across evidence structures, so conclusions from limited structures may be biased. We further introduce a metric, Evidence Preservation Return (EPR), to relate evidence recall to inference FLOPs, and find that it peaks at moderate scales (4B-8B), where recall remains low. Additional output budget mainly benefits already strong models and widens capability gaps, yet the stronger preservation of these models comes at a steep computational cost. These findings highlight the importance for future work to investigate compressors with strong information preservation under a small computation budget, rather than relying on a large output budget or model scaling.
papers.summary: Context compression shortens long inputs for efficiency, but question-answering metrics can hide lost information because a reader may still answer correctly from an unfaithful compression. `KEEP-Bench` measures compression faithfulness directly with 4,102 cases that require keeping evidence for plausible reference resolutions, explicit qualifiers, and minority perspectives. Even with tailored prompting and inputs averaging only 3.1K tokens, the best open-weight model (31B) preserves all required evidence in **only 66.8% of cases**, and the best proprietary model in 61.6%. A new metric, `Evidence Preservation Return` (`EPR`), relates evidence recall to inference FLOPs and peaks at moderate 4B-8B scales, where recall is still low; extra output budget mostly helps models that are already strong, at a steep compute cost.

papers.title: Agent World Model in the Wild: Computer-Use Agent Environment Synthesis
papers.abstract: Agent learning is shifting from learning from human data toward learning through interaction with the world. However, scaling such learning directly in real-world computer systems is challenging and can introduce substantial security risks. We therefore propose Agent World Model in the Wild (WildAWM), a scalable pipeline for synthesizing controllable environments and tasks for training general computer-use agents (CUAs). Whereas existing approaches typically specialize in a single agent interaction interface, we construct executable environments that jointly support graphical user interfaces, model context protocol services, and command-line interfaces, allowing agents to flexibly combine visual interaction, tool use, and code execution. WildAWM is entirely powered by open-source models, demonstrating that high-quality computer-use environments can be generated without proprietary frontier models. Beyond environments, we address three recurring challenges in task synthesis: ensuring solvability, maintaining sufficient difficulty, and producing reliable verifiers, by introducing execution-based quality gates that combine heterogeneous agent rollouts, cross-judge consistency checks, and counterfactual probes of judgment robustness. The resulting pipeline synthesizes 341 long-horizon environment-task pairs that can require over 100 agent steps to solve and remain challenging even for frontier models, with GPT-6-Astra solving only 60% of them. We train two Qwen models of different sizes exclusively in these synthetic worlds. Both models achieve substantial gains across 8 out-of-distribution benchmarks spanning web, claw, and computer-use agents, demonstrating that learning in WildAWM's synthesized worlds generalizes broadly to unseen computer-use tasks. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/MSR-Orchard/WildAWM.
papers.summary: Training computer-use agents (CUAs) by interacting directly with real systems is hard to scale and carries security risks. `WildAWM` is a pipeline built entirely on open-source models that synthesizes executable environments supporting graphical interfaces, model context protocol (MCP) services, and command-line interfaces together. It adds execution-based quality gates for task solvability, difficulty, and verifier reliability, using heterogeneous agent rollouts, cross-judge consistency checks, and counterfactual probes. The resulting 341 long-horizon environment-task pairs can take over 100 steps, `GPT-6-Astra` solves only 60% of them, and two `Qwen` models trained only in these synthetic worlds show **substantial gains across 8 out-of-distribution web and computer-use benchmarks**.

papers.title: ProteinGeoBench: Frontier Structural-Biology Agents Are Fluent at Lookup but Lost in Geometry
papers.abstract: Frontier agents retrieve structural metadata well and compute geometry from coordinates less reliably. We ask how much of a benchmark score reflects that gap and how much reflects the evaluation configuration around the model. We study ProteinGeoBench, a suite of 131 protein-structure tasks, using 4,249 rollouts from four frontier models and 4,486 further trials across 26 models. Three of the four frontier models fall within 0.031 of one another (0.785 to 0.816) with no difference between them resolved, while the fourth scores 0.707 and all three gaps to it exclude zero. Three of the four do better on metadata lookup than on numeric calculation. The fourth is slightly better on numeric. Numeric tasks are 28 of the 131 but half of the twelve tasks that all four models fail. The ranking also depends on the evaluation budget: with one run per task, 23.9% of bootstrap replicates put a different model first. On a selected 15-task slice, removing network access lowers scores more than blocking eight structural-database domains, but the two contrasts were graded in different passes and cannot be cleanly decomposed. Swapping in each model's own command-line agent changes scores by -0.071 to +0.086, a comparison too small to rule out moderate harness effects. Across 26 models, numeric performance rises with non-numeric performance rather than staying flat. The experiments use different task subsets, so they cannot rank model, harness, access and task composition against one another. Evaluations should report results by task family, along with the number of runs, the harness and the access conditions.
papers.summary: Using `ProteinGeoBench`, a suite of 131 protein-structure tasks, the authors examine how much of an agent benchmark score reflects real capability and how much reflects the evaluation setup. Across 4,249 rollouts from four frontier models and 4,486 trials across 26 models, three frontier models score statistically indistinguishably (0.785 to 0.816), and most models do better at metadata lookup than at computing geometry from coordinates. Rankings are fragile: with one run per task, **23.9% of bootstrap replicates put a different model first**, and network access and the choice of agent harness also shift scores. The authors recommend reporting results by task family, together with the number of runs, the harness, and the access conditions.

papers.title: Competing Learning in Hybrid Architectures
papers.abstract: Many modern language models have adopted hybrid architectures that incorporate both linear-time recurrence and softmax attention. Modern recurrence layers provide a highly expressive mixing mechanism while ensuring high throughput by compressing contextual information into a fixed-size state, but underperform softmax attention in contextual information retrieval. In this paper, we reveal a Competing Learning phenomenon where different kinds of mixers compete to learn the same function, and when any layer learns a function, it suppresses the corresponding learning signal for other layers. Layer attribution analysis reveals that under typical data distributions, modern recurrence learns retrieval functions faster than softmax attention, causing attention to fail to learn retrieval in most cases. Stopping weight updates in recurrence in the middle of training helps attention learn retrieval. Based on these results, we propose a staged training procedure for pre-training hybrid architectures on natural language. Empirical results on models up to 1B parameters show that our method results in substantial improvement in language modeling loss, common-sense reasoning, as well as a wide range of retrieval-related tasks across different context lengths.
papers.summary: Hybrid language models that combine linear-time recurrence layers with softmax attention often fail to get the expected retrieval benefit from their attention layers. Layer attribution analysis reveals a **Competing Learning phenomenon**: different mixer types compete to learn the same function, and because recurrence learns retrieval faster under typical data, it suppresses the learning signal that attention would need. Freezing the recurrence weights partway through training lets attention learn retrieval, and this motivates a staged pre-training procedure. On models up to 1B parameters, the procedure improves language modeling loss, common-sense reasoning, and a wide range of retrieval tasks across context lengths.

papers.title: Supervised Learning with Quantum Hamiltonian Embeddings
papers.abstract: Machine learning is widely regarded as a promising application in which quantum computing could offer a computational advantage. However, general quantum machine learning models with provable guarantees on performance, trainability, and efficient inference remain limited. In this work, we introduce quantum Hamiltonian embeddings, a supervised learning framework in which a classical training dataset is encoded into a single effective, parameterized Hamiltonian. Training optimizes the parameters of this data-dependent Hamiltonian, whose approximate ground state defines the classification rule. Once the ground state has been approximated using a quantum algorithm, inference can be performed either classically using a classical representation of the learned state, or with a quantum representation of the state. We establish efficient methods for gradient estimation and prove favorable generalization guarantees. Furthermore, under standard cryptographic assumptions, we show that Hamiltonian embeddings can realize hypothesis functions beyond the reach of efficient classical algorithms. We then demonstrate the framework at scale on IBM Heron processors using a standard benchmark dataset. Together, these results establish Hamiltonian embeddings as a new framework for quantum machine learning, combining theoretical guarantees with a path for experimental investigations at scale on quantum hardware.
papers.summary: Quantum machine learning models with provable guarantees on performance, trainability, and efficient inference remain scarce. Quantum Hamiltonian embeddings encode a classical training set into a single parameterized, data-dependent Hamiltonian whose approximate ground state defines the classifier, and inference can then run classically or on a quantum representation of the state. The authors give efficient gradient estimation methods and generalization guarantees, and show that **under standard cryptographic assumptions the framework can realize hypothesis functions beyond efficient classical algorithms**. They also demonstrate the method at scale on `IBM Heron` processors using a standard benchmark dataset.

papers.title: Kronecker Delta Rule for Long Context Linear Attention
papers.abstract: We propose KronLSTM, a linear attention architecture based on the Kronecker Delta Rule, a novel update rule for associative matrix memories. KronLSTM extends the xLSTM family with a memory-revision mechanism that corrects targeted associations while modifying the memory only along a single direction in matrix space. This minimally invasive memory revision reduces interference with previously stored information compared with delta-rule updates, making it particularly well suited for long-context language modeling. The resulting memory dynamics can be mathematically described as a Markov chain that converges to a steady-state distribution, while the expected norm of the memory matrix remains uniformly bounded throughout the entire input sequence. Hence, KronLSTM ensures stable memory dynamics without requiring additional normalization and stabilization mechanisms for the memory state. Experiments show that KronLSTM is competitive with, and often outperforms, existing linear attention architectures, including models of the (Gated) DeltaNet family, with particularly strong performance on long context benchmarks. These results establish the Kronecker Delta Rule as an effective and analytically tractable foundation for stable associative memory in recurrent linear attention architectures. Our code (https://github.com/NX-AI/KronLSTM) and models (https://huggingface.co/collections/NX-AI/kronlstm) are open-source.
papers.summary: `KronLSTM` is a linear attention architecture in the `xLSTM` family built on the Kronecker Delta Rule, a new update rule for associative matrix memories. It corrects targeted associations while changing the memory along only one direction in matrix space, which causes less interference with stored information than standard delta-rule updates. The memory dynamics form a Markov chain that converges to a steady state with a **uniformly bounded expected memory norm**, so no extra normalization or stabilization is needed. In experiments it is competitive with, and often beats, `DeltaNet` and `Gated DeltaNet`, with especially strong results on long-context benchmarks.

papers.title: Newton-Based Methods for Bilevel Optimization Beyond Lower-Level Strong Convexity
papers.abstract: Bilevel optimization provides a framework for machine learning tasks such as hyperparameter optimization, data reweighting, and meta-learning. Existing Newton-based bilevel methods typically rely on the classical hypergradient formula, which is generally unavailable when lower-level solutions are nonunique and the lower-level Hessian is singular. We develop two Newton-based methods beyond lower-level strong convexity by exploiting curvature shared by the lower-level and multiplier updates. Newton-based GALET handles potentially singular lower-level curvature under a positive spectral-gap condition, exploiting its range structure to avoid the squared-Hessian multiplier system used in GALET. Newton-based BAMM uses a strongly convex aggregation model when the lower-level objective is convex and the upper-level objective is strongly convex in the lower-level variable. We establish convergence guarantees and improved complexity bounds relative to GALET and sl-BAMM under the corresponding assumptions. We further introduce GNBO, a generalized Newton-based framework that captures the shared-curvature structure of the proposed methods and several existing Newton and quasi-Newton bilevel methods. Experiments on synthetic problems, data hyper-cleaning, and GPT-2 data reweighting evaluate the proposed methods across different bilevel learning tasks.
papers.summary: Newton-based bilevel optimization methods, used for hyperparameter tuning, data reweighting, and meta-learning, usually rely on a hypergradient formula that breaks down when lower-level solutions are not unique and the lower-level Hessian is singular. The authors develop two methods that exploit curvature shared between the lower-level and multiplier updates: Newton-based `GALET`, which handles singular curvature under a spectral-gap condition, and Newton-based `BAMM`, which uses a strongly convex aggregation model. Both come with convergence guarantees and **improved complexity bounds over `GALET` and `sl-BAMM`**, and a generalized framework, `GNBO`, unifies them with several existing Newton and quasi-Newton bilevel methods. Experiments cover synthetic problems, data hyper-cleaning, and `GPT-2` data reweighting.

papers.title: LatComm: Reusable Context Compression for Latent Communication between Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Systems that combine several large language models (LLMs) often use one context for many questions. When the context is passed between models as text, the receiving model processes all of its tokens again for every question. Avoiding this cost requires a context representation that is compact, reusable across questions, and readable by a different LLM. Existing compression and latent communication methods each provide only some of these properties. We introduce LatComm, a Latent Communication interface that provides all three by separating encoding from reading: the context is encoded once without the question, and the receiver selects what to read for each question. A frozen context encoder LLM compresses the context into a fixed-size packet and sends it to a different frozen receiver LLM, which reads the packet through cross-attention, with gates computed from its prompt. On 12 multiple-choice question-answering datasets, LatComm improves average accuracy over single-vector baselines by up to 10.2 points. On QuALITY, it reduces the receiver's input by 57x and answers the questions of an article 3x faster.
papers.summary: When several large language models (LLMs) share one context across many questions, passing it as text forces the receiving model to reprocess every token for each question. `LatComm` separates encoding from reading: a frozen encoder LLM compresses the context once, without seeing the question, into a fixed-size packet, and a different frozen receiver LLM reads it through cross-attention with gates computed from its prompt. On 12 multiple-choice QA datasets it improves average accuracy over single-vector baselines by up to 10.2 points, and on `QuALITY` it **cuts the receiver's input by 57x** and answers an article's questions 3x faster.

papers.title: WeAct: Dynamic Weight Switching as Agent Actions
papers.abstract: Long-horizon agents must learn heterogeneous capabilities from interleaved trajectories. Updating shared parameters to learn new capabilities can degrade previously acquired ones, resulting in catastrophic forgetting. As a trajectory unfolds, different stages may require different capabilities, yet conventional joint training and static adapter merging maintain a fixed parameter configuration throughout execution. We introduce WeAct (Weight-level Internal Actions), which trains independent capability-specific LoRA adapters over a frozen backbone and adds adapter selection to the agent's action space. These internal actions use the model's native tool-calling interface for on-demand capability composition in a shared context. Across eight deep-research benchmarks, Qwen3-32B with WeAct improves average accuracy by 6.2% relative to full fine-tuning counterparts despite using less compute, and by 27.5% relative to the strongest static LoRA-merging method. WeAct also supports modular continual adaptation, by adding a new code computation adapter to expand the agent's capabilities and updating the existing writing adapter to improve report quality. Both updates leave the backbone and other adapters unchanged, supporting modular continual adaptation in agents.
papers.summary: Long-horizon agents need different capabilities at different stages of a trajectory, but training shared parameters on all of them causes catastrophic forgetting, and static adapter merging keeps one fixed configuration throughout. `WeAct` (Weight-level Internal Actions) trains independent capability-specific `LoRA` adapters on a frozen backbone and lets the agent switch between them as actions through its native tool-calling interface. Across eight deep-research benchmarks, `Qwen3-32B` with `WeAct` improves average accuracy by 6.2% over full fine-tuning with less compute, and by **27.5% over the strongest static LoRA-merging method**. New or updated adapters, such as a code computation adapter and a revised writing adapter, can be added without touching the backbone or the other adapters.

papers.title: CoopUQ: Robust Multi-Robot Social Navigation via Uncertainty-Aware Cooperative Forecasting
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning enables mobile robots to make fast and scalable navigation decisions in constrained human-shared environments. However, directly extending single-robot approaches to multi-robot settings often fails to ensure safety and efficiency, especially under occlusions and out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios, where individual robots may overlook potential risks or make inaccurate predictions. Leveraging cooperation effectively for both prediction and navigation remains a major challenge. We propose CoopUQ, a multi-robot social navigation framework that bridges uncertainty-aware cooperative occupancy forecasting and robust decision making. CoopUQ predicts future occupancy grid maps through cross-robot spatiotemporal feature fusion and further leverages forecasts and their uncertainty to guide policy via constrained multi-agent reinforcement learning, where the cost penalizes navigation through regions predicted to be occupied or highly uncertain. This design enables the policy to adapt its risk sensitivity under distribution shifts. Experimental results across multiple Unity3D-based simulation environments with both in-distribution and OOD settings, including diverse layouts, pedestrian densities, and rushing behavior, demonstrate improved prediction performance and safety over representative baselines. Real-robot experiments further demonstrate its robustness across various scenes. Our code and videos are available at https://coopuq.github.io/.
papers.summary: Extending single-robot reinforcement learning navigation to several robots in human-shared spaces often fails on safety, especially under occlusions and out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions. `CoopUQ` predicts future occupancy grid maps by fusing spatiotemporal features across robots, then feeds the forecasts and their uncertainty into constrained multi-agent reinforcement learning, where the cost penalizes moving through regions predicted to be occupied or highly uncertain. This lets the policy **adapt its risk sensitivity under distribution shift**. Experiments in several `Unity3D` simulation environments with varied layouts, crowd densities, and rushing pedestrians show better prediction and safety than baselines, and real-robot tests show robustness across scenes.

papers.title: OpenVLHarness: Real World Visual Agentic Tool-Use with Multimodal Memory
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have made rapid progress on visual reasoning, yet many tasks require evidence that is difficult to obtain through internal reasoning alone: our controlled study on 22 benchmarks shows that simply increasing the inference budget of the base model yields only modest gains. Such tasks demand grounded perception, external knowledge, and numerical measurements obtained through heterogeneous tools, whose outputs must be made interpretable to the model and retained across reasoning steps. We introduce OpenVLHarness, a multimodal reasoning harness organized around a capability layer and persistent multimodal memory. The capability layer combines task-level tool interfaces with evidence rendering, providing consistent access to heterogeneous backends and converting their outputs into model-readable observations. Persistent multimodal memory retains the corresponding images, structured data, and web references as addressable artifacts throughout each query. A coding interface executes generated programs over stored data, enabling computations that combine results from multiple tools. Together, these mechanisms support an iterative process of acquiring, inspecting, and composing multimodal evidence. Evaluated on 22 benchmarks with eight open and proprietary backbones, OpenVLHarness improves average scores by 9.7-12.6 points over matched no-tool baselines, including +11.2 with Qwen3-VL-8B, +9.7 with Kimi K3, and +9.9 with GPT-6 Astra. With GPT-6 Luna at medium reasoning effort, OpenVLHarness outperforms the base model, Codex, and Visual Sketchpad at maximum effort by 7.7-8.5 points while incurring at most 37% of their model-token cost.
papers.summary: Many visual tasks need grounded perception, external knowledge, or numerical measurements that multimodal large language models (MLLMs) cannot produce by reasoning alone; a controlled study on 22 benchmarks shows that raising the inference budget yields only modest gains. `OpenVLHarness` pairs a capability layer, which wraps heterogeneous tools and renders their outputs as model-readable observations, with persistent multimodal memory that stores images, structured data, and web references as addressable artifacts, plus a coding interface for computing over stored results. Across eight backbones it improves average scores by **9.7-12.6 points over matched no-tool baselines**. With `GPT-6 Luna` at medium effort it beats the base model, `Codex`, and `Visual Sketchpad` at maximum effort by 7.7-8.5 points while using at most 37% of their token cost.

papers.title: Can It Actually Work? Synthesizing Functional CAD Mechanisms
papers.abstract: While LLM agents can generate visually plausible CAD assemblies, these designs often fail to fulfill their intended physical functions. We study functional CAD design, a setting where agents interpret underspecified requests to construct and iteratively revise mechanisms that satisfy functional requirements in physical simulation. Verifying these requirements is nontrivial: different candidate mechanisms may realize the same function through entirely different components, controls, and operating sequences. To bridge this gap, we propose FunCAD-Harness, a framework that translates abstract requirements into candidate-specific physical tests and uses simulation feedback to guide design revisions. To systematically evaluate this capability, we introduce FunCADBench, a benchmark spanning 46 mechanism families with interdependent and multi-step operations. Experiments across frontier LLM agents show that FunCAD-Harness exposes subtle mechanical failures invisible to visual inspection, substantially improving functional success rates over standard simulation-augmented baselines. Ultimately, our work marks a step toward CAD agents capable of translating human intent into working mechanisms.
papers.summary: LLM agents can generate CAD assemblies that look plausible but fail to perform their intended physical function. The authors define functional CAD design, in which agents interpret underspecified requests and iteratively revise mechanisms until they meet functional requirements in physical simulation. `FunCAD-Harness` translates abstract requirements into physical tests specific to each candidate design and feeds simulation results back into revisions, and `FunCADBench` covers 46 mechanism families with interdependent, multi-step operations. Across frontier LLM agents, the harness exposes mechanical failures invisible to visual inspection and **substantially improves functional success rates** over standard simulation-augmented baselines.

papers.title: Text-to-Image Generative Modeling Without Language Pretraining
papers.abstract: Modern text-to-image (T2I) systems use internet-scale language pretraining for text-conditioned image generation. We ask whether language pretraining is necessary for strong T2I generation. We introduce Halcyon, a family of early-fusion multimodal autoregressive models pretrained entirely from scratch on GPIC, a dataset of 100M image-text pairs. Halcyon-0.52B outperforms LlamaGen-XL/8 (48.0 vs. 63.3 gFD) with 18.2$\times$ less pretraining compute. Further, Halcyon-1.6B outperforms JiT-T2I-XXL/8++ (35.3 vs. 41.0 gFD) with 275$\times$ less pretraining compute. Controlled experiments show that text-only pretraining does not improve T2I generation. Halcyon also learns image captioning by replacing caption dropout with I2T supervision, maintaining competitive T2I generation quality under the same pretraining budget. We show that strong T2I systems can be trained from scratch without internet-scale language pretraining. Code and models are available at https://cs.stanford.edu/~keshik/halcyon
papers.summary: Modern text-to-image (T2I) systems rely on internet-scale language pretraining, and the authors test whether that is actually necessary. `Halcyon` is a family of early-fusion multimodal autoregressive models trained from scratch on `GPIC`, a dataset of 100M image-text pairs. `Halcyon-0.52B` outperforms `LlamaGen-XL/8` with 18.2x less pretraining compute, and `Halcyon-1.6B` outperforms `JiT-T2I-XXL/8++` with **275x less pretraining compute**, while controlled experiments show that text-only pretraining does not improve T2I generation. Replacing caption dropout with image-to-text supervision also lets the model learn captioning without hurting generation quality under the same budget.

papers.title: Navalia: Advancing Cowork Agents through Verifiable Task Synthesis and Long-Horizon Post-Training
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are evolving from conversational assistants into Cowork Agents capable of autonomous planning, tool use, and complex task execution. Financial analysis requires these agents to integrate cross-document evidence and perform multistep numerical reasoning, but expert task authoring is costly, while direct LLM synthesis struggles to produce challenging tasks with reliable answers. We introduce Navalia, a framework for Cowork Agents that combines verifiable task synthesis with long-horizon post-training. Using corporate financial reports as its data source, Navalia semantically selects supporting evidence from complete fact sets and constructs executable computation chains to generate analytical tasks with traceable evidence and actual data dependencies between steps. We further use independent LLM review and programmatic checks to verify evidence consistency and answer correctness. The verified tasks are then used for trajectory collection, cold-start supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and reinforcement learning (RL) to improve long-horizon task execution. Navalia, initialized from Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, achieves consistent gains over the base model across all five benchmarks: OfficeQA Pro, FinSearchComp, Finance Agent Benchmark, APEX-Agents-AA, and Workspace-Bench-Lite. These results demonstrate that Navalia improves evidence integration, tool use, and long-horizon task execution capabilities and generalizes to broader Cowork settings, including general office tasks.
papers.summary: Financial analysis agents must combine evidence across documents and perform multi-step numerical reasoning, but expert-written tasks are costly and tasks generated directly by LLMs are rarely both hard and reliably answerable. `Navalia` builds tasks from corporate financial reports by selecting supporting evidence from complete fact sets and constructing executable computation chains, so every task has traceable evidence and real data dependencies between steps, then checks the tasks with independent LLM review and programmatic tests. The verified tasks drive trajectory collection, cold-start supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and reinforcement learning (RL). Starting from `Qwen3.6-35B-A3B`, the model **improves over the base model on all five benchmarks**, including `OfficeQA Pro`, `FinSearchComp`, and `Workspace-Bench-Lite`, and the gains extend to general office tasks.

papers.title: Disentangling Depression from Cognitive Decline in Elderly Speech Using Concurrent Clinical Assessments
papers.abstract: Detecting depression from speech in elderly patients with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) is complicated by overlapping acoustic effects of cognitive decline. Without disentangling these, classifiers risk learning cognitive rather than depression-specific patterns. We present a Korean elderly speech corpus of 89 MCI speakers collected over three years with concurrent depression (SGDS) and cognitive (MMSE) assessments. Both linear mixed-effects models and partial correlations identify the same pattern: of seven feature groups, only formant features are associated with depression after controlling for cognitive function, while widely used F0 features carry no signal. The F1+F2 subset achieves UAR 0.760 with just 12 features, outperforming both the full eGeMAPS baseline and self-supervised representations. These findings show that concurrent clinical assessments can identify interpretable, depression-specific acoustic markers in populations where cognitive and affective symptoms co-occur.
papers.summary: Detecting depression from speech in elderly patients with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) is difficult because cognitive decline produces overlapping acoustic effects, so classifiers may learn cognitive rather than depressive patterns. The authors collected a Korean corpus of 89 MCI speakers over three years, with concurrent depression (`SGDS`) and cognitive (`MMSE`) assessments. Linear mixed-effects models and partial correlations agree that, of seven feature groups, **only formant features remain associated with depression after controlling for cognition**, while the widely used pitch (F0) features carry no signal. A 12-feature F1+F2 subset reaches an unweighted average recall of 0.760, beating both the full `eGeMAPS` baseline and self-supervised representations.

papers.title: PW-Pruning: Phase-Aware Expert Selection for Speech-Centric Omni-Modal Models
papers.abstract: Sparse routing reduces per-token computation but leaves the full expert bank resident in memory. We study expert pruning for speech-centric omni-modal models, where pooling calibration statistics can obscure the different expert demands of acoustic-input processing and text-answer generation. We propose PW-Pruning, a phase-aware extension of DO-ACP that constructs separate importance-weighted kernels for acoustic-prefill and teacher-forced answer tokens, then combines phase-weighted log-determinant marginal gains to select one static expert bank. On Qwen3-Omni, retaining 32 of 128 experts per layer improves MMAU-mini and MMSU accuracy over matched pooled selection by 3.20 and 4.38 percentage points, respectively, after supervised fine-tuning, averaged over three runs. Single-phase and shuffled-label controls on this public backbone suggest that semantic phase information contributes to these gains. Experiments on a non-public Qwen3.5-Omni backbone and English-only zero-shot evaluation of Nemotron provide complementary evidence. Across the tested Qwen budgets, AU gains are larger under stronger pruning, without inference-time mask switching.
papers.summary: Sparse mixture-of-experts routing reduces per-token computation, but every expert still has to sit in memory, which motivates expert pruning. `PW-Pruning` extends `DO-ACP` for speech-centric omni-modal models by building separate importance-weighted kernels for acoustic-input prefill tokens and answer tokens, then combining phase-weighted log-determinant gains to choose a single static expert set. On `Qwen3-Omni`, keeping 32 of 128 experts per layer improves `MMAU-mini` and `MMSU` accuracy by **3.20 and 4.38 percentage points over pooled selection** after supervised fine-tuning. Control experiments suggest the phase information drives the gains, which grow under stronger pruning and need no mask switching at inference time.

papers.title: Large language model and reinforcement learning based autonomous construction and progress updates
papers.abstract: Due to the rapid growth of the global population, traditional construction methods are gradually unable to meet the current housing demand. The advancement of machine learning algorithms has encouraged researchers to explore their applications in the construction industry, leading to more intelligent and efficient building processes. In particular, the rise of large language models in recent years has provided more possibilities for the transformation from traditional construction to smart construction. In this study, a large language model and reinforcement learning based autonomous construction method is proposed. An enhanced soft actor-critic reinforcement learning algorithm is developed to plan actions for a mobile crane according to construction tasks. Robot kinematics and control algorithms are used to ensure that the actions generated by the reinforcement learning algorithm can be executed by the crane. In addition, a customized embedding model is developed to extract information from the construction environment according to user interests. Then, a large language model, ChatGPT 5, is used to update construction progress, provide safety information to control system, and generate construction progress reports. The feasibility of proposed method is verified through several full-scall retaining wall construction experiments.
papers.summary: Combining a large language model with reinforcement learning, the authors aim to automate construction work and progress reporting. An enhanced soft actor-critic algorithm plans actions for a mobile crane, and robot kinematics and control algorithms ensure the crane can execute those actions. A customized embedding model extracts information from the construction environment, and `ChatGPT 5` updates progress, supplies safety information to the control system, and writes progress reports. The authors report that **full-scale retaining wall construction experiments** demonstrate the method's feasibility.

papers.title: MOSS: A Production Framework for Monitoring and Diagnosing Semantic Failures in Search and Recommendation Systems
papers.abstract:
Detecting semantic failures in production recommendation and search systems is hard: behavioral metrics lag by days, manual review does not scale, and most LLM evaluation frameworks are designed for offline, fixed datasets rather than continuous operational monitoring. We present Model Sanity Service (MOSS), a production framework that addresses this operational gap by embedding LLM-based relevance scoring into a recurring monitoring loop with targeted sampling, strategy-aware prompting, structured alerting, and diagnostic follow-up prompting that categorizes failures into actionable root causes.
  MOSS has been running in production at a large U.S. retailer for over six months across recommendation, search, and offer surfaces, and has surfaced two confirmed serving defects. For one of these, a backfill blending defect, MOSS quantified the impact of the proposed fix offline as a 76.4\% relative reduction in alert rate. On a 498-pair human-annotated recommendation benchmark, frontier LLM judges achieve higher F1 and AUC point estimates than non-LLM baselines (internal production embeddings and SBERT), with the largest gains on strategy-dependent tasks requiring intent-level relational reasoning. The same judge, score scale, and threshold transfer to a 466-pair search benchmark spanning 21 queries with only a surface-specific prompt adaptation, achieving strong F1 and AUC without retuning. These results show that a single LLM monitoring framework can provide useful, actionable quality signals across multiple product discovery surfaces in a large-scale e-commerce setting.
papers.summary: Semantic failures in production search and recommendation systems are hard to catch: behavioral metrics lag by days, manual review does not scale, and most LLM evaluation frameworks assume fixed offline datasets. `MOSS` (Model Sanity Service) runs LLM-based relevance scoring in a recurring monitoring loop with targeted sampling, strategy-aware prompts, structured alerts, and diagnostic follow-up prompts that sort failures into actionable root causes. Over six months at a large U.S. retailer it surfaced two confirmed serving defects, and for one of them it estimated offline that the proposed fix would bring a **76.4% relative reduction in alert rate**. On human-annotated benchmarks, frontier LLM judges score higher F1 and AUC than embedding and `SBERT` baselines, and the same judge settings transfer from recommendation to search with only a prompt adaptation.

papers.title: Pareto-Optimal RTL Code Generation via Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning with Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Recent studies have proposed reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) methods that enable LLMs to generate high-quality RTL circuits from natural-language specifications. Existing approaches optimize circuit PPA (Power, Performance, Area) by aggregating multiple objectives into a single scalar reward, making it difficult to simultaneously generate diverse Pareto-optimal solutions across different trade-offs such as low power, low latency, and small area. However, in practical design, the relative importance of each objective varies depending on product requirements and design constraints; thus, obtaining a diverse and high-quality candidate set is beneficial in that designers can choose a preferred trade-off a posteriori. In this work, we are the first to propose a learning method for LLM-based circuit generation that optimizes, not the quality of a single circuit, but the quality and diversity of the entire circuit set obtained through multiple generations in the PPA objective space. The proposed method consists of (1) a generation-based training pipeline that reformulates coverage improvement of the entire Pareto solution set into a sequential circuit generation problem, and (2) a reward function based on Hypervolume Contribution (HVC) that measures how much a generated circuit contributes to the Pareto front. Evaluation on the RTLLM v2 benchmark shows that the proposed method achieves +13.3 percentage points in relative Hypervolume over a baseline without PPA optimization and +14.4 percentage points over a single-objective reinforcement learning method, while also demonstrating superiority in circuit diversity.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) methods train LLMs to generate RTL circuits from natural-language specifications, but they collapse power, performance, and area (PPA) into one scalar reward, which yields a single trade-off rather than a range of options. The authors instead optimize the quality and diversity of the whole set of circuits produced over multiple generations, framing Pareto-front coverage as a sequential generation problem and rewarding each circuit by its Hypervolume Contribution (HVC). On the `RTLLM v2` benchmark, the method gains **+13.3 percentage points in relative hypervolume** over a baseline without PPA optimization and +14.4 points over single-objective reinforcement learning, while also producing more diverse circuits.

papers.title: Uncertainty Gates the Gradient: Adaptive Updates for Generalized Few-Shot 3D Segmentation
papers.abstract: In generalized few-shot 3D point cloud segmentation, support annotations are often compromised by sparsity and occlusion. Blindly adapting to such low quality samples risks learning spurious geometric patterns rather than robust novel concepts. Although 3D Vision-Language Models have been introduced to sup plement supervision, the potential of uncertainty to actively govern adaptation dynamics remains underexplored. Existing signal-level methods like loss reweight ing fail to prevent unreliable episodes from steering the optimization trajectory. To address this, we propose Uncertainty-Gated Adaptive (UGA), to the best of our knowledge the first framework that elevates uncertainty to update-level gating for generalized few-shot 3D point cloud segmentation. The core mod ule, Uncertainty-Gated Update (UG-Update), estimates episodic reliability via intra-class dispersion over merged support and pseudo-labeled novel supervision, and selectively gates residual gradient updates. This encourages the model to learn novel semantics from reliable episodes while attenuating updates during unreliable ones. Complementing this, we introduce an Uncertainty-Based Pseudo Label Filter (UB-Filter) to enforce learning from high-confidence dense signals. On ScanNet200 and ScanNet++ (1-/5-shot), UGA sets new state of the art with an average +3.08 HM IoU over the strongest prior baseline.
papers.summary: In generalized few-shot 3D point cloud segmentation, the few support annotations are often sparse or occluded, so adapting to them blindly can teach the model spurious geometric patterns. `UGA` (Uncertainty-Gated Adaptive) uses uncertainty to gate the updates themselves, rather than to reweight the loss: its `UG-Update` module estimates how reliable each episode is from intra-class dispersion over merged support and pseudo-labeled data, and dampens residual gradient updates from unreliable episodes. A complementary `UB-Filter` restricts learning to high-confidence pseudo-labels.
