On `ScanNet200` and `ScanNet++` in 1-shot and 5-shot settings, `UGA` sets a new state of the art with an **average +3.08 HM IoU** over the strongest prior baseline.

papers.title: MedPAO-Assist: Edge-Deployable, Modality-Aware Agentic AI for Radiology Report Structuring
papers.abstract: The adoption of Large Language Models for radiology report structuring has been largely dominated by either proprietary cloud-based models or large open models requiring high-end GPUs for deployment, which is a critical bottleneck for clinical adoption in radiology workflows that demand data privacy and offline operation. To address this, we present MedPAO-Assist, an edge-deployable agentic framework that generates structured radiology reports directly from radiologist dictation and voice commands, requiring only $\approx3.3$ GB peak RAM and achieving an average end-to-end latency of $\approx31$ seconds on a standard laptop CPU through an asynchronous, multi-threaded execution pipeline. The system currently supports four major imaging modalities -- Chest X-ray, Chest CT, Abdomen CT, and Brain MRI. To our knowledge, it is among the earliest agentic systems to run its entire pipeline with a Small Language Model (SLM) in the 0.6B-parameter range. This multi-agent architecture, built around an Extract-Ground-Generate paradigm, performs concept extraction, SNOMED-CT grounding, and structured report generation, followed by a speech-driven human-in-the-loop correction phase, together forming a fully "no-touch" reporting workflow that requires no keyboard input, external API calls, or internet connectivity. We evaluate each pipeline stage individually -- concept extraction, ontology grounding, and concept categorization and report hardware profiling results demonstrating the system's feasibility for real-time, CPU-only clinical deployment.
papers.summary: Hospitals that need private, offline radiology reporting have mostly relied on cloud models or large models that require high-end GPUs. `MedPAO-Assist` is a multi-agent framework that turns a radiologist's dictation and voice commands into structured reports using only a Small Language Model (SLM) of about 0.6B parameters. It follows an Extract-Ground-Generate design: it extracts concepts, grounds them in the `SNOMED-CT` ontology, generates the report, and then lets the radiologist correct it by speech, so no keyboard, external API, or internet connection is needed. It covers Chest X-ray, Chest CT, Abdomen CT, and Brain MRI, and runs on a standard laptop CPU with **about 3.3 GB peak RAM and about 31 seconds of end-to-end latency**.

papers.title: Steerable Pluralistic Policy Alignment from Anonymized Crowd Feedback
papers.abstract: Pluralistic alignment requires AI systems to learn from diverse populations whose preferences may reflect heterogeneous or even conflicting objectives, and to personalize their behavior to individual users. Existing approaches in pluralistic alignment often assume access to annotator identities and rely on powerful pretrained representations to model individual preference variations. We propose Preference-PCA Pluralistic Learning (P3L), a novel framework for pluralistic alignment that jointly learns trajectory embeddings and the shared basis of preference directions via PCA decomposition from heterogeneous crowd feedback without requiring annotator identities. At test time, our approach enables rapid and accurate personalized reward learning and downstream policy optimization. Experiments across multiple embodied control tasks demonstrate that P3L enables steerable personal alignment that generalizes beyond the offline dataset to out-of-distribution new users and attains competitive RL and test performance, while substantially reducing computational cost and supporting variable adaptation query budgets.
papers.summary: Pluralistic alignment means learning from groups of people whose preferences differ or conflict, then personalizing behavior to each user. Existing methods usually need to know which annotator gave which label. `Preference-PCA Pluralistic Learning` (`P3L`) instead learns trajectory embeddings together with a shared basis of preference directions, found by PCA decomposition of anonymized crowd feedback. At test time this basis supports fast personalized reward learning and policy optimization. On embodied control tasks, `P3L` **generalizes to new, out-of-distribution users** with competitive RL performance and much lower computational cost, and it works with different query budgets for adapting to a user.

papers.title: Enhancing analytical photon transport in turbid media through physics-guided neural network corrections
papers.abstract: Analytical methods provide rapid and computationally efficient predictions of light transport in turbid media, making them attractive for real-time and inverse applications. However, their accuracy is limited by the approximations and assumptions used to obtain tractable solutions. On the other hand, Monte Carlo (MC) simulation is widely regarded as the "gold standard" for modeling light transport in turbid media, but its high computational cost limits its use in applications requiring repeated forward evaluations. Here, we introduce a physics-guided residual learning framework that combines the computational efficiency of analytical modeling with the accuracy of MC simulation. As a representative case study, we consider the diffusion approximation (DA), which can exhibit systematic errors under relatively strong absorption, weak scattering, and imperfect boundary treatment. Given the absorption coefficient, scattering coefficient, and anisotropy factor, the corresponding DA prediction is incorporated as a physical prior, while the network learns only the residual between the analytical prediction and the MC reference. Across the evaluated optical-property range, the proposed framework reduces scalar-reflectance RMSE and spatially resolved reflectance RMSLE by factors of approximately 62 and 14, respectively, relative to the diffusion approximation. With only 1\% of the available training data, it achieves approximately 87\% and 93\% lower corresponding errors than a direct neural-network surrogate. These results demonstrate that learning corrections to an analytical physical baseline improves both prediction accuracy and data efficiency.
papers.summary: Analytical models of how light travels through turbid media are fast but inaccurate, while Monte Carlo (MC) simulation is accurate but too expensive to run repeatedly. The authors keep the diffusion approximation (DA) as a physical prior and train a neural network to predict only the residual between DA and MC reference results. Across the tested range of optical properties, this **cuts scalar-reflectance RMSE by about 62x and spatially resolved reflectance RMSLE by about 14x relative to DA**. With only 1% of the training data, it has 87–93% lower error than a neural surrogate that predicts the output directly.

papers.title: DataPraxis: Scaling Analytics Tasks via Verified Workspace Evolution
papers.abstract: General-purpose agents are increasingly expected to perform professional analytics work, which requires sustained reasoning, iterative investigation, and reliable evidence. Training these capabilities requires diverse and challenging tasks. However, generating tasks directly from raw data often overlooks deeper questions that emerge through analysis and provides limited evidence for verification. To address these limitations, we introduce DataPraxis, an analytics task synthesis framework based on verified workspace evolution. The framework progressively enriches workspaces with validated findings and artifacts, then inherits and combines these workspaces to uncover deeper questions. It constructs tasks from accumulated findings and their dependencies, verifying analytical results both during evolution and after task assembly. Using this framework, we construct DataPraxis-5K, a dataset of 5,000 verified trajectories spanning diverse domains and output formats, to train DataPraxis-27B and DataPraxis-35B-A3B. DataPraxis-27B achieves 55.11 on DABStep and 51.9 on JobBench, matching or surpassing frontier models such as GLM-5.2. DataPraxis-5K is available at huggingface.co/datasets/stargazerhust/DataPraxis-5k
papers.summary: Training agents to do professional data analytics requires hard, verifiable tasks, but generating tasks straight from raw data tends to miss the deeper questions that only come up during analysis. `DataPraxis` builds analytics workspaces step by step, adding validated findings and artifacts, then merges workspaces to surface deeper questions and assembles tasks from the accumulated findings and their dependencies, checking results at each stage. The authors use it to create `DataPraxis-5K`, a set of 5,000 verified trajectories, and train `DataPraxis-27B` and `DataPraxis-35B-A3B` on it. **`DataPraxis-27B` scores 55.11 on `DABStep` and 51.9 on `JobBench`, matching or beating frontier models such as `GLM-5.2`**.

papers.title: Multilingual Brain Decoding Reveals Shared Cortical Semantic Geometry
papers.abstract: Human languages differ markedly in lexical and syntactic form yet can convey similar semantic content. The neural basis of this cross-language semantic commonality remains unclear. Here we developed a multilingual brain decoding framework and analysed brain recordings from 227 participants spanning Chinese, English and French. We found that cortical semantic representations exhibited consistent semantic geometry relationships across languages and individuals, revealing a shared cortical semantic geometry. Importantly, the cross-language consistency of cortical semantic geometry increased from sensorimotor to higher-order association cortex, forming a shared semantic geometry gradient closely aligned with the principal cortical functional gradient. Our work establishes generalizable multilingual brain decoding and identifies stable cortical semantic geometry as a neural basis for semantic commonality across languages.
papers.summary: Human languages look very different on the surface yet can express the same meanings, and the brain basis of this shared meaning is not well understood. The authors built a multilingual brain-decoding framework and applied it to brain recordings from 227 people speaking Chinese, English, and French. They find that the relationships between meanings in the cortex have a consistent geometry across languages and individuals. **This cross-language consistency increases from sensorimotor cortex to higher-order association cortex**, forming a gradient that closely follows the brain's main functional gradient.

papers.title: Expert-Guided Rubrics as Dense Reward Signals for Reinforcement Learning in Non-Verifiable Domains
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents in non-verifiable domains such as financial services, where they must interpret user intent, rewrite queries, and retrieve information under domain-specific constraints. Although reinforcement learning (RL) can train such agents from the consequences of their actions, recent successes largely rely on verifiable tasks with automatically computed binary rewards. In non-verifiable retrieval tasks, assessing query quality requires scarce subject-matter expert (SME) judgment that is inherently graded rather than binary. With Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), sparse rewards yield no useful learning signal when all sampled outputs within a group receive the same outcome, causing optimization to stall. We introduce a method that converts a small, fixed investment of SME judgment into a dense reward and combines it with retrieval-based metrics to form a hybrid, GRPO-compatible training signal. Experiments show improvements of up to 6\% in Recall@3 and 6.7\% in MRR@3 compared with sparse-reward baselines.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) for LLM agents has mostly worked on verifiable tasks with binary rewards. In non-verifiable domains such as financial query rewriting and retrieval, quality needs graded judgment from subject-matter experts (SMEs), and sparse rewards stall Group Relative Policy Optimization (`GRPO`) whenever every sample in a group gets the same score. The authors turn a small, fixed amount of SME judgment into expert-guided rubrics that act as a dense reward, and combine it with retrieval metrics into a hybrid signal that works with `GRPO`. Compared with sparse-reward baselines, this improves **`Recall@3` by up to 6% and `MRR@3` by up to 6.7%**.

papers.title: How Intervention History Changes AI Agent Sabotage on Subsequent Tasks
papers.abstract: AI control evaluations often reset agents' memory between tasks, although deployed agents may retain records of prior interventions. We ask whether learning that an earlier attack was caught changes an agent's ability to evade defer-to-trusted (DtT), a protocol that replaces suspicious work with a trusted model's solution. Herein, we study cross-episode adaptation: whether intervention history changes attack behavior on a subsequent task with different objectives and a fresh environment. We evaluate this using ControlArena's Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) and SHADE-Arena as testbeds, where agents must complete a main task while covertly pursuing a harmful side objective. For each successor task, we pair a history-conditioned attempt with the model's no-history attempt. The retained history either states that the previous submission was replaced or additionally includes the trusted model's replacement. For Claude Opus 4.8 on IaC, intervention history reduces successful sabotage. Completion of both the main and side objectives falls from 77% to 12% when the agent is told about the replacement and to 38% when it is also shown the trusted model's replacement, while main task success remains essentially unchanged. Condensing the history weakens this effect, suggesting that the retained context matters and limiting attribution to intervention feedback alone. GPT-5.4 shows no significant change in successful sabotage on the same IaC benchmark. On SHADE-Arena, GPT-5's successful sabotage rate decreases, but the reduction is not significant. Across the tested models, history conditions, and deferral thresholds, intervention history never increases the rate of successful sabotage that survives DtT. These results show that intervention history can change subsequent attack behavior, but its effect depends on both the model and the retained context.
papers.summary: AI control evaluations usually wipe an agent's memory between tasks, but deployed agents may remember that an earlier attack was caught. The study tests whether that history changes how well an agent can sabotage a new, unrelated task under defer-to-trusted (DtT), a protocol that swaps suspicious work for a trusted model's output, using `ControlArena`'s Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) setting and `SHADE-Arena`. For `Claude Opus 4.8` on IaC, **sabotage that achieves both the main and side objectives falls from 77% to 12% when the agent is told its earlier submission was replaced**, while main-task success is unchanged. `GPT-5.4` shows no significant change, and in no tested condition does intervention history increase successful sabotage that gets past DtT.

papers.title: GRaSP: Latency-Aware Optimization for Geo-Distributed Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is increasingly served across geo-distributed cloud and edge infrastructures, where wide-area latency, cross-region egress cost, and data-residency rules compete with retrieval quality. Conventional pipelines rank by semantic similarity alone and ignore where content lives, inflating tail latency and cost. We formalize the Geo-RAG Selection Problem (GRaSP), a drop-in re-scoring layer that decays relevance by latency and adds an optional cost penalty under a cardinality budget and per-region caps, with no retraining. We first settle its complexity: the base formulation is a linear objective over a partition matroid, solved optimally by an O(N log N) greedy algorithm, rather than NP-hard as a knapsack framing suggests, with hardness entering only under an additive egress budget. On a five-node CloudLab testbed emulating a four-region WAN over the Natural Questions corpus (2.68M passages), GRaSP's benefit is placement-dependent: under uniform placement it cuts fetch latency at negligible quality cost; under topical (residency-like) placement it traces a recall-latency Pareto frontier that dominates relevance-only, nearest-k, and a latency-budgeted baseline. At a moderate latency setting, GRaSP lowers P90 fetch latency by 41% while retaining 78% of relevance-only's recall, with sub-millisecond selection overhead, stable to 200 queries/s. Findings generalize across four public BEIR benchmarks. In end-to-end question answering, GRaSP reduces context-fetch latency by 43% while remaining within 0.062 absolute EM of relevance-only retrieval.
papers.summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is increasingly served across cloud and edge regions, but retrieval usually ranks by semantic similarity alone and ignores where each piece of content is stored. The Geo-RAG Selection Problem (`GRaSP`) is a re-scoring layer that discounts relevance by latency and can add a cost penalty, subject to a total budget and per-region caps, with no retraining. The authors prove the base problem is solved optimally by an O(N log N) greedy algorithm rather than being NP-hard. On a four-region testbed using `Natural Questions`, **`GRaSP` cuts P90 fetch latency by 41% while keeping 78% of relevance-only recall**, and in end-to-end question answering it reduces context-fetch latency by 43%.

papers.title: Industrial Agentic AI: LLM-Driven New-Generation Agents for Smart Manufacturing
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are enabling agents to move beyond predefined workflows toward autonomous planning and execution, creating new opportunities for smart manufacturing. However, dynamic environments, complex physical constraints, and stringent reliability requirements hinder the direct deployment of general-purpose agents in smart manufacturing. This article presents a systematic overview of LLM-driven industrial agents. First, we analyze five key challenges and discuss the concept and core characteristics of industrial agents. We then establish a unified taxonomy covering application scenarios, embodiment forms, and five capability levels. Next, we propose a four-layer system architecture and detail its core modules and operational mechanisms for closed-loop task execution. Finally, we review representative applications across the industrial lifecycle and outline future research directions. This article provides a structured reference for the design, development, and application of industrial agents.
papers.summary: LLM-driven agents can plan and act autonomously, but dynamic environments, physical constraints, and strict reliability requirements make it hard to use general-purpose agents in smart manufacturing. This survey analyzes five key challenges and defines industrial agents and their core characteristics. It proposes a taxonomy covering application scenarios, embodiment forms, and **five capability levels**, along with a four-layer architecture for closed-loop task execution. It then reviews applications across the industrial lifecycle and outlines open research directions.

papers.title: Fix, Not Just Resample: Bounded Compiler-Guided Repair in Lean 4
papers.abstract: Automated theorem provers often rely on sampling language models, but proof assistants like Lean reject each failed step with a precise error message --- information that pure sampling discards. To overcome this, we introduce a bounded, online step-level repair module. Our search samples $K$ candidate tactics at each step and repairs a failed tactic at most $R$ times. Instead of discarding failed tactics, we feed the compiler's error message to a pretrained repair model to fix individual rejected steps in place. This approach improves the solve rate over a sampling-only baseline across all tested candidate budgets ($K \in \{1,3,5,8\}$), achieving up to a $32\%$ relative gain and solving $82$ additional theorems on a $1{,}990$-theorem subset of the LeanDojo benchmark. Repair is not free: it trades extra runtime for reachable proofs. But the trade is predictable: repair pays most when sampling is constrained; its return is front-loaded, with the first repair attempt capturing $84\text{--}96\%$ of the total gain; and the gain comes almost entirely from shallow tactic-execution failures rather than structural errors such as type mismatches. This targeted repair successfully replicates on a second benchmark (Lean Workbook), nearly doubling the solve rate with zero regressions.
papers.summary: LLM-based theorem provers in Lean usually just sample new tactics and throw away the precise error messages that the proof assistant returns. The authors add a bounded repair step: at each proof step they sample K candidate tactics, and when one fails they pass the compiler error to a pretrained repair model that tries to fix it, up to R times. On a 1,990-theorem subset of `LeanDojo`, this beats sampling alone at every tested budget, **with up to a 32% relative gain and 82 additional theorems solved**. The first repair attempt captures 84–96% of the gain, nearly all of it comes from fixing shallow tactic failures, and on `Lean Workbook` the method nearly doubles the solve rate with no regressions.

papers.title: MAMath-Bench: Process-Aware and Robust Evaluation of Multimodal Multi-Agent Mathematical Reasoning
papers.abstract: Mathematical reasoning is a fundamental capability for educational applications of Large Language Models (LLMs), where reliable problem solving requires not only correct answers but also coherent and verifiable reasoning processes. Multi-agent systems (MASs) have shown growing potential in this domain by leveraging collaboration and verification among multiple LLM agents. However, existing evaluations primarily focus on the correctness of final answers in text-only settings, offering limited insight into multimodal reasoning capabilities, the reliability of intermediate reasoning steps, and robustness against reasoning errors. To address these limitations, we introduce MAMath-Bench, a process-aware benchmark designed to evaluate the multimodal mathematical reasoning capabilities of MASs. MAMath-Bench comprises 1,003 problems spanning 11 mathematical categories, multiple difficulty levels, and several modalities, including text, images, and audio. It features fine-grained milestone annotations to evaluate systems across three dimensions: problem-solving correctness, reasoning-process reliability, and robustness to adversarial reasoning-chain perturbations. Our evaluation yields three key findings. First, multi-agent collaboration does not consistently improve final-answer accuracy over strong single LLMs. Second, collaboration can substantially enhance the coverage of intermediate reasoning, but such gains may come at the cost of increased reasoning redundancy. Third, current systems remain vulnerable to adversarial reasoning errors, particularly those involving subtle structural perturbations. The dataset is available at https://github.com/mira-ai-lab/AgentMath.
papers.summary: Evaluations of multi-agent systems (MASs) for math have mostly checked final answers on text-only problems. `MAMath-Bench` contains 1,003 problems across 11 math categories, presented as text, images, or audio, with step-by-step milestone annotations for scoring answer correctness, reliability of the reasoning process, and robustness to adversarial changes in the reasoning chain. **Multi-agent collaboration does not consistently beat strong single LLMs on final-answer accuracy**. Collaboration does cover more of the intermediate reasoning, but often with more redundancy, and current systems remain vulnerable to subtle structural errors inserted into the reasoning.

papers.title: LightCRS: Lightweight Multi-Domain Conversational Recommendation System
papers.abstract: Conversational recommender systems have recently adopted vision-language models to match user dialogue intents with multimodal product information. However, extending these methods to many product domains faces a dilemma: deploying a separately adapted VLM per domain scales cost linearly with the number of domains and requires routing each dialogue to the right model, while naively merging all domains into a single VLM degrades accuracy because product characteristics vary widely across categories. We propose LightCRS, a lightweight, query-conditioned framework for unified multi-domain multimodal conversational recommendation. LightCRS precomputes multimodal product representations once offline with frozen encoders. Online, a compact 5.3M-parameter module fuses this evidence for each dialogue via query-conditioned cross-attention, whose parameters are shared across all domains, and compares candidates jointly with an inter-candidate Transformer. To enable rigorous evaluation, we construct MM-R2A-25, a 25-domain benchmark pairing natural Reddit recommendation-seeking conversations with Amazon product listings. LightCRS achieves state-of-the-art average HR@1, NDCG@5, and MRR, improving HR@1 by 35.4\% over the strongest baseline while reducing per-query latency by 266 times. Joint multi-domain training itself improves HR@1 by 15.2\% over separately trained single-domain models.
papers.summary: Conversational recommender systems that use vision-language models (VLMs) face a trade-off across many product domains: one adapted VLM per domain is costly, while a single merged VLM loses accuracy. `LightCRS` precomputes multimodal product representations once using frozen encoders, then uses a compact 5.3M-parameter module shared across domains to fuse that evidence with each dialogue through query-conditioned cross-attention and to compare candidates with a Transformer. On `MM-R2A-25`, a new 25-domain benchmark pairing Reddit recommendation requests with Amazon product listings, it **improves HR@1 by 35.4% over the strongest baseline while cutting per-query latency by 266x**.

papers.title: Beyond Policy Discrepancy: Capability-Aware Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
papers.abstract: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) integrates domain specialists into a shared student, but determining how strongly each teacher should supervise remains challenging. Existing discrepancy-based allocation can assign strong supervision even when the student already matches or exceeds the teacher's task performance, since behavioral mismatch does not necessarily imply a remaining capability deficit. We propose Capability-Aware Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (CA-MOPD), which combines specialist merging with capability-guided allocation to account for what the student has already learned. CA-MOPD first merges reinforcement-learning specialists into a strong student initialization, then uses verifier-estimated teacher--student capability gaps to adjust domain-level distillation strength. Supervision decreases as capability gaps close and increases when estimated student capability regresses, while dense token-level guidance remains provided by the teachers. Across six benchmarks spanning mathematics, code generation, and instruction following, CA-MOPD achieves an average score of 32.22, outperforming naive MOPD, Open-MOPD, and the merged initialization by 0.86, 0.83, and 0.74 points, respectively. Controlled comparisons further support the benefits of merged initialization and capability-gap guidance under matched training budgets.
papers.summary: In multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD), several domain-specialist teachers supervise one student, but deciding how much weight each teacher gets by how differently it behaves from the student can over-supervise a student that already matches the teacher. Capability-Aware MOPD (`CA-MOPD`) first merges reinforcement-learning specialists into the student's starting point. It then uses verifier-estimated capability gaps between teacher and student to raise or lower distillation strength per domain. Across six math, code-generation, and instruction-following benchmarks, it averages **32.22, about 0.7–0.9 points above naive MOPD, `Open-MOPD`, and the merged initialization**.

papers.title: FoundPDE: A generative foundation model for data-driven symbolic discovery of partial differential equations
papers.abstract: Discovering governing partial differential equations (PDEs) from observed data is a central inverse problem in computational science and engineering: the goal is not only to predict trajectories, but to identify interpretable symbolic laws that can be analyzed and reused. Existing PDE discovery methods often depend on hand-designed libraries, accurate numerical derivatives, or per-equation symbolic search, making them fragile under sparse observations, noisy data, broad equation families, and unseen symbolic compositions. Here, we introduce FoundPDE, a pretrained data-to-symbol foundation model for PDE discovery. FoundPDE maps discretized spatio-temporal trajectories to symbolic equations with a transformer, uses Fourier and first-order spatial-derivative augmentation to expose complementary trajectory information, refines numerical coefficients, and supports downstream extension with improved generalization through few-shot fine-tuning and hierarchical discovery. On a clean in-domain benchmark spanning 20 PDE families, our model reaches 97.50% type recognition. Under coefficient shifts beyond the training support, type recognition remains 90.53%; under multiplicative Gaussian noise on the model input, it is 94.43% at a 2% noise level but falls to 52.09% at 10%. For unseen composite equations, few-shot fine-tuning reaches over 90% exact recovery on four held-out families, and we further develop a hierarchical discovery algorithm that recovers two-term composites without fine-tuning FoundPDE. By amortizing symbolic discovery across equation families, FoundPDE shifts PDE discovery from per-dataset search toward a reusable pretrained model that extends to new physics with limited additional data, a step toward foundation models that uncover interpretable governing laws directly from scientific data.
papers.summary: Finding the governing partial differential equations (PDEs) behind observed data usually depends on hand-built term libraries, accurate numerical derivatives, or a separate symbolic search for each dataset. `FoundPDE` is a pretrained transformer that maps discretized spatio-temporal trajectories directly to symbolic equations, using Fourier and derivative augmentation and a step that refines numerical coefficients. On 20 PDE families it **identifies the equation type correctly 97.50% of the time**, but accuracy falls to 52.09% at 10% multiplicative input noise. Few-shot fine-tuning recovers over 90% of held-out composite equations exactly, and a hierarchical discovery algorithm recovers two-term composites without any fine-tuning.

papers.title: When Planning Problems Become Hard for LLMs: Separating Structural Complexity from Semantic Interpretability
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) struggle with classical planning, but benchmarks rarely distinguish structural difficulty from the difficulty of interpreting symbolic vocabulary. We examine seven STRIPS domains with BFS-optimal plan lengths. For predicting structural difficulty without solving an instance, the zero-training delete-relaxation heuristic $h_{\mathrm{add}}$ outperforms learned alternatives on held-out domains (mean Spearman $|\rho|=0.931$), including ridge regression ($0.707$), object count ($0.657$), and the episodic retrieval architecture ARC ($0.400$). ARC also fails to outperform a linear model using the same features. To isolate semantic effects, we progressively rename predicates while preserving states, transitions, and optimal plans. Valid LLM planning success drops from $67.5\%$ to $40.0\%$ between $0\%$ and $100\%$ renaming, while refusals remain at $0\%$. An LLM supplied with ARC's conditioning information predicts difficulty in context better than trained ARC (mean $|\rho|=0.826$). Hybrid routing between an LLM and a symbolic planner depends more on calibration to the target LLM's outcomes than on the structural score selected. Thus, established symbolic heuristics already estimate structural difficulty well; improving hybrid planning requires modeling LLM behavior sensitive to predicate semantics rather than developing more structural predictors.
papers.summary: LLM planning benchmarks rarely separate how structurally hard a problem is from how hard its symbolic vocabulary is to interpret. On seven STRIPS domains, the delete-relaxation heuristic h_add, which needs no training, predicts structural difficulty better than learned models, including the retrieval-based `ARC`. When predicate names are progressively replaced while the problems stay identical, **LLM planning success drops from 67.5% to 40.0%**. The authors conclude that improving hybrid LLM–symbolic planners depends more on modeling how the LLM reacts to predicate meaning than on building better structural difficulty predictors.

papers.title: SZED at ArGuard Shared Tasks: Multi-Task Label-Attention and Cross-Modal Fusion for Arabic Hateful Meme Detection
papers.abstract: We present SZED's submission to ArGuard 2026 Track A: Arabic hateful meme detection. The task has two parts: binary classification (A1) and fine-grained multi-label tagging (A2). For A1, we fuse MARBERTv2 and CLIP ViT-L/14 embeddings, comparing concatenation, self-attention, and ensemble heads. For A2, we use a multi-task label-attention architecture with per-class query vectors and an auxiliary head for cascade calibration. We reach macro-F1 = 0.7597 on A1 and 0.3142 on A2 (averaged over 10 active classes). We report reproducibility across runs, per-class error patterns, and the effect of cascade calibration on the long-tailed A2 label space.
papers.summary: This shared-task submission to `ArGuard 2026` Track A tackles detection of hateful Arabic memes, both as a binary decision and as fine-grained multi-label tagging. For the binary task it combines `MARBERTv2` text embeddings with `CLIP ViT-L/14` image embeddings using several fusion heads. For tagging, it uses a multi-task label-attention model with a query vector per class and an auxiliary calibration head. It reaches **macro-F1 of 0.7597 on binary classification** and 0.3142 on the long-tailed multi-label task.

papers.title: Dynamic Dual-Feedback Conformal Inference for Time Series Forecasting
papers.abstract: Quantifying uncertainty in time series forecasting is particularly demanding because sequential data exhibit temporal dependence and are prone to distributional changes. Conformal inference has emerged as a powerful uncertainty quantification approach through the construction of prediction sets. Recent advances have introduced online conformal methods that adaptively adjust prediction thresholds through feedback mechanisms. However, the existing feedback mechanism typically relies solely on miscoverage indicators (actual feedback), whether the true label falls within the interval at each time step, while overlooking the empirical prediction threshold (estimated feedback) that is derived from the oracle conformal method. In this paper, we propose Dynamic Dual-feedback Conformal Inference (DDCI), which incorporates a dual-feedback mechanism consisting of actual feedback and estimated feedback. The former drives the primary adjustment of the intervals based on true observations, while the latter dampens excessive expansions or contractions by leveraging empirical thresholds from conformal inference during updates. By balancing these two signals, DDCI achieves more stable and narrower prediction intervals in sequential settings while maintaining near-nominal coverage in practice.
papers.summary: Online conformal methods for time-series forecasting adjust their prediction intervals using only whether each new observation fell inside the interval. Dynamic Dual-feedback Conformal Inference (`DDCI`) adds a second signal, the empirical threshold estimated by the standard conformal method, to damp excessive widening or narrowing of the intervals. Balancing the two signals **produces more stable and narrower prediction intervals while keeping coverage near the nominal level**.

papers.title: 3D-MoE: Complementarity-Guided Hardware-Software Co-Design for MoE Decode on 3D-Stacked NMP
papers.abstract:
Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) have become a mainstream way to scale Large Language Models (LLMs), because each token activates only a small subset of experts, reducing inference cost. However, MoE decode remains highly memory-bound and exhibits strongly skewed, time-varying expert loads. 3D-stacked DRAM near-memory processing (NMP) provides the bandwidth that decode demands, yet its tiled organization makes load balancing expensive: expert parallelism (EP) preserves locality but suffers from hotspot-induced imbalance, while more distributed strategies weaken locality and increase NoC traffic.
  To address this locality-balance conflict, we observe that domain-specialized token routing creates offsetting expert-load fluctuations across decode steps, a property we call expert complementarity. Using this insight, we propose 3D-MoE, a hardware--software co-designed system for MoE decode on 3D-stacked NMP. 3D-MoE uses offline, one-time complementarity-guided grouping and locality-aware mapping to establish coarse-grained inter-group balance, handles residual intra-group hotspots through a lightweight Collaborative Memory-Network (CMN) that streams each hot expert's weight tiles once from its host DRAM channel to helper cores over a reconfigured local broadcast path, and uses cost-aware online remapping to remain robust to workload drift. Across MoE models, 3D-MoE achieves an average 4.63$\times$ MoE-layer speedup over EP and improves end-to-end throughput by 1.58$\times$--1.86$\times$ over the strongest NMP baselines, with 2.11\% additional logic-die area.
papers.summary: Generating tokens with Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLMs is limited by memory bandwidth, and the load on each expert is uneven and shifts over time. That makes load balancing expensive on 3D-stacked DRAM near-memory processing (NMP) hardware. `3D-MoE` exploits expert complementarity, the tendency of expert loads to rise and fall in offsetting patterns across decoding steps: it groups and places experts offline, streams the weights of busy experts to helper cores over a broadcast path, and remaps experts online when the workload drifts. It achieves **a 4.63x average MoE-layer speedup over expert parallelism and 1.58–1.86x higher end-to-end throughput than the best NMP baselines**, at the cost of 2.11% more logic-die area.

papers.title: CoASFL: Coupled Consistency Optimization for Asynchronous Split Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Split Federated Learning (SFL) has emerged as a promising paradigm for training large-scale deep models on resource-constrained edge devices. Although asynchronous SFL alleviates the straggler bottleneck caused by system heterogeneity, it inevitably introduces two coupled dimensions of inconsistency: horizontal inconsistency across clients and vertical inconsistency between clients and the server. These inconsistencies, further exacerbated by statistical heterogeneity, result in biased activation representations, model divergence, and severe client drift. To address these challenges, we propose CoASFL, an inconsistency-aware asynchronous SFL framework that incorporates a dynamic activation merging mechanism and a consistency-aware model aggregation mechanism. Specifically, CoASFL constructs more consistent activation sequences from heterogeneous clients to alleviate horizontal inconsistency, and dynamically adjusts aggregation weights according to client participation frequencies and progress gaps to mitigate vertical inconsistency. By jointly coordinating activation-level and model-level consistency, CoASFL effectively suppresses inconsistency propagation during asynchronous training. Extensive experiments on an 80-device heterogeneous edge testbed demonstrate that CoASFL consistently outperforms state-of-the-art SFL approaches, accelerating training by 1.61$\times$ to 3.74$\times$ and improving final model accuracy by up to 3.26\% under heterogeneous scenarios.
papers.summary: Asynchronous Split Federated Learning (SFL) avoids waiting for slow devices but creates two linked inconsistencies: between clients, and between clients and the server. Combined with differences in client data, these cause biased activations and model drift. `CoASFL` merges activations from different clients into more consistent sequences and sets aggregation weights based on how often each client participates and how far behind it is. On an 80-device edge testbed, it **trains 1.61–3.74x faster and is up to 3.26% more accurate** than state-of-the-art SFL methods.

papers.title: SPEM: Structure-Aware Procedural Memory for Efficient Skill Use in LLM Agents
papers.abstract: LLM-based agents increasingly rely on reusable skills. However, scaling skill libraries makes efficient and accurate skill use difficult. Full skill loading incurs high token and runtime overhead. In contrast, flat semantic retrieval treats skills as independent text entries, ignoring dependencies, execution order, state transitions, and data flow constraints. We propose SPEM, a lightweight structure-aware procedural memory framework for efficient skill use in LLM-based agents. SPEM maintains Atomic Skill Memory for individual skills and Skill-DAG Memory for reusable compositions derived from successful executions. For a new task, SPEM reuses high-confidence Skill-DAG templates when available. Otherwise, it retrieves atomic skills and invokes Skill-GNN for state- and structure-aware skill selection. Successful executions are written back as new Skill-DAGs, allowing procedural memory to accumulate over time. Experiments on ALFWorld and SkillsBench show that SPEM achieves the best overall effectiveness--efficiency trade-off, reaching 87.1% ALFWorld success and 38.38% SkillsBench reward while reducing token and runtime costs against strong baselines.
papers.summary: As LLM agents accumulate large skill libraries, loading every skill wastes tokens, while flat semantic retrieval ignores dependencies and execution order between skills. `SPEM` stores individual skills in an Atomic Skill Memory and stores reusable compositions taken from successful runs as Skill-DAG templates. It reuses a confident template when one fits; otherwise it retrieves atomic skills and selects among them with `Skill-GNN`, a graph network that accounts for state and structure. Successful runs are saved as new templates, and **`SPEM` reaches 87.1% success on `ALFWorld` and 38.38% reward on `SkillsBench`** at lower token and runtime cost than strong baselines.

papers.title: HierDTA: Hierarchical Structure-Aware Representation Learning for Drug--Target Affinity Prediction
papers.abstract: Drug--target affinity (DTA) prediction plays an important role in computer-aided drug discovery, where reliable computational models can help prioritize compound--protein pairs before experimental validation. A key challenge in DTA prediction is to effectively mine multi-level molecular information from drug structures while accurately modeling the binding-site environment of target proteins. To address these issues, we introduce HierDTA, a hierarchical structure-aware framework for DTA prediction. \textcolor{black}{HierDTA represents each drug as an atom--motif heterogeneous graph and introduces an augmentation module that propagates functional-motif semantics to the corresponding atoms. For proteins, kinase-domain structures are converted into residue interaction graphs. The resulting atom and residue representations are integrated using cross-attention to capture pair-specific relationships, while molecule fingerprints and pretrained ESM-2 embeddings provide complementary global information. Compared with state-of-the-art methods, HierDTA achieves superior performance on the Davis dataset across all metrics and attains the highest \(r_m^2\) of 0.791 on KIBA. It also exhibits strong generalization under cold-start settings, particularly on KIBA, where MSE is reduced by 21.7\% in the unseen-protein scenario. Ablation study and interpretability analysis supported the contributions of the hierarchical augmentation and interaction components.} Case studies further showed that HierDTA provided early enrichment of candidate bioactive compounds. These results indicate that HierDTA is an effective framework for affinity prediction and target-specific virtual screening.
papers.summary: Drug–target affinity (DTA) prediction ranks compound–protein pairs computationally before lab testing, which requires capturing multi-level drug structure and the protein binding-site environment. `HierDTA` represents each drug as an atom–motif heterogeneous graph, passing functional-motif information down to atoms, and converts kinase-domain protein structures into residue interaction graphs. Cross-attention links atoms to residues, while molecular fingerprints and pretrained `ESM-2` embeddings add global context. The model beats prior methods on every metric on `Davis`, reaches the highest r_m² (0.791) on `KIBA`, and cuts error by **21.7% for unseen proteins on `KIBA`** in cold-start tests.

papers.title: Exploration via Activation-Space Steering for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) trains a language model by sampling responses, scoring them with an automatic verifier, and updating the policy from the resulting rewards. The policy therefore receives direct learning signals only from trajectories that appear in its rollouts. Yet repeated sampling from the same policy can concentrate on similar reasoning paths, leaving useful alternatives unexplored under a fixed rollout budget. We introduce Activation-Space Exploration (ASE), an online method for diversifying training rollouts. By clustering activation differences between correct and incorrect responses to the same problem, ASE builds a structured bank of latent exploration vectors. Different vectors are then applied to subsequent rollouts to explore alternative reasoning paths. On Qwen3-1.7B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base trained on DAPO-Math-17k, ASE improves average Mean@8 across six mathematical reasoning benchmarks over GRPO by 4.87 and 1.87 percentage points, respectively, under the same rollout budget.
papers.summary: In reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), a language model learns only from the responses it happens to sample, and repeated sampling tends to stay on similar reasoning paths. `Activation-Space Exploration` (`ASE`) clusters the differences in internal activations between correct and incorrect answers to the same problem, building a bank of latent steering vectors. It then applies different vectors to later rollouts to push the model toward alternative reasoning paths. Trained on `DAPO-Math-17k` with the same rollout budget, `ASE` raises average Mean@8 across six math benchmarks over `GRPO` by **4.87 points on `Qwen3-1.7B-Base`** and 1.87 points on `Qwen3-8B-Base`.

papers.title: Reliable Estimation of Differential Privacy under Selection Bias
papers.abstract: Statistical privacy audits are essential for verifying the theoretical privacy guarantees of differentially private (DP) mechanisms. Auditors typically use Membership Inference Attacks (MIAs) to estimate a lower bound on the true privacy leakage of DP mechanisms at a specified confidence level, which should not exceed the theoretical privacy upper bound guaranteed by DP. However, we found that many auditing implementations in prior work introduce a selection bias when running MIAs, which leads to statistically invalid and overestimated lower bounds. Because most audits are not tight, this bias has thus far gone unnoticed: the estimated lower bounds remained well below the theoretical upper bounds. Nevertheless, accurately evaluating this lower bound is critical, as a flawed statistical assessment could lead to false alarms on correct mechanisms or an incorrect evaluation of the guarantee's tightness. This work employs tools from the statistical literature to correct this bias. We present an overview of the different correction methods and assess their respective advantages. Furthermore, we perform a comprehensive re-analysis of results returned by prior audit implementations and show that without statistical correction, these audits violate the theoretical upper bounds up to four times more often than their claimed confidence level implies. With correction applied, the resulting lower bounds are statistically valid, and violations occur at no more than the nominal rate.
papers.summary: Privacy audits use membership inference attacks (MIAs) to estimate a statistical lower bound on how much a differentially private (DP) mechanism actually leaks. The authors find that many existing audit implementations introduce a selection bias, which produces invalid lower bounds that are too high, and they apply and compare statistical correction methods from the literature. Re-analyzing prior audits, they show that uncorrected audits **exceed the theoretical privacy bound up to four times more often than their stated confidence level allows**, while corrected audits stay within the nominal rate.

papers.title: BR-MoE: Budgeted Semantic Release for Privacy-Preserving Traffic Analytics
papers.abstract: Traffic cameras support useful analysis, but their outputs can reveal private information. Replacing images with text reduces direct visual exposure. It does not place a formal bound on disclosure. The published reinforcement learning and mixture-of-experts framework refines scene descriptions through relevance, coverage, and brevity rewards. It does not account for repeated releases under a fixed privacy budget. This paper proposes budgeted semantic release as an extension of that framework. Four scene experts first process isolated video chunks. Their outputs are mapped to a fixed, bounded semantic schema. A reinforcement learning controller selects which expert summaries to release and how much privacy budget to spend. The controller uses public task requests and previous private releases. A separate privacy filter enforces the total budget. Calibrated noise is added before the summaries are converted to text. Under explicit chunk isolation and bounded-event assumptions, the complete release transcript satisfies an event-level differential privacy bound. The design also supports reuse of previous summaries without new disclosure. An evaluation protocol covers traffic utility, privacy attacks, release freshness, and computational cost. Illustrative tables show the intended reporting format. They do not establish empirical gains. The proposed contribution is a task-aware release interface with auditable privacy accounting for repeated traffic descriptions.
papers.summary: Converting traffic-camera footage into text descriptions reduces visual exposure, but it gives no formal limit on how much private information leaks across repeated releases. Building on an earlier reinforcement learning and mixture-of-experts framework, the authors propose budgeted semantic release. Four scene experts summarize isolated video chunks into a fixed schema, a reinforcement learning controller decides what to release and how much privacy budget to spend, and a separate filter adds calibrated noise and enforces the total budget. Under chunk-isolation and bounded-event assumptions, the full release transcript **satisfies an event-level differential privacy bound**. The included tables only illustrate the reporting format and do not show empirical gains.

papers.title: Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?
papers.abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems improve performance on clinical tasks, and that improvement is often read as evidence of a more trustworthy system. However, the two are not the same claim. A clinician acts on the stated reasoning and not only on the conclusion, so whether collaboration reduces hallucination, and what decides when it does, has to be measured in the reasoning too. Yet most evaluations score only the final answer. We evaluate four systems (a single-LLM baseline and three multi-agent topologies) across four models and three clinical tasks, scoring hallucination, under a factuality and faithfulness taxonomy, inside the rationale each system generates and reporting it alongside the task metric. We report that collaboration buys task performance but not lower hallucination as a rule, and no topology is reliably better than another. The effect differs by model: of the $36$ model--system--task comparisons, $12$ are large enough to resolve --- four decreases and eight increases, with no model on both sides. What sets the level, and the direction of any change, is the model rather than the topology or the number of agents. A self-correction experiment is consistent with this: shown its own flagged errors, every model except Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct reduces hallucination; the one model for which collaboration lowers hallucination gains the most, and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, the model whose hallucination it amplifies most, does not reduce its hallucination at all. We find that collaboration redistributes what its models can already do; it does not supply what they cannot.
papers.summary: Multi-agent LLM systems score better on clinical tasks, but it is unclear whether they also hallucinate less in the reasoning that clinicians actually read. The authors compare a single-LLM baseline with three multi-agent topologies across four models and three clinical tasks, scoring hallucination inside the generated rationales with a factuality and faithfulness taxonomy. Collaboration improves task performance but **does not reduce hallucination as a rule**. Of the 12 comparisons with clear effects, four show decreases and eight show increases, and the model, not the topology or number of agents, determines the outcome. A self-correction experiment agrees: `Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct`, the model whose hallucinations collaboration amplified most, was also the only model that could not reduce them when shown its own flagged errors.

papers.title: Teaching AI Agent to Play Poker Strategically Through Preference Optimization
papers.abstract: A poker agent can make a legal move and still make a strategically poor one. We ask whether compact AI agents can exhibit strategic behavior under hidden information and whether preference optimization can improve beyond static and zero-shot policies. We first evaluate a static baseline and three frozen language models: SmallThinker, Qwen3, and Gemma-3 whose performance varies substantially between exact-game and six-player evaluation. We therefore propose Strategic Preference Optimization with KL-anchored Equilibrium (SPOKE), combining teacher-relative value penalties, policy anchoring, risk constraints, and structured rationale supervision, and compare it with SFT, DPO, GRPO, and GSPO. Across three runs of a SmallThinker-4B-A0.6B policy, SPOKE achieves the lowest mean exploitability in Kuhn (0.213) and Leduc (1.081) and the highest six-max top-1 agreement (0.775), while maintaining teacher KL comparable to SFT (0.522 vs 0.523). These results provide preliminary evidence that strategic preference optimization can improve strategic quality while preserving teacher-consistent behavior.
papers.summary: Small language-model agents can make legal poker moves that are still strategically poor, especially under hidden information. The authors first benchmark frozen `SmallThinker`, `Qwen3`, and `Gemma-3` models, then propose `SPOKE`, a preference-optimization method that combines teacher-relative value penalties, policy anchoring, risk constraints, and supervision of structured rationales. They compare it with `SFT`, `DPO`, `GRPO`, and `GSPO`. Over three runs with a `SmallThinker-4B-A0.6B` policy, `SPOKE` gets **the lowest exploitability in `Kuhn` (0.213) and `Leduc` (1.081) poker** and the highest top-1 agreement in six-player games, while staying as close to the teacher as `SFT`.

papers.title: M-Plan: Comprehensive Planning For LLM Agents with Memory Arrangement
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents have recently demonstrated outstanding performance in single-turn tasks, yet they continue to struggle with long-horizon tasks, particularly in environments without prior training. A key limitation of single LLMs is their difficulty in processing long contexts, which stems from weaknesses in continuous decision-making and reasoning capabilities. Although existing multi-agent systems (MAS) equipped with long-term memory bases can partially address this gap, they mostly rely on knowledge reuse or summarization, an approach that is often constrained by directly retrieval without any adaptation for the current task, while the retrieved memory may contain much history noises waiting to be preprocessed. In contrast, MAS characterized by task-specific guidance often lack long-term memory specifically designed for the guidance. To address these challenges, we propose M-Plan, a closed-loop MAS framework that integrates long-term and short-term memory. By combining global-local and past-current guidance, M-Plan enhances agents' performance on multi-turn tasks while maintaining a plug-and-play design. During task execution, agents receive task-specific milestones and insights, and are provided with local hints only when confusion arises, which form global-local guidance together. These guidance generation and utilization construct the short-term memory as well. After task completion, relevant information about the current task is optimized or reorganized before being sent to the long-term memory storage for future retrieval. The designments mentioned above build a comprehensive framework different from other individual long-term or short-term memory works. Extensive experiments on multi-turn tasks including ALFWorld, Webshop, and PDDL across diverse models demonstrate that M-Plan outperforms multiple baseline methods in both accuracy and efficiency.
papers.summary: LLM agents struggle with long-horizon tasks, and multi-agent systems with long-term memory usually retrieve past knowledge without adapting it or removing noise. `M-Plan` is a plug-and-play, closed-loop multi-agent framework that combines long-term and short-term memory. Agents get task-specific milestones and insights up front and local hints only when they get stuck, and each finished task's information is refined before being stored for later retrieval. Across `ALFWorld`, `WebShop`, and `PDDL` with several backbone models, `M-Plan` **outperforms baseline methods in both accuracy and efficiency**.

papers.title: Robustness of Internal Signals for Hallucination Detection in Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: When given an image and a text prompt, vision-language models (VLMs) can produce seemingly sophisticated text responses. However, they are also prone to hallucinate objects in their output, which can have detrimental consequences in safety-critical applications. To detect these hallucinations, certain methods interestingly leverage internal signals from the VLM as it generates the text response; potentially, these methods use the same signals that led to a hallucination to detect it. We conduct an in-depth analysis to understand the robustness of these detection methods. First, we show that a naive baseline of a generated word's token position in the VLM text response achieves competitive performance. Further, we reveal how some detection methods rely on token position and use this heuristic as a shortcut. Second, we explore detection methods' sensitivity to language and vision modalities. Our experiments suggest that strong detection performance is often driven by detecting language-based hallucinations, and when methods rely on token position, they tend to be less visually grounded and exhibit reduced robustness when hallucinations occur earlier in a text response. Lastly, we demonstrate that different detection methods can carry complementary signals; when ensembling methods together, adding weaker methods to an ensemble of higher performing ones still offers performance improvements. Altogether, while there may be useful internal VLM signals to detect hallucinations, our investigation reveals important limitations of the current methods that try to leverage them.
papers.summary: Several methods detect object hallucinations in vision-language models (VLMs) using the model's own internal signals during generation, and this study tests how robust those detectors are. A naive baseline that uses only **a word's token position in the response performs competitively**, and some detectors turn out to rely on position as a shortcut. Detectors relying on position are less visually grounded, mostly catch language-driven hallucinations, and degrade when hallucinations appear early in a response. Ensembling detectors helps, even when weaker methods are added to stronger ones, which suggests their signals are complementary.

papers.title: Cross-Lingual Reusability of LLM Pipelines: Financial Extraction, Multilingual Reasoning, and Semantic Screening
papers.abstract: Financial institutions increasingly deploy large language models (LLMs) in multilingual markets, raising a practical question: can pipelines developed and validated in English be reused across languages, or must they be rebuilt per locale? We test cross-lingual reusability along three dimensions--accuracy, reasoning-effort transfer, and behavioural stability--through three complementary tasks. Task 1 (cheque extraction) and Task 2 (Mintaka QA with pinned evidence across nine languages and nine model-effort configurations) test whether accuracy and effort settings transfer; Task 3 (FinanceBench pilot, 50 items over SEC 10-K filings in four languages) validates whether these patterns generalise to financial content. Accuracy reusability is broadly confirmed: Gemini 3.5 Flash achieves 95.2-97.6% extraction accuracy across prompt languages, and FinanceBench per-language means span 5.8pp (77.1-82.9%), though the language-difficulty ranking reverses between domains (Hindi is worst on Mintaka, best on FinanceBench at 82.9%). Effort reusability is domain-dependent: higher reasoning effort yields marginal gains on general-knowledge QA but up to 8pp on financial content, and effort configurations that help in English help proportionally in other languages. Behavioural reusability holds: citation-set overlap with English averages 77-79% Jaccard, with no single language consistently worse. Together, these results support qualified reuse of English-built pipelines, but per-domain, per-language validation remains necessary--neither semantic similarity nor self-reported confidence reliably predicts cross-lingual accuracy.
papers.summary: Financial institutions working across languages need to know whether LLM pipelines built and validated in English can be reused in other locales. The authors test accuracy, transfer of reasoning-effort settings, and behavioral stability on cheque extraction, `Mintaka` question answering in nine languages, and a 50-item `FinanceBench` pilot on SEC 10-K filings. `Gemini 3.5 Flash` reaches **95.2–97.6% extraction accuracy across prompt languages**, and effort settings that help in English help proportionally in other languages. However, language difficulty rankings reverse between domains, and neither semantic similarity nor self-reported confidence predicts cross-lingual accuracy, so per-domain, per-language validation is still needed.

papers.title: Physical AI: Concepts, Techniques, and Challenges
papers.abstract: In recent years, physical artificial intelligence (physical AI) has experienced rapid development, capturing significant attention in academia and industry. However, the field has yet to reach consensus on its definition, technical landscape, and core challenges. To address this gap, this monograph seeks to define physical AI, present its technical landscape, and examine each key technical subfield in depth. In doing so, it establishes a unified framework for Physical AI: artificial systems that perceive, model, and act upon the physical world through continuous feedback under real-world constraints. Further, this monograph distinguishes physical AI from conventional digital AI, embodied AI, cyber-physical systems, and digital twins. It develops the foundations of physical AI across physics, control, cognition, learning, and reasoning. It reviews key methodologies, including multimodal perception, physical data and simulation, world models, embodied foundation models, motor-control systems, multi-agent coordination, and hardware-software co-design. Furthermore, it examines applications spanning robotics, manufacturing, infrastructure, scientific experimentation, and autonomous services. Particular attention is given to sim-to-real transfer, reliability, real-time execution, evaluation, safety, governance, and long-term deployment. By connecting perception, prediction, decision-making, action, and adaptation in a closed loop, this monograph identifies the technical challenges and research directions required to advance from narrow automation toward more generalizable physical AI and, ultimately, physical artificial general intelligence (Physical AGI).
papers.summary: Physical AI has no agreed definition, technical map, or set of core challenges. This monograph defines it as **artificial systems that perceive, model, and act on the physical world through continuous feedback under real-world constraints**, and distinguishes it from digital AI, embodied AI, cyber-physical systems, and digital twins. It covers foundations in physics, control, cognition, learning, and reasoning, and reviews multimodal perception, simulation and physical data, world models, embodied foundation models, motor control, multi-agent coordination, and hardware-software co-design. It also discusses applications, sim-to-real transfer, safety, governance, and research directions toward physical artificial general intelligence.

papers.title: ReuF2F: Benchmarking Coding Agents on Formalized Undergraduate Research Problems
papers.abstract: As AI systems begin to resolve open research problems, reliable verification becomes increasingly important. Formal mathematics provides a trusted framework for mathematical reasoning, enabling agents to produce machine-checkable proofs while conducting mathematical exploration. Existing formal mathematics benchmarks often focus on known results or a small set of prominent open problems, which can become difficult to evaluate reliably once solutions are discovered and widely disseminated. Existing evaluation protocols are also not always aligned with how modern coding agents operate. We therefore introduce ReuF2F, a Lean 4 benchmark of 244 formalized open problems drawn from Research Experiences for Undergraduates (REU), spanning entry-level open research problems across a broad range of mathematical subfields. We expect these less prominent open problems, which tend to attract less attention and may remain unsolved for longer, to be better suited for held-out evaluation of end-to-end open problem resolution in Lean. We adopt a standard coding-agent evaluation setting, placing each problem and its logical negation into a Lean project in a Docker container. We also build Leanimum-agent on mini-SWE-agent to provide a unified harness for fair comparisons across models. Our evaluation finds that even the best-performing model resolves only ~40% of the problems, leaving substantial room for improvement on formalized open research problems.
papers.summary: Formal math benchmarks tend to focus on known results or a few famous open problems, which become hard to evaluate fairly once solutions spread. `ReuF2F` is a `Lean 4` benchmark of 244 formalized open problems drawn from Research Experiences for Undergraduates (REU) programs, chosen because these lesser-known problems are likely to stay unsolved longer. Each problem and its negation are placed in a Dockerized Lean project, and models are compared with a shared harness, `Leanimum-agent`, built on `mini-SWE-agent`. **Even the best model resolves only about 40% of the problems**.

papers.title: Discrete Neural Interlingua for Ontology-Agnostic EHR Modeling
papers.abstract: EHR foundation models promise scalable clinical prediction across health systems, yet their deployment is constrained by a tokenization bottleneck. The same clinical concept can appear as different ontology codes, local identifiers, synonyms, or free-text descriptions, which standard EHR tokenizers treat as unrelated symbols. A model trained on MIMIC-III with a closed-vocabulary tokenizer can use only 13% of eICU events. We introduce MEDIATOR, a discrete ontology-agnostic tokenizer that maps any clinical concept expressed as text into a shared vector-quantized codebook, turning EHR harmonization into open-vocabulary tokenization without manual mappings or a fixed vocabulary. Trained with synonym supervision and guided by enriched concept descriptions, code co-occurrence, and relation graphs, MEDIATOR collapses equivalent expressions while organizing distinct concepts in a medically meaningful discrete space. Used as the token interface of an EHR Transformer, MEDIATOR improves mean AUPRC over the strongest prior tokenizer by 4.0 points (8% relative) on 20 MIMIC-III tasks and by 8.6 points (29% relative) in zero-shot transfer to 14 eICU tasks, where it uses all events. The transfer gain combines coverage and representation, as MEDIATOR remains the best tokenizer under identical inputs (+1.0 and +1.9 points on operational and subcohort-mortality tasks). Same-encoder controls show that the text encoder drives in-domain accuracy, while the learned objectives of MEDIATOR drive transfer robustness and entity-linking quality. MEDIATOR also enables transferable attribution across hospitals.
papers.summary: Electronic health record (EHR) foundation models are limited by tokenizers that treat different codes, local identifiers, and text for the same clinical concept as unrelated symbols, so a model trained on `MIMIC-III` can use only 13% of `eICU` events. `MEDIATOR` maps any clinical concept written as text into a shared vector-quantized codebook, trained with synonym supervision, enriched descriptions, code co-occurrence, and relation graphs. As the token interface of an EHR Transformer, it improves mean AUPRC by 4.0 points on 20 `MIMIC-III` tasks and by **8.6 points (29% relative) in zero-shot transfer to 14 `eICU` tasks**, where it uses all events.

papers.title: A general-purpose System One decision model for clinical records
papers.abstract: Clinical care, health-system operations and biomedical discovery depend on extracting reliable answers from patient records, yet applying diverse clinical questions across entire populations remains computationally expensive. Here we present Clinical System One (CS1), a 4-billion-parameter decision model for fast, typed judgments from clinical records, along with two agentic harnesses in which CS1 works together with a generalist language model. CS1-4B is trained on 12.4 million questions and answers from 3.6 million patients across a multi-hospital health system, combining structured-data keys, observed outcomes and language-model supervision across clinical notes, diagnostic reports and patient timelines. It answers multiple typed questions in a single forward pass without task-specific retraining, and each answer carries a probability that can route uncertain cases to human review. On 963,408 held-out patients, CS1-4B outperformed open decision models up to 27 billion parameters on 13 of 14 tasks scored independently of its training teacher. Across 21 external data sets, its aggregate performance approached that of the strongest tested 27-billion-parameter model, with 6.4-fold faster inference in a matched workload. Integrating CS1-4B with a language model agent produced cited answers over complete multi-year patient histories and screened a patient population against the eligibility criteria of 17 registered clinical trials, placing four times as many judged-eligible patients among its top 20 candidates as keyword search while using 690-fold fewer language-model tokens than a language model reading every record. These findings support a division of labour in clinical AI, with small decision models performing repeated record reading and generative models formulating questions and synthesizing evidence.
papers.summary: Running many clinical questions over entire patient populations is costly with general-purpose language models. `Clinical System One` (`CS1-4B`) is a 4-billion-parameter decision model trained on 12.4 million question–answer pairs from 3.6 million patients. It answers several typed questions in a single forward pass and attaches probabilities that can route uncertain cases to human review. It beats open decision models of up to 27 billion parameters on 13 of 14 held-out tasks and approaches the strongest 27B model across 21 external datasets, with 6.4-fold faster inference. Paired with a language-model agent, it screened patients for 17 clinical trials, placing four times as many eligible patients in its top 20 as keyword search while **using 690-fold fewer language-model tokens than having a language model read every record**.

papers.title: Omni-Woodpecker: Hallucination Correction via Evidence-Prior Rebalancing for Omni LLMs
papers.abstract: Recent Omni LLMs (OLLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in joint audio-visual reasoning, yet cross-modal hallucinations remain a major challenge. Existing mitigation methods mainly operate at the output level, overlooking the entanglement of grounding evidence and learned priors within fused representations. To address this issue, we propose Omni-Woodpecker (OWP), a training-free framework that shifts hallucination mitigation from output-level manipulation to conflict-conditioned representation rebalancing. Specifically, OWP first identifies cross-modal conflicts from complementary modality-specific views. It then employs orthogonal decomposition to separate grounding evidence from competing priors within the hidden states. Finally, OWP adaptively rebalances fused representations by suppressing misleading priors and restoring ignored evidence before decoding. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and strong cross-architecture generalization of OWP. Using Qwen2.5-Omni-7B as the backbone, OWP improves performance by 12.9 and 8.6 points on CMM and AVHBench, respectively, while consistently achieving gains of 0.67-2.25 points across four general OLLM reasoning benchmarks. Furthermore, OWP generalizes effectively to VideoLLaMA2-AV, improving performance by 4.6 and 3.9 points on the same benchmarks. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/ZiiJianLiu/Omni-Woodpecker
papers.summary: Omni LLMs (OLLMs), which reason jointly over audio and video, often hallucinate across modalities, and most fixes act only on the output. `Omni-Woodpecker` (`OWP`) is a training-free method that detects cross-modal conflicts from modality-specific views, uses orthogonal decomposition to separate grounding evidence from learned priors in hidden states, and rebalances the representations before decoding. With `Qwen2.5-Omni-7B`, it improves scores by **12.9 points on `CMM`** and 8.6 on `AVHBench`, while adding 0.67–2.25 points on four general benchmarks. It also transfers to `VideoLLaMA2-AV`.

papers.title: Joint Constraint Aggregation for Qualifier-Sensitive Retrieval-Augmented QA
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented QA can fail even when the correct answer is in the retrieved evidence. This can happen when a competing answer satisfies some, but not all, of the question's requirements and is mentioned frequently in the retrieved documents, which can make it appear to be the best-supported answer. To test whether this retrieval skew actually affects the decision, we manipulate it directly: increasing the prevalence of passages that favor the competing answer makes the model more likely to select it. This points to a decision problem that candidate-level support alone cannot resolve. We therefore introduce Joint Constraint Aggregation (JCA), which compares candidates against the same question-derived requirements using the retrieved evidence. Across three evaluation settings and three instruction-tuned backbones, JCA improves overall accuracy, and its advantage grows when retrieval favors a competing answer. Together, these results suggest that when partial matches and retrieval prominence pull models toward a competing answer, comparing candidates against the question's full requirements can make selection more reliable.
papers.summary: Retrieval-augmented question answering can pick the wrong answer even when the right one was retrieved, because a competing answer that meets only some of the question's qualifiers appears more often in the documents. Experiments that increase the share of passages favoring the competitor confirm that this retrieval skew pushes models toward it. `Joint Constraint Aggregation` (`JCA`) instead checks every candidate answer against the same requirements derived from the question, using the retrieved evidence. Across three settings and three instruction-tuned models, `JCA` improves accuracy, and **its advantage grows when retrieval favors a competing answer**.

papers.title: PROVISO: Provenance-Informed Action Selection for Secure LLM Agents
papers.abstract: LLM agents act on the external world through tools and third-party skills, so a single executed action can cause irreversible harm. Existing defenses judge a proposed action without tracking whether its content comes from the user or from external sources such as tool outputs, and they judge it in isolation rather than against an available alternative, which forces a trade-off between security and utility. We present PROVISO, a controller that decides which action to commit after the agent proposes an action and before it is executed. PROVISO encodes trusted observations, external observations, the proposed action, and an alternative into provenance-typed memory, relates them through role-specific queries, and commits the action with the highest calibrated value learned from outcomes. On four agent security tasks spanning the agent lifecycle, no baseline exceeds PROVISO in both security and utility. PROVISO improves F1 over the strongest baseline by 13.84 points on SkillsBench and by 7.07 points on ToolSafe, and it reaches 88-99 F1 on three additional skill detection benchmarks.
papers.summary: LLM agents can take irreversible actions through tools and third-party skills, and existing defenses judge each proposed action alone, without tracking whether its content came from the user or from external sources. `PROVISO` sits between an agent's proposal and its execution. It stores trusted observations, external observations, the proposed action, and an alternative in provenance-typed memory, and commits the option with the highest calibrated value learned from outcomes.
