On four agent security tasks, no baseline beats it on both security and utility. It improves F1 by **13.84 points on `SkillsBench`** and 7.07 on `ToolSafe`, and reaches 88–99 F1 on three skill-detection benchmarks.

papers.title: PORA: Learning When More Reasoning Pays Off for LLM Agents
papers.abstract: LLM agents perform tasks over multiple steps and revise their actions based on feedback. As the total reasoning budget is often limited and must support future steps, the agent must choose between short and long reasoning before each action. Longer reasoning may improve the final task outcome by preventing later errors, but it also uses budget capacity that may be needed for future decisions. This creates two challenges: estimating the downstream value of long reasoning and deciding when that value is worth using the remaining budget. We propose Paired Outcome-guided Reasoning Allocation (PORA), which learns this decision by comparing short and long reasoning from the same interaction state. During training, \method{} completes the task twice from each selected state, once with a short reasoning allowance and once with a long allowance, and compares their final quality and total processing to estimate when longer reasoning is valuable. During inference, a controller weighs this estimate against learned prices on remaining-budget pressure and chooses either short or long reasoning without running both alternatives. We evaluate PORA across application, memory, code, retail, and mathematics tasks, achieving strong results across all settings. On BFCL memory, it exceeds the strongest existing method by 17.4--32.9 percentage points. Within the same agent, it matches or exceeds always using long reasoning on code and mathematics with 50.6% fewer actor tokens and 31.2% fewer model requests, respectively.
papers.summary: With a limited total reasoning budget, an LLM agent has to decide before each step whether long reasoning is worth spending budget it may need later. `Paired Outcome-guided Reasoning Allocation` (`PORA`) learns this by completing tasks from the same state twice during training, once with short and once with long reasoning, and comparing final quality against total cost. At inference, a controller weighs the estimated benefit against learned prices for remaining-budget pressure, without running both options. `PORA` beats the strongest prior method on `BFCL` memory by **17.4–32.9 percentage points**, and on code and math it matches or exceeds always-long reasoning while using 50.6% fewer actor tokens and 31.2% fewer model requests, respectively.

papers.title: EDMA: Entropy-Driven Multimodal Answering
papers.abstract: Multimodal question answering (MMQA) is based on integrating heterogeneous data sources, selectively leveraging relevant modalities, and ignoring distractors. Existing approaches based on Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) improve performance by splitting the task into intermediate steps, but do not quantify how each modality contributes to reaching the final answer. We argue that quantifying the effect that each modality has on the answering process improves process traceability and final performance. Thus, we propose Entropy-Driven Multimodal Answering (EDMA), which uses logical entropy to formalise multimodal QA as an iterative process of entropy reduction and to quantify the contribution of each modality in distinguishing correct from incorrect candidate answers. This enables the construction of quantifiable answering trajectories, where each step is associated with a measurable entropy reduction. EDMA introduces (i) modality-conditioned partitioning to estimate unimodal entropy reduction, (ii) entropy-driven multimodal fusion to capture complementary information across modalities, and (iii) entropy-based selection of the answering trajectory that minimises the most logical entropy. Evaluated across standard MMQA benchmarks, EDMA outperforms competitive prompting baselines, with average gains of 12.8 F1 and 4.6 LLM-J points over Planning Prompting and 18.6 F1 and 8.3 LLM-J points over Chain-of-Thought. Moreover, EDMA outperforms self-consistency baselines and is competitive with the multi-agent system baseline. Moreover, we show that higher entropy correlates with more false positives and, through controlled trajectory selection, demonstrate that logical entropy serves as an effective, monotonic selector for correct reasoning paths, validating entropy level as a reliable proxy for performance.
papers.summary: Multimodal question answering (MMQA) systems built on multimodal large language models split the task into steps but do not measure how much each modality contributes to the answer. `Entropy-Driven Multimodal Answering` (`EDMA`) treats answering as iterative reduction of logical entropy over candidate answers. It estimates each modality's reduction separately, fuses complementary information across modalities, and selects the reasoning trajectory with the largest entropy reduction. On standard MMQA benchmarks it beats `Chain-of-Thought` by **18.6 F1 points** and planning prompts by 12.8, and the authors show that entropy level reliably predicts whether a reasoning path is correct.

papers.title: Reconstruction-Optimized Expert Pruning for Mixture-of-Experts Language Models
papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models reduce computation through sparse expert activation, but deployment still requires storing a large number of expert parameters. We study post-training expert pruning using task-domain calibration data as a subset-selection problem: given a pretrained MoE layer, select a fixed number of experts that best reconstruct its original output. Exact subset search is combinatorial and becomes intractable for modern MoE models with many experts per layer. We develop OptEP, a scalable continuous relaxation that directly optimizes differentiable expert-selection variables, followed by a lightweight reconstruction-based update of the retained expert weights. Across multiple MoE architectures and tasks spanning mathematical reasoning and code generation, our approach improves over the strongest existing expert-pruning baselines, with absolute accuracy gains of up to 15.05% on Qwen3-30B-A3B, 14.55% on Qwen3-235B-A22B, 11.06% on GLM-4.5-Air, and 16.20% on Mixtral-8x7B. The improvements are particularly pronounced under aggressive pruning, demonstrating that reconstruction-driven expert selection and weight adaptation can preserve substantially more of the original model's performance while reducing the number of retained experts.
papers.summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models activate only a few experts per token, but every expert still has to be stored at deployment. `OptEP` treats post-training expert pruning as choosing the subset of experts that best reconstructs each layer's original output on task-domain calibration data, using a scalable continuous relaxation of the selection followed by a lightweight weight update for the retained experts. On math reasoning and code generation, it improves on the strongest pruning baselines with absolute accuracy gains of up to 15.05% on `Qwen3-30B-A3B`, 14.55% on `Qwen3-235B-A22B`, 11.06% on `GLM-4.5-Air`, and 16.20% on `Mixtral-8x7B`, with **the largest gains under aggressive pruning**.

papers.title: Mind Your Boundaries: Boundary-Aware Model Obfuscation against Cross-node Attack
papers.abstract: With the advancement of powerful AI chips, on-device machine learning is gaining traction for its low latency and privacy protection. However, when edge devices are compromised, attackers can obtain white-box access to the deployed models by reversing the apps directly to obtain the knowledge of peer devices, which is known as Cross-Node Attacks, like performing efficient adversarial attacks. Most existing defenses target known vulnerabilities, yet white-box access still enables attackers to uncover more unknown weaknesses. This creates a critical risk for edge-device deployments, where one compromised device can endanger all models distributed from the same source. Motivated by findings that the model robustness is primarily influenced by the curvature of the decision boundary, we investigate how model parameters shape its curvature. In this paper, we propose a novel method, BMO, that obfuscates model parameters to diversify the decision boundary further resisting cross-node attack while preserving its benign accuracy. Specifically, we explore decomposing model parameters into boundary-position and boundary-curvature components based on null-space constraints, then models with differentiated decision boundaries are instantiated by injecting noise into the boundary-curvature component. Across all four major types of adversarial attacks with four widely-deployed on-device models, BMO achieves an average success rate of 68.68% in defense, far exceeding the most competitive baseline, which attains only 22.32% in defending against cross-node attacks. Moreover, BMO achieves comparable performance in benign accuracy compared with baselines.
papers.summary: When one edge device running an on-device model is compromised, attackers gain white-box access that lets them craft adversarial attacks against every device running the same model, which the authors call cross-node attacks. Building on evidence that robustness depends on the curvature of the decision boundary, `BMO` uses null-space constraints to split model parameters into boundary-position and boundary-curvature components, then injects noise into the curvature component to give each deployed copy a different decision boundary. Across four attack types and four common on-device models, `BMO` **defends successfully 68.68% of the time, versus 22.32% for the best baseline**, with comparable accuracy on normal inputs.

papers.title: Ontic state recovery through prediction
papers.abstract: We encounter a system through its responses, yet its state concerns how the system is. Predicting further responses promises knowledge beyond what is immediately observed. What that knowledge tells us about the system's state depends on what we mean by a state in the first place. We give this notion a model-relative meaning: a state is the complete response profile over a specified query universe, and configurations agreeing on every query are regarded as the same state. From this perspective, a learned state is understood through the distinctions between these profiles that it retains. Prediction concerns selected observations; recovery concerns the profile as a whole. We examine their relationship through query ambiguity, state-space geometry, and the choice of prediction targets. Synthetic systems with known response laws and neural recordings provide complementary settings for this investigation. The aim is to clarify how prediction can become a way of knowing a system, and what it would mean for a learned state to preserve the state being studied.
papers.summary: The authors ask what it means for a model learned through prediction to recover the actual state of the system it observes. They define a state relative to a model: a state is the complete response profile over a chosen set of queries, so two configurations that answer every query the same way count as one state. With that definition, the gap between predicting particular observations and recovering the whole profile is analyzed through query ambiguity, the geometry of the state space, and the choice of prediction targets. The framework is studied on synthetic systems with known response laws and on neural recordings, with the goal of clarifying **when a learned state can be said to preserve the state under study**.

papers.title: Representing short-term movement to reveal animal identity and learning progress
papers.abstract: How learning progresses over time and varies across individuals is a longstanding question in cognitive and behavioral science. However, a major challenge is identifying observable behavioral measures that faithfully capture learning progression. Existing approaches commonly rely on predefined behavioral features or task-level performance, while fine-scale posture and movement in freely behaving animals remain less explored. In this paper, we ask: can short-term movement trajectories reveal learning progress and individual identity? We introduce a self-supervised representation learning framework built on a simple hypothesis: behavioral characteristics associated with identity and learning remain relatively stable over nearby time intervals. Using temporal proximity as supervision, our framework learns compact representations directly from movement trajectories without manually defining behavioral states or kinematic features. Using behavior data from freely behaving rats, we show that the learned representations not only improve prediction of identity and learning-related readouts over existing methods, but also provide a tool for investigating broader scientific questions about when and how these signals appear in behavior. Specifically, trajectories as short as one second contain informative learning and identity signals. Egocentric pose dynamics are more predictive of identity, whereas allocentric motion is more predictive of learning-related variation, and both signals are strongest at decision junctions in the alternation cohort. We further use a representation-conditioned diffusion model to inspect movement patterns associated with identity and learning progress. Our findings establish short-term movement as an informative behavioral "fingerprint" for studying learning and individual differences. Our code is available at https://github.com/pizhn/TRAIL.
papers.summary: Fine-scale posture and movement of freely behaving animals are rarely used to measure learning, which is usually tracked through hand-defined behavioral features or task scores. The authors introduce a self-supervised representation learning framework, released as `TRAIL`, that uses temporal proximity as its supervision signal, on the assumption that traits tied to identity and learning stay stable over nearby time windows. On recordings of rats, the learned representations predict identity and learning-related readouts better than existing methods, and **trajectories as short as one second carry informative signals**. Egocentric pose dynamics predict identity better, allocentric motion predicts learning better, and a representation-conditioned diffusion model is used to visualize the associated movement patterns.

papers.title: ICLHerd: Herding-Based Data Selection for LLMs with In-Context Learning as a Proxy
papers.abstract: Data selection plays a central role in modern large language model training, as the quality of training data strongly influences downstream performance. A common approach is to curate a development set that encodes the desired skills (e.g., reasoning or multilinguality) and select data that are similar to them. Existing methods compute similarity using cosine distance over either the model's hidden states or gradients. However, we observe that this max-similarity strategy induces a mode-seeking bias: the selected data clusters tightly around the development samples. To address this, we propose ICLHerd, a data selection framework that leverages the von Mises-Fisher kernel to balance mode-seeking with mode-averaging. We further introduce in-context learning as a validation proxy, enabling efficient hyperparameter search over the balance trade-off. Results show that ICLHerd outperforms existing LLM data selection algorithms, highlighting the importance of balancing mode-seeking and mode-averaging.
papers.summary: A common way to select training data for large language models is to pick examples most similar to a curated development set, using cosine similarity over hidden states or gradients. The authors show this max-similarity approach is mode-seeking: the selected data clusters tightly around the development samples. `ICLHerd` instead uses herding with a von Mises-Fisher kernel to balance mode-seeking against mode-averaging, and uses in-context learning as a cheap validation proxy for tuning that balance. The method **outperforms existing LLM data selection algorithms**.

papers.title: Model Exposure on One Device Endangers Others: Rethinking Edge Neural Network Security across Devices
papers.abstract: Neural networks (NNs) are increasingly deployed on edge devices such as mobile and IoT platforms, offering low latency and improved privacy compared to cloud-based deployment. However, on-device models embedded in mobile applications can be unpacked and exposed to adversaries, enabling cross-node attacks in centrally distributed ecosystems, where adversarial examples crafted on one compromised device transfer effectively to other nodes sharing the same models. To address this threat, we propose VeilNN, a defense framework that reduces adversarial transferability across on-device models via model obfuscation. The core idea of VeilNN is to introduce controlled model diversity while preserving original task functionality. Specifically, VeilNN applies stealthy and irreversible obfuscation at both the architectural and parameter levels through network cell obfuscation and layer assembling, and is applicable to diverse NN architectures, including MLPs, CNNs, and Vision Transformers. Extensive experiments demonstrate that VeilNN effectively defends against cross-node attacks, achieving an average defense success of 49.19% and up to 81.19% across four adversarial attack types, with more than 33.16% improvement over existing defenses.
papers.summary: Neural networks shipped inside mobile and IoT apps can be unpacked by an attacker, and adversarial examples crafted against one exposed copy then transfer to every other device running the same model. `VeilNN` defends against these cross-node attacks by obfuscating the model on each device, making stealthy and irreversible changes at both the architecture and parameter levels through network cell obfuscation and layer assembling, while keeping task behavior intact. It works with MLPs, CNNs, and Vision Transformers. Across four attack types it reaches an **average defense success of 49.19% (up to 81.19%)**, more than 33.16% better than existing defenses.

papers.title: MoSAIK: Motion Search with Artificial Intelligence in K-space
papers.abstract:
Object:
  Motion artefacts remain a major limitation of routine two-dimensional T2-weighted turbo spin-echo (TSE) brain MRI, reducing diagnostic confidence and often necessitating repeated acquisitions. MoSAIK (Motion Search with AI in K-space) retrospectively estimates in-plane rigid-body motion directly from standard multi-coil TSE k-space. Without a motion-free reference, external navigators, or additional acquisitions, MoSAIK infers motion from k-space self-consistency violations and incorporates predicted parameters into model-based, motion-aware reconstruction rather than synthesizing corrected images.
  Materials and Methods:
  Selected complex coil data were represented as log-magnitude and phase channels. A decoupled convolutional embedding and Transformer encoder estimated phase-encoding-line-indexed rotation and two-dimensional translations. Training used motion-free clinical acquisitions with simulated motion; four held-out subjects were evaluated. Component-wise errors assessed estimation; SSIM and PSNR in silico and entropy focus criterion (EFC) in vivo assessed reconstruction.
  Results:
  Motion estimation errors were low for both rotation (MSE $<$ 0.2 deg$^2$) and translation (MSE $<$ 0.2 pixels$^2$), with Pearson correlations of approximately 0.96 and 0.94, respectively. In every in-vivo acquisition, more than 75% of slices showed information gain relative to uncorrected reconstructions. MoSAIK reduced visible artefacts while preserving anatomical detail.
  Discussion:
  Transformer-based k-space motion-trajectory estimation enables fast retrospective correction of standard clinical TSE brain MRI.
papers.summary: Patient motion degrades routine two-dimensional T2-weighted turbo spin-echo (TSE) brain MRI and often forces repeat scans. `MoSAIK` (Motion Search with AI in K-space) estimates in-plane rigid-body motion directly from multi-coil k-space data, with no motion-free reference, navigators, or extra acquisitions. A convolutional embedding feeds a Transformer encoder that predicts rotation and translation for each phase-encoding line, and those estimates go into a model-based, motion-aware reconstruction rather than a synthesized image. Trained on clinical scans with simulated motion, it achieves **Pearson correlations of about 0.96 for rotation and 0.94 for translation**, and in every in-vivo scan more than 75% of slices showed an information gain over uncorrected reconstructions.

papers.title: Understanding the Benefits of Scaffolds through Computational Separations
papers.abstract: Inference-time harnesses, i.e., external procedures that call a model many times and keep state across calls, can substantially improve model capabilities. In this paper, we investigate the benefits of using such harnesses and the extent to which these benefits can be internalized through training. More precisely, we conceptualize a harness $\mathcal{A}$ as an arbitrary wrapper around a base model $M$ and attempt to distill a student model from the harness's traces. Empirically we find that, even with simple scaffolds and small models, the inference-time harness significantly outperforms a distilled student. We then prove that such a gap is due to a fundamental representational limitation: inference-time harnesses can compute a closure of their per-call primitive that is $\NL$-complete even when the primitive is a trivial $\AC^0$ lookup, and that no fixed-depth forward pass can represent under the widely believed conjecture that $\NL\not\subseteq\TC^0$. Our theory suggests that expanding the representational capacity of the student relative to the task at hand, e.g., by enlarging the model, making the task easier, or lengthening its chain-of-thought, is necessary to close the gap, which we verify empirically. Finally, we scale to an agentic harness on competition math, where the same gap reappears. Overall, our results show that a harness confers on the base model a profound gain in representational power, one that training a same-class student on its traces cannot transfer back into the weights.
papers.summary: Inference-time harnesses, meaning external procedures that call a model many times and keep state between calls, often improve capability, and the authors ask whether those gains can be distilled back into a single model. Empirically, even with simple scaffolds and small models, the harness clearly beats a student distilled from its traces. They prove the gap is representational: a harness can compute an `NL`-complete closure of a trivial `AC0` lookup primitive, which **no fixed-depth forward pass can represent if NL is not contained in TC0**. Closing the gap requires more student capacity, such as a larger model, an easier task, or a longer chain of thought, and the same gap reappears with an agentic harness on competition math.

papers.title: Learned Control Variates for Rare Grid-Outage Estimation at Electric Vehicle Charging Stations
papers.abstract: Public charging of electric vehicles (EVs) adds a large and synchronized load to the distribution feeders. In most networks, it is rare to overload a feeder at the same time. When it does happen, the consequences can be severe: an overloaded feeder stresses its transformers and can trigger cascading outages across a city. Planners who design for high reliability therefore need to estimate very small outage probabilities. To that end, plain Monte Carlo estimation with an expensive grid simulator can require a prohibitively large number of runs for this task. To reduce the number of runs, we propose a control variate (CV) built from a learned classifier of the outage, trained on cheap observable features such as temperature and load forecasts. We show that for any binary learner, the variance reduction is an explicit function of its recall and false-positive rate. Furthermore, we show that control variate based on a Gaussian proxy of the load loses its effect as outages become rarer, while a learner with non-vanishing precision keeps removing a fixed fraction of the variance even in the extreme rare-event regime. We verify these results in numerical experiments using a feeder-overload simulator across three orders of magnitude of outage probability and obtain that even weak learner with a single feature can remove a quarter of the variance, while a boosted-tree learner is able to remove about 60%. We then apply the estimator to the feeder network of Surabaya, Indonesia, in which the Gaussian load model leaves every feeder three to seven times the one-day-in-ten-years blackout target. At the same simulation budget, planning the reserve with the learned CV and a 95% confidence limit reduces the city-wide blackout days by a third compared with Monte Carlo. These results show that learned control variates can help planners design distribution grids that stay reliable against rare outages.
papers.summary: Grid planners need to estimate very small probabilities of feeder overloads caused by synchronized public electric vehicle (EV) charging, and plain Monte Carlo with an expensive grid simulator takes too many runs. The authors build a control variate from a learned outage classifier trained on cheap features such as temperature and load forecasts, and show that its variance reduction is an explicit function of the classifier's recall and false-positive rate. A Gaussian load proxy loses its effect as outages get rarer, while a learner with non-vanishing precision keeps removing a fixed share of variance: a boosted-tree learner removes **about 60% of the variance**. Applied to the feeder network of Surabaya, Indonesia, the method cuts city-wide blackout days by a third compared with Monte Carlo at the same simulation budget.

papers.title: Visual Task Modeling and Automated Planning for Humanoid Robots in Education of Individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder
papers.abstract: In robot-assisted education, a robot must understand how to complete a task in order to effectively guide a student through it. We present a novel method that enables a semi-autonomous, camera-equipped robot to recognise the task goal and plan actions to achieve it. Our work focuses on Shoebox Tasks, an activity commonly used in the education of individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). These tasks are designed so that the goal can be inferred directly from their visual structure. We have developed a solver that uses a vision-based Large Language Model to convert photos of a Shoebox Task into a Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL) representation and generate action plans for solving it. We have also implemented a robotic interface that enables a Nao robot to autonomously execute various Shoebox Tasks and assist a student by suggesting next steps or signalling detected failures through action demonstrations, voice commands, or gestures. With an adapted robotic interface, the solver can be integrated into a variety of educational robots. No programming expertise is required from teachers, and the solver operates exclusively on captured images as input. Research in special educational needs indicates that students with ASD can benefit substantially from robot-assisted teaching, and our system aims to strengthen these learning opportunities while also fostering interest in robotics among individuals with ASD.
papers.summary: For a robot to guide a student through a task, it has to understand the task itself. The authors target Shoebox Tasks, visually self-explanatory activities used in teaching people with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). A vision-based large language model converts photos of a task into a Planning Domain Definition Language (`PDDL`) representation, a planner generates action plans, and a `Nao` robot then executes tasks or helps the student by suggesting next steps and flagging failures through demonstrations, speech, or gestures. The system **works only from captured images and needs no programming expertise from teachers**, and it can be adapted to other educational robots.

papers.title: On the Fragility of Tasks under Composition: Implicit Budgeting in Language Models
papers.abstract: Modern language models are increasingly asked to handle several tasks within a single prompt. Doing so requires solving each task correctly while integrating the resulting answers into a coherent response. In this paper, we identify a fundamental limitation in this process, where models make substantially more errors when tasks are composed, even when they can solve every constituent task reliably in isolation. This degradation cannot be fully explained by the accumulation of independent errors. Across both open-weight models and the frontier model Claude Opus 5, our findings instead point to an implicit thinking budget underlying this effect. In particular, under composition, models use substantially fewer tokens per task than in isolation, even when the full sequence remains well within the context window. Tasks that require longer solution traces in isolation are consequently more $\textit{fragile}$ under composition, i.e., models make more errors on prompts containing these tasks. In isolation, non-fragile tasks receive more reasoning than they need and waste compute. However, by grouping tasks according to their fragility, the implicit budgeting can be manipulated to reduce token usage by $43$\% across a range of math and linguistic tasks while also preserving accuracy.
papers.summary: Language models make substantially more errors when several tasks are combined in one prompt, even when they solve each task reliably on its own, and the drop is larger than independent error accumulation would predict. Across open-weight models and `Claude Opus 5`, the authors trace the effect to an implicit thinking budget: under composition, models spend far fewer tokens per task even when the context window has plenty of room. Tasks that need long solution traces in isolation are therefore the most fragile when composed, while non-fragile tasks get more reasoning than they need. Grouping tasks by fragility exploits this budgeting to **cut token usage by 43% while preserving accuracy** across math and linguistic tasks.

papers.title: CARLAR Influence: A Structured Hallucination Risk in Multimodal Cheque Extraction and an Exploratory Compressed-Image Countermeasure
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for structured extraction from financial documents, but their behavior under visual ambiguity is poorly understood. We study CARLAR (Courtesy Amount Recognition and Legal Amount Recognition) influence: a model returns the same amount for both cheque fields even though their annotations differ, including cases with a blank annotation encoded as zero. Across ten visual prompting conditions, we evaluate GPT-4.1 and Claude 4.5 Sonnet on 243 primary cheques (124 with two observed unequal amounts) and 598 strict mismatches from two additional datasets. Under courtesy redaction, GPT-4.1 CARLAR reaches 73.7 percent (95 percent bootstrap interval: 68.3 to 79.0; p below 0.001 versus baseline). Model-reported confidence can remain high when predictions agree; expected calibration error reaches 0.93 among CARLAR cases. We also test a compressed-image few-shot intervention that presents examples as one visual table without model fine-tuning. On the 243-case cohort, Claude's Control condition increases paired joint extraction accuracy by 11.5 percentage points (95 percent interval: 6.2 to 16.9; adjusted p = 0.00054), but its strict-124 gain is smaller and not significant after correction. The intervention's effect on predicted-field agreement is model-dependent: it decreases for Claude and increases for GPT-4.1. These results motivate validation methods that account for visual context and dependencies between extracted fields.
papers.summary: The authors study a structured hallucination in multimodal LLMs that extract amounts from cheques, which they call CARLAR (Courtesy Amount Recognition and Legal Amount Recognition) influence: the model returns the same value for the numeric and written amount fields even when the two actually differ. Testing `GPT-4.1` and `Claude 4.5 Sonnet` under ten visual prompting conditions on 243 primary cheques plus 598 mismatches from two other datasets, they find **GPT-4.1 shows CARLAR in 73.7% of cases when the courtesy amount is redacted**, and expected calibration error reaches 0.93 among those cases. A few-shot intervention that presents examples as a single compressed image table raised Claude's joint extraction accuracy by 11.5 percentage points on the main cohort, but the gain on the strict subset was not significant after correction and the effects differed between models.

papers.title: LSA-PAST: Layer-Specific Adaptation and Prototype Transport for Compositional Incremental Learning
papers.abstract: Class-Incremental Learning (CIL) enables models to recognize new classes over time while retaining prior knowledge, but many real-world problems are compositional, where visual concepts arise from combinations of primitives such as states (i.e., red, shiny) and objects (i.e., shoe, car). Standard CIL methods treat each composition as an independent class, ignoring shared primitives and providing no mechanism to stabilize their representations as new compositions arrive. This causes parameter updates to entangle primitives and induce drift that degrades performance on earlier compositions. Compositional Incremental Learning (composition-IL) formalizes this setting by introducing new state-object compositions across tasks. In this paper, we propose Layer-Specific Adaptation with Prototype-Anchored Adapter-Space Transport (LSA-PAST), a parameter-efficient method tailored to composition-IL. LSA integrates Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) into a frozen ViT with depth-specialized adapters for states, objects, and compositions. PAST then maps past, anchored prototypes into the current adapter space through a rehearsal-free affine transform fit on current-task data, enabling old prototypes to remain compatible with new adapters. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LSA-PAST achieves state-of-the-art (SOA) accuracy-forgetting trade-off performance for composition-IL.
papers.summary: In compositional incremental learning, new state-object combinations such as "red shoe" arrive over time, and standard class-incremental methods treat each combination as an independent class, so updates entangle the shared primitives and degrade earlier compositions. `LSA-PAST` adds Low-Rank Adaptation (`LoRA`) adapters to a frozen `ViT`, with adapters at different depths specialized for states, objects, and compositions. A rehearsal-free affine transform, fitted on current-task data, maps stored prototypes from earlier tasks into the current adapter space so they stay compatible with the new adapters. The method reports a **state-of-the-art accuracy-forgetting trade-off** on compositional incremental learning.

papers.title: LoWAgent: A Low-Resource Multilingual Benchmark for Web Agents
papers.abstract: Web agents are typically evaluated on English-language interfaces, leaving their ability to operate across the world's multilingual websites largely unexplored. This gap is especially significant for low-resource languages, where standardized resources for evaluating web agents remain limited. To address this gap, we introduce Low-Resource Web Agent Benchmark (LoWAgent), a benchmark for evaluating web agents across different low-resource languages (LRLs) in comparison to the default, English. LoWAgent evaluates web agents across English and four LRLs: Hindi, Bengali, Urdu, and Amharic. The benchmark comprises of six fully localized websites, instantiated across five languages to yield 3,000 task instances. We evaluate three closed-source and five open-source models across all five languages on all six websites. Our findings show that both closed-source and open-source models experience performance degradation for LRLs compared to English, with substantially greater performance drops observed among the open-source model agents. We further evaluate the robustness of the models on realistic interface disruptions, such as cookie notices and advertisement pop-ups, and find that these further degrade agentic performance. Finally, we show that post-training on a small subset of LoWAgent traces can significantly improve low-resource language agentic task performance, demonstrating the usefulness of our benchmark.
papers.summary: Web agents are almost always evaluated on English interfaces. `LoWAgent` (Low-Resource Web Agent Benchmark) provides six fully localized websites in English, Hindi, Bengali, Urdu, and Amharic, for 3,000 task instances in total. Across three closed-source and five open-source models, performance drops in the low-resource languages compared with English, with **substantially larger drops for open-source agents**, and realistic disruptions such as cookie notices and pop-up ads degrade performance further. Post-training on a small subset of benchmark traces significantly improves agent performance in the low-resource languages.

papers.title: Language Guidance for Supervised Vision Training: An Empirical Study of Generalization
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks have achieved remarkable success on vision benchmarks, yet they continue to struggle with many generalization challenges. Supervised vision training relies on one-hot labels, which provide limited information about semantic structure and shared attributes between classes. This limited supervision can leave visual representations vulnerable to distribution shifts, spurious correlations, texture bias, adversarial perturbations, and forgetting in sequential learning settings. We study whether pretrained language models can serve as lightweight auxiliary supervision for vision training without requiring paired image-text data, prompt engineering, or contrastive objectives. Specifically, we evaluate two forms of language guidance, Explicit Language Guidance (ExLG) and Implicit Language Guidance (ImLG). We conduct a comprehensive evaluation across six generalization regimes, including in-distribution, out-of-distribution generalization, shortcut and spurious correlation resistance, texture and shape bias, adversarial robustness, and continual learning. Our analyses show that the two mechanisms have complementary strengths, with explicit guidance consistently benefiting in-distribution, low-data performance, and continual learning retention, while implicit guidance is often more useful in shortcut-sensitive settings and under stronger adversarial perturbations. Importantly, both are lightweight and add minimal parameters and training overhead. The analyses characterize when language-derived structure helps supervised vision training and provides a practical roadmap for using off-the-shelf pretrained models from another modality as auxiliary supervision.
papers.summary: Supervised vision training on one-hot labels carries little information about how classes relate, which can leave models vulnerable to distribution shift, shortcuts, texture bias, adversarial attacks, and forgetting. The authors test whether pretrained language models can act as lightweight auxiliary supervision, without paired image-text data or contrastive objectives, comparing Explicit Language Guidance (`ExLG`) and Implicit Language Guidance (`ImLG`) across six generalization regimes. The two mechanisms are complementary: **explicit guidance helps in-distribution, low-data, and continual learning, while implicit guidance helps more in shortcut-sensitive settings and under stronger adversarial perturbations**. Both add minimal parameters and training overhead.

papers.title: Profile-DP: Differential Privacy for User-Controlled Profile Release in Personalized LLM Inference
papers.abstract: Personalized large language models (LLMs) increasingly rely on profile-conditioned inference, pairing public requests with rich, user-specific facts. This paradigm exposes the user profile itself, together with the user's explicit sharing preferences. We introduce Profile-DP, a policy-aware local differential privacy framework designed specifically for user-profile release in personalized LLM inference. Profile-DP provably bounds the release of user-withheld facts while treating public instructions, profile schemas, and authorized facts as public side information. By generating a privatized profile that composes with the public instruction prior to answer generation, our framework decouples formal privacy guarantees from downstream model behavior. We develop two finite-domain mechanisms satisfying Profile-DP: DP-SLOT independently perturbs protected attributes, while DP-BLOCK uses public semantic decisions to coordinate their release and jointly sample related attributes. A positive, public compatibility prior connects these attributes while preserving a profile-level privacy bound. On PEEP, DP-BLOCK leads the utility composite among DP methods at all 13 structured budgets and is closest to the ideal privacy--utility point in 18 of 26 format--budget settings under our composite weighting. Direct measurements reveal complementary strengths: DP-BLOCK discloses less, while DP-SLOT retains more authorized facts. These results make policy-aware profile release a practical basis for studying privacy and personalization.
papers.summary: Personalized LLM inference sends user-profile facts alongside each request, which can expose facts the user wanted to keep private. `Profile-DP` is a policy-aware local differential privacy framework that provably bounds the release of withheld facts while treating the instruction, the profile schema, and authorized facts as public, and it produces a privatized profile before any answer is generated so the guarantee does not depend on how the downstream model behaves. Two mechanisms implement it: `DP-SLOT` perturbs protected attributes independently, and `DP-BLOCK` coordinates related attributes and samples them jointly. On the `PEEP` benchmark, **DP-BLOCK leads utility among DP methods at all 13 structured budgets**, while DP-SLOT retains more authorized facts.

papers.title: Sparse RL Relaxation for LLM Reasoning
papers.abstract: Recent work has explored continuous representations in place of discrete tokens during Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, often referred to as soft CoT. This is motivated by the idea that a mixture of token embeddings can represent a superposition of multiple reasoning possibilities within a single step. However, it remains challenging to train large language models to realize this potential. Existing work has explored reinforcement learning (RL)-style training for soft CoT. However, these approaches treat soft tokens as actions in a Markov decision process rather than as differentiable intermediate computation steps. Thus, they do not propagate gradients across the soft tokens and miss out on the signal of how the choice of one soft token affects the next. In this paper, we propose a sparse relaxation method for RL (called SpaRLax), which leverages the differentiability of soft-CoT reasoning over time steps and makes training more stable and effective. We adopt an entmax sparsity method that adaptively determines the degree of softness, which truncates long-tail noise at confident steps while retaining multiple plausible candidates when uncertain. Across nine reasoning benchmarks, our method achieves the highest average performance compared with baseline methods. Further analyses validate the effective use of soft-token superposition in our approach, and also demonstrate the contribution of adaptive sparsity in our approach.
papers.summary: Soft chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning replaces discrete tokens with mixtures of token embeddings that can hold several reasoning possibilities at once, but existing reinforcement learning (RL) approaches treat soft tokens as actions and do not pass gradients between them. `SpaRLax` is a sparse relaxation for RL that exploits the differentiability of soft CoT across time steps, making training more stable and effective. It uses `entmax` to set the degree of softness adaptively, cutting long-tail noise at confident steps and keeping several candidates when the model is uncertain. It achieves the **highest average performance across nine reasoning benchmarks** compared with baselines, and ablations confirm that both the superposition and the adaptive sparsity contribute.

papers.title: Magnolia: A Persistent-Memory Agent Framework for Computational Chemistry
papers.abstract: Chemistry has recently entered a high-data regime as molecular databases from high-throughput platforms or computational studies have become available. Increasing automation within the chemical sciences leads to a more digital and precision chemistry. Dedicated scientific agents are becoming central to guiding the chemist through an ever-increasing amount of data and findings, including negative ones. Here, we introduce Magnolia, a persistent-memory artificial intelligence agent framework that integrates computational protocols, from docking to quantum chemistry, lab notebooks and chat logs relying on large language models (LLMs). It relies on a three-tier memory system: session-level observations are automatically captured and distilled into structured learnings, confirmed and elevated to project-tier entries and, when human-validated, promoted to cross-project rules that actively guide subsequent work and provide direct chemical feedback. We illustrate Magnolia on four case studies: quantum-chemical evaluation of aromatic systems (COMPAS database), molecular dynamics of butane and of modified DNA, and a protein-peptide docking campaign. Across these projects, Magnolia tracked 317 runs and accumulated 116 project-tier entries, from which four cross-project rules were promoted; in controlled replays of four tasks, runs with memory passed the checks that runs without it failed (for example, ten of ten docking-configuration checks, against one to four of ten). By combining automation, reproducibility, and human-in-the-loop control, our Magnolia framework streamlines docking, molecular dynamics and quantum chemistry calculations with direct analysis and LLM-augmented feedback, offering accelerated access to computational (bio)chemistry.
papers.summary: `Magnolia` is an LLM-based agent framework for computational chemistry that ties together protocols ranging from docking to quantum chemistry with lab notebooks and chat logs. It uses a three-tier memory: observations from each session are distilled into structured learnings, confirmed ones are promoted to project-level entries, and human-validated entries become cross-project rules that guide later work. Across four case studies, including the `COMPAS` aromatic database, molecular dynamics, and protein-peptide docking, it tracked 317 runs and promoted four cross-project rules. In controlled replays, **runs with memory passed checks that runs without it failed**, for example ten of ten docking-configuration checks compared with one to four of ten.

papers.title: MMedAgent-Plus: Scaling Multimodal Medical Agents across Modalities, Tasks and Workflows
papers.abstract: Medical workflows often require multiple interdependent analyses, but existing specialist and generalist AI models are not designed to coordinate them. We introduce MMedAgent-Plus, a multimodal medical tool-use agent that combines a vision-language planner with 18 leading specialist models spanning 12 tasks and 8 modalities. Through a unified tool interface, the planner selects specialists, executes them in sequence, and synthesizes responses grounded in their outputs. The planner is instruction-tuned on 208,928 samples from 32 public medical benchmarks, covering single- and multi-tool interactions across single and multiple rounds. We separately evaluate tool orchestration, response synthesis, and end-to-end execution on held-out samples. MMedAgent-Plus achieves tool-call accuracies of 91.0%, 98.1%, and 80.7% in single-tool multi-round, multi-tool multi-round, and multi-tool single-round settings, respectively. Given correct tool outputs, MMedAgent-Plus achieves scores of 14.4-14.8 out of 15 for faithfulness, completeness, and conciseness across 600 evaluation samples. In end-to-end execution without pre-supplied tool outputs, MMedAgent-Plus correctly invokes the required specialist in 90.6% of 350 evaluation cases spanning seven tasks. Its final-answer accuracy reaches 0.98, matching the dedicated leading specialist and exceeding the strongest baseline (0.28).
papers.summary: Medical workflows often chain several analyses, but neither specialist nor generalist models are built to coordinate them. `MMedAgent-Plus` pairs a vision-language planner with 18 specialist models covering 12 tasks and 8 imaging modalities, behind a unified tool interface; the planner is instruction-tuned on 208,928 samples drawn from 32 public medical benchmarks. It reaches tool-call accuracies of 80.7% to 98.1% across single- and multi-tool settings, and in end-to-end execution it invokes the correct specialist in 90.6% of 350 cases. Its **final-answer accuracy of 0.98 matches the leading dedicated specialist**, far above the strongest baseline at 0.28.

papers.title: EGI-BENCH: An Enterprise General Intelligence Benchmark Suite
papers.abstract: Enterprise adoption of LLMs in agentic workflows is gated by evaluations that span a wide arc of abilities: CRM operations, heterogeneous-document retrieval, personal data understanding, multi-turn planning, tool use, function calling, long-horizon research, and long-context software engineering. These evaluations live today in separate repositories with divergent runners, dependencies, and scoring conventions, which makes cross-benchmark comparison difficult and obscures what a single aggregate number actually represents. We release EGI-BENCH, a unified LLM agent benchmark suite that consolidates eight enterprise facing agent benchmarks (CRMARENA, HERB, PERSONABENCH, USERBENCH, MCP-UNIVERSE, MCPEVAL, BENCHFORCE, LOCOBENCH) behind a single command-line interface with two runtime-budgeted execution modes. On top of the suite we define the Enterprise General Intelligence (EGI) Score, a six-dimensional framework (M1-M6) whose buckets are populated by fine-grained sub-metrics routed from each benchmark rather than by benchmark-level averages. We describe the suite, the sub-metric routing, and the quick/deep budgets, and report results for fourteen frontier and cost-efficient LLMs spanning the GPT, Claude, and Gemini families under quick mode. Top-line EGI ranges from 39.6 (GPT-4o mini) to 65.6 (gpt-5.5), and no single model dominates every capability axis: gpt-5.5 leads task outcome, planning, and retrieval grounding; Claude Sonnet 4.5 leads tool actioning and safety/abstention; and Claude Haiku 4.5 leads engineering quality. Code is available at https://github.com/SalesforceAIResearch/egi-bench.
papers.summary: Enterprise agent evaluations are scattered across repositories with different runners and scoring conventions, which makes cross-benchmark comparison hard. `EGI-BENCH` puts eight enterprise agent benchmarks, including `CRMARENA`, `MCP-UNIVERSE`, and `LOCOBENCH`, behind a single command-line interface with quick and deep runtime budgets. It defines a six-dimensional Enterprise General Intelligence (EGI) Score built from fine-grained sub-metrics routed from each benchmark rather than from benchmark-level averages. Across fourteen models, scores range from 39.6 (`GPT-4o mini`) to 65.6 (`gpt-5.5`), and **no single model leads every capability axis**: gpt-5.5 leads planning and retrieval, `Claude Sonnet 4.5` leads tool actioning and safety, and `Claude Haiku 4.5` leads engineering quality.

papers.title: AutoRedClaw: Automated Red-Teaming for Claw-Style Agents
papers.abstract: Agent systems are shifting from task-scoped tool-use agents to persistent, personalized assistants such as OpenClaw. These claw-style agents maintain configuration files (e.g., AGENTS.md), long-term memory, and reusable skills. Once poisoned, this persistent state is repeatedly reloaded into the agent's context, creating persistent threats across tasks and sessions. Existing security evaluation systems struggle to evaluate these complex claw-style systems since they rely heavily on manually constructed test cases and environments, which limits their scale and coverage; in addition, these manually designed cases quickly become outdated as agents evolve, and their evaluation settings leave a gap with how claw-style agents are deployed in practice. To address this, we introduce AutoRedClaw, an automated red-teaming framework that generates end-to-end attacks together with the environments needed to execute them. AutoRedClaw combines a strict quality-checking protocol with execution-based validation to ensure the correctness, realism, and effectiveness of generated samples, and adopts task-driven environment construction to keep costs low. To achieve broad coverage, it organizes generation along risk categories, attack strategies, attack stages, and attack surfaces, and uses experience-guided exploration to steer generation toward under-explored regions. AutoRedClaw achieves an effective attack rate above 30% at less than $0.10 per successful sample. From its outputs, we construct RedClaw-Bench, a 330-case benchmark that yields substantially higher attack success rates (ASRs) than AgentDojo, AgentDyn, and DTap. Across seven harnesses and four frontier models, most agent systems exceed 50% ASR, showing that our red-teaming pipeline provides a strong evaluation signal even for the most advanced agent systems. Our code and benchmark are released at https://github.com/SaFo-Lab/AutoRedClaw.
papers.summary: Persistent personal assistants such as `OpenClaw` keep configuration files like `AGENTS.md`, long-term memory, and reusable skills, so once that state is poisoned it is reloaded into every later task and session. `AutoRedClaw` automatically generates end-to-end attacks together with the environments needed to run them, filtering samples with strict quality checks and execution-based validation and steering generation toward under-explored risk categories, strategies, stages, and attack surfaces. It achieves an effective attack rate above 30% at under $0.10 per successful sample, and its outputs form `RedClaw-Bench`, a 330-case benchmark that yields higher attack success rates than `AgentDojo`, `AgentDyn`, and `DTap`. Across seven harnesses and four frontier models, **most agent systems exceed 50% attack success rate**.

papers.title: Target-Aware Curation of Hallucination Stress Tests for Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Hallucination stress tests can yield similar average scores across language models even when different prompts elicit hallucinations in each model. We develop a procedure that iteratively edits source-grounded seed prompts to expose hallucinations in a target model. An LLM editor revises each prompt in response to the target's answer and a judge's category-specific score and explanation. In the main setting, the target also receives feedback on its previous response. Experiments cover 500 seeds from seven datasets and ten topics, with intrinsic and extrinsic hallucinations evaluated across open-weight and closed-source models. Editing substantially increases judge-rated severity over the seeds. In the baseline configuration, retained responses fall in the judge's strong-hallucination bin in 77.2% of runs targeting extrinsic hallucination and 74.2% targeting intrinsic hallucination. Later editing rounds account for more than half of the mean score increase. Among 219 prompts that pass model-assisted source-validity checks, 89 elicit responses containing unsupported claims. Across five models, 200 curated prompts yield similar average severity scores, although pairwise Spearman correlations between prompt-level scores are only $\rho=0.0387$ to $0.1897$. Curated prompts can be reused across models, but their diagnostic value depends on source validity and the failures they expose in each model.
papers.summary: Hallucination stress tests can give different language models similar average scores even when different prompts trigger hallucinations in each one. The authors iteratively edit source-grounded seed prompts against a specific target model: an LLM editor revises each prompt based on the target's answer and a judge's category-specific score and explanation. Starting from 500 seeds across seven datasets, editing pushes 77.2% of extrinsic-hallucination runs and 74.2% of intrinsic-hallucination runs into the judge's strong-hallucination bin, and 89 of the 219 prompts that pass source-validity checks elicit unsupported claims. Across five models, curated prompts produce similar average severity, yet **prompt-level score correlations between models are only 0.04 to 0.19**, which shows that each model fails on different prompts.

papers.title: ValiAssist: Scaling LLM-generated Programming Feedback Validation by Demonstration
papers.abstract: Generative AI can create programming feedback at scale, but validating its alignment with instructors' pedagogical goals and strategies remains challenging. Instructors may struggle to fully specify validation criteria upfront, as these often emerge through inspecting concrete examples and revising misaligned feedback. We present ValiAssist, a validation-by-demonstration system that infers reusable validation logic from instructors' revisions of AI-generated feedback and allows instructors to inspect and refine that logic as it is applied across other student submissions. In a comparative study with 16 instructors, ValiAssist helped instructors create and refine validation criteria, producing feedback that better aligned with their pedagogical intent (91% vs. 57%) and more than doubling the accuracy of correcting problematic criteria (77% vs. 32%). Our findings suggest that validation by demonstration can help instructors turn judgments they know how to make on individual cases into explicit, reusable logic, while progressively clarifying where those judgments do and do not generalize.
papers.summary: Generative AI can write programming feedback for students at scale, but checking that the feedback matches an instructor's teaching goals is hard, because instructors often can't state their validation criteria up front. `ValiAssist` is a validation-by-demonstration system: it infers reusable validation logic from the edits instructors make to AI-generated feedback, then applies that logic to other student submissions, where instructors can inspect and refine it. In a comparative study with 16 instructors, feedback validated this way matched the instructors' pedagogical intent **91% of the time versus 57% for the baseline**, and instructors corrected problematic criteria accurately 77% of the time versus 32%.

papers.title: TxnQA: Benchmarking Analytical Reasoning and Evidence Grounding over Transaction Event Sequences
papers.abstract: Analyzing merchant transaction histories requires dynamic temporal filtering, entity resolution, and aggregation over irregular event streams--operations poorly captured by static tabular or time-series forecasting benchmarks. We introduce TxnQA, an analytical QA benchmark comprising 27 task families (81 templates) alongside a 5-scenario fraud-risk reasoning suite that evaluates both verdicts and supporting evidence over synthetic, privacy-mitigated transaction data. Ground-truth answers are computed programmatically, and model performance is decomposed into format-following rate (FFR), conditional content accuracy (CA), and end-to-end correctness (E2E). Evaluating prompted proprietary baselines and six LoRA-adapted open-weight models shows that adaptation reliably enforces output schemas but leaves arithmetic bottlenecks: Gemma-4-31B-IT and Qwen3-8B attain E2E scores of 0.867 and 0.816, whereas evaluated MoE checkpoints reach only 0.632-0.713. Furthermore, on the 500-instance fraud suite, verdict accuracy frequently exceeds 80%, yet joint accuracy (requiring exact evidence attribution) collapses to at most ~23%. These findings identify schema compliance, semantic calculation, and evidence attribution as three distinct bottlenecks in transaction-sequence QA.
papers.summary: Answering analytical questions about merchant transaction histories requires time-based filtering, entity resolution and aggregation over irregular event streams, which existing tabular and time-series benchmarks don't capture well. `TxnQA` covers 27 task families on synthetic, privacy-mitigated transaction data, with programmatically computed answers, plus a 5-scenario fraud-risk suite that grades both verdicts and supporting evidence. Scores are split into format-following rate, conditional content accuracy and end-to-end correctness. LoRA-adapted open-weight models reliably follow the output schema but still struggle with arithmetic: `Gemma-4-31B-IT` reaches 0.867 end-to-end and mixture-of-experts checkpoints only 0.632–0.713. On the fraud suite, verdict accuracy often exceeds 80%, but **joint accuracy with exact evidence attribution collapses to at most about 23%**.

papers.title: When Models Know but Can't Linearly Say: Relational Encoding Limits Linear Vulnerability Classification in Code LLMs
papers.abstract: Large language models can detect vulnerable code, yet the form of vulnerability encoding in their representations remains unclear. We analyze 8 code models spanning 6.7B-15B parameters on C programs using three datasets (DELTASECOMMITS, SVEN, and PRECISE-BUGS), comparing two diagnostic tasks on the same representations: identifying what patterns the code instantiates, and determining whether it is vulnerable. Models encode the first with high fidelity. Under the studied paired C-code datasets and linear-probing setup, vulnerability information is more accessible as a paired relational signal-whether code A is riskier than code B-than as a globally separable categorical label. This structural difference has implications for classification: the model reliably ranks which code is riskier but standard classifiers on isolated samples achieve limited accuracy because vulnerable and secure samples form overlapping distributions in representation space.
papers.summary: The study asks how code language models internally represent whether code is vulnerable. It runs linear probes on 8 code models (6.7B–15B parameters) over C programs from `DELTASECOMMITS`, `SVEN` and `PRECISE-BUGS`. The models encode which code patterns a program instantiates with high fidelity. Vulnerability information, however, is more accessible as a paired relational signal (whether code A is riskier than code B) than as a separable label: **models reliably rank which of two programs is riskier, yet classifiers on isolated samples reach only limited accuracy** because vulnerable and secure samples overlap in representation space.

papers.title: Theorem prover Arend
papers.abstract: This paper is an exposition of the theorem prover Arend developed at JetBrains Research. Arend language has been designed to facilitate the formalization of mathematics within the framework of univalent foundations and with the focus on constructive mathematics. It is based on a variant of homotopy type theory with cubical syntax that is more closely aligned with Martin-L\"of Type Theory (MLTT) than fully computational cubical type theories, while still retaining some of their computational properties useful in practice. Among the most notable features of the Arend language is its powerful system of classes and records supporting subsumptive subtyping, partial implementations and anonymous extensions, which provides extensive flexibility for constructing hierarchies of definitions. Formalization in Arend is streamlined by the IntelliJ Arend plugin, which transforms IntelliJ IDEA into a full-fledged integrated development environment (IDE) for the Arend language. The main Arend library arend-lib includes formalizations in constructive algebra, topology and synthetic homotopy theory.
papers.summary: This is an exposition of `Arend`, a theorem prover from JetBrains Research built for formalizing constructive mathematics in univalent foundations. Its language rests on a variant of homotopy type theory with cubical syntax that stays closer to Martin-Löf Type Theory (MLTT) than fully computational cubical type theories, while keeping some of their practically useful computational properties. Notable features include **a flexible class and record system with subsumptive subtyping, partial implementations and anonymous extensions**, an IntelliJ IDEA plugin that serves as a full IDE, and the `arend-lib` library covering constructive algebra, topology and synthetic homotopy theory.

papers.title: Auditing Safety Preference Supervision with Recorded Derivations
papers.abstract: Preference labels align model training, but the judgments behind them are difficult to inspect or verify. In this paper, we examine how preference construction can be checked when intermediate decisions are recorded, and which of them remain uncertain. We present Symbolic Preference Labeling, a method in which a pretrained language model classifies predefined attributes of prompts and responses. Explicit rules assign response verdicts, and a fixed verdict ranking determines the preference label. Each preference label has a recorded derivation: the response verdicts and preference label can be recomputed from the stored attribute assignments, rules, and verdict ranking without rerunning the language model. On 200 prompts annotated by human raters, the language model produces valid structured outputs for 192 prompts. All eight parsing failures occur in the subset of self-harm prompts marked as harmful. Using 465 preference pairs, we train one policy model with direct preference optimization across five training seeds. Mean measured benign refusal is 40.82 percent on 1,319 benign prompts that resemble unsafe ones, and mean measured toxic refusal is 84.98 percent on 655 toxic prompts. This study distinguishes the reproducibility of preference labels from attribute correctness. The recorded derivations make preference construction open to inspection, while attribute correctness and semantic safety require separate validation.
papers.summary: Preference labels drive alignment training, but the judgments behind them are hard to inspect. `Symbolic Preference Labeling` has a pretrained language model classify predefined attributes of prompts and responses. Explicit rules then assign response verdicts and a fixed ranking turns those verdicts into a preference label, so every label can be recomputed from stored decisions without rerunning the model. On 200 human-annotated prompts the labeler produced valid structured output for 192, and all eight failures were harmful self-harm prompts. A policy trained on 465 pairs with direct preference optimization (`DPO`) refused **84.98% of toxic prompts but also 40.82% of benign look-alike prompts**. The authors stress that reproducible labels are not the same as correct attributes, which need separate validation.

papers.title: Certifying Repeatable Entry-Replay Witnesses for COBOL-to-Java Migration
papers.abstract: Producing synthetic data for comparison testing a migrated COBOL application is a major challenge that agentic migrations face today. Our prior paper, the Agentic Method for Deterministic Validation of Legacy Code Migration, presents a deterministic oracle to facilitate such migrations, the Locksmith Loop. We now propose a novel method for achieving high branch and paragraph coverage through generated synthetic end-to-end test cases, by means of entry-replay test-case certification by observing the code execution trace on a surrogate COBOL program that mocks external interactions via a chronological external-operation tape. We applied our method to a very large COBOL program with 33,429 lines of code to generate 849 synthetic end-to-end test cases covering 2,973/3,806 source branches (78.1%) and 989/1,033 main-AST paragraphs (95.7%). Using the Locksmith Loop's projected-agreement validation, the generated Java code matched the COBOL surrogate on the specified observations across all 849 certified synthetic end-to-end test cases. During the campaign we detected 61 defects and fixed the Java generator accordingly. To test whether the coding agent could silently introduce business logic bugs, we seeded 450 defects into the Java code, such as deleted writes, deleted paragraph calls, and altered rounding, to verify how many of these would be detected by the gating methodology. The gate detected 47.6%, including all deleted writes and paragraph calls in executed code, but was unable to detect the rounding and precision defects.
papers.summary: Agentic COBOL-to-Java migrations need synthetic test data to check that the translated code behaves like the original. The method certifies end-to-end test cases by replaying execution traces on a surrogate COBOL program that mocks external interactions with a chronological tape of external operations, and validates the Java output against it with the authors' earlier `Locksmith Loop` oracle. On a 33,429-line COBOL program, it generated 849 certified tests covering 78.1% of branches and 95.7% of paragraphs, and the campaign surfaced 61 generator defects. Of 450 deliberately seeded Java bugs, **the gate caught 47.6%**, including every deleted write and paragraph call in executed code, but **it missed all rounding and precision defects**.

papers.title: A latent control model for realistic rodent motion
papers.abstract: The development of embodied models of animal behavior is a major goal of the neuro-AI community. Embodied models will enhance our ability to make direct comparisons between biological and artificial agents. To make such comparisons effective, though, we need embodied models that actually move like animals. Previous work has developed virtual animal bodies and techniques for training realistic motion through imitation. However, to date, there is no system for embodied animal modeling that produces natural movements both during trained goal-directed behavior, and during exploration driven by random generation. Here, we introduce Simulated Control via Augmented Motor Priors for Embodied Reinforcement learning (SCAMPER), a system for training an embodied virtual rat model, enabling natural movements during both goal-directed behavior and random exploration. SCAMPER uses a variational architecture with two distinct priors, a motion prior for control and a behavior prior for exploration. We show that combining both of these priors allows SCAMPER to generate realistic behavior during exploration and exploit the task structure effectively. SCAMPER can also learn from sparse rewards as a result of the diverse movements induced by the behavior prior, allowing the system to model realistic sparse-reward tasks from experimental neuroscience. Altogether, SCAMPER provides the neuro-AI community with an effective new system for training embodied models of rodents on realistic tasks.
papers.summary: Comparing biological and artificial agents in neuroscience requires embodied models that actually move like animals, both during trained tasks and during free exploration. `SCAMPER` (Simulated Control via Augmented Motor Priors for Embodied Reinforcement learning) trains a virtual rat with a variational architecture that has two priors: a motion prior for control and a behavior prior for exploration. Combining the two produces **realistic movement during random exploration while still exploiting task structure**, and the diverse movements from the behavior prior let the model learn sparse-reward tasks drawn from experimental neuroscience.

papers.title: VPFlow: Value-Predictive Planning with Imperfect World Models for Offline Goal Reaching
papers.abstract: Offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning enables skill acquisition by reaching any goal from any state without dense rewards. Model-based methods allow for planning by scaling test-time compute to solve complex tasks. Combining both holds appealing promise for pre-training on suboptimal demonstrations and zero-shot adaptation via goal specification and planning. Yet existing methods assume effective planning requires accurate next-state prediction in pixel or latent space. In this work, we show that value prediction is more useful for planning, whereas accurate state prediction is often unnecessary. Our key insight is that offline goal reaching naturally admits a closed-form Monte Carlo return, enabling value regression to replace temporal-difference bootstrapping. We use this return as the sole supervision for latent world models: imagined latents are trained to predict goal-reaching value rather than match future states, implicitly preventing representation collapse. These planning-oriented representations let imperfect world models imagine on the level sets of value field beyond dataset transitions. We then present VPFlow, a value-predictive planner that pairs the world models with a one-step flow policy and plans in its noise space via evolutionary search. It enables policy improvement with imagined generalized advantage and reduces out-of-distribution queries common in action-space planning. On 30 state and pixel OGBench datasets, VPFlow surpasses model-free baselines by at least 30.3 and 10.1 percentage points in success rate, respectively, and outperforms latent planners LeWorldModel, PLDM, and TD-MPC2. It achieves this despite a latent prediction error orders of magnitude larger than with state prediction, while minimizing this error lowers success rate. This demonstrates that value-predictive representations, not exact state prediction, are what offline planning requires.
papers.summary: The authors argue that model-based planning for offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning needs value prediction rather than accurate next-state prediction. Offline goal reaching admits a closed-form Monte Carlo return, so latent world models are trained only to predict goal-reaching value instead of matching future states, which also prevents representation collapse. `VPFlow` pairs these models with a one-step flow policy and plans in the policy's noise space via evolutionary search. On 30 `OGBench` datasets, it **beats model-free baselines by at least 30.3 points (state inputs) and 10.1 points (pixel inputs) in success rate** and outperforms `LeWorldModel`, `PLDM` and `TD-MPC2`. It does this despite much larger latent prediction error, and reducing that error actually lowers success.

papers.title: When Does Hate Transfer? A Large-Scale Study of Cross-Lingual Hate Speech Detection
papers.abstract: Effective detection of hate content is essential for maintaining healthy online communities, yet performance can vary substantially across languages. This work investigates a core practical question: Can training data from one language support hate-speech detection in another language with comparable performance? To answer this question, we conduct a large-scale study across 14 languages. \change{We observe consistent patterns in which certain language pairs transfer more effectively than others. Among the factors we measure, linguistic similarity is the strongest predictor of these patterns, with temporal overlap and dataset-size difference playing smaller roles. These measurable factors do not fully explain the observed patterns; a complementary qualitative analysis suggests that shared cultural cues and communicative norms may be associated with some of the remaining cases, particularly within several clusters. We present this cultural interpretation as a hypothesis from qualitative inspection rather than a measured cause.}{} Our analysis includes low-resource languages, offering practical insights into when cross-lingual transfer can support them and where its limitations emerge. These findings inform the design of more reliable multilingual hate-detection systems.
papers.summary: The study asks whether hate-speech training data in one language can support detection in another, testing transfer across 14 languages, including low-resource ones. Some language pairs transfer consistently better than others, and **linguistic similarity is the strongest measured predictor**, with temporal overlap and dataset-size differences playing smaller roles. A qualitative analysis suggests shared cultural cues and communicative norms may explain some remaining patterns, which the authors present as a hypothesis rather than a measured cause.

papers.title: TEX: Test-Time Scaling Testing Agents via Execution-based Cross-Validation
papers.abstract: Test-case generation is critical but remains challenging for language models. Existing test-time scaling methods either isolate candidates or aggregate traces, which do not scale to long-horizon tasks. We present TEX, a collaborative test-time scaling framework based on execution-driven cross-validation. TEX parallelizes agents to generate tests and patches, cross-executing each test against every patch to form a $K \times K$ feedback matrix. Agents use their matrix slices for refinement, enabling objective validation without verbose trace sharing. On SWT-Bench Verified, TEX achieves 86.4%, establishing a new state-of-the-art and improving +9.0% over single-agent baselines. Moreover, even random selection from TEX outputs (84.4%) surpasses the previous SOTA (84.0%), showing collaborative execution feedback improves solution quality, not just best-case samples. Our results highlight execution-grounded feedback as an effective scaling mechanism for long-horizon agentic tasks.
papers.summary: Generating test cases is hard for language models, and existing test-time scaling methods either treat candidates in isolation or share long reasoning traces, neither of which scales to long-horizon tasks. `TEX` runs parallel agents that each produce tests and patches, executes every test against every patch to form a K×K feedback matrix, and lets each agent refine its work using its slice of that matrix. On `SWT-Bench Verified` it reaches **86.4%, a new state of the art and 9.0 points above single-agent baselines**. Even randomly picking one `TEX` output scores 84.4%, above the previous best of 84.0%, which indicates that shared execution feedback improves typical outputs and not just the best sample.

papers.title: Vulnerability Analysis for Safe Multi-Agent Reinforcement
papers.abstract: Safe Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (SMARL) aims to learn cooperative control policies under prescribed safety constraints. Al- though existing SMARL methods focus on enforcing safety during policy optimization, their vulnerability remains largely unexplored. This paper investigates inference-time observation attacks against SMARL, where an adversary perturbs the observations of a subset of agents, thereby altering the actions produced by their policies. We propose MinMax Attack, an attack framework that jointly selects adversarial target actions for compromised agents while accounting for the Cooperative Resistance of benign agents.
