We further derive a bound on the induced safety cost and characterize its relation- ship with the Compromised-Agent Budget and the Perturbation Budget. Experiments across multiple safety-critical multi-agent benchmarks and representative state-of-the-art SMARL algorithms show that MinMax Attack induces substantially higher safety costs than existing attack baselines while preserving task reward, thereby reducing its detectability and achieving both attack effectiveness and stealthiness.
papers.summary: Safe multi-agent reinforcement learning (`SMARL`) methods enforce safety constraints during training, but their robustness to attacks at inference time has received little study. `MinMax Attack` perturbs the observations of a subset of agents, choosing adversarial target actions for the compromised agents while accounting for how the benign agents will cooperatively resist. The authors bound the resulting safety cost in terms of how many agents are compromised and how large the perturbations are. Across several safety-critical benchmarks and state-of-the-art `SMARL` algorithms, the attack **induces substantially higher safety costs than existing attacks while leaving task reward intact**, which makes it harder to detect.

papers.title: Stronger artificial intelligence breakthroughs hasten their own exhaustion
papers.abstract: Progress in artificial intelligence is widely assumed to scale with effort: more researchers, papers and investment should accelerate discovery. Theories of technological growth instead locate the difficulty of discovery in the space of ideas. Here we show that neither scale nor space is enough: breakthroughs depend on diverse attention, which collective concentration can deplete. Across 36 years of computer science, we analyze 7.2 million papers, 73,089 peer reviews and 3.7 million researchers and their topic shifts. The field expanded while its attention narrowed sharply after the Transformer. Over half of topic-shifting researchers moved into AI, especially mid-career ones, and reviewer confidence fell by a full point on a 5-point scale. Each successive breakthrough, from AlexNet to large language models, raised the field's carrying capacity for ideas but was followed by steeper exhaustion of those ideas. Bigger breakthroughs capture attention more completely, depleting the diversity their successors may draw upon. Structural biology shows the same cycle after cryo-EM and AlphaFold. Simulations show how well-intentioned and widely used policies such as reciprocal reviewing empower prolific authors and further narrow what the field accepts. We call for institutions that protect diverse attention in artificial intelligence rather than reward concentration on the winning paradigm.
papers.summary: The authors argue that progress in AI depends on diverse research attention, not just more effort or a larger space of ideas, and that concentration on a winning paradigm depletes it. They analyze 36 years of computer science: 7.2 million papers, 73,089 peer reviews and 3.7 million researchers. The field grew but its attention narrowed sharply after the Transformer, over half of topic-switching researchers moved into AI, and reviewer confidence fell by a full point on a 5-point scale. Each breakthrough from `AlexNet` to large language models raised the field's capacity for ideas but **was followed by steeper exhaustion of those ideas**, a cycle also seen in structural biology after cryo-EM and `AlphaFold`. Simulations suggest policies such as reciprocal reviewing further narrow what the field accepts.

papers.title: Generalizing Multimodal Foundational Models in Context-Driven Class Incremental Learning
papers.abstract: Class-Incremental Learning (CIL) aims to learn new classes continuously without forgetting the previously learned ones. Recent works in CIL have significantly advanced across various modalities; however, at the intersection of audio-visual modality, this problem remains underexplored. While representations from multimodal foundational models (MFMs) encapsulate rich static priors, our preliminary analysis shows that these representations struggle in incremental settings. Motivated by this, we propose a framework that generalizes frozen MFMs to audio-visual CIL. Specifically, we leverage their dense audio and visual representations and employ an attention-based contextual guidance module, in which the audio representations serve as task-stable contextual guidance for the visual representations, enabling effective class recognition in the incremental setting. To further mitigate catastrophic forgetting and preserve stability across tasks, we employ feature- and logit-level distillation, which are primarily responsible for the reduced forgetting. Extensive evaluations across various audio-visual CIL benchmarks demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Code is available at https://github.com/avigupta2798/MFM-CIL.
papers.summary: Class-incremental learning (CIL) means learning new classes over time without forgetting old ones, and it is underexplored for combined audio and video. The authors find that frozen multimodal foundation model (MFM) representations struggle in this incremental setting. Their framework uses an attention-based module in which dense audio features act as task-stable context guiding the visual features, and adds feature- and logit-level distillation, which accounts for most of the reduction in forgetting. The approach **consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods across audio-visual CIL benchmarks**.

papers.title: Evaluating Context Compaction on the Questions That Come Later
papers.abstract: Language-model agents compact their context for the question at hand, but the compacted context must also serve questions that come later. We evaluate compaction on these later questions, using four corpora that annotate the evidence of several questions per text and recorded agent trajectories, and compare every method with random deletion at the same budget. On MultiRC, keeping the sentences that gpt-6-luna (through the OpenAI Decisions API) judges necessary for the current question raises its accuracy on that question by 11.4 points at 25% of the tokens. On the later questions, however, no method that selects sentences for the current question does detectably better than deleting sentences at random. Deleting words instead of sentences does better: LLMLingua-2, which ignores the question, beats random sentence deletion at the same token count by 12.5 points on the later MultiRC questions. It keeps about twice random deletion's share of the evidence's content words, and at equal content-word retention its gain shrinks to 7.3 points (exploratory). On FEVER, label accuracy can overstate what the kept text supports: the gain of sentence selection is no longer detected when answers are scored against the kept evidence, and the 21.0-point gain of LLMLingua-2 is not shown to rest on the kept text. The ranking also depends on the setting: on Evidence Inference sentence selection beats LLMLingua-2 at a nominal 25% budget, and on $\tau$-bench trajectories, whose later tool calls need exact identifiers, it beats random deletion while LLMLingua-2 shows no detected gain. Scores on the question a compaction was made for do not reliably show how it serves later ones.
papers.summary: Agents compact their context for the question at hand, but the compacted text must also answer later questions. Using four corpora with multiple annotated questions per text and recorded agent trajectories, and comparing every method against random deletion at the same token budget, the study finds that keeping the sentences `gpt-6-luna` judges necessary raises current-question accuracy on `MultiRC` by 11.4 points at 25% of the tokens. On later questions, however, **no sentence-selection method detectably beats random sentence deletion**. Question-agnostic word-level compression with `LLMLingua-2` beats random deletion on later `MultiRC` questions by 12.5 points, partly because it keeps more evidence words. The ranking flips across settings: on `τ-bench` trajectories, where later tool calls need exact identifiers, sentence selection helps while `LLMLingua-2` shows no detected gain.

papers.title: Global Security Blind Spots: Translation as a Safety Bypass in Low-Resource Languages
papers.abstract: Large language models are deployed globally, yet safety alignment and evaluation remain concentrated in English: harmful requests refused in English can elicit unsafe completions when translated into low-resource languages. We evaluate ten widely deployed LLMs across 79 languages (English plus 78 low-resource) under a translation-bypass threat model, using a metric conditioned on English safety, which separates translation bypass from unsafety already present in English. English safety does not transfer reliably: conditioned on safe English completions, mean bypass rates range from 21.9% to 44.4%. Bypass risk concentrates in a subset of language families, a pattern broadly shared across models. The shared ordering is confounded with translation degeneracy, but its variation across models is significant and survives every control we apply. We also show that per-model bypass rates do not identify a stable ranking: nine of ten models change rank across three conditioning schemes that estimate the same quantity, with no change to any underlying response.
papers.summary: Safety alignment is concentrated in English, so harmful requests that models refuse in English may succeed once translated into low-resource languages. Ten widely deployed LLMs were tested across English plus 78 low-resource languages, using a metric conditioned on the model already answering safely in English, which separates translation bypass from unsafety the model already has in English. **Conditioned on a safe English completion, mean bypass rates range from 21.9% to 44.4%**, and risk concentrates in a subset of language families in a pattern broadly shared across models. Per-model rankings proved unstable: nine of ten models changed rank across three conditioning schemes that estimate the same quantity from identical responses.

papers.title: When Does an Added Planning Capability Create Operational Value? An Observable Evidence Standard
papers.abstract: Industrial artificial intelligence (AI) planning systems combine predictive models, optimization logic, controls, and governance rules, but improvement in the complete policy does not show whether one addition made an independent contribution or whether that contribution justifies its burden. We address this attribution problem with an observable evidence standard that separates opportunity to act, executed-plan change, operational consequence, equivalence, uncertainty, and operating scope. Using forecast-to-plan replay on Favorita, M5, and Walmart data, we apply the standard to heterogeneous planning additions. Three limits of single-indicator evaluation emerge. First, a composite policy can conceal negligible component contribution: one control changed only 15 of 681 executed plans. Second, changing execution does not guarantee stable benefit: the evaluated multi-period capability helped in several long-lead settings but was 7.6% more costly under tight capacity. Third, indirect evidence can prioritize review but cannot complete attribution. Independent runs produced different paths in 19 of 599 cases that a rule-based check predicted would be unchanged. Although a lower-cost diagnostic matched the full-evaluation winner in only 55.0% of cases, it selected an option within the $10^{-6}$ cost-equivalence tolerance in 79.5%; the remaining cases prevented the proxy from authorizing acceptance. These experiments establish capability-level contribution evidence; the organization completes the value decision by weighing it against implementation and sustaining burden. The resulting capability evidence record links the observations to validation, deployment scope, fallback, monitoring, redesign, and retirement decisions.
papers.summary: Industrial AI planning systems combine forecasting models, optimization, controls and governance rules, so an improvement in the whole system doesn't show whether any single added component contributed. The proposed evidence standard separates a component's opportunity to act, its changes to executed plans, the operational consequences, equivalence, uncertainty and operating scope. It is applied through forecast-to-plan replay on `Favorita`, `M5` and `Walmart` data. The experiments show that composite policies can hide negligible contributions (**one control changed only 15 of 681 executed plans**), that a component can help in some settings yet cost 7.6% more under tight capacity, and that a cheaper diagnostic picked the full evaluation's winner in only 55.0% of cases.

papers.title: Evolving Self-tuning Benchmarks for Long-Horizon Tool Use
papers.abstract: For AI assistants to move beyond simple chat interfaces and reliably assist users with applications like Gmail, Venmo, and Slack, we need to improve their tool-use capabilities. However, existing tool use benchmarks are still limited and difficult to scale because they rely on human supervision or are too domain-specific. To make data generation scalable, we propose, TURTLE (**T**ool **U**se **R**elated **T**asks with **L**ong-Horizon **E**volution), an Unsupervised Environment Design (UED) approach to evolve existing tasks using a proposer, a solver, and a feedback generator large language model agents. The proposer is rewarded for difficult yet solvable tasks based on the solver's empirical performance, and the feedback generator summarizes the solver's execution traces for the proposer to exploit. TURTLE produces evolving, self-tuning test suites adaptable to different environment requirements, from supporting user simulators and dense document retrieval to interacting across multiple apps. Empirical results on AppWorld, $\tau$-Bench, and AutomationBench using Gemma 4 31B-it show that the evolved tasks target the desired difficulty range (e.g., a 165\% increase in the percentage of hard tasks on AppWorld), increase task diversity (in terms of reasoning and simultaneous tool interactions), and elicit a broader range of failure modes than the original tasks.
papers.summary: Tool-use benchmarks for assistants working across apps like Gmail, Venmo and Slack are hard to scale because they depend on human supervision or are domain-specific. `TURTLE` uses Unsupervised Environment Design (UED) with three LLM agents: a proposer rewarded for creating tasks that are difficult yet solvable, a solver, and a feedback generator that summarizes the solver's execution traces for the proposer. Run with `Gemma 4 31B-it` on `AppWorld`, `τ-Bench` and `AutomationBench`, the evolved tasks hit the targeted difficulty range (**a 165% increase in the share of hard tasks on `AppWorld`**), are more diverse, and expose a broader range of failure modes than the originals.

papers.title: Steering Vision-Language Models for Visual-Contextual Privacy in Location Disclosure
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can infer sensitive information such as geolocation from subtle visual cues, creating privacy risks when responses disclose more detail than the visual context warrants. We study visual-contextual privacy in geolocation disclosure, where a VLM should reveal location information only at the granularity appropriate to the visual context depicted in the image. We first show that this contextually appropriate granularity is recoverable from pre-generation hidden states, even when generated responses are misaligned, with disclosure levels exhibiting an ordered structure along a common hidden-state direction. Motivated by this, we propose an inference-time route-and-steer framework: an ordinal granularity router maps visual-contextual privacy representations to a disclosure route, and a disclosure-level-conditioned steering module applies route-specific hidden-state interventions during decoding. Across four VLM backbones, our method improves visual-context-aware disclosure alignment, better balances over- and under-disclosure, and incurs only modest changes on general capability benchmarks. It further transfers to another dataset with a distinct data distribution and privacy-risk taxonomy.
papers.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) can infer a photo's location from subtle cues and may disclose more detail than the image's context warrants. The authors show that **the appropriate level of location detail can be read from the model's hidden states before generation**, even when the actual response gets it wrong, and that disclosure levels are ordered along a common hidden-state direction. Their inference-time route-and-steer framework uses an ordinal router to choose a disclosure level, then applies level-specific hidden-state interventions during decoding. Across four VLM backbones it improves context-appropriate disclosure, balances over- and under-disclosure with only modest effects on general capability benchmarks, and transfers to a second dataset with a different privacy-risk taxonomy.

papers.title: Unsupervised Tool Evolution for Coding Agents in Data-Lake Analytics
papers.abstract: Coding agents can answer analytical questions over a data lake by discovering, cleaning, and joining the relevant data. However, they discard this work after each question and redo it from scratch for the next one. Tool evolution, which automatically builds and refines reusable tools across tasks, is a natural fit for this repetition. Since a ground-truth label for a data-lake question requires an expert to solve it first, we consider the unsupervised setting. We propose TEAL (Tool Evolution for Analytics over data Lakes), which evolves a library of tools and usage skills for a given Worker agent without labels. Two agents propose tools from complementary evidence, an Explorer from the data lake itself and a Critic from Worker trajectories. A proposed change is kept only if the Worker adopts the tool on a rerun without extra steps and any changed answer is supported by trajectory evidence. We also introduce TEAL-Q, which generates synthetic questions for tool evolution when real ones are unavailable. We evaluate on KramaBench and LakeQA with four Worker LLMs under step budgets, which cap the number of steps the Worker may take per question. With a tight budget of 10 or 15 steps, TEAL improves every Worker on both benchmarks, lifting Sonnet-5 at 15 steps by 9.3 points on KramaBench and 21.7 points on LakeQA. A tighter budget also yields better feedback for evolution. For example, Sonnet-5's LakeQA library evolved at 20 steps and deployed unchanged at 30 steps scores 68.3, above both the baseline (59.6) and a library evolved directly at 30 steps (64.2). Additionally, a library evolved on synthetic questions performs comparably to one evolved on real questions. These results show that useful tools can be evolved without labels, and hopefully inspire future work on what to evolve and how to obtain feedback in unsupervised agent evolution.
papers.summary: Coding agents that answer analytical questions over a data lake redo the same discovery, cleaning and joining work for every question. `TEAL` (Tool Evolution for Analytics over data Lakes) evolves a library of reusable tools and usage skills without labels. An Explorer agent proposes tools based on the data lake and a Critic proposes them based on the Worker agent's trajectories. A change is kept only if the Worker adopts it on a rerun without extra steps and any changed answer is supported by trajectory evidence. With tight step budgets, `TEAL` improves all four Worker LLMs on `KramaBench` and `LakeQA`, **lifting `Sonnet-5` by 9.3 and 21.7 points respectively at 15 steps**. Libraries evolved on synthetic questions from `TEAL-Q` perform comparably to ones evolved on real questions.

papers.title: Modeling Authentic Research Trajectories: A Graph View of Research Ideation
papers.abstract: The research idea in a published paper is rarely the project's initial idea. Between the two lies a closed-loop process in which researchers run experiments, derive insights, identify challenges, explore the literature, and revise the idea, with each step motivated by evidence and reasoning they can articulate. We call the path one idea takes through this process, with the evidence and reasoning behind each step, its authentic research trajectory. Although it underlies every scientific contribution, it is rarely recorded. Existing LLM-based research agents generate an idea once, refine it against reviews, literature, or their own experimental results, or search over candidate ideas and experiments. In all of them the text of the idea evolves, while the evidence and reasoning that connected one version to the next are discarded. We propose the Research Progress Graph (RPG), a representation of authentic and complete research trajectories. An RPG records the evolution of an idea as typed research states connected by cognitive transitions, each annotated with a temporal index and the reasoning behind it, which makes this evolution an explicit object of study. We ground the representation in authentic trajectories whose steps their authors justify in annotations and papers. Comparing the representations of thirty-five research agents with the RPG, we find that each is an incomplete RPG; none keeps the state that changed, the evidence that changed it, and the reasoning connecting them as one evolving record. Modeling ideation with the RPG changes how research agents should be designed, evaluated, and trained. Agents predict the next research state instead of a complete idea, ideas are evaluated as trajectories instead of final texts, and authentic trajectories serve as training data. These directions shift research agents from generating static ideas to modeling how ideas evolve.
papers.summary: The idea in a published paper usually differs from where the project began, and the experiments, insights and literature that reshaped it along the way are rarely recorded. The proposed Research Progress Graph (`RPG`) represents this trajectory as typed research states connected by cognitive transitions, each annotated with a time index and the reasoning behind it, grounded in trajectories whose authors justified each step. Comparing 35 LLM research agents against `RPG`, the authors find **every agent captures only an incomplete version**: none keeps the changed state, the evidence that changed it and the connecting reasoning together. They argue agents should predict the next research state, be evaluated on whole trajectories, and train on authentic trajectories.

papers.title: An LLM-Based Agent for Legal Compliance Assessment: Architecture, Memory, and Evaluation in a Canadian and Quebec Context
papers.abstract: Checking whether a text complies with a body of law is slow when done by hand and fragile when done with keyword rules. This paper presents ComplianceAgent, the legal compliance sub-agent of COMPASS, a multi-agent framework that evaluates texts along four axes: digital sovereignty, carbon impact, compliance, and ethics. The agent relies on a large language model that scores a text on a fixed rubric, grounds its judgment in a reference legal corpus, and, when the score falls at or below a critical threshold, runs a corrective chain made of self-healing rewrites, a compliance label, an explainability report, and escalation to a human reviewer. We describe what the language model does at each step, how the memory of the agent is organized, and how the same implementation can be pointed at different reference corpora. We evaluate the agent in a Canadian and Quebec context, on a corpus of thirteen legal instruments that brings together federal and provincial texts, international treaties, and municipal documents of the City of Trois-Rivi\`eres. The evaluation relies on a hand-annotated gold standard of fifteen texts and combines classification metrics, a repeated-query stability test, retrieval precision, and a composite score. On this gold standard the agent separates every conforming text from every non-conforming one, its scores remain stable under repeated queries, and the index returns relevant passages.
papers.summary: Manual legal compliance checking is slow and keyword rules are brittle, so the authors built `ComplianceAgent`, the compliance sub-agent of `COMPASS`, a multi-agent framework that also scores texts on digital sovereignty, carbon impact, and ethics. The agent uses a large language model to score a text against a fixed rubric, grounds the judgment in a reference legal corpus, and triggers a corrective chain when the score is at or below a critical threshold: self-healing rewrites, a compliance label, an explainability report, and escalation to a human reviewer. Tested on a corpus of thirteen Canadian, Quebec, international, and municipal legal instruments with a hand-annotated gold standard of fifteen texts, the agent **separates every conforming text from every non-conforming one**. Its scores also stay stable under repeated queries, and retrieval returns relevant passages.

papers.title: Refuses When Asked, Complies When Acting: A Runtime Safety Check for Robot Control Loops
papers.abstract: Frontier models can control robots through agent harnesses that loop on one question: what motion comes next toward the user's goal? We show that this default loop carries out harmful instructions. With GPT-6 Astra controlling a low-cost SO-101 arm through the Inspect Robots harness on three household tasks whose hazard is common knowledge, such as "put the knife in the toy basket", the policy refused 0% of 15 trials, attempted the harm every time, and completed it in 27%. Its one exit, give_up, is meant for goals that cannot be achieved, and it never cited the hazard. We add an optional runtime safety check to the loop: before the first motion, the model is asked whether it would carry out the instruction, given the same camera frames. The check would have stopped all 15 hazardous instructions, including the 4 that completed the harm, and flagged none of the 15 harmless controls. Code and data: https://github.com/Arnav-Gr0ver/Refuses-When-Asked-Complies-When-Acting.
papers.summary: When frontier models control robots through an agent harness that keeps asking which motion comes next, they carry out harmful household instructions they would refuse if asked directly. With `GPT-6 Astra` driving a low-cost `SO-101` arm through the `Inspect Robots` harness on tasks such as putting a knife in a toy basket, the policy **refused 0% of 15 hazardous trials**, attempted the harm every time, and completed it in 27% of trials. The authors add an optional runtime check that asks the model, before the first motion and with the same camera frames, whether it would carry out the instruction. This check would have stopped all 15 hazardous instructions and flagged none of the 15 harmless controls.

papers.title: Exposing Vulnerability Monoculture Through Systemic Adversarial Robustness
papers.abstract: Beneath the apparent diversity of foundation models lies an increasingly homogeneous technical stack of common training pipelines, distillation methods, and data. These shared algorithmic choices can expose an otherwise distinct model ecosystem to concentrated risks leading to a vulnerability monoculture. Yet current practice in assessing adversarial robustness is restricted to individual robustness scores and attack transfer rates, leaving open the unexplored fundamental question: how many attacks suffice for catastrophic widespread compromise? In this paper, we investigate the empirical nature of shared vulnerabilities within a model pool and introduce Systemic Adversarial Robustness (SAR), a novel measure of shared vulnerability of a model pool through the attack diversity needed to exploit it. Specifically, SAR interpolates between single-attack transferability and independent per-model robustness: small values reveal a vulnerability monoculture, whereas large values indicate that failures are dispersed across models. We theoretically formulate SAR as a partial set-cover problem with provable approximation guarantees---enabling the development of scalable algorithms to empirically measure the systemic adversarial robustness. We empirically test the shared vulnerability of vision and large language models and characterize their shared collective vulnerability curve. Specifically, we demonstrate that model pools distilled from DeepSeek-R1 and Claude Opus 4.6 exhibit lower estimated systemic robustness than their corresponding parent pools, revealing a potential systemic cost of frontier-model distillation. Our framework seeks to establish vulnerability monoculture as a measurable target for a more wholistic adversarial evaluation of model populations.
papers.summary: Foundation models increasingly share training pipelines, distillation methods, and data, which raises the risk of a vulnerability monoculture where a few attacks compromise many models at once. The authors introduce `Systemic Adversarial Robustness` (`SAR`), which measures how many distinct attacks are needed to compromise a pool of models; it interpolates between single-attack transferability and independent per-model robustness. They formulate SAR as a partial set-cover problem with provable approximation guarantees, which gives scalable algorithms for measuring it. Experiments on vision models and large language models show that **model pools distilled from `DeepSeek-R1` and `Claude Opus 4.6` have lower systemic robustness than their parent pools**, which points to a possible systemic cost of distilling from frontier models.

papers.title: LiBRA: Logit Fingerprints for Byzantine-Robust Client Selection in Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Byzantine-robust aggregation shields federated learning from malicious updates, but the rules that filter out suspect updates do so by comparing clients' parameter vectors. That comparison requires access to every client's update, which secure aggregation exists to withhold, costs $O(n^2 d)$ in the parameter dimension $d$, and is defined only between clients that share an architecture. We propose LiBRA, which compares clients on what their models compute rather than on the parameters that compute them, using a fingerprint of $C^2$ values for $C$ classes, the class-conditional logit response of each client's model to pseudo-patterns optimised against it. We instantiate LiBRA as variants of Krum, Multi-Krum and Bulyan that change only what the dissimilarity score is computed on. On Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10 with three architectures and four backdoor and label-manipulation attacks under i.i.d. partitions, each variant holds every attack its parent holds, and on identical client updates under a backdoor attack the fingerprint ranks malicious clients within 0.006 AUC of the full parameter vector. The variants thus match the robustness of the rules they extend, while their trust decision reads no client parameter, compares up to 49,090 times fewer values, and can by construction compare clients whose architectures differ, at the cost of one pattern optimisation per client per round.
papers.summary: Byzantine-robust aggregation in federated learning filters malicious client updates by comparing parameter vectors, which conflicts with secure aggregation, costs quadratic time in clients times parameters, and only works when all clients share an architecture. `LiBRA` instead compares clients by a small fingerprint of class-conditional logit responses to pseudo-patterns optimized against each client's model, and is instantiated as variants of `Krum`, `Multi-Krum`, and `Bulyan`. On `Fashion-MNIST` and `CIFAR-10` across three architectures and four backdoor and label-manipulation attacks, each variant holds every attack its parent holds. The fingerprint ranks malicious clients within 0.006 AUC of full parameter vectors while **comparing up to 49,090 times fewer values**, and it can compare clients with different architectures, at the cost of one pattern optimization per client per round.

papers.title: On the Limits of Scale: Inverse Scaling in Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Scaling laws suggest that increasing model size, training data, and compute generally yields monotonic performance improvements. While this often holds at the aggregate level, we present systematic evidence that vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit inverse scaling at the subtask level: specific question categories on which larger models perform worse than smaller counterparts within the same model family. We evaluate 19 models from four distinct model families across eight multimodal benchmarks (nine evaluation splits), answering 29,386 questions per model, 558,334 model-question evaluations in total. Using per-question pairwise analysis across all model pairs in each family, we identify 375 subtask-model-pair combinations exhibiting inverse scaling, spanning 4,342 unique queries where a smaller model answers correctly but a larger model fails, and we find that these patterns replicate across independently developed architectures. We identify 13 subtask-dataset pairs that show inverse scaling across multiple families, consistent with the phenomenon being task-driven rather than model-specific. The most affected domains in our study include multi-image spatial reasoning, visual perception, and university-level STEM knowledge, with accuracy gaps exceeding 20 percentage points in several cases, while diagram understanding appears comparatively resistant. These findings challenge the assumption that increasing model size uniformly improves multimodal capabilities and suggest that model selection should be task-aware.
papers.summary: Scaling laws predict that bigger models do better, but this large-scale study of vision-language models (VLMs) finds systematic inverse scaling at the subtask level. The authors evaluated 19 models from four families on eight multimodal benchmarks (558,334 model-question evaluations) and ran per-question pairwise comparisons within each family. They identified 375 subtask and model-pair combinations, covering 4,342 queries, where a smaller model answers correctly and a larger sibling fails, and 13 subtask-dataset pairs where inverse scaling replicates across families, which suggests the effect is driven by the task. Multi-image spatial reasoning, visual perception, and university-level STEM knowledge are hit hardest, with **accuracy gaps above 20 percentage points** in several cases, while diagram understanding is comparatively resistant.

papers.title: Predictive Closure: A Set-Level Characterization of JEPA's Feature Selection
papers.abstract: In joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPA), an encoder and a predictor are trained together to produce a representation that minimizes the error in predicting the representation of the next observation. Because the representations of both the current and the next observation are learned, it is unclear which features they will include. Earlier characterizations describe the features JEPA selects in terms of their individual predictability, raising the concern that unpredictable features, like a traffic light, will not be encoded into the representation. However, the prediction error is also affected by the relationships between features, e.g., the light's color helps predict whether the traffic will stop. We propose the predictive closure characterization, which accounts for these relationships. Based on a reformulation of the JEPA training objective, we show that selection depends on properties of feature sets. This view agrees with earlier works when features evolve independently, but makes new predictions when they do not, for instance that a feature like the traffic light can still be retained. We test this characterization in controlled experiments, which show that unpredictable features can become better represented when they help predict other features, and that changing one feature's predictive relationships can affect how well others are represented. We also demonstrate implications for steering feature selection: targeting one feature with an auxiliary objective, or supplying it to the predictor as side information, can strengthen the representation of another feature whose future values it helps predict, so steering can be indirect.
papers.summary: In joint-embedding predictive architectures (`JEPA`), both the encoder and the predictor are learned, so it is unclear which features the representation keeps; earlier analyses judged features by their individual predictability, implying that unpredictable features would be dropped. The authors reformulate the training objective into a 'predictive closure' characterization, in which selection depends on properties of feature sets rather than of individual features. Controlled experiments show that **unpredictable features can be better represented when they help predict other features**, and that changing one feature's predictive relationships changes how well others are encoded. As a consequence, feature selection can be steered indirectly: an auxiliary objective or predictor side information that targets one feature can strengthen another.

papers.title: Trail-Weighted Influence Scores for Approximate Outcome Prediction in Bayesian Networks
papers.abstract: We study trail-weighted pruning of evidence for Bayesian-network prediction. A traversal enumerates the active trails from each evidence node to the outcome, scores each trail by the product of its edge strengths, and drops evidence whose score falls below a threshold. For collider-free networks (chains and forks) over binary variables, we show that the trail score equals the exact correlation between a trail's endpoints, that a chain and a fork with equal edge strengths have identical joint distributions, and that the pruned posterior is within a computable sum of per-trail terms of the exact posterior when each dropped trail lies in its own branch of the outcome node. We prove this bound, check it exhaustively on all small trees, and show that it fails when dropped trails share a branch. In simulations on random trees, thresholding trail scores gives 1.4 to 13 times lower error than random pruning of the same size. We also apply the score, as an unproven heuristic, to seven bnlearn networks with colliders and loops. Keeping the top half of the active evidence by trail score gives lower error than random pruning on all seven, but it is not clearly better than a mutual-information ranking, and scoring costs more than the inference it saves on six of the seven, so we show no speedup. Models trained on trail, graph and information features and tested on networks they never saw do not beat the trail score or mutual information, but trail features carry most of what they use and clearly outperform generic graph features. A bound for general networks is left to future work.
papers.summary: The authors study pruning evidence for Bayesian-network prediction by scoring each active trail from an evidence node to the outcome as the product of its edge strengths, then dropping evidence whose score falls below a threshold. For collider-free binary networks they prove that the trail score equals the exact endpoint correlation and that the pruned posterior stays within a computable bound when dropped trails lie in separate branches; they also show the bound fails when dropped trails share a branch. On random trees, thresholding gives **1.4 to 13 times lower error than random pruning** of the same size. On seven `bnlearn` networks with colliders and loops, the score beats random pruning but not clearly a mutual-information ranking, and scoring costs more than the inference it saves on six of the seven networks.

papers.title: Fundamental Impossibility Results in AI Safety: Trading Off between Desiderata
papers.abstract: Is there a fundamental tradeoff between desiderata for safe AI systems, such as harmlessness and helpfulness? We answer by formalizing the interaction between AI systems and users as a game with three players: a defender and an attacker that are computationally or informationally bounded, and an AI that provides public advice and is less constrained. Our main result shows that there is a fundamental tradeoff in providing advice that helps the defender while advice remains public. We also consider whether the information that the AI shares can be manipulated to benefit only the defender and conclude with a discussion of how we can use these results in designing safer AI systems.
papers.summary: The authors ask whether safety goals such as harmlessness and helpfulness fundamentally conflict, and model AI-user interaction as a three-player game. In the game, a computationally or informationally bounded defender and attacker both receive public advice from a less constrained AI. The main result proves **a fundamental tradeoff in giving advice that helps the defender while that advice remains public**. The authors also ask whether shared information can be shaped to benefit only the defender, and discuss what the results imply for designing safer AI systems.

papers.title: REM: What to Store, When to Recall, What to Forget in Experience Memory for Coding Agents
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents now autonomously complete long-horizon tasks, such as repository-level coding, through hundreds of think-act steps, yet the experience each run produces is rarely reused on the next. Prior memory systems concentrate on retrieval, finding the most relevant past trajectory. Retrieval cannot observe the running agent, so it cannot decide whether the agent needs an experience, at which point, or for how long. We introduce REM (Reusable Experience Memory), a framework that manages the memory lifecycle from inside the agent's think-act loop through three explicit decisions. What to store: each completed trajectory is consolidated into a phase-structured document, two orders of magnitude smaller than the trajectory. When to recall: the document is injected at the start of the task; the costlier implementation record is withheld until an in-loop gate detects the agent struggling. What to forget: the record is evicted after a single exposure. On repository-level bug fixing (SWE-ContextBench Lite), REM retrieves the related trajectory more accurately than every state-of-the-art memory system (68.7% vs. 55.6% match@1) and improves, in every replicate, end-task resolution (27.6% vs. 24.9%) at 17% lower cost. Injecting the same experience as a summary or raw trajectory, even when oracle-retrieved, does not. Ablating any of the three decisions reduces resolution. Altogether, these results demonstrate that the bottleneck in experience reuse is not retrieval fidelity but how experience is stored and governed across its lifecycle, opening a control-theoretic perspective on agent memory.
papers.summary: Coding agents rarely reuse experience from earlier runs, and existing memory systems focus on retrieval, which cannot see whether, when, or for how long the running agent needs a past experience. `REM` (Reusable Experience Memory) manages memory from inside the agent's think-act loop through three decisions. It stores each trajectory as a compact phase-structured document about two orders of magnitude smaller than the trajectory, injects that document at task start while withholding the costlier implementation record until an in-loop gate detects the agent struggling, and evicts the record after one exposure. On `SWE-ContextBench Lite`, REM matches related trajectories more accurately than prior memory systems (68.7% vs. 55.6% match@1) and **raises resolution from 24.9% to 27.6% at 17% lower cost**, whereas injecting the same experience as a summary or raw trajectory does not help, even with oracle retrieval.

papers.title: Correcting Attribution Patching with a Few Exact Measurements
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability asks which language model components matter for a behavior, and activation patching answers by changing one component's activation and measuring its effect, at a cost growing with components and prompts. Attribution patching estimates these effects from one gradient pass, but its estimates can be far off, and verifying each one restores the cost. Can the structure of these errors reduce this cost? We propose Guided-AP, which uses a few exact measurements to reveal attribution patching's errors and correct unmeasured estimates. On a single prompt, many components' errors share one sign, so a small exact sample yields one correction for the rest. Over many prompts of one task, components are misestimated similarly, so a few measured prompts show what to verify and how to correct each component's average effect. Our analysis shows that choosing what to verify needs error size, while correction also needs sign. On a single prompt, the correction lowers error by up to 26% across three behaviors at the compute of verifying the largest estimates and also on larger models. Over many prompts, learned corrections cut the error of average effects on factual completion by 75% to 79%, repaying their cost in long analyses.
papers.summary: Activation patching measures exactly how much each language model component matters for a behavior, but its cost grows with the number of components and prompts; attribution patching approximates it from one gradient pass but can be badly wrong. `Guided-AP` uses a few exact measurements to estimate and correct those errors. It exploits two patterns: on a single prompt many components' errors share a sign, and across prompts of one task the same components are misestimated in similar ways. On single prompts the correction lowers error by up to 26% across three behaviors at the compute cost of verifying only the largest estimates, and over many prompts learned corrections **cut the error of average effects on factual completion by 75% to 79%**.

papers.title: When PTQ Calibration Helps or Hurts: Dose-Driven Collapse and Validation-Gated Abstention in Quantized Text Embedders
papers.abstract: Learned post-training quantization (PTQ) calibration fits quantizer parameters on a small calibration set, and for a text embedder the natural supervision is retrieval relevance. We ask two questions that are usually conflated: how far to calibrate, and whether to calibrate at all. Across three embedders (e5-base-v2, BGE-M3, EmbeddingGemma-300m) at 4-bit weight quantization, 161 calibration runs, the outcome of a fixed procedure ranges from a gain to catastrophic degradation, and the driver is the dose of the update, measured as the functional displacement D_func of the quantized model from its uncalibrated start. On EmbeddingGemma the same learning-rate grid gives +1.47 to -71.53 points of in-domain NDCG@10 change; a label-free cosine objective collapses at the same dose (-69.52 vs -71.63), so the collapse is a property of learnable calibration rather than of retrieval supervision. Objective sensitivity is heterogeneous: on e5, ranking calibration is substantially more robust than cosine at matched displacement (+14.16 +/- 4.34 pp, 95% t-CI [+3.37, +24.96], three paired slates), whereas on BGE-M3 the ordering is directionally opposite but unresolved ([-5.18, +2.38]). Dose is the main axis but not a sufficient statistic: equal D_func reached along different paths differs by up to 1.61 pp. We therefore treat calibration as an optional intervention. A pre-registered rule that accepts a checkpoint only when a per-query paired confidence interval on a 25% calibration-validation split clears the uncalibrated baseline was run on 6 independent slates and five arms. It never selected a checkpoint below its slate's baseline (0 harmful selections in 30 decisions), retained 8 of 11 beneficial updates, and paid a mean oracle regret of 1.52 pp with one abstention that forfeited 11.13 pp, a safety-opportunity trade-off, not a free improvement. We report what remains open, including label efficiency.
papers.summary: Learned post-training quantization (PTQ) calibration fits quantizer parameters on a small dataset, and the authors find it can either help or catastrophically hurt 4-bit text embedders (`e5-base-v2`, `BGE-M3`, `EmbeddingGemma-300m`) across 161 calibration runs. The main driver is the 'dose' of the update, measured as how far the calibrated model is functionally displaced from its uncalibrated start. On `EmbeddingGemma` one learning-rate grid ranges from a gain of 1.47 to a loss of 71.53 points of NDCG@10, and a label-free objective collapses at the same dose. The authors therefore treat calibration as optional and use a pre-registered rule that accepts a checkpoint only if a paired confidence interval on held-out validation data beats the uncalibrated baseline; this rule **never selected a harmful checkpoint in 30 decisions** and retained 8 of 11 beneficial updates, at a mean regret of 1.52 points.

papers.title: Unified Sharp Bounds on Probabilities of Causation
papers.abstract: Probabilities of causation (PoCs) have developed steadily, from the binary measures first introduced by Pearl to the non-binary setting recently studied by Shu et al. As the theory has matured, PoCs have found applications in a growing range of areas, including personalized medicine, marketing and legal attribution. Shu et al. proposed closed-form bounds for multi-valued treatments and outcomes and proved them valid, but left their sharpness in high dimensions open. We close this gap with a mathematical proof. We further show that $\PNS$, $\PSub$, $\PRep$ and $\PN$ are all special cases of a single, more general formula. Combined with their equivalence classes, this settles the question of sharp bounds for discrete PoCs from experimental and observational data: in every dimension, they are given in closed form by a single theorem.
papers.summary: Probabilities of causation (PoCs), which quantify questions such as whether a treatment was necessary or sufficient for an outcome, are used in personalized medicine, marketing, and legal attribution. Earlier work gave valid closed-form bounds for multi-valued treatments and outcomes but left their sharpness in high dimensions open. The authors prove those bounds are sharp and show that several existing measures (`PNS`, `PSub`, `PRep`, and `PN`) are special cases of one general formula. Together with their equivalence classes, this result means **sharp bounds for discrete PoCs from experimental and observational data are given in closed form by a single theorem in every dimension**.

papers.title: ProMemAgent: Long-Horizon Proactive Assistance with Context-Aware Prospective Memory from Sensory Perceptions
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are moving beyond reactive responses toward proactive assistance that anticipates user needs without explicit requests. However, existing proactive agents primarily address immediate needs, while many everyday situations involve delayed intentions that can only be acted on hours or days later. Humans handle such intentions through prospective memory, the ability to remember to act on an intention when the right moment arises. In this paper, we introduce ProMemAgent, the first proactive agent to incorporate prospective memory over everyday sensory contexts for long-horizon proactive assistance. ProMemAgent organizes past sensory perceptions (e.g., egocentric video and audio) into context-aware memory, generating prospective cues and linking earlier events with subsequent developments for future retrieval. Given the current context, it retrieves relevant past events and performs memory-augmented proactive reasoning to determine whether assistance is needed. We further introduce CPMBench, the first benchmark for evaluating long-horizon proactive assistance over sensory contexts, comprising 1,000 instances across eight everyday categories. Extensive experiments show that ProMemAgent achieves the best memory retrieval performance and consistently outperforms all baselines on long-horizon proactive assistance.
papers.summary: Proactive LLM agents usually address immediate needs, but many everyday intentions can only be acted on hours or days later, which in humans relies on prospective memory. `ProMemAgent` organizes past sensory perceptions such as egocentric video and audio into context-aware memory, generates prospective cues, and links earlier events to later developments. Given the current context, it retrieves relevant past events and reasons over them to decide whether to offer help. The authors also release `CPMBench`, a 1,000-instance benchmark covering eight everyday categories, on which **`ProMemAgent` achieves the best memory retrieval and outperforms all baselines** on long-horizon proactive assistance.

papers.title: More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents
papers.abstract: LLM agents can improve across tasks without updating model parameters by storing experience from their own executions in external memory and reusing it to guide later decisions. A central design question is whether to retain only observed trajectories and outcomes or also the rules, summaries, and skills inferred from them. Retaining these abstractions allows agents to reuse strategies without repeatedly deriving them from raw trajectories. However, errors in stored abstractions can propagate to subsequent decisions through retrieval and reuse. They can also shape execution trajectories, which then become the basis for new abstractions that reproduce the original errors. We term this feedback mechanism error reproduction: errors are regenerated through a cycle of abstraction, execution, and re-abstraction, extending their persistence beyond direct reuse of the original faulty knowledge. We propose Anti-Persistence, a memory design that accumulates trajectories and outcomes while reconstructing task-specific guidance on demand. An adaptive selector uses prior outcomes to decide whether and how to synthesize guidance, which is discarded after execution. This prevents its direct reuse as a stored object, although indirect feedback through retained trajectories remains possible. Across different benchmarks and backbones, Anti-Persistence achieves higher overall held-out success and the lowest average LLM-call cost among the evaluated memory designs. These results support separating experience accumulation from abstraction persistence in memorybased self-improvement.
papers.summary: LLM agents that store rules, summaries, and skills inferred from their own past runs can suffer from what the authors call error reproduction: a flawed abstraction shapes new trajectories, which are then re-abstracted into the same error, so mistakes outlive the original faulty memory. Their `Anti-Persistence` design keeps only trajectories and outcomes in memory. An adaptive selector decides from past outcomes whether and how to synthesize task-specific guidance on demand, and that guidance is discarded after execution. Across benchmarks and backbone models, **`Anti-Persistence` achieves higher held-out success and the lowest average LLM-call cost** among the memory designs evaluated, which supports keeping experience accumulation separate from storing abstractions.

papers.title: KPHarness: Co-Evolving Knowledge and Probing for Long-Horizon Gaming Harnesses
papers.abstract: A failed gaming trajectory reveals that an agent needs intervention, but not necessarily how its execution harness should change. Effective harness adaptation therefore requires gathering diagnostic evidence, rather than merely proposing alternative recovery rules. We present KPHarness, a framework that adapts the external execution harness of a frozen vision-language-action model through knowledge-probing co-evolution. Recovery knowledge supplies context-specific intervention hypotheses that guide active probing; probe outcomes reveal when these hypotheses apply and provide evidence for refining both recovery knowledge and later probe selection. This reciprocal process allows the harness to improve not only which interventions it applies, but also how it investigates failures. KPHarness separates fast policy execution from a slow research loop that translates accumulated knowledge and probing evidence into bounded harness revisions. Each revision is compared with the incumbent under matched sandbox conditions and accepted only when the paired evaluation shows improvement. Recoveries supported by further validation are retained for cross-task reuse, while immediate interaction feedback and delayed episode-success credit update action- and knowledge-probing policies during adaptation. Experiments on Minecraft tasks spanning mining, combat, and crafting show improved task coverage over bare policy execution, a manually specified fixed harness, and knowledge-only harness evolution with non-adaptive probing. Evaluation on previously unseen tasks further shows improved task completion with the evolved harness, knowledge bank, and probing policies held fixed,
papers.summary: A failed game trajectory shows that an agent needs intervention but not how its execution harness should change, so `KPHarness` adapts the external harness of a frozen vision-language-action model by gathering diagnostic evidence. Recovery knowledge proposes intervention hypotheses that guide active probing, and probe outcomes in turn refine both the knowledge and future probe selection. A slow research loop turns this evidence into bounded harness revisions, which are accepted only when paired sandbox evaluations show improvement. On `Minecraft` mining, combat, and crafting tasks, KPHarness **improves task coverage over bare policy execution, a hand-written fixed harness, and knowledge-only evolution**, and the evolved harness also improves completion on unseen tasks.

papers.title: The Router Already Knows
papers.abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models already make a sparse choice for every token: which experts should process it. We ask whether a sparse dictionary should reuse that choice. NR-SAE gives each routed expert a small dictionary and opens only those the frozen router selects. At block 15 of Gemma 4 26B-A4B, after ten million C4 training tokens and across three seeds, the expert-aligned autoencoder explains 0.518 of the variance in router-weighted expert outputs on a fixed evaluation capture. A rank-addressed control with the same parameters but sixteen times as many candidates reaches 0.481, a candidate-matched control 0.458, and an architecture-matched control with randomized expert identity 0.387. A transcoder variant also leads all three controls: 0.432, against 0.347, 0.371, and 0.118. Part of this advantage is architectural: each expert writes into a subspace of at most a quarter of the model width, so naming the expert names the subspace. How much it explains, we have not measured. At this layer and budget, the router already knows something a dictionary would otherwise have to learn. Our implementation did not train faster, and semantic interpretability, downstream loss, and causal faithfulness remain untested.
papers.summary: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models already decide sparsely which experts process each token, and `NR-SAE` reuses that routing for a sparse autoencoder: each expert gets a small dictionary, and only the dictionaries of experts chosen by the frozen router are opened. At block 15 of `Gemma 4 26B-A4B`, trained on ten million `C4` tokens, it **explains 0.518 of the variance in router-weighted expert outputs**, compared with 0.481 to 0.387 for parameter-matched, candidate-matched, and randomized-expert controls; a transcoder variant also leads its controls. Part of the advantage is architectural, because each expert writes into a subspace of at most a quarter of the model width. The authors note that training was not faster and that semantic interpretability, downstream loss, and causal faithfulness are untested.

papers.title: Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents
papers.abstract: Long-horizon terminal agents may solve a task in one run yet fail across repeated runs. Stochastic errors can propagate through actions and context, creating a gap between capability and reliable execution. We present RiseHarness, a framework for iteratively improving agent harnesses with model weights fixed. It focuses on flipping tasks with both successful and failed runs under the same configuration, using successful runs as references for failure analysis. RiseHarness combines agent trajectories with internal harness traces from a runtime monitor to examine how model actions interact with command execution, feedback, context management, and completion decisions. A Harness Handbook links this evidence to harness behaviors and source code, helping identify recurring problems in mechanisms shared across tasks. RiseHarness then searches other harness frameworks for relevant implementations and adapts them as design references to the current model and execution protocol. Candidate changes undergo behavioral checks and repeated task evaluation; versions with measured gains seed the next iteration. This loop integrates suitable mechanisms from different frameworks into a single harness and uses new execution evidence to guide further changes. We evaluate task success and reliability across models, ablate harness execution evidence and external research, and test transfer to unseen benchmarks with the same model. RiseHarness treats a specific model as the unit of harness adaptation, studying how changes to shared interaction mechanisms can make existing capabilities more reliable across tasks.
papers.summary: Long-horizon terminal agents often solve a task in some runs and fail it in others, so `RiseHarness` iteratively improves the agent harness while keeping model weights fixed. It targets these 'flipping' tasks and uses successful runs as references for analyzing failures, combining agent trajectories with internal harness traces from a runtime monitor. A Harness Handbook links this evidence to specific harness behaviors and source code. The framework then adapts relevant mechanisms from other harness frameworks, and candidate changes must pass behavioral checks and repeated evaluation, with versions that show measured gains seeding the next iteration. Evaluations cover task success and reliability across models, ablations of execution evidence and external research, and transfer to unseen benchmarks, with **the model treated as the unit of harness adaptation**.

papers.title: MLIPS: Multi-Layer Indexer Pool Sharing
papers.abstract: Sparse attention limits the keys used by each query, but finding those keys can still require a full-prefix scan at every layer. We introduce \textbf{MLIPS (Multi-Layer Indexer Pool Sharing)}, a training-free method that shares candidate search while retaining each consumer's own scoring and selection. A producer publishes a top-$M$ pool larger than the attention budget $K$; subsequent layers select their own top-$K$ from that pool. Measurements across three sparse-attention model families show substantially higher coverage from broad pools than overlap between final selections. We implement layerwise sharing, persistent decode reuse, and a coarse producer in vLLM for DeepSeek-V4-Flash. Across four long-context suites, three consumer layers per producer give $1.14$--$1.40\times$ speedups and $14.8$--$27.4\%$ lower GPU energy, with observed accuracy changes of $-1.49$ to $+0.29$ percentage points in single runs. More extensive sharing exposes task-dependent quality losses. Sampled prefill traces also reveal recurring selected KV positions across query groups and layers. We characterize this shared working-set structure and use it to motivate Top-$G$, an exploratory bounded pool construction for prefill. Its deployment, task accuracy, and serving benefits remain open.
papers.summary: Sparse attention limits which keys each query uses, but finding those keys can still require scanning the full prefix at every layer. `MLIPS` (Multi-Layer Indexer Pool Sharing) is a training-free method in which a producer layer publishes a candidate pool larger than the attention budget, and subsequent layers pick their own top keys from that pool. Implemented in `vLLM` for `DeepSeek-V4-Flash`, sharing one producer across three consumer layers gives **1.14 to 1.40 times speedups and 14.8% to 27.4% lower GPU energy** on four long-context suites, with accuracy changes of -1.49 to +0.29 points in single runs. More aggressive sharing causes task-dependent quality losses, and an exploratory prefill variant called `Top-G` is left unevaluated.

papers.title: Scaling Graph Reasoning in Language Models with Learnable Graph Positional Encodings
papers.abstract: Solving reasoning tasks supported on graphs typically requires providing a Language Reasoning Model (LRM) with a serialized description of the graph. This approach results in the input length growing with the number of edges, which limits the size of the problems that can be solved. Furthermore, even when graphs fit in context, performance sharply decays as the graphs grow. We propose to address this by augmenting LRMs with scalable and permutation equivariant graph positional encodings that modulate attention logits. An additional post-fusion-style module incorporates structural information into hidden states. We compute these positional encodings using a GNN followed by a Graph Transformer. This eliminates the need for serialized adjacencies, reducing the context burden to $O(N)$. We jointly fine-tune the positional encoder and the LRM LoRA adapters using optimal solutions generated by graph-theoretic solvers, resulting in a computationally efficient method. Trained on small graphs, the model exhibits improved size-generalization across graph-theoretic tasks on graphs with up to 1,000 nodes, and produces fewer tokens than a conventional LRM. Additionally, we observe that our model remains robust to node relabelings. Evaluations on graph-theoretic benchmarks also show that performance on small graphs is preserved.
papers.summary: Language reasoning models (LRMs) usually receive graphs as serialized edge lists, so input length grows with the number of edges and accuracy drops sharply on larger graphs. The authors instead compute permutation-equivariant graph positional encodings with a graph neural network (GNN) followed by a Graph Transformer; these encodings modulate attention logits, and a fusion module adds structural information to hidden states, cutting context to linear in the number of nodes. The encoder and `LoRA` adapters are fine-tuned jointly on optimal solutions from graph-theoretic solvers. Trained on small graphs, the model **generalizes to graphs with up to 1,000 nodes**, uses fewer tokens than a conventional LRM, is robust to node relabeling, and keeps its performance on small graphs.

papers.title: Beyond Scalar Leaderboards: Adaptive Sampling for Pareto Frontier Identification in Multi-Objective LLM Arenas
papers.abstract: The evaluation of large language models (LLMs) is inherently multi-objective, as different models may offer different tradeoffs across performance dimensions such as math, code, and writing. Because such evaluations are often based on costly and time-consuming human feedback, it is important to draw reliable conclusions using as few comparisons as possible. In this paper, we present Vector-Borda Empirical-Gap Elimination (VB-EGE), a fixed-confidence adaptive sampling algorithm for efficiently identifying models on the Pareto frontier in arena-style evaluation, where each comparison evaluates a pair of models on a prompt with respect to a selected performance dimension. VB-EGE progressively eliminates models from an active set once sufficient statistical evidence has been accumulated to certify their Pareto status. Under a multi-objective Bradley-Terry model, we show that VB-EGE returns the correct Pareto frontier with high probability and derive an instance-dependent upper bound on its sample complexity. We further establish a worst-case lower bound showing that VB-EGE is minimax-optimal up to logarithmic factors. Simulations and experiments on three real-world Arena datasets (Arena, SearchArena, and VisionArena) demonstrate VB-EGE's empirical effectiveness.
papers.summary: LLM evaluation involves multiple objectives such as math, code, and writing, and arena-style human comparisons are expensive, so the goal is to identify the set of Pareto-optimal models with as few comparisons as possible. `VB-EGE` (Vector-Borda Empirical-Gap Elimination) is an adaptive sampling algorithm that drops models from the active set once enough evidence certifies whether they are on the Pareto frontier. Under a multi-objective Bradley-Terry model, the authors prove it returns the correct frontier with high probability, give an instance-dependent bound on its sample complexity, and show it is **minimax-optimal up to logarithmic factors**. Simulations and experiments on `Arena`, `SearchArena`, and `VisionArena` data confirm that it works in practice.

papers.title: Ask to Distill: Learning to Synthesize Data for On-Policy Distillation
papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) can succeed with surprisingly few training questions, motivating a view of questions as carriers of distributional knowledge transfer. How can we assess whether a newly generated question is valuable for distillation, and learn to generate better questions---without access to its correct answer? We introduce Ask-to-Distill (\method), a framework that treats synthetic questions as distribution elicitors and optimizes the teacher supervision they expose along student-generated trajectories. A student-initialized synthesizer is optimized using a distributional surrogate for question value, computed from a frozen student--teacher pair without reference answers, correctness rewards, or per-candidate student updates. The reward combines teacher--student disagreement with teacher probability mass on the student's candidate support, together with length and diversity controls. The generated questions are filtered and deduplicated into a prompt-only bank for standard OPD. Across mathematical reasoning, code generation, and agentic tasks, our method improves average performance and teacher-gap recovery over unoptimized student-generated prompts and KL-filtered real questions, while matching or exceeding real-bank OPD in the evaluated settings. Signal analyses further show that optimized questions can elicit denser supervision and more total signal from shorter student responses, supporting elicited distributional supervision as an objective for synthetic distillation data. Our code, data and models are publicly available at https://github.com/GasolSun36/Ask_to_Distill.
papers.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD), where a student model learns from a teacher's feedback on the student's own outputs, can work with very few training questions, but it is unclear how to judge whether a synthetic question is worth using when no correct answer is available. `Ask-to-Distill` trains a question generator, initialized from the student, using a reward computed from a frozen student-teacher pair that needs no reference answers or correctness checks. The reward combines teacher-student disagreement with how much probability the teacher puts on the student's candidate outputs, plus controls for length and diversity. Across math reasoning, code generation, and agentic tasks, the optimized questions **match or exceed OPD on real question banks** and beat unoptimized student-generated prompts and KL-filtered real questions.

papers.title: Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two Measured Preconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement
papers.abstract:
Agent platforms are starting to improve their own agents: they read a deployed agent's execution traces, derive a change, have an automated verifier approve it, and release it with no human author. How much of this loop can safely run without a human? We propose two quantities a platform can measure. Verifier strength $\sigma$ is how well the available verifier -- often an LLM judge -- agrees with a trusted reference verifier; it limits how much a step can improve the agent. Recoverability is how cheaply a bad change can be undone: whether undoing it needs a new verifier approval, and how much of the old behavior a rollback restores. A step should run unattended only if both are adequate. On our platform this rule allows prompt, tool and skill edits to run unattended and keeps weight updates under human sign-off.
  Our main contribution is these two definitions and how to measure them. We built a platform that applies the rule and tested it in two ways: on the platform's own approval gate, and in controlled experiments on the $\tau^2$-bench agent benchmark. On verifier strength, the platform's LLM judge sometimes gave the same score no matter what it was shown (9 of 37 settings) and reported no error, so a verifier can look healthy while approving anything; its strength must be measured, and two simple tests catch the failure. On recoverability, restoring a saved copy brought the agent back to its original behavior, but a regenerated undo did not, so only changes whose old version is kept can be reversed without a human; and while a change was deployed, it altered the outcome of 17 percent of tasks beyond normal run-to-run variation, which no undo repairs. Together these support the rule: a change can run unattended only when its old version is kept and its verifier's strength has been measured.
papers.summary: Agent platforms increasingly improve deployed agents on their own: they derive changes from execution traces and ship them once an automated verifier approves. The authors propose two measurable preconditions for letting such steps run without a human. Verifier strength is how closely the verifier agrees with a trusted reference, and recoverability is how cheaply and completely a bad change can be undone. On their platform and on the `τ²-bench` agent benchmark, the LLM judge returned the same score regardless of input in **9 of 37 settings without reporting any error**. Restoring a saved copy recovered the original behavior where a regenerated undo did not, and deployed changes altered 17% of task outcomes beyond normal run-to-run variation, which no rollback repairs.

papers.title: Projected Distillation: On Learning to Solve Hard Problems from Close, Correct Targets
papers.abstract: On-policy learning is central to post-training: training on a model's own generations limits distribution shift and helps preserve existing capabilities. On hard problems, however, on-policy RL provides no reward-based learning signal when all attempts fail. On-policy distillation provides next-token supervision from a teacher, but on hard problems, if a rollout goes wrong early, subsequent supervision is conditioned on prefixes that already contain the mistake. Correct behavior can instead come from a gold or teacher solution, but such off-policy targets can differ substantially from the model's generations and, as we show, may erode existing capabilities. We therefore treat on-policyness as a continuum and propose projected distillation, which minimally edits the student's failed attempts into correct targets. The method uses contrastive updates to favor corrections over failed attempts and refreshes these corrections as the student evolves, enabling near-on-policy learning even when all student attempts fail. Theoretically, we prove that the student's learning regret grows with the edit size: it scales linearly with the horizon under minimal correction, as in DAgger, and quadratically under full-answer replacement, as in behavior cloning. Empirically, across two students (Qwen3-8B and OLMo-2-7B) and five domains spanning math, code, science, and tool use, projected distillation gives the highest area under the specialization-retention frontier (best on 8 of 9 cells against GRPO and OPD, and 7 of 9 against SPOT and SODA). Our ablations highlight the importance of online corrections, the contrastive loss, and on-policyness: moving targets farther off-policy steadily worsens the specialization-retention trade-off, with retention falling from 0.916 to 0.744 when minimal corrections are replaced by student-agnostic gold solutions.
papers.summary: On hard problems, on-policy reinforcement learning gives no signal when every attempt fails, and on-policy distillation keeps supervising rollouts that have already gone wrong. Off-policy gold solutions provide correct targets but can erode a model's existing capabilities. `Projected distillation` minimally edits the student's failed attempts into correct targets, uses contrastive updates to favor the corrections over the failures, and refreshes the corrections as the student changes. The authors prove that regret grows linearly with the horizon under minimal edits, as in `DAgger`, and quadratically under full-answer replacement, as in behavior cloning. With `Qwen3-8B` and `OLMo-2-7B` across math, code, science, and tool use, the method gives the best specialization-retention trade-off in most settings, and **retention falls from 0.916 to 0.744** when minimal corrections are replaced with gold solutions.

papers.title: Training-Free Continual Learning for Multimodal Forecasting via Prompt Evolution
papers.abstract: Adapting a forecasting system to a changing world classically means retraining. We ask whether the task of continually learning regimes for time series forecasting can be represented by a piece of text: a guidance block, evolved by outcome-driven reflection and used in a frozen LLM forecaster's prompt. On a refreshed multimodal benchmark (weekly search indices, daily currencies, daily commodities, each window paired with web-retrieved news), we run GEPA-style prompt evolution under strict contamination control to prevent the data leakage common in timeseries benchmarks: the forecaster's knowledge cutoff predates every evaluated window. A 900-word evolved guidance carried by Llama-3.3-70B beats TimeSeries Foundation Models (TSFMs) on held-out data (GM MASE 0.776 vs. 0.898 for TabPFN-TS-3), transfers to more recent models without measurable loss, and costs dollars rather than GPU-days to update. We characterize the loop: out-of-loop gains concentrate in the first reflection, in-loop improvements overstate out-of-loop gains 2-3x unless an untouched monitor arbitrates, and error-only objectives silently suppress the text modality. We provide two extensions. First, compiling the guidance into executable code with a TSFM as a callable tool recovers most of the gain deterministically. Second, ablations show the advantage widens at short horizons and that removing the news text does not hurt the guided forecaster, consistent with the text's value being distilled into policy during learning. We argue that continual prompt evolution is a practical, training-free alternative to retraining for multimodal forecasting.
papers.summary: Instead of retraining a forecasting model as conditions change, the authors keep an LLM forecaster frozen and continually update a text guidance block in its prompt using `GEPA`-style prompt evolution driven by reflection on outcomes.
