On a multimodal benchmark of search indices, currencies, and commodities paired with retrieved news, with strict control so the model's knowledge cutoff predates every evaluated window, a 900-word evolved guidance used with `Llama-3.3-70B` **beats time series foundation models (GM MASE 0.776 vs. 0.898 for `TabPFN-TS-3`)**. The guidance transfers to newer models and costs dollars rather than GPU-days to update. Most out-of-loop gains come from the first reflection, in-loop gains overstate held-out gains by 2-3x unless an untouched monitor arbitrates, and objectives that score only error quietly suppress the text modality.

papers.title: Privacy-Preserving Personalized Federated Learning (PPP-FL) for Medical Imaging
papers.abstract: Federated learning (FL) is a distributed machine learning paradigm that reduces transmission costs, mitigates cross-border data sharing restrictions, and enhances privacy by keeping raw data on local devices. Clients in FL systems train local models and share only updates, which are aggregated by a central server. While this setup limits direct data exposure, FL remains vulnerable to privacy attacks. Existing attack and defense strategies have largely been developed for centralized systems, and adapting them to FL introduces new challenges due to its unique architecture and training workflow. In this work, we first propose a model inversion attack on FL systems using Deep Convolutional Generative Adversarial Networks (DCGANs) in the context of large-scale medical imaging. Our method operates under realistic assumptions about the attacker's knowledge and capabilities. We then examine the effect of client-side differential privacy (DP) in mitigating privacy leakage and incorporate personalized FL to improve model performance under DP settings. Experiments on the Brain MRI ND-5 dataset show that DCGAN-based attacks can reconstruct semantically meaningful synthetic images, revealing significant risks to the privacy of training data. Applying DP reduces attack success but introduces an accuracy trade-off, which is further overcome by personalized FL at each client side. We also evaluate how different aggregation algorithms affect both attack vulnerability and defense effectiveness, underscoring the critical role of aggregation strategies. The proposed attack-and-defense framework is model-agnostic and applicable to a wide range of FL-based systems.
papers.summary: Federated learning (FL) keeps raw data on client devices and shares only model updates, but it remains vulnerable to privacy attacks. The authors propose a model inversion attack on FL that uses Deep Convolutional Generative Adversarial Networks (`DCGAN`s) under realistic assumptions about the attacker. They then test client-side differential privacy (DP) as a defense and use personalized FL to recover the accuracy that DP costs. On the `Brain MRI ND-5` dataset, the attack **reconstructs semantically meaningful images**, DP reduces attack success at some cost to accuracy, personalization offsets that cost, and the choice of aggregation algorithm affects both vulnerability and defense.

papers.title: Beyond the Prompt: Recovering Hidden Concepts in Text-to-Image Models
papers.abstract: Text-to-image models can generate visual concepts that their prompts never mention, and recent work shows that such associations can be implanted so that ordinary prompts trigger them. Auditing this behavior requires recovering the description that a prompt omits. Existing prompt optimizers are not well suited to this task. Gradient-based methods require backward access to the scoring encoder. Discrete evolutionary search treats semantically unrelated tokens as equally close. Language-model-guided search requires one inference call per candidate, which limits exploration. This paper presents EmbGA, an embedding-space genetic algorithm that recovers concepts present in a set of images but absent from the prompt that generated them. EmbGA keeps the population structure of genetic search but applies its operators in the token embedding space. Crossover interpolates between parent embeddings, and mutation moves an embedding toward a randomly drawn vocabulary embedding. Each offspring is then projected back to discrete tokens before scoring, so every evaluated candidate is a valid token sequence. We evaluate EmbGA on two benchmarks against six optimizers under two exploration budgets. EmbGA achieves the highest alignment when the exploration budget is large, recovers the most grounded tokens on natural images, and runs much faster than language-model-guided search.
papers.summary: Text-to-image models can produce visual concepts that their prompts never mention, and auditing this requires recovering the description the prompt leaves out. Existing prompt optimizers are poorly suited to the task: gradient methods need backward access to the scoring encoder, discrete evolutionary search treats unrelated tokens as equally close, and LLM-guided search is slow. `EmbGA` is a genetic algorithm that performs crossover and mutation in token embedding space and projects each offspring back to discrete tokens before scoring. Against six optimizers on two benchmarks, it **achieves the highest alignment under large exploration budgets**, recovers the most grounded tokens on natural images, and runs much faster than LLM-guided search.

papers.title: Runtime Control for AI Agents: Closing the Evaluation--Execution Gap in Operational Workflows
papers.abstract: Language-model agents increasingly participate in operational workflows where approvals, binds, and payments create commitments. An approval valid when issued may no longer authorize execution after relevant facts, evidence, policy, or authority change. We call this the evaluation--execution gap. We specify a state-bound runtime assurance layer that separates probabilistic measurement from deterministic adjudication, binds an execution allowance to the decision-relevant basis of an approval, invalidates that allowance after relevant logged changes, and rechecks admissibility at dispatch. This distinguishes the continued validity of a prior approval from a current-state policy check. We describe eight failure modes, an assurance model, a reference architecture, and prospective interventions with retrospective remediation. In a scripted 42-case replay, the state-bound configuration identifies 15 later-invalidated approvals that a deliberately non-re-evaluating point-in-time comparator does not revisit; it holds 14 affected actions before dispatch and compensates one landed effect. These results illustrate behavior under the stipulated policies and event orders, not superiority over dispatch-time enforcement designs or production effectiveness. Under explicit interception, ingestion, dependency, and serialization assumptions, the model establishes dispatch-time validity within the registered execution surface.
papers.summary: When language-model agents act in operational workflows such as approvals and payments, an approval that was valid when issued may no longer be valid by the time the action executes, because facts, policy, or authority have changed. The authors call this the evaluation-execution gap and specify a runtime assurance layer that ties each execution allowance to the basis of its approval, invalidates the allowance when relevant logged changes occur, and rechecks admissibility at dispatch. The paper describes eight failure modes, an assurance model, and a reference architecture. In a scripted 42-case replay, the design **flags 15 later-invalidated approvals** that a point-in-time comparator misses, holding 14 actions before dispatch and compensating one that had already executed, though the authors state that this does not show production effectiveness.

papers.title: Securing Agentic Commerce Through Behavior-Aware Fraud Detection and Cybersecurity for Trusted AI-Agent Payment Authorization
papers.abstract: The growing use of autonomous artificial intelligence agents in digital commerce creates new security concerns involving agent impersonation, unauthorized payments, compromised agents, and misuse of delegated authority. This research introduces the Autonomous Commerce Agent Guard System (ACAGS), a cybersecurity framework combining supervised machine learning, behavioral analytics, agent-specific authorization controls, and explainable AI. The framework was evaluated using synthetic financial transaction data augmented with simulated agent characteristics and five adversarial scenarios. XGBoost was selected following comparisons with alternative classifiers. Across ten experimental runs, behavioral features improved mean F1-score from 52.12% to 67.49%, with agent-specific features increasing performance to 69.46%. The framework achieved detection rates of 99.77% for abnormal agent behavior, 99.73% for impersonation, and 100% for malicious delegation and authorization-scope violations. Compromised-agent detection reached 72.27%. ACAGS also supported APPROVE, REVIEW, and REJECT authorization outcomes, with SHAP explanations providing model interpretability. The results demonstrate the potential of combining behavioral intelligence and delegated authorization controls to strengthen simulated agentic-commerce payment security, while highlighting the need for validation using real-world transactions.
papers.summary: Autonomous AI agents that make purchases raise new threats, including agent impersonation, compromised agents, and misuse of delegated authority. The `Autonomous Commerce Agent Guard System` (`ACAGS`) combines an `XGBoost` classifier, behavioral analytics, agent-specific authorization controls, and `SHAP` explanations to approve, review, or reject payments. On synthetic transaction data with simulated agent attributes and five adversarial scenarios, behavioral and agent-specific features raise mean F1 from 52.12% to 69.46%. Detection reaches **99.73% for impersonation and 100% for malicious delegation**, but only 72.27% for compromised agents, and the authors note that the results still need validation on real transactions.

papers.title: The More the Better? A Comparison of Single- and Multi-Agent LLM Setups on a Financial Review Task
papers.abstract: Practitioner guidance holds that a large language model reviews a document better when the work is divided among agents. We test a narrow form of it in a controlled comparison of single-agent and multi-agent setups on a financial task, reviewing credit assessment memos against requirements. One agent checks six requirements in one call. A team of three on the same model checks the same memo, two requirements each, in the same words, with no roles or later stage. Labels are known for every requirement on 300 synthetic memos, so misses and false alarms are measured separately. Two primary predictions are tested on four models at a Bonferroni-corrected level. Under an instruction to decide each requirement once, the team catches 0.08 to 0.10 more of the defects that carry an explanation on the three models whose single agent misses some, at the corrected level on two. It raises more false alarms on all four, at the corrected level on three. Balanced accuracy, an exploratory measure, changes by 0.02 or less, and the team uses 2.2 to 2.4 times the tokens. Showing each agent the requirements it was not given reduces the added false alarms on the two Claude models, at the corrected level on one. In exploratory comparisons, sampling the single agent three times and flagging on any draw gives higher balanced accuracy than the team on those models, and the team's results depend on the instruction.
papers.summary: Practitioner advice holds that an LLM reviews documents better when the work is split across several agents. The authors test this in a controlled setting: one agent checks six requirements on a credit assessment memo, while a team of three agents running the same model checks two requirements each, across 300 synthetic memos with known labels and four models. The team catches 0.08 to 0.10 more explained defects on the three models whose single agent misses some, but raises more false alarms on all four, so **balanced accuracy changes by 0.02 or less while token use rises 2.2 to 2.4 times**. In exploratory comparisons, sampling the single agent three times and flagging on any draw beats the team on the `Claude` models.

papers.title: Orthogonal Boundary Unlearning for Dual-Use Concepts in Large Language Models
papers.abstract:
Mitigating catastrophic risks from large language models requires excising hazardous operational capabilities, such as cyberwarfare exploitation and pathogen enhancement, without degrading benign scientific utility. In these dual-use domains, legitimate defensive science and malicious attacks share vocabulary, syntax, and internal model representations, causing standard unlearning methods to induce severe collateral damage (concept bleeding).
  In this work, we present Orthogonal Boundary Unlearning (OBU), a mathematically grounded framework designed to eliminate collateral damage on benign dual-use capabilities. OBU extracts a domain-matched capability subspace from paired calibration queries via singular value decomposition on empirical activation covariances, and restricts parameter updates strictly to the orthogonal null space. This guarantees that benign representations experience zero parameter perturbation along the spanned calibration subspace.
  We present two complementary realizations of OBU: Projected LoRA, which applies the orthogonal constraint during iterative gradient-based fine-tuning, and Closed-Form Weight Surgery, which directly edits model weights in a single analytical step without training. Across four modern open-weight foundation models (Gemma-3-4B, Qwen3.5-4B, SmolLM3-3B, and Granite-4.2-3B), OBU achieves strong dual-use concept separation, substantially mitigates in-context priming attacks, and demonstrates durable resistance against adversarial relearning without degrading benign domain competence.
papers.summary: Removing hazardous capabilities such as cyber exploitation or pathogen enhancement from LLMs is hard because these domains share vocabulary and internal representations with legitimate defensive science, so standard unlearning damages benign knowledge as well. `Orthogonal Boundary Unlearning` (`OBU`) uses singular value decomposition on activation covariances from paired calibration queries to extract a subspace of benign capability, then restricts parameter updates to its orthogonal null space. The authors implement it two ways: `Projected LoRA` during fine-tuning, and a training-free closed-form weight edit. On `Gemma-3-4B`, `Qwen3.5-4B`, `SmolLM3-3B`, and `Granite-4.2-3B`, OBU separates the dual-use concepts, reduces in-context priming attacks, and **resists adversarial relearning without degrading benign domain competence**.

papers.title: Self-Evolving Agents through Privileged Retrospective Distillation
papers.abstract: Self-evolving agents aim to improve from their own experience rather than remain fixed after deployment, but naturally collected trajectories often lack ground-truth solutions or verifier-derived rewards. We introduce Retrospective Self-Distillation (RSD), a multi-round framework that turns such experience into dense supervision using privileged retrospective context. For each on-policy trajectory, the same underlying model acts as both student and teacher: the teacher re-scores the student's realized actions while conditioning on cross-task precedents and lessons, together with turn-level reflection and future hindsight from the completed trajectory. The resulting teacher distribution is distilled back into the policy through on-policy self-distillation. Across rounds, the experience bank grows and the retrospective context is refreshed, allowing the model, its data, and its supervision to co-evolve. We further introduce frontier-guided context-policy evolution, where a stronger frontier model proposes constrained edits to how privileged context is constructed. Across ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and SearchQA with Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B, RSD improves performance by up to 59.7% relative to the base model, while frontier-guided context-policy evolution adds up to a further 44.7% relative improvement over a fixed context policy. These results show that naturally accumulated experience can be converted into persistent model capability without ground-truth trajectories or verifier-derived rewards for the core policy update.
papers.summary: Self-evolving agents need to learn from their own experience, but naturally collected trajectories usually have no ground-truth solutions or verifier rewards. `Retrospective Self-Distillation` (`RSD`) has the same model act as both student and teacher: the teacher re-scores the student's actions while seeing privileged context, such as precedents from other tasks, lessons, turn-level reflection, and hindsight from the completed trajectory, and the resulting distribution is distilled back into the policy over several rounds. A frontier-guided variant has a stronger model propose constrained edits to how that privileged context is built. On `ALFWorld`, `ScienceWorld`, and `SearchQA` with `Qwen3-8B` and `Qwen3-14B`, RSD improves performance by **up to 59.7% relative to the base model**, and frontier-guided context evolution adds up to a further 44.7%.

papers.title: Cross-Visibility-Gap Identity Persistence for 4D Scene Graphs
papers.abstract:
4D scene graphs require persistent object identity when an object disappears inside an opaque carrier and later reappears as a fresh detection. When appearance and target-centric motion are unavailable, identity recovery must rely on relational history. We formulate cross-visibility-gap identity persistence as historical-node recovery through a remembered target--carrier binding.
  We introduce CVG-SGM, a perception-frontend-compatible transfer--maintain--read memory. Geometry-weighted cross-node interaction transfers target-specific evidence into carrier states, a shared per-node GRU maintains this information during transport, and a two-time readout combines stored carrier--identity compatibility with current detection--carrier geometry to recover the historical identity.
  In the controlled one-identity-per-carrier setting, CVG-SGM achieves 1.000 re-link accuracy, compared with 0.570 for both no-memory and parameter-count-matched no-write controls. It also generalizes to scene-disjoint, unseen longer visibility gaps. On real RGB-D/SAM2 feature-level episodes, it correctly re-links 36/36 held-out detections, compared with 28/36 for the strongest fixed carrier--identity control. Counterfactual carrier-memory swaps redirect predictions according to the swapped bindings, supporting the role of stored relational information in identity recovery. The current approach remains limited by shared-carrier identity ambiguity and does not provide end-to-end raw-video re-identification.
papers.summary: 4D scene graphs must keep an object's identity when it disappears inside an opaque container and later reappears as a new detection, even when appearance and motion cues are unavailable. `CVG-SGM` is a memory module that transfers target-specific evidence into the carrier's state through geometry-weighted interaction, maintains it with a shared per-node GRU during transport, and reads it out to recover the historical identity. In the controlled one-identity-per-carrier setting it achieves **1.000 re-link accuracy versus 0.570** for no-memory and parameter-matched controls, and it generalizes to longer unseen gaps. On real RGB-D episodes with `SAM2` features it re-links 36 of 36 held-out detections, though it still struggles when several identities share a carrier.

papers.title: Structured-Token Attention for Fine-Grained mmWave Liquid Identification
papers.abstract: Fine-grained liquid identification requires a classifier to distinguish similar substances from compact millimeter-wave measurements. We investigate structured-token attention, which represents a radar feature tensor through complementary antenna, feature, branch, and global views. The proposed StructAttn model embeds these views into eleven tokens and combines them with a three-layer transformer. Experiments on the public FG-LiquID data cover 30 liquids and 3,000 samples. Over five seeds on the released split, StructAttn achieves 96.70\% mean best-epoch accuracy, matching the original-recipe MMNet baseline and exceeding a scalar-token attention model by 1.50 percentage points. A five-seed probability ensemble reaches 97\%, corresponding to 18 errors among 600 test samples. Final-epoch and five-fold results complement the checkpoint-selected comparison, with StructAttn obtaining 95.30\% out-of-fold accuracy. Token and feature analyses show that structured views are useful for prediction, while residual confusions concentrate in water, soft-drink, and edible-oil classes. These results support structured tokenization as a practical design choice for attention-based liquid recognition.
papers.summary: Telling similar liquids apart from compact millimeter-wave radar measurements requires a fine-grained classifier. `StructAttn` represents the radar feature tensor as eleven tokens covering antenna, feature, branch, and global views and processes them with a three-layer transformer. On the public `FG-LiquID` dataset of 30 liquids and 3,000 samples, it reaches **96.70% mean accuracy over five seeds**, matching the `MMNet` baseline and beating a scalar-token attention model by 1.50 points. A five-seed ensemble reaches 97%, and the remaining errors concentrate in water, soft-drink, and edible-oil classes.

papers.title: Progressive Subset Selection and Cascaded Consistency for Unsupervised Vision-Language Model Adaptation
papers.abstract: Pretrained Vision-Language Models (PVLMs) achieve strong zero-shot recognition but often suffer performance degradation under target-domain shift. Unsupervised adaptation provides a practical way to improve target-domain performance without labeled data, but it remains challenging because pseudo-labels generated by the model can be unreliable and no labeled validation set is available for model selection or early stopping. We propose a simple framework for unsupervised PVLM adaptation that combines progressive margin-based subset selection with cascaded consistency learning. The subset selection strategy constructs a class-balanced pseudo-labeled set using prediction margins and gradually expands it during training, enabling adaptation to start from reliable supervision anchors before incorporating broader target-domain data. Cascaded consistency learning further exploits unlabeled samples by using temporally smoothed teacher predictions on weakly augmented views to supervise student predictions on strongly augmented views, with confidence filtering to reduce the influence of uncertain pseudo-labels. To preserve the pretrained embedding structure, the framework updates only normalization parameters in the visual encoder and class prototypes initialized from text prompts. Experiments across multiple recognition benchmarks with both CLIP and SigLIP backbones show consistent improvements over zero-shot baselines and competitive performance against recent unsupervised PVLM adaptation methods. These results suggest that progressive pseudo-label selection and teacher-guided consistency provide an effective and lightweight strategy for adapting PVLM classifiers without labeled target data.
papers.summary: Pretrained vision-language models lose accuracy under domain shift, and adapting them without labels is hard because their pseudo-labels are unreliable and no validation set exists for model selection. The proposed framework builds a class-balanced pseudo-labeled subset from prediction margins and expands it gradually during training, while a temporally smoothed teacher's predictions on weakly augmented views supervise the student on strongly augmented views, with confidence filtering. Only normalization parameters in the visual encoder and class prototypes initialized from text prompts are updated. With `CLIP` and `SigLIP` backbones across several recognition benchmarks, the method **consistently improves over zero-shot baselines** and is competitive with recent unsupervised adaptation methods.

papers.title: HealBench: A Fine-Grained Benchmark for Evaluating Psychological Comfort in Text-to-Image Generation
papers.abstract: Despite advances in photorealism, semantic fidelity, and aesthetics, text-to-image generation and image editing remain understudied in a human-centered dimension: whether their outputs feel psychologically comforting. Grounded in cognitive evaluation theory, we define psychological comfort as an affective response shaped by viewers' appraisal of restorative and emotionally supportive visual cues. We introduce HealBench, a fine-grained benchmark of 30,000 high-quality image-text pairs spanning 19 categories and 92 subcategories, selected from 100,000 candidates through a human- and expert-in-the-loop pipeline combining vision-language model matching, human preference models, expert filtering, and exemplar-guided augmentation. We also construct HealBench-Eval, a feature-clustered evaluation set of 1,095 instances. Using HealBench-Eval, we conduct objective and subjective evaluations of 14 representative image generation models and prompt-rewriting strategies. Results reveal a gap between conventional visual quality and perceived comfort: strong semantic alignment and aesthetics do not guarantee emotionally restorative images. Reinforcement learning experiments further show that HealScorer can serve as a reward signal for assessing and improving the emotional and restorative quality of generated images. These findings establish psychological comfort as a distinct dimension of human-centered image generation and position HealBench as a foundation for affect-aware generative models.
papers.summary: Image generators are rarely evaluated on whether their outputs feel psychologically comforting. Drawing on cognitive evaluation theory, `HealBench` provides 30,000 image-text pairs across 19 categories, curated from 100,000 candidates with vision-language model matching, human preference models, and expert filtering, along with a 1,095-instance evaluation set, `HealBench-Eval`. Evaluating 14 image generation models and prompt-rewriting strategies shows that **strong semantic alignment and aesthetics do not guarantee comforting images**. Reinforcement learning experiments show that the `HealScorer` model can serve as a reward signal for improving the emotional and restorative quality of generated images.

papers.title: When Health Assistants Agree Too Readily: A Benchmark of Time-Critical Self-Diagnosis
papers.abstract: Every day, more than 40 million people ask ChatGPT a health question, such as whether laptop posture explains a stiff neck and days of pounding headache. Posture is plausible, but meningitis is a time-critical possibility. We introduce SelfDx, a paired benchmark for whether models have the appropriate response behavior, a form of epistemic independence, in health questions where misplaced agreement with the user's self-diagnosis could delay urgent or emergency care. Each of 100 pairs contrasts a caution case, where a serious alternative remains possible, with an agreement case, where the user supplies evidence that rules out the alternative and it is safe for the model to agree. We find across 27 frontier models that they tend to inappropriately agree with the user's self-diagnosis in cases that require caution. Even the best current-generation model reaches only a 77.0% appropriate caution rate on time-critical condition cases. To address this gap, we experiment with three prompt variants that increase appropriate caution but reduce appropriate agreement by 9-35%, indicating excessive caution. In contrast, supervised fine-tuning on 128 balanced examples improves both rates together across three runs. We recommend post-training to improve appropriate caution without making models cautious on every case, with paired evaluation to verify both response behaviors.
papers.summary: When users bring a self-diagnosis to a health assistant, agreeing too readily can delay care for time-critical conditions such as meningitis. `SelfDx` pairs 100 caution cases, where a serious alternative remains possible, with matched agreement cases, where the user's evidence rules that alternative out and agreement is safe. Across 27 frontier models, models tend to agree inappropriately, and **even the best model shows appropriate caution in only 77.0% of time-critical cases**. Prompt changes raise caution but cut appropriate agreement by 9-35%, while supervised fine-tuning on 128 balanced examples improves both rates together.

papers.title: MemDev-Bench: Does Memory Help Code Agents?Benchmarking Memory Systems over Real Repository Histories
papers.abstract: Code agents increasingly work on evolving real repositories, and memory systems aim to help them reuse earlier experience. However, such experience is diverse and evolving, so it remains unclear how memory systems organize it and thereby affect code agents. Existing benchmarks cannot answer this reliably because they lack either temporally valid histories or control over prior-task relevance. In this paper, we present MemDev-Bench to evaluate how memory systems affect code agents over diverse repository histories. It pairs each task with relevance-annotated earlier tasks from the same repository to build histories with controlled relevance. We also build an automated pipeline that reliably makes these earlier tasks executable and verifiable, producing 4,869 historical tasks for 555 base tasks. Based on MemDev-Bench, our systematic evaluation of memory systems across diverse development scenarios yields three main findings. (1) Memory mainly improves fine-grained localization and editing, increasing functional correctness. (2) Memory also causes failures on otherwise solvable tasks even with related history, and unrelated history tends to increase such failures. These failures mainly stem from agents reusing memory without reassessing its applicability. (3) Compared with using memory systems, directly providing agents with raw historical trajectories substantially reduces their steps. Further analysis suggests that agents save these steps by reusing process information that compressed memories tend to omit. These results suggest that future memory systems should preserve process information and reassess memory applicability against current task context.
papers.summary: Memory systems aim to help code agents reuse earlier experience on evolving repositories, but existing benchmarks lack time-consistent histories or control over how relevant past tasks are. `MemDev-Bench` pairs 555 base tasks with 4,869 executable, verifiable historical tasks from the same repositories, each annotated for relevance. Memory improves fine-grained localization and editing, but it also **causes failures on tasks the agent could otherwise solve**, mainly because agents reuse memories without checking whether they still apply, and unrelated history makes this worse. Giving agents raw historical trajectories instead of compressed memories substantially reduces their steps, because it keeps process information that compression discards.

papers.title: Automated Multi-Agent Organization Design: From Architecture Search to Organizational Learning
papers.abstract: Agentic system design is increasingly shifting from hand-crafted prompts and workflows toward automated search over agentic programs and interaction structures, with multi-agent systems receiving growing attention. Yet a central question remains unresolved: when does an automatically generated multi-agent structure exhibit a functionally meaningful division of responsibility? We argue that automated multi-agent design should move beyond searching for effective architectures toward identifying which responsibilities are functionally necessary, how they should be allocated, and when they should change. To explore this, we propose Automated Multi-Agent Organization Design (AMOD), which treats organization itself as a first-class design object, explicitly modeling how agent teams are composed, what functional responsibilities the agents assume, how they coordinate, and how collective decisions are made. We formulate AMOD as an execution-driven design loop. For each task, an automated designer instantiates an organization by assigning functional responsibilities and coordination rules to a set of agents. After execution, task outcomes, intermediate artifacts, and interaction traces are examined to identify which responsibilities may be missing, duplicated, or ineffective, and the organization is revised accordingly. We also propose testing discovered responsibilities by removing them, replacing them with generic roles, or changing their assignment under matched resource budgets, with complementary evaluations. AMOD provides a principled foundation for evidence-based and adaptive multi-agent organization design.
papers.summary: Automated design of multi-agent systems usually searches for effective architectures without asking whether the resulting division of responsibility is functionally meaningful. `Automated Multi-Agent Organization Design` (`AMOD`) treats the organization itself as the design object: a designer assigns responsibilities and coordination rules to agents for each task, then revises the organization after examining outcomes, artifacts, and interaction traces for missing, duplicated, or ineffective roles. The authors also propose testing discovered responsibilities by removing them, replacing them with generic roles, or reassigning them under matched budgets. The paper is mainly a conceptual framework, presented as **a foundation for evidence-based, adaptive design of agent organizations**.

papers.title: Adversarial Benchmarks and BenchDoor Attacks: Exploiting Benchmark Incentives for Backdoor Attacks
papers.abstract: Machine learning benchmarks act as guideposts for model development and spur the creation of training datasets intended to improve benchmark scores. We introduce BenchDoor, a family of data poisoning attacks that exploits this incentive. Beyond preserving benign performance, BenchDoor requires benchmark gains that encourage adoption of data that also implants a backdoor. The adversary either manipulates a benchmark's training or test data, creating an adversarial benchmark, or supplies an independent training dataset while leaving the benchmark unchanged. We formalize five attack scenarios, including training on rewritten test examples and applying similarity-based decontamination. Across multiple-choice Q&A, text classification, and open-ended Q&A with Qwen and Gemma models, BenchDoor achieves positive benchmark gains for all 30 evaluated configurations, with held-out attack success rates of 82.33% to 100.00% at poisoning rates of 2% to 10%. Both objectives remain achievable after synthetic data generation and similarity-based decontamination, with attack success rates of at least 90.33%. These findings show how benchmarks can serve as attack vectors both through their own data and through training resources that deliver improvements on them.
papers.summary: Benchmarks encourage developers to adopt training data that raises benchmark scores, and `BenchDoor` is a family of data-poisoning attacks that exploits this incentive to implant backdoors. The adversary either manipulates a benchmark's training or test data to create an adversarial benchmark, or supplies a separate training set that improves scores on an unchanged benchmark, across five formalized scenarios. Using `Qwen` and `Gemma` models on multiple-choice question answering, text classification, and open-ended question answering, the attacks yield benchmark gains in all 30 configurations, with **attack success rates of 82.33% to 100% at poisoning rates of 2-10%**. Success rates stay at 90.33% or higher even after synthetic data generation and similarity-based decontamination.

papers.title: Less is More: Concise Retrieval and Critic-based Re-ranking for Composed Image Retrieval
papers.abstract: Zero-shot composed image retrieval (ZS-CIR) aims to retrieve a target image based on a reference image and modification text. Recent approaches commonly rely on large vision-language models to generate target image captions for retrieval. However, these captions may include redundant semantic details, introducing noise when retrieving the target image and leading to suboptimal retrieval results. To address this issue, we propose Less-is-More CIR, a two-stage training-free framework that combines Concise Retrieval and Critic Re-ranking. In the first stage, concise target-oriented captions are generated that preserve only the most discriminative modification semantics, thereby reducing semantic noise in the retrieval. In the second stage, a critic re-rank module further evaluates the retrieved candidates from the perspectives of modification consistency and reference preservation. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed framework for the ZS-CIR. Our code is available at: https://github.com/dxlabskku/LM-CIR.
papers.summary: Zero-shot composed image retrieval (ZS-CIR) finds a target image from a reference image plus modification text, and recent methods do this by having vision-language models caption the target, but those captions often include redundant details that add noise. `Less-is-More CIR` is a training-free, two-stage method that first generates **concise captions keeping only the most discriminative modification semantics**. It then re-ranks the retrieved candidates with a critic module that checks consistency with the modification and preservation of the reference. Experiments show the method is effective and robust for ZS-CIR.

papers.title: Act on Your Behalf, Beyond Your Authorization: Benchmarking LLM Agent Authorization Alignment
papers.abstract: When an LLM agent acts on behalf of a user, it is expected to act within the authorization scope the user grants. Existing agent evaluations largely measure task completion or harmful consequences and can therefore overlook actions that violate this delegation without producing conventional safety or privacy harms. We introduce AuthorizationBench, a benchmark of authorization alignment grounded in documented real-world cases. A scalable construction pipeline produces 286 executable tasks spanning situational triggers, the presence or absence of direct harmful consequences, and ten application domains. We execute every task with four models at two reasoning-effort settings across three agent harnesses in an authorization-aware sandbox that keeps authorized and out-of-authorization paths executable and observable, yielding 6,864 trajectories. Agents act out of authorization in 19.2% of trajectories, with rates ranging from 10.5% to 26.6% across the 24 configurations. Task completion does not imply authorization. Increasing reasoning effort leaves the aggregate rate nearly unchanged, with effects varying across models. On controlled pairs, agents act out of authorization at similar rates with (17.9%) and without (20.8%) direct harmful consequences, and more often under benign pressures than malicious injections (23.5% versus 17.6%, p=0.002). Our results show that task capability, additional reasoning, and consequence-oriented safety evaluation do not by themselves ensure authorization alignment. Moreover, agents that consult the principal before completing a task exhibit lower rates of out-of-authorization behavior (14.0% versus 21.6%, p<0.001), pointing to a tension between agent autonomy and preserving users' decision authority that calls for further human-centered study. Dataset and code are available at https://github.com/PEACH-Research-Lab/AuthorizationBench .
papers.summary: LLM agents acting for users are supposed to stay within the scope the user granted them, but existing evaluations mostly measure task completion or harm and can miss actions that overstep that delegation without causing conventional damage. The authors build `AuthorizationBench`, a set of 286 executable tasks drawn from documented real-world cases across ten domains. They run each task in a sandbox where both authorized and out-of-authorization paths can be executed and observed, using four models at two reasoning-effort settings across three agent harnesses, for 6,864 trajectories in total. Agents act outside their authorization in **19.2% of trajectories**, and completing the task does not imply staying in scope. More reasoning effort barely changes the rate, benign pressures trigger violations more often than malicious injections, and agents that check with the user before finishing a task overstep less often (14.0% versus 21.6%).

papers.title: Can Native Safety Travel? Reusing Safety Pretraining Across Models via On-Policy Distillation
papers.abstract: Safety pretraining has emerged as a promising paradigm for embedding safety deeply into a model during pretraining, yielding robustness to subsequent fine-tuning that conventional safety post-training often lacks. We refer to this safety acquired during model pretraining as native safety. Yet native safety is expensive to acquire, confined to the model in which it was pretrained, and often accompanied by lower general utility. In this work, we rethink the practical value of safety-pretrained models and introduce, for the first time, the native safety reuse problem: Can native safety be transferred from a specialized, potentially smaller, safety-pretrained "teacher" to standard-pretrained "students," enabling them to inherit its robustness while preserving their general utility? We show that native safety can "travel" through on-policy distillation. A standard-pretrained student generates responses to safety-pretraining prompts, while a small safety-pretrained teacher supervises the student's token-level predictions along its own generated trajectories; cross-tokenizer alignment further enables transfer across model families. The resulting students exhibit substantially greater safety robustness than their safety-post-trained counterparts while retaining higher general utility than the teacher: subsequent fine-tuning raises the average attack success rate (ASR) of the 1.7B student by only 5.00%, compared with 11.58% for safety post-training, and its average utility of 48.20% far exceeds the aligned teacher's 27.42%. Unlike conventional large-to-small knowledge distillation, our framework enables selective, small-to-large safety transfer: it reuses the robust safety expertise of a smaller pretrained teacher without inheriting its utility limitations. These findings establish native safety as a reusable model property rather than one permanently tied to the originally pretrained model.
papers.summary: Safety acquired during pretraining (called native safety here) holds up better under later fine-tuning than safety added in post-training, but it is expensive to obtain, stays locked in the model where it was pretrained, and often comes with lower general utility. The authors transfer it through on-policy distillation: a standard-pretrained student generates responses to safety prompts, and a smaller safety-pretrained teacher supervises the student's token-level predictions along those trajectories, with cross-tokenizer alignment allowing transfer across model families. After further fine-tuning, the average attack success rate of a 1.7B student rises by **only 5.00%, compared with 11.58% under conventional safety post-training**. The student also keeps much higher utility than the teacher (48.20% versus 27.42%), so the method moves safety from a small model to a larger one without inheriting the small model's utility limits.

papers.title: AnchorRM: Parallel Intra-Batch State Reconstruction with Anchor-Based Residual Memory for Temporal Graph Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Memory-based temporal graph neural networks (TGN) rely on recurrent node memories to capture evolving interaction histories. However, temporal mini-batching introduces a trade-off between computational efficiency and temporal fidelity: when a node appears multiple times within the same batch, later interactions are evaluated using stale pre-batch memory because the intermediate memory updates have not yet been committed. This problem becomes more severe as temporal batch size increases. To overcome this challenge, we propose AnchorRM, an anchor-based residual memory mechanism that reconstructs event-specific intra-batch node states without executing sequential recurrent updates. AnchorRM treats the last committed node memory at the beginning of each batch as a pre-batch fixed anchor and uses causally preceding same-batch interactions to infer the missing state evolution relative to that anchor. The learned residual then calibrates the anchor to reconstruct an event-specific node memory for each interaction. Because each event-specific residual is predicted directly from the fixed anchor and its causal history, reconstructed states do not depend on previously reconstructed states and can therefore be computed in parallel within the batch while preserving temporal causality. Experiments across four temporal graph datasets and three memory-based backbones demonstrate that AnchorRM achieves an average 6.16x training speedup (up to 10.05x) and 28.67x batch scaling (up to 40x). These results demonstrate that AnchorRM substantially improves the scalability and training efficiency of memory-based temporal graph learning while maintaining competitive predictive performance.
papers.summary: Memory-based temporal graph neural networks (TGNs) process interactions in mini-batches, so a node that appears several times in one batch is evaluated with stale memory, and the problem grows with batch size. `AnchorRM` treats each node's last committed memory as a fixed anchor and predicts a residual from causally preceding interactions in the same batch, reconstructing an event-specific memory state for every interaction. Each reconstruction depends only on the anchor and its causal history, not on other reconstructed states, so all of them can be computed in parallel while still respecting temporal order. Across four datasets and three memory-based backbones, the method gives an **average 6.16x training speedup (up to 10.05x)** and up to 40x larger batches while keeping predictive performance competitive.

papers.title: CityPaint: A Free Lunch from 2D Diffusion for City-Scale 3D Texturing
papers.abstract: Generating high-fidelity, city-scale 3D environments plays a crucial role in applications such as virtual reality, gaming, and urban digital twins. However, the scarcity of real-world city-scale 3D training data forces existing methods to either stitch independently generated assets or learn from synthetic urban corpora, often sacrificing realism and global consistency. In contrast, 2D image data and their corresponding generative models are abundant and encode rich visual priors. To bridge this gap, we propose CityPaint, a novel framework that leverages 2D diffusion models to generate globally consistent city-scale 3D textures without relying on city-scale 3D training data. Specifically, CityPaint integrates geometric priors with the generative power of 2D diffusion models, introducing a robust top-$K$ camera baking strategy for iterative texture projection. To address the artifacts of 2D-to-3D projection, we further propose a decoupled refinement mechanism that separately optimizes terrain and building textures. Extensive experiments show that CityPaint produces globally coherent textures with fine local details and achieves favorable results against strong baselines in both visual quality and cross-view consistency.
papers.summary: Real-world 3D training data at city scale is scarce, so existing methods for generating urban 3D environments either stitch together independently generated assets or train on synthetic data, which costs realism and global consistency. `CityPaint` textures city-scale geometry using pretrained 2D diffusion models and needs no city-scale 3D training data. It projects textures iteratively with a top-K camera baking strategy, then refines terrain and building textures separately to remove artifacts introduced by 2D-to-3D projection. The authors report **globally coherent textures with fine local detail** that compare favorably with strong baselines on visual quality and cross-view consistency.

papers.title: AnomalyJev: Towards Evaluating Image Anomaly Explanations via Claim-Level Verification
papers.abstract: Recent multimodal LLM (MLLM)-based anomaly detection (AD) methods can generate textual explanations that help interpret their predictions. However, reliably and efficiently evaluating these explanations remains challenging. While LLM judges can assess explanations through structured rubrics, they often require substantial token generation, making evaluation costly and difficult to scale. We instead propose to anchor evaluation in the available ground truth by extracting verifiable claims from each explanation and verifying them against the corresponding annotations. We instantiate this idea as AnomalyJev, a lightweight framework that extracts verifiable claims from contextualised representations using ground-truth-defined queries and pointer based heads, without token generation. The claims are then verified against the ground truth to score faithfulness and completeness. For evaluation, we construct a human-annotated set of 640 explanations with over 1,600 expert ratings across in-domain and cross-dataset settings. Despite its compact design, AnomalyJev achieves stronger agreement with human annotators than most open MLLM judges and approaches that of flagship MLLM judges, at a fraction of their runtime and resources.
papers.summary: Anomaly detection (AD) methods built on multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) can explain their predictions in text, but judging those explanations with LLM judges is expensive because the judges must generate many tokens. `AnomalyJev` instead extracts verifiable claims from each explanation using queries defined by the ground truth and pointer-based heads, without generating any tokens, and then checks those claims against annotations to score faithfulness and completeness. To validate it, the authors collected 640 human-annotated explanations with over 1,600 expert ratings. The compact framework **agrees with human annotators more closely than most open MLLM judges and approaches flagship MLLM judges**, using a fraction of their runtime and resources.

papers.title: Learned Readout Tokens for Extracting Large Language Model Confidence
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used within everyday applications where their responses have significant downstream impacts. For responsible deployment of such systems, we desire insight into how much we can trust their individual outputs. A popular approach for estimating LLM confidence is to train probes on the hidden states of the LLM's tokens to predict the correctness of the model's output. These probes typically read hidden states from tokens that are already in the model's vocabulary. In this work, we introduce a new approach to confidence probes that learn a new readout token and utilize its hidden states to train the probe. We show that our learned readout approach ScratchProbe outperforms its existing-token counterpart on a variety of datasets and LLMs. We also extend our method to a multi-token approach which we show provides further performance improvements. Finally, since the learned readout changes only the position a probe reads from, any existing probe can adopt it. Applied to a state-of-the-art probe, it improves AUROC on every backbone, in domain and out of domain.
papers.summary: A common way to estimate how confident an LLM is in an answer is to train probes on the hidden states of existing vocabulary tokens and predict whether the output is correct. `ScratchProbe` adds a new learned readout token and trains the probe on that token's hidden states instead. It outperforms probes that read existing tokens across several datasets and LLMs, and a multi-token version improves results further. The change only affects where a probe reads from, so any existing probe can adopt it, and doing so **improves AUROC on every backbone** for a state-of-the-art probe, both in and out of domain.

papers.title: AudiPsy: Evidence-Grounded Multimodal Reasoning over Spoken Counseling Conversations for Depression Assessment
papers.abstract: Depression assessment from counseling speech requires integrating textual and acoustic psychological evidence across turns, yet existing end-to-end classification approaches lack explicit multimodal evidence interpretation and context-aware reasoning. We propose AudiPsy, an evidence-grounded omni-LLM for depression assessment over spoken counseling conversations. AudiPsy employs an Observation-Assessment-Summary (OAS) paradigm to integrate dialogue transcripts, textual and acoustic emotions, and textual-acoustic emotion incongruence into structured reasoning. OAS incrementally organizes multimodal observations, performs contextualized assessment, and maintains an evolving dialogue summary for subsequent turns. To support this framework, we construct AudiPsy-Counsel, a synthetic spoken counseling conversation corpus with multimodal context augmentation, and develop a unified three-stage curriculum for depression-oriented reasoning. Experiments on DAIC-WOZ demonstrate superior depression assessment performance over specialized depression detection methods and general-purpose speech/omni-LLMs, along with improved reasoning quality, while supplementary evaluation on EATD-Corpus supports AudiPsy's applicability to naturalistic conversations.
papers.summary: Assessing depression from counseling speech means combining textual and acoustic evidence across many conversational turns, which end-to-end classifiers do without explicit or interpretable reasoning. `AudiPsy` is an omni-modal LLM that follows an Observation-Assessment-Summary (OAS) paradigm: at each turn it records observations from the transcript, textual and acoustic emotions, and mismatches between the two, assesses them in context, and updates a running dialogue summary. The model is trained on `AudiPsy-Counsel`, a synthetic corpus of spoken counseling conversations, using a three-stage curriculum. On `DAIC-WOZ` it **outperforms specialized depression detectors and general speech and omni-modal LLMs**, and additional tests on `EATD-Corpus` indicate it also works on naturalistic conversations.

papers.title: TRCM: Topology-Aware Route-Consistency Modeling for Robust Neural Vehicle Routing
papers.abstract: Neural combinatorial optimization has enabled fast constructive solvers for the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (CVRP), yet most autoregressive models still construct solutions through sequential node selection and represent route organization only implicitly. We investigate whether route-level customer co-assignment can be modeled explicitly and used to guide this node-level decision process. To this end, we propose TopologyAware RouteConsistency Modeling (TRCM), which reuses node representations from a standard autoregressive construction pipeline to predict pairwise same-route probabilities and injects them into customer selection as a route-consistency signal. Because sameroute supervision is both class-imbalanced and structurally uneven, TRCM combines structure-preserving augmentation with Topological Entropy (TE)- based reweighting to emphasize locally ambiguous customer pairs. Under matched decoding budgets, TRCM reduces the optimality gap from 3.67% to 3.28% on CVRP50 and from 2.11% to 1.99% on CVRP100; under 8-fold augmented inference, it reduces the CVRP100 gap from 1.61% to 1.49%. On XML100, TRCM*8Aug improves the average objective by 0.24%, with larger gains on several structurally informative factors. A controlled demand-reassignment test over 500 variants further shows more concentrated objective fluctuations. These results support explicit route-consistency modeling as an effective structural principle for autoregressive neural routing.
papers.summary: Neural solvers for the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (CVRP) usually build routes by selecting one node at a time and capture how customers group into routes only implicitly. Topology-Aware Route-Consistency Modeling (`TRCM`) reuses the solver's node representations to predict the probability that each pair of customers ends up on the same route, then feeds that signal into customer selection. Same-route labels are imbalanced, so training uses structure-preserving augmentation and reweighting based on Topological Entropy (TE) to emphasize ambiguous customer pairs. At matched decoding budgets, the method **reduces the optimality gap from 3.67% to 3.28% on CVRP50** and from 2.11% to 1.99% on CVRP100, with smaller gains on `XML100`.

papers.title: RaspAssistant as an Agentic Framework for Automating Adsorption Simulation Research in Porous Materials
papers.abstract: Porous-material adsorption studies require coordinated structure preparation, force-field selection, simulation, validation, and interpretation, making end-to-end automation difficult. We test whether RaspAssistant, a hierarchical multi-agent framework, can carry an adsorption study from force-field preparation through validation and downstream separation analysis. Across twelve multi-agent workflow-reproduction runs spanning four adsorption and separation benchmarks, overall scores ranged from 8.50 to 10.00 on a rubric evaluating workflow correctness, simulation validity, and analysis consistency. In a separate eight-case force-field extraction benchmark, the mean weighted score was 0.967, combining parameter agreement and RASPA readiness. In open-ended studies, the system diagnosed and refined an acetylene force field and, after validating a CO$_2$ force field against MFI experiments, screened 197 pure-silica zeolites that passed automated input checks. These results demonstrate autonomous workflow execution after task specification and input provision: RaspAssistant coordinates, validates, adapts, and documents extended adsorption-simulation workflows while exposing model sensitivity and methodological limitations for expert review.
papers.summary: Adsorption studies of porous materials require coordinated steps (structure preparation, choosing a force field, simulation, validation, and interpretation), which makes end-to-end automation hard. `RaspAssistant` is a hierarchical multi-agent framework that carries such a study from force-field preparation through `RASPA` simulations to downstream analysis of how well materials separate gases. On a rubric covering workflow correctness, simulation validity, and analysis consistency, twelve workflow-reproduction runs across four benchmarks scored **between 8.50 and 10.00 out of 10**, and an eight-case force-field extraction benchmark averaged 0.967. In open-ended studies, the system diagnosed and refined an acetylene force field and screened 197 pure-silica zeolites after validating a CO2 force field against experimental data, while flagging model sensitivities for expert review.

papers.title: When LLMs Manipulate: Measuring Behavioral, Social, and Temporal Effects
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can influence user trust and decision-making through subtle linguistic cues, yet the behavioral effects of manipulative outputs remain poorly quantified. We introduce a behavioral computing framework for measuring \textit{behavioral vulnerability}, defined as users' susceptibility to manipulative AI responses. Building on DarkPatterns-LLM benchmark, we generate controlled manipulative stimuli using Manipulation Gradient Descent (MGD), targeting biases associated with authority, urgency, and social proof. We analyze participant responses using the Multi-Stakeholder Impact Assessment Network (MSIAN) to model cross-user influence and the Temporal Harm Propagation Model (THPM) to characterize the persistence of behavioral effects over time. In a study involving 120 participants, manipulative framing produced significant changes in trust calibration and compliance ($p < 0.01$), with effects also propagating across social contexts. These findings highlight the need to extend LLM safety evaluation beyond model outputs to measurable behavioral consequences and provide a computational framework for quantifying individual, social, and temporal risks arising from manipulative AI interactions.
papers.summary: LLMs can sway users' trust and decisions through subtle wording, but how much manipulative outputs change actual behavior has rarely been measured. Building on the `DarkPatterns-LLM` benchmark, the authors generate controlled manipulative responses with Manipulation Gradient Descent (`MGD`) that target authority, urgency, and social-proof biases. They model influence between users with a Multi-Stakeholder Impact Assessment Network (`MSIAN`) and track how long effects persist with a Temporal Harm Propagation Model (`THPM`). In a study with 120 participants, manipulative framing **significantly shifted trust calibration and compliance (p < 0.01)**, and the effects spread across social contexts.

papers.title: The Show-Up Attack: When Subagents Win Over Their Supervisor
papers.abstract: Multi-agent systems are increasingly deployed to coordinate multiple large language model (LLM) agents. However, this also creates new attack surfaces: malicious agents may have chances to exploit the coordination. In this paper, we propose and study the \textit{show-up attack}, in which a malicious subagent manipulates the supervisor into involving it in tasks beyond its assigned scope. To evaluate this risk, we propose SUA-Arena, which implements 6 attack strategies and contains 188 test cases. Then, we evaluate 6 frontier LLMs and find that all of them are vulnerable to show-up attacks. For example, GPT-5.6-Sol as a supervisor suffers an ASR of up to 0.93. Mitigation strategies such as prompting and restricted communication fail to reduce the risk consistently. These results show that multi-agent systems need explicit mechanisms for enforcing authority boundaries.
papers.summary: In multi-agent LLM systems, a supervisor delegates work to subagents, which opens a new attack surface. The authors define the show-up attack, in which a malicious subagent manipulates the supervisor into involving it in tasks beyond its assigned scope, and build `SUA-Arena` with 6 attack strategies and 188 test cases to measure it. **All six frontier LLMs tested were vulnerable**, with `GPT-5.6-Sol` as supervisor reaching an attack success rate of up to 0.93. Mitigations based on prompting or restricted communication did not reduce the risk consistently, so the authors argue that multi-agent systems need explicit mechanisms for enforcing authority boundaries.

papers.title: Factual Access States in Diffusion Language Models: From Mechanism to Knowledge Editing and Retrieval
papers.abstract: Factual recall is a lookup: some representation inside the network serves as the key, and what that key is made of decides which queries can retrieve the fact, what an edit must cover, and what a retriever can read. We call it the factual access state. In autoregressive (AR) models the subject position enriches attributes largely independently of the relation, and relation-specific selection happens later, at the readout position. In masked diffusion language models (DLMs) we find the state is assembled differently, and much earlier: in the first attention layer the wording of the relation is routed into the position of whichever entity is visible and the early feed-forward layers look the fact up on this fused representation. The state therefore varies with the relation's surface form and with the query direction, so the queries about one fact occupy a region of state space rather than a point, and an operation on the fact succeeds only for queries that enter it. We treat the state as an interface to a DLM's factual knowledge, and put it to two uses. Writing to the state gives a knowledge editor: from one declarative statement, Multi-View Edit fits one shared value per direction across that region and installs it in the early-MLP block, preserving source-prompt reliability while substantially improving paraphrase and reverse question answering, where AR editors gain near zero. Reading it suggests a complementary use: the state at each entity position can serve as a relation-specific retrieval vector with no training, returning both pieces of evidence for two-entity queries on which pooled, prompted and lexical retrievers almost never return both.
papers.summary: Recalling a fact works like a lookup keyed on some internal representation, which the authors call the factual access state. In autoregressive (AR) models, relation-specific selection happens late, but in masked diffusion language models (DLMs) the state forms early: the first attention layer routes the relation's wording into whichever entity is visible, and early feed-forward layers look up the fact on that fused representation. As a result, queries about a single fact occupy a region of state space rather than a single point. Building on this, `Multi-View Edit` installs an edit across that region from a single statement and **substantially improves paraphrase and reverse-question accuracy where AR editors gain near zero**. Read without any training, the same states also serve as relation-specific retrieval vectors that recover both pieces of evidence for two-entity queries, where pooled, prompted, and lexical retrievers almost never do.

papers.title: DuplexLedger: Benchmarking Transactional Memory in Full-Duplex Speech Agents
papers.abstract: Full-duplex speech agents must update persistent memory while listening and speaking, yet it remains unclear which events should be stored, revised, or excluded. Existing benchmarks isolate interaction timing from memory outcomes, obscuring the state transitions behind a correct answer. We introduce DuplexLedger, a bilingual benchmark of 1,094 persistent sessions aligning four full-duplex scenarios with event-level Write/Update/Ignore/Retain supervision, explicit pre/post memory states, and 6,564 same-session questions and checks. Evaluating five full-duplex models reveals an interaction-memory gap: no system combines strong boundary control with coherent final-state memory, and the best final-state fact coverage is 2.01%. We propose ACT-Mem, an 8.92M-parameter sidecar comprising an event controller, a versioned transactional ledger, and a typed retriever coupled with a frozen MiniCPM-o 4.5 backbone. On 219 held-out sessions, ACT-Mem increases latest-value accuracy from 4.11% to 8.68% while reducing stale assertions and distractor adoption. It improves interaction boundaries but slows interruption stopping. These results motivate selective, auditable full-duplex memory rather than indiscriminate transcript retention. Code is available at https://github.com/lyx-researcher/DuplexLedger.
papers.summary: Full-duplex speech agents listen and speak at the same time, and they must decide which events to store in persistent memory, which to revise, and which to ignore. `DuplexLedger` is a bilingual benchmark of 1,094 persistent sessions labeled at the event level (Write, Update, Ignore, or Retain), with explicit memory states before and after each event and 6,564 questions and checks. Across five full-duplex models, none combines good control of turn boundaries with a coherent final memory state, and **the best final-state fact coverage is just 2.01%**. The authors' `ACT-Mem`, an 8.92M-parameter add-on module with a versioned transactional ledger attached to a frozen `MiniCPM-o 4.5`, raises latest-value accuracy from 4.11% to 8.68%, though it makes the agent slower to stop when interrupted.

papers.title: Beyond Experience: Knowledge-Guided Evolution for NPU Kernel Generation
papers.abstract: LLM agents have become capable kernel engineers on mainstream GPU stacks, but they struggle on emerging accelerators such as Ascend NPUs, whose programming model is barely represented in pretraining data. Recent NPU agents address this gap largely through experience: they accumulate memory from their own generation and optimization trials and reuse it on later tasks. We argue that experience alone is not enough for kernel generation. An agent can only remember what it has tried, and it rarely tries a mechanism it does not know. As a result, such memory offers little help when a new operator calls for a different mechanism, and even familiar operators raise unseen situations as optimization proceeds. We present ASCENDEVOLVE, which grounds every step of an evolutionary kernel search in a large external knowledge base built from platform documentation, toolkit headers, and operator repositories. Because this corpus far exceeds any context window, ASCENDEVOLVE indexes it and routes each agent to a small, task-specific slice of evidence instead of the corpus itself. The retrieved knowledge seeds diverse implementation strategies, guides repair when a candidate fails, and constrains how strong candidates are recombined. On 53 Ascend C operators from CANN-Bench spanning four difficulty levels, ASCENDEVOLVE achieves an overall score of 71.39, improving over Reflexion and OpenEvolve by 11.6% and 17.2%.
papers.summary: LLM agents write GPU kernels competently but struggle on Ascend NPUs, whose programming model barely appears in pretraining data, and existing NPU agents rely mostly on memory of their own past attempts, which cannot suggest mechanisms they have never tried. `AscendEvolve` grounds each step of an evolutionary kernel search in a large knowledge base built from platform documentation, toolkit headers, and operator repositories. Because the corpus far exceeds any context window, the system indexes it and gives each agent a small, task-specific slice. The retrieved knowledge seeds diverse implementation strategies, guides repairs when a candidate fails, and constrains how strong candidates are recombined. On 53 Ascend C operators from `CANN-Bench`, it scores 71.39 overall, **outperforming `Reflexion` by 11.6% and `OpenEvolve` by 17.2%**.

papers.title: Benefit and Cost of Random-Token Replacement under Repeated Data: A Known-Entropy Decomposition and Evidence from Ten Real Corpora
papers.abstract: When unique pretraining data is scarce, models see the same tokens many times and are thought to memorize. Random-token replacement, an input-corruption augmentation, is one remedy reported to lower validation loss, but a lower loss alone does not reveal which source of error it reduces. On a controlled source whose entropy rate is known in closed form, we show that replacement shrinks predictions toward the corpus average. We also introduce a decomposition that separates validation loss into approximation, estimation, and memorization terms. This shrinkage view predicts that replacement's bias cost needs no memorization but its benefit does. Memorization raises validation loss after its minimum, so we report the effect at two points, the minimum validation loss and the end of a fixed budget. Where replacement helps, it reduces this rise by about 60%. At the end of the budget, it turns from harmful to helpful as the controlled source becomes less predictable; at the minimum, it helps at no predictability level under the fixed recipe. On Korean and Japanese web text, replacement removes about a third of the loss rise after the minimum by the end of the budget, but its effect at the minimum is much smaller. Across ten real corpora, replacement lowers the final loss on nine. It harms only the census corpus, program-generated JSON that is the most redundant of the ten and much more redundant than any of 64 further prose and code corpora we measure.
papers.summary: When unique pretraining data is scarce and models see the same tokens many times, random-token replacement (corrupting input tokens as augmentation) is reported to lower validation loss, but it has been unclear which source of error it actually reduces. Using a controlled data source whose entropy rate is known exactly, the authors show that replacement pulls predictions toward the corpus average, and they split validation loss into approximation, estimation, and memorization terms. In this view, replacement's bias cost appears even without memorization, while its benefit requires it: where it helps, it **cuts the post-minimum rise in validation loss caused by memorization by about 60%**, though it does not improve the minimum loss itself. Across ten real corpora, replacement lowers the final loss on nine and hurts only highly redundant program-generated JSON.

papers.title: WORTH Benchmark: Evidence Discovery under Not-Fully-Cooperative Information -- A Two-Episode Pilot
papers.abstract: Existing reasoning evaluations typically provide task-relevant information to models as available premises, rarely examining concurrently how models discover evidence autonomously and how information presentation within narratives guides or obscures judgment. This paper proposes the WORTH Benchmark: models read original mystery narratives without clue annotations, autonomously select key clue sentences, identify case participants, and explain their reasoning process. The narrative materials are designed by professional authors such that evidence facilitating reasoning coexists with narrative arrangements that delay the revelation of truth. We report a pilot experiment under full-story conditions across two episodes, conducting a total of 70 formal runs on models, of which 67 runs are content-scorable. Scoring separately records hits on author-designated key clue sentences and participant selections; natural language explanations are used for case diagnosis and are not scored independently. The results show that clue hits and participant judgments are not synchronized; across 37 content-scorable runs in Episode 02, 31 runs simultaneously selected the same set of incorrect participants, while adjacent suspicion-oriented and exoneration-oriented sentences were selected 25 times and 0 times, respectively. These phenomena illustrate the diagnostic value of component-wise analysis and suggest that not-fully-cooperative informational relationships may influence evidence selection and judgment. This study only implements full-story conditions for two episodes, and does not establish stable model rankings or infer general mechanisms on this basis; human player records have not yet been cleaned, and this version does not report human-model comparisons.
papers.summary: Most reasoning evaluations hand models the relevant premises up front, rather than testing whether they can find evidence that a narrative partly obscures. `WORTH` has models read professionally written mystery stories with no clue annotations, pick out key clue sentences, identify the case participants, and explain their reasoning. Across 67 scorable runs over two episodes, hitting the right clues did not go together with correct participant judgments. In one episode, **31 of 37 runs converged on the same incorrect set of participants**, and models chose suspicion-oriented sentences 25 times but adjacent exonerating sentences 0 times. The authors present this as a pilot that establishes neither stable model rankings nor comparisons with human players.

papers.title: Meta Expert: Cross-Layer Expert Sharing for Storage- and Retrieval-Efficient MoE
papers.abstract: As model parameters scale up, sparsely activated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) approaches have become essential for model scaling. However, mainstream models currently adopt hierarchical architectures, where experts in different layers, although topologically independent, exhibit substantial similarity and redundancy in their stored content. Compared to the hierarchically arranged \textbf{Local Expert} in existing mainstream models, we hypothesize that inter-layer shared \textbf{Meta Expert} hold greater potential. To this end, we conduct a multi-dimensional empirical comparison between Local and Meta Experts, and find that models incorporating Meta Experts exhibit lower parameter redundancy, together with lower cross-entropy loss and higher downstream task accuracy. With the activated quantity and the expert granularity held fixed, \textbf{our model matches the performance of Vanilla MoE using only 70--80\% of the experts}, substantially improving the model's scaling potential. Beyond removing inter-layer redundancy among experts and improving information storage efficiency, our theoretical analysis further shows that, compared with Local Experts, Meta Experts provide hidden states with more flexible residual pathways, thereby improving information retrieval efficiency.
papers.summary: In Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, each layer has its own experts, yet experts in different layers often store similar, redundant content. The authors propose `Meta Expert`, a pool of experts shared across layers, and compare it empirically with conventional per-layer experts. Shared experts reduce parameter redundancy, lower cross-entropy loss, and raise downstream accuracy. With the number of activated experts and their size held fixed, the model **matches vanilla MoE using only 70 to 80% of the experts**, and a theoretical analysis argues that shared experts give hidden states more flexible residual pathways.

papers.title: From Encoding to Generation: Towards Empathetic Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Empathetic interaction involves two distinguishable capacities: representing another person's emotional state (cognitive empathy) and generating an appropriate response to that state (affective empathy). We apply this distinction to examine how emotion-related information is internally organized, selectively attended to, and carried through response generation in Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct across 10 emotion categories from the EmpatheticDialogues dataset. Layer-wise linear probing revealed a broad middle-layer region of peak emotion-category decodability, with the layer-11 L2 probe achieving 63.6% held-out accuracy against a 10% chance level and a 54.6% TF-IDF lexical baseline. During response generation, emotion-related user tokens received 1.89 times as much attention per token as other utterance tokens, concentrated across layers 10-15. Target-emotion alignment then decreased from a mean cosine similarity of 0.239 for input representations to 0.125 for generated responses, with positive drift in 77% of examples and the largest shifts for angry and furious. Emotion-category representation, attention allocation, and response-level alignment therefore emerge as distinguishable components of model processing that can be analyzed through a functional cognitive-affective empathy framework. These findings provide a foundation for monitoring emotion representations during generation and leveraging models' existing affective structure to support more naturally empathetic responses without relying on external prompting or explicit emotion conditioning.
