Its Genese engine separates decisions from state updates, while reusable financial scenarios and application ledgers track consumption, cash, debt and payments. FinL-mlx, a compact decision model trained with SFT + RLCD on 2.93 million examples, achieves 74.55% accuracy and 38.37% question-macro F1 in consumer financial-choice scenarios, outperforming Jev 1.13 and GLM-5.3-Flash on both measures. We evaluate eight financial task families and simulate 12 million distinct household agents in paired purchase-funding conditions. Jointly raising purchase goals and approved credit limits increases consumption, with responses differing across age and income groups. Education, employment and household-size differences persist after age--income standardization and mainly reflect transitions from deferral to purchase. Asset and debt groups differ in cash drawdown, repayment and closing debt. A 24-month panel varies purchase goals under a common credit product, with repayment and arrears updating subsequent offers. S$^2$-MAS links heterogeneous household decisions to evolving consumption, cash and repayment paths, supporting economic experiments across household groups, population scales and time horizons.
papers.summary: `S²-MAS` is a framework for simulating economic behavior at society scale using 500 million synthetic household personas grounded in real survey data. Its `Genese` engine separates agent decisions from state updates, and reusable financial scenarios and ledgers track consumption, cash, debt, and payments. The decision model, `FinL-mlx`, is trained with supervised fine-tuning and `RLCD` on 2.93 million examples and reaches **74.55% accuracy on consumer financial-choice scenarios**, outperforming `Jev 1.13` and `GLM-5.3-Flash`. Simulations of 12 million household agents and a 24-month panel show responses to credit and purchase goals that differ by age, income, education, and debt profile.

papers.title: Give the Model a Finger: Developmentally Aligned Evaluation of Counting in Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are exact on small sets and drift into estimation on larger ones, a profile reminiscent of children before they master counting. Children cross the barrier with epistemic actions: pointing at each item while reciting number words, moving counted items aside, partitioning the array. We give VLMs the same actions as dumb image tools with no visual intelligence of their own in a training-free agent loop. Our central claim is about measurement, not intervention: a model that counts by marking leaves a normally hidden serial procedure on the image, and the developmental principles of counting turn those marks into an interpretable audit of serial visual reasoning: every tag is classified against point-level ground truth as on-target, duplicate, phantom, or omitted, the answer is checked against the number of tags, and order irrelevance is tested by forcing opposite traversal orders. Across 9 models, 682 images, and 7 harness conditions we find that (i) the exact-counting range is a model-specific signature spanning nearly two orders of magnitude (R80 from 3 to 150 dots); (ii) as an intervention the finger mostly fails: tags help 4 of 9 models on small-count photographs, hurt imprecise pointers, and rarely beat a verbal routine or a blind point list; what the loop buys is an auditable trace, not accuracy; (iii) as measurement it succeeds: a tag-perturbation probe shows that precise pointers read their answers off the tags, pointing precision tracks which models benefit, dense scenes fail by omission, and models rarely revise after seeing their own tags; and (iv) the capacities dissociate: models follow an instructed traversal order yet often change their answer when it reverses, and children's regular-over-scattered advantage appears only under the routine and survives lattices that defeat a rows-times-columns shortcut.
papers.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) count small sets exactly and drift into estimation on larger ones, much like children before they learn to count. The authors give VLMs simple image-marking tools, such as pointing at, moving, or partitioning items, inside a training-free agent loop, and use principles from developmental psychology to audit each tag as on-target, duplicate, phantom, or omitted. Across 9 models and 682 images, the exact-counting range is a model-specific signature spanning nearly two orders of magnitude, from 3 to 150 dots. **The marking tools rarely improve accuracy, but they produce an auditable trace** showing that precise pointers read their answers off their tags, that dense scenes fail by omission, and that models seldom revise an answer after seeing their own tags.

papers.title: CrystalAR: Autoregressive Modeling for Symmetric Crystal Generation
papers.abstract: Deep generative modeling has achieved remarkable progress in crystal generation. Given the rich symmetries inherent in crystalline structures, recent work has sought to explicitly incorporate space-group symmetry into generative models, enabling more effective exploration of novel symmetry templates. Yet introducing symmetry templates increases the combinatorial complexity of stoichiometric relationships between atomic species and crystallographic sites, while creating a fundamental tension between flexible exploration of discrete crystallographic templates and faithful realization of these templates as continuous three-dimensional structures. To address these challenges, we propose CrystalAR, a unified autoregressive framework that models Wyckoff symmetry templates and complete crystal structures within a single generative sequence. Specifically, CrystalAR reformulates continuous coordinate generation as a symmetry-conditioned hierarchy of discrete spatial localization decisions, autoregressively refining the positions of all symmetry-inequivalent sites across resolution levels while jointly modeling their spatial configuration within each level. This discrete hierarchical formulation further enables constraint-aware search over both crystallographic templates and geometric realizations. As a result, CrystalAR retains strong symmetry-template generation capability while achieving competitive de novo generation performance and template-free crystal structure prediction (CSP) accuracy. These results suggest that symmetry-template generation can be retained alongside broadly competitive de novo generation performance and competitive CSP without reliance on symmetry templates retrieved from prior data, providing a promising alternative paradigm for symmetry-preserving crystal generation.
papers.summary: Generating crystals under space-group symmetry templates complicates the matching of atomic species to crystallographic sites and creates tension between exploring discrete templates and realizing them as continuous 3D structures. `CrystalAR` handles both in one autoregressive sequence, recasting continuous coordinate generation as a symmetry-conditioned hierarchy of discrete localization decisions refined across resolution levels. Because the formulation is discrete, it supports constraint-aware search over both templates and geometric realizations. The model keeps strong symmetry-template generation while achieving **competitive de novo generation and template-free crystal structure prediction (CSP) accuracy**.

papers.title: How Much Do $\ell_1$ Attacks Need Concentrated Perturbations?
papers.abstract: A global $\ell_1$ budget limits how much an adversary may change an image, not how that change is distributed. We ask how much of an $\ell_1$ attack's observed success remains when large coordinate changes are restricted. We add a per-coordinate cap to the budget, enforce the joint constraint by exact in-loop projection, and sweep the cap for APGD-$\ell_1$, SLIDE, and FMN-$\ell_1$ without altering their objectives. Across 18 standard-model settings, caps of at most $32/255$ retain a median $97\%$ of attack success relative to each method's native uncapped baseline, while median peak magnitude falls by $80\%$ and median effective support nearly triples. At matched realized $\ell_1$, capped perturbations remain structurally distinct; separate ImageNet comparisons also show lower LPIPS and DISTS at selected caps. Direct in-loop constrained optimization preserves up to $88$ percentage points more attack success than post-hoc clipping, highlighting the importance of constraint enforcement. Suitable caps nevertheless vary across attacks and models, and adversarially trained classifiers exhibit more heterogeneous concentration sensitivity. These results establish perturbation concentration as a complementary, model- and attack-dependent axis of $\ell_1$ attack evaluation.
papers.summary: An ℓ1 budget limits the total change an adversarial attack makes to an image but not how concentrated that change is. The authors add a per-coordinate cap, enforce the combined constraint by exact projection inside the optimization loop, and sweep the cap for `APGD-ℓ1`, `SLIDE`, and `FMN-ℓ1` without changing their objectives. Across 18 settings on standard models, **caps of at most 32/255 keep a median 97% of attack success** while median peak magnitude falls by 80% and effective support nearly triples. Enforcing the cap inside the loop preserves up to 88 percentage points more success than clipping afterwards, though suitable caps vary by attack and model, and adversarially trained classifiers respond less uniformly.

papers.title: Radar-Based 3D Human Pose Estimation via Motion-Aware Pose Initialization and Observation-Guided Refinement
papers.abstract: 3D Human Pose Estimation (3D HPE) is used in indoor environments, such as smart homes, to analyze human movement and monitor human states. Millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar is suitable for this task because it is robust to lighting variations and does not capture images of human appearance. However, radar observations often provide insufficient information about certain body parts or contain overlapping reflections from multiple body parts, limiting accurate 3D joint localization. To address these limitations, we propose the Initialization-to-Refinement Pose Framework (I2R-Pose), comprising two stages: Motion-Aware Pose Initialization and Observation-Guided Refinement. In the first stage, joint-wise features are learned by incorporating temporal relationships across consecutive radar observations and human skeletal structure to compensate for insufficient joint information and estimate an initial 3D pose sequence. In the second stage, separately extracted radar observation features predict joint-wise positional corrections that refine the initial pose and generate the final pose sequence. The framework supports individual and fused inputs of time-Doppler/time-range (TD/TR) maps and radar point clouds (PCs). To evaluate performance across indoor activities, we construct the Radar Motion and Spatial Information for 3D Human Pose Estimation (RaMoS-Pose) dataset, providing synchronized TD/TR maps, radar PCs, and 3D joint ground truth (GT). Evaluations on RaMoS-Pose and the publicly available MVDoppler-Pose dataset show that I2R-Pose reduces mean per-joint position error (MPJPE) by 39.50% on MVDoppler-Pose and by 15.13% on RaMoS-Pose with fused inputs, compared with the best-performing existing methods evaluated on each dataset.
papers.summary: Millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar suits indoor 3D human pose estimation (3D HPE) because it is robust to lighting and does not capture appearance, but its reflections are sparse and overlapping. `I2R-Pose` first estimates an initial pose sequence from temporal and skeletal structure, then predicts per-joint corrections from separately extracted radar features, and accepts time-Doppler and time-range maps, radar point clouds, or both. The authors also release the `RaMoS-Pose` dataset of synchronized radar data and 3D joint ground truth. With fused inputs, mean per-joint position error (MPJPE) drops by **39.50% on `MVDoppler-Pose`** and 15.13% on `RaMoS-Pose` compared with the best existing methods.

papers.title: RITE: Evaluating End-to-End Resilience to Silent Tool Errors in E-Commerce Agentic Systems
papers.abstract: Tool-using LLM agents increasingly answer e-commerce queries through multi-step tool interactions. The expected output of a tool call can shift between agent development and execution, allowing a plausible but incorrect value to be returned without an explicit failure signal. These silent errors may propagate through subsequent decisions into final answers. To study agents' resilience across this end-to-end process, we formulate Silent-error Resilience Task, an interactive task that evaluates whether they complete the original query after a silent error corrupts an intermediate state. We introduce RITE, a benchmark built from human-authored industrial workflows and production-log-derived inputs. To enable controlled and reproducible evaluation, we use a semantic error taxonomy to inject errors into fixed workflow prefixes, freeze recorded tool behavior, and let agents continue freely. It contains 167 matched units across nine e-commerce workflows, yielding 501 silent-error, correct-value, and explicit-failure instances. Across 10 recent LLMs, silent errors roughly halve task success and are consistently harder than explicit failures. Recognition, use of an available verification path, and integration of the resulting evidence form successive bottlenecks. We also propose a light State Checker as an intervention to test whether resilience can be improved.
papers.summary: Tool-using LLM agents can receive plausible but wrong values from a tool call with no failure signal, and these silent errors can propagate into final answers. `RITE` is a benchmark built from human-authored industrial e-commerce workflows and inputs derived from production logs: errors from a semantic taxonomy are injected into fixed workflow prefixes, tool behavior is frozen, and the agent then continues freely, across 501 instances in nine workflows. Across 10 recent LLMs, **silent errors roughly halve task success** and are consistently harder than explicit failures. The main bottlenecks, in order, are recognizing the error, using an available verification path, and integrating the resulting evidence; the authors also test a lightweight `State Checker` intervention.

papers.title: GRADUS: Discovering and Recovering Agent Lessons from the Environment's Latent Syllabus
papers.abstract: Training LLM agents for policy-constrained tool environments, such as an airline backend with booking, refund, and cancellation policies, requires tasks that exercise the environment's rules individually and in combination. Existing synthesis pipelines let a model propose tasks and retain only those it immediately solves, biasing training data toward easier behaviors. We introduce Gradus (Graded Rungs of Ascending Difficulty from an Underlying System), which decouples what a task should teach from the concrete task and solution used to teach it. Without seed tasks, Gradus treats a fixed environment as a latent syllabus, extracting guarded behavioral operators that capture how actions depend on current conditions and how their effects reshape subsequent decisions. It composes these operators into increasingly demanding tasks while using corpus-level feedback to target missing outcome combinations. Crucially, Gradus jointly calibrates tasks and solutions against the environment: execution feedback identifies which side to refine while preserving the intended behavioral requirements. Verification thus becomes a recovery signal rather than a terminal filter, coupling coverage-guided exploration with the preservation of difficult examples. From off-the-shelf backbones, the resulting curriculum lifts a 30B model from 59% to 89% on $\tau^2$-Bench and from 47% to 83% on CAR-Bench with an Opus 4.5 proposer, and to 76% and 62%, respectively, with an open-weight Qwen3-235B proposer. These results show the value of jointly controlling which behaviors are explored and which survive into verified training data.
papers.summary: Synthetic training data for LLM agents in policy-constrained tool environments, such as an airline booking backend, tends to favor easy behaviors because pipelines keep only tasks the proposing model solves right away. `Gradus` needs no seed tasks: it extracts guarded behavioral operators from the environment, composes them into progressively harder tasks, and uses corpus-level feedback to cover missing outcome combinations. When verification fails, execution feedback shows whether the task or the solution needs fixing, so hard examples are repaired rather than discarded. The resulting curriculum lifts a 30B model **from 59% to 89% on `τ²-Bench`** and from 47% to 83% on `CAR-Bench` with an `Opus 4.5` proposer, and to 76% and 62% with an open-weight `Qwen3-235B` proposer.

papers.title: RELAY: Scaling Historical Build Restoration through Rule Reuse and Agentic Repair
papers.abstract: Vulnerability benchmarks and software engineering research depend on rebuilding historical software. Yet builds rely on external resources, such as base images and packages, that change independently of the source code. In this study, we examine this environment decay on 14,159 OSS-Fuzz cases. We find that 69.7% no longer complete reconstruction and verification, and that most failures share a small number of recurring failure symptoms. A recurring failure can therefore be diagnosed once and its repair reused. We present Relay, a hybrid framework that uses an LLM to derive and validate deterministic repair rules from representative failures, reuses them without model calls, and escalates cases unresolved by rules to a per-case agent. We evaluate Relay in human-guided and fully automated rule-derivation campaigns and compare it with a per-case agent approach. We find that rule derivation can be fully automated, and that reusable rules restore as many builds as per-case agents with fewer build executions. However, agents restore cases that the rules cannot. Our results show that a hybrid approach that applies rules first and escalates the remaining cases to an agent restores more builds than either approach alone and at a lower cost than using agents alone.
papers.summary: Rebuilding historical software for vulnerability benchmarks breaks as base images and packages change independently of the source code; across 14,159 `OSS-Fuzz` cases, **69.7% no longer complete reconstruction and verification**, mostly because of a few recurring failure patterns. `Relay` uses an LLM to derive and validate deterministic repair rules from representative failures, applies those rules without further model calls, and hands unresolved cases to a per-case agent. Rule derivation can be fully automated, and the rules alone restore as many builds as per-case agents while running fewer builds. The hybrid of rules first and agents for the remainder restores more builds than either approach alone, at lower cost than agents alone.

papers.title: SLM-SS: Token-Based Speech Separation with Speech Language Models
papers.abstract: Speech separation (SS) has witnessed substantial progress in recent years with the advent of neural network-based methods, achieving notable improvements on signal-level evaluation metrics. Existing speech separation systems are mostly optimized with signal-level objectives, and often yield outputs that are acceptable in waveform metrics but suboptimal for intelligibility-sensitive downstream tasks. To address this gap, we propose SLM-SS, a token-based generative speech separation framework that models multi-talker mixtures with speech language models. We first discretize clean speech into multi-codebook token sequences with neural codecs and serialize multi-speaker targets via Serialized Output Training (SOT). An encoder-decoder autoregressive speech language model predicts the zero-order sequence to establish speaker ordering and coarse linguistic content, and a non-autoregressive module then refines higher-order residual codebooks for efficient reconstruction. We further introduce a per-talker non-autoregressive strategy that simplifies high-order modeling and improves the stability. On Libri2Mix, SLM-SS with per-talker NAR achieves $6.92\%$ WER, approaching codec-only reconstruction. The WavTokenizer variant eliminates NAR refinement and achieves the highest mean subjective quality score among evaluated separation systems. Its UTMOS and DNSMOS advantages over discriminative baselines persist on unseen noisy and Chinese mixtures without fine-tuning.
papers.summary: Speech separation systems trained on signal-level objectives can score well on waveform metrics while producing output that suits intelligibility-sensitive downstream tasks poorly. `SLM-SS` treats separation as generation: clean speech is discretized into multi-codebook tokens with neural codecs, speakers are serialized with Serialized Output Training (`SOT`), an autoregressive speech language model predicts the first codebook, and a non-autoregressive (NAR) module refines the rest, optionally per talker. On `Libri2Mix` the per-talker variant reaches **6.92% word error rate (WER)**, close to codec-only reconstruction. A `WavTokenizer` variant without NAR refinement gets the highest subjective quality score among evaluated systems, and its quality advantages hold on unseen noisy and Chinese mixtures without fine-tuning.

papers.title: Toward Agentic AI for the 6G Physical Layer: From Algorithm Discovery to Verified Baseband Silicon
papers.abstract: 6G will be designed faster than it can be built: AI-driven search already proposes physical-layer algorithms at machine speed, while carrying a single one onto embedded baseband silicon remains specialist work. That silicon imposes hard memory and numeric limits, but also exposes cost structures a GPU lacks, and a design flow that never runs on the target sees neither. We present an agentic workflow in which an LLM coding agent implements algorithms on a commercial baseband SoC, optimizes them down to agent-written vector assembly, and validates them on silicon. The agent is guided by a knowledge base of measured platform facts, checked at every step against evaluators it is instructed never to edit, and metered per phase. We showcase the workflow on an AI-discovered orthogonal time frequency space (OTFS) detector portfolio on the open 6G4All platform. It yields twelve kernels that run cycle-exactly on silicon, their optimized versions at 18k-405k cycles (30-660 $\mu$s) per frame. It also yields a new detector shaped by the chip's measured costs that needs 13.9% fewer cycles than the port of the discovered detector while matching its error rate, with a measured edge our evaluation cannot statistically resolve, a structure that a hardware-blind search objective had no reason to find. What is not specific to OTFS is the workflow: an LLM agent exploring an implementation space under real hardware limits, with the cost of every choice measured rather than assumed.
papers.summary: AI search can propose 6G physical-layer algorithms quickly, but implementing them on embedded baseband chips with tight memory and numeric limits remains specialist work. The authors present a workflow in which an LLM coding agent implements and optimizes algorithms on a commercial baseband system-on-chip down to agent-written vector assembly, guided by a knowledge base of measured platform facts and checked at each step against evaluators it is told never to edit. Applied to an AI-discovered orthogonal time frequency space (`OTFS`) detector portfolio on the open `6G4All` platform, it produced twelve kernels that run cycle-exactly on silicon. It also produced a new hardware-aware detector that **needs 13.9% fewer cycles than the port of the discovered detector** at matching error rate.

papers.title: LatBridge: Efficient and Stable Model Replacement in Latent-Communication Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: Multi-agent systems rely on communication to complete tasks, and latent communication passes continuous representations to reduce text generation and re-encoding. However, multi-agent systems must reconfigure agent models, whereas existing latent-communication methods are built for fixed model combinations, so their interfaces may fail after replacement. Our pilot study confirms this interface failure and identifies the requirement for interface reuse after model replacement. We present LatBridge, which connects agent models through a shared Bridge and separate interfaces under a shared latent-communication protocol. After agent model replacement, LatBridge reuses unchanged interfaces, selects matching low-rank interfaces, and combines them through the Bridge, training only missing ones with all models frozen. The Bridge processes source representations in the basic mode and constructs target input without autoregressive generation in the accelerated mode. Experiments support effective communication after model replacement, with mean basic-mode accuracies of 14.8% on MATH and 27.3% on ALFWorld next-action prediction across eight small-model configurations. Analyses examine the factors supporting task accuracy and communication efficiency.
papers.summary: Latent-communication multi-agent systems pass continuous representations between agents instead of text, but their interfaces are built for one fixed set of models and break when an agent's model is swapped out. `LatBridge` connects agent models through a shared `Bridge` with separate low-rank interfaces under one latent-communication protocol, so after a replacement it reuses unchanged interfaces and trains only the missing ones while all models stay frozen. An accelerated mode builds the target model's input without autoregressive generation. Across eight small-model configurations, the basic mode reaches mean accuracies of **14.8% on `MATH` and 27.3% on `ALFWorld` next-action prediction** after model replacement.

papers.title: RAG-NIMBF: A Non-Invasive, Modular Benchmarking Framework for Automated RAG Configuration Analysis
papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has become the dominant paradigm for grounding the outputs of large language models (LLM) in external knowledge. However, practitioners are faced with a vast configuration space comprising chunking, embedding, retrieval, reranking, prompting and generation models, and there is limited guidance on how these components interact. We present RAG-NIMBF, a modular benchmarking framework that attaches to existing RAG pipelines as a non-invasive evaluation layer. It evaluates the configuration space through controlled ablation with end-to-end experiment tracking. The evaluation combines LLM-based answer quality scores, retrieval correctness measures, and runtime indicators. This study validates the framework across multiple generation models on the SQuAD dataset. This process reveals non-obvious interactions and demonstrates how the experiments are tracked. The findings indicate that the retrieval balance of relevance and diversity substantially enhances the relevance and coverage of retrieved context in comparison to a conventional similarity search, with MMR raising nDCG@5 by +4 to +11 percentage points across the swept models. More detailed prompt instructions meaningfully increase how faithfully generated answers stick to the retrieved evidence, especially for capable and reasoning models (+10 to +13pp on Qwen3.6-27B, GPT-4o-mini and Qwen3.5-think, but negligible on the 20B generator). Overall, RAG-NIMBF transforms the configuration space of RAG into reproducible, comparable experiments. By attaching to existing production pipelines in a non-invasive way, it enables practitioners to systematically evaluate and improve deployed systems without disrupting existing workflows. This replaces ad hoc choices with evidence-based decisions.
papers.summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines involve many interacting choices, including chunking, embedding, retrieval, reranking, prompting and generator model, and practitioners have little guidance on how these choices interact. `RAG-NIMBF` attaches to an existing pipeline as a non-invasive evaluation layer and runs controlled ablations with end-to-end experiment tracking. It scores LLM-judged answer quality, retrieval correctness and runtime. On `SQuAD`, Maximal Marginal Relevance (`MMR`) retrieval raises **nDCG@5 by 4 to 11 percentage points** over plain similarity search, and more detailed prompts improve faithfulness to retrieved evidence by 10 to 13 points for capable and reasoning models but barely help a 20B generator.

papers.title: Privacy-preserving inference on hosted models: a learned input-embedding transform for frozen Qwen3.8-27B
papers.abstract: Every prompt sent to a hosted language model is readable by whoever runs it. We study whether the prompt can remain on the client while the host receives transformed vectors that stand in for it. A language model converts text to vectors exactly once, with a public lookup table; we perform that step locally and pass the vectors through a small trained network (55.6M parameters) before they leave the perimeter. The host runs a frozen 27B model (Qwen3.8-27B) on the transformed vectors and never receives text or token ids. We train the transform against the frozen model as a fixed judge, combining a forward-KL utility term with an auxiliary term that pushes each vector away from its original direction. On 1,490 MMLU questions held out from training, the transform costs 1.5 points of accuracy (80.7% vs. 82.3%), breaking 68 of the 1,226 questions the unmodified model answers correctly (5.5%), while 30.1% of content tokens no longer decode to their original token under a nearest-neighbour lookup.
papers.summary: Every prompt sent to a hosted language model is readable by whoever runs the host. In this approach the client performs the embedding lookup locally and passes the vectors through a small trained network (55.6M parameters), so the host runs a frozen `Qwen3.8-27B` on transformed vectors and never sees text or token ids. The transform is trained against the frozen model with a forward-KL utility loss plus a term that pushes each vector away from its original direction. On 1,490 held-out `MMLU` questions, accuracy drops by only **1.5 points (80.7% vs. 82.3%)**, while 30.1% of content tokens no longer decode to their original token under nearest-neighbour lookup.

papers.title: SMART: Semantic Segment Mapping and Assessment of Recognition Transcripts with Contextual Rubrics
papers.abstract: Word error rate (WER) assigns equal cost to lexical edits despite their different semantic consequences, while overall semantic scores cannot identify which individual errors alter the intended meaning. We formulate ASR semantic evaluation as context-aware, segment-level consequence assessment and propose Semantic Segment Mapping and Assessment of Recognition Transcripts with Contextual Rubrics (SMART), a framework for traceable semantic evaluation and targeted ASR correction. SMART maps reference-hypothesis discrepancies into coherent segments and applies a structured contextual rubric to assign explicit consequence labels. These labels support Semantic Impact Error Rate (SIER), which quantifies consequential errors at utterance, chunk, and lexical levels. Against majority-vote human labels, SMART achieves 0.843 F1 versus 0.745 for direct LLM judgment. Evaluation across multiple LLMs further demonstrates that SMART is relatively insensitive to the choice of evaluation model, while MER and SIER reveal different aspects of ASR quality. A separate target-reference-free rubric guides correction using the target hypothesis and surrounding ASR hypotheses, outperforming a matched w/o Rubric baseline on both datasets, with further absolute reductions of 0.85-0.98 percentage points in MER and 1.18-1.65 percentage points in SIER_lex.
papers.summary: Word error rate (WER) treats every lexical edit as equally costly, while whole-utterance semantic scores cannot say which specific speech-recognition errors change the meaning. `SMART` groups reference-versus-hypothesis discrepancies into coherent segments, applies a structured contextual rubric to label each one's consequence, and uses those labels to define a Semantic Impact Error Rate (`SIER`) at utterance, chunk and lexical levels. Against majority-vote human labels it reaches **0.843 F1 versus 0.745 for direct LLM judgment**, and its results change little across judge models. A separate rubric that needs no target reference guides automatic correction and further reduces both `MER` and `SIER` compared with a no-rubric baseline.

papers.title: COMPASS: Routing via Capability-Oriented Model Profiling with Adaptive Search, Selection, and Tool Use
papers.abstract: LLM routing aims to select a capable model at low cost, but specialized routers can require updates as models and tasks change. We propose COMPASS, an agentic router in which an LLM follows a routing recipe, gathers performance and cost evidence through tools, and optionally inspects candidate answers before selecting a model. Our evaluations on LLMRouterBench and DeepSWE show that agentic routing can improve accuracy and lower model-call cost relative to specialized and trained routing baselines, without routing-specific training. On LLMRouterBench, COMPASS reaches 69.85% accuracy at \$139.57, compared with RLCascadeRouter's 69.14% at \$180.22. On DeepSWE under fixed five-fold cross-validation, it reaches 78.1% at \$215, compared with 74.1% at \$500 for the best single model. COMPASS also supports routing across benchmarks and adapts to an expanded model pool by reading new evaluation records, without changing the router's weights or prompt.
papers.summary: LLM routing tries to pick a capable model at low cost, but specialized routers need retraining whenever the available models or tasks change. `COMPASS` is an agentic router: an LLM follows a routing recipe, uses tools to gather performance and cost evidence, and can optionally inspect candidate answers before choosing a model, all with no routing-specific training. On `LLMRouterBench` it reaches 69.85% accuracy at $139.57 versus `RLCascadeRouter`'s 69.14% at $180.22, and on `DeepSWE` it reaches **78.1% at $215 versus 74.1% at $500 for the best single model**. It adapts to an expanded model pool by reading new evaluation records, without changing its weights or prompt.

papers.title: SAPD: Learning from Agent Experience without Environment Interaction
papers.abstract: Scaling the training of Large Language Model (LLM) agents typically requires a large collection of executable environments, whose construction, maintenance, and operation constrain the expansion of training experience. Existing offline trajectories offer an opportunity to reuse interaction experience, yet effectively refining the current policy without revisiting these environments remains challenging: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can lead to catastrophic forgetting, while online reinforcement learning requires real-time interaction with the environment. To address this challenge, we propose Step-Advantage Policy Distillation (SAPD), a method for learning from offline trajectories using relative step advantages. SAPD decomposes multi-turn trajectories into individual decision contexts for on-policy distillation, allowing the student to generate responses conditioned on recorded histories, and introduces relative step advantage signals to stabilize training. The entire process requires neither new environment observations nor additional multi-turn interactions. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-based QA show that SAPD improves performance across different teacher configurations, mitigates catastrophic forgetting compared with SFT, and runs at least $4.7\times$ faster per training step than online OPD. We will release our code soon.
papers.summary: Training LLM agents at scale usually requires many executable environments, and reusing offline trajectories instead is hard: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) causes catastrophic forgetting, while online reinforcement learning needs live interaction. Step-Advantage Policy Distillation (`SAPD`) splits recorded multi-turn trajectories into individual decision contexts, lets the student generate its own responses conditioned on the recorded history for on-policy distillation, and stabilizes training with relative step-advantage signals. No new environment observations or multi-turn rollouts are needed. On `ALFWorld`, `WebShop` and search-based QA, `SAPD` improves performance across teacher configurations, forgets less than SFT, and runs **at least 4.7x faster per training step than online on-policy distillation**.

papers.title: Physical Operating-Condition-Guided Vision-Language Matching for Cavitation Diagnosis in Industrial Pipeline Systems
papers.abstract: Cavitation diagnosis in industrial pipeline systems is challenging because acoustic responses vary substantially with operating conditions, while similar time-frequency patterns may correspond to different cavitation states. To address this issue, we propose a physical operating-condition-guided vision-language matching (POC-VLM) for cavitation diagnosis. POC-VLM first constructs physical operating-condition-aware semantic descriptions by explicitly incorporating sample-specific operating variables into candidate cavitation texts. A time-frequency-conditioned text adaptation module then dynamically aligns these physical semantics with the observed acoustic response, followed by global-local vision-language matching to capture both holistic and localized discriminative patterns. In parallel, a K-nearest neighbours-based non-parametric physical operating-condition prior estimates the physical plausibility of each candidate state and is fused with the vision-language semantic evidence at the decision level. Experiments on three real-world cavitation datasets show that POC-VLM consistently outperforms representative data-driven, multimodal and domain-specific diagnostic methods. Further analyses verify the complementary roles of vision-language semantic matching and physical operating-condition priors, while demonstrating robust performance under varying sampling rates, noise levels and observation durations.
papers.summary: Diagnosing cavitation in industrial pipelines from acoustic signals is difficult because the signals change with operating conditions, and similar time-frequency patterns can correspond to different cavitation states. `POC-VLM` writes candidate class descriptions that include each sample's operating variables, adapts this text to the observed time-frequency response, and performs global and local vision-language matching. It then fuses the result with a K-nearest-neighbours prior that estimates how physically plausible each candidate state is. On three real-world cavitation datasets it **consistently outperforms data-driven, multimodal and domain-specific baselines** and stays robust under varying sampling rates, noise levels and observation durations.

papers.title: VISH-ASR: Viterbi-Guided Selection of Hotwords for Speech-LLM Contextual ASR
papers.abstract: Prompt-based contextual ASR requires selecting a compact hotword subset from large dynamic inventories, yet existing pre-selection methods rely either on discrete ASR hypotheses that may discard acoustic evidence or on separately trained retrieval models. We propose Viterbi-guided Selection of Hotwords (VISH), a training-free, plug-and-play framework that directly verifies candidate-specific acoustic support over frame-level CTC posteriors. VISH formulates pre-selection as constrained posterior search; M-VISH makes large-list verification scalable through frame-synchronous shared-prefix Viterbi search with bounded top-K pruning, while Bi-MVISH exploits complementary backward evidence for robust verification. Across five benchmarks, M-VISH achieves up to 11.7% absolute improvement in Best-F1 over a strong learned-retrieval baseline and reduces candidate-search latency by 75.2% at 2,000 candidates relative to hypothesis-based filtering. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of posterior-level verification for accurate and scalable hotword pre-selection without additional model training.
papers.summary: Prompt-based contextual speech recognition with speech LLMs needs a small subset of hotwords chosen from a large, changing inventory, but existing pre-selection methods either work from discrete recognition hypotheses that discard acoustic evidence or need a separately trained retrieval model. `VISH` is a training-free, plug-and-play method that checks each candidate's acoustic support directly against frame-level CTC posteriors, framed as a constrained posterior search. `M-VISH` scales this to large lists with a shared-prefix Viterbi search and top-K pruning, and `Bi-MVISH` adds backward evidence. Across five benchmarks, `M-VISH` improves Best-F1 by **up to 11.7 points absolute** over a learned-retrieval baseline and cuts search latency by 75.2% at 2,000 candidates compared with hypothesis-based filtering.

papers.title: Hallucinations of Large Language Models in Cross-Language Code Translation: Phenomena and Mitigation
papers.abstract: Code translation converts source code from one programming language to another while preserving its functionality. Although Large Language Models (LLMs) have improved code translation, their outputs still contain hallucinations: generated code that conflicts with the source program, violates target-language facts, or introduces contextually inconsistent dependencies. These failures are especially harmful in translation because small semantic deviations can silently change program behavior. Existing hallucination studies mainly focus on natural-language generation or code generation, leaving the forms, distribution, and mitigation of hallucinations in cross-language code translation insufficiently characterized. This paper presents a systematic empirical study of LLM hallucinations in code translation. Across three benchmark datasets, six language pairs, and seven LLMs, we construct a taxonomy with three major categories: Semantic Consistency Conflicts, Factual Knowledge Conflicts, and Project Context Deviations. We manually annotate 13,919 hallucination cases and analyze how hallucination types vary across models, datasets, and language directions. Guided by the taxonomy, we further propose HaluCodeTran, a mitigation framework that combines BM25-based retrieval of relevant translation examples with taxonomy-aware reflective refinement. The study provides an execution-tested characterization of code-translation hallucinations and a practical baseline for building more reliable LLM-based code migration tools.
papers.summary: When LLMs translate code between programming languages, they can hallucinate in ways that silently change program behavior, and these failures have been studied far less than hallucinations in natural-language or code generation. This empirical study covers three benchmarks, six language pairs and seven LLMs, manually annotating **13,919 hallucination cases** into a taxonomy of Semantic Consistency Conflicts, Factual Knowledge Conflicts and Project Context Deviations, and analyzing how the types vary by model, dataset and translation direction. Guided by the taxonomy, the authors propose `HaluCodeTran`, which combines `BM25` retrieval of relevant translation examples with taxonomy-aware reflective refinement, as a mitigation baseline for LLM-based code migration.

papers.title: Automatic Differentiation with Constraints in Forward and Inverse Problems
papers.abstract: Approximate solutions of partial differential equations (PDEs) on unstructured grids can be represented on a graph. Numerical optimization involving stiff evolutionary and static PDEs often requires solving a large system of equations, which can be treated as a constraint. In this work, we present a fully differentiable graph-based implicit solver that incorporates this constraint. We evaluate its performance across four key tasks: a) linear and nonlinear forward modeling of evolutionary and static problems, b) solving inverse problems to estimate equation coefficients, c) solving inverse problems to estimate the right-hand side, and d) learnable graph coarsening to accelerate forward modeling. The stability and differentiability of our solver enable significant reductions in the complexity of forward modeling while efficiently addressing related inverse problems. These capabilities make it a powerful tool for different physics and engineering applications, in particular for geophysics, where inverse problems are commonly solved in order to reduce the model uncertainty.
papers.summary: Stiff partial differential equations (PDEs) solved on unstructured grids lead to large systems of equations, which become a constraint whenever the solver sits inside an optimization loop. The authors build a fully differentiable, graph-based implicit solver that incorporates this constraint, and test it on linear and nonlinear forward modeling, inverse problems that recover equation coefficients or the right-hand side, and learnable graph coarsening that speeds up forward modeling. They report that the solver's stability and differentiability **substantially reduce forward-modeling complexity** while handling the related inverse problems efficiently, with geophysics as the main target application.

papers.title: Physical-Variable-Informed Deep Learning for Robust Diagnosis in Industrial Fluid Transport Systems
papers.abstract: Industrial fluid transport systems are monitored through heterogeneous sensing streams, but robust fault diagnosis remains difficult because response signals vary with operating conditions and differ from physical variables in sampling rate, observation duration and data granularity. To address these challenges, we propose a physical-variable-informed deep learning framework (PhyNet) for robust fault diagnosis under real-world sampling heterogeneity. PhyNet treats physical variables as global operating constraints and response signals as local diagnostic evidence. Its physical-to-response cross-attention mechanism connects sequence-level physical-variable tokens with a learnable global response token, enabling interaction without strict temporal alignment. Across four benchmarks, including three real-world cavitation datasets and one public two-phase-flow dataset, PhyNet achieves the best performance across all evaluated metrics. Class-wise analyses, together with attention and masking analyses, show improved discrimination of ambiguous states and indicate that physical variables meaningfully constrain local response interpretation. These findings demonstrate a deployment-oriented approach to robust diagnosis in heterogeneous industrial environments.
papers.summary: Fault diagnosis in industrial fluid transport systems is hard because sensor responses shift with operating conditions, and physical variables are recorded at different sampling rates, durations and granularities than the response signals. `PhyNet` treats physical variables as global operating constraints and response signals as local evidence, linking them through a cross-attention mechanism between physical-variable tokens and a learnable global response token, so the two streams do not need strict temporal alignment. Across three real-world cavitation datasets and one public two-phase-flow dataset, it **achieves the best results on every evaluated metric**, and attention and masking analyses indicate that the physical variables help separate ambiguous states.

papers.title: The Shape of the DPO Hyperparameter Landscape: What to Measure, How It Moves with Scale, and When Not to Transfer It
papers.abstract: Direct preference optimisation (DPO) is widely used for language model post-training, but its performance depends strongly on the choice of its hyperparameters, such as the learning rate and the reference-policy regularisation parameter $\beta$. To better understand the DPO hyperparameter landscape, we conduct extensive experiments using a dense hyperparameter grid across different model scales from the same family. This allows us to analyse how the optimal DPO hyperparameters evolve with model size and the number of update steps, with intermediate checkpoints providing an inexpensive signal to accelerate the hyperparameter optimisation process. Furthermore, by evaluating our models on both static and dynamic benchmarks, we identify which benchmarks provide the strongest signal for hyperparameter selection. Finally, we investigate how different state-of-the-art hyperparameter optimisation strategies perform in this setting. Our experiments show that the optimal learning rate varies with model size and that hyperparameters are not transferable across training datasets. We also find that validation loss is a poor proxy for hyperparameter optimisation, as hyperparameters that minimize validation loss only weakly correlate with optimal hyperparameters for downstream benchmarks. Therefore, DPO hyperparameters need to be tuned specifically for the target model, dataset, and evaluation objective. We also show that short candidate training runs can substantially reduce the cost of this selection. We release all our training configurations and evaluation results to support reproducible analysis of selection quality and training cost.
papers.summary: Direct preference optimisation (`DPO`) is sensitive to its hyperparameters, especially the learning rate and the regularisation strength β. Using a dense hyperparameter grid across several model sizes from one family, the study tracks how optimal settings change with scale and training steps, which benchmarks give the most useful selection signal, and how standard hyperparameter-optimisation strategies perform. The optimal learning rate shifts with model size, hyperparameters do not transfer across training datasets, and **validation loss is a poor proxy** because it correlates only weakly with downstream-optimal settings. Short candidate training runs substantially cut the cost of tuning, and all configurations and results are released.

papers.title: CollabSciReM: Aligning Language Models for Scientific Conversations via Science-Aware Reward Decomposition
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used as research collaborators for hypothesis refinement, methodological planning, and technical analysis across multi-turn interactions. In this setting, a useful assistant must be accurate, methodologically justified, logically consistent, and token-efficient. Current alignment approaches rarely achieve all of these together. Instruction-tuned models gain conversational quality through verbosity, and we show that science-agnostic general collaborative rewards compress responses at the expense of scientific rigor. We propose CollabSciReM, a goal-conditioned reward framework that decomposes the session-level reward into conversational quality, scientific rigor, and structural efficiency. We also introduce SciQuality, a pairwise evaluation of multi-turn research conversations grounded in 300 held-out scientific papers and scored on six dimensions: methodological soundness, justification, logical consistency, factual correctness, novelty, and responsiveness. Fine-tuned on 8.62K synthetic research conversations, CollabSciReM is preferred on SciQuality over a science-agnostic reward baseline trained on the same data for all four Llama and Qwen models, including a 65.3% win rate at matched response length. For the 7B and 8B models, CollabSciReM outperforms the science-agnostic reward baseline on the primary metric in 8 of 10 single- and multi-turn benchmark settings. In a blind study, domain experts rated CollabSciReM significantly higher on novelty than the general-reward variant and reported fewer hallucinated responses than both the general-reward variant and the base model.
papers.summary: LLMs used as research collaborators need to be accurate, methodologically justified, logically consistent and concise. Instruction-tuned models tend to get more verbose, and the authors show that general collaboration rewards shorten responses at the cost of scientific rigor. `CollabSciReM` splits the session-level reward into conversational quality, scientific rigor and structural efficiency, and the accompanying `SciQuality` benchmark scores multi-turn research conversations grounded in 300 held-out papers along six dimensions. After fine-tuning on 8.62K synthetic conversations, it is preferred over a science-agnostic reward baseline for all four `Llama` and `Qwen` models, including a **65.3% win rate at matched response length**, and domain experts rated it higher on novelty with fewer hallucinations.

papers.title: Staged Continual Adaptation of Multimodal Foundation Models for Japanese Financial Documents
papers.abstract: Staged post-training of multimodal foundation models chains vision-language alignment, reasoning distillation, and domain tuning, yet how each phase trades capabilities against the others remains under-characterised. Tracking an 8.4B-parameter model from an un-fine-tuned baseline through three training phases on Japanese financial documents (evaluated on five text-input benchmarks), we find the phases interact non-additively: math-only distillation overwrites the financial knowledge acquired earlier even as procedural math skill survives, and the domain phase repairs more than it installs. A skip-phase ablation is best for domain knowledge but forfeits numerical-reasoning gains, so per-phase contributions are not decomposable and the best checkpoint is task-dependent, with implications for checkpoint retention and scheduling rather than added stages.
papers.summary: Staged post-training of multimodal foundation models chains vision-language alignment, reasoning distillation and domain tuning, but how the phases trade capabilities against each other is poorly understood. Tracking an 8.4B-parameter model through three phases on Japanese financial documents, evaluated on five text-input benchmarks, the authors find that the phases interact non-additively. **Math-only distillation overwrites earlier financial knowledge** while procedural math skill survives, and the domain phase mostly repairs that damage rather than adding new capability. Skipping a phase is best for domain knowledge but gives up numerical-reasoning gains, so the best checkpoint depends on the task.

papers.title: Polarity Blindness in LLM Safety: A Systematic Study of Negation, Antonym Substitution, and Adversarial Framing
papers.abstract: Negation remains a persistent challenge for language models across NLP tasks and modalities. We show that this weakness can undermine LLM safety guardrails through a structural vulnerability we term polarity blindness: the failure to recognize harmful intent after polarity-altering linguistic transformations. We study two forms of polarity inversion: grammatical negation and antonym replacement, and use synonym replacement as a polarity-preserving control. We further test whether an adversarial textual wrapper amplifies these failures. Using a 260-prompt benchmark across 10 state-of-the-art LLMs and 3 languages (English, Spanish, Czech), stratified by harmfulness potential and evaluated on a validated 0-5 harm scale, we find that polarity blindness affects most evaluated models, with mean harm scores reaching 4.12 for the most vulnerable model. The effect persists across typologically differing negation systems, suggesting that polarity blindness reflects a broader limitation in semantic robustness rather than a language- or grammar-specific failure.
papers.summary: LLMs have long struggled with negation, and this study shows the weakness can undermine safety guardrails through what the authors call polarity blindness: failing to recognize harmful intent after a request is grammatically negated or has words replaced by antonyms. Using a 260-prompt benchmark across 10 state-of-the-art LLMs and three languages (English, Spanish, Czech), with synonym replacement as a polarity-preserving control and an optional adversarial wrapper, harm is scored on a validated 0-5 scale. Polarity blindness affects most evaluated models, with **mean harm scores up to 4.12** for the most vulnerable one. The effect holds across languages with different negation systems, which suggests a general semantic-robustness gap rather than a grammar-specific one.

papers.title: MMEnterprise-Bench: Evaluating Enterprise Agents over Evolving Multimodal Records
papers.abstract: Enterprise agents answer questions over workplace records that evolve through team collaboration. As information is shared, corrected, and revised across documents, chats, and figures, multiple versions of the same information accumulate in the workspace. Reliable question answering therefore requires agents to reason over sufficient evidence, resolve cross-source and temporal conflicts, and recognize when the available evidence is insufficient to establish an answer. To systematically evaluate these capabilities, we introduce MMEnterprise-Bench, a benchmark comprising 1,613 questions grounded in evolving multimodal records from simulated collaboration projects, covering three categories: Evidence Reasoning, Conflict Resolution, and Unanswerability. We evaluate 10 proprietary and open-source multimodal LLMs and find that even the strongest models struggle when evidence contains cross-source or temporal conflicts or spans multiple images. Moreover, increasing the retrieval budget or employing a larger retriever improves evidence recall but does not consistently translate into higher answer accuracy. These findings highlight the persistent challenges of reasoning over evolving workplace records and establish MMEnterprise-Bench as a testbed for developing more reliable enterprise agents. Code and data are available at https://mlvlab.github.io/MMEnterprise-Bench/.
papers.summary: Enterprise agents must answer questions over workplace records that change as teams share, correct and revise information across documents, chats and figures. `MMEnterprise-Bench` contains 1,613 questions grounded in evolving multimodal records from simulated collaboration projects, split into Evidence Reasoning, Conflict Resolution and Unanswerability. Across 10 proprietary and open-source multimodal LLMs, even the strongest **struggle when evidence conflicts across sources or over time, or spans multiple images**. A larger retrieval budget or retriever improves evidence recall but does not reliably improve answer accuracy.
papers.highlight_summary:
Enterprise agents answering questions over workplace records must cope with information that is shared, corrected and revised across chats, emails, documents and figures, while the old versions stay in the workspace. `MMEnterprise-Bench` tests this with **1,613 questions** over 30 simulated collaboration projects whose superseded records are kept rather than overwritten, so the 7,140-record retrieval corpus contains both cross-source and temporal conflicts.
- Each project starts from a public paper or government report; an LLM plans a timeline of collaborative events, such as sharing a result, spotting an error and issuing a correction, and turns them into Slack messages, Notion entries, emails, slides and PDF pages, with 5,725 textual and 1,415 visual records in total.
- Questions fall into three categories: Evidence Reasoning, which has five subtypes; Conflict Resolution, split into cross-source and temporal; and Unanswerability. They come from rule-based and LLM generation, are filtered by LLM validation, and none of 50 LLM-accepted items was rejected in a blind three-person human check.
- In a RAG setup using `Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B` retrieval, the best of 10 models, `GPT-5.6 Sol`, reaches only **52.6% at k=10** and **68.0% at k=50**, while the best open model, `Qwen3.5-27B`, reaches 50.3% at k=50.
- Conflict questions are the hardest: at k=10, accuracy ranges from **11.8–36.3% on cross-source** conflicts and **13.2–33.5% on temporal** ones, and `GPT-5.6 Sol` drops from **83.3%** on single-text-record questions to **27.5%** when the evidence spans multiple images.
- Better retrieval does not reliably help: a larger 8B retriever and k up to 100 raise evidence recall from 41.3% to 67.3%, but smaller models stagnate or decline. Strong overall accuracy also doesn't mean good abstention, since `GPT-5.6 Sol` scores 65.5% on unanswerable questions against 87.4% for `Gemini 3.8 Flash`. Limitations include records that are simulated and LLM-generated, a small unanswerable set of 87 questions, and an automatic judge (`GPT-5.6 Luna`) that is itself one of the evaluated models.

papers.title: ACE-Compression: An Ability-Centric Evaluation of Compressed Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Model compression makes large language models deployable, but today's evaluation tells an incomplete story. Standard practice measures retained task performance and stops there. This misses a critical fact: compression perturbs the distributed knowledge embedded across billions of weights, and task scores alone cannot reveal which underlying abilities survive and which quietly collapse. To solve this question, we introduce ACE-Compression, an ability-centric evaluation framework. Instead of asking only "does the compressed model still answer correctly?", we ask "which of its core abilities remain intact?" Our framework probes four deployment-facing dimensions: procedural reasoning and constraint execution, knowledge grounding and truthfulness, social cognition and affective understanding, and persona fidelity and stylistic consistency. Across more than 35 compressed checkpoints from six open-weight LLMs-covering quantization and pruning-we find that compression redistributes ability profiles. Coarse, local, and surface-level signals often persist, while fine-grained, long-tail, and context-dependent abilities become fragile. Quantization consistently outperforms pruning in retention, but the practical meaning of that gap depends entirely on which ability an application requires. Based on our findings, deployers can choose compression methods by the ability profile their application needs, not just by a leaderboard average. And algorithm designers gain diagnostic signals to build compression methods that preserve what matters. We believe that ACE-Compression turns compression from a black-box accuracy drop into an interpretable intervention-one we can measure, understand, and ultimately improve.
papers.summary: Compressed LLMs are usually evaluated only by how much task accuracy they keep, which hides which underlying abilities survive. `ACE-Compression` probes four deployment-facing abilities: procedural reasoning and constraint following, knowledge grounding and truthfulness, social and affective understanding, and persona and style consistency. It applies them to more than 35 quantized and pruned checkpoints from six open-weight LLMs. Compression **redistributes ability profiles rather than degrading them uniformly**: coarse, local and surface-level abilities tend to persist while fine-grained, long-tail and context-dependent ones become fragile. Quantization retains abilities better than pruning overall, but how much the gap matters depends on which ability an application needs.

papers.title: Quantum-JEPA: Quantum Born Priors for Latent-Action JEPA World Models
papers.abstract: A single observation can admit several plausible futures, making uncertainty an essential part of world modelling. However, quantum generative models remain underexplored for this task. We introduce Quantum-JEPA, a latent-action JEPA framework that learns distributions of future representations using a conditional quantum Born prior. Circuit measurements generate binary latent actions, which a shared predictor maps to alternative future representations. We train the quantum prior through the quality and diversity of these predictions using a sampled energy objective. Our model learns distinct continuations on constructed multimodal tasks and captures latent-action correlations that support coordinated multi-agent futures. On D3IL, a benchmark of diverse human demonstrations, our trained models generate multiple obstacle-crossing routes from a common starting point without observed motion. On the controlled tasks, our classical and quantum prior implementations improve prediction validity and distributional fidelity over the evaluated variational baselines. Our quantum priors combine competitive predictive quality with a parameter-efficient sampling structure: they avoid an exponentially sized categorical output layer while supporting correlated latent actions. We further validate finite-shot parameter-shift training, including training with readout noise. Unlike most prior work, which focuses on simulation, we also verify the feasibility of inference with trained priors on a real QPU. These results establish a trainable quantum component for JEPA future prediction and a basis for exploring quantum-enhanced world models at larger scales.
papers.summary: World models need to represent uncertainty because one observation can lead to several plausible futures, and quantum generative models have barely been tried for this. `Quantum-JEPA` adds a conditional quantum Born prior to a latent-action `JEPA` world model: circuit measurements produce binary latent actions, a shared predictor maps them to alternative future representations, and the prior is trained on the quality and diversity of those predictions. On `D3IL` it generates multiple obstacle-crossing routes from one starting point, and on controlled tasks its classical and quantum priors improve prediction validity and distributional fidelity over variational baselines while avoiding an exponentially large categorical output layer. The authors also demonstrate training with finite measurement shots and readout noise, and **run inference with trained priors on a real quantum processor**.

papers.title: From Comparison to Selection: Enhancing Cross-Scale Generalization of Pointer Networks Trained with Reinforcement Learning for Capacitated Drone Delivery Routing
papers.abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) enable fast, flexible last-mile and emergency delivery, but their routing remains challenging as the number of clients varies. Classical approaches based on mixed-integer programming and heuristics can scale poorly or require problem-specific design, motivating learning-based alternatives. Reinforcement learning is particularly promising, provided a single policy can generalize across problem sizes without retraining. Although attention-based Pointer Networks are inherently size-agnostic, their solution quality degrades under both upscaling and downscaling. Using the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (CVRP) as a controlled proxy, with fixed capacity reflecting drone payload constraints, we investigate this degradation and identify three contributing factors: shifts in node density, attention dispersion, and dilution of the mean-pooled graph context. We systematically compare architecture-wide, encoder-side, and decoder-side modifications to address these limitations and propose a learned, permutation-invariant graph-context aggregation mechanism, implemented as a weighted average and as Set2Set. Results reveal distinct requirements for transfer in each direction: entropy-based attention scaling reduces the CVRP20-to-CVRP100 performance gap by 1.41 percentage points, while the proposed aggregation methods achieve the largest improvement on the more challenging CVRP100-to-CVRP20 transfer, approximately 0.9 percentage points. Exploiting this complementarity, we introduce an approach selector that chooses the best model for each training-target size pair. The selector reduces cost relative to the reference model across all nine seen train-test pairs and eight of nine pairs involving unseen sizes (CVRP35, CVRP75, and CVRP200), achieving improvements of up to 3.2 percent.
papers.summary: Pointer Networks trained with reinforcement learning can in principle route drone deliveries for any number of clients, but their solution quality degrades when the test problem is larger or smaller than the training one. Using the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (`CVRP`) with fixed capacity as a stand-in for drone payload limits, the authors trace the degradation to shifts in node density, attention dispersion and a diluted mean-pooled graph context. Entropy-based attention scaling helps most when scaling up, while a learned permutation-invariant context aggregation (a weighted average or `Set2Set`) helps most when scaling down. A selector that picks the best variant for each train-test size pair **reduces cost in all nine seen pairs and eight of nine unseen-size pairs**, by up to 3.2%.

papers.title: HypTI: Hyperbolic Geometry-Aware Multimodal Feature Fusion Framework for Dementia Detection Based on Tabular-Image Data
papers.abstract: AI-assisted dementia detection usually requires multimodal fusion of diverse data, such as clinical tabular assessments and neuroimaging data. However, most existing approaches perform feature fusion in Euclidean space. This overlooks the geometric structure of representation, including hierarchical organization in clinical assessments and multi-scale anatomical patterns in neuroimaging data. Recent studies have proved hyperbolic space provides a natural geometry for modelling hierarchical and multi-scale structures due to its exponentially expanding space. Motivated by these, we propose HypTI, a hyperbolic geometry-aware multimodal fusion framework for dementia detection based on clinical tabular assessments and MRI scans. HypTI extends hyperbolic representation learning to an underexplored tabular-MRI setting, jointly modelling clinical tabular, MRI scans, and cross-modal interactions in hyperbolic space. Specifically, clinical tabular variables are represented through learnable Lorentz prototypes to capture hierarchical relationships among assessments, while MRI scans are encoded using ROI-guided multi-scale representation learning to capture anatomical patterns across brain regions and spatial scales in Lorentz space. The multimodal representations are integrated through an adaptive fusion module generates subject-specific scale and shift coefficients to dynamically modulate and integrate the multimodal embeddings, enabling effective patient-level tabular-image representation learning for dementia detection. Experiments on OASIS-3 dataset show that the proposed framework achieves strong performance compared with representative approaches.
papers.summary: AI-assisted dementia detection usually fuses clinical tabular assessments with brain imaging in Euclidean space, which ignores the hierarchical structure of the assessments and the multi-scale anatomy in MRI. `HypTI` performs the fusion in hyperbolic (Lorentz) space: tabular variables are represented with learnable Lorentz prototypes, MRI scans are encoded with region-of-interest-guided multi-scale features, and an adaptive module fuses the two with subject-specific scale and shift coefficients. On the `OASIS-3` dataset it **performs strongly compared with representative fusion approaches**.

papers.title: APRIL: Ambiguity-Aware Expert Routing for Respiratory Sound Domain-Incremental Learning
papers.abstract: Automated respiratory sound classification enables continuous, non-invasive respiratory assessment, yet long-term deployment remains challenging due to domain shifts from evolving recording devices and acquisition periods. When privacy and governance regulations prohibit replaying historical data, sequential learning easily overwrites previously acquired knowledge. Preserving dedicated domain experts prevents parameter interference, but selecting the correct expert at inference is difficult under overlapping acoustic distributions and absent domain labels. To resolve this dilemma, we propose APRIL, an exemplar-free domain-incremental framework for RSC. Built on a shared frozen BEATs backbone, APRIL sequentially inherits and isolates low-rank experts to enable new-domain adaptation without altering earlier models. A multi-level prototype router retrieves the top-two candidate experts and dynamically selects the final model by integrating domain-routing posteriors with classification confidence, adaptively weighted by matching ambiguity. We establish standardized device- and temporal-incremental benchmarks on the ICBHI and SPRSound datasets across forward and reversed domain orders. Evaluated over five random seeds, APRIL consistently achieves the highest final-session average Score among compared continual learning approaches, reaching 64.4% and 65.4% on ICBHI, and 83.1% and 82.2% on SPRSound under forward and reversed sequences, respectively. Crucially, average forgetting remains under 1.0% across all protocols, demonstrating robust domain adaptation and long-term knowledge retention without data replay. Overall, APRIL offers a reliable and privacy-preserving paradigm for deploying continuous respiratory sound classification across real-world healthcare settings.
papers.summary: Respiratory sound classification (RSC) systems deployed over long periods face domain shifts as recording devices and acquisition periods change, and privacy rules often forbid replaying old data, so sequential training tends to overwrite earlier knowledge. `APRIL` is an exemplar-free domain-incremental framework built on a frozen `BEATs` backbone. It adds a new isolated low-rank expert for each domain and uses a multi-level prototype router to pick the right expert at inference without domain labels. The router shortlists two candidate experts and chooses between them by combining domain-routing posteriors with classification confidence, weighted by how ambiguous the match is. On new device- and temporal-incremental benchmarks built from `ICBHI` and `SPRSound`, it achieves the highest final-session scores among the compared continual learning methods, with **average forgetting under 1.0% across all protocols**.

papers.title: Lost in Recovery: Demystifying Recovery Behavior of Computer-Use Agents via Goal-Oriented Action Replay
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large (vision) language models have enabled computer-use agents that automate digital workflows via fine-grained keyboard and mouse operations. However, such agents remain fragile in long-horizon settings, where errors accumulate and executed actions leave unintended side effects, making the ability to recover from failures critical. Yet, existing remedies remain inadequate: environment resets are infeasible in proprietary settings, action replay is prohibitively expensive over long horizons, and API-based rollback is limited to web environments, leaving model-based recovery largely unexplored. To address this gap, we present ReTrace, a scalable evaluation framework for systematically studying recovery behavior in computer-use agents. We formalize Transition-Consistent Recovery: identical downstream actions from the recovered and target states must yield identical outcomes. We operationalize this criterion through goal-oriented action replay following controlled error injection. Using ReTrace, we present the first systematic study of autonomous, model-based recovery, revealing that (i) ideal recovery can unlock model's latent task completion capabilities, (ii) current computer-use agents fail to exploit their latent recovery capabilities, and (iii) accurate model-based recovery yields measurable end-to-end gains. Together, these findings establish recovery as a fundamental capability for building reliable computer-use agents. Our code and dataset is available at https://github.com/BangProx/ReTRACE.
papers.summary: Computer-use agents that operate keyboards and mice are fragile on long tasks: errors accumulate, and executed actions leave side effects that resets, replay, or API rollback often cannot undo. `ReTrace` is an evaluation framework for model-based recovery. It defines Transition-Consistent Recovery, meaning the recovered state and the target state must produce identical outcomes under identical downstream actions, and tests it by injecting controlled errors and then replaying goal-oriented actions. The study finds that ideal recovery unlocks latent task-completion ability, but **current computer-use agents fail to exploit their own latent recovery capabilities**. Accurate model-based recovery also yields measurable end-to-end gains.

papers.title: When Do Humans and Machines Truly Complement Each Other? Formal Conditions and Empirical Evidence for Human-AI Synergy
papers.abstract: Can humans and artificial intelligence cooperate such that their combination yields greater accuracy than either agent alone? This result, termed \emph{synergy} or \emph{complementarity}, is notoriously difficult to achieve, even when both agents possess significant independent accuracy. In this paper, we present a formal framework to model human-AI interaction through the lens of reliance patterns, which characterize the joint correctness structure of human and algorithmic decisions. We derive mathematically necessary and sufficient conditions for synergy, demonstrating that its emergence depends on the ability of either agent to identify and correct the errors of the other, what we call Human and Algorithmic Correction. Beyond its theoretical contribution, the proposed framework provides a foundation for the design and evaluation of knowledge-based decision support systems, where interaction policies must dynamically integrate heterogeneous sources of expertise. We demonstrate this through the analysis of seven clinical case studies. Our empirical results reveal a ``dominance trap,'' where a strong algorithmic advantage can paradoxically inhibit synergy by eroding human corrective intervention. We also show that synergy can persist even in the presence of cognitive biases, such as automation bias, provided there is functional de-correlation between human and AI errors. These results provide a formal foundation for key concepts in the human-AI systems literature and offer actionable insights for designing interaction-centric AI systems that foster complementarity.
papers.summary: Human-AI teams rarely beat the better of the two working alone, even when both are individually accurate. The authors model this through reliance patterns, which describe how human and algorithmic decisions are jointly right or wrong. They derive **necessary and sufficient conditions for synergy, which hinge on each agent's ability to detect and correct the other's errors**. Across seven clinical case studies they identify a "dominance trap", in which a much stronger algorithm suppresses human corrective intervention. They also show that synergy can survive automation bias as long as human and AI errors remain de-correlated.

papers.title: Recast the Past: Stable Long Video Generation with Full Context Memory
papers.abstract: Long-horizon video generation requires retaining an ever-expanding history, but conditioning on its growing token sequence is costly. Existing methods restrict or compress historical context, potentially losing information needed for future generation. This work proposes ReCam, which groups local spatiotemporal blocks of historical latents into vectors and projects them directly into the high-dimensional hidden space of a Diffusion Transformer.
