Today, this obligation depends almost entirely on differential testing: run the new kernel and a trusted reference on randomly sampled tensors, then compare their outputs within a tolerance. This approach has blind spots that additional test cases cannot eliminate. For example, a logical bug may produce an error smaller than the tolerance required to accommodate a correct optimized kernel.
  We propose symbolic equivalence checking, which executes a kernel and its reference on symbolic inputs, turning each output cell into an exact algebraic expression, and then checks whether the paired expressions agree for all inputs. Because these expressions are exact, symbolic equivalence checking distinguishes floating-point error from logical bugs, while a single check covers the entire input space.
  We implement Racer, a PTX-level symbolic equivalence checking engine, with three techniques that make this approach practical for production kernels: (1) Shape Reduction to control checking cost, (2) a lockstep CTA scheduler to handle concurrency, and (3) idiom templates with exact numeric refutation for otherwise inconclusive results. Across 2,408 production kernels from 41 collection targets, Racer found 82 real bugs in 23 libraries, including 76 previously unknown bugs and 41 confirmed so far.
papers.summary: GPU kernels are rewritten for every hardware generation, numeric format, and kernel language, and each rewrite is usually checked by differential testing on random tensors within a tolerance, which misses logic bugs whose errors fall below that tolerance. The authors propose symbolic equivalence checking: run the kernel and a reference on symbolic inputs so each output becomes an exact algebraic expression, then verify the paired expressions agree for all inputs, which separates floating-point error from logic bugs. Their engine, `Racer`, works at the PTX level and uses shape reduction to control cost, a lockstep scheduler for thread blocks to handle concurrency, and idiom templates with exact numeric refutation to resolve inconclusive cases. Across 2,408 production kernels from 41 collection targets, **`Racer` found 82 real bugs in 23 libraries, 76 of them previously unknown**, with 41 confirmed so far.

papers.title: A Digital Twin to Improve Cyber-Social Impact
papers.abstract: The increasing complexity of Industrial Control Systems (ICS) and their integration with IT infrastructures has significantly expanded the cyber threat landscape. Traditional cybersecurity models, primarily based on the Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability (CIA triad), fail to capture the broader societal and operational impacts of cyberattacks. This paper proposes a novel framework that integrates Digital Twin technology with a Cyber-Social Security model to simulate, analyze, and quantify cyber threats in critical infrastructures. Virtualized ICS environments built with Mininet and MiniCPS are used to model attack scenarios and assess their consequences across technical and social dimensions. At the core of the framework lies the Cyber-Social Vulnerability Scoring System (CSVSS), a quantitative metric that extends CVSS with a Social Impact dimension grounded in the Entity and Place pillars, producing a single, reproducible severity score that reflects real-world consequences. Crucially, the framework does not automate risk assessment but keeps the human analyst at its center: a Large Language Model (LLM) performs a first-pass analysis, mapping vulnerabilities and drafting risk reports, while the analyst, supported by explainable AI feedback, validates the findings and retains decision authority over critical cases. Experimental results demonstrate the framework's ability to model and score cyber-social impact, while the human-in-the-loop design is presented as a conceptual principle to preserve oversight.
papers.summary: Security models built on confidentiality, integrity, and availability miss the societal consequences of attacks on industrial control systems (ICS). The proposed framework pairs a digital twin of an ICS, virtualized with `Mininet` and `MiniCPS`, with the `Cyber-Social Vulnerability Scoring System` (`CSVSS`), which extends `CVSS` with a social impact dimension and produces **a single reproducible severity score that reflects technical and social consequences**. A large language model (LLM) does a first-pass vulnerability mapping and drafts risk reports, while a human analyst, supported by explainable AI feedback, validates the results and keeps decision authority. Experiments show the framework can model and score cyber-social impact, though the human-in-the-loop design is presented only as a conceptual principle.

papers.title: Plausible Future, Wrong Choice: Steering World-Action Models toward Intended Future
papers.abstract: World-Action Models (WAMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for embodied generalist policies by jointly modeling future world evolution and robot actions across diverse manipulation tasks. However, representing diverse futures is only the first step: a capable WAM must also generate futures that match the requirements of the current task and execution progress. In long-horizon manipulation where similar observation-action segments occur across different tasks and stages, existing approaches may generate locally plausible yet misdirected rollouts to drift toward wrong task stage, i.e., a phenomenon we term Stage Confusion. To address this problem, we propose TaskWAM, a closed-loop, stage-aware framework that represents fine-grained task requirements with Mode Tokens and tracks execution progress with State Tokens, forming a structured task state to steer world--action generation toward intended future. We further introduce StageBench, a controlled multi-stage manipulation benchmark with parameterized stage variations and automated evaluation.Extensive experiments on both simulation benchmarks and real-world tasks demonstrate that TaskWAM effectively reduces confusion and achieves competitive performance with state-of-the-art methods. Moreover, TaskWAM provides strong plug-and-play transfer across heterogeneous WAM architectures and robot embodiments, including single-arm robots, dual-arm grippers, dexterous hands, and humanoid robots.
papers.summary: World-Action Models (WAMs) jointly predict future observations and robot actions, but in long-horizon manipulation, where similar segments recur across tasks and stages, they can produce locally plausible rollouts that drift to the wrong task stage, a failure the authors call stage confusion. `TaskWAM` is a closed-loop, stage-aware framework that encodes fine-grained task requirements as mode tokens and tracks execution progress with state tokens, steering generation toward the intended future. The authors also release `StageBench`, a controlled multi-stage manipulation benchmark with parameterized stage variations and automated evaluation. In simulation and real-world experiments, `TaskWAM` reduces stage confusion, performs competitively with state-of-the-art methods, and **transfers plug-and-play across different WAM architectures and robot embodiments**, including single- and dual-arm robots, dexterous hands, and humanoids.

papers.title: Every Model Leaves a Trace: Multi-Resolution LLM Fingerprinting
papers.abstract: Large language models leave model-specific traces in their generated text, but it remains unclear how finely these fingerprints can distinguish related models and which signals remain informative as obvious cues are reduced. We study this through fingerprint resolution, considering both model resolution, from different families to distilled and adapted variants, and signal resolution across behavioral, stylometric, lexical, and semantic evidence. We progressively suppress surface cues, paraphrase outputs, vary the amount of available text, and test generalization across prompt distributions and languages. Our results show that fingerprints persist beyond broad family differences, remaining detectable in distilled models and even LoRA adaptations of the same base model. Although attribution weakens as surface and lexical cues are altered, substantial model-specific signal remains. These signals transfer across prompt sources and languages, with semantic representations proving most robust across languages. These findings show that model identity is recoverable at multiple resolutions, but that recoverability depends on model similarity and the evidence available in the text.
papers.summary: The study asks how finely the text a large language model generates can identify the model that wrote it, from different families down to distilled and adapted variants, and which behavioral, stylometric, lexical, and semantic signals remain informative. The authors progressively strip surface cues, paraphrase outputs, vary the amount of text, and test generalization across prompt sources and languages. **Fingerprints stay detectable in distilled models and even across LoRA adaptations of the same base model**, and although attribution weakens as surface and lexical cues are altered, substantial model-specific signal survives. These signals transfer across prompt sources and languages, with semantic representations the most robust across languages.

papers.title: Stratified Sparse Attention: Reducing the Sparse-to-Dense Gap at Extreme Sparsity
papers.abstract: Large Language Model inference over long contexts is increasingly bottlenecked by the cost of attending to a growing Key-Value (KV) cache. Sparse attention reduces this cost by accessing only a fraction of the cache, but existing methods face a trade-off between deterministic retrieval, which captures high-scoring tokens but discards residual attention mass, and sampling, which improves coverage at the cost of higher variance. Hybrid methods combine top-$k$ retrieval with uniform sampling, yet still exhibit a substantial gap from dense attention at aggressive sparsity. We introduce \emph{Stratified Sparse Attention (SSA)}, a unified framework combining deterministic retrieval with score-guided sampling. SSA deterministically attends to high-scoring tokens while sampling the residual using proxy attention scores and correcting for their inclusion probabilities, thereby recovering attention mass beyond the retrieval set. SSA encompasses top-$k$, top-$p$, and hybrid top-$k$+sampling as special cases. Across RULER, LongBench, LOFT, and AIME, and five models ranging from 3B to 27B parameters, SSA consistently improves over the baselines at matched sparsity. On RULER-HARD with Ministral-3-8B, SSA improves accuracy over the strongest practical baseline from 81.8\% to 84.2\% at 32K and from 63.8\% to 69.3\% at 128K under $50\times$ attention sparsity, recovering 94\% and 85\% of dense-attention performance, respectively. With optimized CUDA kernels, SSA achieves up to $2.96\times$ decode speedup over FlashInfer at 1M context, demonstrating that its accuracy gains translate into practical long-context inference acceleration. We open-source our code at https://github.com/skylight-org/SSA-Paper-Code.
papers.summary: Sparse attention cuts the cost of attending over a large key-value (KV) cache during long-context inference, but top-k retrieval discards the remaining attention mass, sampling adds variance, and hybrids still fall well short of dense attention at aggressive sparsity. `Stratified Sparse Attention` (`SSA`) attends deterministically to the highest-scoring tokens and samples the rest using proxy attention scores, correcting for their inclusion probabilities; top-k, top-p, and hybrid methods fall out as special cases. Across `RULER`, `LongBench`, `LOFT`, and `AIME` on five models from 3B to 27B parameters, `SSA` beats baselines at matched sparsity, and on `RULER-HARD` with `Ministral-3-8B` at 50x sparsity it **recovers 94% of dense-attention accuracy at 32K context and 85% at 128K**. With optimized CUDA kernels it decodes up to 2.96x faster than `FlashInfer` at 1M context.

papers.title: Toolflation: Seller Agents Distort Tool Markets Through Spontaneous Generative Engine Optimization
papers.abstract: Agents are starting to sell to other agents. Seller agents write the listings of tools, services and products, and buyer agents read these listings when they choose what to use. We show that seller agents told only to be selected more often practice generative engine optimization on their own, and that this distorts the market for sellers and for buyers. We build tool markets from real data tools on Amazon and Instagram and run every tool on every question, so we know which tools can answer each question. Under all five production models we test, sellers rewrite their descriptions to claim more and more fields, including fields that their tools return for fewer than half of the targets. We call this process toolflation. Nothing in the market limits it, and how far it goes depends on the model, as the number of claims that contradict the sellers' own evidence differs by an order of magnitude between models. Toolflation shifts the buyers' choices between sellers, and the most capable tool loses share in seven of the ten combinations of seller model and platform. Under four models, the choices stay with capable tools and buyer agents keep their task success. Under the fifth, sellers copy one another until the descriptions no longer tell the tools apart. Buyer agents then pick tools by their position in the list, tools that answer almost nothing win a quarter to two fifths of the choices, and task success falls from 89% to about 30% on Amazon, close to random choice, and from 77% to 40% on Instagram. The sellers did only what their vendors asked, and the cost fell on buyers they never dealt with. We therefore argue that honesty toward third parties under competition is part of safety alignment, and that models should be tested as sellers before they are deployed as sellers.
papers.summary: As agents begin selling to other agents, seller agents write the listings that buyer agents read when choosing tools. In tool markets built from real data tools on Amazon and Instagram, where every tool is run on every question so true capability is known, seller agents told only to get selected more often spontaneously practice generative engine optimization, inflating their listings with fields their tools return for less than half of targets; the authors call this toolflation. Under all five production models tested, inflation shifts buyer choices, and the most capable tool loses share in seven of ten seller-model and platform combinations. Under one model, sellers copy each other until listings become indistinguishable, buyers fall back to picking by list position, and **task success drops from 89% to about 30% on Amazon** and from 77% to 40% on Instagram, which the authors use to argue that models should be tested as sellers before they are deployed as sellers.

papers.title: Beyond Trajectory Statistics: Community-Consistent Human Mobility Generation via Evolving User-Location Graphs
papers.abstract: Human mobility data are fundamental to Web-based location services and broader urban applications, and mobility generation provides synthetic trajectories when real data are costly or inaccessible. Although recent mobility generators have incorporated collective mobility patterns, they primarily focus on individual trajectories and aggregate population dynamics, leaving evolving community structures formed by user-location interactions insufficiently modeled. In this paper, we study community-consistent human mobility generation. To this end, we formulate mobility generation as the generation of dynamic user-location graphs to model community structures and propose MOTION, a Multi-agent framework for cOmmuniTy-consIstent human mObility geNeration. MOTION consists of user agents, location agents, and a global manager agent. MOTION first detects coherent communities from historical mobility using the Leiden algorithm and extracts community-conditioned interaction priors to guide the generation process. Guided by these priors, the user agents plan mobility, search destination candidates, and infer user movements from the individual view. In parallel, selectively activated location agents infer likely user arrivals from the community view. The manager coordinates both views, diagnoses interactions causing deviations, and attributes targeted reflection signals to revise user decisions, location attraction, and source-user selection. Experiments on two real-world datasets show that MOTION outperforms baselines by at least 4.05% across reported metrics of individual trajectories, population and flow distributions, and community and graph structures. Further analyses confirm its robustness, privacy preservation, and downstream utility. The code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MOTION-04C4.
papers.summary: Synthetic human mobility generators capture individual trajectories and aggregate population dynamics but largely ignore the evolving community structure formed by interactions between users and locations. `MOTION` frames mobility generation as producing dynamic user-location graphs, using user agents, location agents, and a global manager agent guided by community priors that the `Leiden` algorithm extracts from historical data. User agents plan movements from the individual view, selectively activated location agents infer likely arrivals from the community view, and the manager diagnoses deviations and sends targeted reflection signals to revise decisions. On two real-world datasets, `MOTION` **outperforms baselines by at least 4.05%** on metrics covering trajectories, population and flow distributions, and community and graph structure.

papers.title: Claims of emergence in AI should be grounded in information decomposition
papers.abstract: When a language model develops capabilities not traceable to its individual components, when a multi-agent AI system outperforms each agent on its own, or when a human-AI pair succeeds where either fails in isolation, AI researchers describe it as a case of ``synergy'' or ``emergence''. However, these are usually informal assessments not supported by a theoretical framework, making these claims impossible to compare or even meaningfully dispute. Here we argue that \emph{information decomposition can serve as a unifying formal framework to operationalize assessments about synergy in AI systems}. Information decomposition provides a way to distinguish qualitatively different \emph{types} of information, including unique information available from individual components, redundant information shared across multiple components, and synergistic information accessible only from parts taken together. This gives claims of emergence a precise, falsifiable criterion: a system's behavior is emergent only if it carries synergistic information about task-relevant outcomes. We apply this lens to attention heads, autonomous agents, and human-AI teams, showing how it organizes existing knowledge across scales and substrates, while also generating cross-level conjectures that siloed fields would miss.
papers.summary: Claims of "synergy" or "emergence" in AI, whether about language model capabilities, multi-agent systems, or human-AI teams, are usually informal and hard to compare or dispute. This position paper argues that information decomposition, which separates the unique information carried by individual components, the redundant information they share, and the synergistic information available only from parts taken together, should serve as a unifying formal framework. It proposes a falsifiable criterion: **a system's behavior counts as emergent only if it carries synergistic information about task-relevant outcomes**. The authors apply this lens to attention heads, autonomous agents, and human-AI teams, organizing existing findings and proposing conjectures that cut across levels.

papers.title: Exploring Temporal Context-Aware Physical Grounding in Latent World Models
papers.abstract: Learning latent dynamics is fundamental to building action-conditioned world models for planning. Among existing families, Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) offer a natural framework by modeling transitions directly in latent space rather than at the pixel level. However, two issues remain in JEPA-based world models: (i) physical grounding lacks explicit aggregation of temporal context and (ii) action planning always overly relies on generic sampling distributions. To this end, we propose $\mathcal{G}$-JEPA, which incorporates temporal context into physical grounding for latent world models and couples the learned models with prior-guided action planning. Specifically, during learning, we incorporate a shared causal temporal module that aggregates temporal context within observation and prediction sequences under physical state supervision, grounding both in task-relevant physical states. When planning, we further introduce action inference through stepwise conditioning of a generative action distribution on the current and goal latent representations together with their evolving discrepancy, yielding anchored proposals that guide model-based online refinement. Together, physical state supervision guides temporal representation learning, while the action prior guides search through the learned world model. Experiments demonstrate improved planning performance on manipulation tasks, including tasks with increasing temporal separation between initial and goal observations. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/myl11045/G-JEPA.
papers.summary: World models based on Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) predict transitions in latent space, but they lack explicit aggregation of temporal context for physical grounding and rely on generic sampling distributions for planning. `G-JEPA` adds a shared causal temporal module that aggregates context across observation and prediction sequences under supervision from physical states. For planning, it generates action proposals conditioned step by step on the current and goal latent representations and their evolving gap, then refines them online with the learned model. Experiments show **improved planning on manipulation tasks**, including tasks where the initial and goal observations are far apart in time.

papers.title: Proof-Carrying Contracts: Commitments AI Agents Cannot Break
papers.abstract: AI agents increasingly act on behalf of people or other agents, purchasing services, exchanging information and delegating work. What an agent must respect is written in instructions, policies or agreements, but text alone cannot make it comply. It may make mistakes, be redirected by what it reads, or pursue different interests. For an economy of such agents to function, parties need agreements they can rely on without inspecting or trusting one another's agents. We introduce Proof-Carrying Contracts (PC2), a framework for making agreed constraints enforceable throughout an agent's interactions with a system. Before a requested operation can run, the agent must supply a machine-checkable proof that it preserves the agreed constraints in every case allowed by its model. An execution system called the Airlock checks the proof and controls access to the operation. The parties specify the conditions to preserve, while the agent supplies the reasoning needed to justify its decisions and remains free to adapt its strategy. This avoids having to design a separate permission policy and prove that every decision it permits is safe. We prove that the constraints hold at every instant during execution, even for an adversarial agent, and identify when this implies safety in the world. Reusable capability modules provide tools and guarantees from which contracts can be constructed. PC2 provides a foundation for an agent economy whose agreements protect both those delegating work and those carrying it out.
papers.summary: Agents acting for people or other agents can make mistakes, be redirected by what they read, or pursue other interests, so text instructions alone cannot guarantee they honor an agreement. `Proof-Carrying Contracts` (`PC2`) require an agent to supply a machine-checkable proof that a requested operation preserves the agreed constraints in every case its model allows; an execution system called the `Airlock` checks the proof before granting access. Parties specify only the conditions to preserve, the agent supplies the justifying reasoning and stays free to adapt its strategy, and reusable capability modules provide tools and guarantees from which contracts can be built. The authors **prove that the constraints hold at every instant of execution, even against an adversarial agent**, and identify when this implies safety in the world.

papers.title: Model- and Layer-Level Closed-Loop Forecasting with SSM-Based Spiking Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Deep State-Space Models (Deep SSMs) have shown promising performance and computational benefits in processing of time-series data with complex temporal dependencies. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) constitute a biologically inspired class of deep SSMs, where computing blocks communicate through spikes, discrete single-bit events rather than continuous activation functions. A particularly important task in time-series processing is forecasting, i.e. predicting future values of a sequence from past observations alone. However, how to best perform forecasting with SNNs is an open question, where the standard autoregressive nature of the data processing with SNNs requires values that are not available during the forecasting phase. In this article, we address this challenge. We explore two closed-loop forecasting strategies, in which the network's own generated values are fed back into the network as if they were observed past values: (i) model-level and (ii) layer-level closed-loop forecasting. We evaluate these approaches on the ETT-small datasets, a standard benchmark for time-series forecasting, under both spike-based and continuous activation functions. We compare the proposed closed-loop approaches against state-of-the-art methods such as SpaceTime, as well as the zero-masking baseline in S4. Both of the proposed approaches perform comparably to or better than zero-masking with S4, and in most cases match SpaceTime. These findings highlight the trade-off between continuous and low-bit quantized activations, and demonstrate that the proposed Deep SSM architectures provide a competitive framework for forecasting.
papers.summary: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) are a biologically inspired class of deep state-space models (SSMs) that communicate through single-bit spikes, but their autoregressive processing needs input values that are unavailable while forecasting. The authors test two closed-loop strategies that feed the network's own predictions back in as if they were observations, one at the model level and one at the layer level, using both spiking and continuous activations on the `ETT-small` datasets. **Both strategies match or beat the zero-masking baseline used with `S4`** and in most cases match `SpaceTime`, which the authors present as evidence that SSM-based SNNs are competitive for forecasting despite the trade-off of low-bit activations.

papers.title: BitMTP: When Multi-Token Prediction Meets Low-Bit Large Language Models
papers.abstract: For efficient deployment of large language models (LLMs), methods of ultra-low-bit backbones reduce weight storage, memory traffic, and linear-layer execution cost, while multi-token prediction (MTP) methods reduce sequential decoding steps by predicting multiple future tokens in parallel. Although complementary, the direct combination of these methods cannot accelerate decoding at comparable quality: masked drafting lacks intermediate token input supplied in next-token training, while wider computation and causal key-value (KV) updates can offset the savings from fewer steps. To address these challenges, we propose BitMTP, an algorithm-system co-design framework for efficient MTP on ultra-low-bit LLM backbones. A joint next-token prediction and MTP objective equips a single model with both autoregressive (AR) generation and block-causal drafting. Confidence-only decoding, speculative-only decoding, and hybrid decoding provide different quality-throughput operating points without using separate draft and verifier models. Accepted-prefix alignment keeps the committed prefix, materialized causal KV boundary, and CUDA Graph replay state consistent for continued generation. BitMTP uses this contract to select width-specialized low-bit execution and reuse captured graphs over shared KV storage. On NVIDIA H20, BitMTP with hybrid decoding achieves five-task mean speedups of 2.2x on BitNet b1.58-2B and 2.1-2.4x on 1.7B-4B Bonsai models at comparable task quality. On RTX 3090 and Jetson Orin, it further achieves up to 2.0x in five-task mean throughput and 3.3x on MBPP+, respectively. These results demonstrate that BitMTP accelerates ultra-low-bit LLM generation across backbones, model sizes, and GPU types. The source code is released at https://github.com/PolyU-VCLab/BitMTP
papers.summary: Ultra-low-bit large language models (LLMs) and multi-token prediction (MTP) both speed up inference, but naively combining them gives no speedup at comparable quality, because masked drafting lacks intermediate token inputs and the extra computation and causal key-value (KV) updates offset the savings from fewer steps. `BitMTP` trains one model on a joint next-token and MTP objective, so it supports both autoregressive generation and block-causal drafting without separate draft and verifier models, and offers confidence-only, speculative-only, and hybrid decoding modes. On the systems side, accepted-prefix alignment keeps the committed prefix, KV cache, and CUDA Graph replay state consistent, enabling width-specialized low-bit kernels and graph reuse. Hybrid decoding achieves **2.2x mean speedup on `BitNet b1.58-2B` and 2.1x to 2.4x on 1.7B to 4B `Bonsai` models** on an NVIDIA H20 at comparable quality, with up to 2.0x throughput on an RTX 3090 and 3.3x on `MBPP+` on a Jetson Orin.

papers.title: ECG for laboratory values:A comprehensive physiological and technical analysis
papers.abstract:
Laboratory measurements are essential for clinical decision making but typically require invasive blood sampling. Recent research suggests that ECG recordings may contain information beyond cardiac rhythm and provide information related to laboratory values. This thesis investigates NT-proBNP prediction from ECG recordings and patient metadata using a multimodal deep learning framework, while considering the physiological plausibility of ECG-based prediction. It also compares a 1-lead configuration using lead II with the corresponding 12-lead configuration. Additional experiments on glucose, hemoglobin, and potassium are presented in the appendix.
  Regression, binary classification, and three-class classification experiments were conducted using MIMIC-IV, with the three-class task based on clinically established thresholds. The 12-lead configuration consistently achieved better performance. Regression reached a mean absolute error of 534.98 pg/mL for 1-lead and 514.27 pg/mL for 12-lead. Binary classification achieved AUROCs of 0.849 and 0.876, respectively, while three-class classification achieved macro-averaged AUROCs of 0.738 and 0.752.
  The results indicate that precise NT-proBNP regression remains challenging, whereas broader concentration ranges can be classified more effectively. The findings are consistent with the physiological hypothesis that ECG characteristics and NT-proBNP concentrations reflect shared cardiovascular processes. ECG-based NT-proBNP prediction may therefore provide complementary information, particularly for classifying broader concentration ranges. However, laboratory measurements remain necessary, and validation on independent datasets is required.
papers.summary: Blood tests are invasive, so this thesis asks whether electrocardiogram (ECG) recordings plus patient metadata can predict the cardiac biomarker NT-proBNP using a multimodal deep learning framework. It compares a single-lead (lead II) setup against a full 12-lead setup on `MIMIC-IV` across regression, binary classification, and three-class classification based on clinical thresholds. The 12-lead configuration was consistently better, reaching **a binary classification AUROC of 0.876** against 0.849 for one lead, while precise regression remained difficult with a mean absolute error above 500 pg/mL. The author concludes that ECGs can complement, but not replace, laboratory measurement for sorting patients into broad concentration ranges, and that independent validation is still needed.

papers.title: DecisionPivot: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Decision Models in LLM Systems
papers.abstract: Decision models support routing, guardrails, and output verification in LLM systems. However, item accuracy alone cannot establish whether models make correct decisions across controlled variations or assign reliable confidence to their predictions. We introduce DecisionPivot, a diagnostic benchmark comprising 48 tasks and 40,033 items across seven decision roles. Its core track contains 7,800 items from 13 generated task families, organized into contrast groups with computed answers verified by independently implemented solvers. The complementary reference track contains 32,233 items from 35 public test sets, preserving their original evaluation metrics. We evaluate 40 decision models and 14 general models using documented, model-specific protocols, assessing item and contrast-group accuracy, probability ordering, calibration, and empirical selective coverage. Our results reveal substantial differences obscured by aggregate scores: two 27B models separated by only 2.6 points on the reference track achieve contrast-group accuracies of 70.1% and 44.2%. Across 2,400 binary contrast pairs, Perplexity Decider correctly ranks the positive member above the negative member in 92.3% of pairs but answers both members correctly in only 74.1%, exposing a gap between probability ordering and decision correctness. Models with similar item accuracy also differ in the reliability of their high-confidence predictions. On a separate 1,296-item subset, GLM-5.3 achieves 93.5\% contrast-group accuracy at a higher reasoning setting, compared with 81.5% at its lowest effort. By linking errors to pivotal details and difficulty levels, DecisionPivot provides fine-grained diagnostics of decision failures that aggregate evaluation alone cannot reveal.
papers.summary: Decision models handle routing, guardrails, and output verification in LLM systems, but item accuracy alone does not show whether they decide consistently across controlled variations or report reliable confidence. `DecisionPivot` is a diagnostic benchmark of 48 tasks and 40,033 items across seven decision roles. It pairs a generated core track of contrast groups, whose answers are checked by independent solvers, with a reference track drawn from 35 public test sets. Evaluating 40 decision models and 14 general models shows that aggregate scores hide large differences: **two 27B models only 2.6 points apart on the reference track score 70.1% and 44.2% on contrast-group accuracy**. The benchmark also finds that `Perplexity Decider` ranks the correct item of a contrast pair higher 92.3% of the time but answers both items correctly only 74.1% of the time.
papers.highlight_summary:
Decision models handle routing, guardrails and output verification in LLM systems, but item accuracy alone hides whether they react correctly when one decisive detail changes, and whether their confidence can be trusted. `DecisionPivot` tests both with 48 tasks and 40,033 items across seven decision roles: a generated core track of contrast groups whose answers are checked by independent solvers, plus a reference track of 35 public test sets.

- The core track has **7,800 items** from 13 Python-generated task families, such as `filter_match`, `state_goal` and `toolcall_valid`, in which members of a contrast group differ only in a pivotal detail (for example, a shipping fee that puts a total one cent above or below a limit); a group counts as correct under "pair accuracy" only when every member is answered correctly.
- Aggregate scores hide large gaps: `Perplexity Decider` and `JEV-27B` differ by only **2.6 reference-score points** but reach **70.1% vs 44.2%** core pair accuracy, and **19 of 40** decision models fall below the 16.1% uniform-guess baseline on pair accuracy.
- Probability ordering does not guarantee correct decisions: across 2,400 binary pairs, `Perplexity Decider` ranks the positive member higher **92.3%** of the time but gets both members right only **74.1%** of the time, and models with near-identical accuracy, such as `Kev 27B` (70.6%) and `JEV-27B` (70.3%), differ in how accurate their high-confidence predictions are (93.8% vs 88.9% at confidence ≥0.90).
- Reasoning helps a lot on arithmetic and temporal contrasts: `GLM-5.3` rises from **81.5% to 93.5%** pair accuracy at a higher effort setting, and the authors' `SL-27B AutoThink` reaches **86.9%** versus 75.4% for its one-pass `Instant` variant, although its reference score barely changes (58.9 vs 59.4).
- The main caveats are that the benchmark and the top-ranked `StartLux-Decision` models come from the same team, the selective-coverage numbers are computed after the fact on evaluation labels, the difficulty levels raise case size and complexity together, and the fresh-sample checks only test stability within the existing generator designs.

papers.title: VLM-Guided Contact Retargeting and Generative Partner Modeling for Humanoid-Human Interaction
papers.abstract: Humanoid-human interaction requires robots to operate under severe partial observability: during close physical contact, the human partner is occluded, truncated, or outside the robot's field of view, causing pose estimation to fail and often necessitating external tracking or privileged human state. At the same time, heavy mutual occlusions introduce errors into the human-human motion-capture data used for learning. We present REACT, a framework for learning deployable humanoid-human interaction policies from human-human demonstrations. REACT treats semantic contact structure as the key supervisory signal connecting demonstration processing, interaction learning, and onboard control. First, a VLM-guided contact modeling and retargeting pipeline identifies semantically meaningful contacts and transfers them onto humanoid-human geometry while preserving interaction structure. Using these annotations, privileged interaction policies learn physically grounded behaviors through interaction-aware contact rewards and are then distilled into deployable egocentric depth policies trained entirely from onboard sensing using photorealistic human depth rendering. To address severe partial observability, we introduce generative partner-state modeling objectives that predict partner motion from occluded egocentric views. We evaluate REACT in simulation and on a real Unitree G1 humanoid across five contact-rich interactions. Semantic contact modeling substantially improves preservation of demonstrated interactions, while generative partner-state modeling improves contact recall on four of five interactions, most under heavy occlusion. On real hardware, REACT performs all five interactions using onboard sensing alone.
papers.summary: During close physical contact with a person, a humanoid robot often cannot see its partner, and the human-human motion-capture data used for training is itself corrupted by occlusion. `REACT` learns interaction policies from human-human demonstrations by using semantic contact structure as its main supervisory signal. A vision-language model (VLM) identifies meaningful contacts and retargets them onto humanoid-human geometry, privileged policies learn with contact-aware rewards, and those policies are then distilled into egocentric depth policies trained on photorealistic rendered human depth. Generative partner-state objectives predict the partner's motion from occluded views and improve contact recall on four of five interactions. **On a real `Unitree G1`, the system performs all five contact-rich interactions using onboard sensing alone.**

papers.title: Beyond 4 bits: Data-Centric Post-training Quantization and Recovery
papers.abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) compresses the weights of a trained model with limited compute and data. Down to 4 bits it is near-lossless, but at 2 bits scalar PTQ configurations fall to chance-level accuracy. We study three choices usually treated as implementation details that matter little at 4 bits but decide 2-bit quality: the quantization representation, the calibration data, and the recovery fine-tuning data, across six dense and mixture-of experts models (ranging from $3.8$ to $32$B parameters). Representation is the largest factor and vector codebooks restore usable models where scalar PTQ pipelines collapse. Most of the remaining loss in accuracy is on \emph{generative} tasks, and the amount of performance drop is model-dependent. Furthermore, at a short recovery budget, calibration and recovery data are coupled. The best recovery data depends on the calibration data, so the two must be chosen jointly. The resulting recipe involves a vector codebook representation, a small task-aligned calibration mixture, and an inexpensive codebook-only recovery stage. Including codebooks, it uses about $2.3$ effective bits per weight and retains $89$ to $97\%$ of full-precision question-answering (QA) accuracy where scalar PTQ is at chance, and, including recovery, uses $1.4$ to $30\times$ less compute than the strongest quantization-aware-training (QAT) baseline.
papers.summary: Post-training quantization (PTQ) of model weights is close to lossless at 4 bits, but scalar PTQ falls to chance-level accuracy at 2 bits. The authors study three choices that matter at 2 bits (the quantization representation, the calibration data, and the recovery fine-tuning data) across six dense and mixture-of-experts models from 3.8B to 32B parameters. The representation matters most, with vector codebooks recovering usable models where scalar methods collapse, and calibration and recovery data turn out to be coupled, so they must be chosen together. The resulting recipe uses about 2.3 effective bits per weight, **retains 89 to 97% of full-precision question-answering accuracy**, and uses 1.4 to 30 times less compute than the strongest quantization-aware training (QAT) baseline.

papers.title: Humans Correct Their Judgments Through Debate, but Weaker AI Models Do Not
papers.abstract: How can we effectively oversee AI systems that surpass human intelligence? AI Safety via Debate proposes that two AI systems argue opposing positions and a judge, either a human or a weaker model, decides which is correct. By facilitating supervisors in providing high-quality training signals, debate aims to encourage truthful and safe behavior from AI systems whose capabilities exceed our own. However, human judgment is not neutral: people often rely on biases which advanced AI systems may learn to exploit. Drawing on insights from collective intelligence and social cognition, this paper investigates whether debate can guide human and LLM supervisors toward the truth despite their prior beliefs. We evaluate several protocol configurations. We also explore setups inspired by the wisdom of the crowd such as the number and diversity of judges, as well as interaction mechanisms including deliberation and voting. Overall, we find that debate increases accuracy relative to prior beliefs for human judges, whereas the consultancy baseline, in which a single expert argues for one answer, does not. For weaker language models, however, the results are mixed: debate provides no comparable gains in most settings and can even reduce accuracy. Among multi-judge protocols, weighted voting produces the highest accuracy for human supervisors, whereas for LLMs none of them significantly improves group accuracy, even as the number of judges increases. Notably, the behavior of minority judges in non-diverse deliberation protocols suggests that, under symmetric settings, incorrect positions could be more persuasive than correct ones. These findings support debate as a viable path toward scalable human oversight, but cast doubt on its benefits for weaker AI supervisors, raising concerns about fully automated training and control pipelines in high-stakes settings.
papers.summary: AI Safety via Debate proposes that two AI systems argue opposing sides while a weaker judge, either a human or a smaller model, decides which is right. This work tests whether debate moves judges toward the truth despite their prior beliefs, varying protocol configurations, the number and diversity of judges, and multi-judge mechanisms such as deliberation and voting. **Debate improved accuracy over prior beliefs for human judges, but gave weaker LLM judges no comparable gains in most settings and sometimes reduced their accuracy**, while a single-expert consultancy baseline helped neither group. Weighted voting worked best for groups of human judges, no multi-judge protocol significantly helped groups of LLM judges, and minority-judge behavior suggests incorrect positions can be more persuasive than correct ones in symmetric settings.

papers.title: Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-Set Diffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks
papers.abstract: Discrete diffusion models iteratively denoise a noisy sequence of categorical data such as text, enabling any-order generation with self-correction and in-filling capabilities. This makes them promising candidates for reasoning, planning, and constrained-generation tasks like coding and math. Yet masked and uniform diffusion erase a token's identity in a single corruption event, so their noisy states cannot explicitly represent partially resolved uncertainty in which several alternatives remain plausible. We close this gap with Binary Discrete Diffusion, a family of continuous-time discrete-diffusion processes whose noisy state is a set of candidate tokens per position, represented as a binary membership vector. Binary diffusion changes candidate sets through additions and removals, allowing information to be lost and recovered gradually while the diffusion state itself represents partial uncertainty. On Sudoku-Extreme, Boxoban, and graph coloring, the symmetric formulation of binary diffusion consistently outperforms strong, well-tuned masked and uniform baselines under matched architectures and controlled training, sampling, and tuning budgets, with its largest gains on the hardest instances, while remaining competitive on language modeling (Text8, TinyStories, OpenWebText). These results support candidate sets as an effective intermediate representation for iterative reasoning and show that the corruption kernel can materially change the computation learned by the reverse model.
papers.summary: Masked and uniform discrete diffusion models erase a token's identity in a single corruption step, so their noisy states cannot express partial uncertainty in which several alternatives remain plausible. `Binary Discrete Diffusion` instead represents the noisy state at each position as a set of candidate tokens, stored as a binary membership vector, which gains and loses candidates gradually. Under matched architectures and tuning budgets, the symmetric variant **consistently outperforms masked and uniform baselines on `Sudoku-Extreme`, `Boxoban`, and graph coloring**, with its largest gains on the hardest instances. It stays competitive on language modeling benchmarks (`Text8`, `TinyStories`, `OpenWebText`), which suggests that the choice of corruption process changes what the reverse model learns to compute.

papers.title: Learning Computational Structure for Sample-Efficient Prediction
papers.abstract: Statistical learning in high dimensions suffers from the curse of dimensionality. Fortunately, many functions of practical interest are compositionally sparse, meaning they admit a composition of local functions, each depending on only a few variables, allowing sample complexity to depend on local arity rather than ambient dimension. Yet realizing this benefit requires exploiting hidden compositional structure, which theory does not establish for practical gradient-based training. We study this gap with CSFRBench, a controlled benchmark that hides the target's compositional computation during training but retains it for diagnosis, and find that dense networks and sparsity-based baselines leave much of that benefit unrealized. Inspired by the spatial organization of biological neural circuits, we introduce Learned Wiring (LeWi): each neuron has a learned low-dimensional embedding, only nearby neurons connect, and embeddings and weights are trained jointly. LeWi improves sample efficiency on targets with hierarchical structure, intermediate reuse, or independent modules. Across 32 additional targets generated by independently sampled computation graphs, LeWi is the most sample-efficient method not given the target graph, with 27% lower mean learning-curve area than dense networks. Dense networks perform better on targets with a single high-arity function. LeWi's representations and connectivity align with the target computation. On 17 world-model prediction tasks spanning control, navigation, and manipulation, LeWi beats the dense baseline on 16 and wins 99/119 baseline comparisons. These results show that jointly learning connectivity and weights can exploit computational structure to improve sample efficiency.
papers.summary: Many practical functions are compositionally sparse, meaning they are built from local functions that each depend on only a few variables, which in principle lets sample complexity scale with that local arity instead of the full input dimension. Using `CSFRBench`, a benchmark that hides the target's compositional structure during training, the authors show that dense networks and sparsity-based baselines leave much of this benefit unused. They propose `Learned Wiring` (`LeWi`), inspired by the spatial layout of biological circuits: each neuron learns a low-dimensional embedding, only nearby neurons connect, and embeddings and weights are trained jointly. `LeWi` has **27% lower mean learning-curve area than dense networks** across 32 randomly generated targets and beats the dense baseline on 16 of 17 world-model prediction tasks, though dense networks remain better when the target is a single high-arity function.

papers.title: When Do LLMs Help with Feature Selection? A Systematic Empirical Study
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can leverage semantic feature names alongside summary statistics for tabular feature selection, yet it remains unclear when such information improves subset selection relative to established statistical methods. We investigate this question within an 18-dataset framework comprising 10 datasets for Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) training, 2 for checkpoint validation, and 6 held-out evaluation datasets. We compare five classical baselines, frozen Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.3-70B selectors, and two GRPO-adapted Qwen2.5-7B models, reporting classification ROC-AUC and regression R^2 separately and using dataset-wise ranks for cross-task comparison. Across five seeded evaluation partitions, classical selectors generally achieve higher predictive performance than the tested 7B LLM/RL selectors, including under a pre-specified ~33% feature budget with strict train-only classical fitting, while the 7B selectors retain compact subsets. A cardinality-matched semantic sensitivity experiment shows that, for Zero-shot Qwen-7B, informative feature names improve regression performance over anonymized and shuffled alternatives (+0.1964 and +0.1606 mean R^2), whereas aggregate classification differences are smaller (+0.0159 and +0.0084 ROC-AUC) and dataset-dependent. These results characterize when semantic information benefits LLM-based feature selection and show that classical selectors remain strong baselines for predictive tabular feature selection.
papers.summary: LLMs can read semantic feature names alongside summary statistics when selecting features for tabular data, but it is unclear when this beats established statistical methods. The study uses 18 datasets to compare five classical selectors, frozen `Qwen2.5-7B` and `Llama-3.3-70B` selectors, and two `Qwen2.5-7B` models adapted with Group Relative Policy Optimization (`GRPO`). **Classical selectors generally achieved higher predictive performance than the 7B LLM and RL selectors**, though the LLM selectors chose more compact subsets. In a controlled test, informative feature names improved the regression R² of zero-shot `Qwen-7B` by about 0.16 to 0.20 over anonymized or shuffled names, while the gains for classification were small and depended on the dataset.

papers.title: Large Flow Language Models
papers.abstract: Continuous flow language models offer a path to parallel generation with tools for control and acceleration unavailable to discrete diffusion, yet effective techniques for building them at the billion-parameter scale remain less established. We present Lafa (Large flow language model), a fast, high-performing flow language model scaled to 8B parameters in a data-efficient manner. Lafa is a blockwise flow model with causal attention on the prefix and bidirectional, asynchronous flow within each block. This design enables efficient training by adapting pretrained autoregressive (AR) models and fast inference via prefix caching and blockwise parallel decoding. We train Lafa at 0.5B, 7B, and 8B scales with fewer than 30B tokens, more efficient than previous diffusion models, and evaluate it on instruction following, reasoning, and coding, where the learned flow matches or surpasses the quality of AR and can be distilled into flow maps for one- and few-step generation. Notably, flow training preserves or even improves pretrained AR capabilities via a multi-token prediction effect, which we leverage in a self-speculative decoding scheme that verifies flow-based drafts autoregressively within a single model. This yields 2.54x the throughput of an AR model at comparable quality, outperforming multi-token prediction and discrete diffusion methods. Our findings show that continuous flows can serve as a scalable foundation for language modeling.
papers.summary: Continuous flow language models allow parallel generation, but techniques for building them at the billion-parameter scale are not well established. `Lafa` is a blockwise flow model that uses causal attention over the prefix and bidirectional, asynchronous flow within each block. This design lets it be adapted from pretrained autoregressive (AR) models with fewer than 30B tokens and supports prefix caching at inference. At 0.5B, 7B, and 8B parameters it matches or surpasses AR quality on instruction following, reasoning, and coding, and it can be distilled for one-step or few-step generation. Because flow training preserves or even improves AR capabilities, the authors build a self-speculative decoding scheme that verifies flow drafts autoregressively within one model, achieving **2.54 times the throughput of an AR model at comparable quality**.

papers.title: Agentic Ensemble with Vision-Language Models for Visual Anomaly Detection
papers.abstract: Visual anomaly detection aims to detect abnormal objects, while anomaly samples are often scarce during model training. Assembling multiple pretrained detectors can help by leveraging their transferable image scores and anomaly maps. However, most existing ensemble methods apply fixed fusion rules over saved predictions which struggle when pretrained detectors clearly disagree due to different training objectives, priors, and visual representations. To this end, we design AnomalyAgent, a post-training fusion framework for accurate visual anomaly detection. AnomalyAgent aligns heterogeneous scores and maps, summarizes score- and region-level disagreement, and treats fusion as a finite action-selection problem. It implements two types of actions: 1) score actions that determine how to fuse image-level detector confidence via consensus, robust aggregation, detector weighting, or score-map consistency; 2) map actions that fuse dense anomaly responses via consensus, detector weighting, geometric aggregation, or disagreement correction. A constrained vision-language model (VLM) is introduced to inspect high-conflict samples and select valid score action and map action to produce the final prediction. We evaluate AnomalyAgent on MVTec AD and VisA as primary benchmarks, together with seven additional public anomaly benchmarks and Real-IAD for large-scale score-level evaluation. Across these benchmarks, AnomalyAgent consistently improves over equal-weight fusion and achieves the best mean image AUROC and pixel AP among the compared fusion methods on MVTec AD and VisA, while demonstrating robust transfer across additional anomaly domains.
papers.summary: Visual anomaly detection often combines several pretrained detectors, but fixed fusion rules struggle when those detectors disagree because of their different training objectives and representations. `AnomalyAgent` aligns the detectors' scores and anomaly maps, summarizes where they disagree, and treats fusion as choosing from a finite set of score-level and map-level actions, such as consensus, robust aggregation, or detector weighting. A constrained vision-language model (VLM) inspects high-conflict samples and selects the actions that produce the final prediction. The method **achieves the best mean image AUROC and pixel AP among compared fusion methods on `MVTec AD` and `VisA`**, and transfers well to seven further benchmarks and `Real-IAD`.

papers.title: OptScientist: Automated Discovery of Optimization Laws
papers.abstract: Many scientific phenomena are best understood as outcomes of underlying optimization problems, yet automated scientific discovery has largely focused on recovering equations that describe observed input-output patterns. We introduce OptScientist, a novel automated framework for discovering compact symbolic optimization laws directly from data. OptScientist comprises (i) a model that infers symbolic optimization problems by first learning to represent data as an optimization problem and then extracting its symbolic form, and (ii) an LLM agentic system embedding the model in a discovery process that integrates theoretical priors from scientific literature, discovers candidate laws, abstracts their underlying mechanisms, and suggests new data to collect. We first evaluate OptScientist on OptFeynman, a novel benchmark of 99 physics-derived optimization problems, where OptScientist recovers ground-truth laws for over 80% of the problems and remains robust to noisy contextual information, while substantially outperforming machine-learning, symbolic, and LLM-based model-discovery baselines. On human risky choice and central-bank monetary policy, OptScientist discovers compact symbolic optimization laws that achieve held-out predictive performance competitive with leading baselines, while using few parameters and substantially fewer tokens than LLM baselines. Overall, OptScientist extends automated scientific discovery to uncovering optimization laws that generate observed phenomena, enabling automated theory building across the physical, biological, behavioral, and social sciences.
papers.summary: Automated scientific discovery usually recovers equations that describe input-output data, but many phenomena are better explained as solutions to an underlying optimization problem. `OptScientist` combines a model that infers symbolic optimization problems from data with an LLM agentic system that draws on priors from the scientific literature, proposes candidate laws, abstracts their mechanisms, and suggests new data to collect. On `OptFeynman`, a new benchmark of 99 physics-derived optimization problems, it **recovers the ground-truth law for over 80% of problems** and outperforms machine-learning, symbolic, and LLM-based baselines. On human risky choice and central-bank monetary policy data, it finds compact laws whose held-out predictions are competitive with leading baselines while using few parameters and far fewer tokens than LLM baselines.

papers.title: Evolving Semantic Indexes for Generative Retrieval
papers.abstract: Generative retrieval (GR) casts search and recommendation as autoregressive generation of discrete semantic identifiers (SIDs). SID design largely determines GR quality, but its discrete, interdependent components (SID construction, collision handling, decoding, and training) cannot be optimized end-to-end with gradients and remain largely hand-designed. We introduce a framework that improves these components through LLM-driven evolutionary program search, to our knowledge the first application of this approach to GR. A locally served, open-weight 31B model mutates executable GR components, so no proprietary LLM API is used, and a 1M-parameter proxy decoder provides fast feedback in place of repeatedly training the 1B target generator. Across 21 SID programs on NQ320K, proxy and target Recall@100 show strong rank correlation (Spearman $\rho = 0.90$). Guided by this proxy, evolution improves the seed GR on NQ320K, MSMARCO300K, and a multilingual e-commerce dataset under a fixed training recipe. On NQ320K, jointly evolving SID construction and collision handling improves Recall@1 from 55.8% to 59.3% and Recall@100 from 85.8% to 90.6%. A component study shows that proxy reliability depends on what is evolved: improvements transfer reliably for the semantic index but not for the generator's training objective or the full pipeline. LLM-driven evolutionary search is thus a practical tool for GR design, provided proxy reliability is established for the chosen search space.
papers.summary: Generative retrieval (GR) performs search and recommendation by generating discrete semantic identifiers (SIDs), whose design components cannot be optimized with gradients and are mostly hand-built. The authors apply LLM-driven evolutionary program search, in which a locally served open-weight 31B model mutates executable GR components and a 1M-parameter proxy decoder gives fast feedback in place of retraining the 1B target generator. The proxy's rankings correlate strongly with the target's (Spearman ρ = 0.90), and on `NQ320K` jointly evolving SID construction and collision handling **raises Recall@100 from 85.8% to 90.6%** and Recall@1 from 55.8% to 59.3%. Gains also appear on `MSMARCO300K` and an e-commerce dataset, but improvements transfer reliably only for the semantic index, not for the training objective or the full pipeline.

papers.title: Sage-A1.5: From Long-Horizon Execution to Scientific Exploration with Capability Composition
papers.abstract: In this report, we introduce Sage-A1.5, a 35B Mixture-of-Experts agentic model that builds on A1 to advance long-horizon problem solving through adaptive capability composition. Compared with A1, Sage-A1.5 learns not only to solve individual tasks, but also to organize work and revise its approach during execution. Sage-A1.5 highlights three improvements: agentic orchestration, verification, and open scientific discovery. First, agentic orchestration extends single-agent execution through task delegation and parallel collaboration among subagents with isolated contexts, enabling complex tasks to be decomposed and addressed concurrently and supporting efficient execution while reducing interference across concurrent subagents. Second, agentic verification strengthens long-horizon reliability through progress checking, evidence validation, and reflective strategy revision, allowing the agent to recognize unproductive search paths and pursue alternative approaches. Third, open scientific discovery extends agentic capabilities beyond answering predefined questions to conducting exploratory research, connecting scientific inquiry with interactive analysis and inspectable research artifacts. We showcase these capabilities through complicated agentic tasks and multidisciplinary scientific applications. Besides, we hope Sage-A1.5 provides the community with an accessible foundation for open scientific discovery, offering a practical path from long-horizon task execution to collaborative, verifiable, and inspectable scientific exploration.
papers.summary: `Sage-A1.5` is a 35B mixture-of-experts agentic model, built on `A1`, that aims to solve long-horizon problems by learning to organize its work and revise its approach during execution. It adds three capabilities: orchestration that delegates tasks to parallel subagents with isolated contexts, verification through progress checks, evidence validation and reflective strategy revision, and open-ended scientific exploration that produces inspectable research artifacts. The report demonstrates these capabilities on complex agentic tasks and multidisciplinary scientific applications, and **positions the model as an accessible open foundation for scientific discovery**. The abstract does not report quantitative benchmark results.
papers.highlight_summary:
`Sage-A1.5` is a 35B Mixture-of-Experts agent model built on `Agents-A1`. It targets long-horizon tasks where step-by-step execution degrades: the context keeps growing, searches repeat, and errors compound. Its core idea is to train *capability composition*, meaning how work is decomposed, delegated, checked and revised, as a learned model skill rather than leaving it to rules in an external harness.

- `Agentic Orchestration` has a main agent split work across parallel subagents with isolated contexts, either as alternative hypotheses (exploratory, A∨B∨C) or as complementary subproblems (constructive, A∧B∧C), with each subagent returning a structured self-assessment, its evidence and any open issues.
- `Agentic Verification` is learned from trajectories in which a supervisor model inserted reflections at stalls, repeated searches or key conclusions; the supervisor prompts are then removed, so at inference the model verifies inside its own reasoning, switched on by a system-prompt flag (`Verification protocol:enabled`) and with no online verifier.
- Training first fine-tunes multi-domain teachers on curated data, such as an automated Kaggle-to-task factory for ML engineering with windowed-interaction RL (`WIRL`), leakage-controlled SWE environments, and **3,512** recursively evolved long-context QA pairs on which `Qwen3.5-35B-A3B` scores only **31.57%**; a unified stage then mixes outcome-based RL with multi-teacher on-policy distillation, chosen per sample.
- The authors report that it **beats the much larger `Kimi-K3`, `GLM-5.3` and `GPT-5.6-sol`** on `FrontierScience-Olympiad`, `CMT`, `PinchBench` and `IFBench`, stays competitive on `SWE-Bench Pro` and `BrowseComp`, and **matches or beats same-size `Agents-A1` and `Ornith-1.5` on all twelve benchmarks**, though the extracted text gives no per-benchmark scores.
- Limitations: the verification-driven context compression is only planned future work; the roughly **80%** memory saving claimed for the `pVisor` sandbox comes from preliminary static tests with one run per condition; and much of the capability is distilled from stronger teacher models.

papers.title: Spatially Informed and Direction Sensitive Representation Learning for Spatial Transcriptomics
papers.abstract: Cellular states are shaped by both intrinsic gene expression programs and the spatial microenvironment in which cells reside. Spatial transcriptomics makes this context measurable, but effective representation learning requires capturing both spatially informative molecular signals and intercellular organization. Existing approaches address these challenges only partially: conventional gene selection can overlook spatially structured signals, while methods for encoding cell-cell relationships often either reduce a cell's microenvironment to proximity alone, discarding direction, or rely on absolute coordinates tied to an arbitrary tissue frame. Consequently, cells with similar neighbor distances but distinct spatial organization may receive overly similar representations, despite experiencing different biological contexts that shape their cellular states. We introduce Tessera, a spatial representation learning framework that addresses both molecular selection and cellular context. Tessera combines spatially informed gene selection with a geometric inductive bias that contextualizes each cell within its local tissue environment. By modeling relative cell-cell relationships, Tessera is translation-invariant while preserving direction, allowing neighboring cells to contribute differently according to their spatial context and cellular state. Across held-out tissues and technologies, Tessera outperforms existing spatial foundation models in representation quality and generalizes zero-shot to contexts up to $16\times$ larger than those seen during training.
papers.summary: Representation learning for spatial transcriptomics needs to capture both spatially informative genes and how cells are arranged, yet existing methods often reduce a cell's neighborhood to distances alone or depend on absolute tissue coordinates. `Tessera` combines spatially informed gene selection with a geometric inductive bias that models relative cell-cell relationships. This makes it translation-invariant while still preserving direction, so neighboring cells can contribute differently depending on their spatial context. Across held-out tissues and technologies it outperforms existing spatial foundation models in representation quality, and it **generalizes zero-shot to contexts up to 16 times larger** than those seen in training.

papers.title: Beyond the Sequentiality Bottleneck: A Hybrid Diffusion-Autoregressive Framework for Efficient Multimodal Reasoning
papers.abstract: Autoregressive models (ARMs) face a "Sequentiality Bottleneck" in reasoning, while diffusion language models (DLMs) offer parallelism but lack semantic coherence. To addresses both limitations, we propose Collaborative Reasoning Asymmetric Learning (CoRAL), a hybrid framework via an Asymmetric Planner-Executor (APE) architecture: a DLM Planner generates K diverse reasoning trajectories in parallel, while a large ARM Executor selects the optimal plan and synthesizes the final answer. To train the Planner effectively, we introduce Reward-Guided Denoising for CoT (RDC), which integrates outcome-based rewards into the diffusion process to steer it toward goal-directed reasoning. Experiments on vision-language benchmarks show that CoRAL significantly outperforms prior diffusion-based methods and achieves competitive performance against strong ARMs, achieving both superior efficiency and quality.
papers.summary: Autoregressive models (ARMs) reason one token at a time, while diffusion language models (DLMs) generate in parallel but are less coherent. `CoRAL` (Collaborative Reasoning Asymmetric Learning) pairs the two in a planner-executor design: a DLM planner produces several reasoning trajectories in parallel, and a large ARM executor picks the best plan and writes the final answer. The planner is trained with `Reward-Guided Denoising for CoT` (`RDC`), which builds outcome-based rewards into the diffusion process. On vision-language benchmarks, **`CoRAL` significantly outperforms prior diffusion-based methods** and is competitive with strong ARMs while being more efficient.

papers.title: SceneRig: An Agentic System for Simulation-Ready 3D Scene Reconstruction from Single Images
papers.abstract: Simulation is a powerful tool for robotics, but building diverse, simulation-ready scenes at scale remains difficult. Reconstructing scenes from single images is a promising alternative, but visual similarity alone is insufficient: objects must also be recovered, accurately placed, and physically grounded. Existing methods that rely on post-hoc physics settling often misplace objects, producing scenes that look correct but behave poorly under manipulation. We present SceneRig, an agentic system that turns a single image into an editable, simulation-ready scene. SceneRig combines geometric, visual, and physical tools to reconstruct a faithful 3D scene. An agent then performs edit-and-validate loops inside a physics simulator to achieve physical stability. Across diverse inputs, SceneRig improves instance segmentation, object-centric appearance, and 3D placement while keeping the reconstructed scenes physically stable. Furthermore, SceneRig is effective for downstream robotics: its scenes predict real-robot policy outcomes more accurately than the baseline method and more reliably support replay of recorded manipulations without trajectory adaptation.
papers.summary: Reconstructing simulation-ready robot scenes from single images requires objects that are correctly recovered, placed, and physically grounded, and post-hoc physics settling often produces scenes that look right but behave badly under manipulation. `SceneRig` is an agentic system that combines geometric, visual, and physical tools to build an editable 3D scene, then runs edit-and-validate loops inside a physics simulator until the scene is stable. It improves instance segmentation, object appearance, and 3D placement while keeping scenes stable. In downstream robotics tests, **its scenes predict real-robot policy outcomes more accurately than the baseline** and more reliably support replaying recorded manipulations without adapting the trajectories.

papers.title: Capable Teacher, Myopic Scorer: Reward-Free Teacher Repair for Agentic On-Policy Distillation
papers.abstract: Agentic on-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student agent on its own trajectories while a teacher scores every token. A natural explanation of where it goes wrong is compounding error: the student's mistakes carry its trajectories beyond the region where the teacher is reliable, so recent methods keep training inside that region, through episode-length curricula, teacher-guided turns, prefix replay, or teacher intervention where the two disagree. We show this explanation is incomplete. From the states where the student departs most from the teacher, the teacher's own takeovers still finish the task, yet the student trained on its token scores keeps running out of turns. We attribute this to the myopia of next-token scoring. The teacher rates each token without seeing where the episode ends, so its scores let through the safe, delaying moves that outcome-based RL would punish with zero reward, a penalty agentic OPD lacks. We call this difference between what the teacher does and what it scores the rollout-scorer gap. We propose Rollout-to-Scorer Distillation (R2S), which repairs the scorer before distillation by mining high-disagreement states from the untrained student, running teacher takeovers from them, keeping the states where enough takeovers pass a reward-free check such as consensus or an LLM judge, and fine-tuning the teacher to give its takeover-informed scores on every assistant token from the divergence turn onward, without the takeover in context. The repaired teacher is frozen as the sole scorer for standard OPD, requiring no task reward during repair or training. Across three environments, two teachers and four students, R2S outperforms three state-of-the-art agentic-OPD methods in all twelve teacher-student-environment cells, by 12.8 success points on average over the best of them in each cell. Project page: https://tree-shu-zhao.github.io/r2s/.
papers.summary: In agentic on-policy distillation (OPD), a student agent trains on its own trajectories while a teacher scores every token, and failures are usually blamed on compounding errors that push the student outside the teacher's reliable region. The authors argue instead that the cause is a rollout-scorer gap: the teacher can finish the task from difficult states, but its myopic next-token scores still approve safe, delaying moves that eventually exhaust the turn budget. `Rollout-to-Scorer Distillation` (`R2S`) repairs the teacher before distillation by running teacher takeovers from high-disagreement states, keeping those that pass a reward-free check such as consensus or an LLM judge, and fine-tuning the teacher to score tokens in light of those takeovers. Across three environments, two teachers, and four students, **`R2S` beats three state-of-the-art agentic OPD methods in all twelve settings, by 12.8 success points on average**, without using any task reward.

papers.title: What Do RTL Repair Benchmarks Actually Measure?
papers.abstract: RTL repair benchmarks should measure whether a model can fix broken RTL given a specification. To this end, we construct and hash-bind RTLRepairDataset, 5,784 (broken, fixed) training pairs; RTLRepairBench, 459 held-out cases with 374 syntactic and 85 behavioral mutations; and an evaluation harness supporting simulation and formal equivalence. We then use this infrastructure to identify two measurement confounds. First, simulation and formal scoring give opposite signs for the apparent effect of providing a specification in one evaluated cohort; reset-aware rescoring attributes almost all of the simulation-formal disagreement to reset and first-cycle comparison semantics. Second, on 274 mined model failures, the specification-only minus specification-conditioned recovery point estimate ranges from -8.5 to +18.3 percentage points across six models. Thus, a conventional repair score need not isolate whether the model used the faulty RTL. We translate these findings into evaluation controls: report initialization, reset, first-cycle, and unknown-value semantics; disclose oracle coverage and undecided cases; and include a specification-only baseline. Together, the resources and audit provide both a benchmark for behavioral repair and a protocol for diagnosing what contributes to its measured score. We release the benchmark, the training set, construction code, sanitized aggregate evidence, and reproduction materials at https://github.com/Evaaaz/RTLRepairBench.
papers.summary: Benchmarks for repairing hardware register-transfer level (RTL) code should test whether a model can fix broken RTL given a specification. The authors release `RTLRepairDataset` (5,784 training pairs), `RTLRepairBench` (459 held-out cases with syntactic and behavioral bugs), and a harness that supports both simulation and formal equivalence checking. They identify two measurement confounds: simulation and formal scoring can disagree on the sign of a specification's effect, almost entirely because of differences in reset and first-cycle semantics, and **a specification-only baseline recovers anywhere from 8.5 points less to 18.3 points more than specification-plus-buggy-code across six models**, so standard repair scores need not show whether a model actually used the faulty code. They recommend reporting simulation semantics and oracle coverage and always including a specification-only baseline.

papers.title: Evolving Agent Interfaces
papers.abstract: Computer-use agents are limited by the interfaces humans give them. An agent may type a spreadsheet cell by cell when a single line of code would do, or print all two thousand lines of a file through a shell to find one function.
